questions.stem: A highly skilled subject matter expert (SME) is engaged in a government project where approximately 30% of the deliverables will follow an agile approach. The project manager invites the SME to join the agile team to contribute to these iterations. The SME is reluctant because they think that working on a team is demotivating and slows them down, and they want to achieve the highest-quality output possible. What should the project manager do to address the SME's concerns and encourage them to join the agile team?

options.text: Recommend that the SME develop emotional intelligence by integrating with the team.
options.rationale: Telling a specialist to work on their emotional intelligence assumes a deficit nobody has shown and ignores what they actually said they care about. It reads as a rebuke and makes joining the team less attractive, not more.

options.text: Explain that teamwork fosters continuous improvement and early feedback loops.
options.rationale: The SME's objection is about speed and quality, so the persuasive answer speaks to those: short feedback loops catch defects early and continuous improvement raises output quality. It meets their concern on its own terms.

options.text: Request that the SME conduct the retrospective meetings as an objective observer.
options.rationale: Making the SME an observer of retrospectives sidesteps the invitation to contribute to the work, and puts them in a facilitation role they have not asked for. It does nothing to answer their doubt about teamwork.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to meet with the SME and help improve their attitude towards teamwork.
options.rationale: Sending the sponsor to fix someone's attitude escalates before the project manager has even engaged with the concern, and frames a legitimate professional worry as a behaviour problem.

questions.explanation: Resistance to a new way of working is best met by answering the person's actual concern in their own terms. A specialist who values quality is persuaded by evidence that collaboration improves quality — earlier feedback, fewer late defects, continuous refinement — not by pressure, escalation or a side role that avoids the question.
questions.mindset: Win people over by showing how the new approach serves what they already care about.

questions.stem: An organization recently updated its strategic plan and some of the changes were substantial. During a meeting for an ongoing project, an important stakeholder questioned how the project aligned with the new strategic plan. What should the project manager do first to address this concern effectively?

options.text: Review and revise the project charter to ensure alignment with organizational strategy.
options.rationale: A substantial strategy change can invalidate the assumptions the project was chartered on. Reviewing and revising the charter tests alignment with facts and gives the stakeholder an evidence-based answer.

options.text: Schedule a follow-up meeting with the stakeholder to discuss their concerns.
options.rationale: A meeting is useful, but holding it before the project manager has checked alignment means arriving with nothing to say. It postpones the analysis rather than doing it.

options.text: Remind the stakeholders that the project was initiated prior to the strategy change.
options.rationale: Pointing out that the project predates the strategy is a defence, not an answer. Projects exist to serve current strategy, so the date of initiation does not settle whether it still does.

options.text: Assure the stakeholder that the project is aligned with the new organizational strategy.
options.rationale: Offering assurance without having checked is unfounded and potentially dishonest. If the review later shows misalignment, the project manager's credibility goes with it.

questions.explanation: When organisational strategy shifts, a project's justification has to be re-tested rather than assumed. The charter and business case are where the link between project and strategy is written down, so they are the first place to check and, if needed, revise. Engagement with the stakeholder follows once there is a verified answer to give.
questions.mindset: Check that a project still serves the strategy before telling anyone it does.

questions.stem: A pilot project is underway using an agile approach to development. The project is delivering the planned increments on time, but top management is concerned because they do not see the value that the project is adding. How should the project manager communicate the value of the project to top management?

options.text: Include top management in all future sprint reviews to address their concerns in real time.
options.rationale: Sprint reviews show increments, not strategic value, and asking executives to attend every one is a heavy commitment that still leaves them to infer the value themselves.

options.text: Send top management weekly status reports and invite them to retrospectives.
options.rationale: Weekly status reports describe progress, and retrospectives are the team's internal improvement forum. Neither answers the question 'why does this matter to the organisation?'

options.text: Demonstrate how the project's objectives align with the organization's strategic goals.
options.rationale: Top management judges projects by their contribution to strategic goals. Showing that link directly answers the concern in the terms management uses.

options.text: Customize progress reports to address top management's requirements.
options.rationale: Tailoring reports is sensible practice, but a progress report customised in format still reports progress. The gap here is understanding of value, not the layout of the report.

questions.explanation: Delivering on time is not the same as visibly delivering value. Senior audiences need the connection between outputs and strategic objectives made explicit; more ceremonies or more reports do not supply that link on their own. Communication to executives should be framed in the outcomes they are accountable for.
questions.mindset: Speak to executives in terms of the strategic outcomes they own, not the activities the team performs.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a project that follows the company's predictive approach. The project manager discovers that the project is behind schedule and over budget because a key stakeholder has been submitting an unusually high number of change requests. What should the project manager do to help the company achieve its desired project outcomes?

options.text: Review the risk management plan to determine a mitigation plan.
options.rationale: The problem is not an unmanaged uncertainty but a volume of change requests flowing through. The risk plan does not govern how change requests are assessed and approved.

options.text: Use the contingency reserve to implement a fast-track activity.
options.rationale: Contingency reserve is for identified risks, not for absorbing uncontrolled change, and fast-tracking treats the schedule symptom while the stream of changes continues.

options.text: Review the change control process and implement improvements.
options.rationale: If a flood of change requests is pushing the project off schedule and budget, the control mechanism is not doing its job. Reviewing and tightening the change control process addresses the cause.

options.text: Escalate the problem with the stakeholder to the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Escalating the stakeholder skips the project manager's own responsibility for the change process. Escalation is for when the PM has exhausted what is in their authority.

questions.explanation: When change requests are eroding schedule and budget, the fault usually lies in how changes are evaluated and approved rather than in the stakeholder raising them. A sound change control process makes the impact of each request visible before approval, so the fix is to strengthen the process rather than spend reserves or escalate.
questions.mindset: Fix the process that lets the problem through before treating its symptoms.

questions.stem: An agile team is planning for a 2-week iteration. In the middle of the last few iterations, the product owner made changes and reprioritized features, affecting the team's deliverables. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Escalate the issue to senior management and request that the product owner take action.
options.rationale: Escalating to senior management before talking to the product owner skips the obvious first step and damages a working relationship the team depends on.

options.text: Inform the team to ignore the changes requested by the product owner during the iteration.
options.rationale: Telling the team to ignore the product owner undermines the role that owns priority and creates open conflict inside the team.

options.text: Explain the implications of making changes during an iteration to the product owner.
options.rationale: The product owner may not realise that mid-iteration changes disrupt commitments. Explaining the impact coaches them and preserves both the relationship and the sprint's stability.

options.text: Request the product owner make changes as needed since an agile approach responds to change.
options.rationale: Agile welcomes change between iterations, not a constant reshuffle during them. Accepting the pattern leaves the team unable to commit to anything.

questions.explanation: In agile, change is absorbed at the boundary of an iteration: the backlog can be reprioritised freely, but the sprint's committed work is protected so the team can deliver. When a role is breaking that rhythm, the first step is to coach the person on the impact, directly and early, before any escalation.
questions.mindset: Coach before you escalate — most process breaches come from not seeing the impact.

questions.stem: An agile project manager based in country A is working with a development team and business analyst in country B, and a quality assurance team in country C. During the second sprint, it becomes apparent that all of the test cases have failed. The agile facilitator ascertains that the business analyst changed the acceptance criteria of the stories and only communicated these changes to their local team. What should the agile project manager implement going forward to prevent this from recurring?

options.text: Password protection on the user stories
options.rationale: Locking the stories stops legitimate refinement and treats a communication failure as a security problem. It would not have made the change known to the other teams.

options.text: Signed change control documentation
options.rationale: Signed change documentation brings a heavyweight predictive control into a sprint-level refinement activity and slows the team without addressing where the conversation happens.

options.text: Automated change notifications from the user story tool
options.rationale: Automatic notifications broadcast that something changed, but not why or whether everyone agrees. It is a tool patch for what is really a missing shared conversation.

options.text: Backlog grooming
options.rationale: Regular backlog refinement with all sites present makes changes to stories and acceptance criteria a shared activity, so they cannot be made and known only locally.

questions.explanation: Distributed agile teams fail when a decision is made in one location and the others learn about it at test time. The remedy is a shared, regular forum in which backlog items and their acceptance criteria are refined together, so changes are discussed by everyone they affect rather than locked down or broadcast after the fact.
questions.mindset: Make changes to shared work in a shared conversation, not in a local one.

questions.stem: A multi-year project is underway when a key resource announces that they are retiring. The project manager is concerned about the impact on the project and has identified that several critical tasks will be affected. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Require the remaining team members to work additional hours to complete the impacted tasks.
options.rationale: Extra hours spread the retiree's load across people who lack their knowledge, burning the team out without replacing the capability being lost.

options.text: Advise the stakeholders that the resource's tasks will not be completed on time.
options.rationale: Declaring delay before trying to mitigate it is premature. There is time between the announcement and the departure that should be used.

options.text: Collaborate with the resource manager to identify and train an appropriate replacement.
options.rationale: A known departure is a transfer problem. Working with the resource manager to find and train a replacement uses the notice period to move the knowledge while the person is still there.

options.text: Encourage the retiring team member to postpone retirement to avoid disrupting the project.
options.rationale: Asking someone to postpone their retirement for the project's convenience is inappropriate, and it only defers the same problem to a later date.

questions.explanation: A planned departure of a key resource gives the project something valuable: time. The right response uses that time to secure a successor and transfer knowledge while the departing person is still available, working through the resource manager who controls staffing.
questions.mindset: Treat a known departure as a handover to complete, not a gap to absorb.

questions.stem: The lead sales manager and team are unable to submit a project status report on time for the new sales report integration project. Additionally, the report does not meet the expectations highlighted in the group review meetings. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Evaluate the team's understanding of the action plan by requesting their feedback.
options.rationale: Asking the team for feedback on their understanding of the action plan finds out whether the failures come from confusion about expectations before anything else is changed.

options.text: Confirm the plan is documented and shared among the team and stakeholders.
options.rationale: Confirming the plan is documented is useful, but a document that exists does not mean it is understood. It assumes the cause rather than finding it.

options.text: Increase the frequency of the team meetings for the status report submission.
options.rationale: More meetings add overhead without knowing whether the team is unclear, overloaded or blocked. It treats the symptom with more of the same process.

options.text: Ensure that team members are provided with more time to deliberate and plan.
options.rationale: More time presumes the problem is capacity. Late and off-target reports may instead reflect a misunderstanding that more time would not fix.

questions.explanation: When a team misses a deadline and the output also misses expectations, the first move is diagnosis. Asking the team how they understand the plan surfaces gaps in expectations, which is the commonest cause of this combination. Documentation, meeting cadence or time allowances can only be adjusted sensibly once the cause is known.
questions.mindset: Diagnose with the team before prescribing a fix for the team.

questions.stem: A scrum team is using a hybrid approach with 2-week sprints. The minimum viable product (MVP) release is at the end of the current sprint, and the team has completed the must have and should have features; however, some of the other priority features are still in development. The project manager is preparing the monthly report for the steering committee. What should the project manager recommend?

options.text: Reschedule the MVP release review until all the agreed-on features have been completed.
options.rationale: Holding the MVP for lower-priority features defeats the purpose of a minimum viable product, which is to release the core early and learn from it.

options.text: Update the project management plan to include in the release only the features completed.
options.rationale: Rewriting the project management plan is unnecessary: release content is already governed by prioritisation. The plan does not need a formal change to release what was always the minimum.

options.text: Complete the sprint review and release the MVP with the completed features.
options.rationale: The must-have and should-have features define the MVP. Completing the sprint review and releasing gets feedback on the core product as intended.

options.text: Estimate the effort required and submit a change request to add more resources to the team.
options.rationale: Adding resources to finish could-have features chases scope the MVP never needed, and delays learning for no gain in viability.

questions.explanation: An MVP is defined by the smallest set of features that delivers value and generates learning, typically the must-haves. Once those are done, the product should ship and the remaining features continue through the backlog. Holding a release for lower-priority items turns an MVP back into a big-bang delivery.
questions.mindset: Release the minimum that delivers value, then learn from it.

questions.stem: While validating deliverables, a project manager realizes that one of the project team members used an older version of the scope definition document, causing substantial errors. What should the project manager do to manage this situation?

options.text: Discuss the latest deliverables during the next meeting.
options.rationale: Discussing deliverables at the next meeting leaves substantial errors unaddressed and unrecorded, with no assessment of impact or corrective action.

options.text: Update the project document register.
options.rationale: Updating the document register may help prevent recurrence, but it does not deal with the deliverables that were already built to the wrong baseline.

options.text: Perform a change control process.
options.rationale: Deliverables built against the wrong scope version need corrective action with a known impact. Running it through change control documents the issue, assesses the effect and authorises the rework.

options.text: Share the updated scope definition document with the team.
options.rationale: Sharing the correct document is sensible, but on its own it does not correct the deliverables already produced or evaluate the impact of doing so.

questions.explanation: Work produced against an outdated baseline is a configuration problem whose correction has cost and schedule impact. Corrective action of that size is handled through the integrated change control process so that the impact is assessed, the rework is authorised and the records reflect what was done.
questions.mindset: Route significant corrective work through change control so its impact is visible and approved.

questions.stem: A project manager has just taken over a 5-year project that is at the midpoint. At the steering committee meeting, the CEO asked if the project was on track to deliver the target of a 40% increase in production. The project manager responded that since they only worked on the project for one month, they did not know the status of the project. What should the project manager have done to avoid this situation?

options.text: Reviewed the last status report to understand the project status.
options.rationale: Reading the last status report is helpful but gives only a snapshot from the team's side. It may not cover the business targets that the CEO asked about.

options.text: Validated the project status with the lead developer.
options.rationale: The lead developer knows the technical status but is not the right source for whether the project is on track against a business benefit target.

options.text: Reviewed the last project status with the project sponsor.
options.rationale: The sponsor owns the business case and its targets. Reviewing status with the sponsor on taking over would have prepared the PM to answer questions about benefits such as the production increase.

options.text: Checked the project schedule to understand the project status.
options.rationale: The schedule shows timing, not whether the project is on course to deliver its business outcome. It would not answer a question about benefit realisation.

questions.explanation: A project manager taking over mid-stream must quickly own the project's current status against its objectives. The sponsor is the person accountable for the business case, so a structured handover with the sponsor is the fastest way to understand both progress and the outcomes the organisation expects.
questions.mindset: On inheriting a project, own its status against its objectives from the first week.

questions.stem: While planning a global solution delivery in a multinational organization, the project manager and team drafted all work items and defined the priorities and methodologies for implementation. During one of the daily meetings, a team member expresses concern about the compliance of the technology being used and proposes an alternative that is more aligned with the data privacy policies of the country. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Ask the architecture owner to assess the team member's proposal and evaluate the compliance concerns.
options.rationale: Handing the assessment to the architecture owner delegates before the PM has understood whether there is a real issue, and shifts responsibility for a compliance risk.

options.text: Assess the validity of the concern and evaluate the compliance of the current and newly proposed technology.
options.rationale: A credible compliance concern must be understood first. Assessing its validity and comparing both technologies against the privacy rules gives a sound basis for any decision.

options.text: Meet with the customer and ask if they would be comfortable implementing the newly proposed technology.
options.rationale: Asking the customer whether they are comfortable is premature; compliance is not a matter of comfort, and the PM would have no analysis to present.

options.text: Get support from the information technology (IT) department regarding the feasibility of the new technology.
options.rationale: IT feasibility is a later consideration. The immediate question is whether the current technology is compliant, which feasibility advice does not answer.

questions.explanation: When someone raises a possible compliance breach, the first action is to establish the facts: is the concern valid and how do the current and alternative options measure against the regulation? Decisions, delegation and customer conversations come after that assessment, because compliance obligations are not negotiable preferences.
questions.mindset: Take compliance concerns seriously and establish the facts before choosing a response.

questions.stem: A new project manager has taken over an ongoing project. Progress reports show that the project is within the allocated budget and schedule. However, a key supplier has indicated that they will not be able to supply critical materials as scheduled. What should the project manager do first to address this situation?

options.text: Submit a change request to the change control board (CCB).
options.rationale: A change request needs a known impact. Raising one before the baselines have been checked means proposing a change without knowing what it must fix.

options.text: Review the performance against the project baseline.
options.rationale: Reviewing performance against the integrated baseline shows which activities the late materials affect and by how much, which is the information every later decision depends on.

options.text: Initiate legal action against the defaulting supplier.
options.rationale: Legal action is disproportionate as a first step, damages a supplier relationship that may still be needed, and does nothing to protect the schedule.

options.text: Immediately terminate the contract with the supplier.
options.rationale: Terminating the contract immediately removes the only supplier currently lined up and may breach the contract's own terms. It is a reaction, not an assessment.

questions.explanation: A supplier warning is a trigger for impact analysis. Comparing the situation with the scope, schedule and cost baselines shows which work is affected and how badly, and only then can the project manager choose between workarounds, alternative sources, contract remedies or a change request.
questions.mindset: Measure the impact against the baseline before choosing how to respond.

questions.stem: A risk was identified at the beginning of an agile project and a mitigation plan was established. The risk event occurs but the impact is much higher than anticipated and the originally planned response will be ineffective. The project team developed a more effective response, but it is drastically different from the original mitigation plan and must be implemented as soon as possible. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Implement only the initial response as outlined in the risk management plan.
options.rationale: Applying a response the team already knows will be ineffective is following the plan for its own sake, and lets a larger-than-expected impact run unchecked.

options.text: Update the risk management plan and implement the newly created response.
options.rationale: When the realised impact outstrips the planned response, a better response should be adopted quickly and the plan updated so the change is recorded and visible.

options.text: Defer risk response until the next progress meeting to inform stakeholders.
options.rationale: Deferring action until the next meeting lets a live risk event keep causing damage. Stakeholders can be informed without delaying the response.

options.text: Implement a contingency response and inform the stakeholders afterward.
options.rationale: A generic contingency response is not the more effective response the team has just designed, and informing stakeholders only afterwards loses transparency.

questions.explanation: Risk plans are hypotheses made before the event. When reality proves the planned response inadequate, the project should adapt promptly and keep its documentation truthful by updating the plan. Acting quickly and recording the change are both part of responsible risk management.
questions.mindset: Adapt the response to the risk you actually have, and keep the plan honest about it.

questions.stem: During the execution phase of a project, a project team identifies a previously unforeseen risk that could delay the project for several months. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Update the risk register.
options.rationale: Recording the new risk in the register is the first step: it makes the risk visible, assigns an owner and opens the analysis and response workflow.

options.text: Perform qualitative risk analysis.
options.rationale: Qualitative analysis is the next step, but analysing a risk that has not been recorded skips the point at which the project formally recognises it.

options.text: Update the project sponsors.
options.rationale: The sponsor may need to know, but informing them before documenting and analysing the risk means escalating with no assessment to share.

options.text: Plan for additional budget.
options.rationale: Planning extra budget presumes both the impact and the response. It is premature before the risk has been recorded and analysed.

questions.explanation: Risk management runs in a sequence: identify and record, analyse, plan a response, then implement and monitor. A newly discovered risk enters that sequence through the risk register; analysis, escalation and funding decisions follow from what the recorded risk turns out to mean.
questions.mindset: Record a new risk first so everything that follows has something to act on.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on an agile project with a cross-functional team. The project manager is informed that some team members typically raise additional requirements that are not in the approved scope. What should the project manager do to address this expected behavior?

options.text: Coach the team to manage scope using the appropriate framework.
options.rationale: Coaching the team to route new ideas through the backlog and the product owner lets scope be managed without shutting down the ideas themselves.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor and request replacement team members.
options.rationale: Replacing people for raising ideas is a drastic response to a behaviour that can be coached, and it would punish engagement.

options.text: Conduct daily standup meetings with the team and stakeholders.
options.rationale: Stand-ups are for the team to coordinate daily work. Running them with stakeholders does not address how new requirements should be handled.

options.text: Explain that requirements cannot be changed without approval.
options.rationale: A blanket statement that requirements cannot change contradicts agile's welcome of change and discourages useful input, rather than showing where it belongs.

questions.explanation: In agile teams, new requirements are not forbidden; they are channelled into the backlog where the product owner prioritises them. When team members add scope informally, the fix is to coach them on the framework for handling change so ideas are captured without leaking into committed work.
questions.mindset: Channel new ideas into the backlog instead of shutting them down.

questions.stem: A chief technology officer (CTO) is enthusiastic about an organization's recent adoption of servant leadership practices. The CTO requests that all project managers apply servant leadership practices, but seems to be unsure of the practical applications. Which statement below best represents how the project manager should respond to the CTO's request?

options.text: Explain that servant leadership can be adapted and applied to any project situation.
options.rationale: Servant leadership is a set of principles about enabling the team, and those principles can be adapted to any delivery approach or project context.

options.text: Remind the CTO that servant leadership is more suited for projects using agile methods.
options.rationale: Servant leadership is associated with agile, but it is not restricted to it. Saying so would discourage its use on predictive projects where it also helps.

options.text: Clarify that servant leadership practices typically focus on the client's preferences.
options.rationale: Servant leadership focuses on serving the team's needs and removing obstacles, not on following client preferences.

options.text: Affirm that servant leadership only works for projects with substantial resources.
options.rationale: Nothing about servant leadership depends on project size or budget; it is a way of leading, not a resource-intensive method.

questions.explanation: Servant leadership centres on understanding and meeting the needs of the team so that it can perform at its best. Because it is a leadership stance rather than a method, it adapts to predictive, agile and hybrid settings and to projects of any size.
questions.mindset: Treat servant leadership as a stance that adapts to any context, not a method tied to one.

questions.stem: The opening of a new overseas office faces potential delays as the required permit has not yet been issued by the local government. The project team met to evaluate the appropriate course of action as outlined in the risk register. After a thorough assessment, the team decided to postpone the opening to another date. Which document should the project manager use to update the project management plan?

options.text: Risk management plan
options.rationale: The risk management plan describes how risk work is done on the project. A decision about one specific risk does not change that approach.

options.text: Risk report
options.rationale: The risk report summarises overall and individual risk for stakeholders. It is an output, not the record where a specific risk's response is updated.

options.text: Risk register
options.rationale: The risk register holds each risk's status and response. The chosen response to the permit delay is recorded there and then flows into the plan.

options.text: Lessons learned register
options.rationale: The lessons learned register captures insight for the future. It is not where the project records the current response to an active risk.

questions.explanation: Each risk document has a distinct purpose: the plan sets the method, the register tracks individual risks and their responses, the report summarises risk for stakeholders and the lessons learned register captures knowledge. Decisions about a particular risk are recorded in the register and carried into the plan from there.
questions.mindset: Know which document holds which decision, and update that one.

questions.stem: During a standup, a team member falsely reports the completion of a story which is a dependency for other stories. When the team begins to work on related stories, they are unable to continue with development because the initial story is not finished. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Review the sprint planning with the whole team to understand story interdependencies.
options.rationale: Reviewing interdependencies is useful later, but the immediate problem is a misreport, not a planning gap. It sidesteps the person involved.

options.text: Speak to the team member who falsely reported the completion of the story.
options.rationale: A private conversation with the team member finds out why the story was reported done and addresses accountability directly and respectfully.

options.text: Tell the product owner to review the acceptance criteria before pushing it into the sprint backlog.
options.rationale: The acceptance criteria were not the problem; the story was reported complete when it was not. Pushing this to the product owner misplaces the issue.

options.text: Ask the team to explain their interpretation of the definition of done (DoD) at the end of the sprint.
options.rationale: Waiting until the end of the sprint to discuss the definition of done delays the fix while the dependent work stays blocked.

questions.explanation: When an individual's action causes a team-level problem, the first step is a private, direct conversation with that person. It uncovers the reason — misunderstanding of done, pressure or something else — and addresses it without public blame. Wider process fixes can follow once the cause is understood.
questions.mindset: Address individual behaviour privately and promptly, before reaching for process changes.

questions.stem: A business manager and product owner are requesting a more flexible way to incorporate changes into the product backlog. They want to reduce go-tomarket time in order to react to a competitor's release strategy. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Coach the product owner to prioritize product backlog items in accordance with business goals.
options.rationale: Backlog priority is how agile responds to market change. Coaching the product owner to prioritise against business goals delivers the most valuable items first and shortens time to market.

options.text: Review the assumption log and the project management plan to identify potential changes.
options.rationale: The assumption log and project plan do not control what the team builds next; in an agile product the backlog does.

options.text: Establish a comprehensive change control process and select a change control board (CCB).
options.rationale: A comprehensive change control board adds formality that slows reaction, which is the opposite of what the business wants.

options.text: Authorize all key stakeholders to make modifications in order to deliver the product faster.
options.rationale: Letting every stakeholder modify the backlog removes the single point of prioritisation and creates conflicting direction.

questions.explanation: In agile delivery the product owner owns the backlog and its order. Responding to a competitor means reordering the backlog so that the most valuable features reach the market first; heavier controls or open-access editing undermine that responsiveness.
questions.mindset: Respond to market change by reprioritising the backlog, not by adding bureaucracy.

questions.stem: In an innovative project, the sponsor wants to deliver a creative and large data processing platform to better serve the customers. However, the functionality of the platform cannot be described clearly in the project's requirements. In order to obtain continuous investment, every project output that shows progress will be demonstrated to management. What kind of project approach should the project manager recommend?

options.text: Predictive
options.rationale: A predictive approach needs requirements that can be defined up front. It does not fit a platform whose functionality cannot yet be described.

options.text: Waterfall
options.rationale: Waterfall is a predictive life cycle and has the same weakness: it assumes stable, known requirements and delays visible outputs.

options.text: Agile
options.rationale: Unclear requirements and the need to show progress frequently for continued funding both point to an iterative, incremental agile approach.

options.text: Hybrid
options.rationale: A hybrid could work in some settings, but nothing here calls for a predictive component. The characteristics point squarely to agile.

questions.explanation: Choosing a delivery approach starts with the nature of the requirements and the need for feedback. High uncertainty and a need for frequent demonstrable progress favour agile; well-defined, stable scope favours predictive; hybrids suit mixes of both.
questions.mindset: Let requirement certainty and feedback needs choose the delivery approach.

questions.stem: A midsize project has the objective of developing an innovative product with changing requirements. Several team members are unavailable for two weeks per month during the duration of the project. The project manager realizes that the cost of quality increases substantially during those periods. However, the team velocity is stable. What should the project manager do to address this issue?

options.text: Add resources to the team.
options.rationale: Adding people may be impossible and does not tackle why quality dips when particular members are away.

options.text: Expand the testing effort.
options.rationale: More testing finds more defects but adds cost of quality; it treats the symptom rather than the skills gap causing it.

options.text: Provide cross-training.
options.rationale: Quality drops when certain members are absent, so capability depends on specific people. Cross-training spreads that capability and keeps quality stable.

options.text: Increase the sprint duration.
options.rationale: Longer sprints do not fix a skills gap; they only delay feedback and still leave the team exposed during absences.

questions.explanation: When output quality falls during predictable absences but velocity is stable, the issue is concentrated expertise. Cross-training builds T-shaped skills so team members can cover for each other, reducing both single points of failure and the cost of rework.
questions.mindset: Spread critical skills across the team so quality does not depend on who is present.

questions.stem: An agile team is receiving multiple unplanned requests for product enhancements in an iteration. This impediment is causing the team to miss scheduled tasks. How should the project manager address this?

options.text: Tell the team to increase their efforts to accommodate the requests.
options.rationale: Asking the team to absorb unplanned work leads to burnout and still leaves committed work at risk.

options.text: Ask the product owner to include requested enhancements in the current iteration.
options.rationale: Adding the requests to the current iteration breaks the sprint commitment and repeats the problem the team is already suffering.

options.text: Request that the project team reprioritizes all of the committed activities.
options.rationale: Reprioritising all committed work mid-iteration destabilises the sprint and passes an incoming-demand problem onto the team.

options.text: Ask the product owner to add the enhancement requests to the product backlog.
options.rationale: Putting enhancement requests in the product backlog lets the product owner prioritise them for a future iteration while protecting current commitments.

questions.explanation: Unplanned requests should flow into the product backlog rather than into the running iteration. The product owner weighs them against other work, and the team keeps its focus on its sprint commitment. This protects both flow and predictability.
questions.mindset: Route new demand through the backlog, not into the running sprint.

questions.stem: A project manager in the execution phase of a project discovers several stakeholders identified at project initiation are no longer involved. These removed stakeholders are frustrated with unnecessary communication and express concern that the remaining stakeholders may not be receiving all of the information they require. What should the project manager have done to prevent this situation?

options.text: Identified and documented all stakeholder requirements at the start of the project.
options.rationale: Collecting requirements at the start is necessary but does not keep the stakeholder picture current as people leave or join.

options.text: Reported all project information to every stakeholder throughout the project lifecycle.
options.rationale: Sending all information to everyone is the opposite of targeted communication and is exactly what frustrated the removed stakeholders.

options.text: Updated the stakeholder engagement plan through the change control process.
options.rationale: Stakeholder involvement changes over time. Updating the engagement plan through change control would have kept distribution lists and engagement actions current.

options.text: Relied on existing stakeholders to inform the project manager about missing stakeholders.
options.rationale: Relying on others to report changes is passive; the project manager is responsible for monitoring and updating stakeholder engagement.

questions.explanation: Stakeholder identification is not a one-off. As stakeholders enter and leave, the engagement plan and related communications must be updated through the project's change process so that the right people receive the right information.
questions.mindset: Keep stakeholder plans current as the stakeholder landscape changes.

questions.stem: During week two of a two-week sprint, one of the core team members has an emergency and is unable to work on the project for the rest of the sprint. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Request that the product manager increase the project timeline.
options.rationale: The product manager does not own the project timeline, and extending it before looking for internal options is premature.

options.text: Identify tasks that can be reassigned to other team members.
options.rationale: Seeing which tasks others on the team can pick up is the quickest way to protect the sprint goal before any bigger adjustment.

options.text: Extend the sprint to offset the loss of the core team member.
options.rationale: Sprints are timeboxed. Extending one breaks the cadence and should not be the first reaction to a loss of capacity.

options.text: Get additional resources from other teams to complete the sprint.
options.rationale: Bringing in people from other teams mid-sprint costs onboarding time and disrupts those teams. It is not the first move.

questions.explanation: When capacity drops in the middle of an iteration, the first step is to look within the team for work that can be redistributed. If the sprint goal still cannot be met, the product owner can adjust scope; the timebox itself is kept.
questions.mindset: Adjust within the team first, and keep the timebox fixed.

questions.stem: A strategic project has been launched and a project manager has been assigned. The project is progressing, and the team is delivering successfully, but a key stakeholder calls the project manager and complains about not receiving progress updates. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ensure the stakeholder is copied on the weekly status emails.
options.rationale: Adding the stakeholder to an email list fixes one person's symptom but leaves the plan that missed them unchanged.

options.text: Review and update the project communications management plan.
options.rationale: The complaint shows the communications plan does not meet this stakeholder's needs. Reviewing and updating it fixes the cause and prevents repeats.

options.text: Send the stakeholder a copy of the latest project status report.
options.rationale: Sending the latest report is a one-off reply; next month the same gap will reappear.

options.text: Invite the key stakeholder to attend the next project meeting.
options.rationale: An invitation to one meeting does not establish how and how often the stakeholder will be kept informed.

questions.explanation: A stakeholder who is not receiving updates is evidence that the communications management plan no longer reflects stakeholder needs. Fixing the plan — what they need, in what format, how often — prevents the gap from recurring, rather than patching it once.
questions.mindset: When communication fails, fix the plan, not just the instance.

questions.stem: A key resource approaches the project manager after the kick-off meeting and expresses concern that they will be unable to deliver their assigned tasks due to other priorities. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Schedule a team meeting to assess and manage priorities.
options.rationale: Meeting to assess priorities finds out whether the conflict can be resolved by rebalancing work while keeping the key resource on the project.

options.text: Document the lack of availability as a risk in the risk register.
options.rationale: Logging a risk records the problem without solving it. The concern has already been raised and needs action, not just documentation.

options.text: Escalate this issue to the project sponsor for executive support.
options.rationale: Escalating straight to the sponsor skips the project manager's own ability to resolve resource conflicts.

options.text: Update the project management plan accordingly to reflect a potential delay.
options.rationale: Updating the plan for a delay accepts a problem that has not yet been examined and may be solvable.

questions.explanation: A resource conflict raised early is an opportunity to rebalance before it becomes a delay. Assessing priorities with the team and the individual allows capacity to be levelled and the key skills retained. Escalation or re-planning are later options if that fails.
questions.mindset: Work resource conflicts through with the team before escalating or re-planning.

questions.stem: During a project schedule review meeting, the project team identified that one of the critical path activities has slipped due to external dependencies. The project schedule is now at risk. What should the project manager prioritize as the initial response to address the issue?

options.text: Issue a change request and meet with the customer.
options.rationale: A change request and customer meeting come too early; corrective actions within the PM's control have not yet been considered.

options.text: Rebaseline the schedule and notify the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Rebaselining is a last resort after corrective options are exhausted, and it hides the variance rather than addressing it.

options.text: Update the documentation and identify corrective actions.
options.rationale: Recording the slippage and identifying corrective actions such as fast-tracking or crashing is the proper first response to a critical path delay.

options.text: Notify the customer and request that the timeline be extended.
options.rationale: Asking the customer for an extension concedes the delay before trying to recover it internally.

questions.explanation: Schedule control follows a pattern: record the variance, analyse the options within the project's control, then act. Customer involvement, change requests and rebaselining come only when internal corrective actions cannot recover the schedule.
questions.mindset: Recover schedule internally before asking anyone else to absorb the delay.

questions.stem: An ongoing project has a high degree of change. In order to evaluate how the IT security team will influence the performance of the project, what should the project manager do?

options.text: Update the stakeholder engagement assessment matrix.
options.rationale: The engagement assessment matrix records current and desired engagement levels. It is useful, but on its own it does not work out how the team will influence performance.

options.text: Analyze corporate political and power structures.
options.rationale: Political and power analysis is a broader organisational exercise and does not focus on this team's specific influence on the project.

options.text: Create a project communications management plan.
options.rationale: A communications plan describes how information flows; it does not evaluate a stakeholder group's influence on performance.

options.text: Manage stakeholders' expectations.
options.rationale: Actively managing the security team's expectations surfaces their requirements and constraints and how they will affect the project, which is what the project manager needs to understand.

questions.explanation: On projects with frequent change, a stakeholder group's influence is understood by engaging with it: learning its expectations, constraints and decision rights and aligning them with the project. Documents and matrices support that work but do not replace the conversation.
questions.mindset: Understand a stakeholder's influence by engaging with their expectations directly.

questions.stem: The service provider and their client agree on about 80% of the scope of a project contract they are working on for the delivery of marketing content. The client has a fixed budget and target completion date and wants to get the most business value from the project as possible by increasing the scope based on a best-effort delivery close to the end of the project. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Create the contract based on the agreed scope and plan addendum changes.
options.rationale: Planning addenda for every change is slow and adversarial, and risks missing the fixed completion date.

options.text: Ensure that a change control process is documented in the contract.
options.rationale: A change control clause is standard, but it does not give the client the flexible best-effort scope they want within a fixed budget.

options.text: Propose a dynamic scope contract option and add a fixed number of iterations.
options.rationale: A dynamic-scope contract with a fixed number of iterations fixes cost and time while letting the client prioritise the remaining scope, which is exactly what is being asked for.

options.text: Increase the number of resources in the contract to deliver the requirements.
options.rationale: Adding resources raises cost and does not fit a fixed budget, nor does it create the flexibility the client needs.

questions.explanation: When cost and time are fixed but scope must flex, the contract should fix the capacity — for example a set number of iterations — and let the client prioritise what goes into them. This preserves value delivery without renegotiating the contract for every change.
questions.mindset: Fix time and cost, flex scope, and let the contract say so.

questions.stem: During an iteration, a key project team member announces their resignation. The project manager realizes that one of the product features will be impacted by the resignation. What should the project manager do to address this situation?

options.text: Submit a change request to modify the delivery date based on this unexpected situation.
options.rationale: Asking to move the delivery date before exploring mitigations accepts the delay too early and skips the product owner who owns trade-offs.

options.text: Request that human resources (HR) retain the team member until the end of the project.
options.rationale: HR cannot hold someone who has resigned, and the request ignores the person's right to leave.

options.text: Accelerate knowledge sharing with the cross-functional team to ensure that this situation is understood.
options.rationale: Knowledge sharing helps, but on its own it does not decide whether the affected feature still gets the capacity it needs.

options.text: Discuss the situation with the product owner and determine if resources should be added to the team.
options.rationale: The product owner owns scope and priority trade-offs. Deciding with them whether to add capacity or re-plan the feature keeps delivery aligned with value.

questions.explanation: When a capacity loss threatens a feature, the decision about how to respond — add resources, reprioritise or accept a later delivery — is a value trade-off that belongs with the product owner. The project manager brings the impact and options; the product owner decides with them.
questions.mindset: Take capacity trade-offs to the person who owns value, with the impact in hand.

questions.stem: During a standup meeting, some of the team members strongly disagreed about how tasks were distributed. They feel tired and frustrated because task distribution has been a frequent complaint throughout the project. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Review the project management plan to determine how to manage this situation.
options.rationale: The plan will not resolve a recurring team grievance about fairness; the people involved need to be part of the solution.

options.text: Discuss with other project managers if they had to address similar complaints.
options.rationale: Asking other project managers is background research. It delays action on a problem the team has raised repeatedly.

options.text: Organize a team-building workshop to improve collaboration and communication.
options.rationale: Team-building does not address the specific complaint about task distribution and may feel dismissive to people who are already frustrated.

options.text: Work with the team to develop a plan for addressing the task distribution concerns.
options.rationale: Working the concern through with the team produces a distribution approach they helped design and are therefore more likely to accept.

questions.explanation: Recurring complaints about how work is shared are a signal that the team needs a say in the rules. Collaborative problem-solving produces fairer outcomes and higher commitment than a solution imposed from the plan or distracted by unrelated activities.
questions.mindset: Solve a team's recurring grievance with the team, not around it.

questions.stem: An agile team is doing an excellent job of focusing on high-priority items and completing them in less time than required. Which key performance indicator (KPI) would best demonstrate this information to the project manager?

options.text: The number of defects or missed requirements identified by the product owner.
options.rationale: Defect counts show quality, not how quickly high-priority work is being completed.

options.text: The number of action items coming out of the end-of-iteration retrospective.
options.rationale: The number of retrospective actions reflects the team's improvement activity rather than delivery throughput.

options.text: The number of user stories from the backlog that are completed per iteration.
options.rationale: Stories completed per iteration shows throughput of prioritised backlog items, which is exactly the performance described.

options.text: The team consistently remains within the kanban board work in process limits.
options.rationale: Staying within WIP limits shows flow discipline but does not show how much valuable work was finished.

questions.explanation: A KPI should measure the thing you want to see. To show that a team completes high-priority work quickly, measure completed backlog items per iteration (throughput or velocity), not quality, process adherence or improvement activity.
questions.mindset: Pick the metric that directly measures the outcome you care about.

questions.stem: A project manager used to work on predictive projects and now has started working on a project using a hybrid approach. What should the project manager do to enable the teams to focus on their mission?

options.text: Implement a Scrum method.
options.rationale: Imposing Scrum is a method choice; it does not in itself enable teams to focus on their mission and may not suit the hybrid mix.

options.text: Adopt servant leadership.
options.rationale: Servant leadership removes impediments and supports the team, letting them focus on their mission — the key shift for a PM moving from command-and-control to hybrid.

options.text: Apply lean methods.
options.rationale: Lean methods can help flow, but the question is about the leader's behaviour in enabling focus, not a process toolkit.

options.text: Innovate with new processes.
options.rationale: Inventing new processes adds change and uncertainty rather than creating focus.

questions.explanation: Moving from predictive to hybrid work changes the leader's role from directing tasks to enabling the team. Servant leadership — clearing obstacles, shielding focus and supporting growth — is what lets teams concentrate on their mission, whatever mix of practices they use.
questions.mindset: Enable focus by serving the team rather than directing it.

questions.stem: A project manager believes that the project team could benefit from development activities to improve project performance and outcomes. The project manager decides to plan specific development activities for each team member. What should the project manager do first to ensure the success of this initiative?

options.text: Conduct a skills assessment of the team members.
options.rationale: A skills assessment establishes each person's current strengths and gaps, so development activities can be targeted where they add most.

options.text: Ask the team to determine their development plans.
options.rationale: Team input is valuable, but asking people to design plans without an assessment gives no shared baseline to plan against.

options.text: Distribute clear development plans to the team members.
options.rationale: Distributing plans before knowing the skills gaps puts the output before the analysis.

options.text: Implement a reward system based on performance.
options.rationale: Rewards may motivate, but they do not identify what development each person needs.

questions.explanation: Development planning starts with knowing where people are. A skills assessment provides that baseline, allowing tailored development that closes real gaps and aligns with the project's needs.
questions.mindset: Assess before you develop.

questions.stem: A project manager has just been assigned a new project team and needs to assign tasks for an upcoming project quickly and effectively. To ensure that tasks are assigned to the right resources, what approach should you take?

options.text: Distribute the tasks evenly because the team should all have equal skill sets.
options.rationale: Assuming everyone has equal skills ignores reality and results in mismatched assignments.

options.text: Allocate the most complex tasks to the more senior members of the project team.
options.rationale: Seniority is not the same as the right skills; the most complex task may need a specialist who is not the most senior.

options.text: Evaluate the background, experience, and capabilities of the team, then assign tasks.
options.rationale: Evaluating background, experience and capability first lets tasks be matched to the right people quickly and effectively.

options.text: Assign experienced team members to assist team members who lack experience.
options.rationale: Pairing is useful later, but it presumes the PM already knows who is experienced in what — the step that is missing.

questions.explanation: Effective assignment matches work to capability. Understanding each team member's background and skills is the basis for placing tasks, planning support and spotting gaps.
questions.mindset: Know your team's capabilities before distributing the work.

questions.stem: Discussions during weekly project team meetings are frequently dominated by a senior team member who has a tendency to talk over other team members and openly criticize their point of view. This is causing demoralization of the other team members and resulting in lack of engagement during the meetings. What should the project manager do to address this issue?

options.text: Remove the senior team member from the weekly meeting.
options.rationale: Excluding the senior member loses their contribution and avoids the real issue — behaviour in meetings.

options.text: Organize a team-building activity that encourages finding solutions together.
options.rationale: Team-building is generic. The problem is a specific breach of meeting behaviour that needs to be addressed directly.

options.text: Enforce the existing ground rules for team behavior.
options.rationale: Ground rules exist precisely for this; enforcing them corrects the behaviour and restores safety for the rest of the team.

options.text: Escalate the behavior of the senior team member to the functional manager.
options.rationale: Escalating to the functional manager goes over the PM's own authority to manage meeting conduct.

questions.explanation: Team charters and ground rules set expectations for behaviour. When someone breaches them, the project manager enforces them promptly and consistently; this protects psychological safety and engagement without escalating or excluding anyone.
questions.mindset: Use the team's own ground rules to correct behaviour that harms others.

questions.stem: A project is in a key phase of execution and everyone is dedicated to achieving success. A functional manager suddenly takes away one of the key team members to respond to an emergency without communicating with the project manager. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Check the resource calendar to find another team member.
options.rationale: Finding a substitute from the calendar accepts the loss without addressing it with the person who made the decision.

options.text: Report the situation to the project sponsor and executive management.
options.rationale: Going to the sponsor and executives first is an escalation before the PM has spoken to the functional manager.

options.text: Communicate with the functional manager and request the return of the key member.
options.rationale: Speaking directly to the functional manager and requesting the member back addresses the problem at its source and explains the project's need.

options.text: Review the impact to the project and schedule a meeting with the functional manager.
options.rationale: Reviewing impact first and scheduling a meeting later delays contact with the functional manager while the key phase proceeds without the resource.

questions.explanation: In a matrix organisation resource conflicts are negotiated with functional managers. The first step is direct communication: explain the project's need and ask for the resource back or a workable arrangement. Escalation is reserved for when that fails.
questions.mindset: Resolve resource conflicts directly with the manager who controls the resource.

questions.stem: Due to a lack of locally skilled resources, a company employs an internationally dispersed project team that will work virtually. The project manager has never worked with a virtual team and is concerned about engagement. What should the project manager do to ensure this virtual team remains engaged?

options.text: Ensure the entire virtual team attends the project kickoff meeting.
options.rationale: A kickoff is a single event; engagement across a dispersed team needs ongoing contact.

options.text: Adopt the communications management plan of a past virtual team.
options.rationale: Another team's communications plan may not fit this team's time zones, culture or work.

options.text: Rely on asynchronous communication for all major status reports.
options.rationale: Relying only on asynchronous updates for major status removes the live interaction that builds engagement.

options.text: Conduct recurring check-ins and meetings at scheduled intervals.
options.rationale: Regular check-ins and scheduled meetings give a virtual team a rhythm of contact, trust building and shared focus.

questions.explanation: Virtual teams lose the informal contact that keeps colocated teams engaged. A regular cadence of check-ins and meetings replaces that contact deliberately, building trust and keeping everyone aligned.
questions.mindset: Create regular, deliberate contact where proximity does not provide it.

questions.stem: A delivery team member is complaining about the workload and the number of top priorities they are handling. Another team member is complaining that they cannot do their own work due to the lack of progress from the first team member. They are both frustrated and the dispute is negatively impacting productivity and morale. What should the project manager do to improve team performance and resolve the underlying dispute?

options.text: Find common ground to show them that they agree on workload issues.
options.rationale: Finding common ground is helpful but premature while both people are frustrated and emotions are driving the dispute.

options.text: Recognize that emotions are part of this issue and address them first.
options.rationale: Acknowledging emotions first calms the situation and makes a productive discussion of workload possible.

options.text: Initiate conflict resolution techniques to identify which of them is to blame.
options.rationale: Looking for someone to blame escalates the conflict and damages trust.

options.text: Employ stakeholder engagement mechanisms and escalate the situation.
options.rationale: Escalation through stakeholder mechanisms is excessive for a team-level dispute the PM can handle.

questions.explanation: Emotionally charged conflicts cannot be resolved on facts alone. Recognising and addressing emotions first — listening and acknowledging frustration — lowers the temperature so the underlying workload problem can then be solved collaboratively.
questions.mindset: Address emotions first so the facts can be heard.

questions.stem: A project manager notices that team members are not interacting with each other and believes that the lack of interaction is negatively impacting project performance. The project manager attempts to increase team interaction by hosting an after-work event, but only a few team members attend. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Send a team survey to collect ideas for after-work activities from team members.
options.rationale: Collecting ideas for events assumes that social activities are the answer, which the poor turnout already calls into question.

options.text: Continue to invite team members to events and improve morale incrementally.
options.rationale: Continuing the same approach repeats something that has not worked.

options.text: Provide periodic incentives and bonuses to the highest-performing team members.
options.rationale: Rewarding individual top performers may increase competition and reduce interaction further.

options.text: Confidentially poll the team to identify the root cause of the lack of interaction.
options.rationale: A confidential poll gets honest input about why people are not interacting, so the response can target the real cause.

questions.explanation: When a team-engagement initiative fails, it is a sign that the cause is not understood. Gathering confidential input from the team reveals the real reasons before more effort is spent on solutions.
questions.mindset: Find out why before trying again.

questions.stem: The project manager of a large team notices team members are not interacting together, which is impacting project performance and the quality of the project outcome. What should the project manager do to help grow team dynamics?

options.text: Conduct face-to-face group meetings to understand what the issues are.
options.rationale: Face-to-face group meetings let the PM hear directly what is getting in the way of collaboration and start improving dynamics.

options.text: Notify the project team members' supervisors about the lack of cooperation.
options.rationale: Telling supervisors frames the issue as misconduct and undermines trust before anyone understands it.

options.text: Add the lack of team communication as a risk in the risk register and monitor the situation.
options.rationale: Logging a risk and monitoring is passive; the problem is already affecting quality.

options.text: Refer to the lessons learned to understand how other projects handled similar issues.
options.rationale: Lessons from other projects might help later but will not reveal what is happening in this team.

questions.explanation: Team dynamics are improved by engaging the team directly. Listening in person uncovers the obstacles to interaction, and is the foundation for coaching and building collaboration.
questions.mindset: Improve team dynamics by listening to the team first-hand.

questions.stem: A large-scale project has been consistently progressing. However, the team is experiencing difficulties in completing some complex stories and maintaining velocity. The project manager discovers that inefficient collaboration has led to misunderstandings and frustrations. What should the project manager do to enhance the team's performance?

options.text: Focus on servant leadership.
options.rationale: Servant leadership is valuable but general; the specific diagnosed problem is ineffective collaboration and communication.

options.text: Perform a root cause analysis.
options.rationale: Root cause analysis has effectively been done — the PM already found inefficient collaboration was the cause.

options.text: Seek insight from a mentor.
options.rationale: A mentor might help the PM personally but does not act on the team's communication problem.

options.text: Improve team communications.
options.rationale: The cause is already known — misunderstandings from poor collaboration — so improving team communication directly addresses it.

questions.explanation: Once the cause of a performance problem is known, act on it. When misunderstandings from weak collaboration are slowing the team, improving communication practices — stand-ups, shared understanding of stories, open channels — is the direct lever.
questions.mindset: Once the cause is known, act on the cause.

questions.stem: A project is in the implementation phase. A new project manager discovers that the team members have no previous experience with the technology used for the project. However, there are several functional managers that have experience with the technology. What should the project manager do first to ensure the successful performance of the team?

options.text: Ask functional managers to act as mentors or coaches for the team.
options.rationale: Using the functional managers' experience as mentors or coaches closes the skills gap quickly and within the organisation.

options.text: Request that the sponsor substitute experienced team members.
options.rationale: Swapping team members during implementation is disruptive and expensive when expertise is available to develop the current team.

options.text: Identify the risks associated with team members' inexperience.
options.rationale: Identifying risks documents the problem but does not solve it; the gap is known.

options.text: Develop status reports to monitor the team's skills and competencies.
options.rationale: Status reports on skills monitor the gap rather than close it.

questions.explanation: When a team lacks experience with a technology and experts exist nearby, the fastest and least disruptive response is structured knowledge transfer: mentoring and coaching from those experts.
questions.mindset: Close skills gaps by connecting the team with the expertise that already exists.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned a complex project with significant legal, regulatory, and contractual requirements. However, these requirements have not yet been defined or finalized. Concerns exist regarding a delay in completing these requirements. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Focus on the project deliverables instead as it is not the project manager's responsibility to fulfill these requirements.
options.rationale: Compliance requirements affect whether the project can proceed or release; ignoring them is not an option for the PM.

options.text: Contact the product owner and highlight the project risks related to the delay in fulfilling these requirements on time.
options.rationale: Highlighting the risk to the product owner alone does not engage the legal department, who own defining these requirements.

options.text: Meet with the product owner and the legal department to review the project status and the progress in defining these requirements.
options.rationale: Meeting the product owner and legal department to review progress addresses the delay with the people who can resolve it.

options.text: Delay the finalization of the legal, regulatory, and contractual requirements until the end of the project, and before the go-live date.
options.rationale: Deferring compliance requirements until go-live risks failing to launch at all, or reworking the product late.

questions.explanation: Legal, regulatory and contractual requirements are constraints the project must satisfy, often before it can proceed or release. When their definition lags, the project manager engages the owners of those requirements early to track and accelerate progress.
questions.mindset: Treat compliance requirements as gating work and engage their owners early.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a hybrid project with a self-organizing team. The team is unable to agree on the scope for the next increment. How should the project manager resolve this issue?

options.text: Facilitate a team discussion to understand why the team is unable to agree on the scope for the next increment.
options.rationale: Facilitating a discussion to understand why the team cannot agree surfaces the underlying disagreement and supports the team in reaching its own decision.

options.text: Escalate the issue to the project sponsor so that the risk posed by the disagreements over scope becomes visible.
options.rationale: Escalating to the sponsor takes the decision out of a self-organising team's hands at the first difficulty.

options.text: Collaborate with a suitable subject matter expert (SME) to determine the scope for the next increment.
options.rationale: Having an SME decide the scope overrides the team's self-organisation and skips the product owner's role.

options.text: Request that the team votes on the options and identify the appropriate scope based on a majority vote.
options.rationale: A majority vote may leave a sizeable minority unconvinced and does not uncover the reasons for disagreement.

questions.explanation: With self-organising teams, the project manager's role in disagreement is facilitation: helping the team understand its differences so it can reach a decision it owns. Imposed decisions or votes leave the causes of disagreement unresolved.
questions.mindset: Facilitate the team to its own decision rather than making it for them.

questions.stem: The construction of a building is well-defined through plans and written specifications. The service is to be delivered in two years in a high-inflation environment. What contract type should the project manager use?

options.text: Cost plus incentive fee (CPIF) contract
options.rationale: Cost-plus contracts suit uncertain scope. Here the scope is well defined, so reimbursing cost puts unnecessary risk on the buyer.

options.text: Firm fixed price (FFP) contract
options.rationale: A firm fixed price over two years of high inflation forces the seller to price in large contingencies or face losses.

options.text: Fixed price with economic price adjustment (FPEPA) contract
options.rationale: Well-defined scope favours fixed price, and an economic price adjustment clause handles the inflation risk over a long period.

options.text: Time and materials (T&M) contract
options.rationale: Time and materials suits small or undefined work, not a fully specified building project.

questions.explanation: Contract choice follows scope clarity and risk. Defined scope points to fixed price; long durations with volatile prices add a need for an economic price adjustment mechanism so neither party carries unpredictable inflation risk.
questions.mindset: Match the contract to how well the scope is defined and which risks are external.

questions.stem: At an agile project meeting, a team member gives an update on the status of their important task. A new team member interrupts them when they hear their task mentioned and gives a status update before the first team member has finished their update. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Privately talk to the two team members after the meeting.
options.rationale: A private conversation later does not deal with the interruption now, and involving the person who was interrupted is unnecessary.

options.text: Tell the new team member that they are acting unprofessionally.
options.rationale: Calling the new member unprofessional in front of the team is harsh and damages trust.

options.text: Pause to discuss appropriate meeting protocol with the team.
options.rationale: Pausing the meeting to discuss protocol turns a small moment into a large interruption.

options.text: Ask the new team member to wait until their teammate finishes.
options.rationale: Politely asking the new member to wait restores order immediately and respectfully, and keeps the meeting on track.

questions.explanation: Small breaches of meeting etiquette are best handled lightly and in the moment. A courteous redirection maintains respect for everyone's contributions without embarrassing anyone or derailing the meeting.
questions.mindset: Correct small behaviours lightly and in the moment.

questions.stem: The first iteration of an agile project consists of a minimum viable product (MVP) that is now successfully completed. The team members are eager to hand the product over to the customer. How should the product be confirmed as ready for customer use?

options.text: The scrum master determines that all requirements are satisfied.
options.rationale: The scrum master facilitates; they do not decide whether a product meets requirements.

options.text: The project team agrees the MVP meets the definition of done (DoD).
options.rationale: The team's definition of done sets the criteria for readiness; confirming the MVP against it shows it is fit to hand over.

options.text: The senior manager and customer approve and accept the product.
