options.rationale: Senior management and customer acceptance are separate from confirming the team's own completeness criteria.

options.text: The product owner decides that the MVP passes all required quality tests.
options.rationale: Quality tests are part of the DoD, but the DoD is a shared team agreement, not the product owner's sole judgement.

questions.explanation: The definition of done is the team's shared, explicit standard for when work is complete. Confirming an increment against the DoD is how readiness is established before handover to the customer.
questions.mindset: Judge readiness against the shared definition of done, not individual opinion.

questions.stem: A project manager received a complaint that the project team did not respond correctly to a client's request. However, the project manager understands that the team has received multiple out-of-scope requests from the client. Which action should the project manager take?

options.text: Encourage the team members to ask the "five whys" during their communications with the client.
options.rationale: The five whys might explore requests but do not address that the requests are outside the agreed scope.

options.text: Ask the client to better explain the requests and issues they shared with the team.
options.rationale: Asking the client to explain better misplaces the problem; the issue is scope, not clarity.

options.text: Review the scope with the client so that additional requests can be documented and processed as change requests.
options.rationale: Reviewing scope with the client makes the boundary clear and routes additional requests into change control.

options.text: Request to be included in all future communications between the project team members and the client.
options.rationale: Inserting the PM in every communication creates a bottleneck and still does not clarify what is in scope.

questions.explanation: Out-of-scope requests handled informally lead to disappointment on both sides. Clarifying the agreed scope with the client, and processing new requests as change requests, sets expectations and protects the team.
questions.mindset: Make the scope boundary visible and route new requests through change control.

questions.stem: A project manager is managing several interconnected projects. Some of these projects rely on specific deliverables from other projects. To avoid bottlenecks and facilitate project success, the project manager must assess the consolidated project plans for dependencies. What is the most appropriate action for the project manager to take in this situation?

options.text: Identify and document all inter-project dependencies.
options.rationale: Identifying and documenting inter-project dependencies makes them visible so they can be planned, sequenced and monitored.

options.text: Adjust project timelines to remove dependencies.
options.rationale: Adjusting timelines to remove dependencies is often impossible, and without identifying them first there is nothing to adjust.

options.text: Eliminate all potential inter-project dependencies.
options.rationale: Dependencies between interconnected projects cannot simply be eliminated; they are inherent to the design.

options.text: Ensure that all projects can proceed independently.
options.rationale: Forcing independence ignores the reason the projects are connected.

questions.explanation: Across interconnected projects, dependencies must be identified and documented before they can be managed. Visibility enables coordinated planning, communication and risk management; attempting to remove dependencies usually misunderstands why they exist.
questions.mindset: Make dependencies visible before trying to manage them.

questions.stem: During the project kick-off meeting, the project manager announces that a hybrid approach will be used to deliver the project. Many of the team members raise a concern because they are used to working on predictive projects. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Escalate the issue to the project sponsor to ensure the team is aligned with the project delivery approach.
options.rationale: Escalating team concerns about unfamiliar methods to the sponsor is premature and does not help the team understand the approach.

options.text: Engage the project management office (PMO) since they identify the approach to delivering projects.
options.rationale: The PMO may set standards, but handing off the team's concerns does not address their unfamiliarity.

options.text: Educate the team members on agile and the benefits associated with the use of agile principles.
options.rationale: Educating the team on agile principles and their benefits builds understanding and buy-in for the hybrid approach.

options.text: Change to a predictive approach to be aligned with the skills of the team members.
options.rationale: Changing approach to suit current skills ignores why the hybrid approach was chosen for this project.

questions.explanation: When a team is uneasy with a new delivery approach, the project manager addresses the gap in understanding. Education about the principles and benefits builds confidence, which is the basis for adoption.
questions.mindset: Build understanding before expecting adoption.

questions.stem: A key deadline is approaching specialized team member has suddenly received news that they must leave the office for two weeks. They have approximately three workdays until they leave and they will be unavailable through any communication channels. What should the agile project manager do?

options.text: Adjust the project plan and timeline to accommodate the absence.
options.rationale: Adjusting the plan before understanding which tasks are affected is premature.

options.text: Identify critical tasks and dependencies that may be affected.
options.rationale: Identifying the critical tasks and dependencies that depend on the person shows where the absence will bite and what to do in the three days available.

options.text: Introduce a replacement resource for the leaving team member.
options.rationale: Bringing in a replacement may not be feasible and should follow an impact assessment.

options.text: Ask the team member to quickly complete as much as they can.
options.rationale: Asking the person to rush may lower quality and does not target the work that matters most.

questions.explanation: With a short window before an absence, the first step is impact analysis: which critical tasks and dependencies rely on this person. That tells the team what to prioritise, hand over or re-plan while the person is still available.
questions.mindset: Find what depends on the person before deciding how to cover for them.

questions.stem: A new team is formed for an agile project, in which members are located in three different countries and five time zones. What should the project manager do first to ensure effective communication among team members?

options.text: Schedule a virtual meeting and introduce the team members.
options.rationale: Introductions are useful but do not set how the team will communicate across time zones.

options.text: Establish guidelines for team communications.
options.rationale: Guidelines for communication — channels, response times, meeting hours — give a dispersed team shared expectations from the start.

options.text: Set up recurring meetings until all team members are familiar with each other.
options.rationale: Recurring meetings help later, but without agreed guidelines they may clash with time zones and preferences.

options.text: Colocate the team members for a short duration to enhance communications.
options.rationale: Temporary colocation is expensive and may not be possible; it is not the first step.

questions.explanation: A distributed team needs agreed norms before it can communicate well: which tools, when people are available, how quickly to respond and how decisions are shared. Establishing these guidelines first prevents misunderstandings later.
questions.mindset: Agree how the team will communicate before relying on communication.

questions.stem: A team is working on a new product development project using a hybrid approach. After the fourth sprint, they learn that the exchange rate for imported goods will increase significantly. What should the project manager do in order to make sure the final product gets launched on time and as defined?

options.text: Work with the stakeholders to develop incremental budgeting approaches.
options.rationale: Working with stakeholders on incremental budgeting lets funding adjust as costs change while keeping the product on track.

options.text: Reduce the product’s specifications to use less imported material.
options.rationale: Reducing specifications changes what is launched, contrary to the goal of launching as defined.

options.text: Spend the extra money and plan to compensate for it in the next sprint.
options.rationale: Spending unplanned money and hoping to compensate later is uncontrolled and risks overrun.

options.text: Review the backlog to see the impact of a budget increase.
options.rationale: Reviewing the backlog for a budget increase analyses impact but does not provide a way to fund it.

questions.explanation: When external factors like exchange rates move costs mid-project, rigid up-front budgets break down. Incremental or rolling budgeting, agreed with stakeholders, provides control while allowing funding to follow actual conditions.
questions.mindset: Adapt the funding approach when external conditions change the cost base.

questions.stem: At the end of a large project, the stakeholders realize that the achieved benefits are not the same as the expected benefits. Which item, if poorly defined at the start of the project, could have led to this issue?

options.text: Requirements documentation
options.rationale: Requirements documentation defines what to build, not how the benefits it is meant to produce will be measured.

options.text: Project scope
options.rationale: Scope defines the work and deliverables. A well-defined scope can still yield benefits nobody measured along the way.

options.text: Business case
options.rationale: The business case justifies the investment and names expected benefits, but without defined metrics there is no way to track whether they are being realised.

options.text: Benefits metrics
options.rationale: Benefit metrics define how expected benefits are measured and tracked. If they are vague at the start, nobody notices the gap between expected and achieved benefits until the end.

questions.explanation: Benefits must be measurable to be managed. Defining benefit metrics at the outset lets the project and sponsor track realisation during the life cycle and correct course, instead of discovering a shortfall only at closure.
questions.mindset: If a benefit is not measured during the project, it will not be managed during the project.

questions.stem: As part of a temporary assignment, a project manager is leading a business project. During a daily status meeting, it was discovered that the development team had not completed a critical task. This issue is delaying the current iteration. The ability to take the actions needed to address this issue is beyond the authority of the project team. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Delay the current iteration and inform the stakeholders of the issue.
options.rationale: Delaying the iteration and informing stakeholders accepts the delay without anyone with authority taking the needed decision.

options.text: Invite the project team to a swarming session to define a solution.
options.rationale: Swarming helps when the team can solve the problem itself; here the action required is beyond the team's authority.

options.text: Adjust the project timeline to accommodate the development delay.
options.rationale: Adjusting the timeline is itself a decision the team may not be authorised to make, and it simply absorbs the delay.

options.text: Escalate the issue to the project sponsor to define the next steps.
options.rationale: When a decision exceeds the team's authority, escalating to the sponsor gets it to the person who can decide the next steps.

questions.explanation: Governance defines who can decide what. When an issue needs action beyond the project team's authority, the correct path is escalation to the sponsor, ideally with the options already investigated, rather than stalling or improvising outside delegated limits.
questions.mindset: Escalate decisions to where the authority sits, with options in hand.

questions.stem: Two project managers are working on resourcing their respective projects. Both project managers identified the same subject matter expert (SME) as being beneficial to their project. Project A is using a predictive approach and Project B is using an agile approach. To which project should the SME be allocated?

options.text: The SME should be assigned to Project A because project planning was based on the support of the SME.
options.rationale: Having planned around the SME is a reason to negotiate, but predictive plans can often absorb scheduled specialist input rather than full-time allocation.

options.text: The SME should be assigned to Project B because success in an agile project is determined by technical excellence.
options.rationale: Technical excellence matters in agile, but that alone is not the reason given for prioritising Project B.

options.text: The SME should be assigned to the project with the less experienced project manager to improve the likelihood of success.
options.rationale: The experience of the project manager is irrelevant to where the SME's expertise is most needed.

options.text: The SME should be assigned to Project B because agile approaches prioritize flexibility and adaptability.
options.rationale: Agile work relies on responding to change with the right expertise available continuously, so the SME adds most value embedded in Project B's adaptive environment.

questions.explanation: Contended specialists should go where their continuous presence adds the most value. Adaptive approaches depend on rapid decisions and changing requirements, so embedded expertise has high leverage there, while predictive plans can often schedule specialist input at defined points.
questions.mindset: Place scarce expertise where continuous availability adds the most value.

questions.stem: In a software development project, a stakeholder wants to add a major requirement, which they feel will be a great benefit to the project. However, this requirement is not aligned to the project objectives that the business owner has documented. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Ensure the stakeholder understands the purpose of the project.
options.rationale: Helping the stakeholder understand the project's purpose aligns their expectations with the documented objectives before any requirement is considered.

options.text: Encourage the stakeholder to follow the written business requirements.
options.rationale: Telling the stakeholder to follow the written requirements is dismissive and does not explain why their idea does not fit.

options.text: Include the additional requirement into the project and inform the business owner.
options.rationale: Adding a major requirement that does not fit the objectives bypasses scope control and the business owner.

options.text: Fast-track the project and suggest the new requirement to the business owner.
options.rationale: Fast-tracking to create room for an unaligned requirement solves the wrong problem.

questions.explanation: When a stakeholder proposes something outside the project's objectives, start by aligning understanding of the project's purpose. Shared understanding of objectives is what lets stakeholders judge their own ideas against the project's goals.
questions.mindset: Align stakeholders on the project's purpose before debating individual requirements.

questions.stem: During a hybrid project, a project manager reviews the project team's performance and realizes that the team's velocity is not fast enough to meet the next review gate goal. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Prioritize the contents of the backlog and remove some stories.
options.rationale: Removing stories reduces scope before understanding why velocity is low; the problem may be fixable.

options.text: Increase the sprint duration to allow the team more time.
options.rationale: Longer sprints do not increase velocity and break the cadence.

options.text: Use the standup meeting to assess impediments and problems.
options.rationale: Using the stand-up to surface impediments identifies what is slowing the team so it can be removed.

options.text: Create a change request to modify the review gate goals.
options.rationale: Changing the review gate goals gives up on the target before examining the cause.

questions.explanation: Velocity problems are symptoms. Surfacing and removing impediments addresses their cause and is the first lever before adjusting scope, cadence or targets.
questions.mindset: Investigate impediments before cutting scope or moving goals.

questions.stem: A project manager is developing a project management plan. The project duration is set for three months due to regulatory compliance and dependency on senior staff. Which two project objectives should be defined well enough to be included in the project management plan? (Choose two)

options.text: Improve the processes and reduce rework by keeping senior staff turnover to a minimum level.
options.rationale: This objective ties directly to the constraints — dependence on senior staff — and is concrete enough to plan and track in the management plan.

options.text: Develop detailed process maps to align operational activities with the new software system.
options.rationale: Detailed process maps may be useful, but they are an activity, not a clearly defined objective linked to the project's constraints.

options.text: Enhance the development process by redesigning new templates for the design documentation.
options.rationale: Redesigning the design documentation templates is a concrete improvement that addresses rework and can be defined and measured within three months.

options.text: Reduce the company's environmental footprint by using detailed recycling guidelines for all employees.
options.rationale: Reducing the company's environmental footprint is unrelated to this project's scope and constraints.

options.text: Identify training needs and create a development plan to complete the delivery in three months.
options.rationale: Training plans may be supporting work, but the option describes an activity to reach the deadline rather than a project objective in its own right.

questions.explanation: Objectives included in the project management plan should be specific, relevant to the project's constraints and measurable within its timeframe. Objectives that are generic, unrelated or merely activities do not provide a sound basis for planning and control.
questions.mindset: Write objectives that are specific, relevant to the constraints and measurable in the timeframe.

questions.stem: Due to the complex nature of a predictive project, an organization decides to use an agile approach for a project phase. A team member does not really understand the agile approach and keeps allocating tasks to the rest of the team members. After a while, the team is not able to adjust by itself and conflicts arise, delaying the deliverables. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Replace the team member with someone who has agile experience.
options.rationale: Replacing the team member before trying coaching is premature and loses the person's knowledge.

options.text: Wait until the team is finally able to solve the conflict by itself and reorganize.
options.rationale: Waiting has already failed; conflicts are delaying deliverables.

options.text: Reaffirm the principles and roles of agile to create structures that the team can use.
options.rationale: Reaffirming agile principles and roles gives the team the structure it needs to self-organise and corrects the member's behaviour through shared understanding.

options.text: Take control of the sprint backlog and assign tasks to the team members.
options.rationale: Taking control of the backlog contradicts self-organisation and repeats the behaviour causing the problem.

questions.explanation: Teams new to agile need clarity about roles and principles to self-organise. When behaviour reflects the old model, the project manager coaches the team on the new principles and structures rather than replacing people or taking control.
questions.mindset: Coach the team back to the principles before intervening in its work.

questions.stem: A project manager is handling multiple projects in five different countries and is issued a new directive on workplace attire and office arrangements. This has been met with resistance in three countries, resulting in a series of misunderstandings, resentment, and potential legal issues. What should the project manager have done to better handle this situation?

options.text: Asked senior management for clarity and exceptions before issuing a general directive to all countries.
options.rationale: Senior management clarity and exceptions would not have revealed how people in each culture would receive the directive.

options.text: Evaluated the cultural and personal traits in the various countries before issuing a general directive.
options.rationale: Evaluating cultural norms in each country would have exposed where the directive clashed with local expectations and law before it was issued.

options.text: Determined the socioeconomic status of the team members before issuing a widespread directive.
options.rationale: Socioeconomic status is not the relevant factor for attire and office norms and could be seen as discriminatory.

options.text: Obtained a list of personal preferences from the team members before issuing a broad directive.
options.rationale: Collecting personal preferences addresses individuals, not the cultural and legal differences between countries.

questions.explanation: Organisational change across cultures needs cultural analysis. Norms about dress, workspace and hierarchy vary by country, and a single directive that ignores them can cause resentment and legal risk.
questions.mindset: Understand cultural context before applying one rule everywhere.

questions.stem: A new project manager takes over a construction project. Upon reviewing the project management plan, the project manager realizes that the health and safety requirements have not been adequately addressed. The project manager has serious concerns and wants to address this inadequacy. What is the primary concern in this situation?

options.text: Failing to address health and safety issues could damage the client's trust and reputation.
options.rationale: Reputation matters, but it is secondary to the legal and ethical obligation to protect workers.

options.text: The project must comply with all legal and regulatory requirements and responsibilities.
options.rationale: Health and safety requirements are legal obligations; complying with them is non-negotiable and is the primary concern.

options.text: The project timeline may be jeopardized by implementing additional safety measures.
options.rationale: Schedule impact may follow, but it cannot outweigh a legal duty.

options.text: The project manager knows that it is crucial to meet the established performance metrics.
options.rationale: Performance metrics do not override legal and regulatory requirements.

questions.explanation: Compliance with legal and regulatory obligations — especially health and safety — takes priority over schedule, reputation or performance targets. A project cannot legitimately proceed while breaching them.
questions.mindset: Legal and safety obligations are constraints, not trade-offs.

questions.stem: The sponsor for a multimillion-dollar project has just called the project manager for a crisis meeting. The client submitted a formal request to drastically compress the schedule in order to meet a legal deadline. What should the project manager do to prepare for the meeting?

options.text: Initiate procedures to fast-track the project.
options.rationale: Initiating fast-tracking commits to a response before the request has been assessed or approved.

options.text: Implement the required changes to the project schedule.
options.rationale: Implementing schedule changes before approval bypasses change control.

options.text: Analyze tools to crash the project activities.
options.rationale: Analysing crashing tools looks at one option only; the sponsor needs a full impact picture.

options.text: Prepare a change impact assessment report for review.
options.rationale: A change impact assessment shows the effect on scope, schedule, cost, quality and risk so the decision at the meeting is informed.

questions.explanation: A formal change request must be analysed before it is approved or implemented. Arriving with an impact assessment covering options, costs and risks lets decision-makers make an informed choice.
questions.mindset: Bring impact analysis to the decision, not a decision already made.

questions.stem: A project manager is involved in a project where requirements are constantly evolving. What should the project manager do to achieve success?

options.text: Provide regular updates and request deliverable-based approvals from the product owner.
options.rationale: Regular updates and deliverable-based approvals from the product owner keep an evolving scope aligned with what the customer actually needs.

options.text: Work with the team to ensure they are on track and delivering on schedule.
options.rationale: Keeping the team on schedule is generic and does not deal with requirements that keep changing.

options.text: Maintain a comfortable working atmosphere to improve team cohesion.
options.rationale: A comfortable atmosphere matters but does not handle evolving requirements.

options.text: Ensure documentation and processes are filed appropriately and update the product owner.
options.rationale: Documentation and filing do not create the frequent feedback that evolving scope requires.

questions.explanation: When requirements evolve, success depends on frequent feedback and acceptance from the customer representative. Regular engagement with the product owner keeps delivered increments aligned with changing needs.
questions.mindset: Evolving requirements need frequent customer feedback built into the delivery.

questions.stem: A project is currently behind schedule when a new team member, known for their high performance, is assigned to the team. While assessing the new team member, the project manager realizes that the individual lacks training for the specific project but has the skills and relevant experience to join the team. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ensure that the team member receives training before joining the team.
options.rationale: Holding the person back until training is complete wastes capacity when the project is already behind.

options.text: Assign the new team member to critical activities under close monitoring while they receive training.
options.rationale: Assigning critical activities to someone not yet trained on this project raises the risk on exactly the work that can least afford it.

options.text: Assign the new team member to noncritical activities without close monitoring while training is provided.
options.rationale: Non-critical work lets the new member contribute immediately while training, without exposing the critical path.

options.text: Decline the addition of the new team member to the team.
options.rationale: Declining a capable, experienced person makes no sense for a project that is behind schedule.

questions.explanation: New resources can add capacity quickly if their work is matched to their current readiness. Assigning lower-risk tasks during training balances contribution with the protection of critical activities.
questions.mindset: Match early assignments to readiness, protecting the critical path.

questions.stem: After completing the project charter, the project manager sends it to the project stakeholders. What should the project manager do before starting the project planning process?

options.text: Conduct the project's kick-off meeting.
options.rationale: The kick-off usually follows planning and cannot happen before the project is authorised.

options.text: Develop the risk register.
options.rationale: The risk register is built during planning, after the charter authorises the project.

options.text: Create the work breakdown structure (WBS).
options.rationale: The WBS is a planning artefact; creating it before approval may waste effort if the charter changes.

options.text: Obtain project charter approval.
options.rationale: An approved charter formally authorises the project and the PM's authority; planning should not start without it.

questions.explanation: The project charter formally authorises the project and assigns the project manager's authority. Until it is approved, initiation is incomplete and planning work risks being built on scope that may change.
questions.mindset: Get authorisation before investing in planning.

questions.stem: A project manager is managing a project for a successful startup. The startup has shown exponential growth with multiple benefits to the team members, including flexible work hours and a work-from-home policy. During the last retrospective, one of the team members noted that the team velocity improved when the team was physically gathered in the project room. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Gather feedback and analyze the impact of physical location on team velocity.
options.rationale: Gathering feedback and analysing the effect of location on velocity tests the observation before acting on it.

options.text: Refine the backlog to improve team velocity and maintain current policies.
options.rationale: Refining the backlog does not address the observation about location, and it ignores useful data.

options.text: Share the idea with senior management and suggest updating company policies.
options.rationale: Taking a single observation to senior management as a policy proposal is premature and unsupported.

options.text: Update the resource management plan and team charter to promote colocation.
options.rationale: Changing plans to mandate colocation acts on an unverified observation and could conflict with company policy.

questions.explanation: Retrospective observations are hypotheses for improvement. Before changing working arrangements, the team should gather evidence and weigh trade-offs so decisions are informed and well supported.
questions.mindset: Validate an improvement idea with evidence before changing how people work.

questions.stem: A project manager communicates with a key stakeholder via phone calls only, as indicated in the communication management plan. Three weeks into the execution of a project, the project manager begins receiving an increasing amount of redundant ad-hoc communication requests from that stakeholder. How should the project manager address this issue?

options.text: Continue with phone call communication as it has been effective so far.
options.rationale: Continuing phone calls ignores the signal that the stakeholder's needs are not being met.

options.text: Meet with the stakeholder to discuss their communication needs and expectations.
options.rationale: Meeting the stakeholder to understand their needs lets the PM adjust the communications approach so it works for them.

options.text: Send an email to the stakeholder requesting a change in communication approach.
options.rationale: An email asking the stakeholder to change is one-sided and may feel dismissive.

options.text: Assign a team member to act as a liaison between the project manager and the stakeholder.
options.rationale: A liaison adds a layer without resolving why the stakeholder needs more information.

questions.explanation: An increase in ad-hoc requests indicates the planned communication is not meeting needs. The fix is to understand those needs directly and update the communications approach.
questions.mindset: Treat repeated ad-hoc requests as a signal the communication plan needs revisiting.

questions.stem: During a product acceptance test for a software project, the project sponsor tells the project manager that the software will only pass if the theme color is changed from red to blue. The project manager reviewed the planning documents and confirmed that the theme color should be red. The sponsor insists that the color be changed to blue. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Suggest that the project sponsor submit a formal change request to change the requirement for the theme.
options.rationale: A formal change request lets the colour change be assessed, approved and documented, even when the request comes from the sponsor.

options.text: Tell the project sponsor to accept the theme because the contract clearly states it should be red.
options.rationale: Refusing outright is confrontational and ignores the sponsor's legitimate right to request change.

options.text: Agree with the project sponsor and change the theme color as requested to avoid potential conflict.
options.rationale: Making the change informally bypasses change control and may have impacts nobody has assessed.

options.text: Request that procurement change the theme color to blue to align with the project sponsor's expectations.
options.rationale: Procurement is not responsible for requirement changes.

questions.explanation: Change control applies to everyone, sponsors included. A change to agreed requirements goes through the formal process so impacts are understood and the baseline stays accurate.
questions.mindset: Apply change control consistently, whoever is asking.

questions.stem: A project manager observes that team members are not collaborating or being proactive. What should the project manager have done at the beginning of the project to achieve a better project environment?

options.text: Conducted an assessment of team dynamics.
options.rationale: Assessing team dynamics early reveals collaboration styles and potential friction so they can be addressed before they harden.

options.text: Assigned all tasks at the beginning of the project.
options.rationale: Assigning all tasks up front does not build collaboration and may even discourage initiative.

options.text: Facilitated additional team meetings.
options.rationale: More meetings do not in themselves create collaboration or proactivity.

options.text: Split the project into more iterations.
options.rationale: Splitting the project into more iterations changes cadence, not team dynamics.

questions.explanation: Team performance depends on dynamics as well as skills. Assessing how people work together at the start lets the project manager shape the environment — roles, norms, pairings — to encourage collaboration.
questions.mindset: Assess and shape team dynamics early rather than repairing them later.

questions.stem: At the end of the first phase of a stadium expansion project, the project manager realizes they will be running behind schedule for the next project phase. The delay is due to new safety requirements that must be adhered to. Stakeholders are frustrated that they were not aware of the potential safety requirement changes. What should you have done to avoid this situation and ensure that stakeholders are aware of potential disruptions?

options.text: Increase the project's contingency reserve to accommodate unforeseen safety-related issues.
options.rationale: More contingency may absorb delay, but it would not have made stakeholders aware of the risk in advance.

options.text: Hold regular communication meetings with the site supervisor to stay updated on safety requirements.
options.rationale: Regular updates from the site supervisor help but are reactive and narrow; they do not form a structured risk process.

options.text: Implement a proactive risk assessment process during project initiation to identify potential safety-related delays.
options.rationale: A proactive risk assessment at initiation would have identified potential safety-requirement changes and allowed them to be communicated and planned for.

options.text: Request additional resources and personnel to address safety concerns as they arise.
options.rationale: Extra resources address symptoms as they arise, not foresight and communication of risks.

questions.explanation: Surprises for stakeholders often come from risks that were never identified. Proactive risk assessment early in the project lets potential disruptions be communicated and planned for before they occur.
questions.mindset: Identify risks early so stakeholders are never surprised by them.

questions.stem: A project manager working in an agile environment realizes that some new team members are having difficulty understanding how more senior team members accomplished certain results on the project. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Arrange a review meeting with stakeholders.
options.rationale: A stakeholder review meeting does not transfer know-how between team members.

options.text: Ensure team members focus on their tasks.
options.rationale: Telling people to focus on their tasks ignores the knowledge gap that is holding them back.

options.text: Assess the need for knowledge transfer.
options.rationale: The need for knowledge transfer is already evident; assessing it again delays action.

options.text: Encourage and facilitate peer mentoring.
options.rationale: Peer mentoring lets experienced members pass on tacit know-how directly and builds collaboration.

questions.explanation: Much project knowledge is tacit — how things were achieved rather than what was done. Peer mentoring and pairing transfer that knowledge effectively within agile teams.
questions.mindset: Move tacit knowledge through people, not just documents.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a hybrid project. Several team members recently exited the project, including the only individual with a specific critical skill. At the beginning of a new sprint, the project manager identifies a task requiring this missing skill. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Rescope the project to remove the task requiring the missing skill.
options.rationale: Rescoping to remove the task is a drastic step before knowing how important the task is or whether the skill can be sourced.

options.text: Assess the impact of the missing skill on the project.
options.rationale: Assessing the impact of the missing skill defines the options — internal cover, external help, re-sequencing — before choosing one.

options.text: Postpone the task until a replacement is recruited.
options.rationale: Postponing the task may block dependent work and assumes a recruit will arrive in time.

options.text: Reassign the task to another project team with the necessary skills.
options.rationale: Moving the task to another team may not be feasible and should follow an impact assessment.

questions.explanation: Before responding to a lost capability, understand its impact: which work depends on it, how soon it is needed and what options exist. The response then fits the real size of the problem.
questions.mindset: Assess the impact before choosing the remedy.

questions.stem: A project manager realizes that the team needs training on a specific technology that is required in the project. What should the project manager do to mitigate this risk?

options.text: Assess the team's knowledge of the technology and look for recommended training options.
options.rationale: Assessing current knowledge and finding suitable training closes the specific gap and mitigates the risk proactively.

options.text: Contract with an expert provider to do the piece of work that uses that specific technology.
options.rationale: Outsourcing the work may be an option but does not build the team's capability and adds procurement risk.

options.text: Create an item in the risk log and notify the sponsor.
options.rationale: Logging and notifying records the risk but does not reduce it.

options.text: Fix any training gaps as they arise during the project.
options.rationale: Fixing gaps as they arise is reactive and allows avoidable problems to occur.

questions.explanation: Skill-gap risks are mitigated by acting early: assess what the team knows, then target training to the gap. Reactive or purely administrative responses leave the risk in place.
questions.mindset: Mitigate a known skills risk proactively rather than reacting later.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned to a long-term project with a duration of three years. Which approach should the project manager take to address near-term activities, while long-term work is planned at a high level and detailed later?

options.text: Focus on acquiring a team and deliver as soon as possible.
options.rationale: Delivering as soon as possible without planning is not an approach to managing near- and long-term work.

options.text: Engage the sponsor in the validation and prioritization processes.
options.rationale: Engaging the sponsor in prioritisation is valuable but is not a planning technique for this situation.

options.text: Perform workshops with the client for delivery dates.
options.rationale: Workshops about delivery dates do not create a way to plan near-term detail while deferring long-term detail.

options.text: Validate the requirements and perform rolling wave planning.
options.rationale: Rolling wave planning details near-term work and keeps later work at a high level to be elaborated as information improves.

questions.explanation: Long projects cannot be planned in full detail up front without much of it becoming obsolete. Rolling wave planning — a form of progressive elaboration — details the near term and refines later work as information emerges.
questions.mindset: Plan near work in detail and far work at a level you can honestly know.

questions.stem: A project manager has just taken over an ongoing project. The previous project manager resigned from the organization. During a review of the project documentation, the project manager realizes there are major deviations in the procurement process used by the previous project manager to engage service providers currently working on the project. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Call the previous project manager to understand the rationale for the abnormal procurement process.
options.rationale: Contacting the former PM may be useful later, but a major compliance deviation needs to be reported first, not investigated privately.

options.text: Contact the service providers to discuss the deviation and demand that they resolve the issue.
options.rationale: Demanding that suppliers fix a process the buyer's PM deviated from is unfair and may breach contracts.

options.text: Report the service providers and the previous project manager to the ethics committee of the organization.
options.rationale: Reporting individuals to the ethics committee assumes wrongdoing before the facts are established.

options.text: Flag the abnormal procurement process as a critical issue for the attention of senior management.
options.rationale: Major deviations from procurement policy have legal and regulatory implications; flagging them to senior management ensures they are handled properly.

questions.explanation: Procurement is governed by policy and law. When a new project manager finds major deviations, they should raise the issue through the organisation's governance channels promptly, rather than investigating alone or accusing individuals.
questions.mindset: Raise compliance deviations through governance promptly and without prejudging.

questions.stem: A project manager just started managing agile projects. The project manager realizes that due to the lack of a clear definition of project objectives and definition of done (DoD), their colleague's projects have had many difficulties. Sponsors keep asking for more features and the project is yet to be completed. What should the project manager do to avoid these issues?

options.text: Arrange meetings to ensure every task to complete the project is included in the project management plan.
options.rationale: Listing every task in the plan is a predictive approach and does not define objectives or completion criteria for agile work.

options.text: Convince the project sponsor to incorporate quality experts so the product can be tested and accepted as completed.
options.rationale: Quality experts can test, but they do not define the objectives and 'done' criteria that are missing.

options.text: Convince the product owner to approach the team and define project objectives.
options.rationale: The product owner has a role, but the problem needs agreement among key stakeholders, not one person defining objectives.

options.text: Schedule meetings with key stakeholders to build the agile project charter and set clear expectations for the project.
options.rationale: An agile charter built with key stakeholders sets clear objectives and expectations, including what done looks like, preventing endless feature requests.

questions.explanation: Agile projects still need a shared understanding of purpose, objectives and completion criteria. An agile project charter created collaboratively sets those expectations and gives a basis for saying when the project is done.
questions.mindset: Agree what success and done look like before the work begins.

questions.stem: An agile project team has been successfully releasing updated deliverables each sprint that consistently provide an increased value to users. However, the project is running over the initially allocated budget, and there are still many items in the project backlog. Stakeholders have expressed increasing concerns, and the project manager needs to decide on the best course of action to address the situation and manage stakeholder expectations. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Measure user satisfaction and present the results to the steering committee.
options.rationale: Measuring user satisfaction and presenting it shows the value delivered, so the steering committee can make an informed decision on further investment.

options.text: Remove the deliverables from the backlog that were not part of the project charter.
options.rationale: Removing items not in the charter may be valid, but it does not address concerns about budget versus value.

options.text: Request additional budget based on an updated estimation of the remaining backlog items.
options.rationale: Asking for more budget before demonstrating value gives the committee no basis for the decision.

options.text: Emphasize the expectation that the committed work must be finished on time.
options.rationale: Insisting committed work is finished on time ignores the budget concern and value trade-offs.

questions.explanation: When an agile project exceeds its budget but continues to deliver value, stakeholders need evidence of that value to decide whether to fund more. Measured user outcomes let governance weigh value against cost.
questions.mindset: Give decision-makers evidence of value, not just cost.

questions.stem: During the daily standup meeting, one of the team members informs the team that a user story that was initially part of the sprint planning has become invalid due to a recently announced policy change. What should the project manager do in response to this situation?

options.text: Close the user story related to the policy change and explain that it is no longer valid.
options.rationale: A story made invalid by a policy change no longer has value; closing it with an explanation keeps the sprint backlog accurate and stops wasted effort.

options.text: Remove the user story from the current sprint and schedule it for the next sprint.
options.rationale: Moving an invalid story to the next sprint carries work forward that no longer has any value.

options.text: Notify the stakeholders that user stories committed for a sprint cannot be modified.
options.rationale: Committed stories can be adjusted when they lose their value; refusing to change anything ignores reality.

options.text: Remove the user story from the sprint and ask the team to expedite the completion of the current sprint.
options.rationale: Removing the story is right, but asking the team to rush the rest of the sprint adds pressure for no reason.

questions.explanation: External changes can remove the value of planned work. When a story becomes invalid, it should be removed from the backlog rather than deferred, and the reason explained so the team and stakeholders understand the change.
questions.mindset: Drop work whose value has disappeared rather than carrying it forward.

questions.stem: A project is delivering incremental business value to a customer. The success criteria for the project is a 20% increase in market share for the customer. When should the project be considered a success?

options.text: When the sprint reviews demonstrate that each iteration delivers a 20% increase in market share.
options.rationale: A single sprint cannot deliver a 20% market-share gain; that is a business outcome of the whole product, not an iteration target.

options.text: After the project documentation is completed and the project team has been assigned to other projects.
options.rationale: Completed documentation and reassigned staff mark administrative closure, not achievement of the success criterion.

options.text: At the conclusion of project execution, as part of the project closure report approval process.
options.rationale: Success against a business metric is confirmed when the outcome is assessed at the end of execution as part of the closure approval.

options.text: When 75% of the project has been completed and the Earned Value Management (EVM) diagram indicates that the value is on track.
options.rationale: Earned value measures work performed against plan; it says nothing about the customer's market share.

questions.explanation: Project success is judged against the success criteria agreed at the outset. When they are business outcomes such as market share, they are confirmed through closure evaluation of the results, not through progress metrics or administrative milestones.
questions.mindset: Judge success by the agreed outcome measure, not by activity completed.

questions.stem: A project manager for a building project has been informed that a required permit from the local government has not yet been obtained. Applying for the permit will delay project delivery by 21 days at a cost of US$40,000. The fine for not having the permit in place is US$1,900 a day. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Apply for the permit and delay project delivery by 21 days.
options.rationale: Obtaining the required permit keeps the project legal. A 21-day delay is the price of compliance, and the fines would exceed the cost anyway.

options.text: Ignore the permit requirement and continue with the project.
options.rationale: Ignoring a legal requirement is unethical and exposes the organisation to fines and possible shutdown.

options.text: Attempt to negotiate with the local government for a pardon.
options.rationale: Seeking a pardon for not holding a mandatory permit is not a legitimate or reliable strategy.

options.text: Allocate the fine amount as an additional project expense.
options.rationale: Budgeting for fines treats breaking the law as a cost of doing business, which is unacceptable.

questions.explanation: Legal and regulatory requirements are not optional trade-offs to be priced against schedule. The project must comply and plan around the delay; deliberately incurring penalties is both unethical and usually more expensive.
questions.mindset: Comply with the law and plan around the consequences.

questions.stem: A project manager is working in a regulated industry, and the team is working on a project where the requirements are prioritized in a backlog. The minimum viable product (MVP) for the launch has been defined. The project manager learns the regulatory body for the project requires a prototype for inspection before that product can be launched. The prototype is not part of the MVP definition. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Speak with the product owner to prioritize compliance activities in the backlog to submit a prototype to the regulatory body.
options.rationale: The product owner owns backlog priority. Working with them to prioritise compliance work ensures the prototype needed for launch approval is built in time.

options.text: Identify the missing requirements, prioritize the missing regulatory work directly into the backlog, and assign the work to the team.
options.rationale: Adding work to the backlog and assigning it directly bypasses the product owner's role and the team's self-organisation.

options.text: Reschedule the launch of the product until the team can produce a prototype for inspection, as required by the regulatory body.
options.rationale: Rescheduling the launch assumes the work cannot be absorbed; prioritisation may deliver the prototype without delay.

options.text: Create a new MVP definition that contains the scope requirements for the required prototype and prioritize that scope with the team.
options.rationale: Redefining the MVP is not necessary; the prototype is a compliance requirement for launch, which can be prioritised in the backlog.

questions.explanation: Regulatory requirements are part of what makes a product releasable. In agile delivery they enter the backlog through the product owner and are prioritised so that compliance work is done before the release it gates.
questions.mindset: Treat compliance work as release-gating backlog items, prioritised by the product owner.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a project to deliver a new product in a heavily regulated industry and must prioritize quality management practices. The project manager is considering the management of quality improvements. What should the project manager emphasize to ensure focus on managing quality improvements?

options.text: Prioritize rapid product release and analyze consumer feedback to identify and execute the necessary quality improvements.
options.rationale: Releasing quickly and learning from consumer feedback is risky where regulation demands quality before release.

options.text: Implement a strategy of frequent quality audits and product defect tracking to identify and address any quality issues.
options.rationale: Audits and defect tracking are useful but reactive; without defined targets there is nothing clear to improve against.

options.text: Streamline quality and compliance practices by delegating responsibility for quality control to a designated team member.
options.rationale: Delegating quality to one person fragments responsibility; quality is managed by the whole project.

options.text: Establish clear quality metrics and targets for each project stage to ensure compliance with regulatory quality standards.
options.rationale: Clear quality metrics and targets per stage provide a proactive, measurable framework that supports regulatory compliance and targeted improvement.

questions.explanation: Managing quality improvement requires knowing what good looks like. Defining quality metrics and targets for each stage makes quality measurable, highlights where improvement is needed and supports regulatory compliance.
questions.mindset: Define what quality means before trying to improve it.

questions.stem: A project manager has been working on an internal project for the organization's project management office (PMO). The project was initially sponsored by a PMO leader who has since been replaced. The new leader does not see much value in the project. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Organize a second project kick-off meeting with the new PMO leader and the project team.
options.rationale: A second kick-off revisits the start rather than showing the new leader what the project is delivering.

options.text: Use the previous data to obtain sponsorship from the new PMO leader because the project was effective.
options.rationale: Previous data may help, but the strongest evidence is the benefit tracking that shows value delivered so far.

options.text: Use the benefits that the project manager has been tracking throughout the project to prove the project's value.
options.rationale: Tracked benefits demonstrate the project's value in concrete terms and give the new leader a reason to support it.

options.text: Continue the project as planned because it has already been approved and is in progress.
options.rationale: Continuing without engaging the new leader ignores a sponsor who could withdraw support.

questions.explanation: A change of sponsor is a change of key stakeholder. The project manager engages the new sponsor with evidence of value — tracked benefits — to secure support, rather than assuming the previous endorsement still applies.
questions.mindset: Win a new sponsor with evidence of value delivered.

questions.stem: During a design workshop for a new robot, the engineers ask the project manager about safety and environmental protocols for its operating procedures. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Hire a specialized engineer to support the design team.
options.rationale: Hiring a specialist is expensive and premature when the organisation's own policies may already answer the question.

options.text: Provide the team with the organizational process assets and the project charter.
options.rationale: Organisational process assets and the charter contain the policies and requirements that set safety and environmental expectations for the design.

options.text: Look into lessons learned documentation for similar projects.
options.rationale: Lessons learned may help, but they are experience, not the authoritative policies the team must follow.

options.text: Run a benchmark with similar plants to capture their compliance constraints.
options.rationale: Benchmarking other plants is time-consuming and may not reflect this organisation's own requirements.

questions.explanation: Organisational process assets hold the policies, procedures and standards that projects must apply. When a team asks about required protocols, the first source is the organisation's own assets and the project's authorising documents.
questions.mindset: Use the organisation's own standards before looking elsewhere.

questions.stem: During a project planning session, the project manager is trying to define a release plan to achieve consistent value delivery and customer buy-in. A senior stakeholder suggests having a release at the end of the project to make sure the customer sees all of the product features at once. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the project team to propose a release schedule based on the complexity of specific product features.
options.rationale: Basing releases on complexity alone ignores value and customer feedback.

options.text: Recommend three releases with one at the beginning, one in the middle, and one at the end of the project.
options.rationale: Three fixed releases is arbitrary and still limits feedback.

options.text: Create release plans for each time a product feature is delivered to conduct quality testing and reviews.
options.rationale: Releasing each feature for testing is about quality checks, not value delivery and customer buy-in.

options.text: Propose that the product be delivered over the course of multiple iterations to gather customer feedback.
options.rationale: Delivering over multiple iterations provides value early and gathers feedback continuously, building customer buy-in.

questions.explanation: Consistent value delivery comes from frequent increments that customers can use and comment on. A single big-bang release delays value and feedback, increasing the risk of building the wrong thing.
questions.mindset: Deliver value in increments so feedback shapes what comes next.

questions.stem: After nine months, a project concludes its first phase with the release of a new product to the customer. The client is dissatisfied and states that many key features are missing. What should the project manager do first in order to address this issue?

options.text: Evaluate the missing features with the client and develop a plan to include them in the next nine-month project phase.
options.rationale: Planning to add the features in the next phase assumes they were in scope and that the client's view is accurate.

options.text: Review the project plan to determine if the missing features were part of the original scope or if they were added later.
options.rationale: Checking the scope baseline establishes whether the features were agreed or requested later, which determines the right response.

options.text: Request additional funding in order to reduce the current release cycle timeline so the team can deliver value sooner.
options.rationale: Extra funding to speed releases ignores the question of whether features were missed or never agreed.

options.text: Restart the project by implementing an agile life cycle and incorporate the creation of a minimum viable product (MVP).
options.rationale: Restarting with agile is a drastic reaction before the cause is known.

questions.explanation: When a customer says features are missing, the first step is to compare the complaint with the agreed scope. That tells you whether this is a delivery failure, an unmanaged change or a misunderstanding, each of which needs a different response.
questions.mindset: Check the baseline before accepting or rejecting a claim of missing scope.

questions.stem: An organization has a policy requiring all project managers to conduct a standardized audit of another project manager's project once a month. After an audit review, team members complained that the auditor was not fairly reviewing their deliverables. The project manager reviewed the audit results and agreed with the findings. What should the project manager do to address this situation?

options.text: Request that mandatory audits be conducted less frequently.
options.rationale: Reducing audit frequency undermines a standard organisational control because of a complaint the PM does not agree with.

options.text: Use status meetings to review deliverables instead of formal audits.
options.rationale: Replacing audits with status meetings removes an independent quality check.

options.text: Explain that audits are conducted based on standardized measures.
options.rationale: Explaining that audits use standard measures addresses the team's perception of unfairness while upholding the control.

options.text: Report the project manager who conducted the unfair audit.
options.rationale: Reporting the auditor would be unfair; the PM has reviewed and agrees with the findings.

questions.explanation: Quality audits provide independent assurance using consistent criteria. When a team perceives unfairness but the findings are sound, the project manager explains the standardised basis of the audit and uses the findings for improvement.
questions.mindset: Support sound controls and help the team understand them.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on launching a minimum viable product (MVP) for a new-to-market product. The team has successfully progressed to the third iteration out of a planned total of six. During the upcoming iteration planning meeting, the customer notifies the team that a competitor intends to beat them to market and release a similar product in the next quarter. How should the project manager address this competitive challenge?

options.text: Acknowledge the issue and include comprehensive details in the project's next status report.
options.rationale: Reporting the issue without acting wastes the time available to respond.

options.text: Increase the size of the team to expedite product delivery and launch the product before the competitor.
options.rationale: Adding people late often slows teams down and is not the most direct response.

options.text: Meet with the customer to discuss reducing the project backlog to help accelerate product delivery.
options.rationale: Cutting backlog items with the customer helps, but redefining the MVP around core differentiating features is a more focused response.

options.text: Work with the team to prioritize core features and redefine the MVP to beat the competitor to the market.
options.rationale: Refocusing the MVP on core features lets the team reach the market before the competitor with the most important value.

questions.explanation: When market conditions change, the MVP should change with them. Reprioritising the backlog and redefining the minimum set of features lets the team release sooner while still delivering the core value.
questions.mindset: Let market reality redefine what is minimum and viable.

questions.stem: In a project where a third-party provider is implementing a custom solution, the project manager must ensure that the local team will have the capacity to support the solution. What should the project manager do to ensure that the local team can support the solution?

options.text: Delegate the responsibility of supporting the custom solution to the third-party provider.
options.rationale: Delegating support to the provider creates an ongoing dependency instead of building local capability.

options.text: Conduct comprehensive training sessions for the local team on the new solution.
options.rationale: Training the local team equips them to support the solution after handover.

options.text: Reduce the responsibilities of the local team to minimize the need for support.
options.rationale: Reducing the local team's responsibilities avoids the capability issue rather than solving it.

options.text: Hire additional personnel to provide ongoing support for the local team.
options.rationale: Hiring more people does not give anyone the knowledge needed to support the custom solution.

questions.explanation: Operational readiness requires the receiving team to have the knowledge to support what is delivered. Training and knowledge transfer from the provider are planned project work, not an afterthought.
questions.mindset: Build the receiving team's capability before handing over.

questions.stem: During the planning phase, a project manager is creating the project schedule. The designated project team is finishing an unrelated project, so temporary resources are assigned to assist with planning and task duration estimation. The project team will replace the temporary resources prior to starting the project. What should the project manager do before the project schedule is finalized?

options.text: Review the estimates with the designated team.
options.rationale: Reviewing estimates with the people who will do the work tests their realism and builds commitment.

options.text: Check the task durations of previous projects.
options.rationale: Historical durations can inform estimates but do not reflect this team's skills.

options.text: Update duration estimation in the risk register.
options.rationale: The risk register records risks; it is not where duration estimates are validated.

options.text: Request approval from the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Sponsor approval of a schedule with unvalidated estimates would lock in inaccurate numbers.

questions.explanation: Estimates are most accurate and most owned when made or validated by the people doing the work. If temporary staff estimated, the designated team should review the estimates before the schedule is finalised.
questions.mindset: Have the people doing the work validate the estimates.

questions.stem: A project manager is in the execution phase of a project. A newly identified stakeholder continuously bypasses the project manager to get feedback from the project sponsor directly, thus escalating pressure and frustration for all members of the team. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Call a project meeting of all stakeholders to discuss the matter and develop a suitable action plan.
options.rationale: Calling everyone together to discuss one stakeholder's behaviour is disproportionate and may embarrass them.

options.text: Email the communications management plan to the stakeholder and point out that they agreed to the plan.
options.rationale: Sending the plan with a reminder is confrontational, and a newly identified stakeholder never agreed to it.

options.text: Meet the project sponsor and confirm that the project manager must be the single point of contact.
options.rationale: Asking the sponsor to enforce a single point of contact treats the symptom and ignores the stakeholder's unmet needs.

options.text: Meet with the stakeholder to understand their needs and update the communication management plan.
options.rationale: Meeting the new stakeholder to understand their needs and updating the communication plan addresses why they are going around the PM.

questions.explanation: A stakeholder who bypasses the project manager usually has needs the current plan does not meet. Engaging them to understand those needs and updating the communication approach fixes the cause.
questions.mindset: When stakeholders go around you, find out what they are not getting from you.

questions.stem: A dispersed project team has been working together on a long-term development project. The team just finished an iteration when a new team member was onboarded and added to the project team. During their first virtual retrospective meeting, the newly onboarded team member interrupts and asks everyone to reiterate their roles and past work in previous iterations. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Direct the new team member to review the project management plan after the meeting.
options.rationale: Pointing the new member to the plan is dismissive and does not help them understand the team's work.

options.text: Inform the team member that this question would be best addressed in another meeting.
options.rationale: A retrospective is not the right forum for onboarding; addressing the questions separately keeps the meeting focused and still supports the new member.

options.text: Ask each team member to explain their role and what they worked on in past iterations.
options.rationale: Having everyone recount past work derails the retrospective from its purpose.

options.text: Ask the functional manager of the new team member to review the onboarding process.
options.rationale: Involving the functional manager escalates a simple onboarding need.

questions.explanation: Each meeting has a purpose. Onboarding questions deserve an answer, but in a forum suited to them, so retrospectives can stay focused on improving how the team works.
questions.mindset: Honour the need, but in the right forum.

questions.stem: A project manager has identified that a task on the critical path is behind schedule. The project manager thinks that additional resources will help, but higher management declined a request for the additional funding necessary to add resources. The project manager must work with the approved resources and budget. What would be the best-suited practice for the project manager to address this situation?

options.text: Resource leveling
options.rationale: Resource levelling usually lengthens the schedule and does not recover a critical path delay.

options.text: Crashing
options.rationale: Crashing adds resources and cost, which management has refused.

options.text: Fast tracking
options.rationale: Fast-tracking performs activities in parallel, compressing the schedule without extra resources or budget.

options.text: What-if scenario analysis
options.rationale: What-if analysis models scenarios but does not recover the schedule.

questions.explanation: Schedule compression has two main techniques: crashing adds resources at extra cost, while fast-tracking overlaps activities at the price of extra risk. When no additional funding is available, fast-tracking is the tool to use.
questions.mindset: Choose the compression technique that fits your constraints.

questions.stem: In the middle of an iteration for the development of a project deliverable, a team member suggests a new method of doing the work. The method may require several days of work to implement, but it may help the team work more efficiently. How should the project manager respond to the suggestion?

options.text: Immediately implement the suggested change to improve team efficiency without consulting the team.
options.rationale: Implementing a change without team discussion disrupts the iteration and ignores team ownership of its process.

options.text: Reject the suggestion as it provides no value to the customer and is not aligned with the project's goals.
options.rationale: Rejecting a potential efficiency gain outright discourages improvement ideas.

options.text: Document the idea for future consideration but continue with the current iteration without making any changes.
options.rationale: Documenting the idea is safe, but deferring without assessment may leave a real improvement on the table.

options.text: Acknowledge the suggestion and assess the new method and the potential impact on team efficiency.
options.rationale: Acknowledging and assessing the idea respects the contributor and allows an informed decision about when and whether to adopt it.

questions.explanation: Improvement ideas from the team are valuable and should be assessed rather than dismissed or imposed. Evaluating benefit, cost and timing allows good ideas to be adopted at an appropriate point without disrupting commitments.
questions.mindset: Welcome improvement ideas and assess them before deciding.

questions.stem: A project manager is newly assigned to an ongoing project and determines that the quality has been consistent. There is a considerable budget for quality assurance, and other areas of the project could benefit from these funds. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Implement a budget reduction strategy to reallocate funds.
options.rationale: Reallocating quality funds before understanding why quality is consistent could remove the very effort that keeps it so.

options.text: Perform a full inspection since there is no margin for error.
options.rationale: Full inspection is expensive and unnecessary when quality is already consistent.

options.text: Introduce sampling as a cost-effective way to ensure quality.
options.rationale: Sampling may eventually be appropriate, but changing the approach immediately is premature for a newly assigned PM.

options.text: Keep the budget intact for now and continue monitoring.
options.rationale: Consistent quality may be the result of the current spend. Keeping the budget and monitoring lets the new PM understand the process before changing it.

questions.explanation: Consistent quality is often the product of the prevention and appraisal work being paid for. A new project manager should understand the quality system before cutting it; otherwise costs saved now reappear as failure costs later.
questions.mindset: Understand why something works before cutting its funding.

questions.stem: A project manager assigned to an existing project finds that the deliverable quality has been inconsistent. The project manager finds that the team is not adhering to the development standards. What practice should the project manager employ to ensure higher quality?

options.text: Perform a full inspection since there is no margin for error.
options.rationale: Full inspection is costly and finds defects after the fact rather than fixing the process causing them.

options.text: Introduce sampling as a cost-effective and time-efficient way to ensure quality.
options.rationale: Sampling measures quality; it does not correct non-adherence to standards.

options.text: Implement a continuous improvement process to ensure consistent outcomes.
options.rationale: A continuous improvement process addresses the cause — poor adherence to standards — and raises consistency over time.

options.text: Add a unit of work for a specific period of time to prove the solution is viable.
options.rationale: A spike proves a solution, which is not what is needed; the standards already exist.

questions.explanation: Inconsistent quality caused by poor adherence to standards is a process problem. Continuous improvement fixes the process and embeds the standards, while inspection only catches defects after they are made.
questions.mindset: Improve the process rather than inspecting harder.

questions.stem: A project manager is developing a project budget. After estimating the cost of each activity, the manager adds a contingency reserve by increasing the estimated cost of all activities by the same percentage. However, this resulted in the total cost exceeding the allocated budget even before adding the management reserve. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Request additional budget to ensure that all cost estimations are appropriately funded.
options.rationale: Asking for more budget legitimises an estimation method that has no basis in actual risk.

options.text: Reduce the percentage increase to reduce the total cost of the project.
options.rationale: Lowering an arbitrary percentage is still arbitrary.

options.text: Recalculate the contingency reserve based on identified risks and response strategies.
options.rationale: Contingency reserves should be sized from identified risks and planned responses, which gives a defensible figure.

options.text: Allocate a portion of the contingency reserve to the management reserve.
options.rationale: Moving contingency into management reserve confuses two different reserves and their governance.

questions.explanation: Contingency reserve covers identified risks — the known unknowns — and should be derived from risk analysis. Across-the-board percentage padding hides uncertainty and inflates the budget without justification.
questions.mindset: Size contingency from the risks, not from a flat percentage.

questions.stem: A project manager for a delivery project has engaged a vendor to provide testing services. Which items should the project manager be sure to provide to the vendor before the testing starts?

options.text: Test plan and requirements traceability matrix.
options.rationale: The test plan sets scope and approach, and the requirements traceability matrix links requirements to tests, together giving the vendor what it needs to test everything required.

options.text: Test plan and quality risk assessment.
options.rationale: A quality risk assessment helps, but without traceability the vendor cannot confirm coverage of all requirements.

options.text: Defect reports and test scripts.
options.rationale: Defect reports come from testing, so they cannot exist before it starts.

options.text: Requirements traceability matrix and defect reports.
options.rationale: Defect reports are a testing output, not an input.
