questions.explanation: An external testing provider needs to know what to test and how. The test plan defines the approach, and the requirements traceability matrix ensures every requirement is covered; defect reports only exist once testing has begun.
questions.mindset: Give suppliers the inputs that define the work, not the outputs they will produce.

questions.stem: The quality management plan (QMP) calls for regression testing before each product release, but these tests were not included in the work breakdown structure (WBS). What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Submit a change request to add regression testing work packages to the project scope.
options.rationale: The WBS must include all work, including regression testing required by the quality plan. A change request corrects the scope baseline.

options.text: Request extra test resources from the quality assurance functional manager.
options.rationale: Requesting resources before the work is in scope puts the cart before the horse.

options.text: Suggest to the project client that regression testing be removed from the quality requirements.
options.rationale: Removing required regression testing to fix a WBS omission lowers quality to hide a planning gap.

options.text: Seek approval from the project sponsor to remove regression testing from the QMP.
options.rationale: Changing the QMP to match an incomplete WBS resolves the inconsistency in the wrong direction.

questions.explanation: The WBS should contain all the work needed, including quality activities. When a gap is found, the scope baseline is corrected through change control, rather than dropping required work to match an incomplete plan.
questions.mindset: Fix the plan to include required work; do not drop work to fit the plan.

questions.stem: A team member who is unfamiliar with the subject matter is struggling to complete a complex deliverable. What should the agile project manager do to ensure that the team member is able to take on a similar challenge in the future?

options.text: Ensure that the team member receives adequate training and is comfortable with the subject matter.
options.rationale: Training addresses the specific knowledge gap and prepares the team member for similar challenges in future.

options.text: Encourage the team member to take on more stories on this subject matter until they are completely comfortable.
options.rationale: Giving someone more work they are struggling with, without support, risks quality and morale.

options.text: Ask the team member to avoid taking on stories on this subject matter until the person is comfortable with the subject matter.
options.rationale: Avoiding the subject keeps the gap in place and creates dependency on others.

options.text: Replace the team member with a more experienced team member who will improve the team's velocity.
options.rationale: Replacing the person gives up on their development and damages team trust.

questions.explanation: When a team member struggles because of unfamiliar subject matter, targeted training builds lasting capability. Avoidance or replacement leaves the team less resilient.
questions.mindset: Grow capability rather than working around gaps.

questions.stem: A project manager is working with remote team members who are acting independently. What should the project manager do to promote collaboration among team members?

options.text: Include the team members in all emails regarding the project.
options.rationale: Copying everyone on email increases noise without creating collaboration.

options.text: Call team members individually to collect information and provide updates weekly.
options.rationale: Individual calls route everything through the PM and keep team members isolated.

options.text: Promote regular meetings using video conferencing.
options.rationale: Regular video meetings bring remote members together and build the collaboration they currently lack.

options.text: Ask each team member to fill out a task log for daily updates.
options.rationale: Daily task logs are reporting, not collaboration.

questions.explanation: Collaboration requires interaction between team members, not just information flowing to the PM. Regular face-to-face time, even virtually, builds relationships that encourage people to work together.
questions.mindset: Create shared interaction, not just shared information.

questions.stem: A project manager is assembling a team with a mix of new and experienced team members. The project manager finds out that there are issues with team cohesion. The experienced team members believe new team members lack the technical skills required to perform the necessary work and expect that they will have to compensate for their inexperience. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Offer bonuses or other incentives to experienced team members to mentor the new team members.
options.rationale: Paying experienced members to mentor assumes the new members are the problem and may reinforce resentment.

options.text: Analyze the skills of all team members, identify gaps, and develop plans to address them.
options.rationale: Assessing everyone's skills objectively identifies real gaps and replaces assumptions with facts and development plans.

options.text: Reassign new team members to projects that better align with their skills and experience.
options.rationale: Reassigning the new members accepts an untested assumption about their skills.

options.text: Explain that professional project team members are expected to resolve issues without intervention.
options.rationale: Telling professionals to sort it out themselves abdicates the PM's role in building the team.

questions.explanation: Assumptions about competence damage cohesion. An objective skills assessment of the whole team replaces perception with evidence and enables targeted development, which both closes real gaps and builds trust.
questions.mindset: Replace assumptions about skills with an assessment.

questions.stem: A project manager is not sure if the team has the critical skills needed to implement a key feature of an upcoming deliverable. In order to mitigate the risk of sprint failure, what should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask for support from the sponsor to replace the low performers with new team members with a specific skill set.
options.rationale: Replacing people before confirming a gap exists is premature and labels team members as low performers without evidence.

options.text: Negotiate with the stakeholder to postpone this key feature to a later release while figuring out a better alternative.
options.rationale: Postponing a key feature trades value for a risk that may be manageable within the team.

options.text: Identify the potential skill gap and propose a strategy to address the gaps with training, mentoring, or coaching.
options.rationale: Identifying the specific gap and addressing it with training, mentoring or coaching mitigates the risk while developing the team.

options.text: Embrace the risk, accept the sprint failure, and try to motivate the team toward better performance in the future.
options.rationale: Accepting a foreseeable sprint failure gives up on a risk that can be mitigated.

questions.explanation: A suspected skills gap is a risk to be confirmed and mitigated. Servant leaders identify the gap precisely and close it through development — training, mentoring, pairing — so that the team is stronger for the next challenge too.
questions.mindset: Close skill gaps by developing people, not by replacing them.

questions.stem: As part of a project deliverable, a project manager demonstrates how to use one of the products to a subset of a client's employees through a 30-minute virtual conference call. The client's employees complain that a two-day workshop would have been more effective for training. What should the project manager have done to prevent this complaint?

options.text: Assessed the training needs of the client's employees.
options.rationale: Assessing the employees' training needs would have shown what format and depth they required before the session was designed.

options.text: Included this risk in the risk management plan.
options.rationale: Recording a risk does not reveal what training the users need.

options.text: Provided a contingency reserve for additional training.
options.rationale: Contingency funding pays for a fix after the complaint rather than preventing it.

options.text: Developed an asynchronous training plan.
options.rationale: An asynchronous plan is another format chosen without knowing what the users need.

questions.explanation: Training that does not match its audience fails regardless of quality. Assessing learners' existing knowledge, the product's complexity and the desired outcomes lets the training be designed to meet customer expectations.
questions.mindset: Design training around the learners' needs, assessed up front.

questions.stem: In a review meeting, a project manager detects a misunderstanding about one critical deliverable. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Ask the team members to clarify the deliverable.
options.rationale: The team is building the deliverable; getting them to explain their understanding reveals exactly where it diverges.

options.text: Ask the customer to clarify the deliverable.
options.rationale: Going straight to the customer is premature before knowing what the team has misunderstood.

options.text: Ask the product owner to clarify the deliverable.
options.rationale: The product owner may need to be involved, but first the PM needs to find out how the team understands the deliverable.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to clarify the deliverable.
options.rationale: The sponsor is too far from deliverable detail to be the first point of clarification.

questions.explanation: When a misunderstanding surfaces, the first step is to make everyone's interpretation explicit. Asking the team to describe the deliverable pinpoints the gap, which can then be resolved with the right authority if needed.
questions.mindset: Surface the misunderstanding before seeking a ruling on it.

questions.stem: A project manager has been assigned to a new project with multiple high-level stakeholders. Each stakeholder has provided their expectations for the project, and the project manager realizes some expectations conflict. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Facilitate a meeting to address and resolve conflicting expectations.
options.rationale: A facilitated meeting brings the conflicting expectations into the open so stakeholders can work toward agreement.

options.text: Prioritize the expectations of stakeholders with the highest authority.
options.rationale: Deferring to authority leaves other stakeholders unheard and the conflict unresolved.

options.text: Update the stakeholder register with the stakeholders' expectations.
options.rationale: Updating the register records the conflict but does not resolve it.

options.text: Create a project hierarchy to manage the stakeholders' expectations.
options.rationale: A hierarchy for managing expectations is not a recognised practice and does not resolve the conflict.

questions.explanation: Conflicting stakeholder expectations are best resolved collaboratively. Neutral facilitation helps stakeholders understand each other's needs and reach decisions they can support, which lasts longer than an imposed priority.
questions.mindset: Bring conflicting expectations together and facilitate toward agreement.

questions.stem: A project manager has been assigned a project that involves a virtual, multicultural team including representatives from various countries. The project manager needs to prepare a kickoff meeting. What should the project manager do to prepare for the meeting?

options.text: Set rules and regulations that must be followed during the project.
options.rationale: Imposing rules up front before understanding the team's context may alienate members and ignore local constraints.

options.text: Ask the sponsor for different resources to facilitate the project.
options.rationale: Asking for different resources avoids working with the team as it is.

options.text: Consider various time zones, communication capabilities, and possible constraints.
options.rationale: Considering time zones, communication capabilities and constraints makes the kick-off accessible and inclusive for everyone.

options.text: Set up the project sponsor's language as the official project communication language.
options.rationale: Adopting the sponsor's language by default may exclude team members and ignores preferences.

questions.explanation: Preparing a kick-off for a virtual multicultural team means designing around its environment: time zones, technology, language and cultural norms. This gives everyone a fair chance to participate from day one.
questions.mindset: Design team events around the team's real constraints.

questions.stem: A senior team member is having challenges with a new project team member. The senior team member asks the project manager for advice on how to handle the new team member. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Check the team member's performance and responsibility assignment matrix to assess the conflict.
options.rationale: The RAM and performance data are not the issue; the senior member is asking how to handle a relationship.

options.text: Instruct the senior team member to confront the new team member at the next daily standup meeting.
options.rationale: Confronting someone in a public stand-up embarrasses them and escalates conflict.

options.text: Coach the senior team member on conflict resolution models and how they can be applied to this situation.
options.rationale: Coaching the senior member on conflict resolution approaches empowers them to address the situation directly and constructively.

options.text: Ask for a one-on-one meeting with the new team member and tell them to avoid the senior team member.
options.rationale: Telling the new member to avoid a colleague creates division and does not solve anything.

questions.explanation: When team members ask for help with interpersonal issues, coaching them to resolve the issue themselves builds their capability and keeps ownership with those involved. The PM intervenes directly only if that fails.
questions.mindset: Coach people to resolve their own conflicts before stepping in.

questions.stem: A project manager notices that conflicts between team members are occurring in every sprint. After an investigation, the project manager discovers that the team needs to be trained in agile techniques in order to address these conflicts. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Develop a training plan for the team.
options.rationale: A training plan needs to know which gaps to address; writing it first skips that step.

options.text: Schedule training sessions for the team.
options.rationale: Scheduling sessions before knowing what training is needed may target the wrong topics.

options.text: Conduct a training needs assessment for the team.
options.rationale: A training needs assessment identifies which agile techniques the team actually lacks, so training fixes the real cause of conflict.

options.text: Instruct the team to begin using agile techniques.
options.rationale: Telling the team to use techniques they do not know will not work and may increase conflict.

questions.explanation: Effective training starts with a needs assessment. Knowing precisely which skills are missing lets the training be targeted, which is more effective and less wasteful than generic sessions.
questions.mindset: Assess needs before prescribing training.

questions.stem: A stakeholder has suggested using an off-the-shelf, open-source product to speed up development. The team has analyzed the product and found it feasible and desirable, but it needs to be piloted and requires additional user skills. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Initiate a formal change request.
options.rationale: Adopting the product changes the approach, requires a pilot and new skills; a change request allows the impact to be evaluated and approved.

options.text: Request training for the project team.
options.rationale: Training may follow approval but is premature before the change is authorised.

options.text: Review the cost management plan.
options.rationale: The cost plan does not decide whether to adopt a new component; it is only one aspect of impact.

options.text: Consult the product manager.
options.rationale: Consulting the product manager alone does not authorise a change with project-wide impact.

questions.explanation: Adopting a new component with pilots and skill requirements changes the project's approach, schedule and costs. Such changes go through formal change control so impacts are understood and approved before implementation.
questions.mindset: Route approach-changing ideas through change control, however good they are.

questions.stem: A remote project team consists of members from two countries. One of the teams is expecting to have three days off to celebrate a national holiday. The project manager tells the team that they must work during the holiday to achieve a key deliverable of the current iteration. The team is disgruntled and does not understand why they have to work if it is a national holiday. What should the project manager have clearly defined and communicated at the beginning of the project to avoid this?

options.text: Team agreements
options.rationale: Team agreements set norms for working time, holidays and availability, preventing surprises like this.

options.text: Milestones
options.rationale: Milestones set deadlines but not how the team handles holidays.

options.text: Individual roles
options.rationale: Individual roles define responsibilities, not working norms.

options.text: Team hierarchy
options.rationale: A hierarchy says who reports to whom, not how the team will work together.

questions.explanation: Team agreements, created with the team at the start, capture working norms such as availability, public holidays and communication. They make expectations explicit and reduce conflict when commitments meet local customs.
questions.mindset: Agree working norms with the team before they are tested.

questions.stem: During product development, two functional departments indicate that they are short on resources and cannot build and deliver all the products on time. What should the project manager do to address this concern?

options.text: Escalate the issue to the sponsor and request confirmation of the project scope.
options.rationale: Asking the sponsor to confirm scope does not address the resource shortage.

options.text: Ask the functional manager to hire additional resources to meet the requirements.
options.rationale: Hiring more staff may be impossible and is the functional manager's call.

options.text: Request team members work extra hours to meet the commercial needs.
options.rationale: Extra hours are a short-term fix that risks burnout.

options.text: Analyze the critical path to deliver the minimum viable product (MVP).
options.rationale: Analysing what is needed for a minimum viable product focuses limited resources on delivering an acceptable outcome on time.

questions.explanation: When resources cannot cover the full scope in the time available, the MVP concept lets the project deliver the most valuable subset first. Reducing to the essential scope is more sustainable than overtime or waiting for extra resources.
questions.mindset: When resources are fixed, deliver the most valuable minimum first.

questions.stem: An agile team consistently delivers features on time but recently identified a significant architecture gap leading to rework. Which agile practice should the project manager use to address this issue?

options.text: Increment planning
options.rationale: Increment planning looks forward at scope, not back at why rework happened.

options.text: Team retrospective
options.rationale: The retrospective is where the team analyses root causes and agrees improvements to prevent the rework recurring.

options.text: Demonstration to stakeholders
options.rationale: Demos show increments to stakeholders; they do not diagnose internal technical gaps.

options.text: Daily standup
options.rationale: Stand-ups are for daily coordination and are too short for root-cause analysis.

questions.explanation: Retrospectives are the agile mechanism for inspecting and adapting how the team works. Recurring rework from architectural gaps is exactly the kind of problem to analyse there and improve upon.
questions.mindset: Use the retrospective to fix how the team works, not just what it built.

questions.stem: Members of an agile team are struggling. While there is trust among the team members, the majority of team decisions are made by a few of the more experienced team members. What should the project manager do in order to enable a high-performing team?

options.text: Discourage the experienced team members from speaking first, allowing others to offer ideas.
options.rationale: Silencing experienced members is dismissive and loses their contributions.

options.text: Facilitate meetings to ensure that all team members take part in team decisions.
options.rationale: Facilitating every meeting creates dependence on the PM instead of building the team's own habits.

options.text: Coach the team to ensure all members offer ideas and team consensus is achieved.
options.rationale: Coaching the team on inclusive decision-making builds the lasting behaviour needed for high performance.

options.text: Raise the issue in a retrospective and have the team formalize new team agreements.
options.rationale: Formalising new agreements in a retrospective may help, but without coaching the behaviour may not change.

questions.explanation: High-performing teams share decision-making. A servant leader coaches the team on inclusive participation and consensus so that everyone contributes and the team owns its decisions, rather than facilitating every conversation personally.
questions.mindset: Coach the team to include everyone rather than policing who speaks.

questions.stem: A new project manager is hired to replace a project manager who was recently transferred to another project. The team members tell the new project manager that the project is behind schedule due to delays in document approvals from the customer. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Meet with the customer to discuss the delays and negotiate a new deadline.
options.rationale: Negotiating a new deadline before understanding the situation is premature.

options.text: Talk to the previous project manager to understand the situation better.
options.rationale: The previous PM can explain the history, the causes of the delays and what has already been tried.

options.text: Reach out to the customer and request expedited document approvals.
options.rationale: Requesting expedited approvals may repeat something already attempted.

options.text: Assess the impact of the delays on the project schedule and budget.
options.rationale: Impact assessment is needed, but context from the previous PM makes it accurate.

questions.explanation: A new project manager should use available knowledge before acting. The previous project manager is a direct source of context about causes and actions taken, which helps avoid repeating failed approaches.
questions.mindset: Gather the history before changing the course.

questions.stem: In the early stages of team formation, a project manager is unable to focus on the main tasks because team members are constantly asking for help to resolve conflicts regarding the interpretation of the client's requirements. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Empower the team to resolve conflicts among themselves.
options.rationale: Empowering the team to resolve conflicts builds their capability and frees the PM to focus on project-level work.

options.text: Spend time resolving these conflicts with the team.
options.rationale: Resolving every conflict keeps the team dependent and the PM overloaded.

options.text: Use the conflict resolution committee to help resolve these conflicts.
options.rationale: A formal committee is disproportionate for interpretation disagreements.

options.text: Escalate the conflicts to the program manager.
options.rationale: Escalating everyday disagreements to the program manager is unnecessary.

questions.explanation: Teams in early stages often look to the leader to resolve disagreements. Empowering them to handle their own conflicts — with guidance where needed — builds skills and self-organisation.
questions.mindset: Build the team's ability to resolve its own disagreements.

questions.stem: Halfway through a year-long project, a hardware supplier sends a project manager notice of an intent to increase prices due to fluctuating rates of exchange. The project manager is unsure of their negotiating authority. Which document should the project manager reference?

options.text: Risk register
options.rationale: The risk register records risks, not who holds authority to renegotiate contracts.

options.text: Procurement management plan
options.rationale: The procurement management plan defines procurement roles and authority, including who can negotiate with suppliers.

options.text: Project charter
options.rationale: The charter grants overall authority but rarely details contracting authority.

options.text: Communication strategy
options.rationale: A communication strategy does not define negotiating authority.

questions.explanation: Contracting authority is usually limited and defined in the procurement management plan and organisational policy. Before negotiating with a supplier, the PM should confirm what they are authorised to do.
questions.mindset: Know your contracting authority before you negotiate.

questions.stem: A new project involving team members from two countries has just begun. Due to a time difference, one site finishes work an hour after the other site starts for the day. What should the project manager do to promote communication between the two sites?

options.text: Praise the team members who are available after hours.
options.rationale: Praising after-hours work encourages burnout and does not create shared communication.

options.text: Schedule online meetings during the overlapping hours.
options.rationale: Meetings during overlapping hours allow both sites to communicate live without working outside their hours.

options.text: Ask the team members to adhere to uniform working hours.
options.rationale: Forcing uniform hours ignores local working norms and may be unrealistic.

options.text: Draft a team charter to establish a decision-making method.
options.rationale: A decision-making method helps but does not create time to communicate.

questions.explanation: Distributed teams should make the most of the time they share. Scheduling interaction during overlapping hours enables communication while respecting local working time.
questions.mindset: Use the overlap well rather than stretching people across time zones.

questions.stem: A team is working on a new project and the sponsor refuses to approve a budget increase needed for the current iteration. What should the project manager do to address this situation?

options.text: Submit a change request to get formal approval for a budget increase.
options.rationale: The sponsor has already refused; a change request for the same increase repeats the refused request.

options.text: Work with the stakeholders to develop flexible budgeting approaches.
options.rationale: Working with stakeholders on flexible budgeting may find ways to fund the iteration within constraints.

options.text: Explain to the sponsor the risk of not having the budget approval.
options.rationale: Explaining risk may help, but it restates the argument rather than finding a solution.

options.text: Spend the extra money and plan to compensate in the next sprint.
options.rationale: Spending money that has not been approved is a breach of financial control.

questions.explanation: When additional budget is refused, the project manager looks for alternatives within the constraints — flexible or incremental funding, reprioritising, rephasing — rather than repeating the request or spending without authority.
questions.mindset: Work within financial constraints creatively, never around them.

questions.stem: A project manager has developed a project management plan based on agile methodologies in an effort to deliver the product quickly. However, the project is complex and the requirements are unclear, putting the schedule at risk. What should the project manager do to get the project back on track?

options.text: Rebaseline the schedule to accept additional expectations and potential delays.
options.rationale: Rebaselining accepts the delay without resolving unclear requirements.

options.text: Review the product backlog with the product owner and team to resolve the status.
options.rationale: Reviewing the backlog with the product owner and team clarifies requirements and reprioritises, addressing the cause of the schedule risk.

options.text: Increase the number of standup meetings and implement daily status updates.
options.rationale: More stand-ups and status updates add overhead but do not clarify requirements.

options.text: Adjust the plan to employ more iterative and incremental life cycle features.
options.rationale: The plan is already agile; the issue is backlog clarity, not the lifecycle.

questions.explanation: Unclear requirements in agile work show up as a poorly refined backlog. Refining and reprioritising it with the product owner and team clarifies what to build next and restores predictable progress.
questions.mindset: Fix unclear requirements through backlog refinement, not extra status meetings.

questions.stem: Company A is moving from a predictive approach to an agile one. After the second incremental release of project X, the product owner expresses disappointment with the prototype results and wants to escalate the project to upper management and request a new team. Because of this, the team members start blaming each other and the new agile approach for the product owner's perception of the project. How should the project manager resolve the team's differences?

options.text: Follow the conflict resolution process documented in the project charter.
options.rationale: Conflict resolution processes are rarely in the charter, and a formal process does not suit a team-level learning issue.

options.text: Use retrospective sessions to allow the team to determine the cause of the dispute.
options.rationale: A retrospective lets the team examine what happened and find the cause together, turning blame into improvement.

options.text: Revisit the project vision with the team to ensure that the project goal is understood.
options.rationale: Revisiting the vision may help later but does not address the team's blame and conflict.

options.text: Review the definition of done (DoD) with the product owner and determine the cause of the gap.
options.rationale: Reviewing DoD with the product owner is too narrow and leaves the team's internal conflict untouched.

questions.explanation: Blame after a disappointing result is best redirected into structured reflection. A retrospective gives the team a safe forum to find root causes and agree improvements, which also rebuilds trust.
questions.mindset: Turn blame into learning through structured reflection.

questions.stem: In a hybrid project, the need for customer involvement throughout the project is not understood by the customer. As a consequence, rework is beyond acceptable levels. What should the project manager do to address this issue?

options.text: Submit a change request to obtain the required involvement from the customer.
options.rationale: A change request is not the tool for obtaining customer engagement.

options.text: Add this customer issue to the backlog for prioritization and review.
options.rationale: The backlog holds product work, not relationship issues with the customer.

options.text: Meet with the customer to highlight the importance of their engagement for project success.
options.rationale: Meeting the customer to explain why their engagement matters is the direct way to gain their commitment.

options.text: Instruct senior management to make the customer work closely with the team.
options.rationale: The PM cannot instruct senior management, and escalation is premature.

questions.explanation: Adaptive delivery depends on customer involvement. When a customer does not understand that, the project manager explains the link between their engagement and outcomes such as reduced rework.
questions.mindset: Explain to customers why their involvement matters to their own results.

questions.stem: A project is in the planning phase and requires tremendous time and effort for data collection and analysis. The project sponsor asks the project manager to skip a planned focus group discussion and brainstorming sessions in an effort to accelerate the process. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Report the issue to the project steering committee.
options.rationale: Escalating to the steering committee before speaking to the sponsor damages the relationship.

options.text: Acknowledge the project sponsor's request and skip the sessions.
options.rationale: Skipping sessions without understanding the constraint may undermine planning quality.

options.text: Tell the project sponsor that skipping the sessions will jeopardize the project.
options.rationale: Warning of jeopardy without understanding the sponsor's reasons is confrontational.

options.text: Meet with the project sponsor to understand the reasons for the time constraints.
options.rationale: Understanding why the sponsor feels time pressure allows options to be found that meet both needs.

questions.explanation: When a sponsor asks to cut planning activities, the project manager first understands the constraint behind the request. Knowing the reasons lets the PM propose alternatives that satisfy both speed and adequate planning.
questions.mindset: Understand the constraint behind a request before accepting or resisting it.

questions.stem: At the first meeting about a road construction project, the project manager reminds the team of the importance of observing all rules when carrying out their duties and interacting with stakeholders. Later in the project, team members start coming to meetings late and do not follow other ground rules. To ensure the project outcomes and schedule are not affected, what should the project manager do next?

options.text: Address the issue with the specific team members who violated the ground rules.
options.rationale: Addressing the issue with the specific team members is direct and proportionate.

options.text: Remove the team members who violated the ground rules.
options.rationale: Removal is extreme for lateness and rule-breaking without first trying to correct the behaviour.

options.text: Promote all team members who do not violate any ground rules.
options.rationale: Promoting others as a reward is not within a PM's usual authority and does not correct the breach.

options.text: Allow the team to investigate any team members who violate the ground rules.
options.rationale: Having the team investigate colleagues creates division.

questions.explanation: When ground rules are broken, the project manager deals with the individuals involved, privately and directly. Escalation or formal measures are reserved for continued breaches.
questions.mindset: Address breaches with the people involved, directly and privately.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned to a mobile application development project. The project manager realizes that an agile approach is better suited for the project, but most of the team is not experienced in agile approaches. What should the project manager do next if the organization is open to using an agile approach?

options.text: Request that the project be reassigned to a project team with agile experience.
options.rationale: Reassigning the project abandons the chance to build agile capability in the organisation.

options.text: Ask to replace the team members who have never used agile approaches.
options.rationale: Replacing team members for inexperience is unnecessary and damages morale.

options.text: Arrange training on agile principles and mindset for the existing project team.
options.rationale: Training on agile principles and mindset prepares the current team to use the approach the project needs.

options.text: Use a predictive approach since the project team is already familiar with that approach.
options.rationale: Choosing the wrong approach for the project to fit current skills trades long-term success for comfort.

questions.explanation: When the right delivery approach is unfamiliar to the team, the answer is to build capability through training in both practices and mindset, not to abandon the approach or the team.
questions.mindset: Build capability to fit the right approach, not the reverse.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned to redesign a store's point-of-sale system. The team is currently testing the new functionality when a key stakeholder proposes a change. The change can bring a significant benefit and increase customer satisfaction, but it also requires more resources. What actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Stop the testing and schedule a meeting to review the proposed changes with the resources.
options.rationale: Stopping testing disrupts work before the change has been assessed or approved.

options.text: Complete testing while the project manager meets with the key stakeholder to review the proposed changes.
options.rationale: Meeting the stakeholder may help, but it skips documenting and analysing the change.

options.text: Document the proposed changes and assess any impact on time, cost, and resources.
options.rationale: Documenting and assessing the impact on time, cost and resources gives the basis for an informed decision.

options.text: Postpone the proposed changes and allow the team to complete the testing and implementation activities.
options.rationale: Postponing without assessment may lose a significant benefit.

questions.explanation: A proposed change is documented and its impact analysed before a decision. This allows benefits to be weighed against cost and resources through the change control process.
questions.mindset: Document and assess every change before deciding on it.

questions.stem: While attending a governance meeting with upper management, a project manager is verbally informed about an impending external audit of selected projects. The audit will enable the organization to maintain its quality certification. What should the project manager do first to prepare for the audit?

options.text: Update all relevant project documentation with the current status of the project.
options.rationale: Updating documents is sensible but should be guided by what the audit will examine.

options.text: Put the project on hold to ensure full compliance with the auditing process.
options.rationale: Putting the project on hold is disruptive and unnecessary.

options.text: Contact the auditors to understand the scope and requirements of the audit.
options.rationale: Understanding the audit's scope and requirements lets preparation be focused.

options.text: Meet with the team and inform them of the scope and requirements of the audit.
options.rationale: The team can only be informed once the PM knows the scope and requirements.

questions.explanation: Audit preparation starts with understanding what will be assessed. Clarifying scope and criteria with the auditors lets the project prepare efficiently without disrupting work.
questions.mindset: Understand the audit criteria before preparing for them.

questions.stem: An information technology (IT) project manager was assigned a new team for a software development project in an agile environment. The project manager estimates that the project will take a certain number of days based on past experience in another organization. How should the project manager validate this assumption and properly plan and manage the project schedule?

options.text: Conduct a survey in the organization and generate data to validate claims.
options.rationale: An organisation-wide survey does not tell you how fast this particular team will work.

options.text: Estimate based on sprint review meetings and stakeholder input.
options.rationale: Sprint reviews and stakeholder input show what was delivered, not a basis for estimating the team's pace.

options.text: Study previous sprint planning meetings and the organization's project culture.
options.rationale: Other teams' sprint history and the culture do not measure this team's capacity.

options.text: Ask the team members to estimate the number of story points and observe team velocity.
options.rationale: Having the team estimate in story points and observing velocity over a few iterations replaces the PM's assumption with this team's own data.

questions.explanation: Estimates carried over from another organisation or team are assumptions. In agile, the team estimates relative size and its observed velocity soon calibrates the forecast, making planning self-correcting.
questions.mindset: Replace borrowed estimates with the team's own measured velocity.

questions.stem: A global, cross-functional team has been assembled to deliver a multinational initiative. What should the project manager do to ensure that there is full team participation throughout the project?

options.text: Coordinate time zone information and agree to meeting times.
options.rationale: Agreeing meeting times across time zones makes it possible for everyone to take part throughout the project.

options.text: Ensure software is delivered in multiple languages.
options.rationale: Multilingual software is a product requirement, not a way to secure team participation.

options.text: Translate the project documentation.
options.rationale: Translating documents may help understanding but does not create the opportunity to participate.

options.text: Provide guidance on common tools and practices.
options.rationale: Common tools help, but participation first depends on people being able to attend.

questions.explanation: Participation in a global team depends on practical access. Coordinating time zones and agreeing meeting slots that work for everyone is a basic condition for inclusion.
questions.mindset: Make participation practically possible for every location.

questions.stem: During a meeting, a team member on a construction project presents a proposal to the project manager. The proposal states that dividing the project into two phases will mitigate the risk of delays. The first phase would result in a minimum viable product (MVP) that would provide the client with early benefits. This would limit the extent of the damages and other cost overruns by 90%. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Conduct a feasibility study to assess the risks and benefits of the proposal.
options.rationale: A feasibility study may follow, but changing the phasing of a client's project needs the client's view early.

options.text: Reject the proposal and continue with the project as initially planned.
options.rationale: Rejecting a proposal that could cut overruns by 90% without discussion ignores a strong improvement.

options.text: Instruct the team to implement the proposed changes without further review.
options.rationale: Implementing a major change without review or client input bypasses governance.

options.text: Discuss the proposal with the client and other stakeholders to get their input.
options.rationale: Discussing the proposal with the client and stakeholders gathers input on a change that affects their delivery and benefits.

questions.explanation: A proposal that reshapes delivery into phases changes what the client receives and when. Stakeholders affected by such a change should be consulted before it is formally assessed and approved.
questions.mindset: Involve affected stakeholders early in changes to how value reaches them.

questions.stem: A project manager works for a company involved in complex turnkey projects. During a team assessment, the project manager finds that overall performance is negatively impacted because the team has trouble adjusting to frequent changes in project requirements and status. What should the project manager do to ensure the team is better equipped to adjust to change?

options.text: Request that the sponsor communicate directly with the project team.
options.rationale: Direct sponsor communication does not give the team a consistent way to receive changes.

options.text: Communicate with stakeholders regularly to avoid frequent changes.
options.rationale: Changes in a turnkey project are frequent by nature; communication will not stop them.

options.text: Provide one-on-one guidance to each team member on a consistent basis.
options.rationale: One-to-one guidance is resource-intensive and inconsistent across the team.

options.text: Establish clear and consistent communication channels and protocols.
options.rationale: Clear, consistent communication channels and protocols make sure changes reach the team quickly and reliably, helping them adapt.

questions.explanation: Teams adapt better to frequent change when information reaches them predictably. Defined channels and protocols for communicating changes reduce confusion and lag.
questions.mindset: Make change predictable to receive, even if it is not predictable to happen.

questions.stem: A project team working on a high-priority, change-driven project has repeatedly missed release deadlines. The project manager identifies that this is due to the fact that an experienced team member is assigned to multiple projects and has limited bandwidth. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Report the issue to the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Reporting to the sponsor before understanding the workload is premature.

options.text: Adjust the schedule and issue a change request.
options.rationale: Adjusting the schedule accepts the constraint without trying to resolve it.

options.text: Discuss this issue with the project team immediately.
options.rationale: Discussing with the team is useful, but the specific cause is one person's workload across projects.

options.text: Evaluate the workload of the experienced team member.
options.rationale: Evaluating the team member's workload is the basis for negotiating their allocation or arranging support.

questions.explanation: When a shared resource is the bottleneck, the first step is to understand their workload across projects. That evidence supports negotiating priorities with other projects or managers, or adding support.
questions.mindset: Understand the bottleneck before negotiating to relieve it.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a hybrid project. The organization uses an agile approach and a risk register, but the development team prefers a Scrum approach and views risk management as a predictive process. What should the project manager prioritize?

options.text: Personally manage and own the risk register because this is an organizational requirement.
options.rationale: Owning the register alone isolates risk management from the team that sees risks daily.

options.text: Delegate the responsibility of updating the risk register to the development team lead.
options.rationale: Delegating to a team lead does not resolve the team's view of risk management.

options.text: Ask the developers to use the risk register because this is an organizational requirement.
options.rationale: Mandating the register without adapting it to Scrum creates resistance.

options.text: Consider a hybrid approach and integrate elements from the risk register and Scrum processes.
options.rationale: Integrating the register with Scrum practices keeps organisational visibility while letting the team manage risk iteratively.

questions.explanation: Hybrid projects tailor practices so organisational requirements and team methods fit together. Risk can be identified in Scrum events and recorded in the register, satisfying governance without imposing a foreign process.
questions.mindset: Tailor practices so governance needs and team methods reinforce each other.

questions.stem: A project manager in a manufacturing company was notified of a failure of the delivered machinery during the initial tests. The machine failed to comply with standard design specifications, resulting in malfunctions and safety concerns. What should the project manager do first to address the issue?

options.text: Review the initial testing procedure and execution.
options.rationale: Reviewing the testing procedure and its execution checks whether the failure is real or due to how it was tested, which is the first step to finding the cause.

options.text: Assess the environmental and individual factors.
options.rationale: Environmental and individual factors are vague and not the first line of investigation.

options.text: Evaluate the technical documentation of the machine.
options.rationale: Technical documentation may help, but verifying the tests themselves comes first.

options.text: Check the communications between the stakeholders.
options.rationale: Stakeholder communication does not explain a technical failure.

questions.explanation: When a delivered item fails testing, start by verifying the test itself: was the procedure correct and properly executed? That confirms whether the product or the test is at fault before further investigation.
questions.mindset: Verify the measurement before concluding what it measured.

questions.stem: A project manager is setting expectations with a team that is delivering a hybrid project. For a hybrid project, when should feedback be provided?

options.text: The timing for feedback depends on the performance measurement plan set by the project lead at the start of the project.
options.rationale: Tying feedback only to a plan set at the start makes it infrequent and inflexible.

options.text: The project manager is responsible for communicating feedback during internal meetings.
options.rationale: Assigning responsibility does not say how often feedback should be given.

options.text: With each delivery, the project leader is supposed to receive feedback from the stakeholders and share it with the team.
options.rationale: Feedback only at delivery points limits learning between deliveries.

options.text: For the effective performance of the team, feedback is provided on a regular and continuous basis.
options.rationale: Regular, continuous feedback helps the team improve and adapt throughout the work.

questions.explanation: Feedback is most effective when it is frequent and timely. Short feedback loops let teams correct course quickly, which is central to both agile and hybrid working.
questions.mindset: Keep feedback loops short and continuous.

questions.stem: A new project manager is assigned to a project in the execution phase. The project just completed the deliverables for the first phase. During a workshop to review the scope for the second phase of the project, a couple of stakeholders complain that they were not informed of the benefits already delivered. What should the project manager do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Escalate the issue to the steering committee because the sponsor should have informed stakeholders.
options.rationale: The PM is responsible for communication, so escalating to blame the sponsor is inappropriate.

options.text: Escalate the issue to the sponsor because the question came from some of the senior stakeholders.
options.rationale: Escalation because senior stakeholders asked is unnecessary; the PM can fix the gap.

options.text: Record the issue in the issue log, discuss it with the change manager, and update the communications management plan.
options.rationale: Logging the issue, involving the change manager and updating the communications plan fixes the cause and prevents repetition.

options.text: Record the issue in the register, review the stakeholder matrix, and update the risk management plan.
options.rationale: The risk plan is not where a communication failure is corrected.

questions.explanation: Stakeholders unaware of benefits delivered indicates a communication gap. The project manager records the issue and updates the communications management plan so that benefits are reported to those who need to know.
questions.mindset: Fix communication gaps in the plan, not by escalation.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a project to implement a process improvement software system that was developed in-house. However, the adoption across the organization was less than 50% due to a misalignment with core processes. Which three of the following actions should the project manager have performed to realize the project benefits?

options.text: Conducted a full needs assessment in the design phase.
options.rationale: A thorough needs assessment would have aligned the system with core processes from the start.

options.text: Launched the pilot in a core business unit and collected feedback.
options.rationale: A pilot in a core business unit would have exposed the misalignment early, while it could still be corrected.

options.text: Ensured wider stakeholder engagement to gain greater buy-in.
options.rationale: Wider stakeholder engagement builds buy-in, which drives adoption.

options.text: Instructed the marketing team to collect feedback from customers.
options.rationale: Marketing feedback from external customers is irrelevant to an internal process-improvement tool.

options.text: Developed a clear change management plan that included training.
options.rationale: A change management plan with training helps adoption, but training cannot fix a system that is misaligned with core processes.

questions.explanation: Benefits from internal systems depend on adoption, and adoption depends on fit and buy-in. Understanding needs early, piloting in representative areas and engaging stakeholders widely all reduce the risk of building something the organisation will not use.
questions.mindset: Design for adoption from the start: fit, feedback and buy-in.

questions.stem: In an agile project, the project status indicates that the project is 95% completed. During an iteration review, the stakeholders were concerned about the business value being delivered. What should the project manager do to ensure the project is properly aligned?

options.text: Communicate with the stakeholders to mitigate their concerns.
options.rationale: Communicating to ease concerns without checking alignment leaves the underlying value question unanswered.

options.text: Instruct the project sponsor to review the project goals and work completed.
options.rationale: The PM does not instruct the sponsor, and the product owner is closer to scope and value decisions.

options.text: Meet with the product owner to re-evaluate the project's scope and deliverables.
options.rationale: Re-evaluating scope and deliverables with the product owner checks whether what is being built still delivers business value.

options.text: Request that the business analyst adjust the project goals accordingly.
options.rationale: The business analyst does not change project goals; that would redefine success rather than realign work.

questions.explanation: Percentage complete says nothing about value. When stakeholders question the value being delivered, the product owner and PM reassess the scope and backlog against business goals so that remaining work maximises value.
questions.mindset: Measure progress in value delivered, not work completed.

questions.stem: During the execution phase of a project, a new director joined the management team and introduced a mandatory compliance requirement impacting all project tasks. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Notify the team of the new requirement and proceed with the project as planned.
options.rationale: Proceeding as planned ignores a mandatory requirement.

options.text: Update the project schedule and budget to reflect the demands of the new requirement.
options.rationale: Updating schedule and budget before understanding the impact produces guesses.

options.text: Review the new requirement and assess the impact on project tasks and deliverables.
options.rationale: Reviewing the requirement and assessing its impact on tasks and deliverables establishes what must change.

options.text: Update the risk register to reflect the potential risks associated with the new requirement.
options.rationale: Updating the risk register treats a mandatory requirement as a risk rather than a certainty.

questions.explanation: A new mandatory requirement is not optional and not a risk; it is a constraint. The first step is to understand it and assess its impact, which then feeds schedule, budget and change control.
questions.mindset: Understand a new mandatory requirement fully before re-planning around it.

questions.stem: A project team has completed project deliverables, but the project manager would like to evaluate whether the project has delivered the intended value to the sponsor. What is the most appropriate factor for the project manager to evaluate?

options.text: The alignment of the achieved deliverable against the sponsor's expectations.
options.rationale: Comparing what was delivered with the sponsor's expectations shows whether the intended value was achieved.

options.text: Whether the project's deliverables maximized potential income for the sponsor.
options.rationale: Maximising income may not have been the sponsor's goal; value is defined by their objectives.

options.text: Whether delivery performance variances were within the sponsor's thresholds.
options.rationale: Variance thresholds show delivery performance, not the value of the result.

options.text: The project's overall adherence to scope, time, and budget constraints.
options.rationale: Adherence to scope, time and budget shows efficiency, not whether value was delivered.

questions.explanation: Value is defined by what the sponsor and organisation set out to achieve. Evaluating value means comparing results with those expectations, not only measuring constraint performance.
questions.mindset: Judge value against what the sponsor intended to gain.

questions.stem: A company initiated a project to build a new hydropower plant. Analysis was performed to determine regulatory, safety, and security compliance requirements. After the analysis, it was apparent that some elements necessary to achieve compliance may be difficult and expensive to implement. Stakeholders are concerned about the added cost and complexity and have differing opinions on the importance of compliance and its potential implications. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Meet with the stakeholders and emphasize the importance of compliance and the costs of non-compliance.
options.rationale: Helping stakeholders understand why compliance matters and what non-compliance would cost aligns them around a non-negotiable requirement.

options.text: Review the stakeholder register and determine which stakeholders have the highest authority and influence.
options.rationale: Identifying the most powerful stakeholders to side with does not change the need to comply.

options.text: Escalate the compliance concerns and the disparity between stakeholder opinions to the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Escalating before engaging stakeholders skips the PM's responsibility to align them.

options.text: Identify compliance requirements that can be excluded in order to align with stakeholder expectations.
options.rationale: Dropping compliance elements to please stakeholders exposes the organisation to legal and safety consequences.

questions.explanation: Compliance obligations are not open to preference. When stakeholders resist their cost, the project manager helps them understand the legal, financial and safety consequences of non-compliance so that decisions are made on that basis.
questions.mindset: Make the cost of non-compliance visible when stakeholders question the cost of compliance.

questions.stem: A project is close to completion, and the customer wants to celebrate the success by sharing a business case about the benefits created by the project. The project manager and team feel apprehensive about sharing a business case at this stage. What is the most appropriate action for the project manager to take?

options.text: Collaborate with the customer to create a business case highlighting project benefits.
options.rationale: Creating a business case now may overstate benefits that have not yet been realised or measured.

options.text: Acknowledge the request but emphasize the limitations of a business case at this stage.
options.rationale: Acknowledging the request while explaining that benefits need to be measured first keeps the relationship positive and the claims accurate.

options.text: Refer the customer to the project team for details on the benefits created by the project.
options.rationale: Referring the customer to the team shifts responsibility and may give inconsistent messages.

options.text: Inform the customer that a business case would require additional work and resources.
options.rationale: Citing extra work avoids the real concern: the benefits are not yet proven.

questions.explanation: Benefits are often realised after delivery. Publicising them before they are measured risks inaccurate claims; the project manager can support the customer's goal while explaining the need for evidence.
questions.mindset: Celebrate benefits once they can be evidenced.

questions.stem: A project is currently in progress. The project manager has been notified of a new process that may be helpful if it is incorporated into the project. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Evaluate how the new process can be incorporated.
options.rationale: Planning how to incorporate the process assumes it is worth adopting.

options.text: Issue a priority order for the change.
options.rationale: A priority order commits to the change before its value is known.

options.text: Determine the benefit of the change.
options.rationale: Determining the benefit shows whether the change is worth the effort before planning or approving it.

options.text: Modify the requirements document for the change.
options.rationale: Changing requirements before evaluating the benefit is premature.

questions.explanation: Proposed improvements should be justified by their benefits. Understanding the value first determines whether the change is worth pursuing through planning and change control.
questions.mindset: Establish the benefit before investing in the change.

questions.stem: In the planning stage of an upgrade project, a project manager benchmarked other recent projects that use the same technology. The project manager discovered that longer-than-planned outages occurred in most cases due to frequent maintenance activities. What will be the project manager's next step?

options.text: Benchmark projects using other technologies to establish a more objective baseline.
options.rationale: Benchmarking other technologies does not deal with the risk already identified for this one.

options.text: Compare other similar technologies and recommend the implementation of another technology.
options.rationale: Recommending a different technology is a major decision based on a single risk.

options.text: Create a risk item in the risk register and incorporate the thresholds according to the benchmarks.
options.rationale: Recording the risk with benchmark-based thresholds brings it into risk management with realistic parameters.

options.text: Discuss the probable downtime with the sponsor and obtain approval for outages.
options.rationale: Seeking approval for outages presumes the response before the risk is analysed.

questions.explanation: Benchmarking reveals risks from others' experience. Recording those risks with realistic thresholds lets the project plan responses rather than being surprised.
questions.mindset: Turn lessons from comparable projects into managed risks.

questions.stem: During project execution, a customer asks to replace a piece of planned hardware with one that has more features and a lower price. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Evaluate the new features to ensure they align with the customer's business needs.
options.rationale: Evaluating whether the new features meet business needs is the first step in assessing the change.

options.text: Incorporate the hardware immediately as it will reduce the overall project cost.
options.rationale: Lower price does not guarantee fitness for purpose; implementing immediately bypasses change control.

options.text: Meet with the team to plan the implementation of the new hardware as requested.
options.rationale: Planning implementation before evaluation assumes approval.

options.text: Seek approval from the procurement manager and develop a prototype.
options.rationale: Procurement approval and prototyping come after deciding whether the change is desirable.

questions.explanation: A requested change is evaluated first for value and fit, then for impact, then decided through change control. Cheaper and more features does not automatically mean better for the business.
questions.mindset: Evaluate fit and value before implementing any change.

questions.stem: A project manager calls a meeting to identify risks for a complicated project. Several subject matter experts are invited to this meeting along with the project team. Why has the project manager invited the subject matter experts?

options.text: Subject matter experts have specialized expertise and can help identify and address high-risk issues.
options.rationale: SMEs bring specialist expertise that helps identify high-risk areas the team may miss.

options.text: Identifying risks in a meeting with subject matter experts makes getting better project resources easier.
options.rationale: Risk identification is not about obtaining better resources.

options.text: Risks will be easier to accept if the subject matter experts who attended the meeting work together.
options.rationale: Acceptance of risks is not the purpose of SME involvement in identification.

options.text: The project manager can leverage subject matter experts' resources to follow up on the identified risks.
options.rationale: SMEs are consulted for knowledge, not to use their resources for follow-up.

questions.explanation: Expert judgement is a key input to risk identification. Specialists recognise risks that generalists overlook, especially on complex projects.
questions.mindset: Bring in expertise where risks are hardest to see.

questions.stem: A new product was accepted by the customer, but after two weeks the project manager received a complaint from the customer saying that the product's functionality requirements were not met. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Escalate the issue to the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Escalating without understanding what went wrong is premature.

options.text: Review the scope validation process.
options.rationale: Reviewing how scope was validated shows whether acceptance was based on the right criteria and where the gap arose.

options.text: Schedule an inspection of the product.
options.rationale: Inspecting the product helps later but does not explain how it passed acceptance.

options.text: Validate the scope with the customer.
options.rationale: Validating scope again repeats the process that may be flawed without understanding it.

questions.explanation: Customer acceptance followed by a complaint suggests a weakness in the validation process. Reviewing that process — criteria, reviewers, evidence — identifies the gap and prevents repetition.
questions.mindset: When acceptance fails later, examine how acceptance was given.

questions.stem: A serious quality issue has been identified during the implementation of a major public infrastructure project. The issue is likely to cause a substantial delay to the committed project completion date. As the project manager, what should you do?

options.text: Ignore the issue and hope that it does not cause a substantial delay to the completion date.
options.rationale: Ignoring a serious issue is irresponsible and makes it worse.

options.text: Delay the project until the newly identified quality issue can be completely resolved.
options.rationale: Stopping the project without analysis may be unnecessary and costly.

options.text: Implement a strategy to address the newly identified issue without notifying the stakeholders.
options.rationale: Acting without informing stakeholders breaches transparency on an issue affecting a committed date.

options.text: Meet with the project team and stakeholders to discuss the issue and possible solutions.
options.rationale: Engaging the team and stakeholders ensures transparency and collaborative solutions.

questions.explanation: Serious issues threatening commitments must be communicated openly and solved collaboratively. Transparency lets stakeholders help shape the response and adjust their own plans.
questions.mindset: Share serious problems early and solve them together.

questions.stem: A project is estimated to have a total of 250 story points. The team planned 40 story points for each iteration and delivered 40, 10, 20, and 15 story points in the first four iterations. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Reassign undelivered tasks to team members to complete during the next iteration.
options.rationale: Moving undelivered tasks without changing the plan repeats an unrealistic commitment.

options.text: Work with team members to adjust the planned story points for the next iterations.
options.rationale: Adjusting planned points to reflect actual velocity (about 21) makes iteration planning realistic.

options.text: Remove the features that cannot be delivered from the product backlog and update the customer.
options.rationale: Removing features and telling the customer is drastic without first replanning.

options.text: Negotiate with the customer for an extension of the deliverables due to holiday schedules.
options.rationale: Holidays are not mentioned; this invents a reason rather than addressing velocity.

questions.explanation: Observed velocity is the best guide to future capacity. When actual delivery consistently falls short of planned points, planning should be recalibrated with the team rather than repeating overcommitment.
questions.mindset: Plan to demonstrated velocity, not hoped-for velocity.

questions.stem: A company is working on a hybrid project in which the deliverables have quality issues at the end of one of the sprints. Which action should the project manager take?

options.text: Review the definition of done (DoD).
options.rationale: Reviewing the DoD checks whether the quality criteria are adequate and applied, the most direct lever for sprint quality.

options.text: Look for a clear set of working agreements.
options.rationale: Working agreements cover behaviour, not quality criteria.

options.text: Apply value stream mapping.
options.rationale: Value stream mapping analyses flow and waste, not the quality of sprint deliverables.

options.text: Use a plan-driven approach.
options.rationale: Switching to a plan-driven approach is disproportionate for a quality issue.

questions.explanation: In iterative delivery, quality is embedded through the definition of done. When increments show quality problems, reviewing and strengthening the DoD is the first step.
questions.mindset: Strengthen the definition of done when quality slips.

questions.stem: A senior team member was very influential and played a crucial role in past projects. In this new project, the senior member no longer plays a crucial role and is demotivated. What should the project manager do to address this situation?

options.text: Arrange a team meeting to discuss ways of increasing motivation.
options.rationale: A team meeting on motivation is too general for one person's situation.

options.text: Provide incentives to increase motivation.
options.rationale: Incentives may not address a feeling of reduced importance.

options.text: Ask the functional manager to speak with the team member.
options.rationale: The functional manager is not best placed to handle the project relationship.

options.text: Arrange a one-on-one meeting with the team member.
options.rationale: A private meeting lets the PM understand the member's feelings and find a meaningful role.

questions.explanation: Motivation problems are personal. A one-to-one conversation reveals what the person values and allows the leader to find ways to use their experience meaningfully.
questions.mindset: Address individual motivation individually.

questions.stem: A project manager is overseeing a project aimed at providing customers with real-time shipment tracking capabilities. The project team has encountered ongoing disputes primarily revolving around differing interpretations of how user stories contribute to the project's success. Some team members believe the user stories should prioritize speed, while others emphasize accuracy as the top priority. What should the project manager do to address the team members' disagreements over user stories?

options.text: Ask the product manager to meet with the team and clarify the requirements of the user stories.
options.rationale: The product manager could clarify, but alignment with business objectives resolves the disagreement at its root.

options.text: Schedule a meeting with the business sponsor to obtain clarification regarding the user stories.
options.rationale: Taking a team-level disagreement about story priorities to the business sponsor escalates too early and skips the objectives the stories are meant to serve.

options.text: Consistently revisit the project charter together with the team members to ensure alignment.
options.rationale: Revisiting the charter constantly is inefficient and may be too high-level to settle story priorities.

options.text: Verify that the user stories align with overall business objectives and project goals.
options.rationale: Aligning user stories to business objectives gives an objective basis for deciding priorities like speed versus accuracy.

questions.explanation: Disputes about story priorities are resolved by referring to the value they serve. Mapping stories to business objectives lets the team see which qualities matter most and why.
questions.mindset: Settle priority disputes by tracing work back to business objectives.

questions.stem: A company in a heavily regulated industry is planning to release a new product not previously available in the market. The CEO has asked the project manager to propose a way to ensure that competitors in the industry do not enter the market of this product before this company. Which project delivery approach should the project manager use?

options.text: Use a predictive approach as the company has previous experience with it.
options.rationale: Choosing predictive because it is familiar ignores the need for speed and early feedback.

options.text: Include adequate resources in the budget to fast track the project.
options.rationale: Fast-tracking with extra budget is a schedule tactic, not a delivery approach, and adds risk.

options.text: Implement iterations early in the product development processes, and schedule predictive tasks to be performed just before the rollout phase.
options.rationale: Iterating early for speed and feedback, then applying predictive controls before rollout, combines fast development with regulatory rigour.

options.text: Request an agile coach be included on the agile team to increase the speed of the releases.
options.rationale: An agile coach may help, but a purely agile approach may not satisfy the regulatory steps before launch.

questions.explanation: Delivery approaches can be combined. Where speed to market matters but regulation requires controlled release activities, a hybrid that iterates on development and applies predictive discipline to compliance and rollout serves both needs.
questions.mindset: Tailor the life cycle to both the need for speed and the need for control.

questions.stem: A project team's performance has declined for the last three iterations. Some of the team members are disappointed, and raise their concerns during the retrospective meeting. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Identify potential failure points based on the iteration workload.
options.rationale: Looking at workload failure points focuses on one possible cause before the real one is known.

options.text: Motivate the team to perform better.
options.rationale: Motivational appeals do not address why performance has fallen.

options.text: Focus on remediation, not merely on correcting symptoms.
options.rationale: Remediating the root cause rather than the symptoms prevents the decline recurring.

options.text: Compare the team's performance against other project teams.
options.rationale: Comparing with other teams creates pressure and ignores this team's specific causes.

questions.explanation: Sustained performance decline needs root cause analysis. Fixing the underlying cause prevents recurrence, while treating symptoms or exhorting the team only offers short-lived relief.
questions.mindset: Fix causes, not symptoms.

questions.stem: A project team using a hybrid approach is producing both predictive and incremental deliverables simultaneously. The communications management plan states that written communications are preferred over other types. Problems arise daily regarding the incremental tasks; however, the email backlog is becoming increasingly and unnecessarily complex. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Adopt face-to-face conversations during sprints.
options.rationale: Face-to-face conversation resolves daily issues quickly and cuts the email backlog on the incremental work.

options.text: Adopt judicial communications during sprints.
options.rationale: 'Judicial communications' is not a recognised practice and does not address the problem.

options.text: Adopt disruptive communications during sprints.
options.rationale: Disruptive communication would add to the chaos rather than simplify it.

options.text: Adopt formal conversations during sprints.
options.rationale: More formality would increase complexity, which is the problem already.

questions.explanation: The most efficient way to convey information within a development team is direct conversation. In hybrid projects, the communication approach can be tailored so iterative work uses rapid direct discussion even if written communication is preferred elsewhere.
questions.mindset: Use the most direct channel for fast-moving work.
