questions.stem: At the beginning of an agile project, the project manager is developing the project charter with the team. They are unable to agree on the team values. What should the project manager discuss with the team to address the conflict?

options.text: Sustainable pace
options.rationale: Sustainable pace is a core team value and a common starting point for agreeing how the team will work.

options.text: Definition of done (DoD)
options.rationale: The definition of done is a quality agreement about work items, not a team value.

options.text: Respecting the timebox
options.rationale: Respecting timeboxes is a practice, not an underlying value.

options.text: Project ceremonies
options.rationale: Ceremonies are events in the process, not values.

questions.explanation: Team values in an agile charter describe how the team chooses to work together — sustainable pace, respect, core hours. Discussing such values, rather than practices or artefacts, is how a team resolves disagreement about its norms.
questions.mindset: Agree the values that shape how the team works before the practices.

questions.stem: A project is underway with team members from two different countries and there are complaints from both sides. The team members from Country A believe that team members from Country B are too slow to respond and often have scheduled days off. The team members from Country B believe in a good work/life balance and think more consideration is needed before making decisions. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Reevaluate the team charter with team members.
options.rationale: Reevaluating the team charter together lets both groups agree expectations on response times, availability and decision-making.

options.text: Revisit the communications management plan.
options.rationale: The communications plan covers stakeholders' information needs more than team working norms.

options.text: Remind team members to consider cultural differences.
options.rationale: A reminder about cultural differences does not create a shared agreement.

options.text: Investigate the root cause of misunderstandings.
options.rationale: Investigating root cause is reasonable, but the cause — different working norms — is already clear.

questions.explanation: Conflict from different working expectations is resolved by making norms explicit and shared. A team charter reworked together captures agreements that respect both cultures and sets clear expectations.
questions.mindset: Resolve clashing norms by agreeing shared ones together.

questions.stem: A senior stakeholder was invited to a sprint review meeting and asked a project team member to describe the final product that the project will deliver. The team member was unable to respond and deferred the question to a more senior member of the team. What should have been done differently in this situation?

options.text: The team member should have advised the stakeholder to ask the scrum master.
options.rationale: The scrum master facilitates the process; they are not accountable for the product vision.

options.text: The team member should have advised the stakeholder to ask the product owner.
options.rationale: The product owner owns the product vision and is the right person to describe the final product.

options.text: The stakeholder should have held their questions until the next sprint review meeting.
options.rationale: Holding questions until the next review delays a legitimate stakeholder question.

options.text: The stakeholder should have directed their questions to the project manager.
options.rationale: The project manager may help, but the product owner is accountable for the product.

questions.explanation: In Scrum, the product owner is accountable for the product and its vision. Stakeholder questions about what will be delivered should be directed to them.
questions.mindset: Direct product questions to the person accountable for the product.

questions.stem: An events company is planning a new event for a client that holds biannual conferences. The project is being managed by a new project manager who has reviewed the lessons learned log from the last event and is concerned that a past issue may reoccur. How should the project manager proceed?

options.text: Identify the root cause and consult with stakeholders.
options.rationale: Understanding the root cause of the past issue and consulting stakeholders allows preventive action.

options.text: Handle the issue if it arises during the event planning.
options.rationale: Waiting for the issue to recur ignores what lessons learned are for.

options.text: Recommend rescheduling the upcoming conference.
options.rationale: Rescheduling the conference is disproportionate to a known issue.

options.text: Implement the same strategies used in the last event.
options.rationale: Repeating the same strategies that led to the issue risks the same result.

questions.explanation: Lessons learned are useful only if acted on. When a past issue may recur, analysing its cause and involving stakeholders lets the project plan prevention.
questions.mindset: Use lessons learned to prevent, not just to record.

questions.stem: A gas pipeline construction project was planned for completion in 36 months. After 24 months, the project was suspended by the local government authorities, citing a breach of social impact procedures. What should the project manager have done to avoid this?

options.text: Developed a contingency plan in case of suspension by the local government.
options.rationale: A contingency plan for suspension accepts non-compliance instead of preventing it.

options.text: Reviewed local regulations and procedures and planned for them accordingly.
options.rationale: Reviewing local regulations and procedures and planning to meet them would have avoided the breach.

options.text: Requested additional resources to expedite the construction after the suspension.
options.rationale: Extra resources after suspension address recovery, not prevention.

options.text: Established a regular communication channel with the local government.
options.rationale: Communication with the government helps but does not guarantee compliance with specific procedures.

questions.explanation: Regulatory requirements, including social and environmental procedures, must be identified during planning and built into the project. Compliance is a planning input, not something managed after a breach.
questions.mindset: Plan compliance in from the start.

questions.stem: During sign-off for a strategic project that resulted in additional costs, a project manager was unable to justify the additional expense in relation to the business value realized with the successful implementation. What should the project manager have done to avoid this situation?

options.text: Presented an evaluation of the potential benefits identified in the initial business case as enough to justify additional expense costs.
options.rationale: Initial projected benefits are not proof of realised value.

options.text: Measured and tracked the project benefits identified in the business case throughout the project life cycle.
options.rationale: Measuring and tracking benefits throughout the life cycle provides the evidence to justify decisions about additional cost.

options.text: Performed a reassessment of the current state of the organization after project implementation to show the benefits realized.
options.rationale: Reassessing after implementation is late and cannot guide decisions made during the project.

options.text: Shared nonfinancial or intangible benefits such as customer satisfaction and good reputation as indicators for showing the value realized.
options.rationale: Intangible benefits may help, but without tracked measures they do not justify additional expense.

questions.explanation: Benefits realisation management tracks benefits throughout the project, not just at the start and end. That evidence allows changes and additional costs to be justified against value.
questions.mindset: Track benefits continuously so every cost decision can be tested against value.

questions.stem: A construction project has progressed for about 18 months, and the schedule performance index (SPI) is 0.68. The project manager intends to complete the project as planned without additional cost. What should the project manager do to complete the project on time?

options.text: Crash the schedule.
options.rationale: Crashing adds cost, which the PM wants to avoid.

options.text: Fast track the schedule.
options.rationale: Fast-tracking overlaps activities to recover time without additional cost, though with added risk.

options.text: Reduce the project scope.
options.rationale: Reducing scope needs change control and changes what is delivered.

options.text: Reduce the project quality.
options.rationale: Reducing quality is not an acceptable way to recover schedule.

questions.explanation: An SPI well below 1.0 signals significant delay. To recover without extra cost, fast-tracking — running activities in parallel — is the appropriate compression technique, with its added risk managed.
questions.mindset: Choose the recovery technique that respects the constraints you must keep.

questions.stem: A project sponsor is increasingly anxious about the value returned from the investment made in a project and wants to ensure that the original dates are met. What should the project manager do to convince the sponsor that the project is on track?

options.text: Emphasize the value delivered at the phase gate.
options.rationale: Emphasising phase gate value may not address the sponsor's concern about future dates.

options.text: Increase the number of project status reports.
options.rationale: More reports increase volume, not confidence.

options.text: Present past forecasts and current performance.
options.rationale: Showing how past forecasts compared with actual performance demonstrates the reliability of the current forecast.

options.text: Invite the project sponsor to daily project meetings.
options.rationale: Daily meetings are an unnecessary burden on the sponsor.

questions.explanation: Confidence in a forecast comes from evidence that forecasting has been reliable. Presenting past forecasts against actuals, alongside current performance, gives a sponsor objective grounds to trust projected dates.
questions.mindset: Build trust in forecasts by showing their track record.

questions.stem: During a kick-off meeting, the sponsor informs the project team that they can not attend any meetings for the first half of the project. The sponsor would like to assign a replacement. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Request that the replacement holds substantial influence and decision-making authority.
options.rationale: Asking for authority is reasonable but skips analysing what the absence means and choosing well.

options.text: Set up a meeting with the replacement sponsor as soon as possible to discuss the upcoming agenda.
options.rationale: Meeting a replacement before one has been properly identified is premature.

options.text: Request the full attention of the sponsor and escalate this issue to the project management office (PMO).
options.rationale: Escalating to the PMO against the sponsor's decision damages the relationship.

options.text: Analyze the impact of the change and work with the sponsor to identify a suitable replacement.
options.rationale: Analysing the impact and working with the sponsor to identify a suitable replacement keeps governance and decisions flowing.

questions.explanation: A sponsor's absence affects governance, decisions and support. The PM should analyse the impact and work with the sponsor to delegate to someone with the right authority and availability.
questions.mindset: Protect decision-making when the sponsor steps back.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a project using a hybrid approach. The project team began the project with high morale and performance but both have decreased significantly in the project's later stages. One team member has maintained the initial level of performance and the remaining team members are distracted and showing signs of conflict. What should the project manager do to increase team performance?

options.text: Instruct the team to emulate the member with high performance, praising that member’s work ethic.
options.rationale: Telling the team to emulate one member breeds resentment.

options.text: Mentor the team member who performing well and recommend that he/she work with other team members and train them on iterative development techniques.
options.rationale: Having the strong performer mentor and train others recognises them and spreads skills that lift the team.

options.text: Recommend to the project sponsor that this team should switch back to traditional project management methodologies to not waste additional budget.
options.rationale: Switching back to traditional methods is a drastic reaction to a motivation problem and discards the reasons the hybrid approach was chosen.

options.text: Note the issues in the risk register and address it during the next scheduled standup.
options.rationale: Logging and deferring does not address the declining performance now.

questions.explanation: Peer mentoring uses internal strengths to raise team capability while recognising contribution. It is often more effective than comparison or methodology changes.
questions.mindset: Use strengths within the team to lift the whole team.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned to a top innovation project that has high visibility with the company executives. Recently, one of the project requirements changed and requires the use of new and innovative technology. The change requires the creation of a new position to be filled by someone familiar with the new technology. During a status meeting, a current team member expresses interest in the new role and confirms they are certified in this new technology. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Reassign the team member to the task to support their growth at the organization, and acquire a resource to replace the team member's old role.
options.rationale: Moving a certified team member into the new role puts the right skills where needed and supports growth, with backfill for the old role.

options.text: Ask the team member to continue the current job assignment while also taking on the new assignment as time allows.
options.rationale: Splitting the person across both roles 'as time allows' leaves the new, critical role under-resourced and puts the existing work at risk too.

options.text: Escalate the request to the project sponsor in order to determine if the team member can be assigned to the new assignment.
options.rationale: The PM can make this assignment; escalating is unnecessary.

options.text: Hire a new team member and ask the existing team member to provide the training needed for the new team member to obtain certification.
options.rationale: Hiring and training a new person ignores a qualified internal candidate.

questions.explanation: When a new role needs skills an existing team member already has, reassignment is fast and motivating. The vacated role is then backfilled.
questions.mindset: Put available skills where they are needed most, and backfill.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on a new project. Two key project resources have a disagreement regarding a requirement. The project manager wants to understand both points of view, but one resource is not willing to meet with the project manager. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Escalate the issue to the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Escalating before using available tools is premature.

options.text: Accept the position of the senior project resource.
options.rationale: Accepting the senior view dismisses the other perspective.

options.text: Review the organizational process assets (OPAs).
options.rationale: OPAs rarely resolve an interpersonal disagreement.

options.text: Refer to the team's ground rules and project vision.
options.rationale: Ground rules and the project vision provide an agreed framework for resolving the disagreement.

questions.explanation: When direct conversation stalls, a team's agreed ground rules and shared vision provide a neutral reference point for resolving conflict.
questions.mindset: Use agreed rules and shared vision as neutral ground.

questions.stem: A project manager working in a matrix organization is managing a project that is scheduled to be completed in one month. At today's project meeting, the project manager was informed that errors encountered in the software code are steadily increasing. During discussions with the development team lead, the project manager is told that this is normal when trying to stay on schedule. The development team is pressing to move on so a deadline is not missed, but the project manager is concerned. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Update the work breakdown structure (WBS) and extend the durations in the project schedule to allow more development time.
options.rationale: Extending durations assumes a problem before confirming there is one.

options.text: Direct the team to continue development to avoid missing the deadline, noting that the risk has been mitigated.
options.rationale: Continuing and claiming the risk is mitigated ignores rising defects.

options.text: Examine the quality metrics to determine if the project is complying with the documented quality requirements.
options.rationale: Checking the quality metrics shows whether defects exceed agreed limits, providing an objective basis for action.

options.text: Submit a change request through the change control process to extend the deadline, allowing more time for development.
options.rationale: A change request without evidence is premature.

questions.explanation: Quality metrics define acceptable limits. When concerns arise, comparing actual performance with those metrics determines whether action is needed.
questions.mindset: Test concerns against agreed quality metrics.

questions.stem: While planning a new project, a new project manager finds that the request for proposal (RFP) references several government regulations. However, the project manager discovers that compliance guidelines related to two specific regulations are being created and are not currently available. Senior management advises the project manager that the guidelines will be available when that stage of the project is reached and directs the project manager to continue working on the proposal. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Delay the project and explain the consequences of non-compliance to senior management.
options.rationale: Delaying against senior management's direction is not warranted when guidance has been given.

options.text: Document the interactions with senior management as assumptions in the assumption log.
options.rationale: Documenting the assumption that guidelines will be available keeps it visible and lets it be revisited.

options.text: Verify the requirements for the government regulations and establish a strategy for compliance.
options.rationale: A compliance strategy cannot be completed without the guidelines.

options.text: Continue working on the proposal and update it as more compliance guidelines are understood.
options.rationale: Continuing without recording the assumption leaves a key dependency untracked.

questions.explanation: When the project proceeds on the basis of information not yet available, that basis is an assumption. The assumption log makes it visible so it can be validated later.
questions.mindset: Record what you are assuming so it can be checked.

questions.stem: A marketing team is developing ideas in order to revamp an existing product. The marketing executive reaches out to the project manager to make sure that necessary measures are in place for a successful launch. What should the project manager focus on?

options.text: Ensuring that the scope management plan is in place to cover all related objectives.
options.rationale: A scope plan covers scope, not how launch success will be measured.

options.text: Ensuring that the team is also focused on the overall change management plan.
options.rationale: A change plan supports adoption but does not define success.

options.text: Planning for regular project updates to cover the status of critical deliverables.
options.rationale: Status updates report progress, not outcomes.

options.text: Determining and aligning performance indicators that will help in assessing successful delivery.
options.rationale: Performance indicators agreed up front define and measure launch success.

questions.explanation: A successful launch needs agreed success measures. Defining KPIs in advance makes success measurable and aligns stakeholders on what matters.
questions.mindset: Define how success will be measured before delivering.

questions.stem: In a functional organization, a product analyst is assigned to a short-duration application development effort. The analyst expresses concerns about the task and asks the project manager to provide the support of a peer with expertise in this domain. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Recognize the analyst's concerns and reassign the task to another team member.
options.rationale: Reassigning may not be possible in a functional organisation and misses a development opportunity.

options.text: Enroll the analyst in a capacity-building program, and keep this analyst assigned to the task.
options.rationale: A capacity-building programme may be too slow for a short task.

options.text: Ask the analyst to use skills to develop the tool, then move development to another team member.
options.rationale: Moving the work halfway disrupts it and does not develop the analyst.

options.text: Make sure the analyst has regular pairing meetings with the other team member throughout task execution.
options.rationale: Regular pairing supports the analyst throughout the task and transfers knowledge.

questions.explanation: On short efforts there is rarely time for formal training, so knowledge transfer has to happen while the work is done. Pairing an uncertain team member with an experienced peer gives immediate support and builds lasting capability at the same time.
questions.mindset: Pair people for fast, practical knowledge transfer.

questions.stem: During one of the final incremental deliveries of a project, the end user informed the project leader that they are not satisfied with the outcome and asked to remove a team member which is causing an unfavorable outcome. What should the project leader do?

options.text: Acknowledge the fact, and promise the end user the issue will be resolved.
options.rationale: Promising to resolve an unconfirmed issue risks commitments the PM cannot keep.

options.text: Inform the end user that this is a key member, and promise the issue will be resolved.
options.rationale: Defending the member and promising a fix dismisses the concern.

options.text: Remove the team member as requested to not delay the acceptance.
options.rationale: Removing someone without investigation is unfair.

options.text: Discuss the issue during the regular stakeholder feedback meeting and take action to resolve the issue.
options.rationale: Discussing in the regular feedback meeting lets the facts be established and appropriate action agreed.

questions.explanation: Customer dissatisfaction is investigated before action. Using established feedback mechanisms allows the facts to be clarified and a fair response agreed.
questions.mindset: Establish the facts through proper channels before acting on a complaint.

questions.stem: Working in a continuous delivery environment, a project leader notices that one of the key team members is experiencing low morale, affecting the project delivery and causing a serious delay in the project schedule. While discussing the issue with the team member, the project leader discovers the team member's attitude is because of uncertainty in relation to the performance review set of criteria. What should the project leader have done to avoid this situation?

options.text: Explain the ground rules of the team.
options.rationale: Ground rules address behaviour, not performance review criteria.

options.text: Inform the team about incentives and rewards.
options.rationale: Incentives do not remove uncertainty about how performance is assessed.

options.text: Share feedback and performance results.
options.rationale: Sharing regular feedback and performance results removes uncertainty and supports morale.

options.text: Define the team-building strategies.
options.rationale: Team-building strategies do not address performance criteria.

questions.explanation: Uncertainty about performance expectations undermines morale. Regular, transparent feedback clarifies expectations and helps people perform.
questions.mindset: Give regular feedback so people know where they stand.

questions.stem: A project management organization has a project that leverages waterfall for the requirements gathering phase and agile for development and testing phases. Not everyone on the project team is familiar with both approaches and the project encounters delays due to project team uncertainty. What should have been done to prevent this scenario?

options.text: Train the project team on the benefits of hybrid project management.
options.rationale: Training on the benefits of hybrid does not help the team respond to day-to-day uncertainty.

options.text: Have the project team members familiar waterfall be responsible for the requirements gathering phase and those familiar with agile handle development and testing phases.
options.rationale: Splitting work by familiarity isolates groups and does not build shared understanding.

options.text: Schedule daily standup meetings to keep the team informed of progress and address issues as they occur.
options.rationale: Daily stand-ups surface uncertainty and issues quickly so they are resolved before they cause delay.

options.text: Request that the PMO leverage either waterfall or agile for the full project as the team cannot be trained in time for the project to succeed.
options.rationale: Abandoning the hybrid approach because some people are unfamiliar with it is disproportionate and ignores why the approach was chosen.

questions.explanation: When unfamiliarity creates uncertainty, fast feedback loops help. Daily coordination surfaces confusion early so that it can be resolved before it becomes a delay.
questions.mindset: Shorten feedback loops when uncertainty is high.

questions.stem: While executing a critical iterative phase of a project, a problem previously identified as a risk just became a confirmed issue, which has halted progress. After entering the new item in the issue log, what should the project manager do next?

options.text: Increase communications and involve stakeholders in the resolution whenever necessary.
options.rationale: Increasing communication and involving stakeholders brings the right people into resolving an issue that has halted progress.

options.text: Change the communications management plan and assign ownership to a team member.
options.rationale: Changing the communications plan is heavier than needed.

options.text: Escalate the issue within the team during the next project retrospective meeting.
options.rationale: Waiting for the retrospective delays a blocking issue.

options.text: Add the issue to the product backlog to bring it into focus during the current sprint.
options.rationale: Adding an issue to the product backlog confuses impediments with product work.

questions.explanation: An issue that halts progress needs faster, wider communication, not slower. After logging it, the project manager increases the frequency of updates and brings in the stakeholders who can help resolve it, rather than waiting for a scheduled event or re-planning communications.
questions.mindset: Communicate more, not less, when an issue stops progress.

questions.stem: A new Scrum project manager at a company is contracted to build a traffic measurement and control application for a municipality. The project manager is notified that the municipality has just rejected the traffic measurement portion of the application because it does not comply with longstanding national regulations. What should the project manager have done to avoid this situation?

options.text: Requested that the product owner handle the regulation compliance.
options.rationale: Handing compliance to the product owner makes it someone else's problem without ensuring expertise.

options.text: Allocated an experienced team member to validate regulatory compliance.
options.rationale: Assigning an experienced team member to validate regulatory compliance catches issues before delivery.

options.text: Made the scrum master solely responsible for regulatory compliance.
options.rationale: Scrum masters facilitate; they are not compliance owners.

options.text: Discussed the importance of regulation compliance with the sponsor.
options.rationale: Discussing importance with the sponsor does not validate compliance.

questions.explanation: Regulatory compliance must be verified during delivery. Assigning someone with the right expertise ensures regulations are checked before the customer rejects the product.
questions.mindset: Build compliance verification into delivery.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on a hybrid (predictive-agile) project. During a standup meeting, a team member mentions that because of experience on a previous project, they think that one of the upcoming deliverables may need to comply with government regulations. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Escalate the issue with the project management office (PMO) so they can determine if any compliance is required.
options.rationale: Escalating to the PMO before checking the facts is premature.

options.text: Stop the project until it is confirmed that the deliverable is subject to any regulations.
options.rationale: Stopping the project for an unconfirmed possibility is disproportionate.

options.text: Review lessons learned from the previous project to determine if any compliance is required.
options.rationale: Reviewing lessons learned is a quick way to check whether compliance applies.

options.text: Remove the task from the critical path and assign the resource to work on another requirement.
options.rationale: Removing the task from the critical path ignores the question.

questions.explanation: A team member's hunch about regulation is a question to answer, not a fact to act on. Checking readily available knowledge such as lessons learned from the earlier project establishes quickly whether compliance applies, before escalating or disrupting the work.
questions.mindset: Investigate a possible compliance issue before escalating it.

questions.stem: A project for an accounts receivable system that was recently launched into production received a fine from a regulatory body because the system did not comply with local regulations. What should the project manager have done to avoid this situation?

options.text: Defined risk control management.
options.rationale: Risk control would track the possibility of non-compliance but would not verify that the product actually conformed.

options.text: Defined a control quality process.
options.rationale: A control quality process verifies deliverables against specifications, including regulatory ones, before release.

options.text: Implemented an issue control log.
options.rationale: An issue log tracks problems once they occur; it would not have prevented the non-compliance.

options.text: Involved the audit department in project planning.
options.rationale: Involving audit in planning helps, but compliance must also be verified in the delivered product.

questions.explanation: Regulatory requirements are part of the specification. Control quality measures and inspects deliverables against all specified requirements, so non-conformance is caught before the product reaches production.
questions.mindset: Verify conformance, including regulatory conformance, before release.

questions.stem: A company is going through an organizational change. Most of the senior management has changed, including the project manager's direct supervisor. The supervisor has an aggressive working style, and has made critical comments to the project manager regarding the ongoing project, without really understanding the situation. The project manager feels uncomfortable working with the new supervisor. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Hold a project review meeting to explain the key points of the project to the new supervisor.
options.rationale: A review meeting may help later, but the PM first needs to understand what the change means for the project.

options.text: Apply the new supervisor's recommendations to the project.
options.rationale: Applying recommendations based on a poor understanding of the project could harm it.

options.text: Evaluate the impact of the organizational change to the project.
options.rationale: Evaluating the impact of the organisational change gives the PM an objective footing to engage the new supervisor and plan.

options.text: Communicate to the project team that they need to be ready to embrace change.
options.rationale: Telling the team to embrace change does not assess or manage its effect.

questions.explanation: Organisational change can alter priorities, sponsorship and constraints. The project manager responds objectively by assessing the impact of the change on the project, which then informs how to engage new leadership.
questions.mindset: Assess what organisational change means for the project before reacting to people.

questions.stem: A project manager had just started a long-term project when the government implemented new legislation that all engineers working in the state need to be registered. Registration is based on work area, experience, and professional development completed in the last 3 years. Due to budget constraints in the company for the past three years, there were limited opportunities for engineers to gain formal professional development. How should the project manager handle the situation?

options.text: Send a request to the change management board to assess the situation.
options.rationale: A change request is not needed just to assess the situation.

options.text: Review the team's skills matrix and update the resource management plan.
options.rationale: Reviewing the skills matrix shows which engineers meet the new requirements, and updating the resource plan lets registration and training be scheduled without stalling the project.

options.text: Send all of the engineers to professional development to meet the requirements.
options.rationale: Sending everyone to training before knowing who needs it is wasteful and could strip the project of staff.

options.text: Inform the engineers that they need to be registered to keep working for the company.
options.rationale: Simply telling engineers they must register does not help the project plan for compliance.

questions.explanation: New external legislation affecting people's eligibility to work is a resource constraint. Assessing who is affected and updating the resource plan lets the project comply while maintaining capacity.
questions.mindset: Translate external rule changes into resource planning.

questions.stem: During project execution, the project manager realizes that a team member is not completing tasks in accordance with the project management plan. What is the first action the project manager should take?

options.text: Build a matrix team to review the relationships on all project teams.
options.rationale: A matrix-wide relationship review is unrelated to one person's performance.

options.text: Ask all the team members to focus more on the project.
options.rationale: A general appeal to the team does not address one individual's issue.

options.text: Reassign the uncompleted tasks to another team member.
options.rationale: Reassigning tasks deals with symptoms and may overload others.

options.text: Engage the team member to determine the reasons for poor performance.
options.rationale: Engaging the team member to understand the reasons addresses the cause and supports improvement.

questions.explanation: Individual performance issues are addressed by talking to the individual first. Understanding the cause — skills, workload, clarity, personal factors — allows an appropriate response.
questions.mindset: Understand the person before correcting the performance.

questions.stem: An agile practitioner has been assigned to lead a software development project in a relatively new industry where the external compliance standards are not clearly defined. What should the agile practitioner do to ensure that the project succeeds?

options.text: Speak to agile managers in other organizations with the same challenges to learn how they address issues.
options.rationale: Talking to peers may help but does not give a solid framework for undefined compliance standards.

options.text: Develop a set of standards that work for the role and support the team in implementing them.
options.rationale: Creating home-grown standards risks non-compliance when official standards emerge.

options.text: Use global best practices as a guide for project implementation incorporating the new technology trends and monitoring compliance standards.
options.rationale: Global best practices provide a credible baseline, and monitoring compliance standards as they emerge keeps the project aligned.

options.text: Refer to other previous data that exists from related industries.
options.rationale: Data from related industries may not apply to a new one.

questions.explanation: Where regulations are immature, recognised global standards and best practices offer a defensible baseline. Monitoring the environment lets the project adapt as formal compliance requirements develop.
questions.mindset: Anchor to recognised standards and keep watching for new rules.

questions.stem: A business environment has become unstable because a stakeholder has altered the project deliverables and outcomes in the middle of the execution phase. Taking the stakeholder into consideration, how should the project manager ensure the project benefits are delivered?

options.text: Ensure the project team agrees to the project management plan and provide the stakeholder with constant updates.
options.rationale: Constant updates do not manage a stakeholder who is changing deliverables.

options.text: Combine both agile and predictive approaches and manage changes to the overall scope with minimal deviations.
options.rationale: Mixing approaches does not by itself manage the stakeholder's influence.

options.text: Ensure the project's deliverables and objectives are tailored to the initial requirements.
options.rationale: Holding to initial requirements ignores legitimate changes and the stakeholder's influence.

options.text: Engage the stakeholder based on level of impact and ensure their requirements are captured adequately according to change management process.
options.rationale: Engaging the stakeholder according to their impact and capturing their requirements through change management channels their influence constructively.

questions.explanation: High-impact stakeholders who change direction mid-project need proportionate engagement and a formal route for their requirements. Change management ensures their needs are assessed without destabilising delivery.
questions.mindset: Channel influential stakeholders' changes through engagement and change control.

questions.stem: During a project governance assessment, and after expending 40% of the approved project budget, management approved the auditor's recommendation to have the project terminated. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Compute the expected monetary value of the project and document it in lessons learned.
options.rationale: Expected monetary value belongs to risk analysis, not to closing a terminated project.

options.text: Engage an independent consultant to justify project continuation.
options.rationale: Seeking justification to continue defies an approved governance decision.

options.text: Initiate the project closeout process and document lessons learned for future reference.
options.rationale: Initiating closure and capturing lessons learned complies with the decision and preserves knowledge.

options.text: Prepare a financial report to recognize the actual costs expended as sunk costs.
options.rationale: Recognising sunk costs is a finance matter and not the next step.

questions.explanation: When governance terminates a project, the project manager executes closure promptly: release resources, finalise records and capture lessons learned so the organisation benefits from the experience.
questions.mindset: Close terminated projects properly and learn from them.

questions.stem: A project team is working on a regulatory application that has a fixed duration for delivery. The team is using a hybrid approach and has divided development into three sprints. The first two sprints have not produced the required results mainly due to delays from functional units. The finance director is agitated due to the imminent sanctions if the application is not completed, and the project team is demoralized. Who is responsible for inspiring the project team?

options.text: Product Owner
options.rationale: The product owner focuses on value and backlog, not on inspiring the team.

options.text: Financial Director
options.rationale: The finance director's focus is financial outcomes.

options.text: Functional Manager
options.rationale: Functional managers supply resources rather than lead the project team.

options.text: Project Manager
options.rationale: The project manager is responsible for leading, removing blockers and inspiring the team.

questions.explanation: Inspiring and motivating the project team is part of the project manager's leadership role, especially when external pressures and delays affect morale.
questions.mindset: Leading the team includes keeping it motivated under pressure.

questions.stem: A project manager new to an organization has been tasked with running the first agile project. The project manager has decided to begin by assessing the organization's ability to adapt to an agile project. Which three characteristics of the organization will help to set up the project for success? (Choose three)

options.text: Safe work environment
options.rationale: A safe environment lets people raise issues and experiment, which agile depends on.

options.text: Key performance indicators (KPIs)
options.rationale: KPIs give a baseline of current performance against which agile outcomes can be judged.

options.text: Willingness to experiment
options.rationale: Willingness to experiment is central to iterative, feedback-driven work.

options.text: Speed to market
options.rationale: Speed to market is a desired outcome, not an organisational characteristic that enables agility.

options.text: Predictability
options.rationale: An emphasis on predictability can pull toward rigid plans rather than adaptation.

questions.explanation: Agile readiness depends on culture and data: people must feel safe, be willing to try things, and have measures to see whether they are improving. Outcomes like speed are what agile aims for, not preconditions.
questions.mindset: Assess culture and data before introducing agile.

questions.stem: A company has undertaken a large transformation project to prepare itself for the changing economy. During the execution of the transformation project, a new technology emerges that was not foreseen in the risk management plan. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Escalate this to the IT department and organize training for the impacted team members.
options.rationale: Training may follow, but the first step is to plan for the emerging risk.

options.text: Revisit the procurement management plan and identify the impacted contracts for upcoming purchases.
options.rationale: Procurement impacts may be part of the analysis but are not the starting point.

options.text: Revisit the risk management plan and apply the project risk planning process.
options.rationale: Revisiting the risk plan and applying risk planning brings the new technology into structured risk management.

options.text: Escalate the issue to the next steering committee and facilitate a brainstorming meeting.
options.rationale: Escalation and brainstorming skip the risk process the project already has.

questions.explanation: Emergent risks are handled by feeding them into the risk management process: identify, analyse and plan responses. Risk management is continuous, not a one-time planning event.
questions.mindset: Bring emergent risks into the risk process as soon as they appear.

questions.stem: An agile project is in its last iteration. During the daily standup, the team realizes that they will not be able to complete all the activities that were planned for the sprint. The team members create a contingency plan. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Discuss the contingency plan with the product owner.
options.rationale: The product owner decides scope trade-offs, so the contingency plan should be discussed with them.

options.text: Discuss the contingency plan with stakeholders.
options.rationale: Stakeholders are informed after the product owner decides.

options.text: Discuss the contingency plan with the project sponsor.
options.rationale: The sponsor is not the first point for sprint-level scope decisions.

options.text: Execute the contingency plan immediately.
options.rationale: Executing without product owner input bypasses the role that decides priority.

questions.explanation: When a sprint cannot deliver everything, the product owner decides what matters most. Contingency plans affecting scope are agreed with the product owner before execution.
questions.mindset: Take scope trade-offs to the product owner.

questions.stem: A project team has recently finished a sprint for developing two features for a fleet management system. Although the team delivered the required features, they encountered several issues and conflicts during the sprint. Team members were upset about this experience and are now showing a lack of motivation due to what has occurred. What can the project manager do to help increase the team's motivation and engagement with the project?

options.text: Set up one-on-one meetings with the project team members.
options.rationale: One-to-ones may help individuals but miss the team-level problems.

options.text: Review sprint progress with the project team members.
options.rationale: Reviewing progress focuses on output, not the conflicts that upset the team.

options.text: Review sprint planning procedures with the project team members.
options.rationale: Reviewing planning procedures is narrow and may not address the conflicts.

options.text: Perform a sprint retrospective with the project team members.
options.rationale: A retrospective lets the team discuss what went wrong and decide improvements, restoring engagement.

questions.explanation: Retrospectives give teams ownership over improving their working environment. Addressing conflict openly and deciding changes together increases engagement.
questions.mindset: Let the team fix its own process to rebuild engagement.

questions.stem: A new project manager is assigned to lead an agile project. The project manager wants to use motivation to encourage the team to perform well throughout the project. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Implement a reward system aimed to keep the team engaged and motivated.
options.rationale: A reward and recognition system is a legitimate tool to keep the team engaged.

options.text: Use the management reserves to fund some team-building activities.
options.rationale: Management reserve is held for unforeseen in-scope work under management control; spending it on team events misuses it.

options.text: Inflate project estimates to provide a financial buffer for team activities.
options.rationale: Inflating estimates to create a hidden fund is dishonest padding that undermines the credibility of the plan.

options.text: Ask project sponsor to fund more for team building activities.
options.rationale: Asking the sponsor for more money is not the first step.

questions.explanation: Recognition and reward systems, designed fairly, support motivation. They should be funded legitimately and aligned with team values.
questions.mindset: Recognise and reward in ways that are fair and transparent.

questions.stem: A senior business stakeholder with many years of experience is pressuring an agile team to deliver most of the promised functionality to the customer 18 months in the future as opposed to multiple, incremental deliveries over the course of the 18 months. What should the project lead do next?

options.text: Work with the agile team to schedule the incremental deliveries to enable delivery of business value sooner to the customer.
options.rationale: Scheduling increments without addressing the stakeholder ignores their pressure.

options.text: Schedule meetings with the customer to determine their ability to support multiple incremental deliveries.
options.rationale: Asking the customer first sidesteps the stakeholder raising the concern.

options.text: Provide details of the concern to the agile team and adjust their goals and release plans to conform to the stakeholder's request.
options.rationale: Conforming to a single delivery abandons agile benefits without understanding the concern.

options.text: Work with the stakeholder to understand what the concerns are while, at the same time, conveying the benefits of incremental deliveries.
options.rationale: Understanding the stakeholder's concerns while explaining incremental benefits aligns expectations.

questions.explanation: Resistance to incremental delivery often hides concerns such as disruption or integration. Understanding those concerns and explaining the benefits aligns expectations rather than forcing one view.
questions.mindset: Understand resistance before persuading.

questions.stem: A project manager has been assigned to a project to implement an asset health management system. The executive business sponsor has indicated that the system is expected to improve the quality of operations and extend the life span of the assets. What should the project manager do in order to demonstrate the business value once the system is in production?

options.text: Establish critical success criteria, potential cost savings, and ongoing performance metrics for the project.
options.rationale: Success criteria, cost savings and ongoing performance metrics allow the business value to be measured once the system is live.

options.text: Write test cases to align with the business values and ensure that acceptance criteria are clear during user acceptance testing (UAT).
options.rationale: Test cases confirm function, not business value in production.

options.text: Verify that all requirements and acceptance criteria are in alignment with the business value and expectations.
options.rationale: Requirement alignment helps delivery but does not measure value after go-live.

options.text: Validate the return on investment (ROI), review the current asset performance, and use it as a benchmark for future measurements.
options.rationale: ROI validation and benchmarks help, but without success criteria and ongoing metrics value is not demonstrated.

questions.explanation: Demonstrating business value needs measures defined in advance and tracked over time. Success criteria and performance metrics link the delivered system to the outcomes the sponsor expects.
questions.mindset: Define how value will be measured before claiming it.

questions.stem: A project execution phase overlaps with a holiday in the country where the majority of team members are based. This phase is critical, and all team members are required to work through the holiday. This negatively impacts team morale. What should the project manager have done to avoid this?

options.text: Requested help from other teams based in other countries
options.rationale: Calling on other teams is reactive and often impractical.

options.text: Postponed project activities
options.rationale: Postponing critical activities delays the project.

options.text: Prepared the stakeholder engagement plan
options.rationale: The stakeholder plan does not address resource availability.

options.text: Better developed the resource management plan
options.rationale: A thorough resource plan accounts for holidays and availability, avoiding forced working.

questions.explanation: Resource planning includes calendars and non-working days. Planning around known holidays protects morale and schedules.
questions.mindset: Plan around people's calendars, not through them.

questions.stem: Midway through project execution, several stakeholders raise concerns about team performance and delivery. The project manager believes the project is progressing per the approved scope, budget, and schedule. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Email the stakeholders to assure them of action.
options.rationale: Assurances without understanding the concerns are empty.

options.text: Consult the communications management plan to manage stakeholders' expectations.
options.rationale: Consulting the communications plan helps understand stakeholders' expectations and how to address them.

options.text: Ask the project sponsor to intervene.
options.rationale: Asking the sponsor to intervene is unnecessary.

options.text: Ask stakeholders to escalate their concerns to the CEO.
options.rationale: Directing stakeholders to the CEO is inappropriate escalation.

questions.explanation: Stakeholder concerns despite good performance often indicate a gap between what they expect and what they see. Using the communications plan to understand and meet their needs aligns perception with reality.
questions.mindset: Close the gap between performance and perception through communication.

questions.stem: A project manager learned that the project deliverables will not meet the quality requirements unless a change is made to a component. After issuing a formal change request, the project manager emailed details of the change to all stakeholders. Most stakeholders received the information promptly and are fully aware of the change. However, the project manager finds out that some stakeholders did not receive the email or did not read it. What could the project manager have done to prevent this?

options.text: Reviewed the communications management plan.
options.rationale: Reviewing the communications plan would have shown each stakeholder's preferred channel, avoiding reliance on one email.

options.text: Developed a detailed work performance report.
options.rationale: A performance report does not change how information reaches people.

options.text: Met with the project sponsor to discuss communication.
options.rationale: The sponsor meeting does not address channels.

options.text: Questioned the stakeholders about technological literacy.
options.rationale: Questioning technological literacy is condescending and misses the point.

questions.explanation: Different stakeholders need information through different channels. The communications plan records those needs; following it ensures important information reaches everyone.
questions.mindset: Send important information through each stakeholder's agreed channel.

questions.stem: A project manager learns that in-house resources are insufficient to produce a critical component of a deliverable. This poses a significant threat. The quality of the component is integral to the project, and the in-house resources cannot guarantee high-quality output. In response to this threat, the project manager decides to outsource the production of the component by contracting a third-party vendor. Which threat response strategy did the project manager use?

options.text: Accept
options.rationale: Accepting a threat means taking no proactive action; here the project manager acted to change the outcome.

options.text: Mitigate
options.rationale: Outsourcing to a capable vendor reduces the probability of poor quality, which is mitigation.

options.text: Enhance
options.rationale: Enhance is a response to an opportunity, used to increase its probability or impact; it does not apply to a threat.

options.text: Escalate
options.rationale: Escalation passes the threat to a higher authority, which is not what happened.

questions.explanation: Threat responses include avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept and escalate. Mitigation reduces probability or impact; engaging a capable supplier to reduce quality risk is mitigation.
questions.mindset: Know which response you are choosing and why.

questions.stem: A project manager has been made aware of a recent weather event that could potentially impact the project. Forecasters are unable to predict the path or strength of the event. Any delays would extend the project's finish date and cause cost overruns. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Notify the stakeholders and revise the budget.
options.rationale: Revising the budget before understanding the risk is premature.

options.text: Take preventive action based on new information.
options.rationale: Preventive action should be based on the risk information.

options.text: Check the risk register for more risk information.
options.rationale: The risk register shows whether this risk was identified and what responses were planned.

options.text: Record information about the event in the issue log.
options.rationale: The storm's effect is still uncertain, so it is a risk to analyse rather than an issue that has already happened.

questions.explanation: When a potential risk emerges, first check whether it was already identified and what response was planned. The register provides that information.
questions.mindset: Check what the plan already says before improvising.

questions.stem: A project manager completed plans for a project and submitted all documents for approval but did not allocate time for delays in obtaining approvals. In addition to selecting a risk owner to address this potential risk, what should the project manager have done?

options.text: Asked the risk owner to escalate with approvers so that approvals are obtained as soon as possible.
options.rationale: Escalating approvals is one action, not a planned strategy.

options.text: Adjusted the project plans by lowering work completion estimates so that the work can be completed on time despite the delay.
options.rationale: Lowering estimates to hide delay is dishonest.

options.text: Developed specific actions to implement the agreed-upon risk response strategy, including primary and backup strategies.
options.rationale: Developing specific actions including primary and backup strategies makes the risk response executable.

options.text: Used a real options analysis to perform an economic analysis of alternative risk response strategies.
options.rationale: Real options analysis is an unnecessary method for this risk.

questions.explanation: Risk response planning includes specific, assigned actions — primary and fallback — so the response is ready when needed.
questions.mindset: Make risk responses specific and executable.

questions.stem: A technology project for a multinational bank is in the testing stage. The project manager learns that a security breach has exposed the personal data of thousands of end users. The project sponsor suspends work while the cause is investigated. The threat of a security breach was identified during the risk management planning process, and the impact is significant. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Refer to the stakeholder engagement plan to determine the risk owner.
options.rationale: The owner is in the risk register, not the stakeholder plan.

options.text: Perform a decision tree analysis to calculate the optimal path to resolution.
options.rationale: Decision tree analysis is not the immediate step.

options.text: Meet with the project sponsor to negotiate a new requirements management plan.
options.rationale: Negotiating a new requirements plan does not address the breach.

options.text: Update the issue log and review the risk response strategy outlined in the risk register.
options.rationale: Logging the issue and reviewing the planned response prepares the PM to act.

questions.explanation: A risk that occurs becomes an issue. Record it in the issue log and apply or adapt the planned response in the risk register.
questions.mindset: When a risk materialises, log it as an issue and execute the planned response.

questions.stem: While conducting a retrospective meeting, team members were surprised from the performance results of the team shared by the project lead. The team have all expressed their ignorance of the measurements and availability of the different tools in place. What should have the project lead done to avoid this situation?

options.text: Ask the HR to explain the different performance measurement tools
options.rationale: HR has no role in explaining project performance tools.

options.text: Inform the team members to fill in feedback on a regular basis
options.rationale: Asking for regular feedback forms collects opinions but does not tell the team how their performance will be measured.

options.text: Provide Team members with continuous feedback about their performance
options.rationale: Continuous feedback helps but assumes a framework exists.

options.text: Planning and define a clear performance measurement framework
options.rationale: A clear, planned measurement framework shared with the team avoids surprises.

questions.explanation: Teams should know how performance will be measured. Defining and sharing the measurement framework makes results understandable.
questions.mindset: Share measures in advance so results are never a surprise.

questions.stem: A project is in the execution phase, and product testing is almost complete. A team member proposes that the testing can be fast-tracked by removing some of the tests. The team member believes this will help to finish the job earlier and give the project more float. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Request more information from the team member.
options.rationale: Requesting more information delays a clear decision.

options.text: Reject the team member's proposal.
options.rationale: Removing tests to gain float compromises quality without need.

options.text: Discuss this proposal with the project team.
options.rationale: Discussing with the team gives credence to an unacceptable proposal.

options.text: Ask the quality manager to consider the proposal.
options.rationale: Deferring to the quality manager is unnecessary.

questions.explanation: Planned testing is part of the quality commitment. Removing tests for schedule convenience is unacceptable when no schedule pressure exists.
questions.mindset: Do not trade quality for convenience.

questions.stem: A virtual project team is composed of members from various countries with cultural differences. The project manager is concerned that cultural differences may lead to miscommunication and conflict. What should the project manager do to effectively mitigate against potential conflicts?

options.text: Collaboratively define and communicate the project-specific ground rules.
options.rationale: Defining ground rules together prevents conflict by setting shared expectations.

options.text: Require that all communications within the project team are in written form.
options.rationale: Written-only communication does not bridge cultural differences.

options.text: Appoint the senior member of one country's team to act as arbitrator if a conflict arises.
options.rationale: An arbitrator from one country may appear biased.

options.text: Make all conflict resolution decisions and then inform the team.
options.rationale: Deciding conflicts unilaterally disempowers the team.

questions.explanation: In culturally diverse virtual teams, conflict often starts from different assumptions about how to communicate and behave. Ground rules defined together make those assumptions explicit and shared, preventing misunderstandings rather than arbitrating them afterwards.
questions.mindset: Agree the rules together before conflict arises.

questions.stem: A project has been closed and customer care needs to measure customer satisfaction with the deliverables. What should be done next?

options.text: Negotiate additional contract with customer for similar service.
options.rationale: Selling a follow-on contract is a commercial move, not a measurement of how satisfied the customer is with what was delivered.

options.text: Schedule meeting with stakeholders and customer to discuss lessons learned.
options.rationale: A lessons learned meeting captures how the project went for the team, but it is not the tool for measuring customer satisfaction with deliverables.

options.text: Evaluate project deliverables and review customer feedback documents.
options.rationale: Evaluating the deliverables alongside the customer's documented feedback gives a direct, evidence-based measure of satisfaction.

options.text: Audit project success by reviewing closing documentation for each project phase.
options.rationale: An audit of phase closing documents checks process compliance; it tells you little about how the customer feels about the result.

questions.explanation: Customer satisfaction is measured against what the customer actually received and said about it. Combining an evaluation of the delivered outputs with the customer's own feedback gives a grounded view, distinct from internal lessons learned or process audits.
questions.mindset: Measure satisfaction from the customer's own feedback on what they received.

questions.stem: The client agreed to the standards that would be used to assess final deliverables prior to hand-off, but is now asking for improvements because the deliverables do not meet the standards. Which document should the project manager consult to resolve this issue?

options.text: Scope management plan
options.rationale: The scope plan explains how scope is defined and controlled, not the standards deliverables are assessed against.

options.text: Quality management plan
options.rationale: The quality management plan holds the agreed standards and how conformance is demonstrated, so it settles whether the deliverables meet them.

options.text: Requirements documentation
options.rationale: Requirements documentation says what is needed, but the agreed assessment standards and methods sit in the quality plan.

options.text: Project charter
options.rationale: The charter is too high level to contain acceptance standards for individual deliverables.

questions.explanation: When a client disputes whether deliverables meet agreed standards, the reference point is the quality management plan, which records those standards and how compliance is shown. Using the agreed document turns an argument into a check.
questions.mindset: Settle quality disputes against the standards both sides agreed.

questions.stem: A customer is concerned that the current project deliverable will not fulfill stated project requirements. What could be done to alleviate customer concerns?

options.text: Schedule a meeting to remind the customer of requirements previously communicated to the team.
options.rationale: Reminding the customer of earlier requirements is defensive and assumes the team has understood them correctly.

options.text: Document the customer's concern as a risk in the risk register and plan accordingly.
options.rationale: Logging a risk records the concern but does nothing to reassure the customer or align expectations.

options.text: Manage the concern at the review of each deliverable with the customer.
options.rationale: Waiting until each deliverable review to address the concern leaves the customer worried and risks rework.

options.text: Ask a product owner to review the acceptance criteria previously discussed with the customer.
options.rationale: Having the product owner revisit the acceptance criteria with the customer confirms, in concrete terms, what done looks like for each requirement.

questions.explanation: Customer anxiety about whether requirements will be met is best answered by making acceptance criteria explicit and shared. Clear criteria, agreed with the customer by the product owner, align expectations before delivery rather than after.
questions.mindset: Turn customer concerns into explicit, agreed acceptance criteria.

questions.stem: A major project deliverable is completed. What should the project manager and team do to confirm that specifications have been met?

options.text: Check the organizational process assets.
options.rationale: Organisational process assets are templates and policies; they do not test whether this deliverable meets its specifications.

options.text: Validate the quality audit reports.
options.rationale: Quality audits examine processes, not whether an individual deliverable conforms.

options.text: Verify the scope.
options.rationale: Scope validation is the customer's formal acceptance and comes after the team has verified the deliverable internally.

options.text: Perform quality control.
options.rationale: Quality control inspects and tests the deliverable against its specifications, confirming correctness before customer validation.

questions.explanation: Quality control checks deliverables for correctness against specifications; scope validation then obtains the customer's acceptance. Internal verification comes first so that what is presented for acceptance has already been confirmed to conform.
questions.mindset: Verify correctness internally before seeking acceptance externally.

questions.stem: A project manager leads two highly motivated teams who typically work on 3-4 concurrent short projects with tight deadlines. Recently, communication, morale, and project performance have declined across teams and the project manager wants to improve team effectiveness and project success. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Implement a new collaboration tool to facilitate communication between both teams.
options.rationale: A new tool may help later, but introducing it before understanding the causes of decline risks solving the wrong problem.

options.text: Conduct individual performance reviews to identify and address performance issues within each team.
options.rationale: Individual reviews treat a cross-team decline as individual failings and may damage trust further.

options.text: Organize team-building activities to increase team cohesion and boost morale.
options.rationale: Team-building can lift morale briefly but does not uncover what is actually driving the decline.

options.text: Facilitate open communication sessions to identify and address underlying challenges.
options.rationale: Open sessions let both teams surface what is getting in the way, giving the PM real causes to act on and the teams ownership of the fix.

questions.explanation: When communication, morale and performance decline together, the causes are usually systemic — workload, priorities, handoffs. Facilitated, open conversation surfaces those causes and engages the teams in solving them, which is more effective than prescribing tools or events.
questions.mindset: Let the team name the problem before prescribing the cure.

questions.stem: A project team has not been performing user acceptance tests on a deliverable because the product has been working as expected in other projects. However, after implementation, the product is not operational. What should the project manager do to identify the source of the problem?

options.text: Review the quality metrics document.
options.rationale: The quality metrics document describes what to measure; it does not explain why this product failed.

options.text: Develop a scatter diagram.
options.rationale: A scatter diagram shows correlation between two variables and is not the right starting tool for finding a single failure's cause.

options.text: Conduct a root cause analysis.
options.rationale: Root cause analysis finds the underlying reason for the failure, such as the skipped acceptance tests, so it can be fixed and prevented.

options.text: Perform an audit.
options.rationale: An audit reviews compliance with processes more broadly and is slower to pinpoint the cause of this particular failure.

questions.explanation: When a product fails in operation, root cause analysis establishes why, rather than just what. Here it is likely to expose the decision to skip user acceptance testing on the assumption that success elsewhere guarantees success here.
questions.mindset: Find the root cause before fixing the failure.

questions.stem: A project team in the middle of an incremental delivery project decided they need the help of a subject matter expert (SME) who is working in a different department. The project team asked the SME to join their team and assist in a specific task and they informed the project leader about this action. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Check the project budget and assess the impact and feasibility of adding an additional resource
options.rationale: Budget checks may matter, but the team has acted within its working agreement; the PM's job is to support coordination.

options.text: Talk with the project sponsor and get approval, explaining that this resource is important and crucial
options.rationale: Going to the sponsor for approval treats a routine team coordination as an exceptional request.

options.text: Talk to the functional manager of this needed resource and check their availability and bandwidth
options.rationale: Checking availability with the functional manager is part of coordination but is only one piece of it.

options.text: Facilitate the coordination of resources with the needed resources based on the teams working agreement
options.rationale: Facilitating coordination according to the team's working agreement supports the self-organising team while respecting other departments.

questions.explanation: Self-organising teams often coordinate directly with specialists elsewhere. The project manager supports that coordination within the team's working agreement, clearing organisational obstacles rather than re-centralising the decision.
questions.mindset: Support the team's self-organisation by smoothing coordination, not taking it over.

questions.stem: A new member joined a project during the execution phase. The work requires strong collaboration with other team members. What should the project manager do to foster a collaborative environment?

options.text: Send an email to the project team asking them to collaborate with the new team member.
options.rationale: An email asking people to collaborate is passive and unlikely to build working relationships.

options.text: Share all information available and allocate time to explain in detail the work in progress.
options.rationale: Sharing all information is thorough, but it is one-way and does not build connections with teammates.

options.text: Ask each member to describe their interests and experience in the next team meeting.
options.rationale: Introductions at the next meeting help but are too brief to establish collaboration on complex work.

options.text: Organize a one-day workshop with the entire team to bring the new member up to speed.
options.rationale: A focused workshop brings the new member up to speed with the whole team, building relationships and shared understanding at once.

questions.explanation: Collaboration depends on relationships and shared context. Deliberately investing time to integrate a new member with the team, not just transferring documents, sets the conditions for effective joint work.
questions.mindset: Invest time to integrate new members, not just inform them.

questions.stem: A project leader and a product owner had a side conversation about the status of the next delivery. The product owner raised concerns about the way the architecture owner is dealing with the coming delivery. What should the project leader do to address this issue?

options.text: Reassure the product owner not to worry and ask them to attend the daily meetings.
options.rationale: Reassuring the product owner not to worry dismisses a legitimate concern.

options.text: Share the product owner's concerns with the architecture owner and ask for their opinion.
options.rationale: Passing the concern only to the architecture owner keeps it bilateral and misses the team's perspectives.

options.text: Ask the product owner not to get involved and ignore the concerns until after the delivery.
options.rationale: Telling the product owner to ignore the concern suppresses information the team may need.

options.text: Make sure that team members attend daily meetings to discuss and resolve issues.
options.rationale: Bringing the issue into the team's daily forum lets it be discussed openly and resolved with everyone's input.

questions.explanation: Agile teams resolve issues openly. Concerns raised in side conversations should be brought into team forums where all perspectives can be heard and solutions agreed collectively.
questions.mindset: Move side-conversation concerns into the open team forum.

questions.stem: A project manager is reviewing work performance data in preparation for the close project process. The data reveals that one of the deliverables was not accepted. The estimated work required to complete acceptance of the deliverable will delay the project completion date by two months. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Allocate the contingency reserve to procure resources needed for completion.
options.rationale: Using contingency reserve to fund unapproved extra work bypasses the decision about a two-month delay.

options.text: Update the schedule and perform the work.
options.rationale: Updating the schedule and doing the work without approval changes the baseline informally.

options.text: Issue a change request for review by the change control board (CCB).
options.rationale: A change request lets the CCB decide how to handle the unaccepted deliverable and the two-month schedule impact.

options.text: Update the watch list in the risk register.
options.rationale: The watch list is for low-priority risks; this is a confirmed problem with significant impact.

questions.explanation: When a deliverable fails acceptance and completing it would change the schedule baseline, the corrective work goes through integrated change control. The decision about delay and cost belongs to the change authority, not to the project manager alone.
questions.mindset: Let the change authority decide on baseline-changing corrective work.
