questions.stem: A project manager notices that a project is not running well and deliverables are falling behind. What is the first step the project manager should take in order to make a decision on how to progress with the project?

options.text: Identify the problem.
options.rationale: Identifying the problem clearly is the first step, because everything else depends on understanding what is actually wrong.

options.text: Brainstorm solutions.
options.rationale: Brainstorming solutions before defining the problem risks solving the wrong thing.

options.text: Establish a measurement criteria.
options.rationale: Measurement criteria follow once the problem and goal are understood.

options.text: Set a goal.
options.rationale: A goal cannot be set sensibly until the problem is defined.

questions.explanation: Problem-solving follows a sequence: define the problem, analyse causes, generate options, choose and implement, then measure. Skipping the definition step leads to effort spent on symptoms or the wrong issue.
questions.mindset: Define the problem before solving it.

questions.stem: A project manager begins to notice disengaged members arriving late, not delivering on time, not attending meetings, and producing low-quality deliveries. What action should the project manager take?

options.text: Investigate the reason for the team members' disengaged behavior and boost morale and participation.
options.rationale: Investigating why people are disengaged, then acting to rebuild morale and participation, addresses the cause of the behaviours.

options.text: Ask the team members to change the way they are working to match the newest work trends.
options.rationale: Asking people to adopt new work trends assumes the cause without evidence.

options.text: Encourage the team to double their efforts to pick up the slack from the disengaged team members.
options.rationale: Asking others to compensate overloads them and spreads disengagement.

options.text: Request that the team members abandon the process that is slowing their progress.
options.rationale: Abandoning a process without knowing if it is the cause is a guess.

questions.explanation: Disengagement shows up as lateness, missed deadlines and poor quality, but these are symptoms. Understanding the causes — workload, clarity, recognition, conflict — is what allows the project manager to restore engagement.
questions.mindset: Treat disengagement as a symptom to be understood.

questions.stem: A project manager needs to close out a project and does not have time to update the lessons learned register. What could be a consequence of this failure to act?

options.text: Work performance data would be incomplete and unavailable for analysis.
options.rationale: Work performance data is collected during execution and is not affected by the lessons learned register.

options.text: Opportunities to prevent similar problems in future projects could be missed.
options.rationale: Without captured lessons, the organisation loses the chance to avoid the same problems on future projects.

options.text: The project management plan could be inaccurate and misleading.
options.rationale: The management plan is not made inaccurate by an un-updated lessons register.

options.text: Key stakeholders would refuse to engage in future projects.
options.rationale: Stakeholder refusal to engage in future projects is speculative and unrelated.

questions.explanation: Lessons learned exist to transfer experience to future work. Skipping them at closure means repeating avoidable mistakes and missing reusable practices.
questions.mindset: Capture lessons so the next project starts wiser.

questions.stem: A delivery milestone for a project is fast approaching, but an item that is planned to be completed is at risk. A team member begins to act defensively and is blaming others for this issue. How should the project manager have acted to avoid this?

options.text: Established ground rules for interaction that the whole team must follow.
options.rationale: Ground rules for interaction set expectations for how the team handles problems, discouraging blame when pressure rises.

options.text: Established and maintained meaningful relationships between team members.
options.rationale: Relationships help, but without agreed norms pressure can still produce defensiveness and blame.

options.text: Established formal patterns of authority, responsibility, and accountability.
options.rationale: Formal authority structures define who decides, not how people should behave under pressure.

options.text: Established clear delegation and accountability-sharing principles.
options.rationale: Delegation principles clarify responsibilities but do not govern how team members speak to each other.

questions.explanation: Pressure brings out defensive behaviour unless norms exist for how issues are raised and discussed. Ground rules agreed early give the team a standard to hold each other to when things go wrong.
questions.mindset: Agree how to handle problems before the problems arrive.

questions.stem: A project is in the testing phase, and the quality control team informs the project manager that the quality of the deliverables from one vendor is poor. Their investigation found that the staff assigned does not have the required certifications. How did this issue arise?

options.text: The vendors' proposal did not include the list of people assigned to the project.
options.rationale: A missing staff list may be a symptom, but the root cause is that certification requirements were not specified.

options.text: The project sponsor did not mandate three references from previous customers.
options.rationale: References show past performance, not whether current staff hold required certifications.

options.text: The Procurement Management Plan did not include the certifications required
options.rationale: The procurement plan should specify required qualifications and certifications; leaving them out allowed unqualified staff to be assigned.

options.text: The quality control team had too high of standards and tested too thoroughly
options.rationale: The quality team was doing its job; the fault lies upstream in procurement requirements.

questions.explanation: Supplier quality depends on the requirements set in procurement. Qualifications, certifications and standards must be written into the procurement plan and contracts so they can be enforced.
questions.mindset: Specify supplier qualifications before the contract, not after the defects.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a Scrum team. During Business Acceptance Testing (BAT), the client rejects the deliverable due to poor quality, traced back to a lack of collaboration between team members. What should have the project manager done to prevent this?

options.text: Provided detailed instructions on how and when the work should be done.
options.rationale: Detailed instructions micromanage the team and undermine the self-organisation Scrum relies on.

options.text: Requested detailed documentation and sign-offs between project phases.
options.rationale: Documentation and sign-offs between phases add process but do not create collaboration.

options.text: Implemented detailed tracking of project progress, productivity, and costs.
options.rationale: Tracking progress and cost monitors output without building collaboration.

options.text: Provided a detailed vision and empowered the team making them accountable.
options.rationale: A clear vision combined with empowerment makes the team accountable for outcomes, encouraging collaboration and quality.

questions.explanation: Scrum teams produce quality when they share a vision and own the outcome. Empowerment with accountability fosters collaboration, while command-and-control or heavy tracking works against it.
questions.mindset: Give the team a clear vision and the authority to achieve it.

questions.stem: A project to develop a new product is nearing its closing phase after 6 months of contributions from the project team and vendor. The project manager has confirmed that the project satisfied the strategic goal it was meant to achieve and received formal documented acceptance from the client and sponsor. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Review all contracts with the project team and suppliers.
options.rationale: Reviewing contracts confirms all parties have met their obligations so that procurements can be formally closed.

options.text: Disband the project team and return resources to their functional location.
options.rationale: Releasing the team before contracts are closed risks losing people who can resolve open items.

options.text: Ensure customer care teams have the training to perform their role.
options.rationale: Customer care training is operational readiness work, which should already be complete by acceptance.

options.text: Document lessons learned for future reference.
options.rationale: Lessons learned are important but contract closure comes first to avoid open obligations.

questions.explanation: After formal acceptance, closure includes confirming all contractual obligations are satisfied and closing procurements. Resources are released and lessons captured once open commitments are resolved.
questions.mindset: Close contracts before closing the team.

questions.stem: A project manager is involved in an e-commerce development project. The project has been completed successfully using the hybrid model and initiated operations handover. The project manager notices that the development team is relaxed and not spending time on the handover process, which is impacting application support. How should the project manager handle this situation?

options.text: Confront the development team and demand their immediate attention to the handover process.
options.rationale: Confrontation damages relationships and may produce minimal compliance.

options.text: Meet with the development team to discuss the importance of the handover process and its impact on application support.
options.rationale: Explaining why the handover matters and its impact on support gets the team's genuine engagement.

options.text: Delegate the responsibility of the handover process to another team member to ensure it gets done properly.
options.rationale: Delegating to one person may overload them and still lacks the development team's knowledge.

options.text: Disregard the issue and expect that the development team will address and resolve the issue on their own.
options.rationale: Ignoring the problem risks poor support after go-live.

questions.explanation: Handover is part of delivery. Teams sometimes see it as optional after the main work ends; explaining its importance and impact on operations restores focus.
questions.mindset: Treat handover as part of delivery, not an afterthought.

questions.stem: A project manager is managing a project that has a component using agile. The project sponsor asks the project manager to add a new component to this project which is government regulated with new complex tax-rules with enough time provided to implement these rules. The sponsor suggests implementing this new component using predictive non-agile approach due to its complexity. Which methodology will the project manager use for this new component?

options.text: Inform the project sponsor that you will manage the new component using agile methodology as agile supports one-size-fits-all.
options.rationale: No single method fits every situation; imposing agile ignores the sponsor's valid concern.

options.text: Use hybrid approach by continuing to manage the existing component using agile, and the new component using predictive.
options.rationale: Keeping agile for the existing component and predictive for the regulated one tailors each to its needs.

options.text: Manage the existing component as well as the new component using predictive plan-based approach.
options.rationale: Switching everything to predictive loses the benefits for the existing agile component.

options.text: Seek guidance from project sponsor for which methodology will suit best for new component.
options.rationale: Deferring the choice to the sponsor abdicates the PM's responsibility for tailoring the approach.

questions.explanation: Hybrid approaches let different components use the life cycle that suits them. Stable, rule-driven regulatory work may suit predictive planning while evolving features continue iteratively.
questions.mindset: Tailor the approach per component.

questions.stem: Project completion will be delayed because an essential component will not be delivered on time. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Consult with stakeholders and revise the project schedule to reflect the delay.
options.rationale: Revising the schedule before understanding the impact is premature.

options.text: Review the scope management plan to understand how acceptance of project deliverables could still be obtained.
options.rationale: Acceptance criteria are not the issue; the component is late.

options.text: Check the procurement contract for penalties that can be imposed on the supplier of the component.
options.rationale: Penalties may be relevant later but do not address the project's needs now.

options.text: Evaluate the impact of the delay before deciding what actions are necessary.
options.rationale: Evaluating the delay's impact on successors and the finish date comes before choosing a response.

questions.explanation: A late supplier delivery is first analysed for impact: which activities depend on it and what the finish date consequences are. Options such as workarounds, re-sequencing or contract remedies follow from that analysis.
questions.mindset: Analyse impact before choosing a response to a delay.

questions.stem: A project has components that are outsourced and the project manager is in the control phase of the procurement process. What should the project manager focus on doing?

options.text: Finalize the contract and pay the vendors.
options.rationale: Finalising contracts and paying vendors belongs to closing, not control.

options.text: Develop a procurement plan and identify potential vendors.
options.rationale: Developing the procurement plan and identifying vendors is planning.

options.text: Issue requests for proposals and select vendors.
options.rationale: Issuing RFPs and selecting vendors is conducting procurement.

options.text: Evaluate the performance of one of the major project vendors.
options.rationale: Evaluating vendor performance against the contract is the focus of control procurements.

questions.explanation: Procurement has stages: plan, conduct, control and close. During control, the project manager monitors vendor performance, manages changes and resolves issues against the contract.
questions.mindset: In control, monitor what was contracted.

questions.stem: A project manager needs to close a project phase. What step should project manager take?

options.text: Ensure deliverables have full buy-in according to decision process established for phase.
options.rationale: Buy-in is part of acceptance, but closure requires confirming all phase objectives are met.

options.text: Compare project deliverables with project charter and request customer sign off.
options.rationale: Comparing with the charter is too high level and sign-off is only one part.

options.text: Review high-level strategic and operational assumptions and constraints with stakeholders.
options.rationale: Strategic assumptions are not reviewed at phase closure.

options.text: Review project management plan to ensure phase objectives have been met.
options.rationale: Reviewing the management plan confirms the phase's work and objectives are complete before it is closed.

questions.explanation: Closing a phase requires confirming that all planned work is complete and objectives are met. The project management plan is the reference for what the phase committed to deliver.
questions.mindset: Close against the plan's objectives.

questions.stem: A project was cancelled during its initiation phase due to lack of adequate resources. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Inform all team members according to guidelines in the communications management plan.
options.rationale: Team members may not yet be assigned in initiation, so the communications plan may not exist.

options.text: Refer to the company's project closure guidelines.
options.rationale: Company closure guidelines define how to close a cancelled project properly.

options.text: Perform a risk analysis to determine the impact of terminating the project.
options.rationale: Risk analysis of termination is not needed after the decision.

options.text: Reassign all resources and reallocate budget.
options.rationale: Resources and budget may not yet be allocated during initiation.

questions.explanation: Even cancelled projects must be closed properly. Organisational closure procedures specify the steps, ensuring records and knowledge are preserved.
questions.mindset: Follow closure procedures even when cancelling early.

questions.stem: A project has begun to develop a new software application that will be used by the company's sales team. The project is expected to take six months to complete and has a budget of $100,000. The project manager has identified software development tools, hardware, and training to be procured. What is the most important thing for the project manager to do while developing the procurement plan?

options.text: Ensure that all resources will be procured within budget.
options.rationale: Staying within budget is the key constraint to respect when planning procurement.

options.text: Ensure that the project is on schedule with no delays.
options.rationale: Schedule is important but procurement planning here focuses on the budget constraint.

options.text: Ensure that all procured resources are of great quality.
options.rationale: Quality matters, but 'great quality' without regard to budget is not the planning priority.

options.text: Ensure that all resources will be procured on schedule.
options.rationale: Timing matters but budget is the stated constraint.

questions.explanation: Procurement planning must fit the project's constraints. With a fixed budget, ensuring purchases fit within it is the primary planning consideration.
questions.mindset: Plan procurement within the project's binding constraint.

questions.stem: A project stakeholder has been missing scheduled facilitation workshops and has delegated assigned tasks to another member of the stakeholder community. What should the project manager do to engage this stakeholder?

options.text: Review with the stakeholder the roles and responsibilities of everyone involved as specified in the project charter.
options.rationale: Reviewing roles and responsibilities reminds the stakeholder of their commitments.

options.text: Explain to the stakeholder the differences among the tasks assigned to each project team member.
options.rationale: Explaining task differences does not address missed participation.

options.text: Ask the program manager to brief this stakeholder and to require the stakeholder's attendance at all relevant meetings.
options.rationale: Using the program manager to enforce attendance escalates too early.

options.text: Pair the stakeholder with a more experienced team member who can act as a mentor.
options.rationale: Mentoring is not appropriate for engagement issues with a stakeholder.

questions.explanation: When stakeholders disengage, clarifying their roles and responsibilities as agreed in the charter re-establishes expectations.
questions.mindset: Re-anchor disengaged stakeholders to their agreed roles.

questions.stem: An intern is replacing a critical resource midway through a sprint. To help the intern get up to speed, the project manager assigns a senior engineer in the team as the intern's mentor. Two months later, the project goes into critical status, delaying the release milestone by a month. What should the project manager have done to avoid this scenario?

options.text: Convinced the critical resource to remain on the project.
options.rationale: The critical resource was leaving; trying to hold them does not address how the project absorbs a much less experienced replacement.

options.text: Requested an experienced resource as a replacement.
options.rationale: An experienced replacement might not have been available, and the question is about planning for the replacement the project actually got.

options.text: Negotiated additional time to complete the project.
options.rationale: Replacing a critical resource with an intern who needs mentoring lowers capacity for both the intern and the mentor, so negotiating extra time up front reflects the real capacity.

options.text: Allocated additional time for mentoring.
options.rationale: Adding mentoring time recognises the cost of mentoring but, without extending the schedule, takes that time from the senior engineer's own critical work.

questions.explanation: Swapping an experienced resource for a trainee reduces team capacity twice: the trainee is slower and the mentor loses time. The schedule must reflect that reality, which means renegotiating time when the substitution is made rather than discovering the slip at the milestone.
questions.mindset: When capacity drops, reset the schedule to the capacity you actually have.

questions.stem: The headquarters of a multinational company is in Europe, with many regional offices in other countries around the world. The operations director of a regional office decides to establish a project management office (PMO). A project manager has been selected to manage the project, which is in its initial phase. The project manager needs to align stakeholder expectations with the benefits of the project process and the business strategy. Which document should the project manager develop for this purpose?

options.text: Business case
options.rationale: The business case justifies the investment but is usually prepared before the PM is assigned and is not the alignment document for the project itself.

options.text: Benefits management plan
options.rationale: The benefits management plan explains how benefits are realised and tracked, but it does not formally align stakeholders on the project's purpose and authority.

options.text: Project charter
options.rationale: The charter sets out objectives, high-level scope, stakeholders and the link to strategy, and is the document stakeholders agree to at initiation.

options.text: Project management plan
options.rationale: The management plan is a planning output developed after initiation and is too detailed for aligning expectations at this stage.

questions.explanation: At initiation, the project charter is the vehicle for aligning stakeholders: it links the project to business strategy, states objectives and success criteria, and authorises the project manager. Later documents build on that agreed foundation.
questions.mindset: Align stakeholders on purpose and authority in the charter before planning detail.

questions.stem: A majority portion of a local company was recently sold to an international company. The new parent company is mandating the use of health, safety, and environmental (HSE) regulations for all projects in the local company. What should the project managers do to remain compliant?

options.text: Wait for the functional department responsible for HSE regulations to communicate the process change.
options.rationale: Waiting for the HSE function to announce changes is passive and risks non-compliance in the meantime.

options.text: Ask the functional department responsible for HSE regulations to assign a new team member.
options.rationale: Asking for a new team member presumes the solution before understanding what the regulations require.

options.text: Speak with the project sponsor to get clarification about the new HSE regulations.
options.rationale: The sponsor may not know the regulatory detail; the HSE specialists are the right source.

options.text: Meet with the HSE team to understand the impact of the new regulations on the projects.
options.rationale: Meeting the HSE team to understand the impact lets each project identify what must change to comply.

questions.explanation: When new compliance requirements are mandated, project managers act proactively: they engage the specialists who own the requirements to understand their impact on each project, then adjust plans accordingly.
questions.mindset: Go to the owners of a new requirement to understand its impact on your project.

questions.stem: A complex technology project is in the execution phase. New technologies are added to the backlog based on customer requirements, which will involve significant changes to the deliverable. What should the project manager do to satisfy the customer?

options.text: Replan the sprints and releases to meet every expectation of the customer.
options.rationale: Trying to meet every expectation leads to endless replanning and loses sight of business value.

options.text: Manage customer expectations based on the organization's business needs.
options.rationale: Managing the customer's expectations against the organisation's business needs keeps additions focused on value and feasible within constraints.

options.text: Accept the new requirements, and schedule meetings to plan a new release schedule.
options.rationale: Accepting all new requirements and replanning ignores their impact on value, cost and time.

options.text: Push the project team to increase flexibility and accept the new challenge.
options.rationale: Pushing the team to absorb significant changes risks burnout without deciding whether the changes are worthwhile.

questions.explanation: Satisfying customers does not mean saying yes to everything. It means aligning their expectations with the business goals the product serves, so that changes are judged by value and fit rather than accepted automatically.
questions.mindset: Satisfy customers by aligning expectations with business value, not by accepting every request.

questions.stem: A project manager is managing a hybrid project with a fixed time and fixed price agreement. The project manager is having difficulty getting the team to submit their time sheets. The feedback received from the team is that work will be delivered every two weeks, so no time sheets are required. However, the project manager needs the time sheets to complete a cost assessment of the project. What should the project manager do to ensure all team members submit their time sheets as required?

options.text: Ask the project management office (PMO) to ensure the team submits their time sheets.
options.rationale: Asking the PMO to enforce submission avoids explaining the reason and relies on authority rather than understanding.

options.text: Send a weekly reminder to each team member notifying them to submit their time sheets.
options.rationale: Reminders address forgetting, but the team has told you they think time sheets are unnecessary.

options.text: Explain the impact of not submitting time sheets on the project's cost assessment.
options.rationale: Explaining how time sheets feed the cost assessment answers the team's objection and gives them a reason to comply.

options.text: Change the submission frequency for the time sheets from biweekly to weekly.
options.rationale: Changing the frequency adds burden without addressing why people are not submitting.

questions.explanation: When a team resists an administrative requirement because it seems pointless, explain the purpose. Understanding how data is used, here for cost assessment on a fixed-price agreement, is more effective than enforcement or reminders.
questions.mindset: Explain why a requirement matters before enforcing it.

questions.stem: A department store chain is in the implementation stage of a project to replace the payment systems across all of its stores in multiple countries. The project planning followed a predictive approach, and implementation is based on multiple iterations for each country. Implementation in country C is stalled due to new laws regulating the security of the new payment solution implementation. Which two actions should the project manager take to avoid a significant delay on the project? (Choose two)

options.text: Monitor compliance with the laws of each country continuously during planning and after implementation in each country.
options.rationale: Continuous monitoring of each country's legal requirements catches changes early and prevents similar stalls elsewhere.

options.text: Document the legal compliance risks in the project management plan for country C in the implementation phase and iterations.
options.rationale: Documenting risks for country C is useful but does not reduce the current delay.

options.text: Deploy alternative systems compatible with the security standards and legal framework for country C.
options.rationale: Deploying an alternative system is a major decision that may not be feasible or compliant without analysis.

options.text: Execute another country's implementation phase after validating the compliance standards while a solution is prepared for country C.
options.rationale: Resequencing to implement in another compliant country while a solution for country C is prepared keeps the project moving.

options.text: Communicate the delay in the project to the steering committee, and place the project on hold until a decision is reached.
options.rationale: Putting the whole project on hold spreads one country's problem to all the others.

questions.explanation: In multi-country rollouts, legal changes in one jurisdiction should not halt everything. Monitoring compliance continuously and resequencing work so compliant countries proceed while issues are resolved limits delay.
questions.mindset: Keep delivering where you can while you solve where you cannot.

questions.stem: During a new technology project, confusion arises due to the lack of a clearly defined and communicated future state of the product. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Create and get approval on a benefits management plan.
options.rationale: A benefits management plan defines the intended future state, the benefits and how they will be realised, removing the confusion.

options.text: Ask the project sponsor what the project outcome should be.
options.rationale: Asking the sponsor for the outcome is a start, but it does not produce an agreed, documented definition.

options.text: Discuss the scope and objectives with the functional owner.
options.rationale: The functional owner may help with scope but not with defining the benefits and future state.

options.text: Review the project's business case to identify alternatives.
options.rationale: The business case justifies the investment; reviewing it for alternatives does not clarify the target state.

questions.explanation: Confusion about the future state is a benefits clarity problem. A benefits management plan articulates what the project should achieve, how value will be realised and measured, and gives the team a shared target.
questions.mindset: Make the intended future state explicit and agreed.

questions.stem: A new regulation has been approved that will impact the deliverables in the fourth phase of the project. The delivery is following an iterative approach and is currently completing the second phase. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Consult with the project sponsor to discuss a cost increase.
options.rationale: Discussing cost increases assumes an impact that has not been assessed.

options.text: Get approval for the additional budget from the steering committee.
options.rationale: Asking for budget before knowing the impact is premature.

options.text: Meet with subject matter experts (SMEs) to assess the impact to objectives.
options.rationale: Meeting SMEs to assess the impact on objectives is the right first step before deciding on changes.

options.text: Acquire approval for an exception to the implementation of the new regulation.
options.rationale: Seeking an exemption from a new regulation is rarely appropriate and presumes non-compliance.

questions.explanation: A regulatory change affecting future deliverables should be analysed before it is acted on. Expert assessment of the impact on scope, cost, schedule and risk informs whatever changes follow.
questions.mindset: Assess the impact of external change with expert input first.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a wastewater treatment project for a factory. During project execution, the government unexpectedly releases new environmental protection standards that are stricter than the previous standards. To ensure compliance with these updated regulations, what should the project manager's initial course of action be?

options.text: Meet with the project team to assess the implications of the new government regulations on the project requirements.
options.rationale: Assessing the implications with the team establishes exactly how the new standards affect requirements before any decision.

options.text: Review the project's risk register to determine if this change was previously documented as a potential risk to the project.
options.rationale: Checking the risk register is useful, but the standards are now certain and the impact must be analysed regardless.

options.text: Draft a formal change request detailing the adjustments and submit it to the change control board (CCB) for evaluation.
options.rationale: A change request needs the impact assessment as its content, so it cannot come first.

options.text: Initiate discussions with the government agency to negotiate a revised timeline for adopting the new environmental standards.
options.rationale: Negotiating a timeline with the regulator presumes the project cannot comply and is not the first step.

questions.explanation: When regulations change during execution, the team first analyses the impact on requirements, scope, schedule and cost. That analysis becomes the basis for change requests and stakeholder communication.
questions.mindset: Understand the impact of new rules before deciding how to comply.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a critical project to deliver a new solution. The CEO is highly invested in the project, and the CFO is the product owner. During the testing phase, the CFO requests an additional nonfunctional requirement to shorten the frequency of transaction processing. This new requirement will impact the launch date, and the CFO is insistent on having it implemented. What should the project manager do to minimize the impact of the new requirement on the launch date and manage the expectations of the CEO and CFO?

options.text: Meet with the CFO and suggest delaying the implementation of the new requirement to the post-launch phase.
options.rationale: Suggesting a post-launch delay before understanding the impact may be the right answer, but it is premature.

options.text: Ask the CEO to intervene and stop the implementation of the new requirement, as development is complete.
options.rationale: Asking the CEO to block the product owner's request escalates prematurely and damages the relationship.

options.text: Tell the project team to update the product backlog with the new requirement and adjust the project plans.
options.rationale: Updating the backlog and plans without assessment accepts an unknown impact on the launch date.

options.text: Assess the scope of the new nonfunctional requirement to determine its specific impact on the planned go-live date.
options.rationale: Assessing the scope and specific impact on go-live gives the facts needed to discuss options with the CFO and CEO.

questions.explanation: When an influential stakeholder demands a late change, the project manager's credibility depends on facts. A precise impact assessment allows informed options — defer, phase or accept a delay — and helps manage expectations.
questions.mindset: Bring facts about impact to conversations with powerful stakeholders.

questions.stem: A team member suggests using a new product to speed up feature development, but this will increase the project budget. The project team is taking an incremental approach to product development, and the product owner is responsible for prioritizing and managing the product backlog. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Consult the product owner and present the benefits and drawbacks of using the new product.
options.rationale: The product owner decides trade-offs between value and cost in the backlog, so presenting benefits and drawbacks to them is the first step.

options.text: Review and update the cost management plan to accommodate the potential budget impact.
options.rationale: Updating the cost plan before a decision assumes approval.

options.text: Request additional funding for the implementation of the new product from the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Requesting funding before deciding the product is worth it skips the value decision.

options.text: Revise the acceptance criteria for the user stories to incorporate the new product effectively.
options.rationale: Changing acceptance criteria presumes the product will be used.

questions.explanation: In incremental delivery, trade-offs between speed, cost and value are decided by the product owner. The PM supports that decision with a clear view of benefits and costs.
questions.mindset: Give the value owner the information to make trade-offs.

questions.stem: A new customer relations database is being deployed. The schedule calls for migration from the previous system to occur over one weekend. However, some key stakeholders believe it may take more time for the migration. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Assess the concerns and risks of not deploying within the scheduled time frame and react accordingly.
options.rationale: Assessing the stakeholders' concerns and the risk of overrunning the weekend informs a proportionate response.

options.text: Change the deployment plan such that additional resources are available to perform the weekend deployment.
options.rationale: Adding resources assumes the problem is capacity without analysis.

options.text: Review and revise as necessary the risk management plan
options.rationale: Revising the risk management plan changes how risk is managed, not this specific risk.

options.text: Modify the schedule to increase the time frame of the deployment plan.
options.rationale: Extending the window may not be possible and presumes the concern is correct.

questions.explanation: Stakeholder concern that a plan is unrealistic is a risk signal. Assessing that risk — likelihood, impact and response options — lets the project respond proportionately rather than overreacting or ignoring it.
questions.mindset: Treat stakeholder doubts as risk signals and analyse them.

questions.stem: A team is working on a new product using a gated approach. After the third sprint they noticed that the market needs may be changing, and the product may not fit the new market needs. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Survey the market for possible impacts on the project.
options.rationale: Surveying the market establishes whether the needs really have changed and how they affect the product.

options.text: Change the product’s scope to meet the new needs.
options.rationale: Changing scope before confirming the market shift may waste effort.

options.text: Finalize the product on time and budget to launch as planned.
options.rationale: Launching as planned risks delivering a product the market no longer wants.

options.text: Review the backlog to see the impact of the new needs.
options.rationale: Reviewing the backlog is useful after the new needs are understood.

questions.explanation: External market changes must be understood before scope decisions are made. Gathering evidence about the market's new needs allows the team to adjust scope deliberately rather than guess.
questions.mindset: Check the market before changing the product.

questions.stem: A new system is being developed to replace an existing manual process. During a sprint demo, business stakeholders expressed the concern that they would not gain any value from using this system. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Discuss this with the product manager and identify new user stories to address business concerns.
options.rationale: Creating new stories assumes the concern is valid before checking against agreed metrics.

options.text: Call a steering committee meeting to determine critical success factors for the project.
options.rationale: Critical success factors should already exist; a steering meeting to create them is late.

options.text: Create a project benefits management plan and review it with the stakeholders.
options.rationale: A benefits plan should already exist; creating one now does not answer the immediate concern.

options.text: Review the performance metrics with stakeholders to ensure the system accomplished agreed-upon metrics.
options.rationale: Reviewing the agreed performance metrics with stakeholders checks objectively whether the system delivers the expected value.

questions.explanation: When stakeholders doubt the value of what is being delivered, return to the agreed measures of success. Objective metrics show whether concerns reflect a real shortfall or a need for better communication.
questions.mindset: Answer doubts about value with the agreed measures.

questions.stem: After several interviews with key stakeholders and checking the project charter, a project manager found that the current project organizational structure is no longer appropriate for the project's strategic goals. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Assess the lessons learned documents and validate which organizational structure was used in the past for similar projects.
options.rationale: Past structures may not fit this project's strategic goals.

options.text: Ask the team to document the risk in the project risk register and develop a risk response plan accordingly.
options.rationale: Treating the misfit as a risk to log delays addressing a known problem.

options.text: Evaluate the gaps between the current organizationalstructure and the expected project benefits to determine required actions.
options.rationale: Evaluating the gaps between the current structure and the expected benefits identifies the changes needed.

options.text: Ask the team to review the project charter and evaluate the project objectives for relevance.
options.rationale: The charter's objectives are not in question; the structure is.

questions.explanation: Project structures should support the project's goals. When they no longer fit, a gap analysis between current structure and what is needed to realise benefits identifies the required governance or organisational changes.
questions.mindset: Shape the project structure to the outcomes it must deliver.

questions.stem: During the last iteration of planning in an agile project, the team discovers that mandatory regulations were not included in the minimum viable product (MVP). What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the team to include this regulatory requirement in the iteration backlog.
options.rationale: The team does not set backlog priority; the product owner does.

options.text: Ask the product owner to review the priority of this regulatory requirement.
options.rationale: The product owner orders the backlog and can prioritise mandatory regulatory requirements into the MVP.

options.text: Ask the stakeholders to review the priority of this regulatory requirement.
options.rationale: Stakeholders provide input, but priority decisions sit with the product owner.

options.text: Ask the sponsor for approval to include this regulatory requirement in the iteration backlog.
options.rationale: Sponsor approval is not needed to reorder the backlog.

questions.explanation: Mandatory regulatory items are part of a viable product. In agile, the product owner prioritises them in the backlog so the MVP is compliant.
questions.mindset: Make mandatory items part of the minimum.

questions.stem: The local government regulator has issued a notification to all companies regarding a new project aimed at facilitating information reporting to an international regulator. However, due to the dynamic nature of the project, there is a possibility of changing requirements while the delivery date remains fixed. The project manager assigned to this initiative is concerned about the uncertainty and the short timeline for delivery. How should the project manager best prepare to address this situation?

options.text: Implement iterative and incremental approaches in relevant areas of the project to adapt to changing requirements.
options.rationale: Iterative and incremental approaches let the team deliver while requirements evolve within the fixed date.

options.text: Meet with the sponsor to determine a detailed project schedule to ensure that the project is completed on time.
options.rationale: A detailed schedule assumes stable requirements, which is not the case.

options.text: Develop a detailed contingency plan using the crashing technique to expedite project activities as needed.
options.rationale: Crashing adds cost and does not deal with changing requirements.

options.text: Enhance communication strategies and engagement with the local government to ensure alignment and timely updates.
options.rationale: Better communication helps but does not provide a delivery approach for uncertainty.

questions.explanation: Fixed deadlines with changing requirements favour iterative and incremental delivery. The team can prioritise, adapt and deliver usable increments while the requirements settle.
questions.mindset: When requirements move and dates do not, iterate.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned to a legacy system modernization project. The project management plan is solidified and the requirements have been handed off to the IT department for development. However, the company's CEO announces the company's new strategic direction and upcoming plans for an enterprise resource planning (ERP) implementation. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the project sponsor for recommendations to keep the project on track.
options.rationale: Sponsor recommendations help, but the key question is whether the project still fits the strategy.

options.text: Understand and clarify how the existing project aligns with the overall organization vision.
options.rationale: Clarifying how the project aligns with the new vision determines whether it should continue, change or stop.

options.text: Conduct a project team meeting to plan and confirm resource assignments for the new project.
options.rationale: Planning resources for a new project is outside the PM's current remit.

options.text: Review the project schedule to ensure the project will be completed on time.
options.rationale: Checking the schedule assumes the project should continue unchanged.

questions.explanation: When strategy changes, every project's alignment must be rechecked. Continuing unchanged risks delivering something the organisation no longer needs.
questions.mindset: Recheck alignment whenever strategy changes.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a project that received a request for additional scope caused by changes in market demand. The change request also seeks a more rapid delivery time frame. Which two actions should the project manager take? (Choose two)

options.text: Assess company performance and the scope of other projects to ensure minimal impact.
options.rationale: Assessing other projects is not the priority for evaluating this change.

options.text: Organize a workshop with the sponsors and ask them to increase the project budget.
options.rationale: Asking for more budget before validating the change is premature.

options.text: Collect data and analyze the business environment to validate the business benefits.
options.rationale: Analysing the business environment validates whether the change delivers the claimed benefits.

options.text: Assess new technologies and competitors, then benchmark the change against them.
options.rationale: Benchmarking against competitors is useful but secondary to validating the benefits.

options.text: Organize a risk workshop, then update the risk management plan and the risk register.
options.rationale: A risk workshop and register update capture the new risks introduced by more scope in less time.

questions.explanation: A change driven by market demand needs its business benefits validated and its risks understood. Both feed the change request so decision-makers can weigh value against risk.
questions.mindset: Validate benefits and assess risk for every significant change.

questions.stem: A project manager is developing a project charter, but a key stakeholder is failing to provide information about the expected project benefits. Why should the project manager meet with the project sponsor about this issue?

options.text: The project sponsor is the key person responsible for managing both tacit and explicit project knowledge.
options.rationale: Knowledge management is the PM's responsibility, not the sponsor's.

options.text: The project sponsor is the party who can address internal political and strategic issues that can affect project quality.
options.rationale: The sponsor can address political and strategic issues that prevent a stakeholder from contributing.

options.text: The project sponsor can request that the change control board (CCB) make a change in the stakeholder community.
options.rationale: The change control board decides on changes to baselines; it does not add or remove people from the stakeholder community.

options.text: Disciplinary actions regarding stakeholders are managed by the project sponsor.
options.rationale: The sponsor may have no disciplinary authority and discipline is not the aim.

questions.explanation: Sponsors provide authority and influence the PM lacks. When a key stakeholder is not engaging, the sponsor can resolve organisational obstacles and secure their contribution.
questions.mindset: Use the sponsor's influence where yours does not reach.

questions.stem: Due to a downturn in the business environment, a customer is only able to make a project's payment in part, rather than the fully committed monthly payment. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Discuss it with management and pause the project because of the customer's budget constraint.
options.rationale: Pausing the project creates a lose-lose outcome.

options.text: Deliver the features with the highest business value, based on the available budget.
options.rationale: Delivering the highest-value features within the available budget maximises value for the customer.

options.text: Deliver the features that have small independent components, based on the available budget.
options.rationale: Choosing small independent components optimises for ease, not value.

options.text: Continue with the planned development and deliver only when full payment is made.
options.rationale: Waiting for full payment stalls delivery and value.

questions.explanation: When funding shrinks, the question becomes what to deliver with the money available. Prioritising by business value ensures the customer gets the features that matter most, rather than pausing, waiting or choosing work by ease of delivery.
questions.mindset: Spend reduced funds on the highest-value work.

questions.stem: A critical software development project has been in development for the past six sprints. A demonstration for stakeholders took place two days before the final sprint, in which a new stakeholder voiced that the product would not meet expectations for the market. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Discuss the matter with the project sponsor and new stakeholder and request them to fix the expectation issue.
options.rationale: Asking the sponsor and stakeholder to fix it themselves abdicates the PM's role.

options.text: Review the scope and plan of the project with the new stakeholder.
options.rationale: Reviewing the scope and plan with the new stakeholder clarifies what was agreed and exposes any real gap.

options.text: Review the list of required tasks with the development team and new stakeholder.
options.rationale: A task list is too detailed and misses the scope conversation.

options.text: Follow the change management plan and revise the scope and plan upon the stakeholders' request.
options.rationale: Revising scope before understanding the concern assumes the stakeholder is right.

questions.explanation: Late-joining stakeholders may not know the agreed scope. Reviewing it with them clarifies expectations and reveals whether the concern warrants a change.
questions.mindset: Bring new stakeholders up to speed before changing course for them.

questions.stem: During the execution phase of a project, a new project manager is assigned to replace the previous project manager. As the project manager starts managing the project, they discover that team performance is significantly decreasing, which is impacting the project's key performance indicators (KPIs). This team has delivered good performance on similar projects in the past. What should the project manager do next to improve this situation?

options.text: Review the resource management plan and organizational assets.
options.rationale: Plans and assets do not reveal why a proven team is struggling.

options.text: Implement compression techniques to bring the project back on track.
options.rationale: Compression techniques treat the schedule symptom.

options.text: Call for a team meeting to identify the root cause for the declining performance.
options.rationale: A team meeting to find the root cause — possibly the change of leader — builds trust and targets the real problem.

options.text: Estimate the baseline impacts and submit a change request.
options.rationale: A change request is premature before understanding causes.

questions.explanation: When a previously high-performing team declines after a change of leader, the cause may be the transition itself. Engaging the team openly to find the root cause is the first step.
questions.mindset: When performance changes, ask the team why.

questions.stem: A project manager recognizes the need to improve team dynamics and knowledge sharing during a megaproject. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Conduct knowledge-sharing sessions where experienced team members present their expertise.
options.rationale: Presentation sessions are one-way and do not reveal the team's actual needs.

options.text: Assign junior team members tasks that push their skill level and offer minimal support.
options.rationale: Stretch assignments with minimal support can lead to failure and discouragement, and they do nothing to improve how the team shares knowledge.

options.text: Implement a formal mentoring program with structured goals and regular meetings.
options.rationale: Formal mentoring is valuable but heavyweight without knowing what the team needs.

options.text: Facilitate open team discussions to identify and address individual challenges and concerns.
options.rationale: Open discussion identifies individual challenges and builds dynamics and knowledge sharing.

questions.explanation: Improving team dynamics starts by understanding the team's challenges. Open discussion creates a safe space and shows what knowledge-sharing is needed.
questions.mindset: Start improvement with the team's own view of its challenges.

questions.stem: A team is assembled for a new project that will be using a predictive approach through requirements gathering and an agile approach for development and testing. Not everyone on the team has experience working in agile. The schedule has started slipping due to the unclear structure of the agile development approach. What should the project manager have done to avoid this situation?

options.text: Set up weekly status meetings to review team progress and regularly escalate delays.
options.rationale: Weekly meetings are too infrequent and escalation does not create structure.

options.text: Met with the team, allowed team members to make decisions about what to do, and established performance goals.
options.rationale: Empowering the team and setting clear performance goals gives structure and ownership to the agile work.

options.text: Established daily standup meetings to track team progress and escalate delays to stakeholders as appropriate.
options.rationale: Daily stand-ups track progress but do not by themselves clarify structure or goals.

options.text: Conducted routine meetings and identified team members who are under performing.
options.rationale: Identifying underperformers focuses on blame.

questions.explanation: Teams new to agile need clear goals and the authority to organise their work. Empowerment with explicit performance expectations provides structure.
questions.mindset: Give new agile teams clear goals and real authority.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned to a water treatment investment project. The local government has recently passed a law that requires compliance with clean water according to global standards. This is a new regulation that was initiated in the last month and was quickly passed. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Inform the stakeholders and continue with the project according to the original plans since the law was passed after the project started.
options.rationale: A law passed after the project started still applies to it; continuing on the original plan knowingly ignores a legal requirement.

options.text: Meet with the project sponsor and recommend that the project continue because the new legal requirements can be delivered.
options.rationale: Recommending continuation before analysing the impact assumes the new requirements can be delivered without evidence.

options.text: Conduct an analysis of the impact of the regulation on the project and the business and communicate it to stakeholders.
options.rationale: Analysing the regulation's impact on the project and the business, then communicating it, gives stakeholders a sound basis for decisions.

options.text: Recommend that all work on the project be stopped immediately until the impact of the regulation is understood.
options.rationale: Stopping all work immediately is disproportionate; much of the work may be unaffected, and analysis can proceed while work continues.

questions.explanation: New legislation that affects a project must be analysed for its impact on scope, schedule, cost and business outcomes, and the results communicated. Neither ignoring the law nor halting everything is a considered response; understanding the impact is.
questions.mindset: Analyse and communicate the impact of new law before deciding on the response.

questions.stem: A startup in its early stages has been acquired by a major company. In light of this new scenario, the project manager has been requested to review the project's roadmap. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Determine the definition of value with the stakeholders and reprioritize the project's backlog accordingly.
options.rationale: After an acquisition, what counts as value may have changed; redefining it with stakeholders and reprioritising the backlog aligns the roadmap with the new reality.

options.text: Reprioritize the project's backlog by prioritizing those features that maximize the return on investment (ROI).
options.rationale: ROI is one lens on value, but prioritising on it alone assumes the new owners' definition of value without asking.

options.text: Reprioritize the roadmap by focusing on long-term benefits and reducing the technical debt.
options.rationale: Focusing on long-term benefits and technical debt is a particular strategy that may not match the new stakeholders' priorities.

options.text: Launch a customer survey to better evaluate the key project features prior to reprioritizing the roadmap.
options.rationale: A customer survey may inform prioritisation, but internal stakeholders' definition of value after the acquisition comes first.

questions.explanation: Backlog priority rests on an agreed definition of value. When ownership or strategy changes, that definition should be revisited with the stakeholders who now set direction, and the roadmap reprioritised accordingly.
questions.mindset: Redefine value with the people who now own it, then reprioritise.

questions.stem: A project manager works in a matrix organization and manages an internal software development project to improve the company's tracking system. The project is scheduled to be completed in one month. Some benefits will be realized once the system is online, however, full benefits will not be realized for a while. Although the project manager will track benefits through project closure, they are concerned about tracking the benefits of post-project activities. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Request that a new project be initiated to monitor and report the achievement of benefits.
options.rationale: Starting a new project to monitor benefits is heavy and unnecessary when an owner already exists in operations.

options.text: Revise the benefits management plan to extend the project until all benefits are realized.
options.rationale: Extending the project until all benefits are realised keeps a temporary organisation alive for operational monitoring.

options.text: Update the work breakdown structure (WBS) and project schedule with tasks to track benefits realization.
options.rationale: Adding tracking tasks to the WBS only covers the period before closure, not the benefits that arrive afterwards.

options.text: Coordinate with the benefits owner to monitor the achievement of benefits after the project closes.
options.rationale: Coordinating with the benefits owner hands over responsibility for measuring benefits after closure to someone who stays with the business.

questions.explanation: Many benefits are realised after a project closes. The benefits management plan should assign an owner in the business to track them, and the project manager ensures a clean handover of that responsibility.
questions.mindset: Hand benefits tracking to an owner who outlives the project.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on a project that will deliver a solution in country A. Due to the potential for a security breach, country A's government is banning the technology that will be used in the project's solution, adversely affecting the project. The project manager is close to completing the installation for the project after already procuring the materials and the banned technology. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Review the project management plan and follow the process for change control.
options.rationale: Following the change control process defined in the plan assesses the impact of the ban and routes decisions through the proper authority.

options.text: Request that the legal team review the change and determine the appropriate response.
options.rationale: Legal review may be part of the assessment, but it is not a substitute for the defined change process.

options.text: Meet with the project sponsor about the issue and request direction for next steps.
options.rationale: The sponsor will be involved through change control; seeking direction informally bypasses the process.

options.text: Inform the customer that the project cannot deliver the defined scope.
options.rationale: Declaring the scope undeliverable before assessing options is premature.

questions.explanation: An external event that changes what can be delivered is handled through the project's change control process. That ensures impacts are analysed, options considered and decisions made by the right authority.
questions.mindset: Route externally forced changes through the same change control as any other.

questions.stem: A project is developing a product where the time to market is critical. During the execution phase, the client submits a change request to include the latest technology that will enhance the product features and provide a competitive advantage. The change will impact the project constraints, but the benefits outweigh the cost and effort. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Adopt an incremental delivery approach and release essential features of the product into the market first to counter competition.
options.rationale: Releasing essential features first through incremental delivery protects time to market while the enhancement is added.

options.text: Start a separate project to adopt the new technology incrementally to enhance the product features as the technology matures.
options.rationale: A separate project splits ownership and delays the benefit.

options.text: Perform an integrated change control process and review the project constraints to effectively manage the enhanced scope.
options.rationale: Change control is needed, but on its own it does not address the time-to-market pressure.

options.text: Close the current project and start a new project with an incremental delivery approach.
options.rationale: Closing and restarting is disruptive and wasteful.

questions.explanation: When change adds valuable scope to a time-critical product, incremental delivery lets the team release core value first and follow with enhancements. Tailoring the delivery approach can resolve tension between scope and speed.
questions.mindset: Protect time to market by delivering core value first.

questions.stem: A project manager is asked to manage a project that will allow the company to comply with a new, upcoming regulation. Just after project kick-off, the scope is modified to have the project team now work on specific tasks, while a global team will manage the program for several countries in parallel. The project management plan has not yet been shared, and the deadline to complete the project is fixed. What should the project manager do to handle the scope and changes?

options.text: Create a risk entry in the risk management plan due to the lack of a global project management plan.
options.rationale: Logging the absence of a global plan as a risk records the gap but does not start delivering.

options.text: Formalize the change in the scope with the project sponsor to limit accountability for the specific tasks.
options.rationale: Formalising scope to limit accountability is defensive and does not progress the work.

options.text: Review the organizational process assets (OPAs) from similar situations and the approaches that were implemented.
options.rationale: OPAs may help, but with a fixed regulatory deadline the team needs to begin work now.

options.text: Define an initial backlog and start working on the clearest tasks, then incrementally refine the scope.
options.rationale: An initial backlog, starting on the clearest tasks and refining as the programme defines more, balances action with changing scope.

questions.explanation: When scope is uncertain and the deadline fixed, waiting for full definition wastes time. Starting with the clearest work and refining scope incrementally lets the team make progress while details emerge.
questions.mindset: Start with what is clear and refine the rest as it becomes known.

questions.stem: A complex project has multiple participants. The project manager agrees with the team that they need to better understand the perspective of all project participants for the optimal success of the project. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Review the stakeholder analysis.
options.rationale: Reviewing the stakeholder analysis shows each participant's interests, influence and expectations, building an understanding of their perspectives.

options.text: Create a communication plan.
options.rationale: A communication plan is built on stakeholder analysis, so it is not the first step.

options.text: Conduct a SWOT analysis.
options.rationale: SWOT analyses the project or organisation, not individual stakeholder perspectives.

options.text: Perform a risk analysis.
options.rationale: Risk analysis looks at uncertainties, not stakeholder viewpoints.

questions.explanation: Understanding participants' perspectives is the purpose of stakeholder analysis. It captures interests, influence and expectations, forming the basis for engagement and communication planning.
questions.mindset: Understand stakeholders through analysis before planning how to engage them.

questions.stem: A project team discovers an opportunity to enhance software without impacting the budget or schedule. The team makes the enhancement without proper documentation, which later causes production issues. What process should have been conducted to prevent this?

options.text: Control Schedule
options.rationale: Control Schedule monitors timing, not whether changes are authorised.

options.text: Perform Qualitative Risk Analysis
options.rationale: Qualitative risk analysis prioritises risks; it would not have stopped an undocumented change.

options.text: Plan Scope Management
options.rationale: Plan Scope Management defines how scope is managed but does not govern individual changes during execution.

options.text: Perform Integrated Change Control
options.rationale: Integrated change control requires even apparently free enhancements to be documented, assessed and approved, preventing unintended consequences.

questions.explanation: Unauthorised enhancements, even well-intended ones, can create defects and inconsistencies. Integrated change control ensures every change is recorded and assessed, whether or not it seems to affect cost or schedule.
questions.mindset: No change is free of consequences; control them all.

questions.stem: A pilot project is ready to close and the project team wants to capture the challenges that were overcome and the opportunities for future work. Where will they document this information?

options.text: Organizational process assets updates
options.rationale: OPA updates happen when lessons are archived, but the working record during the project is the lessons learned register.

options.text: Work performance report
options.rationale: Work performance reports describe status, not lessons and opportunities.

options.text: Project management plan
options.rationale: The management plan describes how the project is run, not what was learned.

options.text: Lessons learned register
options.rationale: The lessons learned register captures challenges overcome and opportunities for future work.

questions.explanation: The lessons learned register records what the team learned — challenges, solutions, opportunities — throughout the project. At closure it is transferred to the organisation's knowledge base for reuse.
questions.mindset: Record lessons where future teams will find them.

questions.stem: A key stakeholder refuses to sign off on a product because it does not meet the expectations outlined in the project scope. What should the project manager have done to avoid this situation?

options.text: Solicited stakeholder feedback throughout the life cycle of the project.
options.rationale: Gathering stakeholder feedback throughout would have revealed the mismatch with expectations long before sign-off.

options.text: Conducted risk assessments based on the stakeholder's expectations.
options.rationale: Risk assessments do not replace ongoing engagement.

options.text: Implemented conflict management techniques during sign-off.
options.rationale: Conflict techniques at sign-off are too late.

options.text: Involved the key stakeholder during the testing phase.
options.rationale: Testing-phase involvement is late in the life cycle and may still expose major gaps.

questions.explanation: Stakeholder acceptance is built through engagement across the life cycle. Continuous feedback aligns deliverables with expectations incrementally, avoiding surprises at sign-off.
questions.mindset: Engage stakeholders continuously so sign-off holds no surprises.

questions.stem: While executing a project that is nearly behind schedule, a project manager must commission a new piece of equipment. Two local parties who will be impacted by this commission ask that the project be stopped immediately because they were not given an opportunity to provide project approval. How would implementing a stakeholder engagement plan have helped the project manager avoid this situation?

options.text: By using the conflict management techniques described in the plan, the project manager could have gotten approval from the local parties.
options.rationale: Conflict techniques do not help if the parties were never identified.

options.text: Including the local parties in the plan would have ensured their sign-off and approval of the project charter.
options.rationale: Stakeholders do not typically approve the charter; the problem is that they were overlooked.

options.text: By understanding the local parties' expectations, the project manager could have used appropriate negotiating techniques to engage them.
options.rationale: Negotiation assumes the parties were known and engaged.

options.text: By identifying the local parties as stakeholders, they would have been included in relevant communications.
options.rationale: Identifying the local parties as stakeholders would have ensured they received relevant communications and were engaged in time.

questions.explanation: Stakeholder identification must include everyone affected by the project, including local communities. Once identified, they can be engaged and informed appropriately.
questions.mindset: Identify everyone affected, not just those who fund or direct the work.

questions.stem: A project manager compiling a list of project stakeholders discovers an interested stakeholder with little to no authority. How should they manage this stakeholder?

options.text: Keep satisfied.
options.rationale: Keep satisfied is for high-power, low-interest stakeholders.

options.text: Manage closely.
options.rationale: Manage closely is for high-power, high-interest stakeholders.

options.text: Monitor.
options.rationale: Monitor is for low-power, low-interest stakeholders.

options.text: Keep informed.
options.rationale: Keep informed fits a stakeholder with high interest but little authority.

questions.explanation: The power/interest grid suggests engagement strategies: manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed and monitor. High interest with low power calls for keeping the stakeholder informed.
questions.mindset: Match engagement effort to stakeholder power and interest.

questions.stem: A project schedule requires that two teams work simultaneously on separate parts of a complex project. The two parts of the project are dependent on each other. The project manager needs to ensure there are no conflicts when the outputs from the two teams are combined. What should the project manager do to manage any potential conflicts first?

options.text: Set up weekly meetings between the teams to monitor each other's work.
options.rationale: Regular meetings between the teams let them see each other's work and resolve integration conflicts early.

options.text: Prioritize conflict resolution for the part of the project that is on the critical path.
options.rationale: Prioritising one part does not prevent conflicts where the parts meet.

options.text: Review the lessons learned register to anticipate potential conflicts and plan their resolution.
options.rationale: Lessons learned may inform, but ongoing coordination is what prevents conflict.

options.text: Engage project stakeholders to ensure their support through any conflicts as they arise.
options.rationale: Stakeholder engagement does not resolve technical integration between teams.

questions.explanation: Parallel work on interdependent parts needs continual coordination. Regular cross-team meetings surface conflicts in interfaces and outputs before integration.
questions.mindset: Coordinate interdependent teams continuously, not at integration time.

questions.stem: During a project's execution, a previously unidentified stakeholder within the customer's organization requests a change that could affect the project's scope. The stakeholder's influence within the customer's organization is strong. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Schedule a meeting and, based on the outcome, update the project management plan.
options.rationale: A meeting may be needed later, but the stakeholder should first be identified and analysed.

options.text: Issue a change request to the change control board (CCB).
options.rationale: A change request is premature before understanding the stakeholder and consulting others.

options.text: Identify the new stakeholder and update the stakeholder register.
options.rationale: Adding the new stakeholder to the register and analysing their influence is the first step.

options.text: Meet with all stakeholders to discuss the change.
options.rationale: Calling all stakeholders together before understanding the new stakeholder and their request is premature and may create unnecessary alarm.

questions.explanation: When an influential new stakeholder appears, they should be identified and analysed before their request is processed. The register captures their influence and expectations.
questions.mindset: Know who a stakeholder is before acting on their requests.

questions.stem: Due to a budget issue, the project team decides to use low-cost equipment with higher testing uncertainty to reduce cost. However, the test results are unstable and are creating discrepancies. One of the team members is aware of the situation and proposes to use high-resolution equipment with lower test uncertainty to increase the testing quality. How should the project manager respond to this proposal?

options.text: Reject the proposal due to budget constraints and follow the quality management plan.
options.rationale: Rejecting the proposal outright ignores a real quality problem.

options.text: Accept the proposal because the high-resolution equipment produces precise test results with lower test uncertainty.
options.rationale: Accepting on the assumption that it will work skips evaluation.

options.text: Evaluate the proposal to determine if the high-resolution equipment produces precise test results with lower test uncertainty.
options.rationale: Evaluating the proposal confirms whether the better equipment solves the problem and justifies the cost.

options.text: Accept the proposal because budget is not an issue when quality assurance is taken into consideration.
options.rationale: Budget always matters; ignoring it is irresponsible.

questions.explanation: Quality improvement proposals should be evaluated on evidence: does the change solve the problem, at what cost, with what risk? That lets the project balance quality and budget.
questions.mindset: Evaluate improvement proposals on evidence before accepting or rejecting them.

questions.stem: A new project manager joins a project during the delivery of a critical milestone. This project has multiple stakeholders, and each has a different level of interest.
