The project manager needs to determine how much detail to provide to the stakeholders about the delivery. Which document should the project manager refer to?

options.text: Communications management plan
options.rationale: The communications plan describes information flows, but tailoring detail to each stakeholder's engagement is in the engagement plan.

options.text: Stakeholder register
options.rationale: The register lists stakeholders but not how much detail to share.

options.text: Stakeholder engagement plan
options.rationale: The engagement plan describes strategies for each stakeholder, including information needs.

options.text: Project management plan
options.rationale: The project management plan is the umbrella document; the specific guidance on how much to share with each stakeholder is in the engagement plan.

questions.explanation: The stakeholder engagement plan sets strategies per stakeholder, including the level of detail and involvement. It guides how the PM tailors communications.
questions.mindset: Tailor communication using the engagement strategy for each stakeholder.

questions.stem: A project manager is managing an agile project which has many risks identified in the risk register. The current sprint deals with a critical aspect of the project. During the iteration, an identified risk occurs which ceases project development. The project manager logs the risk occurrence. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Raise the frequency of communications and leverage stakeholders to assist in resolving issues.
options.rationale: Increasing communication and involving stakeholders helps resolve an issue that has stopped development.

options.text: Assign responsibility for the communication management plan to a senior team member.
options.rationale: Reassigning the communications plan does not address the issue.

options.text: Invite the stakeholders to the next retrospective meeting and inform them of the issue.
options.rationale: Waiting for the retrospective delays resolution.

options.text: Delay development of the critical aspect to the next sprint and work on items currently in the backlog.
options.rationale: Deferring the critical work to the next sprint is a scope decision taken too early.

questions.explanation: When a risk materialises and stops development, the project manager steps up communication and draws in stakeholders who can help, rather than waiting for scheduled ceremonies or deferring critical work.
questions.mindset: Mobilise communication and help when work stops.

questions.stem: During an agile retrospective session, several team members mentioned that they were confused about the iteration's progress. What should the project manager do to avoid this confusion?

options.text: Coach the team to review the iteration board.
options.rationale: Coaching the team to use the iteration board gives them a real-time view of progress.

options.text: Prepare a daily project status report and share it with the team.
options.rationale: Daily status reports duplicate what the board shows and add overhead.

options.text: Ask the team to refer to the iteration backlog report.
options.rationale: Backlog reports are less visible than a live board.

options.text: Address the issue at the next retrospective session.
options.rationale: Waiting for the next retrospective leaves confusion in place.

questions.explanation: Agile teams use visible information radiators to track progress. Coaching the team to use them maintains shared understanding without extra reporting.
questions.mindset: Make progress visible to the team all the time.

questions.stem: A project manager complains that three engineers from different cultural backgrounds leave project meetings twice a day and assumes that they are "gossiping and smoking" for 15 minutes. The engineering manager replies that their absence is due to prayer time. What should the project manager do first to rectify their assumption?

options.text: Apologize for the unconscious bias.
options.rationale: Apologising for the assumption acknowledges the bias and begins repairing trust.

options.text: Develop a plan to improve work ethic.
options.rationale: A work ethic plan continues the biased assumption.

options.text: Set up a meeting to raise cultural awareness.
options.rationale: Cultural awareness helps later but the immediate step is to correct the assumption.

options.text: Follow and watch to make an informed observation.
options.rationale: Watching the engineers is intrusive and continues distrust.

questions.explanation: Unconscious bias can damage trust and inclusion. When it becomes clear an assumption was wrong, acknowledging it promptly is the first step to repairing relationships.
questions.mindset: Own your assumptions when they turn out to be wrong.

questions.stem: A project manager identifies that the work started by the project team is inconsistent with industry regulations. What should the project manager update?

options.text: Organizational process assets
options.rationale: OPAs capture organisational knowledge; they are not where an active issue is tracked.

options.text: Work performance data
options.rationale: Work performance data is raw observation, not an issue record.

options.text: Issue log
options.rationale: Non-compliance is a current issue and should be recorded in the issue log for action.

options.text: Project management plan
options.rationale: The plan may need updating later, but the first record is the issue log.

questions.explanation: Non-compliance discovered during the work is an active problem that needs an owner and a resolution. Recording it in the issue log makes it visible and tracked; plans and assets are updated later as the fix is agreed.
questions.mindset: Log issues so they are owned and resolved.

questions.stem: A key project team member is leaving the organization at the halfway point of the project. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Meet with remaining team members to reassign workloads.
options.rationale: Reassigning workload before understanding the impact may miss critical gaps.

options.text: Work with the functional manager to find a replacement.
options.rationale: Finding a replacement is likely, but understanding impact first shapes what is needed.

options.text: Evaluate the impact of the loss of the team member on the project.
options.rationale: Evaluating the impact of the loss determines the response.

options.text: Reassess the resource roles and team composition.
options.rationale: Reassessing roles is part of the response after impact analysis.

questions.explanation: Before responding to the loss of a key team member, the project manager assesses the impact on work, skills and schedule.
questions.mindset: Assess impact before choosing a replacement strategy.

questions.stem: A project manager must ensure stakeholder responsibilities are clear, concise, and promote successful completion while maintaining stakeholder engagement. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Collaborate with the stakeholder to define their manageable workload.
options.rationale: Collaborating to define a manageable workload makes responsibilities clear and keeps the stakeholder engaged.

options.text: Assign new responsibilities only after prior deadlines have been met.
options.rationale: Tying new responsibilities to past deadlines is arbitrary.

options.text: Assign as many responsibilities as they believe the stakeholder can handle.
options.rationale: Assigning as much as possible risks overload.

options.text: Add at least two new responsibilities after prior deadlines are met.
options.rationale: Adding a fixed number of new responsibilities is arbitrary.

questions.explanation: Stakeholders stay engaged when their responsibilities are clear and realistic. Agreeing a manageable workload with them, rather than assigning by arbitrary rules or by maximum capacity, produces commitments they can keep.
questions.mindset: Agree responsibilities with stakeholders rather than imposing them.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on the development of a business case to secure funding and resources. What is needed to ensure that the right priority is assigned to the project?

options.text: Developing the most efficient delivery plan
options.rationale: An efficient delivery plan does not establish priority.

options.text: Developing a clear and detailed project schedule
options.rationale: A detailed schedule is a planning output and says nothing about how important the project is to the organisation.

options.text: Aligning the project with company’s goals and objectives
options.rationale: Aligning the project with company goals shows its strategic importance and justifies priority.

options.text: Aligning the project with company’s roadmap
options.rationale: A roadmap is narrower than company goals and objectives.

questions.explanation: Portfolio priority depends on strategic contribution. A business case that clearly aligns the project with company goals supports appropriate prioritisation.
questions.mindset: Show strategic alignment to earn priority.

questions.stem: During acceptance testing of a deliverable, some senior stakeholders complain that a feature essential to their department was not included. What should the project manager have done to prevent this?

options.text: Consulted lessons learned from similar projects to adapt processes
options.rationale: Lessons learned may help, but a structured approach to scope is what was missing.

options.text: Prepared a change management plan and logged changes during project implementation
options.rationale: Change management tracks changes but not missing requirements.

options.text: Analyzed the project charter and developed a scope management plan
options.rationale: Analysing the charter and defining a scope management plan establishes how scope is collected and validated, preventing omissions.

options.text: Prepared a prototype and conducted a product demo with stakeholders
options.rationale: A demo may catch issues but a scope management approach is the preventive foundation.

questions.explanation: Missing requirements often reflect weak scope management. A scope management plan defines how requirements are gathered, defined and validated so that essential features are not missed.
questions.mindset: Plan how scope will be captured so nothing essential is missed.

questions.stem: A project manager working in a global organization decides to use a low-cost social media platform to exchange information, knowledge, and experience within the organization. Which three challenges should the project manager be prepared to deal with? (Choose three)

options.text: Lack of physical interaction
options.rationale: An online platform removes face-to-face contact, so trust and rapport have to be built without it.

options.text: Time differences
options.rationale: A global organisation spans time zones, which limits real-time exchange on any shared platform.

options.text: Competing priorities
options.rationale: People always have competing priorities, but that is not a challenge specific to a low-cost knowledge-sharing platform.

options.text: Lack of funding
options.rationale: The platform is low-cost by design, so funding is not the challenge the project manager needs to prepare for.

options.text: Cultural differences
options.rationale: Cultural differences affect how people share knowledge, give feedback and interpret messages across a global network.

questions.explanation: Virtual knowledge-sharing across a global organisation faces three characteristic challenges: no physical interaction, dispersed time zones and cultural diversity. Planning for them — asynchronous norms, overlap windows, cultural awareness — makes the platform useful rather than silent.
questions.mindset: Plan for distance, time and culture when collaboration goes virtual.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on a complex project that includes many stakeholders with conflicting priorities. What should the project manager do to reduce conflict?

options.text: Document and sign off on all deliverables in the project.
options.rationale: Documenting deliverables and obtaining sign-off turns conflicting expectations into an explicit, agreed baseline, reducing later disputes.

options.text: Take the lead in all aspects of the negotiations.
options.rationale: Leading every negotiation personally makes the PM a bottleneck and does not create lasting agreement among stakeholders.

options.text: Negotiate all aspects with help from the project management office (PMO).
options.rationale: The PMO can support, but negotiating everything through it moves ownership away from the project and its stakeholders.

options.text: Negotiate all aspects using agile for easy deliveries.
options.rationale: Choosing agile to avoid conflict misunderstands the problem; agile still requires agreement on priorities.

questions.explanation: Conflict among stakeholders with different priorities is reduced by making agreements explicit. Documented, signed-off deliverables provide a shared reference, and later changes are handled through change control rather than renegotiated informally.
questions.mindset: Make agreements explicit so they can be referred to, not re-argued.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on a complex project with many stakeholders and conflicting priorities. Senior management asked the project manager to avoid "noise" specifically for political projects. Although it is difficult to find resources for the project, what should the project manager do to ensure smooth progress of the project?

options.text: Apply "If you do something nice for me I'll do something nice for you."
options.rationale: Trading favours ties resource decisions to personal deals rather than project needs, which breeds more noise.

options.text: Be consistent with words and actions to avoid conflicts with the stakeholders.
options.rationale: Consistency builds credibility, but it does not solve the practical problem of scarce resources.

options.text: Utilize compliments to obtain resources, and cooperate toward mutual goals.
options.rationale: Flattery to obtain resources is manipulative and unsustainable.

options.text: Allocate the scarce resources efficiently to meet the needs of the project.
options.rationale: Allocating scarce resources efficiently to the project's most important needs keeps progress smooth without political manoeuvring.

questions.explanation: Resource scarcity is one of the most common sources of project conflict. Allocating what is available to the work that matters most, transparently and on the project's merits, keeps progress steady and avoids the noise of personal bargaining.
questions.mindset: Allocate scarce resources on merit, not on favours.

questions.stem: A project team is working on determining dependencies for approximately 350 activities for an ongoing project. Which actions should the project team take to manage dependencies successfully? (Choose 2).

options.text: Communicate the dependencies to the sponsor.
options.rationale: The sponsor does not need detail on hundreds of dependencies; this is not a management action.

options.text: Assess and document the dependencies.
options.rationale: Assessing and documenting dependencies makes them explicit so the schedule can be built correctly.

options.text: Communicate the dependencies to the customer.
options.rationale: Customers rarely need activity-level dependencies communicated to them.

options.text: Ensure that the dependencies are monitored.
options.rationale: Monitoring dependencies throughout the project catches changes before they disrupt the schedule.

options.text: Ensure you use only finish-to-start dependencies.
options.rationale: Restricting to finish-to-start ignores legitimate start-to-start and finish-to-finish relationships.

questions.explanation: Managing dependencies means identifying and documenting them, then keeping them under watch as work progresses. Other relationship types exist for good reasons, and communication should be targeted to those affected.
questions.mindset: Document dependencies, then keep watching them.

questions.stem: A customer requested a change in functionality for a product that will be delivered in the next sprint. The responsible specialist for this change is also assigned to a deliverable for another project. The project manager needs to negotiate the availability of the specialist. Who is responsible for confirming the specialist's availability?

options.text: Project sponsor
options.rationale: The sponsor supports the project but does not control a functional specialist's allocation.

options.text: Functional manager
options.rationale: The functional manager controls the specialist's time and confirms their availability across projects.

options.text: Product owner
options.rationale: The product owner prioritises work but does not allocate people from functional departments.

options.text: Human resources
options.rationale: HR supports employment matters, not day-to-day allocation to projects.

questions.explanation: In matrix organisations, functional managers own their staff's allocation. Project managers negotiate with them for availability, especially when a specialist is shared across projects.
questions.mindset: Negotiate for people with whoever controls their time.

questions.stem: A project manager has been on a complex project that began eight months ago. The project manager has a quality team that has been working hard, is motivated, and successful. What type of management and leadership should the project manager use at this stage?

options.text: Empower them to improve results
options.rationale: A motivated, successful team in a mature stage benefits most from empowerment to push results further.

options.text: Support with periodic iterations and feedback
options.rationale: Periodic feedback is useful but under-uses a high-performing team.

options.text: Help with conflict resolution
options.rationale: There is no indication of conflict to resolve.

options.text: Feedback, coaching, or help only when they ask for it
options.rationale: Offering help only on request can feel distant; empowerment is a more active leadership choice.

questions.explanation: Leadership style should match team maturity. Newly formed teams need direction; experienced, motivated teams perform best when empowered with authority and trust to improve their own results.
questions.mindset: Match leadership style to team maturity.

questions.stem: A project team is actively engaged in the preparation of the last delivery before the final product is live in production. What should the project manager do to make sure that the whole team is in full sync?

options.text: Ensure the team is attending the daily meetings and participating actively
options.rationale: Active daily meetings keep everyone synchronised and surface dependencies before the final release.

options.text: Ensure that the needed information is available and accessible to each and every member
options.rationale: Accessible information is useful, but availability does not guarantee people are aligned.

options.text: Ensure to visualize the work to be done on a white board visual and accessible to all
options.rationale: A visual board helps, but without the daily conversation the team may still work out of step.

options.text: Ensure there is a room for the team to have regular conversation whenever needed
options.rationale: Space for conversation is good, but ad-hoc chats do not guarantee the whole team is in sync.

questions.explanation: Near a critical release, daily synchronisation is essential. Active participation in daily meetings exposes blockers and dependencies quickly, keeping the team aligned.
questions.mindset: Synchronise daily when the stakes are highest.

questions.stem: A new project manager has been assigned to a project during its execution stage. During a review of the work breakdown structure (WBS), the project manager discovers that some deliverables were overlooked. The project manager needs to ensure that no work is left out of the project scope and no extra work is performed. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Add the work to the WBS and recalculate the project metrics.
options.rationale: Adding overlooked approved work to the WBS makes it complete and recalculating metrics keeps performance measurement accurate.

options.text: Ask the stakeholders if these deliverables need to be added to the WBS.
options.rationale: If the deliverables are part of the approved scope, asking stakeholders whether they belong is unnecessary.

options.text: Roll up the lower-level deliverables into higher-level work already accounted for in the WBS.
options.rationale: Rolling deliverables up hides work rather than defining it.

options.text: Initiate a Change Control Request with the project management office (PMO).
options.rationale: Change control is needed for new scope, but these are overlooked deliverables of existing scope.

questions.explanation: The WBS must represent the entire approved scope — no more and no less. When approved deliverables are missing, they are added and the dependent measures recalculated so the baseline matches reality.
questions.mindset: Keep the WBS a complete picture of approved scope.

questions.stem: A project integrates with several systems developed by various vendors and one of these vendors has gone out of business. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Meet with this vendor to identify a replacement.
options.rationale: Meeting a vendor that has gone out of business is not possible.

options.text: Review the risk register and update the issue log.
options.rationale: Reviewing the risk register for planned responses and logging the issue starts a controlled response.

options.text: Calculate the delay and notify the project sponsor of the new timeline.
options.rationale: Calculating delay before exploring responses may be unnecessarily pessimistic.

options.text: Negotiate with another vendor to produce the deliverable.
options.rationale: Negotiating with another vendor may be the response, but first check what was planned.

questions.explanation: A vendor failure is a risk that has materialised. The project manager checks the risk register for planned responses and logs the issue to track corrective action.
questions.mindset: Turn a materialised risk into a tracked issue and use the planned response.

questions.stem: During a retrospective meeting, team members show disengagement, stating that they are repeating the same ideas over and over. How can the project manager best handle this situation?

options.text: Ask the team members to pay more attention to the session even if they think they know what is coming.
options.rationale: Asking for attention does not make repetitive retrospectives more useful.

options.text: Ask the team members to give their feedback, even if it is the same as other team members, to stress their points.
options.rationale: Repeating the same feedback reinforces the problem.

options.text: Encourage the team members to provide better feedback as they know the questions already.
options.rationale: Asking for better feedback puts the burden on the team without changing the format or follow-through.

options.text: Encourage the team to provide ideas for process improvement and support changes based on the feedback received.
options.rationale: Encouraging improvement ideas and acting on them shows retrospectives produce change, restoring engagement.

questions.explanation: Retrospectives lose value when nothing changes afterwards. Focusing on actionable improvements and visibly implementing them re-engages the team.
questions.mindset: Show that retrospectives lead to change.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading an agile project that is in the execution phase. After a couple of sprints, the project manager realizes that the team's estimates are not realistic. What action should the project manager take to remove this impediment?

options.text: Ask the team to address this issue at the next the retrospective to avoid impacting the sprint in progress.
options.rationale: Waiting for the retrospective delays improving estimates.

options.text: Obtain approval from project sponsor to add a contingency buffer to the sprint, and change the end date.
options.rationale: Adding a buffer and moving the end date violate the sprint timebox.

options.text: Ask the team to address this issue at the next standup, and meet the commitment for the sprint in progress.
options.rationale: The stand-up is for coordination, not estimation work.

options.text: Organize product backlog refinement sessions to better understand the scope and review estimations.
options.rationale: Backlog refinement improves shared understanding of scope, which is the basis for better estimates.

questions.explanation: Poor estimates usually reflect poor understanding of the work. Backlog refinement clarifies stories and improves the team's estimation skill, without changing sprint length or adding buffers.
questions.mindset: Improve estimates by improving understanding of the work.

questions.stem: During a daily meeting, the project team raised an impediment that one of the business subject matter experts is frequently changing the definition of done, and expressed their fear that this is a sign of distrust. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Remind the team to focus on their work, and commit to speak with the SME
options.rationale: Telling the team to focus and handling the SME alone does not address the team's concern about trust.

options.text: Remind the product owner to support the team and speak with the SME
options.rationale: Asking the product owner to intervene treats the SME's input as a problem.

options.text: Remind the SME to keep the definition of done that was initially agreed
options.rationale: Freezing the definition of done ignores legitimate learning about what the business needs.

options.text: Remind the team that continuous feedback is important for success
options.rationale: Reminding the team that continuous feedback is part of agile reframes the SME's changes as engagement, not distrust.

questions.explanation: In agile, changing understanding is expected. Frequent stakeholder feedback, even on the definition of done, reflects engagement; the team should see it as input to deliver the right product.
questions.mindset: Treat stakeholder feedback as engagement, not distrust.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on a hybrid project. The team performance has been suffering and multiple team members have identified one of the stakeholders as a constant obstacle. They say that the stakeholder regularly asks team members for status updates and tries to implement project changes directly through the project team. How can the project manager improve project performance?

options.text: Identify the stakeholder as a risk in the risk register and work with the team on a mitigation strategy.
options.rationale: Logging the stakeholder as a risk documents the problem without removing it.

options.text: Have the team direct all project requests from the stakeholder to the project manager.
options.rationale: Routing all requests through the PM may help but can create a bottleneck.

options.text: Work with the project management office (PMO) to remove the stakeholder from the project.
options.rationale: Stakeholders cannot simply be removed from a project.

options.text: Meet with the project sponsor to address and remove impediments and obstacles for the team.
options.rationale: Engaging the sponsor to address the obstacle removes it with the authority needed and lets the team focus.

questions.explanation: Removing impediments for the team is part of servant leadership. When an influential stakeholder disrupts the team, the PM uses the sponsor's authority to address the behaviour and protect the team.
questions.mindset: Use the right authority to clear obstacles from the team's path.

questions.stem: A project manager just completed a project in an organization that values lessons learned. Leadership encourages all the project stakeholders to use the process, tools, and results from the lessons learned repository in future projects. Preparing to update the lessons learned repository, the project manager has gathered relevant project data and feedback. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Store all the comments and recommendations received for future reference.
options.rationale: Storing raw comments makes the repository a dump rather than a source of insight.

options.text: Analyze and organize the findings with the stakeholders to extract insights.
options.rationale: Analysing and organising findings with stakeholders turns raw feedback into usable insights.

options.text: Document and share the findings with the stakeholders for review and feedback.
options.rationale: Sharing findings for review is useful, but it comes after the data has been analysed and organised into insights.

options.text: Retrieve all of the comments and recommendations received in the past.
options.rationale: Retrieving past comments is not the next step.

questions.explanation: Lessons learned are only valuable if future teams can use them. Raw comments must be analysed and organised, ideally with the stakeholders who lived the project, to extract insights before they are stored and shared.
questions.mindset: Turn feedback into insight before storing it.

questions.stem: An organization has decided to implement agile and a project manager with Scrum Master has been selected to coach the project team to understand agile delivery. One of the team members asks the project manager what servant leadership hierarchy means. How should the project manager respond?

options.text: Team members are supposed to serve their manager.
options.rationale: Team members serving the manager describes a traditional hierarchy, the opposite of servant leadership.

options.text: Managers are supposed to serve their team members.
options.rationale: Servant leadership inverts the hierarchy: leaders serve the team by removing impediments and enabling growth.

options.text: Clients are supposed to serve the team members.
options.rationale: Clients serving the team is not what servant leadership means.

options.text: Team Members are supposed to serve their clients.
options.rationale: Serving clients is a value, but not the meaning of servant leadership hierarchy.

questions.explanation: Servant leadership puts the leader in service of the team: creating an environment for growth, removing obstacles and facilitating rather than commanding.
questions.mindset: Lead by serving the team.

questions.stem: A functional manager has been making changes to a project outside of the established management plan. The functional manager recently went straight to the project sponsor to request another change. What should that project manager do?

options.text: Determine if the change control board (CCB) needs to review the changes.
options.rationale: The CCB reviews changes as defined; there is nothing to determine.

options.text: Tell the functional manager that all changes must go through the change control process.
options.rationale: Telling the functional manager that all changes must go through change control enforces the agreed process.

options.text: Modify the project management plan to allow flexibility in the change control procedures.
options.rationale: Loosening change control rewards bypassing it.

options.text: Meet with the project sponsor to discuss details about the requested changes.
options.rationale: Discussing details with the sponsor legitimises bypassing the process.

questions.explanation: Change control applies to all stakeholders. When someone bypasses it, the PM reinforces the process so every change is assessed and approved consistently.
questions.mindset: Enforce change control consistently.

questions.stem: The change control board (CCB) has evaluated and approved several change requests in a timely manner in the last several weeks. However, implementation of the changes is taking more time than anticipated. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Revise the change control system to allow only critical changes to be raised.
options.rationale: Restricting changes does not address slow implementation of approved ones.

options.text: Acquire additional resources to ensure the project milestones are met.
options.rationale: Adding resources assumes the delay is a capacity problem before anyone has looked at how the changes are being implemented.

options.text: Perform a detailed risk analysis to determine the impact of the time required to implement the changes on the success of the project.
options.rationale: A detailed risk analysis is premature when the immediate question is whether implementation follows the agreed procedures.

options.text: Monitor implementation of the changes to ensure that change management procedures are being followed.
options.rationale: Monitoring implementation checks procedures are followed and reveals why changes are slow.

questions.explanation: Approved changes still need controlled implementation. Monitoring it ensures procedures are followed and shows whether delays come from process gaps or other causes.
questions.mindset: Control changes through implementation, not just approval.

questions.stem: During the execution phase of your project, a Resource Manager informed you that one of the experts allocated to your project had to be motivated in order to perform very well. What would be the recommended actions to address this issue?

options.text: Remind the functional manager that is his duty to motivate his team
options.rationale: Motivation cannot be delegated back to the functional manager.

options.text: Remind the team member that there are penalties for bad behaviours.
options.rationale: Threatening penalties demotivates skilled professionals.

options.text: Remind the team member that there are financial incentives for the team.
options.rationale: Team-wide financial incentives do not address the individual's needs.

options.text: Remind the team member their important role and how it will be rewarded.
options.rationale: Recognising their important role and how it will be rewarded motivates skilled individuals effectively.

questions.explanation: Highly skilled people are often motivated by recognition and meaningful contribution. Showing how their role matters is more effective than threats or generic incentives.
questions.mindset: Motivate experts by recognising their contribution.

questions.stem: During project execution, a team member made a mistake resulting in a 1-week delay to the project schedule. What should the project manager do with regard to this error and delay?

options.text: Discuss the issue with the team, look for solutions, and offer to help and support the team.
options.rationale: Discussing the issue with the team, finding solutions and offering support builds a safe environment and resolves the delay.

options.text: Make sure the impact of this mistake is understood by the team member who made the mistake.
options.rationale: Focusing on the individual's mistake creates blame.

options.text: Escalate the issue to senior management to make sure a similar mistake won't happen again.
options.rationale: Escalating a one-week delay is disproportionate.

options.text: Find a solution, communicate it to the team, and reinforce that it should be implemented now.
options.rationale: Dictating a solution misses the team's input.

questions.explanation: How leaders respond to mistakes shapes team culture. Supportive problem-solving encourages openness and faster recovery.
questions.mindset: Respond to mistakes with support and problem-solving.

questions.stem: A project manager is managing an agile project. In order to make sure there is enough funding available for the project, the project sponsor is asking the project manager for an estimate when the project will be completed. How should the project manager respond to the sponsor?

options.text: Inform the sponsor that an estimate is not necessary, as agile supports responding to change over following a plan.
options.rationale: Agile does plan and estimate; refusing is based on a myth.

options.text: Remind the sponsor that agile projects are not judged based on budget and schedule.
options.rationale: Agile projects still manage budget and schedule.

options.text: Provide the estimate to the sponsor, as agile supports estimating.
options.rationale: Providing a forecast based on velocity and backlog supports funding decisions.

options.text: Influence the sponsor to add a contingency buffer to the cost in case of a cost overrun.
options.rationale: Adding contingency without estimation is unfounded.

questions.explanation: Agile teams forecast too. Using the backlog and observed velocity, they can give sponsors a completion estimate that is updated as they learn, which is exactly what funding decisions need.
questions.mindset: Agile forecasts too.

questions.stem: An organization decides to implement the Scrum delivery framework. The project manager is using an impediment board with the Scrum team to identify and raise impediments. What should happen after the impediments are recorded?

options.text: Address the highest priority impediments from the log and ensure that it is removed so that the team can continue to reach the sprint’s objective.
options.rationale: Acting on the highest priority impediment requires prioritisation first.

options.text: Prioritize impediments based on their levels of importance and in relation to those that are already on the log.
options.rationale: Prioritising impediments by importance relative to others ensures effort goes to the most critical.

options.text: Publish and post the impediments log and make it visible to everyone.
options.rationale: Publishing is useful but prioritisation is the next step.

options.text: Communicate that the impediment is removed to the involved parties and update the impediments log.
options.rationale: Communicating removal happens after resolution.

questions.explanation: Impediments are recorded, prioritised, resolved and communicated. Prioritisation ensures effort targets the blockers that matter most.
questions.mindset: Prioritise impediments before attacking them.

questions.stem: The project manager for a complex project discovers that a certain team member has missed several targets. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Determine if the team member has been assigned to a concurrent project.
options.rationale: Checking concurrent assignments is part of understanding, but talking to the person comes first.

options.text: Impose a penalty for each day the team member misses a target.
options.rationale: Penalties are punitive and unlikely to fix the cause.

options.text: Ask the team member's functional manager to address the issue.
options.rationale: Going to the functional manager avoids the direct conversation.

options.text: Discuss the issue with the team member and offer any needed assistance.
options.rationale: Discussing the issue and offering help addresses the cause directly.

questions.explanation: When a team member repeatedly misses targets, the first move is a direct, supportive conversation. It uncovers the cause — overload, unclear expectations, skills or personal issues — and lets the project manager offer the right help instead of punishing or deflecting.
questions.mindset: Talk to people before judging their performance.

questions.stem: A project manager learns that a functional manager is assigning a two-week task in another project to a team member. Loss of this resource for two weeks will jeopardize the project schedule. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Review the resource management plan to determine how to negotiate with the functional manager.
options.rationale: The resource management plan defines how resources are allocated and gives a basis for negotiating with the functional manager.

options.text: Submit a change request to the change control board (CCB) to obtain a replacement resource from another department.
options.rationale: A change request is not the tool for resource negotiation.

options.text: Meet with the project sponsor to discuss the priority levels of the two projects.
options.rationale: Priority discussions with the sponsor are an escalation.

options.text: Assign another team member to perform the work of the team member who will be missing for two weeks.
options.rationale: Quietly moving the work to someone else accepts the loss without negotiating and may overload another team member on a schedule that is already at risk.

questions.explanation: The resource management plan describes how resources are acquired and managed. It supports negotiation with functional managers over conflicts.
questions.mindset: Negotiate resources using the agreed resource plan.

questions.stem: A project manager identifies conflicts among local and virtual team members' understanding of the deliverables. How can the project manager resolve these conflicts?

options.text: Ask the project sponsor to meet with the team
options.rationale: Bringing in the sponsor to settle a team's differing understanding of deliverables escalates a problem the team can resolve itself.

options.text: By collaborating with team members to address the conflicts
options.rationale: Collaborating with team members addresses different understandings and creates shared agreement.

options.text: Host a mediation session that brings a degree of satisfaction to all team members
options.rationale: Mediation aiming at partial satisfaction is compromise, not collaboration.

options.text: By emphasizing areas of agreement rather than areas of difference
options.rationale: Emphasising agreement is smoothing and leaves differences unresolved.

questions.explanation: When team members understand deliverables differently, collaboration — working through the differences together to reach a shared understanding — produces a real resolution and commitment. Compromise, smoothing or escalation leave the underlying gap in place.
questions.mindset: Collaborate to create shared understanding.

questions.stem: A new project manager has been assigned to a global project team. In the next few days, the project team must create a resource breakdown structure (RBS) for the project. However, the resource management plan states that the RBS should be created and reviewed only at the beginning of the project. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Update the resource management plan.
options.rationale: The resource management plan must be updated first to allow the RBS to be revised.

options.text: Update the project management plan.
options.rationale: Updating the overall plan does not directly change the resource approach.

options.text: Update the resource breakdown structure.
options.rationale: Updating the RBS contradicts the current plan.

options.text: Update the work breakdown structure.
options.rationale: The WBS decomposes the work, not the resources, so updating it does nothing to allow the RBS to be revisited.

questions.explanation: When a plan component stops the team doing something it now needs to do, the plan is updated first through the proper process, and the activity is then carried out in line with it. Acting against the plan leaves documentation and practice out of step.
questions.mindset: Fix the plan before breaking it.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a project that entails transitioning to agile. The project will pilot the agile delivery modeled around using four resources from a vendor, working alongside two internal resources with no agile experience. The project manager needs to act as a coach for the project team and help them understand the differences between the functioning of a traditional project team and an agile team. What is the most important thing the project manager needs to do to establish agile team behavior?

options.text: Focus on the produced result of the team.
options.rationale: Focusing on results before the team knows how to work together pushes output ahead of the behaviours that make agile teams productive.

options.text: Build trust within the team.
options.rationale: Trust is the foundation of self-organisation: without it a mixed vendor and internal team will not share information, take decisions together or raise problems early.

options.text: Encourage collaboration among the team.
options.rationale: Collaboration is essential, but people only collaborate openly once they trust each other; it is a consequence of trust rather than its starting point.

options.text: Hold each team member accountable.
options.rationale: Holding individuals accountable in a new, mixed team can make people defensive and reinforce the traditional behaviours the transition is trying to change.

questions.explanation: Agile team behaviours — self-organisation, collaboration, shared ownership — all rest on trust. When a team mixes vendor staff with internal members new to agile, deliberately building trust is the first leadership task, because every other agile practice depends on people feeling safe to share, commit and admit problems.
questions.mindset: Build trust first; the other agile behaviours grow from it.

questions.stem: In the middle of project execution, the project sponsor leaves, and a new sponsor is assigned. The new sponsor is requesting major revisions to the deliverables. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Implement all the changes to the deliverables.
options.rationale: Implementing every change because a new sponsor asked bypasses change control and could derail cost, schedule and quality.

options.text: Request additional resources to adjust the deliverables.
options.rationale: Requesting more resources presumes the changes will be approved and what they need, before anyone understands the impact.

options.text: Evaluate the possible impacts of the changes.
options.rationale: Evaluating the impact of the requested changes on scope, schedule, cost and quality gives the new sponsor a sound basis to decide.

options.text: Extend the project timeline to include the changes.
options.rationale: Extending the timeline commits to the changes and one particular consequence before they have been assessed or approved.

questions.explanation: A new sponsor has every right to request changes, but major revisions still go through impact analysis and change control. Presenting the consequences clearly lets the sponsor make an informed decision rather than simply having their wishes absorbed into the plan.
questions.mindset: Analyse a new sponsor's changes before committing to them.

questions.stem: In the implementation phase of a project, the project manager receives news that a team lead will be leaving the organization. The project sponsor has been made aware and has suggested a replacement. What is the first action the project manager should take in response to this change?

options.text: Determine the competence levels of the suggested new resource.
options.rationale: The replacement's competence matters, but judging it before knowing what the departure affects puts the solution ahead of the problem.

options.text: Review the project baselines to assess the impact of the change.
options.rationale: Reviewing the baselines shows which scope, schedule and cost elements depend on the departing lead, so the response can be sized properly.

options.text: Document the change according to the change management plan.
options.rationale: Documenting the change is part of the process, but the record needs the impact analysis to be meaningful.

options.text: Edit the communications management plan to reflect the change.
options.rationale: Updating the communications plan is administrative and does not address the risk to delivery.

questions.explanation: Losing a team lead mid-implementation is a change whose impact must be understood first. Reviewing the baselines identifies what is at risk, which then shapes decisions about the replacement, handover and any change requests.
questions.mindset: Size the impact of a change before choosing the fix.

questions.stem: A company has decided to form agile teams within the organization to improve project results and take advantage of new opportunities in the market. A project manager with extensive agile experience was recruited to oversee the process. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Recruit, appoint, and evaluate new agile project practitioners.
options.rationale: Recruiting practitioners before deciding where agile will be used risks hiring for projects that do not suit the approach.

options.text: Implement an agile project management office (PMO).
options.rationale: An agile PMO may come later, but setting up structure before defining when agile applies puts governance ahead of purpose.

options.text: Determine the criteria for when to launch agile projects.
options.rationale: Criteria for when to launch agile projects ensure the approach is applied where it fits and gives the organisation a consistent basis for adoption.

options.text: Perform a retrospective analysis of prior project experiences.
options.rationale: Retrospective analysis of past projects is useful input, but it does not by itself decide how the organisation will adopt agile.

questions.explanation: Introducing agile across an organisation starts with deciding where it fits. Clear criteria for selecting agile projects — uncertainty, customer involvement, team readiness — prevent misapplication and give the transformation a coherent foundation.
questions.mindset: Decide where an approach fits before rolling it out.

questions.stem: During the project planning phase, the stakeholders neglected to document an essential system feature. The client realizes the oversight during an initial review of the deliverables. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Review the procurement management plan to determine if the missed feature can be added to the final deliverables.
options.rationale: The procurement plan governs buying from suppliers, not whether a missed requirement can be added to the project.

options.text: Determine what effect overlooking the feature will cause and submit a change request to the change control board (CCB).
options.rationale: Assessing the impact of the missing feature and submitting a change request follows the agreed process for adding essential scope.

options.text: Ask the project sponsor to authorize a price discount for the client.
options.rationale: A discount does not deliver the essential feature and is not the project manager's decision to make.

options.text: Work with the customer to agree on a new price to compensate for the omission.
options.rationale: Renegotiating price informally bypasses change control and does not deliver the missing feature.

questions.explanation: When a necessary requirement was missed in planning, it enters the project as a change: its impact is analysed and a change request submitted for decision. Commercial arrangements follow from that decision, not in place of it.
questions.mindset: Bring missed requirements in through change control, with their impact known.

questions.stem: A parent company announces an integration project for all of its subsidiary companies. The integration project covers the legal, human resources (HR), and finance departments of the subsidiary companies. Senior management is investing in this as the company's first agile project and a new project manager has been assigned. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Meet with the stakeholders to discuss risks.
options.rationale: Discussing risks with stakeholders is necessary, but without a plan for how the organisation will move to agile there is no frame for them.

options.text: Develop a team charter.
options.rationale: A team charter sets working norms for a team, but the challenge here is organisational transition across legal, HR and finance.

options.text: Plan to enhance the team's agile maturity level.
options.rationale: Improving agile maturity is part of the journey, but it needs a strategy that says where the organisation is going and how.

options.text: Develop a transition strategy.
options.rationale: A transition strategy provides the roadmap for moving several departments to agile ways of working for the first time.

questions.explanation: An organisation's first agile project, spanning several functions, is as much an organisational change as a delivery. A transition strategy describing the current state, target state and path between them gives coherence to training, team formation and stakeholder engagement.
questions.mindset: Plan the transition before expecting the transformation.

questions.stem: A large-scale, multiyear transformation project was completed as per the defined requirements and within the approved budget and schedule. The requirements were also validated and confirmed by the business. However, the post-delivery analysis of the project revealed that the project did not provide benefits as expected. What should the project manager have done to avoid this?

options.text: Ensured the requirements were properly captured in the product backlog.
options.rationale: Capturing requirements well does not ensure those requirements still deliver value as circumstances change.

options.text: Created a business strategy to assist with organizational change management.
options.rationale: Organisational change management helps adoption, but the gap here is that value was never checked during the project.

options.text: Improved the status reporting processes to highlight specific project results.
options.rationale: Better status reports describe results; they do not validate that benefits are on track.

options.text: Measured and demonstrated business value throughout the project lifecycle.
options.rationale: Measuring and demonstrating value throughout the life cycle would have revealed the gap between requirements and benefits while there was time to act.

questions.explanation: On-time, on-budget delivery of validated requirements does not guarantee benefits. Measuring business value throughout the project, including revisiting the business case at phase gates, reveals when delivered outputs stop leading to intended outcomes.
questions.mindset: Measure value during the project, not only at the end.

questions.stem: During a product backlog refinement meeting, a stakeholder from the legal department and the product owner disagree on the prioritization of a particular item. The product owner states that the current prioritization is adding maximum value to the project, and the stakeholder states that the item should be prioritized because it is a governmental compliance requirement. What should the project manager do in this situation?

options.text: Yield to the product owner's prioritization authority and remind the stakeholder that it is not their responsibility.
options.rationale: Deferring to the product owner and dismissing the legal stakeholder ignores a compliance requirement that may be mandatory.

options.text: Examine previous situations in the lessons learned register to find a solution and prioritize the backlog accordingly.
options.rationale: Past situations may help, but the disagreement needs the two parties to understand each other now.

options.text: Use negotiation techniques to convince the product owner to prioritize the backlog as suggested by the stakeholder.
options.rationale: Pushing the product owner to comply removes their authority without exploring the value and compliance trade-off.

options.text: Facilitate a discussion between the product owner and the stakeholder to discuss their perspectives and concerns.
options.rationale: Facilitating a conversation lets both perspectives be understood so the product owner can prioritise with full knowledge of the compliance obligation.

questions.explanation: Compliance requirements often trump pure value ordering, but the product owner still owns the backlog. The project manager helps both sides understand each other's concerns so priorities reflect both value and obligation.
questions.mindset: Help value owners and compliance owners understand each other.

questions.stem: A company is developing a breakthrough product in a highly competitive and rapidly evolving market. The project manager acknowledges that, due to the significantly competitive environment, the definition of done (DoD) is likely to shift. What should the project manager do to ensure the project's successful delivery of value?

options.text: Implement robust project tracking and reporting procedures.
options.rationale: Robust tracking and reporting show quickly when the definition of done shifts, allowing the team to adapt while keeping focus on value.

options.text: Expand the project timeline and budget to address potential risks.
options.rationale: Expanding time and budget up front guesses at the size of change instead of managing it as it happens.

options.text: Allocate additional resources to expedite product development.
options.rationale: Extra resources speed delivery but do not help the team adapt to shifting criteria.

options.text: Restrict project scope and focus on meeting project deadlines.
options.rationale: Restricting scope to hit deadlines trades value for predictability in a market that rewards adaptation.

questions.explanation: In fast-changing markets the target moves. Close monitoring of progress and changing criteria gives the team the information to adapt quickly, which is how value is protected when the definition of done cannot stay fixed.
questions.mindset: When the target moves, watch it closely and adapt quickly.

questions.stem: An international company is implementing an innovative technology at one of its production plants. The technology has already demonstrated positive returns at another site. What should the project manager consider as a key aspect of the successful implementation of this technology?

options.text: Assess the business case to ensure the return on investment (ROI) meets or exceeds the performance indicators of the first site.
options.rationale: Comparing ROI with the first site checks the numbers but ignores local culture, which often decides whether change succeeds.

options.text: Consult with the technology manager to ensure the technology can fit in the new site.
options.rationale: Technical fit matters, but the question points to the human side of implementation at a new site.

options.text: Conduct an information-sharing workshop to present the new technology and its benefits to the new site's stakeholders.
options.rationale: An information-sharing workshop prepares the new site's stakeholders and addresses local culture, building acceptance for the change.

options.text: Develop the project charter for implementation at the new site using the lessons learned from the first site.
options.rationale: Lessons from the first site help planning, but they do not engage the new site's people.

questions.explanation: Success at one site does not transfer automatically. Local culture, concerns and practices shape adoption, so sharing information and engaging stakeholders at the new site is a key part of implementing a proven technology.
questions.mindset: Transfer proven change by engaging the people who must adopt it.

questions.stem: During final inspection of a deliverable, the quality team observes that there is a deviation on a particular component. The customer, however, has not indicated anything with regard to this in its specifications. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Raise the matter to a technical expert.
options.rationale: A technical expert gives an opinion on one issue but does not check the deliverable against the quality standards.

options.text: Conduct a quality assurance audit.
options.rationale: A quality assurance audit compares the deliverable with established standards and determines whether the deviation is acceptable.

options.text: Approve the deliverable as it does not deviate from any customer specifications.
options.rationale: Approving because the customer did not specify it ignores internal quality standards that may still apply.

options.text: Reject the deliverable, citing deviation from the project specifications.
options.rationale: Rejecting assumes the deviation breaches specifications without evaluating it.

questions.explanation: A deviation not covered by customer specifications may still breach organisational or industry standards. A quality audit establishes objectively whether it is acceptable before approving or rejecting.
questions.mindset: Judge deviations against standards, not assumptions.

questions.stem: A project manager is currently overseeing a project from its inception and is aware that there are several assumptions and dependencies integral to the project's success. What action should the project manager take in this situation?

options.text: Seek support from the project sponsor to allocate a dedicated resource to monitor and track benefits realization.
options.rationale: A dedicated benefits resource tracks outcomes, not the assumptions and dependencies the plan rests on.

options.text: Instruct the project team to record all the assumptions and track all the changes.
options.rationale: Recording assumptions and tracking changes makes the plan's foundations visible so they can be validated and managed.

options.text: Facilitate a brainstorming session with the project team to formulate a comprehensive risk mitigation plan.
options.rationale: A risk mitigation plan is useful, but first the assumptions must be recorded to know what could turn into a risk.

options.text: Ask the project management office (PMO) to implement a benefits measurement system to verify benefit metrics and associated risks.
options.rationale: A benefits measurement system addresses benefits, not the assumptions underneath the plan.

questions.explanation: Assumptions and dependencies are the unseen foundations of a plan. Recording them in an assumption log and tracking changes allows the project to test them and react when they prove false.
questions.mindset: Write down what the plan depends on, and watch it.

questions.stem: During a business status meeting, the project manager acknowledges that several market conditions have recently changed dramatically. As a result, the expected value of the project in progress may be threatened. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Stop the project immediately due to uncertainty that the project will deliver the expected value.
options.rationale: Stopping immediately is premature; the market change may not invalidate the project.

options.text: Continue with the project since the project manager has not been formally informed of any change in market conditions.
options.rationale: Waiting for formal notice ignores information the project manager already has.

options.text: Ask the project team to investigate the evolution of market conditions during the last 6 months.
options.rationale: A historical investigation delays the key conversation with the sponsor.

options.text: Meet with the project sponsor to discuss the information and ask if the organization still supports delivery of the project.
options.rationale: Discussing the changes with the sponsor and confirming organisational support tests whether the business case still holds.

questions.explanation: The value of a project rests on assumptions about the market. When those change, the sponsor, who owns the business case, should decide whether the project still merits investment.
questions.mindset: Take changes to the business case to its owner.

questions.stem: A project manager has started developing a plan for a new project. During the first planning meeting, the stakeholders ask about the project's value and how it relates to the organization's goals. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Refer the stakeholders to the scope management plan.
options.rationale: The scope plan explains how scope is managed, not why the project matters.

options.text: Refer the stakeholders to the project charter.
options.rationale: The charter records the project's purpose, value and link to organisational goals.

options.text: Invite the project sponsor to join the meeting to address questions.
options.rationale: The sponsor may help, but the answer is already in the charter.

options.text: Ask the project management office (PMO) to provide the necessary documentation.
options.rationale: The PMO is not the source of project purpose.

questions.explanation: The project charter captures why the project exists and how it contributes to organisational goals. It is the reference when stakeholders ask about value in early planning.
questions.mindset: Point stakeholders to the charter for the project's purpose.

questions.stem: A client requests a major scope change due to a change in the market environment, which will significantly add to the project cost. This change is approved through the change control process. What should the project manager do to put the project on track?

options.text: Reevaluate the scope baseline and impact on the project objectives.
options.rationale: Reevaluating the scope baseline and its impact on objectives is a sensible step after a major approved change, but the key here is funding the change.

options.text: Use the management reserve to account for the schedule uncertainty.
options.rationale: Management reserve is held for unplanned but in-scope work and can be released by management to fund an approved change's uncertainty.

options.text: Monitor risks to ensure the effectiveness of the risk management process.
options.rationale: Monitoring risk is ongoing and does not put the project back on track.

options.text: Reevaluate the cost management plan to address the impact of the change.
options.rationale: Revisiting the cost plan changes how cost is managed, not how this change is funded.

questions.explanation: After an approved scope change, the baselines are updated and funding must be provided. Management reserve, under management control, can be released for that purpose; contingency reserve covers identified risks.
questions.mindset: Know which reserve funds what, and who controls it.

questions.stem: A project manager is tracking an infrastructure project that is dependent on a service provider. The service provider informed the project manager that some of the third-party components will no longer be manufactured or supported. Upon an initial review, this would significantly delay the schedule and increase the budget. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Escalate this issue to the project sponsor.
options.rationale: An external problem that significantly affects budget and schedule is beyond the project manager's authority and should go to the sponsor.

options.text: Update the risk register.
options.rationale: Updating the risk register records the risk, but the impact is significant and already evident.

options.text: Convene a review with the team.
options.rationale: A team review helps understand options but does not reach the authority needed.

options.text: Update the project status to reflect these findings.
options.rationale: Updating status reports communicates but does not seek a decision.

questions.explanation: Issues with major budget and schedule consequences that are beyond the project manager's authority are escalated to the sponsor with the initial impact assessment.
questions.mindset: Escalate what exceeds your authority, with the impact in hand.

questions.stem: A project is under scrutiny for its amount of water usage. The government's water licensing branch is changing its policy to be more restrictive. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Align project resources to oppose the new water license standard.
options.rationale: Mobilising project resources to oppose a government policy is outside the project's mandate and wastes effort on something it cannot control.

options.text: Cancel the project because of the uncertainty introduced with the policy change.
options.rationale: Cancelling because of uncertainty is premature; the policy's effect on the project has not yet been assessed.

options.text: Assess the impact of the policy change on the project scope.
options.rationale: Assessing how the tighter water policy affects scope and requirements is the first step to deciding how the project must adapt.

options.text: Create a new project schedule based on potential changes to the water policy.
options.rationale: A new schedule built on potential changes guesses at the outcome before the impact has been analysed.

questions.explanation: Changes in the external environment — regulation, policy, market — must be assessed for their impact on scope and requirements. Only once the impact is understood can the project decide whether to adapt, re-plan or escalate.
questions.mindset: Assess the impact of external change on scope before reacting.

questions.stem: Following the start of a sprint, a key stakeholder constructed an email to a project team voicing displeasure of the work that just commenced, despite being inexperienced in agile. The stakeholder is insistent about changing the internal and external deliverables. What next step should the project manager take?

options.text: Request the team’s assessment of the matter at the next standup meeting.
options.rationale: Waiting for the team's view at the next stand-up leaves an insistent stakeholder unaddressed and pulls the team into a scope debate.

options.text: Change the backlog and comply with the stakeholder’s request.
options.rationale: Changing the backlog mid-sprint to comply bypasses the product owner and breaks the sprint's commitment.

options.text: Facilitate a meeting with the product owner and the key stakeholder to align on deliverables.
options.rationale: Bringing the product owner and stakeholder together aligns expectations about deliverables through the role that owns the backlog.

options.text: Encourage the stakeholder to participate in a discussion regarding backlog clarification.
options.rationale: Encouraging a discussion is vague and does not ensure the product owner, who decides priority, is involved.

questions.explanation: Stakeholder dissatisfaction with sprint work is resolved through the product owner, who owns what is built. The project manager facilitates alignment between them, protecting the sprint while ensuring the stakeholder is heard.
questions.mindset: Align stakeholders with the product owner rather than changing work around them.

questions.stem: A key project stakeholder showed interest in the beginning of a complex agile project but has become less involved as the sprint has progressed due to additional responsibilities. A few sprints later, the key stakeholder rejected a feature deliverable. The team is reworking the rejected deliverable for the next sprint. What should the project manager have done to avoid this situation?

options.text: Documented the project vision and objectives.
options.rationale: A documented vision helps alignment but does not keep a busy stakeholder engaged in feature decisions.

options.text: Analyzed the changes in stakeholder attributes.
options.rationale: Analysing changes in stakeholder attributes might have spotted the drop in involvement, but it would not by itself have secured their input.

options.text: Involved the key stakeholders in the decision-making process.
options.rationale: Involving the key stakeholder in decisions ensures their expectations shape the feature before it is built, avoiding rejection and rework.

options.text: Customized stakeholder communications based on the stakeholders' needs.
options.rationale: Customised communications keep the stakeholder informed but do not give them a say in decisions.

questions.explanation: Stakeholders who will accept or reject deliverables need to be part of the decisions that shape them. When involvement drops, the project manager finds ways to keep them in the decision loop so that acceptance is built in rather than tested at the end.
questions.mindset: Involve the people who will accept the work in deciding what the work is.

questions.stem: A company begins to implement Scrum. About halfway through the first sprint, communication issues develop. Some project team members are not in sync with other team members. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Educate the team on the importance of communication in Scrum.
options.rationale: Educating the team assumes the problem is awareness, which may not be the cause.

options.text: Establish clear communication guidelines.
options.rationale: New guidelines may help, but without knowing the cause they may not address it.

options.text: Identify the root cause of the communication issues.
options.rationale: Identifying the root cause — unfamiliarity with Scrum, conflict, tools — shows what intervention will work.

options.text: Monitor the team's communication and provide feedback.
options.rationale: Monitoring and feedback is useful after the cause is known and a fix is in place.

questions.explanation: Communication breakdowns have many possible causes. Diagnosing the real cause before intervening ensures the response fits, rather than applying a generic fix.
questions.mindset: Diagnose communication problems before prescribing a fix.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on a project in its implementation phase when a stakeholder informs them that sales have suddenly decreased significantly. Upon investigation, the project manager finds out that an unexpected shift in market conditions resulted in a significant reduction in demand for the product, leading to decreased sales. What should the project manager do first to address this issue?

options.text: Identify the potential risks associated with the market shift and develop plans to address them.
options.rationale: Identifying the risks from the market shift and planning responses gives the project a structured way to adapt.

options.text: Use forecasting formulas to generate a high-level estimate of the impact of the decreased demand.
options.rationale: A high-level forecast of impact is useful but addresses only cost, not the range of risks.

options.text: Increase the contingency reserve to compensate for the cost of responding to the unexpected shift.
options.rationale: Increasing contingency without analysis is guesswork.

options.text: Use earned value management (EVM) techniques to calculate an estimate at completion (EAC) forecast.
options.rationale: EAC forecasting measures cost performance, not the market risk.

questions.explanation: A sudden market shift creates new risks for project value and scope. Identifying and planning for those risks allows the project to respond deliberately, whether by adjusting scope, approach or business case.
questions.mindset: Treat market shifts as sources of risk to analyse and plan for.

questions.stem: During project execution, an issue arises that requires additional budget and time to resolve the issue. The project team did not identify this issue as a risk during risk management planning. The project sponsor points out that this risk has occurred on past projects. What should the project manager have done to avoid this oversight?

options.text: Reviewed the risk management plan.
options.rationale: The risk management plan describes the method, not specific risks from past projects.

options.text: Confirmed organizational risk appetite.
options.rationale: Risk appetite affects how risks are treated, not whether they are identified.

options.text: Reviewed the lessons learned register.
options.rationale: Reviewing the lessons learned register would have revealed that this risk occurred on past projects.

options.text: Allocated additional contingency reserves.
options.rationale: More contingency does not identify the risk; it only funds unknown impacts.

questions.explanation: Historical information is a primary source for risk identification. Lessons learned from past projects surface recurring risks that should be anticipated.
questions.mindset: Mine past projects for risks before they surprise this one.

questions.stem: During the development of a project management plan, the project team inadvertently omitted an essential component required for a product. The team quickly developed a workaround, but during a quality compliance review, the project management office (PMO) determined that the workaround was not effective. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Design a revised prototype of the workaround with a new modification to resolve the issue.
options.rationale: Designing another workaround repeats an approach that has already failed review.

options.text: Review the requirements traceability matrix to determine the business value of the missing component.
options.rationale: The business value of an essential component is not in question; it must be addressed.

options.text: Follow the formal integrated change control process to submit a change request to the change control board (CCB).
options.rationale: A change request through integrated change control defines and approves the proper fix with its impacts understood.

options.text: Perform a qualitative risk analysis to assess the impact of designing a replacement for the workaround.
options.rationale: Qualitative risk analysis is not the mechanism for authorising the needed change.

questions.explanation: When a gap in the plan requires a real fix, the change goes through integrated change control so scope, schedule and cost impacts are assessed and approved.
questions.mindset: Replace failed workarounds through controlled change.

questions.stem: A software development project is in the testing phase. New government regulation requires that additional documentation be delivered under the contract. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Terminate the project.
options.rationale: Terminating the project is disproportionate to a documentation requirement.

options.text: Submit a change request.
options.rationale: New mandatory documentation changes the contract scope, so a change request is the first step.

options.text: Update the schedule forecast.
options.rationale: Schedule forecasts are updated after the change is approved.

options.text: Review the project budget.
options.rationale: Budget review follows once the change is assessed.

questions.explanation: Mandatory new regulatory requirements change project scope. They are brought into the project through a change request so their impact is assessed and the baseline updated.
questions.mindset: Bring mandatory new requirements in through change control.

questions.stem: While reviewing project documentation, a project manager discovers that modifications were made without proper approvals. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Escalate the issue to the project management office (PMO).
options.rationale: Escalating to the PMO before understanding what the process requires is premature.

options.text: Review the change management plan.
