options.rationale: The change management plan sets out how changes are to be approved and how unauthorised changes are handled.

options.text: Review the requirements management plan.
options.rationale: The requirements plan does not govern change approvals.

options.text: Escalate the issue to the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Escalating to the sponsor skips the PM's own responsibility.

questions.explanation: When changes bypass approval, the project manager goes back to the change management plan to understand the process and how to bring those changes under control.
questions.mindset: Return to the agreed change process when changes slip through.

questions.stem: A project management team is developing a project management information system (PMIS) as a collaboration tool for internal and external stakeholders. The project manager wants to develop a dashboard component within the system that will be updated with information on projects' performance. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Identify the data that will be displayed.
options.rationale: Choosing data first risks displaying what is available rather than what people need.

options.text: Select the appropriate visualization tools.
options.rationale: Visualisation choices depend on what is being communicated.

options.text: Determine the frequency of dashboard updates.
options.rationale: Update frequency depends on how stakeholders use the information.

options.text: Define the communication needs of the stakeholders.
options.rationale: Defining stakeholders' communication needs first ensures the dashboard shows the right information.

questions.explanation: Dashboards are communication tools, so their design starts with the audience. Knowing what each stakeholder needs to see and when determines the data, visualisations and update frequency; starting with the data or the tools risks showing what is easy rather than what is useful.
questions.mindset: Design reporting tools around the audience's needs.

questions.stem: A project manager is managing a technology project that is in the implementation phase. A key stakeholder communicates the need for changes to the project. The stakeholder and team members disagree about the need for the changes and how to implement them. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Meet with the stakeholder and the team members separately to understand their concerns.
options.rationale: Meeting each party separately allows the PM to understand concerns without confrontation, laying the basis for a resolution.

options.text: Conduct a risk assessment to determine the impact of the changes.
options.rationale: A risk assessment is useful but premature before understanding the disagreement.

options.text: Present the pros and cons of the changes to the stakeholder and team members.
options.rationale: Presenting pros and cons without understanding concerns may miss the points that matter.

options.text: Make the changes without consulting the stakeholder or team members.
options.rationale: Making changes without consultation bypasses the stakeholders.

questions.explanation: Where a stakeholder and the team disagree about a change, the project manager first understands each side's reasons. That understanding makes a collaborative resolution possible.
questions.mindset: Understand each side before bringing them together.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on a software development project. Several team members have become overly focused on delivering individual features and cannot reach a consensus on which features to prioritize. A stakeholder contacts the project manager and expresses concerns about value delivery. What action should the project manager take?

options.text: Meet with the team to develop a plan to prioritize features based on value.
options.rationale: Developing a value-based prioritisation plan with the team resolves disagreements and addresses the stakeholder's concern.

options.text: Request that the stakeholder provide a checklist of the most important features.
options.rationale: A checklist from one stakeholder may miss the broader value picture.

options.text: Mandate a specific prioritization schema to the team after receiving approval.
options.rationale: Imposing a prioritisation scheme, even with approval, undermines the team's ownership and does not help them understand why value should drive priority.

options.text: Perform quality inspections and document the results in a report to the stakeholder.
options.rationale: Quality inspections do not address prioritisation.

questions.explanation: Prioritisation by value gives teams an objective way to agree what comes first and assures stakeholders that value drives the work.
questions.mindset: Let value settle priority debates.

questions.stem: A key stakeholder requests new features to be added to a product during the project implementation phase. The stakeholder insists that the new features will add value to the product. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Meet with the project sponsor to discuss the benefits of the new features.
options.rationale: Discussing benefits with the sponsor comes after the impact is understood.

options.text: Review the stakeholder engagement plan to determine the key stakeholder's level of involvement.
options.rationale: The engagement plan is not relevant to assessing the change.

options.text: Assess and review how the changes will impact the project budget and schedule.
options.rationale: Assessing the impact on budget and schedule is the first step in evaluating the requested change.

options.text: Implement the change and document the outcome in the lessons learned repository.
options.rationale: Implementing without approval bypasses change control.

questions.explanation: Requests for new features, however valuable, need their impact assessed before a decision. That assessment feeds the change control process.
questions.mindset: Assess impact before approving any new feature.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a business transformation project at a company facing significant financial challenges due to a declining market share. The project manager's stakeholders are skeptical of the need for change and are reluctant to invest in the project. What should the project manager do to demonstrate the urgency and benefits of the change?

options.text: Create a detailed communication plan outlining project goals, milestones, and benefits.
options.rationale: A communication plan informs but does not quantify why change is needed.

options.text: Delegate tasks and provide necessary resources to team members for success.
options.rationale: Delegating tasks does not persuade sceptical stakeholders.

options.text: Hold regular stakeholder meetings to keep them updated and address their questions.
options.rationale: Regular meetings keep stakeholders informed but do not provide evidence of benefits.

options.text: Develop a business case quantifying project benefits and aligning with company goals.
options.rationale: A business case quantifying benefits and aligning with goals provides evidence to convince sceptical stakeholders.

questions.explanation: Sceptical stakeholders need evidence. A business case that quantifies benefits and links the change to company goals creates urgency and justification.
questions.mindset: Persuade sceptics with quantified benefits.

questions.stem: A project leader noticed that a new team member is demotivated and always arrives late to work, causing a delay in the deliverables. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask HR to deal with the team member's attendance, advise them to arrive on time, and remind them of the incentives at the end of the project.
options.rationale: Handing attendance to HR and pointing to incentives avoids the conversation.

options.text: Ask a senior team member to speak with the team member, share personal experiences, and find out the reasons for the performance issues.
options.rationale: Asking another team member to handle it delegates the PM's responsibility.

options.text: During the daily meeting, ask all team members to arrive on time, and plan an event after working hours to celebrate the project progress.
options.rationale: A general reminder does not address the individual's motivation.

options.text: Talk with the team member on a one-to-one basis, emphasizing the importance of teamwork and the value of each member's contributions.
options.rationale: A one-to-one conversation lets the PM understand the member's situation and reinforce the value of their contribution.

questions.explanation: Individual performance and motivation issues are addressed personally. A one-to-one conversation uncovers causes and builds commitment.
questions.mindset: Address individual issues individually.

questions.stem: A key stakeholder's input is essential to a project's success. However, the stakeholder is always late on critical project decisions. What can the project manager do to re-engage this stakeholder?

options.text: Meet with the stakeholder to understand the reason for the delay.
options.rationale: Understanding why decisions are late lets the PM help the stakeholder engage effectively.

options.text: Remove the stakeholder from the project.
options.rationale: Removing an essential stakeholder is neither possible nor desirable.

options.text: Brief the steering committee on the stakeholder's delays.
options.rationale: Briefing the steering committee escalates before trying to fix the problem.

options.text: Add the stakeholder's delay to the issue log.
options.rationale: Logging the delay records it but does not re-engage the stakeholder.

questions.explanation: Re-engaging a stakeholder starts with understanding the causes of their disengagement. Solutions can then be tailored to their constraints.
questions.mindset: Understand disengagement before trying to fix it.

questions.stem: An agile project team is implementing a supporting technology platform across departments. They're planning a readiness review for the delivery. Who should the project manager propose to conduct the readiness review?

options.text: The product owner is responsible for product vision and backlog management.
options.rationale: The product owner owns vision and backlog, but judging technical and functional readiness of a cross-department platform needs deeper platform knowledge.

options.text: The quality control (QC) manager is responsible for ensuring delivery quality and efficiency.
options.rationale: A QC manager checks conformance to quality standards but may lack the detailed understanding of how the platform must serve each department.

options.text: The quality assurance (QA) manager is responsible for proposing measures for delivery improvement.
options.rationale: A QA manager focuses on improving processes, which is not the same as judging whether this platform is ready to go live.

options.text: The subject matter expert (SME) is responsible for a deep understanding of the platform and requirements.
options.rationale: The SME understands the platform and the departments' requirements in depth, so they are best placed to judge whether it is ready.

questions.explanation: A readiness review asks whether a solution will work as intended for the people who depend on it. That judgement needs someone with deep knowledge of both the platform and the requirements, which is why subject matter expertise is central to it.
questions.mindset: Ask the people who understand the solution and its users to judge its readiness.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned to a complex IT project that is expected to deliver significant benefits to the organization. The project manager has a team of experienced engineers and analysts, but no dedicated data scientist or business intelligence specialist. The project manager must enable data capture and reporting related to benefits realization. What is the most appropriate approach for this task?

options.text: Recruiting an external consultant to supervise data capture and business value reporting procedures.
options.rationale: An external consultant adds cost and moves ownership of benefits reporting away from the team that knows the project.

options.text: Implementing a single data collection and analysis system for all stakeholders and all benefits.
options.rationale: A single system for all stakeholders and benefits ignores that different benefits need different measures and sources.

options.text: Collaborating with the team to define key performance indicators (KPIs) and data collection methods.
options.rationale: Defining KPIs and data collection methods with the team aligns measurement with project goals and uses the team's expertise.

options.text: Using a variety of data collection methods and tools to meet the needs of different stakeholders.
options.rationale: Many tools and methods without agreed KPIs produce data without a clear link to the benefits being tracked.

questions.explanation: Benefits reporting depends first on agreeing what to measure. Defining KPIs and how data will be collected, with the people who understand the work, creates a coherent basis for tracking benefits even without specialist analysts.
questions.mindset: Agree what to measure before worrying about tools to measure it.

questions.stem: What should a project manager do first when people are not following the project compliance process?

options.text: Escalate the issue to senior management or the sponsor
options.rationale: Escalating before understanding why people are not complying treats a possibly fixable issue as a disciplinary one.

options.text: Initiate an audit process
options.rationale: An audit confirms non-compliance but does not explain it.

options.text: Log the non-compliance and watch the progress
options.rationale: Logging and watching lets the non-compliance continue.

options.text: Understand the reasons for non-compliance
options.rationale: Understanding the reasons — unclear process, burden, lack of training — shows how to restore compliance.

questions.explanation: Non-compliance with a process usually has a cause: people do not understand it, find it impractical or lack the means to follow it. Understanding that cause lets the project manager fix the real problem rather than just enforce.
questions.mindset: Understand why a process is not followed before enforcing it.

questions.stem: During a meeting with project stakeholders, two stakeholders have a disagreement regarding how a software component is being developed. The disagreement escalates as the stakeholders raise their voices. What should the project manager do in this situation?

options.text: Adjourn the meeting and meet with the other stakeholders on how to proceed.
options.rationale: Adjourning and excluding the two parties avoids the conflict without resolving it.

options.text: Identify what is causing the conflict, attempt to de-escalate the situation, and focus on finding a common solution.
options.rationale: Identifying the cause, calming the situation and moving toward a shared solution resolves the conflict constructively.

options.text: Take detailed notes of both stakeholders' positions and ask the remaining stakeholders to vote on the best option.
options.rationale: Voting on positions produces winners and losers and may deepen the conflict.

options.text: Inform the sponsor about the conflict and ask them to find a solution.
options.rationale: Passing the conflict to the sponsor abdicates the PM's role.

questions.explanation: When a disagreement escalates in a meeting, the project manager de-escalates, identifies what is really causing the conflict and steers toward a collaborative solution.
questions.mindset: De-escalate first, then solve together.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned to an existing project, replacing the previous project manager. Soon after joining the project, the project manager sees that the project’s key performance indicators (KPIs) are decreasing, as is the project team’s overall enthusiasm for the project. The project manager reviews earlier projects completed by the team and sees that they previously performed well together. What should the project manager do to address the performance issues?

options.text: Meet with the sponsor to express concerns regarding the team performance.
options.rationale: Raising concerns with the sponsor before speaking with the team avoids the PM's own responsibility.

options.text: Work on identifying other resources to replace the current team.
options.rationale: Replacing a team that has performed well before is drastic and ignores likely causes such as the transition.

options.text: Meet with the project team to discuss the current level of performance.
options.rationale: Meeting the team to discuss current performance uncovers the reasons for the decline and builds a relationship with the new PM.

options.text: Meet with the functional managers of the team asking them to address the decreasing performance.
options.rationale: Asking functional managers to fix it deflects the PM's responsibility.

questions.explanation: A team that previously performed well but is now struggling after a leadership change needs direct engagement. Discussing performance openly with the team reveals causes and starts building trust.
questions.mindset: Engage the team directly when its performance changes.

questions.stem: A project manager must make decisions daily, regardless of the decision's level of importance or criticality. What should a project manager do to ensure their decisions are unbiased and rational?

options.text: Utilize data without checking for accuracy
options.rationale: Using unchecked data introduces errors into decisions.

options.text: Understand they cannot achieve everything
options.rationale: Accepting that not everything can be achieved guards against optimism bias, leading to more realistic decisions.

options.text: Make decisions quickly
options.rationale: Speed alone does not make decisions rational.

options.text: Make decisions only when the results are certain
options.rationale: Waiting for certainty paralyses decision-making.

questions.explanation: Optimism bias leads people to overestimate what can be achieved. Recognising limits helps project managers make realistic, rational decisions.
questions.mindset: Guard against optimism when deciding.

questions.stem: The team informed the project leader that they are not sure of the stakeholder needs, despite the multiple collection requirements efforts and engagement in status meetings. How should the project manager approach this issue?

options.text: Require the team to work with the stakeholders to analyze their detailed requirements and sign off on the specification
options.rationale: More detailed analysis and sign-off repeats efforts that have not produced clarity.

options.text: Discuss with the team the option of canceling the project since the risk is too great to continue
options.rationale: Cancelling the project because requirements are unclear is disproportionate when there are practical ways to clarify stakeholder needs.

options.text: Ask the team to write a collection of user stories to capture the needs, prioritize and manage the stories
options.rationale: Writing user stories captures what the team thinks but does not validate it with stakeholders.

options.text: Document what the team believes the stakeholders need, show it to stakeholders, and ask for their feedback to share with the team
options.rationale: Documenting the team's understanding and asking stakeholders for feedback tests assumptions and clarifies needs.

questions.explanation: When repeated requirement collection fails, showing stakeholders something concrete — a documented interpretation or prototype — and asking for feedback is often the fastest way to understand their needs.
questions.mindset: Show your understanding and ask for feedback.

questions.stem: A project manager is managing a project with a very aggressive delivery schedule and a firm completion date. The project requires expensive and fragile components that are prone to rework and rejections. The project manager is developing the vendor selection criteria. What should be the strategy for vendor selection?

options.text: Lowest price regardless of the vendor's warehouse location.
options.rationale: Lowest price ignores the risk of delay from distant replacements for fragile components.

options.text: Acceptable price if the vendor is closer to the project site.
options.rationale: An acceptable price from a nearby vendor reduces replacement lead times for fragile, rework-prone components on a tight schedule.

options.text: Project sponsor'srecommendation based on past experience.
options.rationale: The sponsor's recommendation may not consider this project's specific constraints.

options.text: Team members' recommendations based on past experience.
options.rationale: Team recommendations may help but do not address the specific logistic risk.

questions.explanation: Vendor selection criteria should reflect project risks. With fragile items and a tight schedule, proximity reduces delay risk from replacements and may outweigh price.
questions.mindset: Select vendors against the project's real risks, not just price.

questions.stem: A project manager oversees a complex project in which a vendor is responsible for delivering several essential components. The project manager and the vendor team are located in different time zones, and this time zone difference has become a significant challenge, leading to productivity issues within the project. Team members from both sides often struggle to coordinate meetings, share updates, and communicate effectively due to the time zone disparities. What should the project manager do to solve this issue?

options.text: Closely monitor the project schedule and take action if milestones are missed.
options.rationale: Monitoring milestones reacts after the fact without addressing coordination.

options.text: Ask both teams to change their working hours to a common time zone.
options.rationale: Adjusting working hours to create a common window enables synchronous communication.

options.text: Find a common space and relocate the vendor team with the project team.
options.rationale: Relocating the vendor is expensive and impractical.

options.text: Terminate the engagement and find a new vendor in the local time zone.
options.rationale: Terminating an essential vendor over a coordination problem is disproportionate and would itself cause major delay.

questions.explanation: Time-zone gaps hinder collaboration. Creating shared working time, even partially, allows synchronous coordination and reduces delays.
questions.mindset: Create shared time for collaboration across time zones.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on a complex software project. Two team members must team up and work together on a critical module of the project. Before long, the two team members begin to argue and these arguments are impeding progress. How should the project manager resolve this conflict?

options.text: Ignore the conflict and hope that they can work it out on their own.
options.rationale: Ignoring conflict lets it continue to impede progress.

options.text: Assign them to work separately on different tasks to avoid further conflicts.
options.rationale: Separating them avoids conflict but loses collaboration on a critical module.

options.text: Schedule a team meeting to discuss the issues openly and find a resolution.
options.rationale: An open discussion to find a resolution moves the conflict into constructive problem-solving.

options.text: Reassign one of them to a different project to eliminate the conflict entirely.
options.rationale: Reassigning one of them removes the conflict but loses a contributor.

questions.explanation: Conflict that impedes critical work needs to be addressed, not avoided. Bringing it into an open discussion aimed at a resolution turns the disagreement into problem-solving and preserves the collaboration the module depends on.
questions.mindset: Bring conflict into the open and solve it together.

questions.stem: A project manager learns that the project team is involved in an ongoing conflict with an overseas supplier team. The conflict is beginning to impact the performance of the project team. After reviewing the team charter, what should the project manager do next?

options.text: Meet with the manager of the supplier team in person to find a resolution.
options.rationale: Meeting in person overseas is slow and costly.

options.text: Organize a virtual meeting with the supplier team to address and resolve the conflict.
options.rationale: A virtual meeting brings both teams together quickly to address and resolve the conflict.

options.text: Send a copy of the procurement agreement to the manager of the supplier team.
options.rationale: Sending the contract signals a legal dispute and escalates the conflict rather than resolving it.

options.text: Send an email to the manager of the supplier team explaining the issue and asking for a response.
options.rationale: Email is slow and may deepen misunderstanding.

questions.explanation: Conflict with overseas partners is best addressed through direct, synchronous conversation. Virtual meetings allow timely resolution.
questions.mindset: Address supplier conflict directly and quickly.

questions.stem: During the initial planning phase of a complex development project, a project team has identified several stakeholders, including the project sponsor, endusers, regulatory authorities, and the development team. What should the project manager do to ensure that they have a thorough understanding of the various degrees of influence these stakeholders have on project requirements?

options.text: Conduct one-on-one interviews with each stakeholder to gather their input and preferences.
options.rationale: One-to-one interviews gather input but do not show relative influence.

options.text: Send a questionnaire to stakeholders to gather their feedback on project requirements.
options.rationale: Questionnaires collect feedback but provide little insight into influence dynamics.

options.text: Hold a stakeholder workshop to discuss and prioritize project requirements collectively.
options.rationale: A workshop allows stakeholders to discuss and prioritise together, revealing their relative influence on requirements.

options.text: Review historical project documents to identify stakeholder influence patterns.
options.rationale: Historical documents may not reflect current stakeholders.

questions.explanation: Understanding the relative influence of stakeholders is easier when they interact. Workshops reveal how priorities are negotiated.
questions.mindset: See influence in action by bringing stakeholders together.

questions.stem: A product owner has been attending daily standups but seems focused only on the budget and costs of each iteration. When addressing these inquiries, the project manager explains the rationale of the spend and the impact on the product development. The product owner does not seem interested in the rationale, only in the amount spent. What should the project manager do in this scenario?

options.text: Adjust the daily standups to first address the budget, then discuss the project status once the product owner leaves the meeting.
options.rationale: Rearranging stand-ups around one person splits the team's information.

options.text: Modify the communications management plan to send daily budget status updates to the product owner.
options.rationale: Daily budget updates reinforce a cost-only focus.

options.text: Meet with the product owner to educate them on the value delivered by the project, not just the cost of development.
options.rationale: Educating the product owner on value delivered shifts the focus from cost to value.

options.text: Breakout the budget to reflect daily spend and provide this to the product owner to address their concerns.
options.rationale: Daily spend breakdowns feed the same narrow focus.

questions.explanation: Product owners must weigh value against cost. When they focus only on spend, the PM helps them understand the value being delivered.
questions.mindset: Shift the conversation from cost to value.

questions.stem: Stakeholders in a multinational project are experiencing cross-cultural misunderstandings. A seemingly small cultural misinterpretation during the planning phase resulted in the failure to approve the project management plan. What should the project manager have done to avoid this situation?

options.text: Reviewed the lessons learned register to understand previous cultural mistakes made by the organization.
options.rationale: Lessons learned may not cover these specific cultures.

options.text: Researched common cultural mistakes made when dealing with stakeholders from the countries involved with the project.
options.rationale: Research helps, but does not create shared understanding.

options.text: Monitored direct and indirect communication during initial interactions to minimize the chance of a misunderstanding.
options.rationale: Monitoring communication reacts after misunderstandings occur.

options.text: Held a workshop with the stakeholders before the initial meeting to develop a common communication language.
options.rationale: A workshop to develop common communication conventions prevents cultural misunderstanding.

questions.explanation: Proactively establishing shared communication norms with multicultural stakeholders prevents misunderstandings that can derail approvals.
questions.mindset: Build shared communication norms before they are needed.

questions.stem: The project manager's last IT transformation project was canceled due to a misalignment of a business process with the accounting department. A similar project will begin soon, and a process alignment activity will be planned to identify potential scope changes. What should the project manager do to ensure a collaborative and incremental approach to the process alignment work is utilized?

options.text: Identify an external expert team to research and apply best practices in adapting businesses to IT transformation.
options.rationale: External experts may help but do not create collaboration among internal units.

options.text: Plan for an early, two-week activity where impacted units work together to finalize adaptations to the business processes.
options.rationale: A single two-week activity may not allow enough iteration.

options.text: Plan for iterations early in the project to allow cross-functional stakeholders to agree on steps to adapt the business processes.
options.rationale: Early iterations let cross-functional stakeholders align processes incrementally and identify scope changes early.

options.text: Plan for iterations late in the project to allow cross-functional stakeholders to adapt the processes according to delivered work.
options.rationale: Late iterations discover misalignment too late.

questions.explanation: Aligning business processes with a new system benefits from early, iterative collaboration. It surfaces scope changes while they are still inexpensive to address.
questions.mindset: Iterate early on alignment to discover changes early.

questions.stem: In the middle of a three-year-long project, the company committee overseeing the project becomes uncertain about whether the final outcome will meet their expectations and provide the anticipated value. As the project manager, what proactive step can you take to address the committee's concerns and ensure that the project delivers the expected value?

options.text: Extend the project timeline to allow for more thorough testing.
options.rationale: Extending the timeline for more testing adds delay without showing the committee anything about the value of the result.

options.text: Develop a prototype to present to the committee.
options.rationale: A prototype lets the committee see and evaluate the likely outcome, addressing their concerns early.

options.text: Increase the project budget to accommodate potential changes.
options.rationale: Adding budget for potential changes spends more money without addressing the committee's doubt about value.

options.text: Update the project schedule with detailed milestones.
options.rationale: Adding detailed milestones to the schedule shows progress in activity terms, not whether the outcome will meet expectations.

questions.explanation: When a governing body doubts whether a long project will deliver the value it expects, something tangible — a prototype, a demonstration — lets them judge for themselves and steer early, which is far more convincing than more time, money or plans.
questions.mindset: Show value early to build confidence.

questions.stem: A project team meeting is focused on examining if the business value and vision for a project are being delivered by all parties. During the meeting, it was discovered that a few team members were unaware of the project's vision and business value. What should the project manager do to ensure everyone is aware of the vision and business value the project is expected to bring moving forward?

options.text: Schedule regular meetings between the team and senior management to remind them what the vision and business value are.
options.rationale: Occasional meetings with senior management are infrequent and one-way; they will not give team members a working understanding of the vision.

options.text: Tell the team members to refer to the company vision statement and other high-level strategy documents for clarity.
options.rationale: Company strategy documents are too general to explain this project's specific vision and business value.

options.text: Hold the team accountable as they have had ample time to become aware of the project vision and business value.
options.rationale: Blaming the team does nothing to close the gap in understanding and damages the trust needed to fix it.

options.text: Engage with the team regularly regarding the business case and ensure that all doubts are addressed properly and cleared.
options.rationale: Regular engagement with the team about the business case, answering their questions, builds and maintains a shared understanding of the vision and value.

questions.explanation: A shared understanding of purpose is not created once at kick-off; it is maintained. The project manager keeps the business case and vision present in day-to-day conversation with the team so that decisions and deliverables stay connected to the value they are meant to produce.
questions.mindset: Keep the vision alive in everyday conversations, not just in documents.

questions.stem: A team is working on a complex and fast-changing new product development project. After a recent process evaluation, the team decides to add an agile toolkit to the predictive approach they are using. This addition is intended to improve the overall project delivery, success, and productivity. Which of the following describes how this change is intended to add value to the overall delivery, success, and productivity?

options.text: Use the agile toolkit to leverage the ability of agile methods to respond effectively to change, while maintaining the benefits of a predictive approach to project management.
options.rationale: A hybrid combines agile's responsiveness to change with the structure of a predictive approach, which is exactly the value this addition is meant to bring.

options.text: Use the agile toolkit to replace all predictive methods with new agile methods, and by doing so, reduce poor productivity.
options.rationale: Replacing every predictive method goes far beyond adding a toolkit and throws away the structure that still helps the project.

options.text: Use the agile toolkit to compare agile against predictive methods, then choose the best approach for future projects.
options.rationale: Running a comparison to pick an approach for future projects does not improve delivery on this one.

options.text: Use the agile toolkit and ask team members to choose between agile and predictive methods so that they will work more effectively and productively.
options.rationale: Letting each person choose a method fragments the team's way of working and undermines coordination.

questions.explanation: Hybrid approaches tailor delivery by combining practices. Adding agile tools to a predictive framework lets a team respond to change in uncertain areas while keeping planning and control where they add value.
questions.mindset: Combine approaches to get the strengths of each.

questions.stem: An application developer took a story card to work that read "Customer can pay using credit card". After the implementation, the functionality was rejected because the application could not accept foreign credit cards. What should the project manager have done to avoid this issue?

options.text: Described the user story in more detail.
options.rationale: A more detailed story, with acceptance criteria covering card types, would have made the foreign-card requirement explicit before implementation.

options.text: Scheduled the user story for the next iteration.
options.rationale: Rescheduling the story does not add the missing detail.

options.text: Performed iterative backlog grooming with the team.
options.rationale: Backlog refinement is where detail is added, but the specific failure was the story's lack of detail about which cards to accept.

options.text: Gathered more detailed requirement specifications from end users.
options.rationale: Detailed specifications are one route, but in agile the story and its acceptance criteria are where this detail belongs.

questions.explanation: User stories are placeholders for conversation, and acceptance criteria record what the conversation concluded. When a story lacks criteria that define important variations, developers build the obvious case and miss the rest.
questions.mindset: Make acceptance criteria explicit enough to cover the cases that matter.

questions.stem: In an industrial plant, the owner has decided to add more capacity to the plant by installing a new machine and updating the software used in production. This capacity enlargement will occur while the plant is still functioning and producing. The software update will be accomplished using an agile approach in order to minimize risk. The machine procurement, installation, and integration will be accomplished using predictive approaches. What types of communications will the project manager have to design into the schedule management plan to ensure the project will be on schedule?

options.text: Weekly colocated meetings with the relevant stakeholders
options.rationale: Weekly face-to-face meetings with the relevant stakeholders allow fast coordination between the agile software work and predictive machine work.

options.text: Biweekly written status reports from the relevant stakeholders
options.rationale: Written reports every two weeks are slow and one-way for coordinating interdependent streams in a live plant.

options.text: Weekly one-on-one meetings with each of the relevant stakeholders
options.rationale: One-to-one meetings do not bring the interdependent parties together to coordinate.

options.text: Biweekly conference calls with the relevant stakeholders
options.rationale: Fortnightly calls are less frequent and less rich than colocated meetings.

questions.explanation: When agile and predictive streams must be coordinated in a live environment, frequent, rich communication among the relevant stakeholders keeps the schedule on track.
questions.mindset: Coordinate interdependent streams with frequent, direct communication.

questions.stem: All quality controls have passed, and a project deliverable is ready to be released to the customer. However, a change request to add new quality criteria has been approved. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Update the project management plan.
options.rationale: Updating the plan is necessary but the immediate risk is releasing a deliverable that does not meet the approved criteria.

options.text: Stop the release of the deliverable to the customer.
options.rationale: Stopping the release prevents delivering something that no longer meets the approved quality criteria.

options.text: Use the new quality criteria for future deliverables.
options.rationale: Approved criteria apply to all deliverables, including this one.

options.text: Update the risk register.
options.rationale: The change is approved, not a risk; the register is not the priority.

questions.explanation: An approved change to quality criteria takes effect immediately. Deliverables not yet released must meet the new criteria, so release should be halted until conformance is confirmed.
questions.mindset: Apply approved quality changes before releasing, not after.

questions.stem: An impact assessment reveals that a deliverable could be delayed by two weeks. A key resource has not been available to work on a non-critical activity due to other priorities. This could cause work overload on the other remaining resources. Since cost is a major constraint for this project, what should the project manager do immediately?

options.text: Determine if the task has available float to meet the project end date.
options.rationale: Checking float shows whether the non-critical activity's delay actually threatens the end date before spending any money.

options.text: Hire a temporary resource to do the job.
options.rationale: Hiring a temporary resource adds cost when cost is the main constraint.

options.text: Consult the team and reduce the scope.
options.rationale: Reducing scope is a significant change and may be unnecessary.

options.text: Change the resource calendar to avoid major delays.
options.rationale: Changing the resource calendar may not reflect availability.

questions.explanation: Delays on non-critical activities may be absorbed by float. Checking the schedule first prevents unnecessary cost when cost is the binding constraint.
questions.mindset: Check float before spending to recover a delay.

questions.stem: During a team meeting, team members asked the project manager to advise them on project dependencies. What should the project manager ask the team to do for internal dependencies?

options.text: Become familiar with the latest organizational changes.
options.rationale: Internal organisational changes can shift responsibilities and priorities within the organisation, creating internal dependencies for the team.

options.text: Read about the merger with a competing organization.
options.rationale: A merger is an external event whose effects on internal dependencies are indirect.

options.text: Check the changes related to the work-from-home policy.
options.rationale: A work-from-home policy may affect how people work, but not directly the project's internal dependencies.

options.text: Become familiar with the upgrade of the Internet provider.
options.rationale: An internet provider upgrade is an external service change.

questions.explanation: Internal dependencies arise from within the organisation — reorganisations, other teams' priorities and decisions. Staying aware of organisational changes helps teams anticipate how those dependencies might shift.
questions.mindset: Watch the organisation around you for changes that affect your dependencies.

questions.stem: A key supplier has become unavailable and the project manager has found a replacement that will meet project approval. Bringing the new supplier onboard will add 10 days to the project timeline. However, a key stakeholder does not want to extend the schedule. The new supplier must be used to move to the execution phase. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Meet with the stakeholder to explain that using the new supplier will increase the timeline but will meet the overall project goals.
options.rationale: Arguing that the longer timeline still meets goals presents the delay as settled without engaging the stakeholder in reviewing it.

options.text: Let the stakeholder know that the current schedule will require updates, and continue with periodic reviews to discuss the updates.
options.rationale: Telling the stakeholder the schedule will need updating and reviewing it periodically keeps them informed and involved as the change is managed.

options.text: Inform the stakeholder that there will be a 10-day delay in the schedule to onboard the new supplier, but critical path tasks will be fast tracked.
options.rationale: Promising fast-tracking commits to a solution without analysis.

options.text: Communicate to the stakeholder that using the new supplier will require a restart at the beginning of the next planning phase.
options.rationale: A restart is not implied by changing suppliers.

questions.explanation: When unavoidable changes affect the schedule, the project manager is transparent with stakeholders and keeps them involved in reviewing updates, managing expectations over time.
questions.mindset: Be transparent about unavoidable change and keep stakeholders involved.

questions.stem: A project manager wants to develop their own leadership capability during a long project. Select three ways to improve and practise leadership skills. (Choose 3)

options.text: Engage the team in the project process.
options.rationale: Engaging the team in the project process builds leadership through involvement and shared ownership.

options.text: Be actively involved in the project tasks.
options.rationale: Being actively involved gives the leader first-hand understanding of the work and credibility with the team.

options.text: Treat each team member the same way.
options.rationale: Treating every team member the same ignores that effective leaders adapt their style to individuals.

options.text: Ask for feedback and analyze the results.
options.rationale: Seeking feedback and analysing it helps leaders see their impact and improve.

options.text: Use democracy for all team decisions.
options.rationale: Using democracy for every decision is not always appropriate; some decisions need other approaches.

questions.explanation: Leadership skill grows through engagement with the team, involvement in the work and honest feedback. Effective leaders tailor their approach rather than applying one style to everyone or every decision.
questions.mindset: Grow as a leader by engaging, staying close to the work and seeking feedback.

questions.stem: A company is using a predictive approach for the development of a particular component as defined in the scope management plan. Due to regularly changing regulatory requirements, the development team has requested to utilize agile approaches. What should the project manager do about the development team's request?

options.text: Escalate the request for additional financial resources.
options.rationale: Asking for more money does not address the choice of method.

options.text: Analyze the requirements that will need to be addressed under the requested method.
options.rationale: Analysing which requirements would be handled under the agile approach shows whether and how a hybrid would work.

options.text: Forward the request to the project management office (PMO) to amend the organizational process assets.
options.rationale: Changing organisational process assets is premature.

options.text: Ask the project sponsor to obtain approval for implementation of the new approach.
options.rationale: Asking for approval before analysing leaves the sponsor without a basis for decision.

questions.explanation: Requests to change delivery approach should be analysed on their merits. Understanding which requirements are volatile identifies where agile practices would help, enabling a tailored hybrid proposal.
questions.mindset: Analyse where a new approach would help before asking to adopt it.

questions.stem: During the design process for a multinational construction project, the project manager conducted a cost-benefit analysis based on current foreign exchange rates. The risk of changes to the exchange rate had been recorded in the risk register. During the project implementation phase, the exchange rate has fallen to such a degree the project manager believes the project might not be successful. What should the project manager do as a proactive action?

options.text: Update the risk management plan.
options.rationale: Updating the risk management plan changes the method, not the project's viability.

options.text: Escalate the issue to the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Escalating without new analysis gives the sponsor no basis for a decision.

options.text: Submit a budget increase change request.
options.rationale: A budget increase request assumes the project should continue.

options.text: Conduct a new cost-benefit analysis.
options.rationale: A new cost-benefit analysis shows whether the project still makes sense at the new exchange rate.

questions.explanation: When a recorded risk materialises and threatens viability, re-running the cost-benefit analysis shows whether the business case still holds.
questions.mindset: Re-test the business case when its assumptions change.

questions.stem: A project manager is managing a hybrid project. After attending an iteration review, a stakeholder tells the project manager that they are very busy and asks why these reviews are held so frequently. How should the project manager respond?

options.text: Discuss with the stakeholder the benefits of the hybrid project and how frequent reviews lead to greater value and less rework.
options.rationale: Explaining how frequent reviews lead to greater value and less rework helps the stakeholder see why their time is worthwhile.

options.text: Negotiate a reduced review attendance with the stakeholder and update the stakeholder engagement plan to reflect this reduced attendance.
options.rationale: Reducing attendance may be a later option, but explaining the value comes first.

options.text: Explain to the stakeholder that the stakeholder engagement plan requires their attendance at all reviews.
options.rationale: Invoking the plan as a requirement is coercive.

options.text: Record the issue in the issue log and escalate the conflict to the project sponsor for assistance.
options.rationale: Logging an issue and escalating a stakeholder's question about review frequency is disproportionate and damages the relationship.

questions.explanation: Stakeholders are more willing to participate when they understand the benefits. Explaining how reviews reduce rework secures engagement more effectively than insisting on attendance.
questions.mindset: Explain the benefit to win participation.

questions.stem: In the early stages of a project, two key stakeholders have different opinions about a project's goals. Why should the project manager negotiate an agreement between the two stakeholders?

options.text: To understand the stakeholders' ability to influence the project's direction
options.rationale: Understanding influence is part of stakeholder analysis but is not the purpose of negotiating agreement here.

options.text: To obtain approval of the project charter
options.rationale: Agreement on goals is required to approve the project charter.

options.text: To engage the stakeholders in the conflict resolution
options.rationale: Engaging stakeholders in conflict resolution is a means, not the purpose.

options.text: To allow the stakeholders to discuss their opinions at the kick-off meeting
options.rationale: Discussing opinions at kick-off does not settle the goals.

questions.explanation: Early disagreement about goals must be settled before the charter can be approved, because the charter records the project's objectives and authorises it. Negotiating agreement at this stage prevents the project from starting on a contested foundation.
questions.mindset: Resolve disagreements on goals before chartering the project.

questions.stem: An agile team has been struggling to keep up with the planned pace, which is frequently resulting in sprint failures. What should the project manager do to help avoid this situation in the future?

options.text: Ask the project sponsor to approve overtime to compensate for the lack of performance while adjusting the plan.
options.rationale: Overtime to make up for overcommitment is unsustainable and hides the planning problem rather than fixing it.

options.text: Review the velocity of the team over the last several sprints and adjust the plan accordingly.
options.rationale: Using historical velocity to adjust the plan aligns commitments with actual capacity.

options.text: Replace junior team members with more experienced ones, and negotiate the project scope to compensate for the budget gap.
options.rationale: Replacing people and negotiating scope are disruptive.

options.text: Switch to a Kanban approach to have better control on the planned pace by limiting work in progress.
options.rationale: Switching to Kanban changes the method without addressing overcommitment.

questions.explanation: Repeated sprint failures usually mean the team is committing to more than its demonstrated capacity. Reviewing velocity over several sprints and planning to it aligns commitments with reality, which is more sustainable than overtime or restructuring.
questions.mindset: Plan sprints to demonstrated capacity.

questions.stem: A large corporation is transforming itself from a predictive to agile approach. A project team with knowledge of agile practices is experiencing significant conflicts with the executives regarding the processes to be followed. How should these conflicts be resolved?

options.text: Negotiate with the executives and agree on a process.
options.rationale: Negotiating a process with executives who do not understand agile risks a compromise that keeps the old ways and undermines the transformation.

options.text: Train the executives on agile practices.
options.rationale: Training executives in agile practices gives them the understanding they need to support the process rather than resist it.

options.text: Include the executives in team retrospectives.
options.rationale: Retrospectives are a team improvement forum; inviting executives there without grounding in agile may inhibit the team.

options.text: Request that the executives use agile practices.
options.rationale: Asking executives to use agile practices they do not understand is unlikely to change their behaviour.

questions.explanation: Agile transformations fail when leaders do not understand what they are asking the organisation to become. Executive education creates the shared understanding that lets leaders support new processes instead of pulling teams back to old ones.
questions.mindset: Transform leaders' understanding before expecting them to support new ways of working.

questions.stem: A project manager is managing a hybrid project. A stakeholder has directly contacted a team member and has requested a change. Due to the request, the team member was distracted from their work, which caused a loss in productivity. What should the team member do?

options.text: Inform the stakeholder that the correct procedure for new requirements is to provide it directly to the project manager.
options.rationale: Telling the stakeholder to go to the project manager is reasonable, but the team member should raise the impediment so its root cause is addressed.

options.text: Inform the stakeholder that the correct procedure for new requirements is to provide it directly to the change control board (CCB).
options.rationale: Directing stakeholders to the CCB for a hybrid team's backlog items may not reflect how the team handles new requests.

options.text: Inform the scrum master regarding the stakeholder's request for a change and the impact this has had on productivity.
options.rationale: Informing the scrum master about the request and its impact on productivity lets the impediment be removed and prevented.

options.text: Inform the scrum master so that the change can be discussed directly with the stakeholder.
options.rationale: The scrum master does not negotiate the change itself with the stakeholder; changes go through the product owner.

questions.explanation: When outside requests disrupt team members, the disruption is an impediment. Raising it with the person responsible for removing impediments ensures the source is addressed and the team is protected.
questions.mindset: Raise disruptions as impediments so they are removed at the source.

questions.stem: A project manager is managing a project with a hybrid approach and has requested a senior team member to perform a quantitative risk analysis. The team member responds that they do not have the knowledge to perform such an analysis. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Escalate the issue to the functional manager.
options.rationale: Escalating to the functional manager treats a development need as a performance problem.

options.text: Contact the project management office (PMO) and request them to assign another team member who has the knowledge to perform this task to the team.
options.rationale: Replacing the person through the PMO misses the chance to build the team's capability.

options.text: Help the team member to perform the quantitative risk analysis through coaching, mentoring, and training.
options.rationale: Coaching, mentoring and training help the team member build the skill and complete the task.

options.text: Perform the quantitative risk analysis for the team member.
options.rationale: Doing the analysis for them solves today's task but leaves the capability gap.

questions.explanation: Servant leaders develop their people. When a team member lacks a skill for a task, support them with coaching and training so the capability stays in the team.
questions.mindset: Develop the skill rather than working around the gap.

questions.stem: Due to a recent incident, a dissatisfied stakeholder files a complaint about a project that has been closed. What can the project manager do to help resolve this?

options.text: Execute the relationship management plan.
options.rationale: A relationship management plan is not a standard project artefact and is unlikely to help with a complaint about a closed project.

options.text: Consult with the project sponsor to manage the dissatisfied stakeholder.
options.rationale: The sponsor may be involved, but the facts must be established first.

options.text: Review the project management information system (PMIS) archives.
options.rationale: Project archives in the PMIS hold the records needed to understand what was agreed and delivered, allowing the complaint to be addressed on facts.

options.text: Update the risk register.
options.rationale: The risk register is not relevant to a closed project.

questions.explanation: Archived project records allow complaints raised after closure to be investigated objectively. They show what was agreed, delivered and accepted.
questions.mindset: Use the project's records to address complaints after closure.

questions.stem: While working on a project, the project team realizes that recent data center upgrades could impact the project's outcome. Certain modules of the project deliverable are incompatible with the new environment. The team identifies the appropriate steps to address the issue. What is the next step for the project manager?

options.text: Request a budget increase.
options.rationale: A budget request is premature before the change is approved.

options.text: Submit a change request.
options.rationale: The steps to address the incompatibility change the project, so a change request is the next step.

options.text: Change the project schedule.
options.rationale: Changing the schedule without approval bypasses change control.

options.text: Update the requirements document.
options.rationale: Updating requirements without approval is premature.

questions.explanation: Once a team has identified how to respond to an external change, the response goes through change control for approval before plans are updated.
questions.mindset: Submit the fix for approval before changing the plan.

questions.stem: A new warehouse facility is under construction. The project manager implements team development efforts such as training that will result in a lower defect ratio. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Introduce a training program.
options.rationale: The training has already been introduced; introducing it again is not the next step.

options.text: Update the resource management plan.
options.rationale: Team development activities, including training, are part of the resource management plan, which should be updated to reflect them.

options.text: Increase quality control reviews.
options.rationale: More quality reviews do not document the team development.

options.text: Add training costs to the budget.
options.rationale: Budget updates may follow but the plan is the primary record.

questions.explanation: Team development activities are recorded in the resource management plan so that they are planned, resourced and tracked.
questions.mindset: Record team development in the resource plan.

questions.stem: During project execution, a project manager learns that a team member's functional manager wants to remove them from a project because they believe they should not execute a certain task due to conflicting priorities. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Check the responsibility assignment matrix (RAM).
options.rationale: The RAM shows who is responsible for which task, giving a factual basis for discussing the assignment with the functional manager.

options.text: Check the work breakdown structure (WBS).
options.rationale: The WBS lists deliverables but not who is assigned.

options.text: Check the organizational chart.
options.rationale: The organisation chart shows reporting lines, not project assignments.

options.text: Check the resource management plan.
options.rationale: The resource plan describes how resources are managed but not specific task responsibilities.

questions.explanation: When an assignment is questioned, the RAM clarifies agreed responsibilities, which supports a discussion with the functional manager.
questions.mindset: Check agreed responsibilities before negotiating over them.

questions.stem: During project implementation, an issue arises that requires the execution of the project's contingency plan, which will impact the project schedule. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Initiate a risk audit.
options.rationale: A risk audit examines the effectiveness of risk management, not the current issue.

options.text: Issue a change request.
options.rationale: Executing a contingency plan that affects the schedule requires a change request to update the baseline.

options.text: Review the cost impact.
options.rationale: Cost impact is part of the change request analysis.

options.text: Update the contingency plan.
options.rationale: The contingency plan is being executed, not updated.

questions.explanation: Executing a contingency plan may be pre-approved as a response, but if it changes the schedule baseline, a change request formalises the update. That keeps the baseline accurate and decision-makers informed of the new plan.
questions.mindset: Formalise baseline changes even when planned for.

questions.stem: A newly formed project team features members from several countries and continents, with significant age differences and a variety of social circles. How should the project manager address this challenge?

options.text: Help the team discover how their different perspectives can expand their skill sets and strengthen team productivity.
options.rationale: Helping the team see how different perspectives expand skills turns diversity into strength.

options.text: Appoint a delegate for each ethnic/social group to contribute to inclusive decision making.
options.rationale: Appointing group delegates reinforces divisions.

options.text: Require all team members to attend a virtual class on diversity and inclusion.
options.rationale: Mandatory training assumes a problem that has not appeared.

options.text: Plan to intervene authoritatively if confrontations occur between incompatible team members.
options.rationale: Planning authoritarian intervention assumes conflict.

questions.explanation: Diverse teams perform better when members value each other's perspectives. Leaders help the team see diversity as a resource.
questions.mindset: Help the team value its diversity.

questions.stem: While preparing a project charter for a new project, a project manager reviews lessons learned from previous projects. The lessons learned documents show frequent issues with low engagement levels and stakeholder misalignment on project objectives. What should the project manager do to avoid repetition of this issue in the new project?

options.text: Allow any stakeholder to join the change control board (CCB) at any time in the project.
options.rationale: Open CCB membership creates chaos in decision-making.

options.text: Include all stakeholders in the responsibility assignment matrix (RAM) for acceptance of the deliverables.
options.rationale: Including everyone in acceptance dilutes accountability.

options.text: Gather all the requirements provided by every individual stakeholder and include in the work breakdown structure (WBS).
options.rationale: Adding every requirement to the WBS ignores prioritisation and alignment.

options.text: Build a common understanding among stakeholders about key deliverables described in the approved project charter.
options.rationale: Building common understanding of key deliverables aligns stakeholders and improves engagement.

questions.explanation: Past projects show that low engagement and misalignment come from stakeholders not sharing an understanding of what the project will deliver. Building that common understanding early around the approved charter aligns expectations without opening every decision to everyone.
questions.mindset: Build shared understanding early.

questions.stem: A new project has high uncertainty in the cost required for completion. What approach should the project manager use to determine the expected costs?

options.text: Analogous estimating
options.rationale: Analogous estimating needs comparable past projects.

options.text: Statistical techniques estimating
options.rationale: Statistical techniques estimating is not a standard named technique.

options.text: Parametric estimating
options.rationale: Parametric estimating needs reliable historical relationships.

options.text: Three-point estimating
options.rationale: Three-point estimating accounts for uncertainty using optimistic, most likely and pessimistic values.

questions.explanation: When cost uncertainty is high and no reliable comparables exist, three-point estimating captures the range between optimistic, most likely and pessimistic outcomes. The resulting expected value and spread are more honest than a single-point figure.
questions.mindset: Estimate ranges when uncertainty is high.

questions.stem: A multinational company is locally developing a digital product using a new technology platform. The only expert on this platform is located in the company's headquarters, and they are responsible for providing support to different countries. How can the local project manager ensure the involvement of this expert?

options.text: Design a travel schedule so that timely, onsite assistance can be provided.
options.rationale: Travel is slow and takes the expert away from other duties.

options.text: Include the expert on the team using a virtual environment.
options.rationale: Including the expert virtually lets them contribute regularly while supporting other countries.

options.text: Ask the project sponsor to assign the expert as a full-time member of the team.
options.rationale: Full-time assignment is unrealistic given their responsibilities.

options.text: Ask team members to contact the expert as an external expertise source on an as-needed basis.
options.rationale: Ad hoc contact risks the expert not being available when needed.

questions.explanation: Scarce experts who serve several locations can still be part of a team through virtual collaboration. Including them virtually secures regular input without taking them away from their other responsibilities or relying on ad hoc requests.
questions.mindset: Integrate scarce experts virtually.

questions.stem: A project manager engaged in the delivery of a global project is in the process of recruiting a project team. After the team is formed, what should the project manager do?

options.text: Send a welcome email and host a team introductory event with the team members so they get to know each other.
options.rationale: A welcome and introductory event helps team members get to know each other, forming the basis for collaboration.

options.text: Send a project management plan and charter to team members to familiarize them with project goals and procedures.
options.rationale: Sending documents is informative but does not build relationships.

options.text: Arrange a meeting for team members to discuss any concerns regarding requirements and project scope.
options.rationale: Opening a scope-concerns discussion before people know each other is premature and may start the team on a negative note.

options.text: Send the team members a survey to learn more about each member, share the results via email.
options.rationale: A survey with results by email is impersonal and slow compared with meeting each other directly.

questions.explanation: A newly formed global team needs to build relationships before it can collaborate well. A welcome and introductory event helps people put names to faces and start forming trust; documents and scope discussions follow.
questions.mindset: Start a team by connecting its people.

questions.stem: Some team members assigned to a new technology project expressed their lack of knowledge about the technology and the challenges they will face during implementation. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Due to the project due dates, replace the members with more knowledgeable staff.
options.rationale: Replacing members because they need training is disruptive, slow and wastes the chance to build capability.

options.text: Ask the team members to do some research and self-learning efforts about the technology.
options.rationale: Self-learning alone is less effective than structured training.

options.text: Reallocate the members to work on and complete different tasks for which they have experience.
options.rationale: Moving members away from the new technology avoids the skills gap rather than closing it.

options.text: Reassure the team members that a training path is in place to learn the new technology.
options.rationale: Reassuring members that training is planned addresses their concern and builds capability.

questions.explanation: When a team is anxious about unfamiliar technology, the leader provides a path to competence and says so. Structured training, and reassurance that it is in place, builds capability and confidence better than replacement or avoidance.
questions.mindset: Provide the path to capability.

questions.stem: Following project approval, a project team is assigned and the project management plan is created. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Hold a kickoff meeting with the project team and stakeholders.
options.rationale: A kickoff aligns team and stakeholders on goals, roles and approach after planning.

options.text: Develop a detailed project schedule.
options.rationale: The schedule is part of the plan already created.

options.text: Initiate procurement processes for required resources.
options.rationale: Procurement follows from the approved plan, but the team and stakeholders should first be aligned at the kickoff.

options.text: Conduct individual performance reviews.
options.rationale: Individual performance reviews happen during execution, not before the work has started.

questions.explanation: With the plan approved and the team assigned, a kickoff meeting launches execution by aligning team and stakeholders on objectives, roles, approach and next steps. It turns an approved plan into shared commitment.
questions.mindset: Launch execution with shared understanding.

questions.stem: A project manager wants to recruit another team member to replace an architect who recently resigned. What document should be consulted for this change?

options.text: Stakeholder register
options.rationale: The stakeholder register lists stakeholders, not recruitment procedures.

options.text: Project management plan
options.rationale: The management plan may reference resource management but not recruitment procedures.

options.text: Responsibility assignment matrix (RAM)
options.rationale: The RAM shows responsibilities, not how to recruit.

options.text: Organizational process assets (OPA)
options.rationale: OPAs include policies and procedures for recruiting and staffing.

questions.explanation: Organisational process assets contain policies and procedures, including recruitment processes, that project managers follow.
questions.mindset: Follow the organisation's procedures for staffing.

questions.stem: In the company cafeteria, a project manager overhears an unengaged stakeholder mocking the style of language used in the project manager's status report. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Meet with the stakeholder privately to find out how to make communication more engaging.
options.rationale: A private conversation turns overheard mockery into useful feedback about how to make communication engaging for this stakeholder, and starts re-engaging them.

options.text: Ask the company's public relations officer for tips on how to make written communications more captivating.
options.rationale: PR tips address external messaging style, not the specific needs of an unengaged internal stakeholder.

options.text: Stop sending the status reports to the stakeholder and use only direct email to communicate with them.
options.rationale: Cutting the stakeholder off from status reports reduces engagement further and removes their information.

options.text: Update the project social contract to prohibit disrespectful communications when referring to project members.
options.rationale: Changing the social contract to police comments treats the stakeholder's disengagement as a discipline issue instead of a communication gap.

questions.explanation: Criticism of project communication, even when expressed poorly, is a sign that it is not meeting a stakeholder's needs. Talking directly with the stakeholder about what would work for them improves the communication and helps re-engage someone who has drifted away.
questions.mindset: Turn criticism of your communication into a conversation about what would work better.

questions.stem: A project manager is in a matrix organization environment. The project manager notices the team is not working well together, performing poorly, and delivering poor quality results. How should the project manager address this with the team?

options.text: Conduct a team meeting to discuss the issue.
options.rationale: A team meeting lets the whole team discuss how they are working together and find the root causes of poor collaboration and quality.

options.text: Meet with each team member individually to get their perspective.
options.rationale: One-to-one meetings gather individual views but miss the group dynamics behind the team's problems.

options.text: Create a communication plan to improve communication between team members.
options.rationale: A communication plan may help later, but it presumes the cause is communication before discussing it.

options.text: Reassign team members to different roles.
options.rationale: Reassigning roles is a solution chosen before understanding the problem.

questions.explanation: When a team is collaborating poorly, the issue is collective and best addressed collectively. Bringing the team together to discuss it surfaces shared causes and builds joint commitment to fixing them.
questions.mindset: Address team-level problems with the whole team.

questions.stem: A project manager is overseeing the development and launch of a new product. In order to comply with the Project Management Office (PMO)'s guidelines, the project manager is required to ensure a Benefits Realization Plan outlining the business value to be delivered is created. The project manager is currently documenting the Roles and Responsibilities for this task in the form of a RACI chart. Who will be accountable for ensuring the project brings value to the organization?

options.text: Project sponsor
options.rationale: The sponsor is accountable for the project delivering value to the organisation and for its alignment with strategy.

options.text: Project manager
options.rationale: The project manager is responsible for delivering the project's outputs but is not usually accountable for the organisation realising value.

options.text: Solution architect
options.rationale: The solution architect is responsible for technical design, not business value.

options.text: Steering committee
options.rationale: The steering committee oversees and decides but is not the single accountable owner of value.

questions.explanation: In a RACI, accountability sits with one role. For business value, that is normally the sponsor, who owns the business case; the project manager is responsible for delivery that enables it.
questions.mindset: The sponsor owns the value; the project manager owns delivering what enables it.

questions.stem: After preparing the project management plan, a project manager schedules a meeting with key stakeholders to finalize the planning phase. The project manager is now preparing for the executing phase. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Define the project and create the project charter.
options.rationale: Defining the project and creating the charter happens in initiating, which is already complete.

options.text: Put the project plan into action.
options.rationale: Executing means putting the approved plan into action: assigning work, engaging stakeholders and producing deliverables.

options.text: Ensure all deliverables are completed.
options.rationale: Completing deliverables is the outcome of execution, not the next step.

options.text: Address risks to make sure the project is on track.
options.rationale: Addressing risks is ongoing but does not describe starting execution.

questions.explanation: Once the plan is agreed, execution begins: the project manager directs and manages the work defined in the plan, coordinating people and resources to produce deliverables.
questions.mindset: Once the plan is agreed, execute it.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on a complex project. The project includes many stakeholders with conflicting priorities. Which two actions should the project manager take to be prepared for negotiations and gain support from all of the stakeholders? (Choose two)

options.text: Allow enough contingency to cope with scope changes.
options.rationale: Contingency helps cope with change but does not prepare the PM to negotiate among stakeholders.
