questions.explanation: Teams moving from predictive to agile often wait for the manager to decide. The servant leader coaches them through their own decisions until self-management becomes habit.
questions.mindset: Coach teams into making their own decisions.

questions.stem: During a retrospective meeting, the project team confirmed that all deliverables were completed according to the specifications provided in the product backlog. However, the number of errors found during testing increased dramatically. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Meet with quality assurance specialists to clarify the issue and seek resolutions.
options.rationale: Working with QA specialists to understand the rise in errors identifies root causes and resolutions.

options.text: Review the risk management plan to determine the mitigation strategy.
options.rationale: The risk management plan does not diagnose a current quality problem.

options.text: Perform a Monte Carlo analysis to identify possible scenarios and actions.
options.rationale: Monte Carlo analysis models schedule or cost uncertainty, not defect causes.

options.text: Register the risk in the risk register and monitor it during the next iteration.
options.rationale: Treating a present problem as a risk to monitor delays action.

questions.explanation: When deliverables meet the stated specifications but defects rise, something in the specifications or process is wrong. Quality assurance specialists help find the cause and correct the process.
questions.mindset: Investigate rising defects with quality experts.

questions.stem: A company has an existing contract to maintain and enhance a client's customer database. The company's legal department informs the project manager that a new piece of legislation requiring stricter protection of customer information might soon be signed into law. The law will require additional security features to be implemented into the database the project manager is maintaining. These features are not included in the scope of the current contract. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Seek the project sponsor's support to influence the client to amend the contract immediately.
options.rationale: Pushing the client to amend the contract immediately is premature for a law not yet signed.

options.text: Ask the legal department to raise the issue in the next contract negotiation with the customer.
options.rationale: Waiting for the next contract negotiation is passive.

options.text: Update the risk register with the issue and plan risk response with the project sponsor and client.
options.rationale: Recording the risk and planning responses with the sponsor and client prepares for the possible law.

options.text: Wait until the legal requirements are finalized so the change in scope can be concretely defined.
options.rationale: Waiting until the law is final leaves no time to prepare.

questions.explanation: Pending legislation is a risk. Recording it and planning responses with key stakeholders prepares the project to act quickly if the law passes.
questions.mindset: Plan for pending rules as risks.

questions.stem: The team and product owner are reviewing user stories in the iteration planning meeting. While reviewing stories, it is identified that some of the highvalue stories have more associated risks. What should the agile project manager do?

options.text: Recommend that the team include risky stories in early iterations rather than later ones.
options.rationale: Scheduling risky, high-value stories early exposes problems while there is time to respond.

options.text: Recommend that the team choose stories with low risk for easy completion to keep team motivation high.
options.rationale: Choosing easy stories postpones risk to later, when it is costlier.

options.text: Work with the product owner to decide on the stories that should go during the iteration.
options.rationale: The product owner sets priority, but the risk-aware sequencing is what needs recommending.

options.text: Use the Pareto analysis to decide which stories can be completed the fastest.
options.rationale: Pareto analysis focuses on frequency, not risk.

questions.explanation: Agile teams reduce risk by tackling high-value, high-risk work early. Early feedback reveals problems while options remain.
questions.mindset: Tackle risky, valuable work early.

questions.stem: A newly formed team has become accustomed to agile practices. The project lead has noticed that while they are performing according to expectations, there is boredom with daily team practices among many of the team members. What should the project lead do in this situation?

options.text: Allow the team to self-organize and have them analyze the situation in their retrospective session and self correct.
options.rationale: The team is new to agile and may need a push to explore improvements beyond self-analysis.

options.text: Challenge the team to find new ways to achieve higher levels of performance to improve the situation.
options.rationale: Challenging the team to find new ways to perform better re-engages them and supports improvement.

options.text: Speak with individual team members to determine what they would like to do to improve the situation in the team.
options.rationale: Individual conversations are slow and fragment what is a team issue.

options.text: Have the team inform senior management of the situation and ask for recommendations.
options.rationale: Involving senior management is disproportionate.

questions.explanation: Boredom with routine practices signals a plateau. Challenging the team to raise performance through new approaches restores energy and drives continuous improvement.
questions.mindset: Challenge teams to keep improving.

questions.stem: An agile project is running its fifth iteration out of 10. After the last retrospective, the team members realize that they had to work extra hours to deliver the committed work. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the team to have a lower commitment for the next iteration.
options.rationale: Lowering commitment treats the symptom without understanding the cause.

options.text: Ask for additional team members to maintain the velocity.
options.rationale: Adding people assumes the cause is capacity, and new members usually slow a team down before they speed it up.

options.text: Conduct a focused retrospective to help the team to discover the root cause.
options.rationale: A focused retrospective helps the team find the root cause of the overtime.

options.text: Implement a checkpoint in the iteration to verify if the team is on track.
options.rationale: A mid-iteration checkpoint does not reveal the cause.

questions.explanation: Sustained overtime is a warning. A focused retrospective helps the team understand whether estimation, interruptions or other factors are responsible.
questions.mindset: Find out why the team is working extra hours.

questions.stem: A project is being executed. The project's life cycle is defined as predictive; however, a major deliverable will be handed over incrementally to the customer. The assigned resources are experienced and reliable and are willing to make decisions that the project manager used to make after each incremental delivery on other projects. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Inform the team that although this is a hybrid environment, the project manager must still be responsible for making decisions.
options.rationale: Keeping all decisions with the PM ignores the team's readiness.

options.text: Consult the product owner about letting the resources make decisions.
options.rationale: The product owner does not decide how the team is empowered.

options.text: Support the decisions of the team and transfer the decision making responsibility to them.
options.rationale: Supporting the team's decisions and transferring responsibility builds ownership.

options.text: Schedule a steering committee meeting and obtain their approval on the request.
options.rationale: Seeking steering committee approval to let the team make its own decisions escalates a matter the project manager can handle.

questions.explanation: Experienced, reliable teams should be empowered to make decisions. Servant leaders support and delegate, increasing ownership.
questions.mindset: Delegate decisions to teams that are ready.

questions.stem: During a project steering committee meeting, the project manager reports that a formerly supportive key team member has become resistant to and negative about changes. Where should this information be captured?

options.text: Responsible, accountable, consult, and inform (RACI) matrix
options.rationale: A RACI matrix records who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed; it does not capture attitudes or engagement.

options.text: Stakeholders engagement assessment matrix
options.rationale: The engagement assessment matrix records current and desired engagement, capturing the shift to resistance.

options.text: Risk register and issue log
options.rationale: The risk register and issue log are not where engagement levels are tracked.

options.text: Work performance reports
options.rationale: Performance reports summarise status, not engagement.

questions.explanation: The stakeholder engagement assessment matrix compares current and desired engagement. Changes in attitude are recorded there to plan re-engagement.
questions.mindset: Track engagement changes where they can be acted on.

questions.stem: During a project's initiation phase, the project manager reviews the business case and finds that information is incomplete. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Add an information gap to the risk register.
options.rationale: Logging a gap as a risk does not resolve missing information.

options.text: Review the project statement of work (SOW) to create the project charter.
options.rationale: Creating the charter from the SOW with an incomplete business case risks misalignment.

options.text: Revise the business case to narrow the project scope and create the project charter.
options.rationale: Revising the business case unilaterally exceeds the PM's authority.

options.text: Review the business case with the sponsoring organization to confirm that the project aligns with business needs.
options.rationale: Reviewing the business case with the sponsoring organisation confirms alignment with business needs.

questions.explanation: The business case justifies the project. If it is incomplete, the project manager works with the sponsoring organisation to confirm alignment before proceeding.
questions.mindset: Confirm the justification with its owners.

questions.stem: A research and development department is planning to develop a product that will introduce a new line of business for the organization. What should the project manager do to increase the project's chances of success?

options.text: Start developing the project management plan based on a previous project template from the project management office (PMO).
options.rationale: Starting the plan from an old template before the initiative is defined risks planning the wrong thing in detail.

options.text: Conduct an impact analysis of the new initiative to determine how the project should be rolled out.
options.rationale: Impact analysis is useful, but it needs a clear definition of the initiative to analyse.

options.text: Plan a working session focusing on the scope, vision, and mission of the initiative.
options.rationale: A working session on scope, vision and mission gives everyone a shared understanding of what the new business line is meant to achieve.

options.text: Conduct benchmarking to determine the business viability of the initiative.
options.rationale: Benchmarking viability is a business-case activity; the project needs a clear vision to act on.

questions.explanation: For a new line of business, the first step towards success is shared clarity about purpose. Defining vision, mission and high-level scope together gives the team and stakeholders a common direction before detailed planning, benchmarking or impact analysis.
questions.mindset: Define the purpose together before planning the details.

questions.stem: At which stage in the Tuckman team development model should the project manager put the most focus on increasing team motivation?

options.text: Forming
options.rationale: In forming, the team sets its tone and expectations; motivation built now creates a positive foundation for the rest of the project.

options.text: Storming
options.rationale: In storming, attention is on resolving conflict, and motivation efforts compete with those tensions.

options.text: Norming
options.rationale: In norming, the team has settled its ways of working; motivation matters but the foundation is already set.

options.text: Performing
options.rationale: In performing, a motivated team largely sustains itself; the leader's focus shifts to delegation.

questions.explanation: The Tuckman model describes stages teams go through. Leaders invest heavily in motivation and direction in the forming stage because it sets the tone and expectations that shape how the team moves through the later stages.
questions.mindset: Set the tone for motivation when the team is forming.

questions.stem: A project team is arranging user testing to be completed for a project but does not have a strong enough server to do so. The team orders a new server and postpones user testing. What should the project manager do moving forward?

options.text: Eliminate the user testing from the project plan.
options.rationale: User testing is essential for acceptance; removing it trades quality for convenience.

options.text: Utilize the current server to complete user testing.
options.rationale: Testing on inadequate infrastructure risks invalid results and wasted effort.

options.text: Request to expedite the new server from the supplier.
options.rationale: Expediting may help, but the immediate need is to realistically re-plan around the delivery.

options.text: Await the arrival of the new server and reevaluate timelines for user testing.
options.rationale: Waiting for the proper server and re-evaluating timelines ensures valid testing and realistic scheduling.

questions.explanation: When a physical resource needed for a key activity is unavailable, the project re-plans around its arrival rather than skipping the activity or proceeding with inadequate tools.
questions.mindset: Re-plan around missing resources rather than compromising the activity.

questions.stem: A team member approaches the project manager immediately after the end of the project meeting about his need for help to complete a late-due-date task. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ignore the team member's request, and ask for double the efforts to complete the task
options.rationale: Ignoring a request for help and demanding more effort damages trust and does not address the problem.

options.text: Discuss the issue during the daily meeting, and decide the course of action with the team
options.rationale: Raising the issue in the daily meeting lets the team decide together how to help, using the team's collective knowledge.

options.text: Ask the team member to step out from the task and re-allocate the task to someone else
options.rationale: Removing the team member from the task is abrupt and may harm their confidence.

options.text: Ask a junior team member to help in the completion of the task on the due date
options.rationale: Assigning a junior member presumes the solution without team input.

questions.explanation: When a team member asks for help, the team is often the best source of support. Discussing it openly in the daily meeting lets the team swarm on the problem and share ownership.
questions.mindset: Let the team help its own members.

questions.stem: While preparing a project's third progress report, the project manager identifies that the project will experience delays due to late material deliveries. The two previous project reports indicated that the project was on track. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Discuss it with the project team to determine the most appropriate way to respond.
options.rationale: Discussing the response with the team is useful, but the issue must first be recorded and reported transparently.

options.text: Add it to the issue log and include it in the project report.
options.rationale: Adding the delay to the issue log and reporting it gives stakeholders an accurate picture.

options.text: Contact the procurement manager to expedite delivery of the material.
options.rationale: Expediting may help, but it is a response that should follow recording and reporting.

options.text: Escalate the issue to the project owner and request a schedule change.
options.rationale: Escalating and requesting a schedule change is premature.

questions.explanation: Status reports must reflect reality. When a new issue changes the forecast, it is logged and reported transparently, even if earlier reports were positive.
questions.mindset: Report bad news as soon as it is known.

questions.stem: A project is set to install three MRI units in a hospital; one unit has passed acceptance testing and two are under construction. The client requests a change order to add a fourth unit with slightly different requirements. What should the project manager do to accurately estimate the additional unit's delivery?

options.text: Rely on historical data from similar projects.
options.rationale: Historical data from other projects may not reflect the differences in this unit.

options.text: Break the work down into smaller tasks and estimate each individually.
options.rationale: Breaking the work into tasks and estimating each gives the most accurate estimate for a unit with different requirements.

options.text: Use industry formulas or models based on project characteristics.
options.rationale: Parametric models may not capture the new unit's specific differences.

options.text: Compare the new unit to the existing ones and adjust the existing estimates.
options.rationale: Adjusting existing estimates may miss differences hidden in the details.

questions.explanation: Bottom-up estimating is the most accurate technique when requirements differ and detail is available. It accounts for specific tasks and resources.
questions.mindset: Estimate bottom-up when accuracy matters.

questions.stem: A project manager has made compliance-related changes by adopting a new project delivery approach. During external validation, an audit revealed that some of the component work did not conform to the organization's standards. What should the project manager have done?

options.text: Executed only compliant deliverables.
options.rationale: Executing only compliant deliverables presumes knowing what compliant means.

options.text: Clarified interpretation of compliance guidelines.
options.rationale: Clarifying how compliance guidelines apply to the new approach would have prevented non-conforming work.

options.text: Translated business requirements to design.
options.rationale: Translating requirements to design does not ensure compliance interpretation.

options.text: Researched regulations in the public sector.
options.rationale: Public sector regulations may not apply to organisational standards.

questions.explanation: Compliance depends on correctly interpreting the standards. When changing approach, the PM should clarify how the guidelines apply before work begins.
questions.mindset: Clarify compliance interpretation before changing how work is done.

questions.stem: A project vendor has informed a project manager that an outsourced project deliverable will be available 6 months later than the agreed project schedule. The vendor stated that they are focusing on other project deliverables with priority dependencies, and this particular deliverable had no stated dependencies. What should the project manager do to avoid schedule delays in future?

options.text: Monitor the dependencies and respond to challenges.
options.rationale: Monitoring helps but cannot recover dependencies that were never specified.

options.text: Ensure that all new dependencies are finish to start
options.rationale: Restricting to finish-to-start is not relevant.

options.text: Specify any dependencies if they exist.
options.rationale: Specifying dependencies to the vendor ensures they prioritise the deliverable appropriately.

options.text: Conduct a meeting to inform the customer.
options.rationale: Informing the customer does not prevent recurrence.

questions.explanation: Vendors prioritise according to the dependencies they know. Making dependencies explicit in contracts and plans prevents deliverables being deprioritised.
questions.mindset: Make dependencies explicit to suppliers.

questions.stem: What can a project manager do to communicate the formal project announcement and relevant information to stakeholders, and then gain their commitment?

options.text: Create the project charter.
options.rationale: The charter authorises the project but is not a communication strategy for stakeholders.

options.text: Conduct a kick-off meeting.
options.rationale: A kick-off meeting announces the project and seeks commitment, and is often seen as the natural answer.

options.text: Develop the communications management plan.
options.rationale: The communications management plan defines how announcements and information reach stakeholders and how their engagement is sought.

options.text: Prepare and distribute the responsible, accountable, consult, and inform (RACI) matrix.
options.rationale: A RACI matrix clarifies roles but does not announce the project.

questions.explanation: How a project announces itself and keeps stakeholders informed is defined in the communications management plan, which sets out audiences, methods and timing.
questions.mindset: Plan how stakeholders will be informed and engaged.

questions.stem: A project manager considers compliance to be part of the organization's process assets. The project team, however, has decided to include compliance as inputs to the relevant processes rather than document these rules as requirements. What is the project manager's compliance responsibility?

options.text: Acts as coordinator for the resources and activities
options.rationale: Coordinating resources and activities supports the team's approach to compliance.

options.text: Conducts audits for the compliance requirement
options.rationale: Compliance audits are an independent assurance activity; performing them is not the project manager's core compliance role here.

options.text: Performs risk analyses of compliance risks
options.rationale: Risk analysis is only one element of compliance.

options.text: Changes process assets of the organization
options.rationale: The PM does not change organisational process assets.

questions.explanation: In team-led compliance approaches, the project manager coordinates resources and removes obstacles so compliance inputs are applied.
questions.mindset: Coordinate and support compliance work led by the team.

questions.stem: A project manager is helping an organization transition from traditional methods to agile. The infrastructure, data warehousing, and enterprise architecture teams operate very differently than the application development teams. How should the project manager implement agile in this organization?

options.text: Ask every team in the organization to implement the same agile methodology so that a one-size-fits-all solution can provide consistency across all teams.
options.rationale: One-size-fits-all ignores differences between teams.

options.text: Tailor the implementation by deliberately adapting the approach to make it more suitable for the given environment and work at hand.
options.rationale: Tailoring the approach to each environment makes agile work for different teams.

options.text: Force the top-down transition approach by asking the CEO to provide support for implementing agile in every team in the organization.
options.rationale: Forcing a top-down rollout with CEO backing ignores how different these teams' work is and tends to breed resistance.

options.text: Ask one team to implement scrum as a pilot so that all other teams in the organization can also implement scrum by learning from this team.
options.rationale: A scrum-only pilot assumes scrum fits all teams.

questions.explanation: Agile adoption must be tailored. Infrastructure and architecture teams may need different practices from application teams.
questions.mindset: Tailor agile to each team's work.

questions.stem: An agile coach is counseling a large software organization that has been using waterfall methodology and now plans to start using agile or hybrid methodology. What would be a project manager's suggestion?

options.text: Continue using waterfall, since hybrid does not fit with the organizational structure.
options.rationale: Continuing waterfall ignores the organisation's plan to change.

options.text: Start with agile and then move to hybrid, although agile takes time to implement.
options.rationale: Starting with agile lets the organisation experience iterative benefits, then adapt into hybrid where appropriate.

options.text: Start using hybrid methodologies because waterfall knowledge is transferable.
options.rationale: Hybrid may be an end state, but the key choice is the starting point.

options.text: Start using hybrid, the more appropriate methodology for software organizations.
options.rationale: Declaring hybrid best for all software organisations is too general.

questions.explanation: Transitioning from waterfall involves learning new ways of working. Starting with agile allows the organisation to learn and then settle into the right mix.
questions.mindset: Learn a new approach before tailoring it.

questions.stem: A project team often asks questions about the rationale for their work and how the client perceives their progress and deliverables. What should the project manager do to build trust and get the team engaged?

options.text: Share feedback and invite team members to status meetings with the stakeholders.
options.rationale: Sharing client feedback and inviting the team into stakeholder status meetings shows them why their work matters.

options.text: Assure the team that the client is happy and you are handling the expectations.
options.rationale: Reassurance without evidence does not build trust.

options.text: Present the project plan and progress report to the team with regular updates when revised
options.rationale: Plans and progress reports inform but do not connect the team to the client.

options.text: Compare the pending tasks to the completed tasks so the team has a sense of accomplishment.
options.rationale: Counting completed tasks does not answer their questions about purpose.

questions.explanation: Teams engage when they understand why their work matters and can see how the client perceives it. Sharing feedback openly and bringing team members into stakeholder conversations builds trust and connects effort to purpose.
questions.mindset: Connect the team to the client's view of their work.

questions.stem: Project manager B has been assigned to take over a project from Project Manager A. Project Manager A informs Project Manager B that the project is on schedule, only because Project Manager A constantly pushes the team to perform. What is the first action Project Manager B should take as the new project manager?

options.text: Check the risk status.
options.rationale: Checking risk status is useful, but it does not address the bigger question of how to lead a team that has been kept on track only by pressure.

options.text: Check the cost performance.
options.rationale: Cost performance matters, but it does not tell the new PM how to sustain a team that is being pushed to its limits.

options.text: Determine a management strategy.
options.rationale: Deciding a management strategy lets the new PM choose how to lead a team that has been pushed hard.

options.text: Tell the team the new objectives.
options.rationale: Announcing new objectives before understanding the team is premature.

questions.explanation: A project on schedule only through constant pressure may not be sustainable. The new PM decides how to lead before acting.
questions.mindset: Choose your leadership approach before acting.

questions.stem: During an important project, one of the contractors complains that the approval process is difficult to handle and may delay the project schedule. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Hire additional resources for the team to mitigate this risk.
options.rationale: Hiring more people is a costly response chosen before the risk has even been recorded or analysed.

options.text: Discuss with the team to find options to mitigate the risk.
options.rationale: Discussing mitigation options with the team is a good next step, but the risk should first be formally recorded.

options.text: Escalate the risk to upper management as critical for timely delivery.
options.rationale: Escalating as critical before recording and analysing the risk skips the team's own chance to respond.

options.text: Add the risk to the risk register to be monitored and reviewed.
options.rationale: Adding the risk to the register makes it visible and owned, which starts the analysis and response process.

questions.explanation: A contractor's concern about a process that may delay the schedule is a newly identified risk. Recording it in the risk register comes first, so that it is tracked, owned and analysed; responses and any escalation follow from that analysis.
questions.mindset: Capture a new risk formally before deciding how to respond to it.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a project with a scope partially delivered by a vendor. The vendor's processes and tools differ from the project team's, which may pose a risk. How should the project manager mitigate this risk?

options.text: Coach the internal project team to use the vendor's processes and tools.
options.rationale: Making the internal team adopt the vendor's tools can reduce efficiency and increase errors for the larger group.

options.text: Train the vendor to use the same processes and tools as the internal team.
options.rationale: Training the vendor to use internal tools can be expensive and may disrupt processes they depend on.

options.text: Develop a strategy to align the internal and vendor processes and tools.
options.rationale: A strategy to align internal and vendor processes and tools finds common ground and reduces integration risk for both sides.

options.text: Recommend engaging a new vendor that uses the internal processes and tools.
options.rationale: Replacing the vendor over process differences is disproportionate and causes delay.

questions.explanation: When a vendor's ways of working differ from the project team's, the risk is at the interfaces. Aligning processes and tools — agreeing handoffs, formats and shared artefacts — reduces friction without forcing either side to abandon what works.
questions.mindset: Align at the interfaces rather than forcing one side to change completely.

questions.stem: A project manager has just completed the initiation phase of a project and needs to identify and analyze the stakeholders. The project charter focused on scope and budget approval only. What should the project manager do to identify stakeholders?

options.text: Review lessons learned from previous projects.
options.rationale: Lessons learned from similar projects reveal stakeholders who were involved or affected before and may be relevant here.

options.text: Review the project charter.
options.rationale: The charter focused only on scope and budget, so it will not provide a full stakeholder list.

options.text: Conduct a brainstorming session with the project team.
options.rationale: A brainstorm with the team helps, but the team may not have the history of who is affected by such projects.

options.text: Review the organization chart.
options.rationale: The organisation chart shows internal structure but misses external and indirect stakeholders.

questions.explanation: When the charter provides little stakeholder information, historical information from similar projects is a valuable source for identifying who may be involved, affected or influential.
questions.mindset: Use history to find the stakeholders the charter did not name.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a project to develop a new system for a government agency using a predictive approach. The project's governance framework is designed to ensure that the system meets the needs of the stakeholders and complies with all applicable regulations. The project manager receives an approved change request related to a project's governance framework. What should the project manager do to implement this change?

options.text: Review the changes to the governance framework and update relevant planning documents.
options.rationale: Reviewing the approved changes and updating the relevant planning documents implements the change in a controlled way.

options.text: Recalculate the durations of project activities affected by the change to the governance framework.
options.rationale: Recalculating durations may follow, but it assumes schedule impact before the change has been reviewed.

options.text: Put the project on hold until the impact of the governance framework can be assessed.
options.rationale: Putting the project on hold is unnecessary for an already approved change.

options.text: Submit the formal change request to the project steering committee for final approval.
options.rationale: The change is already approved; resubmitting it adds needless delay.

questions.explanation: Once a change is approved, the project manager implements it by understanding what changed and updating the affected plans and documents so the project operates under the new framework.
questions.mindset: Implement approved changes by updating the plans they affect.

questions.stem: Due to increased price volatility, a vendor asks the project manager of a large development project to make a price change that will affect the project contract. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Request the change control board (CCB) to meet with the vendor to discuss the change.
options.rationale: The CCB does not negotiate with vendors directly; the impact needs analysis first.

options.text: Execute the price change requested by the vendor and update the project contract.
options.rationale: Executing the price change and updating the contract without approval bypasses change control.

options.text: Comply with the vendor's request and update the project management plan.
options.rationale: Agreeing and updating the plan without analysis or approval accepts an unassessed contract change.

options.text: Analyze the impact and submit a formal change request, if appropriate.
options.rationale: Analysing the impact and submitting a formal change request if warranted keeps the contract change controlled.

questions.explanation: Vendor requests that alter contract terms go through analysis and formal change control. The project manager assesses impact on cost, schedule and scope before any change is agreed.
questions.mindset: Treat contract change requests like any other change: analyse, then approve.

questions.stem: A project manager with a directive behavioral orientation is leading a virtual team of software developers. The project manager wants to build a highperforming team that is motivated and productive. The team is working on a complex project with a tight deadline. How should the project manager lead this team?

options.text: Build rapport and develop strong relationships with team members.
options.rationale: Building rapport is valuable but is a supportive-style action, not what a directive orientation emphasises under a tight deadline.

options.text: Motivate team members with achievement awards.
options.rationale: Achievement awards may motivate but do not reflect the directive, results-focused approach described.

options.text: Influence team decisions and control the delivery process.
options.rationale: Controlling decisions and delivery can suppress a high-performing team's autonomy and motivation.

options.text: Implement communication channels to announce task completion.
options.rationale: Clear channels to announce task completion suit a directive, results-driven style while keeping a virtual team informed of progress.

questions.explanation: Leadership behaviour should fit both the leader's orientation and the team's context. A directive, results-focused leader with a virtual team on a tight deadline benefits from clear, structured communication of progress.
questions.mindset: Use your natural style in ways that help the team.

questions.stem: A vendor informs a project manager that the project's equipment can be delivered earlier than anticipated. The project manager recognizes that this is an opportunity to complete the project ahead of schedule. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Request management approval.
options.rationale: Management approval is premature before analysing the offer.

options.text: Use the equipment offered.
options.rationale: Accepting the equipment immediately may introduce new risks, such as storage or readiness.

options.text: Revise the project schedule.
options.rationale: Revising the schedule before analysis may commit to an unrealistic plan.

options.text: Determine if there is a risk.
options.rationale: Determining whether early delivery introduces risk ensures the opportunity is exploited safely.

questions.explanation: Opportunities can carry risks: storage, readiness, quality or cash-flow impacts. Analysing them first allows the project to take advantage without introducing new problems.
questions.mindset: Check opportunities for hidden risks before taking them.

questions.stem: A supplier for a regulatory project is responsible for making the component changes. The supplier is unlikely to meet the project schedule. Based on the risk response plan, the project manager secured stakeholder approval to use paper forms until the component changes go live. It is still possible, however, that the paper form changes may not be ready in time. Which risk type is the project manager facing in this situation?

options.text: Secondary risk
options.rationale: A secondary risk is a new risk created by a response, not the remaining chance the response itself fails.

options.text: Residual risk
options.rationale: Residual risk is the risk that remains after a response has been implemented — here, that paper forms may still not be ready.

options.text: Primary risk
options.rationale: The primary risk is the supplier missing the schedule, not what remains after the response.

options.text: Compliance risk
options.rationale: Compliance risk describes a category, not the relationship to the response.

questions.explanation: Responding to a risk rarely eliminates it completely. Residual risk is what remains after the planned response; secondary risks are new ones created by the response.
questions.mindset: Know what risk remains after you respond.

questions.stem: A project manager in an organization is considering implementing an agile project delivery. The organization has a strong project management office (PMO) and a well-defined change control process. What key aspect of agile project delivery should the project manager emphasize as the most compelling argument for its adoption?

options.text: Agile delivery can improve quality through incremental delivery and efficient defect repair.
options.rationale: Quality improvement is a benefit, but not the most compelling argument where formal processes already handle planned change well.

options.text: Agile teams offer flexibility in accommodating planned changes while streamlining the approval process.
options.rationale: Handling planned change is something a strong change control process already does.

options.text: The product owner utilizes a list known as the backlog to prioritize work items, including planned changes.
options.rationale: The backlog is a mechanism, not a compelling benefit.

options.text: Agile delivery is well-suited for handling unforeseen changes and shifting business expectations.
options.rationale: Agile's strength with unforeseen change and shifting expectations complements a strong change control process.

questions.explanation: Where formal change control handles planned changes, agile's distinct value is adapting to the unforeseen. Framing the argument around that complements what the organisation already does well.
questions.mindset: Argue for change on what it adds, not what already works.

questions.stem: The project manager is having difficulties persuading stakeholders to adopt new technlogy in the project. What should the project manager have done to avoid this resistance?

options.text: Invest in stakeholders' communication
options.rationale: Communication investment helps, but it does not involve stakeholders in the decision.

options.text: Provide technical support to stakeholders
options.rationale: Technical support comes after adoption decisions.

options.text: Propose an agreement to stakeholders
options.rationale: Proposing an agreement is too late once resistance has formed.

options.text: Engage stakeholders as early as possible
options.rationale: Engaging stakeholders early lets their input shape the choice and reduces resistance.

questions.explanation: Resistance to new technology is minimised by involving stakeholders early, so they help shape decisions rather than having them imposed.
questions.mindset: Involve people early to reduce resistance later.

questions.stem: A long-term agile project has just reached its midway mark and a new project manager is appointed to take over. Additional to the project manager, a current stakeholder was interchanged with another who has more experience regarding the projects’ technology. What next step should the project manager take?

options.text: Discuss expectations from the stakeholder and revise the engagement plan accordingly.
options.rationale: Discussing expectations and revising the engagement plan is useful but may bypass the product owner.

options.text: Encourage the new stakeholder to convene with the product owner to review pertinent information.
options.rationale: Having the new stakeholder meet the product owner gives them the product context and aligns them with the backlog.

options.text: Notify all stakeholders after revising the project plan with new contents added.
options.rationale: Revising the plan and notifying everyone is premature.

options.text: Hold all upcoming sprint review meetings with the new stakeholder in attendance and revise the project plan.
options.rationale: Attendance at reviews is helpful but does not provide the initial alignment.

questions.explanation: In agile projects, the product owner is the hub for product decisions. New stakeholders are best brought up to speed by the product owner.
questions.mindset: Connect new stakeholders with the product owner.

questions.stem: A project manager is working with a Scrum team that is continually missing deadlines. The steering committee is concerned about the project as it is not clear that it will deliver the expected value. After some analysis, the project manager discovers there is a mismatch of competencies in one of the teams. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Accept the risk of the project missing deadlines due to the mismatch.
options.rationale: Accepting missed deadlines ignores a fixable cause.

options.text: Provide appropriate training to compensate for the mismatch.
options.rationale: Training closes the competency gap causing missed deadlines.

options.text: Update the project schedule to reflect the delay.
options.rationale: Updating the schedule to show the delay accepts the slippage without addressing the skills gap causing it.

options.text: Emphasize to the teams the importance of meeting the agreed deadlines.
options.rationale: Emphasising deadlines does not address capability.

questions.explanation: When missed deadlines stem from a skills mismatch, training addresses the root cause and restores confidence in delivery.
questions.mindset: Fix capability gaps with development.

questions.stem: A lengthy, ongoing project exhausts a project team. Due to deadline issues, the project manager cannot extend the project schedule. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Review the project charter.
options.rationale: The charter does not address team exhaustion.

options.text: Provide more recognition to team members.
options.rationale: More recognition is helpful but does not reduce workload.

options.text: Discuss the situation with the team.
options.rationale: Discussing the situation with the team shows their concerns are heard and draws on their ideas for relief.

options.text: Request additional resources.
options.rationale: Requesting more resources assumes they exist and can be onboarded in time, and skips hearing from the exhausted team first.

questions.explanation: Exhausted teams need to be heard. Involving them in finding solutions builds trust and surfaces practical ideas to reduce workload.
questions.mindset: Listen to tired teams and solve with them.

questions.stem: A team receives outsourced deliverables and determines that they do not meet the agreed-upon acceptance criteria. What should the project manager reference to verify this with the vendor?

options.text: Procurement management plan
options.rationale: The procurement plan describes how procurement is managed, not what the vendor must deliver.

options.text: Request for proposal (RFP)
options.rationale: The RFP invited proposals; the agreed work is in the SOW.

options.text: Statement of work (SOW)
options.rationale: The SOW describes the contracted work and acceptance criteria.

options.text: Inspections
options.rationale: Inspection is how conformance is checked, not the reference.

questions.explanation: The statement of work defines contracted deliverables and acceptance criteria. It is the reference for disputes about vendor deliverables.
questions.mindset: Check deliverables against the contracted statement of work.

questions.stem: A project manager is managing the build of an off-shore data center. In addition, the project manager is the custodian of the assets procured by the project. The project manager is informed by a team member that an asset was lost, and the team member is ready to pay for the missing asset. How should the project manager handle this situation?

options.text: Request your team member to purchase, replace and update the asset register with a new asset tag
options.rationale: Letting the team member quietly buy a replacement hides the loss from the customer and management and skips finding out how it happened.

options.text: Inform the customer, purchase the new asset, and update the asset and risk register
options.rationale: Replacing the asset and informing only the customer omits management and skips the investigation into the cause.

options.text: Inform management, replace the asset with the help of an insurance claim, and update the asset register
options.rationale: An insurance claim and register update deal with the cost but not with understanding what went wrong or the customer's right to know.

options.text: Inform customer and management immediately, launch an investigation, update the risk register and take action based on outcome
options.rationale: Informing customer and management, investigating and acting on the findings deals with the loss transparently and prevents recurrence.

questions.explanation: When an asset the project holds in custody is lost, transparency and investigation come first. Informing those accountable, understanding how it happened and updating the risk register protect trust and prevent repetition; quietly replacing the item hides a control failure.
questions.mindset: Handle losses transparently and learn why they happened.

questions.stem: A company, which is conducting a critical bidding process, included a penalty clause in an agreement specifying that the selected supplier must pay a significant liquidated damages penalty in the event of non-performance. Given that this bidding process is extremely attractive to the supplier with a medium risk threshold, how should the supplier's project manager budget for it?

options.text: Increase the quote to mitigate the risk and support the above clause.
options.rationale: Simply raising the quote may price the supplier out of an attractive bid and does not move the risk anywhere.

options.text: Advise management not to participate in the request for proposals (RFP) since it is a big risk.
options.rationale: Declining an attractive opportunity ignores that the risk can be managed within a medium risk threshold.

options.text: Advise management to purchase insurance coverage to transfer the risk and include it in the budget.
options.rationale: Insurance transfers the financial impact of the penalty to a third party for a known premium, which can be budgeted.

options.text: Record it as a risk in the risk register and review it regularly to avoid the penalty.
options.rationale: Recording and monitoring the risk does not provide financial protection against a significant penalty.

questions.explanation: Transfer shifts the impact of a threat to a third party, usually for a premium. Insurance or bonds let a supplier take on attractive work with large penalties while keeping exposure within its risk threshold, and the premium becomes a budgeted cost.
questions.mindset: Transfer large financial risks you can insure, and budget for the premium.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a complex initiative with diverse stakeholders and must cultivate strong stakeholder relationships. The project manager also has to build a shared understanding of the project with all stakeholders. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Facilitate interactive workshops to discuss goals and expectations.
options.rationale: Interactive workshops let stakeholders discuss goals and expectations together, building relationships and a common understanding.

options.text: Conduct detailed stakeholder mapping exercises.
options.rationale: Stakeholder mapping is preparation; it analyses stakeholders but does not engage them in building shared understanding.

options.text: Deliver formal presentations summarizing project updates.
options.rationale: Formal presentations are one-way and do little to build relationships.

options.text: Distribute comprehensive project documentation for individual review.
options.rationale: Distributing documents for individual review is passive and leaves interpretation to each reader.

questions.explanation: Shared understanding among diverse stakeholders is built through interaction. Workshops where people discuss goals and expectations together create common ground and relationships in a way that presentations or documents cannot.
questions.mindset: Build shared understanding by bringing people together to discuss it.

questions.stem: During project closure, the project manager finds it difficult to obtain successful project completion feedback. Some stakeholders disagree with the project's success criteria and have been frustrated with the project from the beginning. To what should the project manager refer to address these concerns?

options.text: Project charter
options.rationale: The charter records the agreed objectives and success criteria that the project is measured against at closure.

options.text: Quality management plan
options.rationale: The quality plan covers quality standards, not the overall success criteria.

options.text: Scope statement
options.rationale: The scope statement describes deliverables, not the business success criteria.

options.text: Requirements documentation
options.rationale: Requirements documentation lists requirements but not how overall success is judged.

questions.explanation: Project success criteria should be agreed and recorded in the charter at the start. At closure, they are the reference for resolving disagreements about whether the project succeeded.
questions.mindset: Judge success against the criteria agreed at the start.

questions.stem: A project manager is creating a software project's quality management plan. While reviewing lessons learned from past, similar projects, the project manager discovers that rework due to quality issues resulted in cost overruns. What should the project manager do to ensure that quality is addressed throughout the software development life cycle?

options.text: Conduct recurring retrospectives to regularly check on the effectiveness of quality processes.
options.rationale: Recurring retrospectives check the effectiveness of quality processes regularly, catching problems before they turn into costly rework.

options.text: Assign a resource to focus solely on the project’s quality.
options.rationale: One dedicated quality resource concentrates responsibility that the whole team should share.

options.text: Ensure that quality is tied to performance reviews.
options.rationale: Tying quality to performance reviews may encourage hiding problems.

options.text: Identify new quality policies and procedures for the project.
options.rationale: New policies may help, but without regular review their effectiveness is unknown.

questions.explanation: Quality issues that caused rework in the past are prevented by building regular inspection and adaptation of quality practices into the life cycle, so the whole team keeps improving how it builds quality in.
questions.mindset: Inspect and adapt quality practices regularly.

questions.stem: A senior manager informs a project manager that the project is not performing as well as other projects. What can the project manager use to improve performance for the next series of iterations?

options.text: Retrospective session
options.rationale: A retrospective helps the team identify what is holding performance back and agree improvements for the next iterations.

options.text: Backlog analysis
options.rationale: Backlog analysis looks at work items, not how the team works.

options.text: Team building
options.rationale: Team building may help morale but does not target specific performance issues.

options.text: Team motivation
options.rationale: Motivation alone does not diagnose performance problems.

questions.explanation: Retrospectives are the agile mechanism for continuous improvement, letting teams inspect their performance and adapt their practices for upcoming iterations.
questions.mindset: Use retrospectives to raise performance.

questions.stem: A project manager has noticed apparent interpersonal conflict between some team members during the initiation of a project. When should the project manager address this problem?

options.text: At the earliest time possible to prevent the conflict from escalating later in the project
options.rationale: Addressing conflict early prevents it from escalating and harming the project.

options.text: Prior to every meeting by reminding the project team to be respectful with each other
options.rationale: Reminding everyone before each meeting is generic and does not address the specific conflict.

options.text: Directly after an outburst or dispute between members to determine which member is right
options.rationale: Waiting for an outburst and judging who is right escalates and polarises.

options.text: At the end of the project to let the conflict de-escalate and record it in the lessons learned
options.rationale: Leaving conflict until the end allows it to damage the project throughout.

questions.explanation: Conflict is easiest to resolve early, before positions harden. Project managers address it proactively rather than waiting for escalation.
questions.mindset: Address conflict early.

questions.stem: An organization conducted an external audit in an Offshore Data Centre (ODC). The audit team noticed that the project manager is using an old version of the risk register template. The auditor raised a Non-Conformity (NC). How could the project manager have avoided this gap?

options.text: It is not the project manager’s mistake since they are using the risk register template provided by their organization
options.rationale: Using an outdated template is still the project's responsibility; blaming the organisation does not prevent recurrence.

options.text: It is always better to conduct one round of internal audit before allowing an external audit to avoid such a gap
options.rationale: Internal audits help, but the root issue is how the risk process was planned.

options.text: It is suitable to conduct a risk management plan before preparing the risk register
options.rationale: A risk management plan defines the process, tools and templates to use, ensuring current templates are applied before the register is built.

options.text: It is appropriate to update the risk register with a new template and close the NC
options.rationale: Updating the template after the finding corrects the symptom, not how the gap arose.

questions.explanation: The risk management plan specifies the methodology and templates for risk management. Preparing it first helps ensure the project uses current organisational standards.
questions.mindset: Plan the process before producing its outputs.

questions.stem: The stakeholders and project team working on an agile project meet with the project manager at the end of an iteration. The project manager learns that the schedule is slipping, although all work was planned to meet the high-level objectives outlined in the project scope. What should the project manager have done to keep the project on track?

options.text: Worked with the team to understand their expectations of using the agile approach.
options.rationale: Understanding the team's expectations helps, but does not keep work aligned with objectives.

options.text: Empowered team members to self-organize specific tasks to meet the objectives.
options.rationale: Empowering team members to self-organise tasks around the objectives creates practical plans with high buy-in.

options.text: Prioritized work that could have had an early finish to allow for early benefits realization.
options.rationale: Prioritising early-finish work is a PM-driven choice that may not serve the objectives.

options.text: Selected and sequenced the work in order to meet the high-level objectives.
options.rationale: Selecting and sequencing work for the team is directive and reduces ownership.

questions.explanation: In agile, the project manager explains objectives and empowers the team to self-organise tasks to meet them, leading to realistic plans with strong ownership.
questions.mindset: Explain the objective, let the team organise the work.

questions.stem: A project manager participates in a focus group that implements project management changes across the organization. The goal is to improve project effectiveness and success. Which process should the project manager suggest for lasting and successful change within projects?

options.text: Conduct individualized skills assessments and provide targeted training for each team member.
options.rationale: Individual training helps but does not ensure organisational adoption.

options.text: Monitor external regulations and adapt project management practices accordingly.
options.rationale: Monitoring regulations is not a change management process.

options.text: Facilitate open communication and build buy-in from all project stakeholders.
options.rationale: Communication and buy-in are important parts but not the whole process.

options.text: Implement a project management change management plan aligned with industry best practices.
options.rationale: A structured change management plan aligned with best practice defines how changes are introduced, communicated and sustained.

questions.explanation: Lasting organisational change needs structure: defined changes, timelines, communication and support. A change management plan provides that structure.
questions.mindset: Manage organisational change deliberately.

questions.stem: A project manager has engaged the sponsor and discussed concerns regarding noncompliance. The project manager understands that this could be a potential audit situation. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Do nothing and continue to work as before, assuming there will be an audit.
options.rationale: Doing nothing ignores a known compliance problem.

options.text: Disengage the noncompliant department, as this is problematic.
options.rationale: Cutting out the noncompliant department hides the problem rather than resolving it, and may breach obligations of its own.

options.text: Disclose the source of the problem to the auditors and let them decide.
options.rationale: Disclosing the problem to auditors is transparent and allows appropriate action.

options.text: Gain the commitment and approval from leadership on noncompliance.
options.rationale: Seeking approval for non-compliance is unethical.

questions.explanation: Known non-compliance should be disclosed transparently to auditors. Concealment or approval of non-compliance violates ethical standards.
questions.mindset: Be transparent about compliance problems.

questions.stem: During the planning of a project with incremental deliveries, the team realizes that they will need specific expertise for one of the deliverables towards the end of the project. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Enroll the team in training so they can be equipped with the needed expertise.
options.rationale: Training the team may not produce the depth of specialist expertise needed in time for the late deliverable.

options.text: Request the availability of the needed resources with expertise from the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Requesting the needed expertise from the sponsor early secures it for the later deliverable.

options.text: Ask the team members to acquire expertise through self-paced learning.
options.rationale: Self-paced learning gives no assurance that anyone will have the expertise when the deliverable is due.

options.text: Define and share the work agreement with the team to coordinate activities to acquire expertise.
options.rationale: A working agreement helps coordinate the team, but it does not bring in the expertise the deliverable requires.

questions.explanation: When planning reveals that specialist expertise will be needed later, securing it early is part of resource planning. Requesting the resource through the sponsor while there is lead time avoids a gap when the deliverable is reached.
questions.mindset: Secure specialist resources ahead of need.

questions.stem: At the end of an iteration, a team member tells the project manager that a planned task is unfinished because of an issue that appeared days ago but could not be resolved. Why should the project manager discuss the issue during the retrospective to prevent this type of situation in the future?

options.text: It is a timely opportunity to discuss issues and ideas for improvement to encourage team-based problem solving.
options.rationale: The retrospective is a timely forum for discussing issues and improvements through team problem solving.

options.text: It allows the project manager to address the issue during a demo, which leads to high levels of buy-in from the team members.
options.rationale: Demos are for the product, not process issues.

options.text: The team member will have the opportunity to resolve the issue before the retrospective.
options.rationale: The issue is unresolved; waiting until the retrospective for the team member to resolve it is not the point.

options.text: The project manager can emphasize how to maximize the time available to resolve the issue.
options.rationale: Maximising time does not address the underlying process issue.

questions.explanation: Retrospectives give the team a timely, safe forum to examine what stopped progress — such as a problem that sat unresolved for days — and agree improvements together, for example raising blockers sooner and swarming on them.
questions.mindset: Turn unresolved blockers into process improvements.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned to a project that is already in progress because the original project manager left the organization unexpectedly. Unfortunately, the previous project manager did not adhere to the organization's knowledge transfer procedures prior to leaving the organization. What can the new project manager do to fill the knowledge gaps? (Choose 3)

options.text: Review the project documentation, including the project plan, requirements document, and risk register.
options.rationale: Reviewing the plan, requirements and risk register recovers the explicit knowledge the previous project manager left behind.

options.text: Proceed with the project as planned and engage in job shadowing activities.
options.rationale: Proceeding as planned while job shadowing assumes the plan is sound and there is no one left to shadow.

options.text: Meet with key stakeholders to understand their expectations and priorities.
options.rationale: Meeting key stakeholders reveals expectations and priorities that may never have been written down.

options.text: Interview team members to learn about their areas of expertise and experience with the project.
options.rationale: Interviewing team members captures tacit knowledge about the work, history and expertise within the team.

options.text: Reach out to the previous project manager and request a comprehensive knowledge transfer.
options.rationale: The previous project manager has left the organisation, so a comprehensive knowledge transfer from them is unlikely to be available.

questions.explanation: When a predecessor leaves without handing over, the new project manager rebuilds knowledge from the sources that remain: documents for explicit knowledge, stakeholders for expectations, and the team for tacit knowledge of the work. Together they fill most of the gap.
questions.mindset: Rebuild lost knowledge from documents, stakeholders and the team.

questions.stem: A project team has an after-hours get-together. One of the team members who was recently hired and new to the team did not receive an invitation to the get-together. At the next few standups, the new employee is visibly upset and does not participate much during the sessions. How should the project manager address this situation?

options.text: Schedule another after-hours get-together and invite the new team member.
options.rationale: Arranging another event assumes the cause and may feel like a token gesture.

options.text: Meet with the new team member to talk about their concerns.
options.rationale: Meeting the new team member privately lets the project manager understand what is upsetting them — which may or may not be the event — and respond appropriately.

options.text: During the next standup, ask the new team member to participate more.
options.rationale: Asking them publicly to participate more puts pressure on someone who is already upset.

options.text: Invite the new team member to meet after-hours to discuss the project.
options.rationale: An after-hours project discussion does not address how they feel.

questions.explanation: A visible change in a team member's behaviour is a cue to check in privately. Sensitive issues, such as feeling excluded, are best explored one-to-one so the real cause can be understood and addressed.
questions.mindset: Handle sensitive issues privately and start by listening.

questions.stem: A project manager is managing a project involving a few vendors. The project sponsor asks how the project will acquire goods and external services. Where should this information be documented?

options.text: In the Procurement Management Plan
options.rationale: The procurement management plan describes how the project will acquire goods and services from outside the organisation.

options.text: In the Master Service Agreement
options.rationale: A master service agreement sets general terms with a supplier, not the project's approach to acquisition.

options.text: In the Bill of Materials Contract
options.rationale: A bill of materials lists items, not how services will be procured.

options.text: In the Service Level Agreement
options.rationale: A service level agreement defines service standards, typically in operations.

questions.explanation: The procurement management plan documents how the project will acquire external goods and services — contract types, approach, roles and processes — and is the place to answer a sponsor's question about acquisition.
questions.mindset: Describe how the project buys in the procurement plan.

questions.stem: A project manager recently joined a new organization. The project sponsor is a subject matter expert and wants to manage scope by delivering in small increments and changing the scope based on feedback. Which of the following approaches should be the recommended option?

options.text: Scrum
options.rationale: Scrum supports small increments and changing scope from feedback, with a knowledgeable sponsor able to guide the backlog.

options.text: Waterfall
options.rationale: Waterfall fixes scope early and does not adapt to feedback during delivery.

options.text: Kanban
options.rationale: Kanban optimises flow but has no built-in cadence of increments and reviews for changing scope.

options.text: Predictive
options.rationale: Predictive approaches fix scope early and control changes formally, which runs against the sponsor's wish to change scope from feedback.

questions.explanation: When a sponsor wants to deliver small increments and adjust scope based on feedback, an iterative framework such as Scrum fits: regular increments, reviews and backlog reprioritisation.
questions.mindset: Choose an approach that matches how the sponsor wants to manage scope.

questions.stem: A project requires the services of a specialized vendor to install a very complex and expensive piece of equipment. The project manager sent an email a week ago to a partner to request a specialist come on-site. Unfortunately, the vendor has not replied to confirm. What communication method was used in this case?

options.text: Pull
options.rationale: Pull communication is made available for recipients to access, such as a portal.

options.text: Interactive
options.rationale: Interactive communication is a real-time exchange, such as a call or meeting.

options.text: Push
options.rationale: Email is push communication: sent to recipients but with no guarantee it was read or understood.

options.text: Interpersonal
options.rationale: Interpersonal describes face-to-face exchange, not email.

questions.explanation: Push communication sends information to specific recipients but does not confirm it was received and understood. Critical requests sent by email need follow-up or an interactive method.
questions.mindset: Confirm that pushed messages were received and understood.

questions.stem: A project manager is managing an agile project. A new team member, who has never worked in an agile team, joins the project. The new member asks the project manager to explain why an agile approach is used. What should the project manager's response be?

options.text: To eliminate the risk and increase the predictability and visibility
options.rationale: Agile does not eliminate risk; it manages uncertainty through feedback.

options.text: To deliver value faster and change the scope based on feedback
options.rationale: Agile delivers value faster and adapts scope based on feedback.

options.text: To reduce the costs and increase the quality of the end deliverables
options.rationale: Agile does not promise lower costs; its benefit is earlier value and adaptation, and quality comes from practices rather than the label.

options.text: To eliminate the need for documentation by delivering working products
options.rationale: Agile values working product over comprehensive documentation but does not eliminate documentation.

questions.explanation: Agile's purpose is early, frequent value delivery and adapting to feedback. It trades up-front certainty for learning and responsiveness.
questions.mindset: Explain agile as faster value and learning, not as fewer costs or documents.

questions.stem: A key stakeholder has submitted several requests for new functions for a product under development. The project manager just completed the scope definition for the product's next version release and communicated the scope statement to all stakeholders. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Revise the communications management plan to define the number of new feature and function requests that can be submitted.
options.rationale: Limiting the number of requests through the communications plan is not how scope changes are governed.

options.text: Review the acceptance criteria for the product deliverables as defined in the scope statement.
options.rationale: Acceptance criteria define completed deliverables, not how new requests are handled.

options.text: Meet with stakeholders to emphasize their alignment with product objectives and the goals of the project.
options.rationale: Emphasising alignment helps but does not tell anyone how the requests will be processed.

options.text: Review the scope management plan to determine how new functionality requests are to be accommodated.
options.rationale: The scope management plan defines how scope changes are handled, guiding what to do with the new requests.

questions.explanation: New requests after scope definition are handled according to the scope management plan, which sets out how changes are submitted, assessed and controlled.
questions.mindset: Handle new requests the way the scope plan says.

questions.stem: A team lead is assigned to an ongoing project. The team members have been working together for a while. How should the team lead start building relationships?

options.text: Distribute tasks and observe the quality of the deliverables.
options.rationale: Observing deliverable quality is evaluation, not relationship building.

options.text: Talk about personal preferences and make sure the team understands your approach.
options.rationale: Talking about your own preferences centres the leader, not the team.

options.text: Ask some team members to share information about other members to become familiar with the team.
options.rationale: Collecting information about members from others risks gossip and damages trust.

options.text: Ask the team members directly about both personal and work-related matters.
options.rationale: Asking team members directly about personal and work matters shows interest and builds trust.

questions.explanation: A new leader builds relationships by showing genuine interest in the people on the team, their work and their preferences, directly rather than through others.
questions.mindset: Build relationships by showing interest in people.

questions.stem: A project manager wants to establish an incentive and rewards strategy for the project team. What approach should be taken?

options.text: Ask Human Resources department which incentives should be provided.
options.rationale: HR may advise, but it does not know what motivates each team member.

options.text: Check on budget availability in order to determine specific reward amounts.
options.rationale: Budget determines limits, not what motivates people.

options.text: Provide an opportunity for publicly presenting the outcomes.
options.rationale: Public presentation may motivate some but not others.

options.text: Identify the specific needs for each team member to determine incentives.
options.rationale: Identifying individual needs lets incentives match what motivates each person.

questions.explanation: Effective incentives are tailored. Not all rewards are financial, and understanding individual preferences makes recognition meaningful.
questions.mindset: Tailor rewards to what motivates each person.

questions.stem: A team member is working on a critical task for a project, and approaches the project manager immediately before the start of a project meeting and informs the project manager that the task was not completed on time. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Dismiss the team member from the meeting and ask him/her to continue working on the task.
options.rationale: Sending the member away isolates them and removes the problem from team discussion.

options.text: Reallocate the task to another team member and emphasize the importance of finishing it on a time.
options.rationale: Reallocating the task without discussion may overload others and ignores the cause.

options.text: Send an e-mail to the whole team and ask them for support in completing this specific task.
options.rationale: A group email is slower and less collaborative than discussing it in the meeting.

options.text: During the meeting, review all open tasks with the team and jointly decide on which action to take.
options.rationale: Reviewing open tasks together and deciding jointly uses the team's collective knowledge.

questions.explanation: When critical work slips, the team is often best placed to decide how to recover. Reviewing open work together produces better options and shared ownership.
questions.mindset: Solve slippage with the team's collective judgement.

questions.stem: A project manager has identified stakeholders for a software development project: the sales team will be the primary users of the new software application; the IT department will be responsible for deploying and maintaining the new software application; and the project sponsor is the executive who is responsible for approving the project and providing funding. The project manager is in the planning phase of the project, and must engage the stakeholders. What is the most important thing for the project manager to do to build shared understanding?

options.text: Hold a kick-off meeting with all stakeholders.
options.rationale: A kick-off meeting is valuable but needs understanding of needs to be meaningful.

options.text: Create a stakeholder register and communication plan.
options.rationale: A register and communication plan document stakeholders but build on understanding their needs.

options.text: Identify the stakeholders' needs and expectations.
options.rationale: Identifying stakeholders' needs and expectations is the foundation of shared understanding.

options.text: Document the stakeholders' concerns and risks.
options.rationale: Documenting concerns and risks is useful but narrower than needs and expectations.

questions.explanation: Shared understanding starts with knowing what each stakeholder needs and expects. That understanding informs plans, communication and engagement.
questions.mindset: Understand needs before building agreement.

questions.stem: A product team is using a prototyping approach to deliver a multiyear business initiative. The project manager notices that a few user stories are taking longer to be delivered. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Review the project timeline and reallocate resources.
