options.rationale: Reallocating resources before understanding bottlenecks may not help.

options.text: Conduct a retrospective with the team to identify bottlenecks.
options.rationale: A retrospective lets the team identify bottlenecks and improve its process.

options.text: Escalate the issue to senior management for intervention.
options.rationale: Escalating to senior management before the team has looked for the cause of the slow stories is premature and removes ownership from the team.

options.text: Modify the project scope to remove the delayed user stories.
options.rationale: Removing delayed stories reduces value without diagnosing the problem.

questions.explanation: When some work takes longer than expected, a retrospective helps the team find bottlenecks and improve. Actions follow from understanding.
questions.mindset: Diagnose delays with the team before acting.

questions.stem: A transportation company is transforming its operational processes and the main system this company uses to move freight. The scope statement is in place. An iterative delivery approach has been agreed by all stakeholders. What does the project manager need to do next to help the team understand the work that needs to be done?

options.text: Start working on the project management plan with work packages, a detailed schedule, and work assignments for team members.
options.rationale: Creating a detailed plan and assignments before decomposing scope with the team skips the step that builds understanding.

options.text: Work directly with stakeholders on the work breakdown structure (WBS) and assign tasks with a required timeline for each team member to start the work.
options.rationale: Working on the WBS with stakeholders and assigning timelines excludes the team that will do the work.

options.text: Work with the team to decompose the scope into a WBS and work packages in order to create required deliverables and timelines.
options.rationale: Decomposing scope with the team into a WBS and work packages builds shared understanding of deliverables and timelines.

options.text: Create the requirements management plan to outline how project requirements will be collected, analyzed, and documented, and then assign requirements to team members.
options.rationale: A requirements plan describes process, not the work to be done.

questions.explanation: Decomposing the scope with the team helps them understand the work and creates the basis for estimates, schedules and assignments.
questions.mindset: Decompose the work with those who will do it.

questions.stem: A project manager has started a new project with a 24 month timeline. Soon after the kickoff, the sponsor informs the project manager that the timeline needs to be shortened to 6 months. What should the project manager do in this scenario?

options.text: Focus on developing a minimum viable product (MVP) by referencing the product backlog for items with the highest prioritization that can be completed in the new timeline.
options.rationale: Focusing on an MVP from the highest-priority backlog items delivers the most value in the shorter timeline.

options.text: Refer to the product backlog to identify the items that can be completed in the shortest amount of time and add them to the project to complete in the new timeline.
options.rationale: Choosing items by speed of completion ignores value.

options.text: Work with the sponsor to increase the budget to hire vendors to develop the deliverables in the compressed timeline.
options.rationale: Hiring vendors adds cost and may not achieve the compression.

options.text: Implement fast tracking and record this timeline change in the risk register.
options.rationale: Fast-tracking a 24-month plan into 6 months is unrealistic.

questions.explanation: When time is cut drastically, scope must be reduced to what matters most. An MVP built from the highest-priority items preserves value.
questions.mindset: When time shrinks, deliver the most valuable minimum.

questions.stem: A newly-hired project manager is running a project for the first time and is worried about rising tensions. Project team members are arguing during an effort-intensive phase and stakeholders have voiced some doubts about the project's performance. In a discussion with a senior project manager, the new project manager admits that they have a fear of conflict and asks the senior project manager how they perceive conflict. How should the senior project manager respond?

options.text: Conflict in projects is inevitable - focus on managing it.
options.rationale: Conflict is a normal part of projects; the skill is managing it so that it leads to better decisions rather than damage.

options.text: Conflict in projects is preventable - replan the mitigation.
options.rationale: Not all conflict can be prevented, and treating it as a planning failure encourages avoidance.

options.text: Conflict in projects is disastrous - prepare a recovery plan.
options.rationale: Calling conflict disastrous reinforces the new project manager's fear and ignores that conflict can be productive.

options.text: Conflict in projects is healthy - refrain from interfering.
options.rationale: Some conflict is healthy, but refusing to intervene lets destructive conflict escalate.

questions.explanation: Conflict is inevitable wherever people with different priorities work under pressure. Fear of it leads to avoidance, which restricts communication and creativity. Treating conflict as something to manage — early, openly and constructively — turns it into better decisions.
questions.mindset: Expect conflict and manage it; do not fear or ignore it.

questions.stem: A project team has identified a number of defects with some deliverables and intends to resolve these as soon as possible. The project manager will need to submit a change request to the change control board (CCB). What should the project manager do before the request is submitted?

options.text: Implement the changes immediately due to time constraints.
options.rationale: Implementing changes before approval bypasses change control, however pressing the timeline.

options.text: Send the change request to the client for approval.
options.rationale: The client may be involved, but the change request needs impact analysis before anyone can approve it.

options.text: Complete an impact analysis of each requested change.
options.rationale: An impact analysis of each change shows its effect on scope, schedule, cost and quality, which the CCB needs to decide.

options.text: Send the change requests to the sponsor for approval.
options.rationale: Sponsor approval without impact analysis gives them nothing to base a decision on.

questions.explanation: Every change request needs an impact analysis before it goes to the approving body. Without it, decision-makers cannot weigh the benefit of the change against its cost, schedule and risk consequences.
questions.mindset: Analyse impact before asking for approval.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a project team composed of members from different departments, including engineering, marketing, and sales. During the development process, a conflict arises between the engineering and marketing teams. The engineering team is focused on delivering the product on time and within budget, while the marketing team is focused on ensuring that the product meets the needs of the target market. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Suggest that the engineering and marketing teams each give up something to reach an agreement.
options.rationale: Compromise makes both teams give something up and may satisfy neither schedule nor market needs.

options.text: Suggest that the engineering and marketing teams work together to find a solution that works for both teams.
options.rationale: Collaboration lets both teams work toward a solution that meets delivery and market needs together.

options.text: Suggest that the engineering team is correct and ensure that the product is delivered on time and within budget.
options.rationale: Siding with engineering dismisses the market's needs and the marketing team's contribution.

options.text: Suggest that the engineering and marketing teams compete to see who can come up with the best solution.
options.rationale: Competition between teams deepens division and produces winners and losers.

questions.explanation: When teams have legitimate but different priorities, collaboration seeks a solution that satisfies both. It takes more effort than compromise or forcing, but produces better outcomes and commitment.
questions.mindset: Collaborate across teams when both priorities matter.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on a new compliance project that is different from regular projects as it will involve multinational partners and several government departments. The project will result in the adoption of new standards and procedures. What must the project manager do from the onset?

options.text: Ensure that the business requirements are defined and met
options.rationale: Defining business requirements is needed on every project and does not address the compliance challenge.

options.text: Ensure solution design is available from the start of the project
options.rationale: Solution design from the start is not what the compliance context demands first.

options.text: Ensure execution and handover are done effectively
options.rationale: Effective execution and handover matter for all projects, not specifically compliance ones.

options.text: Ensure the interpretation of compliance guidance and validation
options.rationale: Interpreting and validating compliance guidance from the outset prevents misreading requirements from multiple government bodies.

questions.explanation: Compliance projects involving several government bodies and partners depend on correctly interpreting the guidance. Establishing interpretation and validation early prevents costly rework and non-compliance later.
questions.mindset: Get compliance interpretation right before building.

questions.stem: A complex construction project entails the meeting of several regulations throughout project execution. The project team is brainstorming how to implement an effective method to ensure compliance throughout the term of the project. Which compliance review process is suitable for this situation?

options.text: Conduct a gated review throughout the project phases.
options.rationale: Gated reviews at phase boundaries check compliance throughout the project, catching issues early.

options.text: Review at the end of the project.
options.rationale: A review only at the end finds problems when they are hardest to fix.

options.text: Review before the closure of the project.
options.rationale: Reviewing just before closure is too late for regulations that apply throughout.

options.text: Conduct an informal review only that is based on need.
options.rationale: Informal, as-needed reviews are inconsistent for complex regulations.

questions.explanation: Where compliance must be maintained through execution, structured reviews at phase gates provide regular, formal checkpoints and catch issues early.
questions.mindset: Check compliance at every gate, not just at the end.

questions.stem: A group of stakeholders at a financial institution are conducting a project closure review. Some of the stakeholders are concerned that the project deliverables do not satisfy the established closure criteria. What is the first thing that the project manager should do to address this issue?

options.text: Assure the stakeholders that the project deliverables satisfy all established closure criteria.
options.rationale: Assuring stakeholders without evidence ignores their concern.

options.text: Propose that the closure criteria be amended by removing the criteria that have not been met.
options.rationale: Removing unmet criteria to force closure is dishonest.

options.text: Take corrective measures by adapting the closure criteria and extending the project timeline.
options.rationale: Adapting criteria and extending the timeline is a remedy chosen before the gap is understood.

options.text: Perform a thorough analysis to determine why the closure criteria have not been satisfied.
options.rationale: Analysing why the criteria are not met identifies the gaps and the right remedy.

questions.explanation: When stakeholders question whether closure criteria are met, the first step is an honest analysis of the gaps and their causes. Remedies follow from understanding.
questions.mindset: Analyse the gap before deciding how to close it.

questions.stem: During a complex project, a stakeholder informs the project manager about a requirement and proposes to call a meeting to inform team members midsprint. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Schedule a meeting with the stakeholder and a team member.
options.rationale: Meeting with one team member mid-sprint still disrupts the sprint and bypasses the product owner.

options.text: Ask the stakeholder to explain and implement the requirements immediately.
options.rationale: Implementing immediately breaks sprint focus and skips prioritisation.

options.text: Host a meeting with all team members to discuss the requirements.
options.rationale: Gathering the whole team mid-sprint maximises disruption.

options.text: Request the product owner add to the product backlog to be treated in the next iteration.
options.rationale: Having the product owner add the requirement to the backlog lets it be prioritised for a future iteration.

questions.explanation: New requirements during a sprint go to the product owner and the backlog, protecting the team's focus and allowing proper prioritisation.
questions.mindset: Route mid-sprint requirements through the product owner.

questions.stem: An agile project team has implemented design changes over several iterations. The data privacy officer is concerned because their team wasn't involved in these decisions. How should the project manager address these concerns?

options.text: Ensure that a data privacy team member attends every future daily standup.
options.rationale: Attending every stand-up is heavy and does not define how requirements are met.

options.text: Request the data privacy officer assign a data privacy team member to join the project team.
options.rationale: Adding a full-time data privacy member may be more than is needed and still does not settle how privacy requirements enter decisions.

options.text: Set up a meeting with the data privacy officer to identify and implement a process to meet requirements.
options.rationale: Meeting the data privacy officer to agree a process integrates privacy requirements into future work.

options.text: Meet with the project owner to reverse the changes the project team made without consulting the data privacy team.
options.rationale: Reversing the changes is drastic before knowing whether they breach requirements.

questions.explanation: When a compliance stakeholder feels excluded, the fix is to agree with them how their requirements will be built into the team's process, rather than prescribing a mechanism or reversing work.
questions.mindset: Design the engagement process with the compliance owner.

questions.stem: A project manager is responsible for a new agile project that is global in nature. After a few sprints have been completed, the quality assurance team, based in a different country from the PM, has generated a long defect list. The PM is certain that these issues are not related to project quality, but are from language misinterpretation. What should the project manager do to address these issues?

options.text: Request additional budget to hire a local quality assurance team.
options.rationale: Hiring a local QA team adds cost and avoids the communication issue.

options.text: When the project is nearing completion, merge the development team with the quality assurance team to test the deliverables.
options.rationale: Merging development and QA only near completion leaves the misunderstandings in place for the rest of the project.

options.text: Meet with the quality assurance team to criticize the list they provided.
options.rationale: Criticising the QA team damages relationships and does not fix misunderstandings.

options.text: While performing sessions with the full project team, review the project requirements and their descriptions.
options.rationale: Reviewing requirements and descriptions together builds a common understanding across language barriers.

questions.explanation: In global teams, defects can stem from misunderstanding rather than poor quality. Reviewing requirements with the whole team establishes shared meaning.
questions.mindset: Check shared understanding when defects look like misunderstandings.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading an agile project. The product owner complains that the project team is constantly completing fewer story points than the Scrum team working on another project. What should the project manager do to address this issue?

options.text: Ask the team to address this issue as part of the retrospective to improve their velocity in the next sprint.
options.rationale: Asking the team to raise velocity treats a meaningless comparison as a performance problem.

options.text: Tell the product owner that it is incorrect to compare velocity across teams because story points are specific to each team.
options.rationale: Story points are relative to each team, so comparing velocity across teams is invalid.

options.text: Get approval from the product owner to add a contingency buffer to the sprint, and change the duration to increase velocity.
options.rationale: Changing sprint duration to increase velocity misunderstands the metric.

options.text: Take full responsibility for the team’s low performance as compared to the other team and apologize.
options.rationale: Apologising for 'low performance' accepts a comparison that is invalid because story points are team-specific.

questions.explanation: Velocity is a planning tool specific to each team. Comparing it across teams is misleading and can encourage point inflation.
questions.mindset: Do not compare velocity across teams.

questions.stem: In an agile environment, a project leader should always consider a time for open and free discussions between team members on how the team can increase their performance. Why is this practice important for the team?

options.text: Teams should take actions to continuously increase productivity
options.rationale: Productivity follows from better processes but is not the point of the discussion.

options.text: Teams should continuously experiment new ways of doing things
options.rationale: Experimentation is part of improvement but not its purpose.

options.text: Teams should continuously seek to improve their processes
options.rationale: Continuously improving processes is the purpose of regular team reflection.

options.text: Teams should continuously push their members to work harder
options.rationale: Pushing people to work harder undermines sustainable pace.

questions.explanation: Agile teams regularly reflect on how they work in order to improve their processes. Better processes lead to better performance.
questions.mindset: Improve the process, not the pressure.

questions.stem: After monitoring a product’s development after the first three releases, the product owner wants to launch a product even though it lacks some features identified in the minimum viable product (MVP). A stakeholder is not satisfied with this version and feels it needs to meet the previously agreed-upon MVP definition. How should the project manager proceed?

options.text: Review the positives and negatives of releasing the product in its current format and bring this analysis to the project sponsor to decide.
options.rationale: Bringing the decision to the sponsor bypasses the product owner's authority.

options.text: Work with the stakeholder and the product owner to try and find alignment but support the product owner as they are ultimately responsible for the product.
options.rationale: Seeking alignment while supporting the product owner's accountability for the product respects agile roles.

options.text: Schedule a meeting with all stakeholders and the product owner to review the project’s Pareto Chart.
options.rationale: A Pareto chart does not address the disagreement.

options.text: Empower the project team to decide how to proceed as the product’s development is the project team’s responsibility.
options.rationale: The team does not own product release decisions.

questions.explanation: In agile, the product owner is accountable for the product. The PM facilitates alignment with stakeholders but supports the product owner's decision.
questions.mindset: Facilitate alignment, but respect the product owner's authority.

questions.stem: During the fourth iteration of an agile project, the customer requests a technical change to the development of the project deliverable. What should the project manager do in this situation?

options.text: Update the project scope for this change and inform the sponsor
options.rationale: Updating scope and informing the sponsor treats a technical request as a formal scope change and bypasses the team that owns the how.

options.text: Inform the project team of the request, have them decide how to proceed with development, and have them coordinate the changes with the stakeholders.
options.rationale: A technical change to how the deliverable is developed is the team's domain; letting them decide and coordinate with stakeholders respects self-organisation.

options.text: Work with the stakeholders to decide how best to proceed and communicate the process changes to the project team.
options.rationale: Deciding with stakeholders and then telling the team takes a technical decision away from the people best placed to make it.

options.text: Calculate the impact of the customer’s request on the schedule performance index (SPI) and communicate this to the sponsor.
options.rationale: Calculating SPI impact for the sponsor is a predictive reporting step that does not decide how to handle the request.

questions.explanation: In agile, the team decides how to build the product. When a customer requests a technical change, the project manager passes it to the team, which assesses options and coordinates with stakeholders, while the product owner handles any priority implications.
questions.mindset: Let the team decide how the work is done.

questions.stem: A project manager is overseeing a project with an extremely tight schedule. During a meeting, the project stakeholders express concerns about the project's ability to meet critical business demands. What should the project manager do in response to these concerns?

options.text: Work with the sponsor to revise the project scope to address stakeholder concerns.
options.rationale: Revising scope with the sponsor alone leaves the stakeholders and team outside a decision that affects both.

options.text: Meet with the project team and stakeholders to identify the minimum viable product (MVP).
options.rationale: Defining an MVP with the team and stakeholders shows what critical value will be delivered within the tight timeline.

options.text: Assure the stakeholders that the project is on schedule and will meet all business demands.
options.rationale: Assuring stakeholders without evidence does not address their concerns.

options.text: Update the schedule and the communication plans to ensure the stakeholders are updated.
options.rationale: Updating schedules and communications does not change what will be delivered.

questions.explanation: When stakeholders doubt a tight schedule can meet critical needs, defining a minimum viable product together clarifies what will be delivered first and focuses the team on the highest-value work.
questions.mindset: When time is tight, agree the minimum that meets critical needs.

questions.stem: A project manager conducts a lessons learned meeting and project team members mention that they are not always aware of the progress occurring during sprints. What can the project manager do to address this concern?

options.text: Mentor the team about how to use the project iteration board.
options.rationale: Mentoring the team to use the iteration board gives everyone a live view of sprint progress.

options.text: Assign a project team member to prepare daily status reports and distribute to all team members.
options.rationale: Daily status reports add overhead and keep the team dependent on someone else.

options.text: Coach the team about how to use the project backlog report.
options.rationale: The backlog report is mainly for stakeholders and shows less current sprint progress.

options.text: Establish a process to address the confusion at the next retrospective session.
options.rationale: Waiting for the next retrospective leaves the confusion unaddressed.

questions.explanation: Agile teams maintain awareness through visible information radiators such as the iteration board. Teaching the team to use it lets them see progress themselves.
questions.mindset: Teach teams to use their information radiators.

questions.stem: A new college graduate with a degree in computer science was recently hired by an organization. The new employee has been assigned to work on a shortterm application development project. The employee is excited but nervous about the new assignment. What should the project manager do to better ensure success?

options.text: Request that the sponsor replace the new employee with someone more familiar with the organization to ensure project success.
options.rationale: Replacing a new hire denies them the chance to develop and signals mistrust.

options.text: Fast-track the new employee’s new-hire training so that they better understand the organization.
options.rationale: New-hire training helps with the organisation but not with the immediate project work.

options.text: Assign the new employee to less important tasks on the project.
options.rationale: Low-importance tasks may bore the employee and waste their skills.

options.text: Pair the new employee with a more experienced project team member so that they can work together.
options.rationale: Pairing with an experienced colleague supports the new employee and speeds up learning on a short project.

questions.explanation: Pairing is an effective way to integrate new team members on short projects. It provides support, accelerates learning and uses their skills from the start.
questions.mindset: Pair newcomers with experienced colleagues.

questions.stem: A company has been following a predictive approach and always waits for the preceding phase to be completed before evaluating the quality of their products. A new project manager with experience in hybrid approaches has been assigned to help increase the efficiency of the company's quality management process. What should the new project manager do to address the process improvements?

options.text: Continue with the process as is, and wait until the next phase to suggest any improvements.
options.rationale: Continuing as is delays improvements the PM was hired to make.

options.text: Define a ground rule to comply with the quality standard and ask the team members to apply it.
options.rationale: Imposing a ground rule without understanding the process may not fix the real issues.

options.text: Discuss the process improvement with the project management office (PMO) lead to update the project delivery framework.
options.rationale: Updating the PMO framework is a broader change and skips understanding the current process with the team.

options.text: Understand the context and interdependencies of the process from the team members and then define improvements.
options.rationale: Understanding the process context and interdependencies from the team lets improvements be defined that actually work.

questions.explanation: Process improvement starts with understanding how the current process works and why. Engaging the team to map context and interdependencies produces improvements they own.
questions.mindset: Understand a process with the people in it before changing it.

questions.stem: Operations for a new technology-based project are being transitioned to a new project team. Early in the execution phase, the project manager discovers major gaps in the documentation, which will hamper knowledge transfer. The solution launch date cannot be delayed, and the budget cannot be increased. How should the project manager structure the project to optimize the work within the project constraints?

options.text: Double the team size by assigning less expensive, outsourced resources.
options.rationale: Doubling team size with outsourced staff adds coordination and does not fix the knowledge gaps.

options.text: Split knowledge transfer and knowledge testing to run in parallel.
options.rationale: Running transfer and testing in parallel risks testing knowledge that has not been transferred.

options.text: Eliminate all slack and re-plan the tasks using a rolling wave approach.
options.rationale: Removing slack and rolling wave planning does not directly improve knowledge transfer.

options.text: Use agile sprints and Kanban to accelerate learning and fault-finding.
options.rationale: Short sprints with Kanban accelerate learning and surface gaps quickly within fixed time and budget.

questions.explanation: When documentation gaps threaten knowledge transfer under fixed constraints, iterative working accelerates learning. Short cycles expose gaps early and let the team fill them in priority order.
questions.mindset: Use short cycles to learn fast when documentation is lacking.

questions.stem: Midway through a project, a project manager learns that the project management planning application is failing to record updates to the project. What should the project manager do in this situation?

options.text: Task a project team member to manually update the project plan from now on.
options.rationale: Assigning a team member to manual updates takes them away from deliverables.

options.text: Inform the project management office (PMO) and have them resolve this issue.
options.rationale: The PMO may help, but the project still needs its plan updated now.

options.text: Update the project plan to allow the project team to focus on the project deliverables.
options.rationale: Updating the plan himself keeps records accurate and protects the team's focus.

options.text: Record this issue in the issue register and work with the sponsor to implement a new project management application.
options.rationale: Implementing a new application is a separate project and delays the immediate need.

questions.explanation: When tools fail, the project manager absorbs the impediment to keep records accurate while protecting the team's focus, and seeks a longer-term fix.
questions.mindset: Absorb administrative impediments so the team can keep working.

questions.stem: During nondestructive testing at a construction site, it was discovered that certain components are failing workability tests. The project team has identified the root cause of these failures and proposed a solution. However, the project deadline is tight and the solution would require an increase in the budget. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Invite suppliers to submit bids for a lower-cost solution.
options.rationale: Seeking lower-cost bids delays action and may not be feasible.

options.text: Submit a change request to the change control board (CCB).
options.rationale: A change request lets the CCB evaluate the solution's cost and impact.

options.text: Request additional funding from the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Asking the sponsor for funds bypasses the change process.

options.text: Update the risk management plan to include the solution.
options.rationale: The risk plan is not where solutions to current failures are approved.

questions.explanation: Solutions that require more budget go through change control, so their cost and impact are evaluated and approved formally.
questions.mindset: Route budget-changing solutions through change control.

questions.stem: A project is experiencing delays because cultural differences are causing misunderstandings among some stakeholders. What should the project manager do to handle this situation?

options.text: Review the stakeholder register to identify potential replacements for the stakeholders having difficulties.
options.rationale: Looking for replacement stakeholders is rarely possible and avoids the real task of improving communication across cultures.

options.text: Review the stakeholder engagement plan to determine the strategies to improve stakeholder communication.
options.rationale: The engagement plan sets strategies to improve communication with stakeholders.

options.text: Submit a change request to the change control board (CCB) to replace the stakeholders.
options.rationale: Stakeholders cannot be replaced through change control.

options.text: Monitor the communication between the stakeholders to identify any misunderstandings.
options.rationale: Monitoring alone does not improve communication.

questions.explanation: Cultural misunderstandings are addressed through engagement and communication strategies, which the stakeholder engagement plan defines.
questions.mindset: Adapt engagement strategies to bridge cultural differences.

questions.stem: A project manager is on a hybrid project. The project manager meets with the sponsor to get the project milestones. The sponsor requests for more specific information in the project charter. How should the project manager respond to this request?

options.text: Provide the sponsor with a project charter from a similar project as a reference.
options.rationale: A charter from another project does not address the sponsor's request.

options.text: Meet with the project stakeholders to get the project schedule approved first.
options.rationale: Schedule approval comes after the charter is approved.

options.text: Inform the sponsor that before detailed team planning can occur, the project charter needs approval first.
options.rationale: Explaining that the charter must be approved before detailed planning clarifies sequence.

options.text: Invite the sponsor to the team retrospective meeting so the sponsor can get the information requested.
options.rationale: Retrospectives are not the place for charter information.

questions.explanation: The charter's approval authorises detailed planning. Detailed milestones follow once high-level objectives and scope are approved.
questions.mindset: Approve the charter before planning details.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned to join a several year project mid-way. The project was stopped years ago due to organizational change and a local financial crisis. It has now been restarted. 70% of the budget is already consumed. The performance indices are CPI= 0.42 and SPI= 0.2.During a meeting with stakeholders, the project manager also finds there are major scope changes that could lead to delay. What is the best course of action to take as project manager?

options.text: Change the earned value management tracking technique.
options.rationale: Changing the earned value technique changes how performance is measured, not the performance itself.

options.text: Change the contract according to new changes.
options.rationale: Changing the contract does not address the project's viability.

options.text: Negotiate scope changes with stakeholders and keep it minimized as possible.
options.rationale: Negotiating scope changes keeps a failing project alive.

options.text: Close this project and request a new project from the project sponsor.
options.rationale: With 70% of budget spent, very poor indices and major scope change, closing and re-chartering is the sensible choice.

questions.explanation: Sometimes the right decision is to stop. When performance is very poor and scope has changed fundamentally, closing and re-chartering gives a fresh, realistic baseline.
questions.mindset: Know when to close and restart.

questions.stem: A functional manager wants to use resources already allocated to a project. What should the project manager of that project do?

options.text: Escalate the issue to the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Escalating to the sponsor before negotiating is premature.

options.text: Ask the functional manager to delay their project.
options.rationale: Asking the functional manager to delay their project ignores relative priorities.

options.text: Accept the project delay due to reassignment of resources.
options.rationale: Accepting the delay without trying to negotiate gives up on protecting the project's schedule.

options.text: Negotiate the resource requirement with the functional manager.
options.rationale: Negotiating the resource requirement with the functional manager seeks a workable arrangement.

questions.explanation: In a matrix organisation, functional managers control resource allocation. When they want to reassign project resources, the project manager negotiates the requirement with them first — explaining impact and exploring options — before accepting a delay or escalating.
questions.mindset: Negotiate for resources before escalating.

questions.stem: A project manager has been assigned to a new project that revisits a previously completed project. Why should the project manager refer to the previous project lessons learned knowledge base and historic information first?

options.text: To identify resources who worked on the previous project
options.rationale: Identifying past team members is useful, but it is not the main value of lessons learned for a revisited project.

options.text: To define the project requirements and finalize the scope
options.rationale: Requirements and scope come from the new project's stakeholders; lessons learned inform but do not define them.

options.text: To determine a baseline for the project budget
options.rationale: Historical cost data may help estimating, but the key purpose here is learning what went wrong before.

options.text: To understand issues in the previous project
options.rationale: Understanding the issues the previous project faced lets the new project avoid repeating them.

questions.explanation: When revisiting a previous project, its lessons learned and history show what did not go as planned and how problems were resolved. Understanding those issues first shapes planning so the same mistakes are not repeated.
questions.mindset: Learn what went wrong last time before planning this time.

questions.stem: A team for a project is composed of individuals from different backgrounds, ages, and interests. The team is struggling to work together. How would meeting with the team to develop mutual values and a shared vision enable the project manager to facilitate better teamwork?

options.text: An official team meeting to discuss the importance of teamwork would motivate the team and improve project performance.
options.rationale: A meeting about the importance of teamwork motivates briefly but does not create shared understanding among diverse members.

options.text: A better understanding of team members' priorities would create a common language that would foster cooperation.
options.rationale: Understanding each other's priorities builds a common language and mutual values, which enables cooperation across differences.

options.text: Understanding each team member's viewpoint would pinpoint areas where education and training was necessary.
options.rationale: Identifying training needs is a side benefit, not how shared values improve teamwork.

options.text: By developing its own understanding of the goals and objectives of the project, the team would gain confidence.
options.rationale: Confidence from understanding goals helps, but the key mechanism is mutual understanding among team members.

questions.explanation: Diverse teams struggle when members do not understand each other's priorities and assumptions. Developing shared values and vision together creates a common language that lets people cooperate across their differences.
questions.mindset: Build a common language before expecting common action.

questions.stem: A stakeholder requests more frequent and detailed project status reports than a previous agreement. The stakeholder also expresses interest in getting more involved with the project. How should the project manager address this situation?

options.text: Provide the stakeholder with an update on the project's status and send detailed status reports as soon as possible.
options.rationale: Sending detailed reports as a one-off does not change the agreed arrangements or align the team.

options.text: Revise the stakeholder engagement assessment matrix to show the stakeholder's engagement level as supportive.
options.rationale: Changing the engagement label does not deliver the information the stakeholder requested.

options.text: Update the stakeholder communication plan and ensure that the team is aligned on the new reporting requirements.
options.rationale: Updating the communication plan formalises the new reporting needs and ensures the team delivers them consistently.

options.text: Develop a stakeholder cube that defines the relationship between the stakeholder and the project.
options.rationale: A stakeholder cube is an analysis tool and does not meet the reporting request.

questions.explanation: When a stakeholder's information needs change, the communications plan is updated so the new frequency and detail become part of how the project reports, and the team knows what is expected.
questions.mindset: Update the plan when stakeholders' information needs change.

questions.stem: During the planning phase for the expansion of a services company, stakeholders conducted a feasibility study to establish the type of new service the company should provide. During an alternatives analysis, another type of service was determined to be more effective. The change control board (CCB) has approved the change request for the alternative service. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Implement the change as approved.
options.rationale: Implementing the approved change is the project manager's role once the CCB has decided.

options.text: Modify the change to reduce the impact on the schedule and budget.
options.rationale: Modifying an approved change without approval undermines change control.

options.text: Request justification from the CCB for the change.
options.rationale: Requesting justification from the CCB questions a decision within its authority.

options.text: Conduct a cost-benefit analysis of the alternative service.
options.rationale: A cost-benefit analysis should have been part of the evaluation before approval.

questions.explanation: Once a change is approved by the authorised body, the project manager implements it and updates plans accordingly. Re-litigating or altering approved changes undermines governance.
questions.mindset: Implement approved changes as approved.

questions.stem: A project is entering the user acceptance testing phase. After several business end users raised questions and concerns, the project manager discovered that critical business requirements were omitted from the business requirements analysis. What should the project manager do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Interview the team that conducted the analysis to learn why these business requirements were omitted.
options.rationale: Interviewing the analysis team may explain the omission, but it does not add the missing requirements.

options.text: Modify the requirements management plan and communicate to the stakeholders that the project schedule might be impacted.
options.rationale: Changing the requirements management plan does not add the missing requirements to scope.

options.text: Schedule a meeting with the project sponsor to report end users' concerns.
options.rationale: Reporting concerns to the sponsor raises awareness without resolving the gap.

options.text: Meet with the change control board (CCB) to review change requests.
options.rationale: Reviewing change requests with the CCB brings the missing critical requirements into scope through the proper process.

questions.explanation: Critical requirements discovered late must be added through change control. The CCB evaluates their impact and approves how they are incorporated.
questions.mindset: Bring late-found requirements in through change control.

questions.stem: A new project is about to start and is subject to strict time and budget constraints. When reviewing the lessons learned repository, the project manager learns that constant scope creep caused a similar project to fail. What should the project manager do now to avoid project failure?

options.text: Refuse to accept out-of-scope change requests that would increase project duration and budget.
options.rationale: Refusing all out-of-scope changes is rigid and ignores legitimate needs.

options.text: Manage stakeholder expectations to exclude the possibility of changes in order to meet project goals.
options.rationale: Excluding any possibility of change is unrealistic.

options.text: Adjust the project scope and schedule to stay within constraints and avoid potential changes.
options.rationale: Adjusting scope to avoid changes presumes changes will not happen.

options.text: Establish formal change approval processes to guide teams to deliver essential features first.
options.rationale: Formal change approval processes control scope creep and help teams deliver essential features first.

questions.explanation: Scope creep is controlled by a formal change process that evaluates every change against constraints and priorities, not by banning change.
questions.mindset: Control scope with a process, not a ban.

questions.stem: While developing the initial schedule baseline, the project manager learns that a functional manager reassigned two resources needed for a critical task to another strategic project. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Perform a quantitative risk analysis to determine the impact of the change on the project.
options.rationale: Quantitative analysis is premature if replacements can be negotiated.

options.text: Request a review of the reassignment by the change control board (CCB).
options.rationale: The CCB does not normally review resource allocations.

options.text: Meet with the functional manager to negotiate allocation of replacement resources.
options.rationale: The functional manager controls resources and can provide suitable replacements.

options.text: Escalate the issue to the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Escalating to the sponsor before negotiating is premature.

questions.explanation: When functional managers reassign resources, negotiating with them for replacements is the first step, since they control allocation.
questions.mindset: Negotiate replacements with whoever controls the resources.

questions.stem: A complex manufacturing project has multiple stakeholders in multiple locations. The project is entering a high-activity phase and the project manager needs to ensure that all stakeholders are kept informed with timely updates. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Schedule training sessions on effective communications with all stakeholders.
options.rationale: Training stakeholders in communication does not deliver the more frequent updates the high-activity phase requires.

options.text: Determine the most appropriate technology to use to communicate with all stakeholders.
options.rationale: Choosing technology comes after deciding what and how often to communicate.

options.text: Schedule regular status reports to be sent to all stakeholders.
options.rationale: Scheduling reports without updating the plan is ad hoc.

options.text: Revise the communications management plan to have a more frequent update schedule.
options.rationale: Revising the communications plan for more frequent updates suits the high-activity phase.

questions.explanation: Communication needs change with project phases. Updating the communications plan to reflect higher frequency ensures stakeholders stay informed during intense periods.
questions.mindset: Adapt communication to the phase of the project.

questions.stem: A project manager learns that a stakeholder thinks that only certain stakeholders are getting all the project updates and feels left out of the information loop. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Prepare a status update report and send it to all stakeholders.
options.rationale: Sending an update does not fix whether the stakeholder is included going forward.

options.text: Meet with all stakeholders together and ask them to compare information.
options.rationale: Asking stakeholders to compare information is awkward and unproductive.

options.text: Review the communications management plan to ensure that all stakeholders are included.
options.rationale: Reviewing the communications plan ensures all stakeholders are included.

options.text: Revise the project communications strategy to ensure more frequent distribution of status reports.
options.rationale: More frequent reports do not help if the stakeholder is not on the list.

questions.explanation: Feeling left out usually reflects a gap in the communications plan. Reviewing it ensures all stakeholders receive the information they need.
questions.mindset: Fix the distribution, not just the message.

questions.stem: During a project status meeting, the project manager discovers that stakeholders have different expectations that are not aligned. None of these expectations have been met, which has created tension in the meeting. What should the project manager do to keep things moving on the project?

options.text: Update the risk register to reflect the difference in expectations as a high risk.
options.rationale: Updating the risk register records the problem but does not align expectations.

options.text: Ask stakeholders to send their expectations by email to ensure that they are included in the project plan.
options.rationale: Collecting expectations by email does not resolve conflicts between them.

options.text: Meet with stakeholders privately and update the responsibility matrix.
options.rationale: Private meetings help understand each stakeholder's expectations, and updating the responsibility matrix clarifies who owns what.

options.text: Show stakeholders that the current status is aligned with the work breakdown structure (WBS).
options.rationale: Showing alignment with the WBS dismisses the concerns.

questions.explanation: Misaligned expectations often stem from unclear ownership. Understanding each stakeholder's view privately and clarifying responsibilities helps align them.
questions.mindset: Clarify who owns which expectation.

questions.stem: A project manager identifies a risk during the implementation phase of a project which was not anticipated during planning. How would facilitating a brainstorming session allow the project manager to mitigate the risk while keeping the project on schedule?

options.text: Brainstorming would enable the project manager to apply qualitative data analysis techniques.
options.rationale: Brainstorming generates ideas; it is not a qualitative analysis technique.

options.text: Brainstorming with the project team can identify multiple ideas in a short amount of time.
options.rationale: Brainstorming with the team generates many response ideas quickly, keeping the project on schedule.

options.text: Brainstorming with project stakeholders can result in new assumptions regarding risk tolerance.
options.rationale: Revisiting stakeholders' risk tolerance is not why a quick brainstorm helps respond to a newly found risk.

options.text: Brainstorming ways to add funding can help mitigate the risk and compress the schedule.
options.rationale: Adding funding is not a brainstorming outcome.

questions.explanation: Brainstorming quickly generates a range of response ideas from the people closest to the work, useful for unexpected risks.
questions.mindset: Brainstorm with the team to respond quickly.

questions.stem: While reviewing the quality of deliverables with the team, the project manager determines that several quality issues could have been avoided by using a checklist. The project manager implements a checklist to ensure future deliverables would align with the project management plan. What did the project manager do in this situation?

options.text: Defined new quality metrics.
options.rationale: New quality metrics are defined in quality planning.

options.text: Used corrective action.
options.rationale: Implementing a checklist to realign future work with the plan is corrective action.

options.text: Facilitated a retrospective.
options.rationale: A retrospective is a meeting, not the action taken.

options.text: Conducted a lessons learned meeting.
options.rationale: A lessons learned meeting captures knowledge, not realignment.

questions.explanation: Corrective action realigns project performance with the plan. Adding a checklist after quality issues is a classic corrective action.
questions.mindset: Correct the process when outputs drift from the plan.

questions.stem: A project manager has been assigned to a newly approved multi-national project. The successful implementation of the project relies on deliverables from a variety of departments. What is the most important thing the project manager can do to ensure the successful implementation of the project?

options.text: Work with the project team members to create ground rules for communications and develop a project plan.
options.rationale: Ground rules and a plan are needed but do not secure the departments' commitment.

options.text: Facilitate sessions with key stakeholders to gather relevant information and define detailed product requirements.
options.rationale: Detailed requirements are important but assume the departments will deliver.

options.text: Meet with the functional managers of the relevant departments to ensure alignment with project objectives.
options.rationale: Aligning functional managers with project objectives secures commitment from the departments that provide deliverables.

options.text: Develop a resource management plan to define the resources required from each department.
options.rationale: A resource plan defines needs but not alignment.

questions.explanation: When success depends on multiple departments, aligning their managers with project objectives is critical to securing resources and priorities.
questions.mindset: Secure alignment with the managers who control the contributing departments.

questions.stem: The project sponsors for a multinational project have put a process in place that generates emails and reports at the end of each phase. The goal is to ensure the project remains unified across the company. The company plans to use the process as a model for future, similar projects. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Update the communications management plan to include details about the emails and reports.
options.rationale: Updating the communications plan documents the new emails and reports so they can be applied and reused.

options.text: Include a formal sign-off at the end of each phase to engage the stakeholders.
options.rationale: Formal sign-off is a governance step, not a communication one.

options.text: Hold status meetings to solicit input from project sponsors for the emails and reports.
options.rationale: Status meetings to gather sponsor input do not record the reporting process so it can be applied and reused.

options.text: Update the stakeholder engagement plan at the end of each phase to maintain their commitment to the project's success.
options.rationale: The engagement plan describes engagement strategies, not report templates.

questions.explanation: Sponsor-defined communications processes should be captured in the communications management plan, which records methods, templates and timing for reuse.
questions.mindset: Document communication processes in the communications plan.

questions.stem: A project manager is hired by an organization and is given a project that has a vague scope and unclear deliverable requirements. How should the project manager proceed with this project?

options.text: Schedule a meeting with the project team and the sponsor to clarify the scope.
options.rationale: Meeting the team and sponsor to clarify the scope establishes what the project must deliver before planning begins.

options.text: Develop the project plan based on the current scope by breaking down the deliverables and requirements.
options.rationale: Breaking down a vague scope produces a detailed plan built on unclear foundations.

options.text: Escalate to the project management office (PMO) to clarify the unclear scope.
options.rationale: Escalating to the PMO deflects the project manager's responsibility to clarify scope with the sponsor.

options.text: Submit a request to the PMO to be paired with someone familiar with the organization’s project management approach.
options.rationale: Pairing with someone familiar with the methodology may help, but it does not clarify this project's scope.

questions.explanation: A vague scope cannot be planned reliably. The project manager clarifies scope and deliverable requirements with the sponsor and team first, then decomposes the agreed scope into a plan.
questions.mindset: Clarify scope before planning it.

questions.stem: A project manager for an important agile project has a key stakeholder who was actively involved at the beginning of the project. Early in the project, the stakeholder received a promotion and has significantly reduced their participation in the project. Nearing the end of the project, the stakeholder did not accept a deliverable, resulting in significant rework that threatens the project deadline. What should the project manager have done to avoid this situation?

options.text: Update the risk management plan to document the stakeholder’s promotion.
options.rationale: A promotion is not in itself a project risk, and documenting it does not re-engage the stakeholder.

options.text: Monitor the stakeholder attributes and make necessary adjustments to engage the key stakeholder actively.
options.rationale: Monitoring changes in stakeholder attributes and adjusting engagement would have kept the key stakeholder involved.

options.text: Reach out to the sponsor to manage stakeholder engagement.
options.rationale: Delegating engagement to the sponsor removes the project manager's responsibility.

options.text: Removed the key stakeholder from the decision-making process.
options.rationale: Removing a key stakeholder from decisions guarantees rejection later.

questions.explanation: Stakeholders' availability, influence and interest change over time. Monitoring those changes and adjusting engagement keeps key stakeholders involved enough that acceptance is not a surprise.
questions.mindset: Watch for changes in stakeholders and adjust engagement accordingly.

questions.stem: After completing a project, the team meets to conduct a lessons learned session. During this meeting, the team sees that all deliverables were completed to the defined parameters. However, during the testing, there were a large number of errors identified. What should the project manager have done in this situation?

options.text: Set up a meeting with the testing team to get more information about the testing methods to be used.
options.rationale: Meeting the testing team about methods may improve testing but does not deal with variability in error counts.

options.text: Evaluated when the mitigation strategy will be implemented to prepare for future projects.
options.rationale: Evaluating when a mitigation strategy will be used presumes a strategy existed.

options.text: Conducted a Monte Carlo analysis which will determine potential outcomes and responses.
options.rationale: Monte Carlo analysis models the range of possible outcomes for variability risks such as error counts, supporting planned responses.

options.text: Planned for these errors in the risk register as something to look for in future projects.
options.rationale: Logging errors for future projects does not help this project anticipate them.

questions.explanation: Some risks are about variability rather than discrete events — the number of defects may be higher or lower than expected. Simulation techniques such as Monte Carlo model that range so responses can be planned.
questions.mindset: Model variability risks as ranges, not single events.

questions.stem: Multiple stakeholders express dissatisfaction with a project deliverable. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Review the final scope statement.
options.rationale: Reviewing the scope statement may help later, but it does not reveal what the stakeholders are dissatisfied about.

options.text: Update the risk management plan.
options.rationale: Updating the risk plan is not the immediate response to dissatisfaction.

options.text: Review the documented project requirements.
options.rationale: Reviewing requirements is useful after hearing the specific concerns.

options.text: Schedule a meeting with the stakeholders.
options.rationale: Meeting the stakeholders lets the project manager understand their concerns and work on solutions together.

questions.explanation: When multiple stakeholders are dissatisfied, the project manager engages them directly to understand the specifics before checking documents or updating plans.
questions.mindset: Hear the concerns before checking the documents.

questions.stem: A local government passes a law that affects the scope of a project that is currently in the execution phase. The regulation change was unforeseen and will take effect within weeks of the law passing. The project manager knows that the project schedule and budget will be impacted as a result. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Immediately halt the project until the regulation change can be incorporated into the project plan.
options.rationale: Halting the project may be unnecessary and costly.

options.text: Delegate the responsibility for assessing the impact of the regulation change to a team member.
options.rationale: Delegating the impact assessment may lose the expertise needed.

options.text: Proceed with the project as planned until the new regulation is implemented and the impacts are known.
options.rationale: Proceeding without assessing impact risks non-compliance and rework.

options.text: Seek expert judgment to assess the impact of the regulation change on the project schedule and budget.
options.rationale: Expert judgement gives an accurate assessment of the new law's effect on schedule and budget.

questions.explanation: Assessing the impact of new regulations often needs specialist knowledge. Expert judgement helps the project understand effects accurately and plan changes.
questions.mindset: Use expert judgement to assess regulatory impact.

questions.stem: A large project involving functional groups in four countries is nearing completion. The project manager is meeting with the functional managers to prepare closeout documents. Why should the project sponsor sign off on the acceptance of project deliverables?

options.text: Because the project sponsor is responsible for procuring funding and committing resources to the project
options.rationale: The sponsor provides funding and resources, so they formally accept the deliverables that investment produced.

options.text: Because the project sponsor communicates directly with the customer regarding acceptance of deliverables
options.rationale: The sponsor may not communicate with the customer directly.

options.text: Because the functional managers have authority to approve project objectives but not final deliverables
options.rationale: Functional managers' authority over objectives is not the reason.

options.text: Because the functional managers are too geographically dispersed to sign off on the deliverables
options.rationale: Geographic dispersion does not prevent sign-off.

questions.explanation: The sponsor secured the funding and committed the resources, and is accountable for the business case. That is why the sponsor formally accepts the project's deliverables at closure, whatever role functional managers played in producing them.
questions.mindset: The one who funds the project accepts its results.

questions.stem: During a project team meeting, the project manager notices a conflict between three key team members who have very different personalities. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Plan a team-building event where different personality types are required to solve problems.
options.rationale: A team-building event may help later but does not address the specific conflict.

options.text: Remind the team members that emotions should not impair their work performance.
options.rationale: Telling people to keep emotions out is dismissive.

options.text: Assign project tasks to avoid contact between the three members.
options.rationale: Keeping the three apart avoids the conflict but prevents the collaboration the project needs from key team members.

options.text: Identify the root cause of the conflict and support a resolution between the team members.
options.rationale: Understanding the root cause and supporting a resolution addresses the conflict effectively.

questions.explanation: Effective conflict resolution starts with understanding the cause. Interventions based on the real issue work better than generic ones.
questions.mindset: Understand the cause of conflict before intervening.

questions.stem: The company's top executives are embarking on a pivotal project that holds immense importance for the organization's future. This project involves a comprehensive overhaul of their production system. Given the project's high-risk nature, the executives emphasize that its success is non-negotiable. What should the project manager prioritize as the initial step?

options.text: Implementing an appropriate method for the project rollout, prioritizing the components with the highest business value.
options.rationale: Rollout methods matter later but depend on agreed scope.

options.text: Developing a comprehensive communication management plan to ensure timely project progress updates for everyone.
options.rationale: A communications plan is important but secondary to agreement on scope and deliverables.

options.text: Ensuring unanimous agreement among stakeholders and the project sponsor about the project plan, scope, and deliverables.
options.rationale: Ensuring agreement among stakeholders and the sponsor on plan, scope and deliverables establishes a clear foundation.

options.text: Collaborating closely with the marketing team to ensure the end products align seamlessly with customer communication.
options.rationale: Marketing alignment is narrower than overall stakeholder agreement.

questions.explanation: For high-risk, high-importance projects, agreement among key stakeholders on scope and deliverables is the foundation for everything else.
questions.mindset: Secure agreement on what success means before starting.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a team that is developing a new software product. The deadline for the product launch is approaching, but the team is very behind schedule. The project manager has tried to motivate the team and help them catch up, but they have been unwilling and unsuccessful. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Meet with the project sponsor to discuss and develop a revised project plan.
options.rationale: Meeting the sponsor to develop a revised plan addresses the reality of the schedule transparently.

options.text: Request a project deadline extension and continue motivating the team.
options.rationale: Requesting an extension without a plan is incomplete.

options.text: Use the forcing method to require the team to work overtime to meet the deadline.
options.rationale: Forcing overtime harms morale and is unlikely to succeed.

options.text: Escalate the issue to the functional manager for additional resources.
options.rationale: Additional resources may not solve the problem.

questions.explanation: When motivation and recovery efforts have failed and the deadline is at risk, continuing to push is not a plan. The project manager is transparent with the sponsor and works with them on a realistic revised plan — scope, dates or resources — while there is still time to choose.
questions.mindset: Face schedule reality with the sponsor early.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned to join a mega industrial project already underway. The latest performance indices are CPI=0.42 and SPI=0.20. This project is:

options.text: Ahead of schedule and under budget
options.rationale: CPI and SPI below 1 mean the project is not ahead or under budget.

options.text: Ahead of schedule and over budget
options.rationale: SPI below 1 means behind schedule, not ahead.

options.text: Behind schedule and under budget
options.rationale: The project is behind schedule, but a CPI below 1 means it is over budget, not under.

options.text: Behind schedule and over budget
options.rationale: CPI 0.42 and SPI 0.20 are both below 1: over budget and behind schedule.

questions.explanation: Earned value indices are read against 1.0. A CPI below 1 means each unit of cost is buying less than planned (over budget); an SPI below 1 means less work has been done than planned (behind schedule). Values as low as 0.42 and 0.20 signal serious trouble.
questions.mindset: Read indices against 1.0: below means worse than plan.

questions.stem: During a daily standup, a stakeholder unexpectedly joins the meeting and criticizes the performance of one of the team members. After this, the team member is very distracted from their work and their productivity noticeably decreases. What should the team member do in this scenario?

options.text: Schedule a meeting with the stakeholder to discuss the stakeholder’s actions during the standup.
options.rationale: Confronting the stakeholder directly may escalate the situation.

options.text: Email the stakeholder to request that future communications should come through the project manager.
options.rationale: An email request does not address the impact.

options.text: Meet with the scrum master to discuss what occurred and how it has affected productivity.
options.rationale: Discussing it with the scrum master lets the impediment be removed and the stakeholder guided.

options.text: Meet with the project manager and sponsor to request reassignment to a different project.
options.rationale: Asking to leave the project over one incident is drastic and leaves the impediment unaddressed for the rest of the team.

questions.explanation: A stakeholder criticising a team member in a stand-up is interference that affects productivity. Raising it with the scrum master lets the impediment be addressed and the stakeholder guided to appropriate channels, instead of the team member confronting them alone.
questions.mindset: Raise interference as an impediment.

questions.stem: A project manager is new to the organization and is assigned to replace the project manager of an active project. What should be one of the first things the project manager does?

options.text: Schedule meetings with the project stakeholders to learn more about the project deliverables.
options.rationale: Stakeholder meetings are important but come after understanding status from the team.

options.text: Setup meetings with the team members to discuss the project’s status and risks.
options.rationale: Meeting the team to discuss status and risks gives the new PM a first-hand picture.

options.text: Conduct a Pareto analysis to identify which tasks need to be prioritized.
options.rationale: A Pareto analysis of tasks is premature before the new project manager understands the project's status and risks.

options.text: Prepare by reviewing the risk register and mitigation strategies.
options.rationale: Reviewing the risk register alone misses the team's view.

questions.explanation: A project manager taking over an active project needs an accurate picture quickly. Talking with the team about status and risks gives a first-hand view that documents alone cannot, and prepares the PM for stakeholder conversations.
questions.mindset: Learn a project's reality from its team.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a daily standup meeting when a team member requests that other team members take on some of their assigned work because they are feeling overwhelmed with an upcoming deadline. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Reassign the team member's work to other team members without asking for their input.
options.rationale: Reassigning without input ignores team collaboration.

options.text: Ask the team member to identify the tasks they need assistance with in another meeting.
options.rationale: Following up in another meeting keeps the stand-up focused while supporting the member.

options.text: Tell the team member to go for training to figure out how to complete their work on time.
options.rationale: Sending them to training dismisses a workload concern.

options.text: Dismiss the team member's concerns and move on with the daily standup meeting.
options.rationale: Dismissing a team member's concern about overload damages trust and risks the deadline they are worried about.

questions.explanation: Stand-ups are for coordination; detailed problem-solving happens afterwards. When a team member says they are overwhelmed, the project manager acknowledges it and follows up straight after, working out with them which tasks need help.
questions.mindset: Take detailed problem-solving out of the stand-up, but always follow up.

questions.stem: Which of the following steps should an Agile project manager of a newly formed virtual team take to help the organization succeed? (Choose 2).

options.text: Provide clear goals, direction, or priorities.
options.rationale: Clear goals help any team, but in an agile context the manager should avoid directing roles and priorities for a self-organising team.

options.text: Help establish cooperation and trust.
options.rationale: Establishing cooperation and trust is essential for a new virtual team, where people cannot rely on proximity to build relationships.

options.text: Let the team decide and evolve their roles and responsibilities.
options.rationale: Letting the team define and evolve its roles builds ownership and self-organisation.

options.text: Neglect "Face time" and regular check-ins with team members.
options.rationale: Neglecting face time and check-ins weakens communication and trust in a virtual team.

questions.explanation: Newly formed virtual agile teams need trust and ownership. The leader creates conditions for cooperation and lets the team shape its own roles, rather than directing every detail or withdrawing contact.
questions.mindset: Build trust and let the team shape how it works.

questions.stem: An agile team finds it difficult to complete a checklist because they have different interpretations of what the project aims to achieve. How can the project manager help them gain a common understanding of the project's overall purpose?

options.text: Review the project vision.
options.rationale: Reviewing the project vision gives the team a shared understanding of the overall purpose that guides their interpretations.

options.text: Review the full list of user stories.
options.rationale: User stories describe pieces of work, not the overall purpose.

options.text: Review the Agile Manifesto.
options.rationale: The Agile Manifesto describes values for agile work, not this project's purpose.

options.text: Conduct the first sprint retrospective.
options.rationale: A retrospective improves process; it does not clarify the project's purpose.

questions.explanation: A project vision expresses why the project exists and what it aims to achieve. When team members interpret goals differently, revisiting the vision aligns them on purpose.
questions.mindset: Return to the vision when interpretations diverge.

questions.stem: During an iteration the team realizes that the project will overrun the budget. This is due to the support resources being involved for longer than planned. Company policy requires immediate notification when there is any change to the budget. What should project manager do to manage the project budget?

options.text: Estimate the additional project cost and plan to propose the new budget to the change review board.
options.rationale: Estimating and proposing a new budget accepts the overrun before trying to reduce it.

options.text: Reduce the resources and ask the team to manage tasks within the planned cost.
options.rationale: Cutting resources and asking the team to cope may harm delivery without addressing why support was used longer.

options.text: Discuss with the project team to reduce the use of support resources by the project.
options.rationale: Working with the team to reduce reliance on support resources addresses the cause of the overrun.

options.text: Accept the cost overrun risk, depending on the contingency amount of the project.
options.rationale: Accepting the overrun against contingency ignores a controllable cause.

questions.explanation: Budget pressure caused by a specific driver — here, support resources used longer than planned — is best tackled by working with the team to change how those resources are used.
questions.mindset: Tackle the cost driver with the team.

questions.stem: A project manager in a project management office (PMO) is tasked with implementing an agile framework. The leadership team expects a seamless transition to agile practices. However, the project team has no experience with agile projects. The project manager recognizes that the team will face challenges in this transformation. Which three factors should the project manager prioritize to ensure a successful transition to agile practices?

options.text: Identifying key stakeholders and involving them in the agile transformation process.
options.rationale: Involving key stakeholders secures support and aligns expectations for the transformation.

options.text: Providing extensive training and coaching to team members on agile principles and practices.
options.rationale: Training and coaching give the team the skills to adopt agile.

options.text: Promoting a culture of collaboration, transparency, and continuous improvement among team members.
options.rationale: A culture of collaboration, transparency and improvement sustains agile ways of working.

options.text: Ignoring customer feedback at the beginning of the project and focusing solely on internal team dynamics.
options.rationale: Ignoring customer feedback contradicts agile principles.

options.text: Establishing a rigid and inflexible project plan to ensure strict adherence to timelines.
options.rationale: A rigid plan undermines the adaptability agile needs.

questions.explanation: Agile transformations succeed when stakeholders are engaged, teams are trained and coached, and the culture supports collaboration and improvement.
