questions.mindset: Transform people, skills and culture together.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned a project for a customer with a history of being demanding and unclear about requirements. The customer has refused to accept previous deliverables without providing clear feedback. How should the project manager proceed with this project?

options.text: Meet with the sponsor to define a detailed schedule leading to project completion on time.
options.rationale: A detailed schedule does not address unclear expectations.

options.text: Work with the customer and the product owner to clearly define the minimum viable product (MVP).
options.rationale: Defining the MVP with the customer and product owner creates clear, agreed expectations.

options.text: Implement an iterative approach in order to obtain formal acceptance of each deliverable.
options.rationale: Iterating without clear expectations risks repeated rejection.

options.text: Request to terminate the project until the customer is able to provide concrete expectations.
options.rationale: Stopping the project until the customer is perfectly clear is disproportionate; the project manager's job is to help them get there.

questions.explanation: Customers with unclear expectations need help defining what success looks like. Agreeing an MVP creates concrete, shared acceptance targets.
questions.mindset: Make vague expectations concrete through an agreed MVP.

questions.stem: A software developer who is working on a critical component has to take emergency leave from the project. Due to time constraints, the project manager cannot hire a new replacement developer for the team. What should the project manager do to manage the situation?

options.text: Move the critical component to the final iteration it can be worked on after the developer returns from leave.
options.rationale: Moving the component to the end creates risk and delays value.

options.text: Request the project sponsor to extend the project until the developer returns and finishes the work.
options.rationale: Extending the whole project to wait for one person ignores the team's ability to cover the work.

options.text: Prolong the iteration to allow time for the developer to return and complete the component.
options.rationale: Stretching the iteration to wait for the developer breaks the timebox and delays everything else in it.

options.text: Ask team members to find a way to complete the missing developer's work in this iteration.
options.rationale: Asking the team to find a way to complete the work uses their self-organisation to keep to schedule.

questions.explanation: Self-organising teams can often redistribute work when someone is unavailable. The PM invites the team to find a solution first.
questions.mindset: Let the team solve capacity gaps first.

questions.stem: A project manager is running an agile project that is half completed. During the most recent sprint retrospective, the team members see that they worked more hours than were originally scheduled. How should the project manager address this situation?

options.text: Note the additional hours in the budget and leverage the budget reserves.
options.rationale: Absorbing the extra hours into budget reserves hides the problem and lets it recur every sprint.

options.text: Reach out to the sponsor asking for additional project team members to increase velocity.
options.rationale: Adding people assumes the cause is capacity, and new members typically slow a team before they help.

options.text: Work with the project team to identify why this occurred and what can be done to prevent it in future sprints.
options.rationale: Working with the team to find causes and prevent recurrence addresses the issue.

options.text: Empower the team to address this issue and present the sponsor with the proposed resolution.
options.rationale: Empowering the team without involvement misses the PM's support role.

questions.explanation: Working more hours than planned is a warning sign of overcommitment, poor estimates or hidden work. Investigating the cause with the team and agreeing preventive actions leads to a sustainable pace, instead of hiding the extra effort.
questions.mindset: Find the cause of overtime with the team.

questions.stem: A project manager is part of a project that has a scrum team. The team members are unfamiliar with the distinction between risks and issues and prefer to use the concept of impediments. For which of the following would the team be unable to apply the concept of impediments?

options.text: One of the junior members of the team cannot work at full capacity for a week.
options.rationale: A team member working at reduced capacity is an impediment to the team's work.

options.text: One of the competitors announced the imminent release of a new version of their product.
options.rationale: A competitor's announcement does not stop the team working, so it is a market risk rather than an impediment.

options.text: The administration of the building announced that for the next couple of weeks there will be maintenance work on the air conditioning system.
options.rationale: Building maintenance can hinder the team's work and is an impediment.

options.text: The project manager is on leave and scrum master has to take a lead for distinguishing risk from issues.
options.rationale: The project manager's absence affecting decisions can be an impediment.

questions.explanation: Impediments are obstacles blocking the team's progress now. External market events such as a competitor launch are risks to the product, not impediments to the team's work.
questions.mindset: Distinguish what blocks the team from what threatens the product.

questions.stem: Midway through a project, the project manager identifies new stakeholders. Each of these new stakeholders plays a different project role. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Meet with the project sponsor to learn if new roles have been created.
options.rationale: Asking about new roles is not needed; the stakeholders are identified.

options.text: Review the stakeholder register.
options.rationale: The register will be updated, but engagement strategies must also be planned.

options.text: Submit a change request to the change control board (CCB).
options.rationale: No change to requirements means no change request.

options.text: Update the stakeholder management plan.
options.rationale: Updating the stakeholder management plan defines how each new stakeholder will be engaged.

questions.explanation: New stakeholders mid-project need more than a name in the register. The stakeholder management plan is updated to define how each will be engaged, given their different roles, interests and influence.
questions.mindset: Plan engagement for new stakeholders.

questions.stem: Team members express frustration because their functional manager does not listen to their opinions. They seem reluctant to devote themselves to the remainder of the project. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Demonstrate support for the team by discussing their goals and beliefs.
options.rationale: Demonstrating support and discussing the team's goals and beliefs rebuilds motivation.

options.text: Break the remaining work into smaller tasks and divide the tasks among the team.
options.rationale: Breaking work down does not address frustration.

options.text: Ask the team to prioritize the tasks remaining in the project.
options.rationale: Prioritising tasks does not address feelings of not being heard.

options.text: Discuss the team's concerns with the functional manager.
options.rationale: Raising concerns with the functional manager may help later, but the team first needs support.

questions.explanation: When team members feel unheard by their functional manager and lose commitment, the project manager shows support by listening to their goals and views. Feeling valued restores engagement more than restructuring the work.
questions.mindset: Listen to teams that feel unheard.

questions.stem: During project initiation, the project manager learns that a key stakeholder will leave the project for a month to consult on another strategic project. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Update the issue log and notify the other stakeholders.
options.rationale: Logging the issue and notifying stakeholders makes the absence visible so plans can adjust.

options.text: Ask the functional manager to provide a replacement while the stakeholder is unavailable.
options.rationale: A replacement may be needed, but first the issue is recorded and communicated.

options.text: Interview the stakeholder to gather relevant information and expert judgment.
options.rationale: Interviewing the stakeholder is useful but secondary.

options.text: Update the risk management plan to include the impact of the stakeholder's absence.
options.rationale: The risk management plan describes methods, not specific issues.

questions.explanation: A key stakeholder's known absence is a current issue that will affect decisions and input. Recording it and informing the other stakeholders lets everyone plan around the gap before choosing specific mitigations.
questions.mindset: Record and share known issues first.

questions.stem: During a project's execution phase, two stakeholders complain that they receive insufficient information on the project's status. The stakeholders have been included in the regular status meetings, and status reports are being shared with them. Why should the project manager meet with these stakeholders?

options.text: To gather data on the issue in order to update the issue log.
options.rationale: Updating the issue log does not identify what information is missing.

options.text: To determine what information they are lacking and develop an understanding of their communication needs.
options.rationale: Meeting them reveals what information they lack and their communication needs.

options.text: Send the stakeholders copies of the Emails previously sent to prove that they are included in the project's communications plan.
options.rationale: Sending old emails as proof of inclusion is defensive and ignores the possibility that the information does not meet their needs.

options.text: To develop a better working relationship with these stakeholders in order to prioritize and rank their requirements.
options.rationale: Ranking their requirements is not the aim; the stakeholders' complaint is about the information they receive.

questions.explanation: When stakeholders receive regular reports but still feel uninformed, the content or format does not meet their needs. Meeting them to learn what information they lack lets the project manager tailor communication accordingly.
questions.mindset: Ask what information people actually need.

questions.stem: An organization is redesigning and relaunching a key product. The stakeholders are all company executives and want to ensure that the product launch will be a success. What should the project manager do to ensure project success?

options.text: Implement a detailed communication management plan so that stakeholders are kept informed of the project status.
options.rationale: A detailed communication plan informs but does not define success.

options.text: Communicate the critical nature of this project to the team and escalate any issues to the sponsor.
options.rationale: Stressing the project's importance and escalating issues does not define how the launch's success will be judged.

options.text: Ensure that all of the stakeholders attend the daily standups so that they can adjust the project as needed.
options.rationale: Daily stand-ups are not suited to executives.

options.text: Work to identify and align performance indicators with the deliverable.
options.rationale: Aligning performance indicators with the deliverable defines and measures success.

questions.explanation: Success must be defined and measurable. Performance indicators agreed with executives guide delivery toward what matters.
questions.mindset: Define success measures upfront.

questions.stem: A project manager needs to hire suppliers for an international project that has a performance period of several years. The project manager needs to allow for conditions such as changes in inflation rates. What type of contract should the project manager use?

options.text: Time and material (T&M)
options.rationale: Time and materials suits small or undefined work, not a multi-year international supply agreement.

options.text: Cost plus fixed fee (CPFF)
options.rationale: Cost plus fixed fee puts all cost risk on the buyer and does not specifically deal with inflation.

options.text: Cost plus incentive fee (FPIF)
options.rationale: A cost-plus incentive arrangement rewards cost performance but is not designed for predefined inflation adjustments.

options.text: Fixed price with economic price adjustment (FPEPA)
options.rationale: A fixed price with economic price adjustment allows predefined adjustments for inflation over a long performance period.

questions.explanation: Long-duration contracts are exposed to inflation and currency changes. Fixed price with economic price adjustment keeps a fixed-price structure while allowing agreed adjustments for such external conditions.
questions.mindset: Use economic price adjustments when time exposes prices to inflation.

questions.stem: A project is in the execution phase when the project manager needs to assign new resources to the existing project team. What should the project manager do to ensure the team works effectively and meets project requirements on time?

options.text: Create accessible library services.
options.rationale: A library of resources is passive and does not ensure new members become effective.

options.text: Conduct a brainstorming session.
options.rationale: Brainstorming generates ideas but does not build new members' skills.

options.text: Integrate skills development activities.
options.rationale: Integrating skills development ensures new members gain what they need to work effectively and meet requirements.

options.text: Monitor project team cohesiveness.
options.rationale: Monitoring cohesiveness observes the team but does not build capability.

questions.explanation: When new people join mid-project, integrating skills development into execution helps them become productive quickly and keeps the whole team effective.
questions.mindset: Build new members' skills as part of the work.

questions.stem: A project manager has been assigned to a new project. The client has mentioned that the project's inception is based on ideas and assumptions put forward by their business partners. What should the project manager do to ensure that they have a clear understanding of the project objectives?

options.text: Conduct in-depth interviews with the client's business partners to uncover their expectations and objectives.
options.rationale: Interviewing only business partners misses the client and other stakeholders.

options.text: Meet with stakeholders, including the client's business partners, to gather input and define project objectives.
options.rationale: Meeting stakeholders, including the business partners, to gather input and define objectives builds a shared, clear understanding.

options.text: Initiate the project and develop a comprehensive project plan based on available information and assumptions.
options.rationale: Planning on unvalidated assumptions risks building the wrong thing.

options.text: Meet with the client to discuss the project's initial ideas and assumptions and seek clarification on their vision.
options.rationale: Meeting only the client misses the partners whose ideas started the project.

questions.explanation: When a project is based on others' ideas and assumptions, clarity comes from involving all contributing stakeholders in defining objectives together.
questions.mindset: Define objectives with everyone whose assumptions shaped the project.

questions.stem: During project execution, the team finds that changes must be made to a component sourced from an outside supplier. The component is being used in the project. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Meet with the component supplier to discuss the product warranty.
options.rationale: Warranty discussions may not apply to a change the project needs.

options.text: Review the contract terms and the Procurement Management Plan.
options.rationale: The contract terms and procurement plan define how changes to supplied components are handled.

options.text: List the potential risks that would result from the change.
options.rationale: Listing risks is useful but does not establish how to proceed with the supplier.

options.text: Process a change request to modify the project management plan.
options.rationale: A change request may follow, but the contract governs how changes with the supplier are made.

questions.explanation: Changes to supplier-provided components are governed by the contract. Reviewing the contract terms and procurement plan first ensures the change is handled within agreed obligations.
questions.mindset: Let the contract guide changes with suppliers.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned to a new multinational project. This will be the project manager's first time working with team members from different countries. What should the project manager do to prepare themselves for the project?

options.text: Attend cultural sensitivity training to understand and respect cultural differences.
options.rationale: Cultural sensitivity training prepares the project manager to understand and respect differences across the team.

options.text: Brush up on language skills if necessary to facilitate effective communication.
options.rationale: Language skills help, but cultural understanding is broader than language.

options.text: Conduct team-building exercises to foster collaboration and trust among team members.
options.rationale: Team-building comes after the project manager understands the cultures involved.

options.text: Develop an awareness of local customs with the understanding that culture is learned.
options.rationale: Awareness of local customs is useful but narrower than structured cultural training.

questions.explanation: Leading multicultural teams starts with the leader's own cultural competence. Training helps them understand differences in communication, hierarchy and working norms.
questions.mindset: Develop your own cultural competence before leading across cultures.

questions.stem: A project's statement of work (SOW) requires that the project be delivered in nine months. The project manager believes that the timeline is not realistic. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Involve the change control board (CCB) in the Perform Integrated Change Control process
options.rationale: The CCB evaluates changes, but the timeline has not yet been assessed.

options.text: Submit a written request to the project sponsor for additional resources and budget
options.rationale: Requesting resources without evidence is premature.

options.text: Meet with subject matter experts (SMEs) and the project sponsor to set expectations
options.rationale: Meeting SMEs and the sponsor gives evidence about realistic duration and sets expectations.

options.text: Negotiate a new timeline with the project sponsor
options.rationale: Negotiating a new timeline needs evidence first.

questions.explanation: When a timeline appears unrealistic, the project manager gathers expert evidence and uses it to set realistic expectations with the sponsor.
questions.mindset: Bring evidence when challenging a timeline.

questions.stem: In which stage of Tuckman's stages of team development do the team members begin to resolve conflicts effectively?

options.text: Forming
options.rationale: In forming, members are polite and uncertain; conflict has not yet surfaced.

options.text: Storming
options.rationale: In storming, conflict arises but is not yet resolved effectively.

options.text: Norming
options.rationale: In norming, the team develops norms and begins to resolve conflicts effectively.

options.text: Performing
options.rationale: In performing, the team works at a high level; conflict resolution is already established.

questions.explanation: Teams move through forming, storming, norming and performing. Norming is when members establish working norms and start resolving conflict constructively.
questions.mindset: Recognise the team's stage to lead it appropriately.

questions.stem: During project execution, key stakeholders request a change to ensure that the final product will satisfy their requirements. Why should the project manager submit a change request?

options.text: To record the requirements needed for the stakeholders' sign-off in order to update the issues log.
options.rationale: The issue log is not where change requests are recorded.

options.text: To ensure that the request is formally documented and incorporated according to the integrated change control process.
options.rationale: A change request ensures the change is documented and processed through integrated change control.

options.text: To provide justification for any impact the change might have on the project's budget or schedule.
options.rationale: Justification is part of analysis, not the purpose of submitting.

options.text: To ensure stakeholder responsibility regarding potential impact of the change on project budget and schedule.
options.rationale: Stakeholder responsibility is not the purpose.

questions.explanation: A change request is how a proposed change enters integrated change control. It documents the change formally so it can be assessed for impact, approved or rejected by the right authority, and then tracked and communicated.
questions.mindset: Document every change formally.

questions.stem: While reviewing the approved project schedule, the project manager realizes that the milestones are unrealistic due to longer-than-expected procurement lead times for certain key project components. The project manager needs to update the schedule baseline to reflect the long lead times. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Modify the work breakdown structure (WBS).
options.rationale: The WBS does not change because lead times are longer.

options.text: Update the assumption log.
options.rationale: The assumption log may need a note, but baseline change needs approval.

options.text: Modify the procurement management plan.
options.rationale: The procurement plan describes how buying is managed; the problem is that the schedule baseline does not reflect known lead times.

options.text: Submit a change request.
options.rationale: Changing the baseline requires a change request.

questions.explanation: Approved baselines can only be changed through integrated change control, even when the change corrects an error such as unrealistic lead times. A change request documents the correction and gets it approved before the baseline is updated.
questions.mindset: Change baselines only through change control.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned to a project that has completed the planning phase. The project sponsor is confident that the project management plan has allowed for sufficient budget and scheduled time. The project manager believes that unforeseen events could affect the ability to complete the project successfully. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Identify and evaluate potential risks and develop a risk action plan.
options.rationale: Identifying and evaluating risks and developing a response plan prepares for unforeseen events.

options.text: Meet with the project sponsor to request additional funding to mitigate potential risks.
options.rationale: Requesting funds is premature before risks are understood.

options.text: Discuss the risk potential with the functional manager and identify resources that could ensure project success.
options.rationale: Lining up extra resources with the functional manager is premature before the risks have been identified and analysed.

options.text: Document potential constraints and limitations in the risk management plan.
options.rationale: Constraints are not documented in the risk management plan.

questions.explanation: Proactive risk management identifies, analyses and plans responses for uncertainties, even when sponsors feel confident.
questions.mindset: Plan for uncertainty even when confidence is high.

questions.stem: A project manager and the project team identified risks, performed a qualitative risk analysis, and prepared a risk response plan. However, delays in the response to risk events are affecting the project schedule. How would assigning risk owners to the risk responses help avoid these delays?

options.text: Risk owners work with the project sponsor to ensure the risk response plan will be effective.
options.rationale: Working with the sponsor is not the risk owner's defining responsibility.

options.text: Risk owners identify likely constraints and assumptions before the risk events occur.
options.rationale: Identifying constraints is not the risk owner's role.

options.text: Risk owners are responsible for implementing the appropriate risk response strategy.
options.rationale: Risk owners implement the planned responses when triggers occur, avoiding delays.

options.text: The risk report assigns management of delays in the project schedule to the appropriate risk owner.
options.rationale: A risk report summarises risk information; it does not assign anyone to act when a risk event occurs.

questions.explanation: Delays in responding to risk events often mean nobody was clearly responsible for acting. Assigning a risk owner to each risk makes one person accountable for watching its triggers and implementing the planned response promptly.
questions.mindset: Give every risk an owner who acts.

questions.stem: A project manager for a cross-functional team realizes that there is a lack of commitment from stakeholders to the project following a review meeting. This could lead to project failure. Which three of the following actions should be avoided to mitigate this risk? (Choose 3).

options.text: Creating a weak communication plan
options.rationale: A weak communication plan leaves stakeholders uninformed and uncommitted.

options.text: Allowing stakeholders to use information radiators
options.rationale: Information radiators support transparency and engagement, so they should not be avoided.

options.text: Not prioritizing stakeholders’ communication needs
options.rationale: Ignoring stakeholders' communication needs erodes commitment.

options.text: Using fishbowl windows and remote pairing
options.rationale: Fishbowl windows and remote pairing support collaboration.

options.text: Not updating the communication plan
options.rationale: An outdated communication plan fails as needs change.

questions.explanation: Stakeholder commitment depends on effective, prioritised and current communication. Weak or outdated plans erode engagement.
questions.mindset: Keep communication plans strong and current.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a complex system improvement project. During the integration phase, an upgrade to one component causes an outage on an existing critical component that is currently in use by all departments to access inventory data. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Consult the operations plan to determine the best way to resolve the issue.
options.rationale: The operations plan may not cover project-caused outages.

options.text: Follow the communications management plan to notify the stakeholders of the issue.
options.rationale: Notifying stakeholders is necessary, but first know the planned strategy.

options.text: Update the issue log with details about a final solution for the issue.
options.rationale: Recording a 'final solution' before the response has been worked out is premature; the issue is still live.

options.text: Review the strategy documented in the risk management plan to manage the issue.
options.rationale: Reviewing the risk management plan identifies the prepared strategy for such an issue.

questions.explanation: When a risk the project anticipated turns into a live issue, the risk management plan and register hold the strategy prepared for it. Reviewing that strategy first lets the project manager respond quickly and consistently rather than improvising.
questions.mindset: Use prepared strategies when risks materialise.

questions.stem: During a status review meeting, it was determined that the product will not meet project scope requirements in a particular scenario. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Perform risk analysis and update project scope.
options.rationale: Updating the scope as part of a risk analysis changes the baseline outside the change process.

options.text: Initiate integrated change control process.
options.rationale: Initiating integrated change control lets the gap be assessed and any scope or product change approved properly.

options.text: Review the baselines to determine the critical path.
options.rationale: Reviewing the critical path does not address the product failing a scope requirement.

options.text: Inform customer and negotiate an extended deadline.
options.rationale: Negotiating a deadline extension presumes the response before the change has been assessed.

questions.explanation: When a product will not meet a scope requirement in some scenario, any correction — changing the product or the requirement — affects the baseline. Integrated change control ensures the options are assessed and the decision is made by the right authority.
questions.mindset: Route scope gaps through change control.

questions.stem: A new project is initiated to develop several new financial products and services for a company with offices in several countries. The project manager has researched the regulations for each of the countries. Based on the research, the project manager is concerned that some new products and services do not offer enough protection for the consumer. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Identify all of the project risks.
options.rationale: Identifying all project risks, including regulatory and consumer-protection risks, is the first step of risk management.

options.text: Quantify the project risks in the risk register.
options.rationale: Quantifying risks needs them to be identified first.

options.text: Develop a risk response strategy.
options.rationale: A response strategy cannot be developed before risks are identified and analysed.

options.text: Perform scheduled risk audits.
options.rationale: Risk audits evaluate risk management effectiveness later in the project.

questions.explanation: Concerns raised by regulatory research are the start of risk management. Risks are identified and documented first, then analysed and responded to.
questions.mindset: Identify before you analyse or respond.

questions.stem: A project manager is managing an agile project where the team is regularly missing user story due dates. What should the project manager do to resolve this situation?

options.text: Work with the sponsor to move out the deliverable hand over date.
options.rationale: Moving the handover date accepts the problem without understanding it.

options.text: Review the time allotted to iterations and sprints, adjusting them as needed.
options.rationale: Adjusting iteration length breaks the cadence and does not address the cause.

options.text: Meet with the project team to identify if further agile methodologies training is necessary.
options.rationale: Meeting the team to identify whether they need more agile training investigates a likely cause of the missed stories.

options.text: Implement a reward program for the project team to encourage completing stories on the due dates.
options.rationale: A reward programme encourages effort, but it does not fix a skills or process gap that keeps stories slipping.

questions.explanation: When a team repeatedly misses story commitments, the project manager investigates the cause with the team. Gaps in agile practice are common and addressed through training.
questions.mindset: Investigate with the team before changing dates or incentives.

questions.stem: A customer wants to add new features to the project deliverable. Before the project manager can begin work on these new features, what should the project manager do first?

options.text: Document the list of additional features in an email to the customer as a notification that the team will start working on the new features.
options.rationale: Notifying the customer that work is starting bypasses approval entirely.

options.text: Draft the change request in the appropriate format to seek approval from the change control board (CCB) and start working on the new features only after approval is given.
options.rationale: Drafting a change request and waiting for CCB approval before starting the work follows change control.

options.text: Notify the project sponsor that the customer wants to add new features and wait for their approval to work on these new features.
options.rationale: Sponsor approval alone may not be the defined authority for changes.

options.text: Consult a subject matter expert (SME) and start working on the new features after there are no further concerns raised.
options.rationale: SME consultation does not authorise a change.

questions.explanation: New features change the project's scope. No work should start on them until a change request has been reviewed and approved by the defined authority.
questions.mindset: Approve changes before you work on them.

questions.stem: A new project manager joins a project overseen by a senior project manager. The sponsor asks the new project manager to develop the quality management plan. Why should the project manager initially consult with the senior project manager?

options.text: To learn the established quality processes and plans and how appropriate standards were selected.
options.rationale: Learning the established quality processes and how standards were chosen gives the new PM a sound basis for the plan.

options.text: To determine what product requirements have already been collected and to gather more as needed.
options.rationale: Product requirements are not captured in the quality management plan.

options.text: To develop cost-benefit analyses and benchmarking samples to be used for risk management.
options.rationale: Cost-benefit analysis and benchmarking for risk management are not the purpose of consulting.

options.text: To draft a change request for revision to the quality metrics and quality checklists.
options.rationale: Drafting a change request presumes changes are needed before understanding what exists.

questions.explanation: Before writing a quality management plan on an established project, a new project manager learns what quality processes and standards are already in place and why.
questions.mindset: Understand existing standards before planning new ones.

questions.stem: After all deliverables have been completed, a project manager needs to formally close a project. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Update the project documents with quality control measurements to prove deliverables have been met.
options.rationale: Updating quality documents is part of closure, not the key step.

options.text: Obtain stakeholder acceptance and initiate project closeout.
options.rationale: Obtaining stakeholder acceptance and initiating closeout formally closes the project.

options.text: Release the project team and estimate any unused funds.
options.rationale: Releasing the team and estimating funds are closure activities after acceptance.

options.text: Incorporate the issue log into the lessons learned register to produce the final report.
options.rationale: Merging the issue log into lessons learned is part of closeout.

questions.explanation: Formal closure starts with acceptance of the deliverables by the appropriate stakeholders, followed by closeout activities.
questions.mindset: Close with formal acceptance.

questions.stem: A project manager is part of a project management strategy focus group that is brainstorming the ways projects will be used to add business value to the organization in the upcoming quarter. Which statement(s) describes broadly how organizations use projects to add business value?

options.text: Projects are used to develop new products, processes, or services.
options.rationale: Developing new products is part of the answer but incomplete.

options.text: Projects are used to modify existing products, processes, or services.
options.rationale: Modifying existing products is part of the answer but incomplete.

options.text: Projects are used to deliver day-to-day activities, processes, or services.
options.rationale: Day-to-day activities are operations, not projects.

options.text: Projects are used to develop and modify products, processes, or services.
options.rationale: Projects add value by developing new and modifying existing products, processes and services.

questions.explanation: Projects create business value through change: developing new or modifying existing products, processes and services. Ongoing operations are not projects.
questions.mindset: Projects create value by changing things.

questions.stem: A local government provides subsidies for healthcare activities. An organization plans to leverage this subsidy for a project to provide health testing services for at-risk populations. After the project has started, the government announces that this testing service might not qualify for the subsidy. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Escalate the project risk to a higher level.
options.rationale: The subsidy uncertainty affects the organisation's strategy beyond the project, so it is escalated to the appropriate level.

options.text: Meet with the project sponsor to redefine project benefits.
options.rationale: Benefits have not changed yet; redefining them is premature.

options.text: Inform the stakeholders of the need to develop a contingency plan.
options.rationale: A contingency plan may be needed later, but first the risk goes to those who can decide.

options.text: Submit a change request to the change control board (CCB).
options.rationale: A change request needs something concrete to change.

questions.explanation: Risks whose impact reaches beyond the project, such as funding or strategic viability, are escalated to the level of management that owns the decision.
questions.mindset: Escalate risks to the level that owns them.

questions.stem: A megaproject had reached 10% completion when there was a sudden change of company ownership. After being put on hold for a few years, the project is now under study to resume. Who is responsible for approving the updated budget, assigning key resources and relaunching the project?

options.text: Project sponsor
options.rationale: The sponsor is appointed by the organisation and may not have authority to relaunch a megaproject.

options.text: Project management office (PMO) director
options.rationale: The PMO director supports governance but does not usually relaunch megaprojects.

options.text: Chief executive officer (CEO)
options.rationale: The CEO may be involved but formal governance sits with the steering committee.

options.text: Steering committee
options.rationale: The steering committee has authority for organisation-level decisions such as budgets, resources and relaunch.

questions.explanation: Governance bodies such as steering committees make decisions about starting, stopping and relaunching projects, approving budgets and assigning key roles.
questions.mindset: Know which governance body holds each decision.

questions.stem: A project manager has been awarded a firm-fixed-price (FFP) contract to develop a new mobile app for a client. The contract scope is well-defined and the client has approved the project plan. However, during the course of the project, the team encountered some unexpected technical challenges. These challenges will require additional time and resources to resolve. Which of the following is the most suitable course of action to take?

options.text: Terminate the contract with the client and return the advance payment immediately.
options.rationale: Terminating the contract and returning the payment is a drastic reaction to technical difficulties that may be solvable.

options.text: Proceed with the project as planned and try to resolve the challenges within the existing budget and schedule.
options.rationale: Absorbing the challenge silently may be unrealistic.

options.text: Notify the client and request a change order to increase the project budget and extend the project schedule.
options.rationale: Informing the client and requesting a change order is transparent and uses the contract's change process.

options.text: Attempt to resolve the technical challenges using existing resources, even if this means sacrificing quality.
options.rationale: Sacrificing quality to stay within resources breaches the agreed requirements and damages the client relationship.

questions.explanation: When unexpected challenges affect a fixed-price contract, the seller communicates early and uses the contract's change process. Transparency protects the relationship.
questions.mindset: Be transparent about challenges and use the change process.

questions.stem: A project management office (PMO) normally runs projects using the waterfall approach. A project currently in development is impacted by local regulations which are being updated regularly. The project team feels that implementing agile techniques would benefit the project due to the constantly changing regulations. What should the project manager do in this scenario?

options.text: Leverage budget reserves to add vendors familiar with the regulations to the project team.
options.rationale: Using reserves to add regulation-savvy vendors does not answer the team's question about changing the delivery approach.

options.text: Conduct an analysis of how incorporating agile methodologies will impact the project.
options.rationale: Analysing how agile techniques would affect the project provides the basis for any change.

options.text: Present this request to the PMO and the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Taking the request to the PMO and sponsor without analysis gives them nothing to base a decision on.

options.text: Implement the request and train the project team on agile methodologies.
options.rationale: Switching approach and training the team before analysing the impact commits the project to an untested change.

questions.explanation: A team's request to adopt a different approach should be analysed for its impact and benefits before it is presented or implemented. The analysis shows where agile techniques would help with changing regulations and what adopting them would cost the project.
questions.mindset: Analyse before changing approach.

questions.stem: An agile team is determining which activities to complete first during an upcoming project iteration for a new product development. Which factor should they use to rank the order of activities that will be delivered?

options.text: Size of the activity
options.rationale: Size tells the team how much fits in the iteration, not which activities matter most.

options.text: Value of the activity to stakeholders
options.rationale: Ranking by value to stakeholders ensures the most important outcomes are delivered first.

options.text: Cost of the activity
options.rationale: Cost is a factor but value leads prioritisation.

options.text: Ease of completion of the activity
options.rationale: Ease of completion optimises effort, not value.

questions.explanation: Agile teams order work by the value it delivers to stakeholders, so each iteration produces the most important outcomes first. Size, cost and ease inform planning but do not set the order.
questions.mindset: Deliver the most valuable work first.

questions.stem: A project manager in a predictive environment has recently completed agile training and is starting to manage projects in an agile fashion. The organization is new to agile and not everyone understands the principles. How should the project manager gain support going forward?

options.text: Hold a session with the stakeholders explaining the business value of prioritization, mindset, accountability, and improved quality.
options.rationale: Explaining the business value of agile practices to stakeholders builds understanding and support.

options.text: Conduct a cost benefit analysis for the new project comparing predictive and agile approaches and present it to the stakeholders.
options.rationale: A cost-benefit comparison is narrow and may not help stakeholders understand how agile works or why it matters.

options.text: Invite the stakeholders to a backlog grooming session so that they understand the scope of work and the development approach.
options.rationale: Backlog grooming does not explain agile's value.

options.text: Send the stakeholders video links explaining agile approaches as well as supporting case studies from the industry.
options.rationale: Sending video links is passive and does not engage stakeholders or answer their specific questions.

questions.explanation: Stakeholders support new approaches when they understand the value. Direct explanation of business benefits builds support.
questions.mindset: Explain the value to win support.

questions.stem: A project team is brainstorming the best project management methodology to recommend to senior management for adoption. The project team's idea is characterized by frequent requirement changes, incremental and iterative changes, customer focus, and defined stages with specific documents produced to meet industry regulatory standards. Which project management methodology is preferred in this case?

options.text: Agile
options.rationale: Agile fits frequent change and customer focus, but on its own it does not provide the defined stages and regulatory documents required.

options.text: Hybrid
options.rationale: A hybrid combines agile's responsiveness and customer focus with predictive stages and documentation for regulatory standards.

options.text: Predictive
options.rationale: A predictive approach provides stages and documentation but struggles with frequent requirement changes.

options.text: Waterfall
options.rationale: Waterfall is a predictive life cycle and has the same weakness with changing requirements.

questions.explanation: When a project needs both adaptability to change and formal stages with regulatory documentation, a hybrid approach tailors the life cycle to combine iterative delivery with the necessary predictive controls.
questions.mindset: Blend approaches when the work demands both adaptability and formal control.

questions.stem: A project manager has been assigned to a new project. During the initial review of the project charter, the project manager reaches out to the project sponsor to discuss important information that is missing in the document. What piece of information is appropriate for the project manager to request?

options.text: Measurable objectives of critical success factors
options.rationale: Measurable objectives and success criteria are high-level charter content the sponsor should provide from the business case.

options.text: Detailed description and requirements of the final deliverable
options.rationale: Detailed deliverable requirements are developed later in planning, not requested from the sponsor for the charter.

options.text: Work breakdown structure (WBS)
options.rationale: The WBS is a planning output created by the project team.

options.text: Performance measurement baseline
options.rationale: The performance measurement baseline comes from planning, not from the sponsor.

questions.explanation: The charter should state measurable objectives and success criteria, which the sponsor derives from the business case. Detailed requirements, WBS and baselines are developed by the project team afterwards.
questions.mindset: Get the success criteria from the sponsor before planning the detail.

questions.stem: A project team has adopted a new project management methodology which entails holding regular review and retrospective meetings every two weeks. In addition, there are daily status meetings and whiteboards are the main tool used to document decisions and action points. Which project management methodology has the team adopted?

options.text: Traditional
options.rationale: Traditional methodologies rarely use daily stand-ups, whiteboards and fortnightly retrospectives.

options.text: Agile
options.rationale: Daily stand-ups, fortnightly reviews and retrospectives, and lightweight visual documentation are hallmarks of agile.

options.text: Waterfall
options.rationale: Waterfall relies on phase documentation rather than daily meetings and whiteboards.

options.text: Iterative
options.rationale: Iterative development shares some features, but the combination of ceremonies described is agile.

questions.explanation: Agile frameworks rely on short cycles with reviews and retrospectives, daily coordination and lightweight, visible artefacts. Recognising these characteristics identifies the approach in use.
questions.mindset: Recognise an approach by its practices.

questions.stem: A project manager is midway through project delivery. The project manager decides to hold a stakeholder engagement meeting with senior management and the clients to examine if the project deliverables are achieving business value. Which of the documents contains critical information to help the project manager with this?

options.text: Work breakdown structure
options.rationale: The WBS decomposes work; it does not state the value the project is expected to deliver.

options.text: Project management plan
options.rationale: The management plan describes how the project is run, not why it was justified.

options.text: Project scope statement
options.rationale: The scope statement describes deliverables, not the business value expected.

options.text: Business case
options.rationale: The business case records the justification and expected business value, the reference for checking whether deliverables are achieving it.

questions.explanation: The business case sets out why the project was undertaken and what value it should deliver. Reviewing it mid-project lets stakeholders test whether deliverables are still on course to produce that value.
questions.mindset: Check value against the business case.

questions.stem: Due to regulatory changes, a government agency is now a key stakeholder in a complex project. An agency representative has asked the project manager to explain how well the advantages derived from the project align with the agency's business strategies. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Meet with the other stakeholders to discuss the project objectives.
options.rationale: Meeting other stakeholders does not answer the agency's question directly.

options.text: Review the assumption log.
options.rationale: The assumption log records assumptions, not benefits alignment.

options.text: Update the stakeholder engagement plan.
options.rationale: Updating the engagement plan is useful but does not answer the question.

options.text: Refer to the benefits management plan.
options.rationale: The benefits management plan describes benefits and how they align with strategy, directly answering the agency.

questions.explanation: The benefits management plan explains what benefits the project will deliver, how they are measured and how they align with strategy. It is the reference for questions about value alignment.
questions.mindset: Answer questions about benefits from the benefits plan.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned to a project with a lot of stakeholders and competing priorities. What will be the main objective to initiate and conduct negotiations?

options.text: To define the scope
options.rationale: Scope definition may follow from agreement but is not the main purpose of negotiation here.

options.text: To resolve conflict
options.rationale: With competing priorities, negotiation's main objective is to resolve conflict between stakeholders.

options.text: To minimise the cost
options.rationale: Lower cost may follow from a negotiated agreement, but it is not the main reason to negotiate among competing stakeholders.

options.text: To reduce the delivery time
options.rationale: Reducing delivery time may be a secondary outcome.

questions.explanation: Where stakeholders have competing priorities, negotiation is the tool for resolving the conflicts so the project can move forward.
questions.mindset: Negotiate to resolve conflict between competing priorities.

questions.stem: A project manager for a cross-functional team is finding it difficult to schedule regular meetings and communicate with all team members and stakeholders due to various time zones. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Use asynchronous communication tools.
options.rationale: Asynchronous tools let team members and stakeholders communicate across time zones without needing to meet at the same time.

options.text: Schedule two meetings that accommodate most.
options.rationale: Two meetings still exclude some people and duplicate effort.

options.text: Rotate the meeting time on a weekly basis.
options.rationale: Rotating times spreads inconvenience but still limits participation.

options.text: Meet with team members in the same time zone.
options.rationale: Meeting only same-zone members fragments the team.

questions.explanation: When time zones make regular synchronous meetings impractical, asynchronous tools keep communication flowing, complemented by occasional live sessions.
questions.mindset: Use asynchronous channels when time zones make meetings hard.

questions.stem: A stakeholder that is not experienced with agile has emailed the project team expressing frustration and displeasure with their work. In the email, the stakeholder is demanding significant changes in both the project scope and deliverables. How should the project manager address this situation?

options.text: At the next team standup, ask the team why the stakeholder is upset.
options.rationale: The stand-up is not the forum for discussing a stakeholder's dissatisfaction.

options.text: Update the scope and project plan to meet the stakeholder’s requests.
options.rationale: Updating scope and plan to meet demands bypasses the product owner and team.

options.text: Communicate with both the stakeholder and the product owner to foster project alignment.
options.rationale: Communicating with both the stakeholder and product owner aligns expectations through the role that owns the backlog.

options.text: Meet individually with the stakeholder to review the project backlog.
options.rationale: Meeting the stakeholder alone about the backlog excludes the product owner.

questions.explanation: Stakeholder demands for change in agile projects are handled with the product owner, who owns scope and priority. The project manager facilitates alignment.
questions.mindset: Align stakeholders through the product owner.

questions.stem: A project manager is on a project with a very involved customer. The customer demands regular updates on the project, including the current project status and planned next steps. What is the best way to communicate with the customer?

options.text: Email the customer weekly updates including the project risk register and notes from daily standups.
options.rationale: Emailing the risk register and stand-up notes overwhelms the customer.

options.text: Document a detailed summary of the project along with a list of stakeholders, and send it to the customer monthly.
options.rationale: Monthly summaries are too infrequent for an involved customer.

options.text: Schedule daily meetings to provide a brief project summary and details on what the project team is currently working on.
options.rationale: Daily meetings are excessive for customer updates and take time from both the customer and the team.

options.text: Schedule weekly meetings with the customer to present incremental project updates and to have the customer validate project progress.
options.rationale: Weekly meetings presenting increments with customer validation meet the customer's needs and secure agreement.

questions.explanation: A highly involved customer needs regular, structured updates and a chance to confirm that progress matches expectations. Weekly presentations of incremental progress with customer validation provide both without overwhelming anyone.
questions.mindset: Give involved customers regular updates they can validate.

questions.stem: A project manager is halfway through a project using a predictive methodology when the organization announces a transition to a hybrid approach. The project sponsor instructs the team to transition to this new hybrid approach immediately, even though the team has no prior experience with hybrid projects. What is the best course of action for the project manager to take?

options.text: Finish project delivery with the predictive methodology.
options.rationale: Finishing predictively ignores the sponsor's instruction.

options.text: Extend the project timeline to accommodate the change.
options.rationale: Extending the timeline is not necessarily needed.

options.text: Reevaluate project scope and prioritize critical tasks.
options.rationale: Reevaluating scope and prioritising critical tasks focuses the team during the transition.

options.text: Request a complete overhaul of the project plan.
options.rationale: Overhauling the entire plan mid-project is disruptive and unnecessary when the team can refocus on what matters most.

questions.explanation: Switching approach halfway through a project, with a team new to hybrid, needs focus. Re-evaluating scope and prioritising the critical work lets the team adapt incrementally while protecting the project's key outcomes.
questions.mindset: Prioritise ruthlessly during a mid-project transition.

questions.stem: During a meeting with stakeholders, the project manager received multiple concerns about the quality of the project’s deliverables. The customer feels so strongly about these concerns that they decide they will not approve any future deliverables. What should the project manager do in this scenario?

options.text: Inform the sponsor that the project has ended explaining the reason for the project termination.
options.rationale: Declaring the project over because the customer is unhappy is premature; the concerns may well be resolvable.

options.text: Leveraging notes from the meeting, work with the project team to improve the deliverables.
options.rationale: Improving deliverables from notes alone may miss what the stakeholders need.

options.text: Meet with the stakeholders to identify how to address the identified issues and how to proceed with the project.
options.rationale: Meeting the stakeholders to agree how to address the issues and proceed restores confidence.

options.text: Document the concerns presented and send them to the change control board (CCB) for guidance on how to proceed.
options.rationale: The CCB is not the forum for resolving stakeholder dissatisfaction.

questions.explanation: When a customer threatens to reject all future deliverables, the project manager engages directly to agree how to resolve the concerns and move forward.
questions.mindset: Engage directly when a customer loses confidence.

questions.stem: The project manager's company won a digital transformation project request for proposal (RFP) with clear scope, time and cost. As part of the RFP clause, the project manager's company also provided the number of resources required to complete the project. This is a very high investment project, and the customer wants to monitor the progress regularly. Since it is a fixed price project, what approach should the project manager use?

options.text: Use a predictive approach and send the daily status report to the customer.
options.rationale: Daily reports are excessive and do not show working progress.

options.text: Use an Agile approach and showcase each successful completion of the story.
options.rationale: Pure agile is less suited to a fixed scope, time and cost.

options.text: Use a hybrid approach and showcase each successful completion of each module.
options.rationale: A hybrid approach plans predictively and shows completed modules incrementally.

options.text: Use a predictive approach and showcase each successful completion of each module.
options.rationale: Predictive with module showcases is close, but hybrid better reflects incremental delivery.

questions.explanation: Fixed-scope contracts benefit from predictive planning, while incremental demonstration of completed modules gives customers visibility.
questions.mindset: Plan predictively, show progress incrementally.

questions.stem: A project manager notices a potential conflict between a remote developer and an on-site tester during a sprint; the developer feels the tester is being overly critical of their code, while the tester is concerned about potential bugs impacting the release schedule. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Categorize the conflict as "interpersonal" and direct the team members to handle it themselves.
options.rationale: Labelling it interpersonal and leaving them to it risks the conflict festering and affecting the release.

options.text: Publicly discuss the conflict during the next daily standup to encourage open communication.
options.rationale: Discussing a conflict between two people in the public stand-up can embarrass them and harden positions.

options.text: Schedule a private one-on-one meeting with each team member to understand their perspective.
options.rationale: Private one-to-one meetings let each person explain their view safely, revealing both technical and interpersonal causes.

options.text: Add the conflict to the shared project backlog and prioritize its resolution alongside other tasks.
options.rationale: A conflict is not a backlog item; putting it there delays and depersonalises something that needs direct attention.

questions.explanation: Conflicts with both technical and interpersonal dimensions need to be understood before they can be resolved. Private conversations with each party create a safe space to uncover the root cause, from which the project manager can guide them to a solution.
questions.mindset: Understand each side privately before resolving a conflict.

questions.stem: A global organization that has always used predictive project management is now moving towards agile project management. In the first agile project of the organization, members from remote teams are failing to attend the daily standup meetings. How can the project manager resolve this issue?

options.text: Replace remote project team members with co-located team members.
options.rationale: Replacing remote members is disruptive and ignores why the organisation uses a global team.

options.text: Assign tasks of lower priority to the remote team members.
options.rationale: Giving remote members low-priority work marginalises them and does not solve attendance.

options.text: Leverage online meeting platforms for the standups and consider the working hours of remote team members when scheduling.
options.rationale: Online platforms and scheduling around remote members' working hours make stand-ups accessible to everyone.

options.text: Use some of the project budget to provide training on agile methods for all remote team members.
options.rationale: Agile training may help, but the attendance problem is practical, not a lack of knowledge.

questions.explanation: When remote members miss agile ceremonies, the cause is often practical: tools and timing. Designing ceremonies for distributed teams — online platforms and times that respect time zones — enables participation.
questions.mindset: Design ceremonies that distributed members can attend.

questions.stem: A project is currently halfway through its timeline when one of the external resources becomes unexpectedly unavailable for the rest of the project. This unavailability puts the project's successful completion within budget and on time at risk. What should the project manager do as the initial step in addressing this?

options.text: Update the resource management plan and record the necessary skills in the issues log.
options.rationale: Updating the resource plan and recording the needed skills in the issue log captures the problem and what a replacement must bring.

options.text: Engage with stakeholders to find a qualified replacement for the external resource.
options.rationale: Looking for a replacement is likely, but the skills needed should first be documented.

options.text: Initiate training for an internal resource on the required skills and assign the remaining tasks.
options.rationale: Training an internal resource presumes the solution before the skills are defined.

options.text: Revise the project's schedule and budget estimates and submit a change request.
options.rationale: Revising schedule and budget and submitting a change request is premature before the impact is assessed.

questions.explanation: When an external resource becomes unavailable, the project manager first documents the issue and the skills required. That clarity guides the choice between internal cover, training or a new external resource.
questions.mindset: Define exactly what you have lost before replacing it.

questions.stem: A project manager is planning a worldwide product launch. Manufacturing the product is subject to rigid time constraints related to the production line and raw material availability. There are also uncertainties around regional labeling regulations that are expected to evolve within the launch period. How can the project manager integrate planning and development for the unknown labeling requirements?

options.text: Use a hybrid approach, integrating predictive labeling work streams into an agile roll-out schedule.
options.rationale: Making labelling predictive inside an agile roll-out reverses the need: labelling is the uncertain part.

options.text: Use a hybrid approach, integrating an agile labeling workflow into a predictive roll-out schedule.
options.rationale: An agile labelling workflow within a predictive roll-out adapts to changing regulations while manufacturing follows its fixed constraints.

options.text: Apply agile planning to both the manufacturing and labeling work streams to align the workflows.
options.rationale: Agile planning for manufacturing ignores the production line's rigid time constraints.

options.text: Apply predictive planning to the labeling work stream and streamline the change control process.
options.rationale: Predictive labelling with faster change control still fights the uncertainty rather than planning for it.

questions.explanation: Hybrid approaches let each part of a project use the life cycle that fits its certainty. Rigid manufacturing constraints suit predictive planning, while evolving labelling regulations suit an adaptive workflow.
questions.mindset: Put adaptive methods where the uncertainty is.

questions.stem: An organization is launching a new product that is critical to the company's success. The stakeholders have identified three key factors for success: market adaptation, rapid response to market offerings, and agility. What should the project manager do to ensure the project's success?

options.text: Work closely with the marketing team to promote the product and adapt to market changes.
options.rationale: Working closely with marketing directly supports the success factors of market adaptation and rapid response.

options.text: Ensure that the project has sufficient budget and resources to address any challenges.
options.rationale: Budget and resources help but do not address adaptation to the market.

options.text: Be actively involved in the project by monitoring progress, making necessary changes, and capturing data.
options.rationale: Monitoring and changing is generic and not linked to the market factors.

options.text: Invite the stakeholders to attend all standups to ensure they are actively involved in the project’s success.
options.rationale: Inviting stakeholders to all stand-ups is inefficient.

questions.explanation: Aligning project work with the stakeholders' stated success factors — here, market adaptation and responsiveness — focuses effort on what will make the launch succeed.
questions.mindset: Work toward the success factors stakeholders have named.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned to a new environmental project. When reviewing a vendor's proposal, the project manager identifies a technical risk that will have an impact on the project manager's company's operational cost. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Consult with their functional manager.
options.rationale: Consulting the functional manager may help later, but the risk should first be recorded.

options.text: Accept the risk and move on.
options.rationale: Accepting the risk without analysis is premature.

options.text: Update the project risk register.
options.rationale: Recording the risk in the register starts formal risk management.

options.text: Assess the risk in a workshop.
options.rationale: A workshop to assess the risk follows recording it.

questions.explanation: Risks identified while reviewing vendor proposals are recorded first so they can be analysed and responded to, including in contract negotiations.
questions.mindset: Record risks as soon as you see them.

questions.stem: A looming fuel price increase was identified as a risk during the planning stages of a large construction project. The identified risk was assigned high probability with low impact; the price increase would not be more than 2%. The project begins and a 20% fuel price increase goes into effect. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Update the risk register.
options.rationale: The event has happened, so it is no longer a risk to update.

options.text: Update the assumption log.
options.rationale: The assumption log is not where current problems are tracked.

options.text: Update the issue log.
options.rationale: A 20% increase has occurred and must be managed as a current issue in the issue log.

options.text: Update the lessons learned register.
options.rationale: Lessons learned may be captured later but are not the immediate update.

questions.explanation: A risk that has actually occurred is no longer a risk but an issue. The fuel increase — ten times the size planned for — is recorded in the issue log so its impact on cost can be actively managed, and the gap between estimate and reality can inform lessons learned later.
questions.mindset: Once it happens, it is an issue.

questions.stem: A complex project is in the planning stage when the sponsor identifies a need for a specialist who is a citizen of a foreign country. The project manager knows that the budget does not allow for this specialist's travel expenses. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Train a resource on the existing team in the special skills.
options.rationale: Training a team member may not give the special skills needed.

options.text: Submit a change request for additional budget.
options.rationale: Asking for more budget is unnecessary if virtual work is possible.

options.text: Find a local replacement.
options.rationale: A local replacement may not have the specialist skills.

options.text: Assign the specialist to a virtual team.
options.rationale: Including the specialist virtually gets their expertise without travel costs.

questions.explanation: Virtual teams widen access to talent. When a specialist abroad is needed but travel is unaffordable, bringing them into the team virtually secures their expertise within budget, supported by the collaboration tools now widely available.
questions.mindset: Use virtual collaboration to access scarce skills.

questions.stem: A manufacturing project is in the implementation phase. During a status meeting, a team member tells the project manager that a solution has been found for a persistent failure on equipment used in the implementation; however, this solution is temporary, and the equipment could fail again in the future. Which document should the project manager update?

options.text: Issue log
options.rationale: The issue log tracks the equipment problem and its temporary resolution.

options.text: Risk management plan
options.rationale: The risk management plan describes how risk is managed, not specific issues.

options.text: Assumption log
options.rationale: The assumption log records conditions taken as true for planning, not the status of an equipment problem.

options.text: Stakeholder register
options.rationale: The stakeholder register records stakeholders.

questions.explanation: The issue log tracks active issues and their resolution status. A temporary fix is recorded there so the issue remains visible.
questions.mindset: Log temporary fixes so issues stay visible.

questions.stem: A project manager is committed to the success of a multinational project with tight deadlines. A new team member is continually late or misses status meetings. In a one-on-one with the project manager, the team member expresses the belief that working on deliverables is more important than attending status meetings. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Reassign the team member to another project with more flexible deadlines.
options.rationale: Reassignment is premature before expectations are clarified.

options.text: Document this behavior in the team member's personnel file.
options.rationale: Documenting in a personnel file is punitive and premature.

options.text: Encourage this team member's attendance, but be flexible if critical work is not affected.
options.rationale: Flexibility contradicts the expectation the PM needs to set.

options.text: Meet with the team to ensure they understand that attendance at status meetings is required.
options.rationale: Meeting with the team to clarify that attendance is required sets clear expectations for all.

questions.explanation: When a team member does not see the value of a team practice, the project manager restates the expectation clearly and openly with the team, so everyone understands what is required and why. Formal consequences come only if the behaviour continues.
questions.mindset: Set expectations clearly and openly.

questions.stem: A construction project is in the execution phase when several new team members from different countries are assigned to the project. Which document should the project manager update first?

options.text: Procurement management plan
options.rationale: New team members do not change how the project buys goods and services, so the procurement plan is not the first update.

options.text: Risk management plan
options.rationale: The risk plan may need updates, but communication is the priority.

options.text: Project charter
options.rationale: The charter authorises the project and is not affected by adding team members.

options.text: Communications management plan
options.rationale: The communications plan must reflect new members' languages and time zones.

questions.explanation: New international team members change communication needs. Updating the communications plan ensures effective communication.
questions.mindset: Update communication plans when the team changes.

questions.stem: A customer has informed the project manager that they do not accept the project deliverables. What should the project manager do to gain approval?

options.text: Review the acceptance criteria with the customer to address deliverable requirements.
options.rationale: Reviewing acceptance criteria with the customer identifies what must be met for approval.

options.text: Review the project charter and stakeholder engagement plan with the customer.
options.rationale: The charter and engagement plan do not contain acceptance criteria.

options.text: Examine the quality management plan with the customer.
options.rationale: The quality plan does not define deliverable acceptance criteria.

options.text: Ascertain the customer's objections and perform a risk analysis.
options.rationale: Risk analysis is not the remedy for acceptance.

questions.explanation: Acceptance is judged against agreed criteria. When a customer refuses deliverables, reviewing those criteria with them identifies exactly which requirements are unmet, turning a rejection into a list of gaps to close.
questions.mindset: Resolve acceptance disputes against the agreed criteria.

questions.stem: After comparing actual results to the performance measurement baseline, the project manager discovers that the project's work and cost performance measures are better than expected. The project manager doubts that these positive variances can continue until the end of the project. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Conduct performance reviews with the team members.
options.rationale: There is no sign of a performance problem with individuals, so reviews with team members are not warranted.

options.text: Update the risk register.
options.rationale: Recording the risk that performance may deteriorate prepares a response.

options.text: Notify the stakeholders.
options.rationale: Notifying stakeholders of a possible future deterioration is premature before the risk has been analysed.

options.text: Review the project management plan.
options.rationale: Reviewing the plan does not address the risk.

questions.explanation: Doubts that good performance will continue are a concern about the future, which makes them a risk. Recording it in the risk register allows it to be analysed and, if needed, a response planned before any deterioration occurs.
questions.mindset: Treat doubts about the future as risks.

questions.stem: As a predictive project enters the execution phase, a functional manager discovers that one of the materials to be used in the product will have a detrimental effect on the environment and urges the project manager to switch to a more environmentally friendly material. What should the project manager's initial response be?

options.text: Develop a proof of concept plan to assess the feasibility and impact of the change and present it to the project sponsor.
options.rationale: A proof of concept assesses feasibility and impact before presenting to the sponsor.

options.text: Immediately authorize the change in materials and initiate the transition to an environmentally friendly material.
options.rationale: Authorising a material change immediately bypasses analysis of feasibility, cost, schedule and quality impacts.

options.text: Inform the functional manager that material changes are not permitted during the execution phase of the project.
options.rationale: Refusing ignores a legitimate environmental concern.

options.text: Instruct the functional manager to submit a formal change request through the established change management process.
options.rationale: A change request needs analysis; the PM can support it with a proof of concept.
