questions.explanation: Environmental concerns raised during execution deserve evaluation. A proof of concept tests feasibility and impact before a decision.
questions.mindset: Test proposed changes before deciding.

questions.stem: A project sponsor assigns a project manager to a new, critical project. This project has tight budget and time constraints. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Meet with functional managers to schedule team resources.
options.rationale: Scheduling resources before knowing what the project is for risks booking the wrong skills.

options.text: Meet with stakeholders to obtain their buy-in and support.
options.rationale: Seeking buy-in before the PM can explain the purpose and requirements gives stakeholders little to support.

options.text: Meet with the project sponsor to understand the project's purpose and high level requirements.
options.rationale: Meeting the sponsor to understand the project's purpose and high-level requirements is the foundation for the charter and everything after.

options.text: Update the requirements management plan to reflect the budget and time constraints.
options.rationale: Updating a requirements plan before understanding the requirements puts the process ahead of the content.

questions.explanation: A newly assigned project manager starts by understanding why the project exists and what it must achieve, typically from the sponsor. With tight constraints, that clarity is even more important, because it guides every trade-off that follows.
questions.mindset: Understand the purpose from the sponsor before anything else.

questions.stem: After receiving the project charter, a project manager starts to prepare the project management plan. Although there is a limited amount of detailed activity information in the project management office (PMO), the project manager needs to calculate the expected duration of the project. What should the project manager use to determine this?

options.text: Analogous estimating
options.rationale: Analogous estimating uses historical data from similar projects, which suits early estimates when detailed information is limited.

options.text: Bottom-up estimating
options.rationale: Bottom-up estimating needs detailed activity information that is not yet available.

options.text: Kick-off meeting feedback
options.rationale: Kick-off feedback is not an estimating technique.

options.text: Input from the project sponsor
options.rationale: Sponsor input may help but is not a structured estimate.

questions.explanation: Early in planning, detail is scarce. Analogous estimating uses parameters from similar past projects to produce a quick, if less precise, estimate that can be refined as detail emerges.
questions.mindset: Use analogy when detail is scarce.

questions.stem: A project is showing a negative schedule variance. The project manager sees that one team is causing the delays. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Meet with the team to identify strategies to resolve the delays.
options.rationale: Meeting the team causing the delays to identify strategies addresses the problem where it arises and uses their knowledge.

options.text: Meet with the project sponsor to determine an approach to getting back on schedule.
options.rationale: Going to the sponsor first skips the team that can best solve the problem.

options.text: Run a risk analysis to determine the impact of the delays on project success.
options.rationale: Risk analysis quantifies impact but does not resolve the delays.

options.text: Meet with human resources to discuss possible actions to get project back on schedule.
options.rationale: Human resources is not the route to schedule recovery.

questions.explanation: When a specific team is behind, the project manager works with that team to understand causes and agree recovery actions. Escalation is reserved for issues the team cannot resolve.
questions.mindset: Solve delays with the team that has them.

questions.stem: A customer identifies performance issues on a newly implemented product. Why should the project manager estimate the cost of quality (COQ) for this project?

options.text: To find the optimal cost to prevent failures in future iterations of this product.
options.rationale: Prevention for future iterations is one use of COQ, but the question concerns this product's life.

options.text: To assess the conformance and non-conformance cost during the life of this product.
options.rationale: COQ assesses conformance costs (prevention, appraisal) and non-conformance costs (failures) over the product's life.

options.text: To assess the quality of the product to minimize future appraisal costs.
options.rationale: Appraisal is only one element of cost of quality; COQ also covers prevention and the cost of failures.

options.text: To minimize rework and scrap associated with failure costs during project execution.
options.rationale: Rework and scrap during execution are only part of non-conformance costs.

questions.explanation: Cost of quality captures both what is spent to achieve quality and what is lost through failures, across the product's life. It helps decide where investment in quality pays off.
questions.mindset: Weigh the cost of good quality against the cost of poor quality.

questions.stem: A project is in development when a functional manager leaves the company and is no longer involved with the project. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Update the change log.
options.rationale: The change log records changes to the project, not stakeholder changes.

options.text: Update the risk register.
options.rationale: The risk register may need updating later, but the register of stakeholders comes first.

options.text: Update the stakeholder register.
options.rationale: The stakeholder register must reflect that the functional manager is no longer involved.

options.text: Update the assumption log.
options.rationale: The assumption log records planning assumptions and is not where a change in stakeholders is recorded.

questions.explanation: When a stakeholder leaves, the stakeholder register is updated first so engagement and communication reflect the current stakeholder community.
questions.mindset: Keep the stakeholder register current.

questions.stem: A project manager in a global organization is responsible for a project involving six different companies. Midway through the project, one stakeholder moves from one company to another. Which document should the project manager update?

options.text: Stakeholder engagement plan
options.rationale: The engagement plan describes strategies, which may not change.

options.text: Project charter
options.rationale: The charter is not affected by a stakeholder moving company.

options.text: Stakeholder register
options.rationale: The stakeholder register records organisation and contact details, which have changed.

options.text: Project management plan
options.rationale: The project management plan describes how the project is run; a stakeholder changing company does not alter it.

questions.explanation: The stakeholder register holds each stakeholder's organisation, role and contact details. When a stakeholder moves to another company, the register is updated so that engagement and communication reach the right person in the right organisation.
questions.mindset: Update records when stakeholder details change.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a development project for an external customer in another country. The project manager's company is required to comply with certain regulations, and the project manager's project has been selected for an audit. The customer does not think the audit is necessary and has asked the project manager not to disturb the project team. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Exclude the project development team from the compliance audit as requested by the customer.
options.rationale: Excluding the team from a mandatory audit breaches compliance obligations.

options.text: Initiate the audit without informing the customer because the company is required to comply.
options.rationale: Proceeding without telling the customer lacks transparency.

options.text: Schedule a steering committee meeting with all stakeholders to discuss and come to a common understanding.
options.rationale: A steering committee meeting is disproportionate.

options.text: Meet with the customer to explain the need to meet the compliance requirements and proceed with the audit.
options.rationale: Explaining the compliance need to the customer and proceeding with the audit is transparent and compliant.

questions.explanation: Compliance obligations cannot be waived for customer convenience. The project manager explains the need and proceeds transparently.
questions.mindset: Explain compliance; do not skip it.

questions.stem: A project manager leading an agile project wants to motivate the project team to improve performance. How should the project manager accomplish this?

options.text: Set up a benefits system to keep the team driven and involved in the project
options.rationale: A benefits and rewards system keeps the team engaged throughout the project.

options.text: Work with the sponsor to finance a celebration once the project has been completed.
options.rationale: A celebration only at the end does not motivate during the work.

options.text: Work with the human resources department to provide financial bonuses for all team members.
options.rationale: Financial bonuses for all may not motivate performance.

options.text: Monitor the team's daily accomplishments and recognize them after the successful Go-Live of the project.
options.rationale: Recognising achievements only after go-live is too late to motivate the team during the work.

questions.explanation: Motivation is sustained by recognition and reward during the work, not only at the end. A system of benefits and recognition that operates throughout the project keeps an agile team engaged and driving to improve.
questions.mindset: Recognise progress throughout, not only at the end.

questions.stem: A project manager is having difficulty managing stakeholders because the stakeholder register does not distinguish how aware of the project they need to be in order for the project to be successful. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Meet with the change control board (CCB) to assess the impact of identifying new stakeholders.
options.rationale: The change control board decides on changes to baselines; it does not assess stakeholders' required awareness.

options.text: Update the stakeholder communication plan.
options.rationale: The communication plan depends on knowing desired engagement levels.

options.text: Determine each stakeholder's risk threshold.
options.rationale: Knowing stakeholders' risk thresholds does not show how engaged each needs to be for the project to succeed.

options.text: Develop a stakeholder engagement assessment matrix.
options.rationale: The engagement assessment matrix compares current and desired engagement levels.

questions.explanation: The stakeholder engagement assessment matrix compares each stakeholder's current engagement — unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive, leading — with the level the project needs. The gaps show where engagement effort is required.
questions.mindset: Map current and desired engagement.

questions.stem: During iteration planning, a project manager discusses user stories with the team. While prioritizing the user stories, some with a higher value are also identified as having greater risks. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Suggest that the stories with higher risk are included in the earlier sprints instead of the later ones.
options.rationale: Scheduling high-risk, high-value stories early exposes problems while there is time to respond.

options.text: Suggest that the stories with lower risk are included in the earlier sprints to increase team motivation.
options.rationale: Putting low-risk stories first to lift motivation pushes the risky, valuable work later, when problems are costlier to fix.

options.text: Work with the product stakeholders to schedule which user stories should be worked on in which sprints.
options.rationale: Stakeholders do not schedule stories into sprints.

options.text: Conduct a Monte Carlo analysis to identify which user stories should be completed first.
options.rationale: Monte Carlo analysis is not needed for story ordering.

questions.explanation: Agile teams reduce risk by tackling high-value, high-risk stories early. If problems emerge, there is still time to adapt, and early feedback on the most important work shapes the rest of the project.
questions.mindset: Tackle risk early.

questions.stem: A project team is regularly missing milestones. Stakeholders are concerned that the project will miss the deliverable due date. The project manager has been aware of team conflict and learns that a team member is missing some skills needed for project completion. What should the project manager do in this scenario?

options.text: Reassign the team member who is missing the skills to another task.
options.rationale: Moving the team member elsewhere avoids both the skills gap and the team conflict rather than addressing them.

options.text: Meet with the team to discuss the issues and develop a plan to address them.
options.rationale: Discussing issues with the team leads to a plan addressing both conflict and skills.

options.text: Tell the stakeholders that the project will miss the deadline and nothing can be done.
options.rationale: Telling stakeholders nothing can be done gives up before the causes have even been tackled.

options.text: Fire the team member who is missing the skills and hire someone else.
options.rationale: Firing someone for a skills gap is drastic, slow to replace and damages trust across the team.

questions.explanation: When conflict and a skills gap are behind missed milestones, the project manager brings the team together to discuss the issues openly and agree a plan — for example conflict resolution and targeted training — that addresses both root causes.
questions.mindset: Address team problems with the team.

questions.stem: A project manager is attempting to engage project stakeholders in a new project and has invited them to daily standup meetings. However, none of the stakeholders have attended any of the project meetings. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Reach out to stakeholders individually to understand their reasons for non-attendance.
options.rationale: Reaching out individually uncovers why stakeholders are not attending.

options.text: Continue with the daily standup meetings as scheduled and wait for stakeholders to join.
options.rationale: Carrying on and waiting for stakeholders to turn up is passive and leaves them disengaged.

options.text: Cancel the daily standup meetings and explore alternative communication methods.
options.rationale: Cancelling meetings without understanding is premature.

options.text: Escalate the issue to higher management and request their intervention.
options.rationale: Escalating to higher management before asking stakeholders why they are not attending is premature.

questions.explanation: When stakeholders ignore invitations, the project manager finds out why before changing the approach. Individual conversations reveal whether the format, timing or perceived value is the problem, so engagement can be tailored.
questions.mindset: Ask why before changing approach.

questions.stem: A project manager identifies new risks that might affect the completion of critical tasks. The project manager needs to present these new risks to project stakeholders in the monthly status report. In addition to the risk report, which document should the project manager reference when preparing the status report?

options.text: Risk register
options.rationale: The risk register holds details of identified risks and responses for reporting.

options.text: Assumption log
options.rationale: The assumption log concerns assumptions, not risks.

options.text: Risk management plan
options.rationale: The risk management plan describes how risk is managed, not the details of specific identified risks.

options.text: Probability and impact matrix
options.rationale: The probability and impact matrix is a scoring tool, not a record of the risks and their responses.

questions.explanation: The risk register holds each identified risk, its analysis and planned response. Status reports on new risks draw on the register, alongside the risk report that summarises overall exposure.
questions.mindset: Report risks from the register.

questions.stem: A multinational company with a cross-border project wants to implement new software that will impact several departments. The project manager needs to guarantee alignment of stakeholder expectations with the final product. What should the project team develop?

options.text: Project statement of work (SOW)
options.rationale: The statement of work describes what is to be delivered but does not set out how stakeholder expectations will be managed.

options.text: Stakeholder engagement plan
options.rationale: The stakeholder engagement plan defines how stakeholders will be engaged to align their expectations with the final product.

options.text: Stakeholders engagement assessment matrix
options.rationale: The engagement assessment matrix shows current and desired engagement but is not the plan for achieving alignment.

options.text: Risk breakdown structure (RBS)
options.rationale: A risk breakdown structure categorises risks and does not manage stakeholder expectations.

questions.explanation: Aligning expectations across many departments and countries needs a deliberate strategy. The stakeholder engagement plan sets out how each stakeholder group will be involved and informed so that expectations and the final product converge.
questions.mindset: Plan engagement deliberately when expectations must converge across groups.

questions.stem: A project manager recognizes that certain components must be imported to meet the project's requirements. However, due to the potential impact of an unfavorable exchange rate, the project manager decides that incurring a loss is not justifiable and chooses not to take any action to mitigate it. Which risk response strategy did the project manager employ?

options.text: Transfer
options.rationale: Transfer shifts the risk to another party, for example through hedging or insurance, which did not happen.

options.text: Avoid
options.rationale: Avoid removes the risk by changing the plan, such as sourcing locally, which was not done.

options.text: Minimize
options.rationale: 'Minimise' is not a standard response; reducing the risk would be mitigation, and no action was taken.

options.text: Accept
options.rationale: Choosing to take no action and bear the potential loss is acceptance.

questions.explanation: Acceptance means acknowledging a risk without acting on it, either passively or with a contingency reserve. It is appropriate when the cost of responding outweighs the likely impact.
questions.mindset: Accepting a risk is a decision, not an oversight.

questions.stem: A project is nearing completion when the project manager learns that a change in market regulations may impact the project. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Check the stakeholder register.
options.rationale: The stakeholder register does not guide the response to regulatory risk.

options.text: Update the cost baseline.
options.rationale: Updating the cost baseline is premature before the impact is known.

options.text: Review the risk management plan.
options.rationale: The risk management plan sets out how to identify, analyse and respond to emerging risks such as regulatory change.

options.text: Perform a cost-benefit analysis.
options.rationale: A cost-benefit analysis may follow once the risk is assessed.

questions.explanation: Emerging external risks are handled according to the risk management plan, which defines how they are identified, analysed and responded to.
questions.mindset: Use the risk process for emerging external risks.

questions.stem: As a result of a drastic cut to the budget, a project's steering committee is replaced with a single sponsor. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Draft a new project update and share it with the project sponsor
options.rationale: An update to the sponsor may be needed, but the communication approach must first be adjusted.

options.text: Modify the communications management plan to reflect the change in stakeholder community
options.rationale: The change from a committee to a single sponsor changes who receives what information, so the communications plan must be updated.

options.text: Submit a change request to the change control board (CCB) to record the change in stakeholder structure
options.rationale: A change request is not needed to record stakeholder changes.

options.text: Schedule a meeting with the sponsor to discuss the change to the budget
options.rationale: Discussing the budget with the sponsor is useful but does not address communications.

questions.explanation: When governance changes, communication must change too. Updating the communications management plan tailors reports and channels to the new decision-maker.
questions.mindset: Adapt communication when governance changes.

questions.stem: During a standup, a project team member suggests modifying some features to benefit from a new opportunity. Another team member expresses concern regarding the user experience resulting from the proposed feature. How should the project manager address this situation?

options.text: Meet with the product owner to discuss both the opportunity and concern about the proposed modification.
options.rationale: The product owner is responsible for the product and should weigh the opportunity against the user-experience concern.

options.text: Have the project team vote whether or not to include the modification.
options.rationale: A team vote bypasses the product owner's accountability.

options.text: Note the opportunity in the project backlog and table the discussion. Ask the project team to consider the modification and decide on how to proceed at the next scheduled meeting.
options.rationale: Tabling the discussion delays a decision the product owner can make.

options.text: Meet with stakeholders and the project team to discuss how to proceed regarding the proposed modifications.
options.rationale: Involving all stakeholders is heavier than needed.

questions.explanation: When a proposed feature change brings both an opportunity and a user-experience concern, the trade-off is a product decision. The product owner, who is accountable for the product's value, weighs both sides; votes or broad meetings dilute that accountability.
questions.mindset: Take product trade-offs to the product owner.

questions.stem: An organization has implemented agile for its recent projects, but all of the recent agile projects have missed their delivery milestones. The sponsors for the agile projects are regularly adding new requests to the projects. A project manager is given a new agile project and finds that it has a vague project objective and no clear definition of done (DoD). What should the project manager do?

options.text: Set up a meeting with the project stakeholders to ensure the communication management plan is clearly defined.
options.rationale: A communication plan does not resolve a vague objective.

options.text: Ensure the sponsor allows the project team to include the most technical resources to better ensure project success.
options.rationale: More technical resources do not fix unclear goals.

options.text: Work closely with the project team to develop and clearly define the project vision.
options.rationale: Developing a clear vision with the team gives direction, and supports defining done.

options.text: Work with the project stakeholders to ensure that the project charter and deliverables are clearly defined.
options.rationale: Charter and deliverables help, but the team needs a shared vision in agile.

questions.explanation: Agile projects with vague objectives drift. A clear, shared vision gives direction and a basis for defining done and managing change.
questions.mindset: Start with a shared vision.

questions.stem: A project manager is struggling to keep a technical system implementation on track after the loss of a key team member two months ago. The project has missed multiple milestones and is now in critical status. What should the project manager have done to prevent this situation?

options.text: Replaced the key member with a more experienced one.
options.rationale: Replacing the member is reactive and may not be possible.

options.text: Reassigned the key member's tasks to other team members.
options.rationale: Reassigning tasks after the fact may overload the team.

options.text: Motivated the team to meet all milestones and deadlines.
options.rationale: Motivating the team does not replace the capability lost with a key member, so milestones would still slip.

options.text: Identified the risks early and developed a mitigation plan.
options.rationale: Identifying key-person risk early with a mitigation plan would have prevented the crisis.

questions.explanation: Loss of key team members is a foreseeable risk. Identifying it early and planning mitigation — cross-training, documentation, backup — reduces impact.
questions.mindset: Plan for key-person risk before it happens.

questions.stem: An agile project that the current project manager has been managing for three years is replacing one of the stakeholders with one more familiar with the project’s technology. Additionally, the current project manager is being moved to a more urgent project and is instructed to hand off project management duties to a new project manager. The project is scheduled to run for another three years. What step should the current project manager take next?

options.text: Recommend that the new stakeholder meet with the product owner to ensure expectations are in alignment.
options.rationale: Sending the new stakeholder to the product owner helps, but the outgoing PM should first capture their expectations for the handover.

options.text: Clarify the new stakeholder's expectations for the project and update the engagement plan.
options.rationale: Clarifying the new stakeholder's expectations and updating the engagement plan gives the incoming PM a solid basis.

options.text: Meet with the new stakeholder to learn their expectations for this project and update the other stakeholders on these proposed revisions.
options.rationale: Updating other stakeholders on proposed revisions is premature.

options.text: Ensure that the new stakeholder can attend all future sprint meetings and update the project plan with the stakeholder’s proposed revisions.
options.rationale: Committing the new stakeholder to every sprint meeting and revising the plan around them is premature before their expectations are understood.

questions.explanation: During handover, the outgoing project manager captures the expectations of new stakeholders and updates the engagement plan, so the successor inherits an accurate picture.
questions.mindset: Hand over an up-to-date stakeholder picture.

questions.stem: Two agile teams are collaborating on a project. Team A's output is not complete enough for Team B to integrate into their backlog. According to servant leadership and agile principles, how will the project manager resolve this situation?

options.text: The project manager helps Team A solve the issue, and Team A decides how to implement the solution.
options.rationale: The PM helps Team A solve the issue while Team A decides how, respecting its autonomy.

options.text: Team B submits a change request to Team A, and Team A validates the change.
options.rationale: A change request between teams is bureaucratic.

options.text: Team B decides how Team A implements the change, project manager supervises.
options.rationale: Team B deciding Team A's implementation undermines Team A's ownership.

options.text: The project manager decides how Team A implements the change, and defines acceptance criteria.
options.rationale: The PM deciding the implementation is directive.

questions.explanation: Servant leaders help teams remove blockers, including those between teams, while respecting each team's ownership of how it works. The project manager supports Team A in solving the problem, and Team A decides how to implement the solution.
questions.mindset: Help teams solve problems; let them own the solution.

questions.stem: A project manager typically conducts retrospective sessions at the end of a project. However, the sponsor believes that retrospectives are a waste of time and budget, and instructs the project manager to significantly reduce or eliminate retrospectives in future projects. What potential outcome could arise from the sponsor's directive?

options.text: The focus shifts towards discussing issues instead of identifying ways to improve for future projects.
options.rationale: Without retrospectives, discussion tends to dwell on issues rather than on identifying improvements for future projects.

options.text: The opportunity to improve team processes based on specific project observations is missed.
options.rationale: Missing the chance to improve team processes is also a consequence, and many would choose it.

options.text: The emphasis is placed on stakeholder observations about project performance.
options.rationale: Stakeholder observations are not the focus of retrospectives.

options.text: The time management plan is not properly updated.
options.rationale: Retrospectives do not feed a 'time management plan', so this is not a likely consequence of dropping them.

questions.explanation: Retrospectives turn experience into improvement. Removing them tends to leave problems discussed but not converted into better ways of working, and the organisation loses a structured source of learning for future projects.
questions.mindset: Protect the time teams use to improve.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a development project for a high-profile client with strict deadlines. During a sprint, the project manager notices that the team is struggling to complete user stories as planned due to unforeseen technical complexities. What is the most appropriate action to take?

options.text: Request additional resources to accelerate development and mitigate the impact of delayed user stories and technical complexities.
options.rationale: Adding resources mid-sprint rarely speeds things up and does not address why the work is harder than expected.

options.text: Meet with the team to analyze the root causes of the complexities and ask the product owner to adjust the sprint backlog.
options.rationale: Analysing the root causes with the team and having the product owner adjust the sprint backlog keeps the sprint focused on value while dealing with reality.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to extend the sprint duration to accommodate the delays caused by unforeseen technical complexities.
options.rationale: Extending the sprint breaks the timebox and simply delays the same problem.

options.text: Arrange a meeting with the client and request an extension of the project's timeline to compensate for the delayed user stories.
options.rationale: Asking the client for a timeline extension before understanding the causes or reprioritising is premature.

questions.explanation: When unexpected technical complexity threatens a sprint, the team investigates the cause and the product owner adjusts scope so the most valuable work is delivered. Timeboxes stay fixed; scope flexes.
questions.mindset: Understand the complexity, then let the product owner adjust scope.

questions.stem: A project manager secures project approval with a constrained budget due to fiscal limitations. The sponsor emphasizes no additional funds are available during the current fiscal year. The product owner is concerned that the tight budget will impact the project. What should the project manager prioritize?

options.text: Monitoring the budget throughout the project and demonstrating the value of the project to the company.
options.rationale: Monitoring the budget closely and demonstrating the project's value works within the constraint and sustains support.

options.text: Meeting with the sponsor to express the need for a potential budget increase or the project will be delayed.
options.rationale: Asking for more money after the sponsor has said none is available ignores the constraint.

options.text: Removing secondary deliverables from the project plan and monitoring the budget after each iteration.
options.rationale: Removing deliverables up front reduces value before it is clear that it is needed.

options.text: Requesting the sponsor to allocate funds from the next fiscal year to supplement the current budget.
options.rationale: Borrowing from next year's funds contradicts the sponsor's instruction.

questions.explanation: When budget is fixed and firmly limited, the project manager's job is to manage within it: track spending carefully and show the value being delivered, so decisions about scope can be made on evidence if pressure arises.
questions.mindset: Work within a fixed budget and keep showing value.

questions.stem: A project manager receives an email from a customer detailing reservations about the project deliverables. How should the project manager address the customer’s reservations?

options.text: Meet with the customer to discuss the project scope.
options.rationale: Discussing scope in general may not resolve specific concerns about deliverables.

options.text: Note the reservations in the risk register and prepare a mitigation plan.
options.rationale: Logging and mitigating treats a customer's concern as a risk rather than engaging with it.

options.text: Schedule additional time during the deliverable hand over to discuss the customer’s reservations.
options.rationale: Waiting until hand-over to discuss reservations risks rejection at the last moment.

options.text: Set up a meeting with the product owner and the customer to discuss the criteria for an acceptable deliverable.
options.rationale: Bringing the product owner and customer together to agree acceptance criteria aligns expectations before delivery.

questions.explanation: Customer reservations about deliverables are best resolved by making acceptance criteria explicit. The product owner works with the customer to describe what an acceptable deliverable looks like.
questions.mindset: Resolve reservations by agreeing acceptance criteria.

questions.stem: A key stakeholder requests a change that will solve a critical issue that might affect continuity of operations. However, the project is nearing completion and the change would increase the overall project cost and delay the completion date. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Assign the decision regarding the critical nature of the change to a more knowledgeable stakeholder.
options.rationale: Handing the decision to another stakeholder bypasses the defined change process.

options.text: Submit a change request to the change control board (CCB).
options.rationale: Submitting a change request lets the CCB weigh the operational benefit against cost and schedule impact.

options.text: Revise the work breakdown structure (WBS) and the project scope statement to include the change.
options.rationale: Revising the WBS and scope before approval bypasses change control.

options.text: Communicate the impact on the budget and schedule to the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Informing the sponsor is part of the process, but the change still needs formal evaluation.

questions.explanation: Even compelling changes late in a project go through the defined change process, so their benefits and impacts are evaluated and decided by the right authority.
questions.mindset: Evaluate even urgent changes through the change process.

questions.stem: An expert resource avoids assignments that include working with a foreign contractor. How should the project manager resolve the situation?

options.text: Question the expert privately about their reluctance or biases and insist on an inclusive attitude.
options.rationale: A private conversation explores the reasons for the reluctance and sets clear expectations of inclusive behaviour.

options.text: Issue a disciplinary warning to the expert and advise their functional manager to send them to diversity training.
options.rationale: Disciplinary warnings before understanding the cause are premature and may be unfair.

options.text: Prevent delays and conflicts by hiring a consultant that the expert is willing to work with.
options.rationale: Hiring around the expert's preferences accommodates possible bias.

options.text: Reprimand the expert about their discriminatory behavior during a team meeting to set the right example.
options.rationale: Public reprimand humiliates and hardens positions.

questions.explanation: Suspected bias is addressed privately and directly: understand the reasons, then set clear expectations of respectful, inclusive behaviour. Formal measures follow only if needed.
questions.mindset: Address suspected bias privately, clearly and firmly.

questions.stem: The supplier of a tool for a manufacturing project informs the project manager that delivery of the tool will be late. The project manager orders the tool from another supplier. After the tool from the second supplier arrives, the original supplier delivers the tool and submits an invoice according to the procurement agreement. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Return the tool to the original supplier and refuse to pay the invoice because delivery was late.
options.rationale: Refusing payment unilaterally may breach the contract.

options.text: Keep the extra tool as a spare, pay the invoice from the contingency reserve, and update the lessons learned log.
options.rationale: Paying without checking the contract ignores late-delivery terms.

options.text: Consult the original supplier's procurement agreement to apply late delivery terms, and inform legal counsel of the issue.
options.rationale: Consulting the agreement's late delivery terms and informing legal counsel ensures a response grounded in the contract.

options.text: Compare the quality of both tools, select the tool that gives the best value, and return the other tool.
options.rationale: Comparing tools and returning one ignores contractual obligations.

questions.explanation: Disputes over supplier performance are resolved according to the contract. Checking late-delivery clauses and involving legal or procurement experts protects the organisation.
questions.mindset: Let the contract decide supplier disputes.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a complex infrastructure project that is vital for the company's growth. During the project's initial stages, the project manager identifies a highly influential stakeholder who is resistant to the project. This stakeholder's support is crucial for the project's success, but they have expressed concerns and reservations. How should the project manager handle this situation?

options.text: Develop a stakeholder engagement plan that includes strategies to address the concerns of the resistant stakeholder.
options.rationale: A tailored engagement plan addresses the resistant stakeholder's concerns and builds their support.

options.text: Exclude the resistant stakeholder from the project to prevent potential disruptions and maintain project focus.
options.rationale: Excluding an influential stakeholder increases resistance.

options.text: Assign the task of managing the resistant stakeholder to a team member and focus on engaging other stakeholders.
options.rationale: Delegating a crucial stakeholder to a team member reduces the attention they need.

options.text: Seek senior management's intervention to convince the resistant stakeholder of the project's importance.
options.rationale: Senior management intervention may feel coercive.

questions.explanation: Influential but resistant stakeholders need engagement strategies designed around their concerns, building trust and support.
questions.mindset: Engage resistant stakeholders deliberately.

questions.stem: A project manager must get approval for a complex project management plan from multiple stakeholders in various countries before the project can be kicked off. The time to gain approval is limited. What should the project manager first do?

options.text: Schedule a meeting with the stakeholders and walk them through the project plan to gain their approval.
options.rationale: Walking through the plan without prior review makes the meeting long.

options.text: Distribute the plan to the stakeholders for their review days before scheduling a meeting to obtain approvals.
options.rationale: Distributing the plan in advance lets stakeholders review before the approval meeting.

options.text: Tell the project sponsor that the stakeholder approvals will require more time and adjust the schedule.
options.rationale: Asking the sponsor for more time ignores the stated constraint when a better-prepared approval meeting could meet it.

options.text: Obtain partial stakeholder approvals and track incomplete approvals as a risk to be managed later.
options.rationale: Partial approvals leave the plan unauthorised.

questions.explanation: When approval must come quickly from many stakeholders in different countries, sending the plan in advance lets them review it in their own time. The approval meeting can then focus on questions and decisions rather than a first read-through.
questions.mindset: Send material ahead so meetings can decide.

questions.stem: A project manager notices schedule performance issues due to the expertise levels of project resources. Some experienced resources check unnecessary details, and some junior-level resources take a long time to complete tasks. What should the project manager do to help the team enhance their performance?

options.text: Identify each individual's knowledge gaps and address those gaps through training.
options.rationale: Identifying individual knowledge gaps and training addresses both over-checking and slow work.

options.text: Note this in the risk register and address this with the team during a retrospective session.
options.rationale: Logging the issue and waiting for a retrospective delays action on a performance problem already affecting the schedule.

options.text: Inform the sponsor that the deliverable will not be available on time due to insufficient expertise.
options.rationale: Declaring the deliverable late ignores fixable causes.

options.text: Meet with human resources to have them address the individuals that are missing skills.
options.rationale: Human resources is not the right channel for developing the specific skills project work requires.

questions.explanation: When schedule problems come from uneven expertise — experienced people over-checking, junior people working slowly — the fix is individual. Identifying each person's knowledge gaps and addressing them through training raises the team's overall performance.
questions.mindset: Target development to individual gaps.

questions.stem: Upon completion of a long-term contract, the project manager confirms with the release manager that all planned features are functioning properly as verified by the quality assurance team. The project manager informs the same to the customer and project stakeholders and obtains the approval to close the project. The project is now closed. For ensuring that the knowledge gained during this project remains available for future reference, what should the project manager do next?

options.text: Update the lessons learned knowledge base.
options.rationale: Updating the lessons learned knowledge base preserves knowledge for future projects.

options.text: Update the risk register before informing project team members.
options.rationale: The risk register is not the knowledge repository.

options.text: Update and archive the final procurement file.
options.rationale: Archiving procurement files is part of closure but not knowledge sharing.

options.text: Close out the seller performance evaluation documentation.
options.rationale: Seller performance evaluation is part of procurement closure; it does not make the project's knowledge available to future teams.

questions.explanation: At closure, the knowledge the project gained is transferred to the organisation's lessons learned repository, where future projects can find and reuse it. Procurement records and the risk register serve other purposes.
questions.mindset: Transfer lessons to the knowledge base at closure.

questions.stem: A project team lead meets with the project manager before a scheduled kick-off meeting. The team lead is worried that expectations regarding project deliverables might not be realistic. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Review the project business case and the results of the feasibility study.
options.rationale: Reviewing the business case and feasibility study tests whether expectations for deliverables are realistic.

options.text: Facilitate a meeting between the project sponsor and the team lead to discuss the concerns.
options.rationale: A sponsor meeting may be needed after reviewing the evidence.

options.text: Meet with the stakeholders to discuss the concerns and record their conclusions in the stakeholder engagement plan.
options.rationale: Recording conclusions in the engagement plan skips analysis.

options.text: Identify the risks and agreed-upon risk responses and modify the risk register accordingly.
options.rationale: Risk identification is useful but does not test feasibility.

questions.explanation: Doubts about whether expectations are realistic are checked against the business case and feasibility study before kick-off.
questions.mindset: Check expectations against the feasibility evidence.

questions.stem: A functional manager questions whether certain aspects of a project are in compliance with the project's goals. Which document should the project manager review to address the functional manager's concern?

options.text: Statement of work (SOW)
options.rationale: The SOW describes deliverables, not the project's overall goals.

options.text: Project charter
options.rationale: The charter defines the project's objectives, which is the reference for alignment questions.

options.text: Project management plan
options.rationale: The management plan describes how the project is run.

options.text: Project management information system (PMIS)
options.rationale: The PMIS is the set of tools used to manage information; it does not define the project's goals.

questions.explanation: The charter, issued by the sponsor, records the project's objectives and constraints and authorises the work. It is the reference point when anyone asks whether parts of the project are consistent with its goals.
questions.mindset: Check alignment against the charter.

questions.stem: During a periodic review with stakeholders, the project sponsor asks how the project will measure satisfactory completion of the deliverables and how those measurements are applied. Where can the project manager find this information?

options.text: Scope management plan.
options.rationale: The scope management plan describes how scope is defined and controlled.

options.text: Requirements management plan.
options.rationale: The requirements management plan describes how requirements are analysed, documented, measured and managed.

options.text: Quality management plan.
options.rationale: The quality management plan covers quality standards, which some would see as the answer.

options.text: Work performance reports.
options.rationale: Work performance reports describe current status; they do not define how satisfactory completion is measured.

questions.explanation: The requirements management plan explains how requirements will be analysed, documented and verified, including how satisfaction is measured.
questions.mindset: Know where measurement of requirements is defined.

questions.stem: A project team implements a change that was approved by the change control board (CCB). The change was intended to minimize a risk but it had the opposite effect. What should the project manager have done to avoid this outcome?

options.text: Confirmed the effectiveness of the risk response and monitored progress.
options.rationale: Confirming the effectiveness of responses and monitoring progress catches responses that backfire.

options.text: Updated the assumption log with details concerning the risk.
options.rationale: The assumption log does not track response effectiveness.

options.text: Performed a risk analysis to quantify project risk exposure.
options.rationale: Quantitative analysis measures exposure, not response effectiveness.

options.text: Developed a probability and impact matrix to determine the risk's priority level.
options.rationale: A probability-impact matrix prioritises risks, not responses.

questions.explanation: Implemented risk responses can fail or even make things worse. Monitoring risks includes confirming that each response is having the intended effect, so that a response that backfires is caught early and corrected.
questions.mindset: Check that risk responses actually work.

questions.stem: A stakeholder learns that the equipment purchased for a project is of higher quality than originally agreed upon. The stakeholder is concerned that this deviation has negatively impacted the budget. The stakeholder contacts the project manager and demands clarification. What action should the project manager have taken to avoid the situation?

options.text: Updated the communications management plan.
options.rationale: Updating the communications plan would not have authorised or explained a change to what was purchased.

options.text: Shared results of risk analysis for the equipment.
options.rationale: Sharing a risk analysis does not replace approval of a change to the agreed specification.

options.text: Performed integrated change control procedures.
options.rationale: Integrated change control would have assessed and approved the higher-quality equipment before purchase, with its budget impact visible.

options.text: Conducted regular equipment quality assessments.
options.rationale: Regular quality assessments check equipment but do not authorise a change from what was agreed.

questions.explanation: Any departure from agreed scope, quality or cost — even an apparent improvement — should go through integrated change control. That makes the impact visible and gives stakeholders the chance to approve it before it happens.
questions.mindset: Even improvements are changes that need approval.

questions.stem: A project manager is concerned that team members spend too much time assisting operations and maintenance staff with a recently completed and delivered project component. The project manager has referred to the organizational process assets document to validate that the component was signed off and ownership was transferred. To which additional documents should the project manager refer?

options.text: Procurement statement of work (SOW) and work performance report
options.rationale: The procurement SOW and work performance reports belong to earlier stages and do not confirm the handover terms.

options.text: Requirements management plan and change management plan
options.rationale: The requirements and change management plans describe processes, not the completed transition.

options.text: Procurement management plan and project charter
options.rationale: The procurement plan and charter are early documents that do not record final handover.

options.text: Final report and project document updates
options.rationale: The final report and updated project documents confirm what was delivered and handed over, clarifying the team's ongoing obligations.

questions.explanation: At closure, the final report and updated project documents record completion and transition. They help confirm that ownership has passed to operations, so the project team can stop providing unplanned support.
questions.mindset: Use closure records to confirm the handover is complete.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a project to deliver a new product to the market. The project sponsor has asked for a broadened scope and to deliver a "scaled-up version" of the final product. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Request a formal confirmation of the change.
options.rationale: A formal confirmation records the request but does not evaluate its impact.

options.text: Get stakeholder approval to revise the budget.
options.rationale: Seeking budget approval assumes the change is accepted and focuses only on cost.

options.text: Initiate integrated change control process.
options.rationale: Initiating integrated change control evaluates the scaled-up scope's impact on all baselines before any decision.

options.text: Update project management plan.
options.rationale: Updating the plan before approval bypasses change control.

questions.explanation: A request to broaden scope, even from the sponsor, affects baselines and must be evaluated through integrated change control before approval and implementation.
questions.mindset: Route scope increases through change control, whoever asks.

questions.stem: A project has the following characteristics: The project manager is being asked to deliver a business result in a compressed timeline; the original timeline was one month, but the new requested timeline is two weeks. In the resource planning activity, the project manager heard from another team member that no technical resources are available to join the team; however, the project manager knows the technical resource manager from a previous project. What is the first action the project manager should take?

options.text: Ensure the product owner knows that there is an issue with acquiring a technical resource.
options.rationale: Informing the product owner before confirming the facts may raise a false alarm.

options.text: Escalate the technical resource issue to upper management.
options.rationale: Escalating to upper management on the strength of a colleague's remark raises an alarm that may be unfounded.

options.text: Verify the availability of resources by meeting with the previously known technical resource manager.
options.rationale: Verifying availability directly with the known resource manager checks the facts and may secure resources.

options.text: Contact a third-party vendor to obtain a technical resource.
options.rationale: Hiring a third-party resource before checking internal availability adds cost and onboarding time that may be unnecessary.

questions.explanation: Second-hand information about resource availability should be verified directly. Personal relationships can help secure resources quickly.
questions.mindset: Verify before escalating.

questions.stem: A company that is heavily focused on delivering projects using predictive approaches on-boards a new project manager who uses hybrid approaches. The scope of the project contains a number of unclear requirements. How should the project manager plan the delivery of the project?

options.text: Escalate the issue of unclear requirements to the management team and wait for final authorization.
options.rationale: Escalating and waiting for authorisation stalls a project that could start on the requirements already understood.

options.text: Break down the requirements and prioritize the requirements into iterative work packages.
options.rationale: Breaking down and prioritising requirements into iterative work packages lets the team progress while details emerge.

options.text: Ignore the unclear requirements and focus on the delivery plan of the project.
options.rationale: Ignoring unclear requirements risks building the wrong thing.

options.text: Wait for the requirements to be more clear before any further action is taken on the project.
options.rationale: Waiting for every requirement to be clear wastes time that iterative planning could use.

questions.explanation: Hybrid approaches let a team make progress on what is known while unclear requirements are refined. Breaking requirements down and prioritising them into iterative work packages turns uncertainty into a sequence of manageable steps.
questions.mindset: Progress on the known while refining the unknown.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on an IT project. During an iteration review meeting, a couple of key stakeholders enter into a heated discussion about the prototype's capabilities. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Plan a brainstorming session with the project team to find a resolution to the problem.
options.rationale: Brainstorming with the team does not address a conflict between stakeholders.

options.text: Identify the source of the conflict between the stakeholders and address the issue.
options.rationale: Identifying and addressing the source of the conflict is the first step to resolving it.

options.text: List the positives and negatives of the situation to determine the impact of this conflict.
options.rationale: Listing pros and cons does not uncover the cause.

options.text: Invite the project sponsor to intervene and act as a negotiator for the key stakeholders.
options.rationale: Calling in the sponsor to negotiate before the project manager has understood the disagreement escalates prematurely.

questions.explanation: Resolving conflict requires understanding its source. The project manager identifies what is driving disagreement before addressing it.
questions.mindset: Find the source of conflict first.

questions.stem: An approved change request adds an incentive to a lump sum contract if the contractor is able to maintain the current baseline schedule. What should now be updated?

options.text: Scope baseline
options.rationale: The change adds an incentive, not new work, so the scope baseline is unchanged.

options.text: Project management plan
options.rationale: The plan components other than cost are unaffected.

options.text: Cost baseline
options.rationale: The incentive adds potential cost, so the cost baseline is updated.

options.text: Schedule baseline
options.rationale: The incentive rewards keeping the existing schedule; the schedule baseline itself does not change.

questions.explanation: An approved change updates the baselines it affects. An incentive payment tied to meeting the current schedule adds potential cost but changes neither the scope nor the schedule, so only the cost baseline is updated.
questions.mindset: Update the baseline that the change affects.

questions.stem: A hybrid project has the following characteristics: It is in the early stages. It has a brand new team. The project manager will be very busy executing other projects during the first two weeks of the project. During this early stage, how should the project manager develop the new project team?

options.text: Ensure the team understands self-organizing principles.
options.rationale: Ensuring the team understands self-organising principles lets it function while the PM is busy.

options.text: Plan and host several team-building events to normalize the team.
options.rationale: Team-building events early on need the project manager's presence, which is exactly what is missing for two weeks.

options.text: Provide daily project status updates to keep the team informed.
options.rationale: Daily updates from an absent PM are impractical.

options.text: Get to know each team member through one-on-one conversations.
options.rationale: One-to-one conversations with every member take time the project manager will not have in this period.

questions.explanation: When the leader will be largely unavailable while a new team forms, the best investment is making sure the team understands how to self-organise — taking decisions and leadership as needed — so it can function effectively in the meantime.
questions.mindset: Prepare teams to organise themselves.

questions.stem: A project is using a hybrid approach and team performance is consistently excellent during the predictive stages. During the incremental stages, the team begins to show signs of low morale, low commitment, conflicts, and confusion. However, one team member continues to be very confident and excels in performance during this stage. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Recognize the high-performing team member as an example to be followed by the others.
options.rationale: Holding up one member as an example may breed resentment.

options.text: Provide additional training to the team on agile processes.
options.rationale: Training may help, but prescribing it before talking to the team assumes a cause that has not been identified.

options.text: Discuss the issue with the project sponsor and revert the project to use only a predictive approach.
options.rationale: Reverting to a purely predictive approach is a drastic reaction that abandons the reasons the hybrid was chosen.

options.text: Meet with the team to discuss the issues and develop a plan to address them.
options.rationale: Meeting the team to discuss issues identifies root causes and a plan.

questions.explanation: When morale and performance drop only in the incremental stages, something about how the team is working in those stages is not right. Meeting the team to discuss the issues surfaces the causes and produces a plan the team owns.
questions.mindset: Diagnose with the team before prescribing.

questions.stem: A goal has been set at four months for a project team to distribute a product. Unfortunately, it will be difficult to adhere to that time frame due to team members having individual tasks to complete. How should the project manager handle this situation?

options.text: Encourage members of the team to alter their tasks in order to not impede with meeting the project deadline.
options.rationale: Asking members to alter their tasks ignores legitimate work.

options.text: Aid team members in prioritizing their personal tasks against the project's goals.
options.rationale: Helping team members prioritise tasks against project goals balances competing work.

options.text: Postpone the delivery date of the project to a later time so the team can complete their personal tasks.
options.rationale: Postponing the delivery date to fit personal tasks gives up on the project goal without trying to balance the workload.

options.text: Request a delay to the teams’ individual tasks and offer assistance finding alternative times to complete tasks outside of work hours.
options.rationale: Pushing individual tasks outside working hours is unsustainable and damages morale.

questions.explanation: When team members have competing commitments that threaten a project goal, the project manager helps them prioritise their work against the project's objectives, so that critical delivery tasks are protected without ignoring other legitimate work.
questions.mindset: Help people prioritise competing work.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on an complex project with multiple stakeholders and competing priorities. Each stakeholder wants to maximize its share of the allocated resources for the requested functionality. What should the project manager focus on?

options.text: Meeting the personal interests of stakeholders.
options.rationale: Meeting personal interests leads to deals that serve individuals rather than the project, and cannot satisfy everyone.

options.text: Meeting the mutual interests of all stakeholders.
options.rationale: Focusing on mutual interests finds solutions that serve all stakeholders and the project, reducing the competition for resources.

options.text: Preserving the relationships and rapport with stakeholders.
options.rationale: Good relationships matter, but preserving rapport alone does not resolve competing claims on resources.

options.text: Pushing stakeholders to accept the project manager's viewpoint.
options.rationale: Pushing one's own viewpoint produces compliance at best and resentment at worst.

questions.explanation: When stakeholders compete for a share of limited resources, principled negotiation focuses on interests rather than positions. Identifying what they have in common lets the project manager craft solutions that meet shared needs and are accepted more readily.
questions.mindset: Negotiate on shared interests, not competing positions.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a key flagship solution initiative prioritizing agility, market adaptation, and rapid response to market trends. Which activity should the project manager prioritize first to ensure success?

options.text: Conduct periodic reviews of project plans, objectives, and deliverables to ensure all data is captured.
options.rationale: Periodic reviews to capture data are useful, but they do not establish agreed, achievable goals first.

options.text: Request more funding from the sponsor to hire additional skilled resources and improve quality.
options.rationale: More funding does not address alignment on what the initiative must achieve.

options.text: Collaboratively review project objectives with the sponsor to agree on achievable plans and deliverables.
options.rationale: Reviewing objectives with the sponsor to agree achievable plans and deliverables aligns expectations while leaving room to adapt to market trends.

options.text: Create a business case after a market review to adjust project deliverables based on new objectives.
options.rationale: Creating a business case after a market review delays action on a flagship initiative already under way.

questions.explanation: For initiatives that must adapt quickly to the market, clear and achievable goals agreed with the sponsor provide a stable anchor. Shared understanding of priorities lets the team respond to change without losing direction.
questions.mindset: Agree achievable goals with the sponsor so the team can adapt with confidence.

questions.stem: An organization just implemented agile and forms a development team where members are not co-located. The organization’s management style is known for setting clearly defined rules and objectives for team members. What should the agile project manager do to align the team to the desired outcomes?

options.text: Arrange an in-person kick-off meeting to improve upon working relationships.
options.rationale: An in-person kick-off helps relationships but is a one-off and may not be feasible for a distributed team.

options.text: Discuss options with management that would align individual goals to project goals.
options.rationale: Aligning individual goals with management is top-down and does not build team ownership.

options.text: Schedule a speaker to inspire a collective vision across the team.
options.rationale: An inspirational speaker provides a moment of motivation, not lasting alignment.

options.text: Foster commitment through team engagement and planning.
options.rationale: Engaging the team in planning builds shared commitment to the desired outcomes.

questions.explanation: Agile teams align around outcomes they help plan. Involving the team in engagement and planning builds commitment, especially in an organisation used to imposed rules and in a team that is not colocated.
questions.mindset: Build commitment by involving the team in the plan.

questions.stem: A product company is transforming the way it develops and releases products in the market. Executives believe that this is a high-risk initiative, and this initiative must be successful. What should the project manager do in this scenario?

options.text: Develop a communications management plan to inform the employees about the new business model.
options.rationale: A communications plan helps, but it does not reduce the risk of the transformation itself.

options.text: Develop a detailed sprint plan with clear deliverables.
options.rationale: A detailed sprint plan presumes the rollout approach is decided.

options.text: Adopt an iterative rollout approach that delivers the highest business value earlier.
options.rationale: An iterative rollout delivers the highest business value early and reduces risk by learning as it goes.

options.text: Develop a business case with assumptions for the new model.
options.rationale: A business case with assumptions may already exist and does not manage delivery risk.

questions.explanation: High-risk transformations benefit from iterative delivery: early releases of the most valuable elements provide feedback and results, reducing the risk of a single large failure.
questions.mindset: Reduce transformation risk by delivering value in increments.

questions.stem: A new product is being constructed by an agile team, but the team has a limited amount of time to complete it. Due to these circumstances, it is important for the team to sustain collaboration for the duration of the project. To build team solidarity, what should the project leader do?

options.text: Institute protocols for handling sprints in a team meeting.
options.rationale: Protocols for sprints set process but do not build a shared understanding of goals.

options.text: Facilitate meetings with each member of the team to comprehend project goals.
options.rationale: Meeting each member to make sure they understand the project goals builds solidarity around a common purpose.

options.text: Confer product progress with team members by utilizing a burndown chart.
options.rationale: Burndown charts show progress but do not build solidarity.

options.text: Analyze the project map for release of product with team members.
options.rationale: Reviewing the release map is useful but less effective at building shared purpose.

questions.explanation: Teams under time pressure collaborate best when everyone understands and shares the goals. Investing time to make sure each member understands them builds solidarity.
questions.mindset: Build solidarity through shared understanding of goals.

questions.stem: During the execution of a project, the finance team identified that they were not involved in building the business case for the project and will not approve the estimated return on investment (ROI). What should the project manager do?

options.text: Continue developing based on the project management plan and address the issue post-delivery.
options.rationale: Postponing the issue until after delivery risks the finance team blocking the project later.

options.text: Revisit the scope management plan and note this as a risk to the entire project.
options.rationale: Recording a risk does not resolve an actual disagreement.

options.text: Schedule a meeting with the product owner and finance team to agree on course corrections.
options.rationale: Meeting the product owner and finance team to agree course corrections resolves a critical stakeholder issue promptly.

options.text: Revisit the communications management plan and make necessary adjustments.
options.rationale: Adjusting communications does not address the ROI disagreement.

questions.explanation: When a critical stakeholder rejects the project's justification mid-execution, the project manager brings the relevant parties together to agree corrective action rather than postponing.
questions.mindset: Resolve critical stakeholder objections promptly.

questions.stem: Members from an agile team have been consistently tardy for stand-up meetings and are not meeting project target dates. The project leader assumes the issue may be difficulty with self-managing tasks within the team. What action should the project leader take?

options.text: Aid the team to construct an agreement amongst them that details coveted behavioral norms.
options.rationale: Helping the team create an agreement on behavioural norms lets them hold themselves accountable.

options.text: Convene with the team to review the issues and detail actions to solve them.
options.rationale: Reviewing issues and prescribing actions keeps the leader central.

options.text: Adopt a higher leadership role and set an example for the behavior needed.
options.rationale: Taking a stronger leadership role undermines self-management.

options.text: Assemble agile and time management training for the team to complete.
options.rationale: Training may help but does not create accountability.

questions.explanation: Self-managing teams need norms they own. Facilitating a team agreement makes expectations explicit and puts accountability with the team.
questions.mindset: Let teams set and own their norms.

questions.stem: A project manager learns that a few stakeholders have a disagreement regarding the results of one project deliverable. What is the next step the project manager should take?

options.text: Review and analyze the project requirements document.
options.rationale: Reviewing requirements helps but does not resolve the disagreement.

options.text: Review the approved version of a scope statement.
options.rationale: Reviewing the scope statement may inform discussion.

options.text: Organize a meeting with the stakeholders.
options.rationale: Meeting the stakeholders lets them discuss and reach agreement.

options.text: Modernize documented project risks and their responses.
options.rationale: Updating risks does not resolve the disagreement.

questions.explanation: Disagreement among stakeholders about a deliverable is resolved by bringing them together to discuss it, supported by documents as needed.
questions.mindset: Bring disagreeing stakeholders together.

questions.stem: A project's deliverables due date is approaching, but one team member's performance is negatively impacting the schedule. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Acquire a more skilled resource.
options.rationale: Acquiring another resource does not address the underlying issue.

options.text: Remove the team member from the project.
options.rationale: Removing the team member is drastic and does not address whatever is behind their performance.

options.text: Mentor the team member.
options.rationale: Mentoring develops the team member and addresses underlying issues.

options.text: Ask the team member's line manager to provide training.
options.rationale: Line manager training may not arrive in time.

questions.explanation: When one person's performance threatens the schedule, coaching and mentoring address the underlying issue and help them contribute at a higher level. Replacement or outsourced training are slower and do not deal with the cause.
questions.mindset: Develop people through mentoring.

questions.stem: A product owner presented the backlog to the team, and the team raised concerns over implementing some of the features due to various impediments. What should the project manager suggest that the product owner do next?

options.text: Estimate the financial impact of the impediments and request additional funding.
options.rationale: Requesting funding before understanding which impediments matter is premature.

options.text: Capture the impediments and inform management that their assistance is needed in resolving the impediments.
options.rationale: Asking management for help is appropriate only for impediments the team cannot remove.

options.text: Ensure that the impediments are captured and prioritized based upon the highest valued features.
options.rationale: Capturing impediments and prioritising them by the value of the features they block ensures the most important ones are cleared first.

options.text: Begin to remove the impediments, starting with the easiest ones first, to foster team accomplishment.
options.rationale: Removing the easiest impediments first ignores value.

questions.explanation: Impediments should be tackled in order of the value they block. Linking them to backlog priorities ensures the right ones are cleared first.
questions.mindset: Clear impediments in value order.

questions.stem: A project manager is managing a project where requirements are not fully known and a high level of uncertainty exists. Which methodology should be used for this project?

options.text: Agile
options.rationale: Agile's iterative cycles suit projects where requirements are not fully known and uncertainty is high, letting scope emerge through feedback.

options.text: Hybrid
options.rationale: A hybrid could work, but nothing here calls for predictive elements; the situation points to agile.

options.text: Predictive
options.rationale: A predictive approach needs requirements defined up front, which is not possible here.

options.text: Waterfall
options.rationale: Waterfall is a predictive life cycle with the same need for known requirements.

questions.explanation: Life cycles sit on a continuum. Predictive approaches define deliverables up front; adaptive approaches develop them over iterations. High uncertainty and incomplete requirements point strongly toward the adaptive end.
questions.mindset: Match the life cycle to how much is known.

questions.stem: An agile project manager is leading a new software system development project that is in the user acceptance testing phase. The project manager has received positive feedback from the majority of business stakeholders, but the IT director is dissatisfied. What should the agile project manager do first?

options.text: Review previous project meeting attendance to determine the IT director's participation.
options.rationale: Reviewing meeting attendance looks for blame rather than understanding the concern.

options.text: Analyze the requirements that were approved for the project with the IT director.
options.rationale: Re-analysing requirements with the IT director assumes the issue is about requirements before hearing it.

options.text: Discuss the IT director's concerns with the project team.
options.rationale: Discussing the concern with the team before hearing it from the IT director relies on second-hand information.

options.text: Collect forthright feedback from the IT director.
options.rationale: Collecting candid feedback directly from the IT director reveals the specific concerns so they can be addressed.

questions.explanation: When one key stakeholder is dissatisfied while others are happy, the first step is to hear that stakeholder's concerns directly. Specific, honest feedback allows a targeted response.
questions.mindset: Get the dissatisfied stakeholder's feedback first-hand.

questions.stem: One of the retrospective action items that has recurred for the past two iterations is related to the verification and validation of the delivered functionality before production readiness. Which two solutions should the project manager use? (Choose two)

options.text: Adjust velocity for the project team to address additional testing.
options.rationale: Adjusting velocity for more testing changes planning but does not define what adequate verification is.

options.text: Incorporate unit and integration test criteria as part of the validation.
options.rationale: Adding unit and integration test criteria to validation makes verification an explicit part of completing work.

options.text: Modify the methodology of delivery to test-driven development.
