options.rationale: Switching to test-driven development is a major methodology change for a recurring retrospective item.

options.text: Review the working agreement for acceptance criteria with the project team.
options.rationale: Reviewing the working agreement on acceptance criteria clarifies what 'done' means for verification and validation.

options.text: Include a product backlog item to build an integration test suite.
options.rationale: Building an integration test suite may help, but it is a single piece of work rather than a change to how completion is judged.

questions.explanation: When verification before production readiness keeps coming up in retrospectives, the fix is to make it part of the definition of done: explicit test criteria and a working agreement that the team applies consistently.
questions.mindset: Build verification into what 'done' means.

questions.stem: A project manager is planning for a project team that will soon start work on a critical subsystem. There are two technical alternatives identified for the subsystem, but it is not clear if either alternative will perform satisfactorily. The project will be compromised if the performance of the critical subsystem falls short. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Direct the team to assess and evaluate the alternatives for the subsystem.
options.rationale: Having the team assess and evaluate the alternatives produces the data needed to choose one before work is scheduled.

options.text: Add subsystem performance to the issue log and assign an owner for that issue.
options.rationale: The performance question is a risk, not yet an issue, and logging it does not resolve the uncertainty.

options.text: Schedule work for the most promising alternative and add management reserve for the other alternative.
options.rationale: Scheduling the most promising option and reserving money for the other commits to a choice without evidence.

options.text: Advise stakeholders of the major risk to the project posed by the subsystem's performance.
options.rationale: Advising stakeholders is appropriate, but first the team should gather the evidence about the alternatives.

questions.explanation: When a critical choice rests on uncertain technical performance, the first step is to reduce the uncertainty by evaluating the options — for example through spikes or prototypes — before committing the plan.
questions.mindset: Reduce technical uncertainty before committing to a path.

questions.stem: The project manager schedules an iteration review and learns that a few key stakeholders do not approve of how a feature has been developed. What should the project manager do first in order to address this issue?

options.text: Invite project team members to a brainstorming session to identify an appropriate response.
options.rationale: Brainstorming responses before understanding the stakeholders' concerns may solve the wrong problem.

options.text: Address the issue only after evaluating why these stakeholders are concerned.
options.rationale: Evaluating why stakeholders are concerned before acting ensures the response addresses the real issue.

options.text: Determine the impact of the conflict by listing the pros and cons of the situation.
options.rationale: Listing pros and cons does not uncover the stakeholders' reasons.

options.text: Ask the project sponsor to act as a neutral party in negotiation with those stakeholders who are dissatisfied.
options.rationale: Bringing in the sponsor as mediator escalates too early.

questions.explanation: When stakeholders object to how a feature was built, the project manager first understands the reasons behind the concern, then works directly and collaboratively toward a resolution.
questions.mindset: Understand the concern before responding to it.

questions.stem: A project manager observed that a team member is becoming increasingly disengaged from an ongoing project. What should the project manager do to help ensure participation from this team member?

options.text: Speak to the team member, understand the problem, and ask the team member to work on corrective actions.
options.rationale: Speaking with the team member to understand the problem and agree corrective actions addresses the cause and involves them in the solution.

options.text: Ask another team member to mentor the disengaged team member.
options.rationale: Assigning a mentor before understanding the problem may not help.

options.text: Call a team meeting to discuss team engagement expectations.
options.rationale: A team meeting on engagement expectations singles the person out indirectly without understanding the cause.

options.text: Ask the team member to undergo additional training to improve their communication skills.
options.rationale: Communication training assumes a cause that has not been established.

questions.explanation: Disengagement is a symptom. The project manager first talks privately with the person, with empathy, to understand what is happening, then agrees actions together.
questions.mindset: Understand disengagement before prescribing remedies.

questions.stem: A project manager has been assigned to lead a cross-functional project team. During a brainstorming session, the project manager realizes that some team members do not see the need for a change, and this is affecting the team's output. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Restate the objectives of the project to the team.
options.rationale: Restating objectives repeats information the team already has without addressing their doubts.

options.text: Ask the project sponsor to review the project charter.
options.rationale: Having the sponsor review the charter does not address the team members' concerns.

options.text: Engage team members to understand their doubts and get their buy-in.
options.rationale: Engaging team members to understand their doubts and gain buy-in addresses resistance directly.

options.text: End the brainstorming session and adopt interview methods.
options.rationale: Ending the session and switching to interviews abandons the team discussion.

questions.explanation: Resistance to change within a team is overcome by understanding the doubts behind it and involving people, not by restating the case.
questions.mindset: Engage doubters to win their buy-in.

questions.stem: A project manager notices that one team member seems increasingly unhappy during team meetings. The team member is not making progress on a key work package, and this lack of progress is now impacting the critical path. The team member feels that they are not in the correct role within the project team. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Reassure the team member about their abilities by reminding them that they were chosen for a reason.
options.rationale: Reassurance may be unwarranted and does not address the concern about role fit.

options.text: Meet with the team member to discuss where they can contribute, based on their strengths.
options.rationale: Meeting to discuss where they can contribute based on strengths addresses the core concern and may improve performance.

options.text: Enroll the team member in targeted training to acquire the needed skills for their assigned role.
options.rationale: Training for the current role ignores that the person believes the role is wrong for them.

options.text: Schedule weekly touchpoints with the team member to discuss barriers that may impact their work.
options.rationale: Weekly touchpoints create activity without resolving the role question.

questions.explanation: When someone believes they are in the wrong role, the servant leader takes the concern seriously and explores where their strengths fit.
questions.mindset: Put people where their strengths fit.

questions.stem: A large transformation project that requires cross-functional effort from various business teams is in progress. Which two actions should the project manager take first to complete the stakeholder register? (Choose two)

options.text: Hold a workshop with key project team members to brainstorm and identify potential stakeholders.
options.rationale: A workshop with key team members uses their knowledge to identify stakeholders across the business.

options.text: Ask for referrals from the business sponsor or senior leadership.
options.rationale: Referrals from leadership help but are not the first steps.

options.text: Analyze the interest, influence, and impact of potential stakeholders from each business team.
options.rationale: Analysing the interest, influence and impact of potential stakeholders completes the register meaningfully.

options.text: Discuss the project with team members and put together the register at a team meeting.
options.rationale: Compiling the register in a single team meeting skips structured identification and analysis.

options.text: Contact each potential stakeholder directly and ask if they are interested in joining the project.
options.rationale: Asking stakeholders whether they want to join confuses identification with engagement.

questions.explanation: Building a stakeholder register means identifying stakeholders comprehensively and then analysing them. Team brainstorming and interest-influence-impact analysis do both.
questions.mindset: Identify stakeholders broadly, then analyse them.

questions.stem: A project manager working with a culturally diverse team discovers major intra-team conflicts during project execution. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Schedule a project team meeting to understand the conflicts.
options.rationale: A team meeting to understand the conflicts engages the team in identifying causes and solutions.

options.text: Advise the team members to work harmoniously.
options.rationale: Advising people to be harmonious does not resolve conflict.

options.text: Update the resource management plan.
options.rationale: Updating the resource plan does not address conflict.

options.text: Engage members in team-building activities.
options.rationale: Team-building may help later but not before causes are understood.

questions.explanation: Conflicts in diverse teams are resolved by understanding them with the team, rather than issuing general advice or activities.
questions.mindset: Understand conflict with the team before treating it.

questions.stem: A contractor is late with a critical project deliverable due to resource challenges. There is a 22% buffer in the budget for cost overruns. What is the first thing a project manager should do?

options.text: Look into alternative vendors that can assist with project deliverables despite resource constraints.
options.rationale: Exploring alternative vendors assesses options to protect delivery, using the budget buffer if justified.

options.text: Hire a new vendor to replace the current vendor and ask the new vendor to send a contract.
options.rationale: Replacing the vendor immediately is premature before options are assessed.

options.text: Hold a discussion with the vendor regarding the legal implications of this slippage.
options.rationale: Discussing legal implications does not solve the delivery problem.

options.text: Update the project schedule after first accepting the cost overrun.
options.rationale: Accepting the overrun and updating the schedule concedes the delay.

questions.explanation: When a critical supplier falters, the project manager looks for alternatives that protect delivery, then presents a recommendation to the sponsor.
questions.mindset: Protect delivery by exploring alternatives early.

questions.stem: A project manager is managing multidisciplinary teams. During the last project review meeting, the project manager realized that there is friction between some of the team members. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Identify the team members and review their project performance.
options.rationale: Reviewing individual performance targets people instead of the conflict.

options.text: Consult with the sponsor to find replacements for the team members.
options.rationale: Replacing team members over friction is drastic and loses their skills before the cause is even understood.

options.text: Evaluate the issue and apply conflict resolution techniques.
options.rationale: Evaluating the issue and applying conflict resolution addresses the cause.

options.text: Report the issue in the monthly project executive summary.
options.rationale: Reporting to executives does not resolve friction.

questions.explanation: Friction between members of multidisciplinary teams often comes from different priorities or working styles. The project manager evaluates what is behind it and applies an appropriate conflict-resolution technique, rather than judging individuals or escalating.
questions.mindset: Resolve friction at its cause.

questions.stem: A team member is scheduled to visit an overseas client site next week. However, the project manager overheard the team member tell a project coordinator that their functional manager denied the team member's request for time off as compensation for the client visit. The project manager needs to ensure that the team member will visit the client site next week. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Meet with the team member directly to tell them about what they overheard.
options.rationale: Repeating overheard information may embarrass the team member.

options.text: Confirm with the team member that the client visit can take place.
options.rationale: Confirming with the team member that the visit can happen checks the facts directly without escalation.

options.text: Confront the functional manager about the team member's time off.
options.rationale: Confronting the functional manager escalates on hearsay.

options.text: Log the issue as a risk in the risk log and assign another team member.
options.rationale: Logging a risk and reassigning the visit acts on overheard information before checking whether there is any problem.

questions.explanation: Information picked up second-hand may be incomplete or wrong. The project manager checks the key fact directly with the person concerned — here, whether the client visit will go ahead — before escalating or re-planning.
questions.mindset: Verify directly before acting on hearsay.

questions.stem: A director is acting as the product owner for a government software project. The director is repeatedly unable to engage with the team and provide regular and important feedback on project artifacts. What should the project manager do to resolve this?

options.text: Determine communication preferences and review responsibilities.
options.rationale: Determining the director's communication preferences and reviewing responsibilities helps engage the product owner.

options.text: Obtain alternative feedback from the customer.
options.rationale: Customer feedback cannot replace the product owner's input.

options.text: Recommend an open-door policy for the project.
options.rationale: An open-door policy does not address the product owner's specific engagement problem.

options.text: Adopt a collaborative approach.
options.rationale: A collaborative approach is too vague to resolve the issue.

questions.explanation: When a product owner cannot engage, understanding how they prefer to communicate and clarifying responsibilities creates a workable engagement pattern.
questions.mindset: Tailor engagement to how the product owner can participate.

questions.stem: A customer is not satisfied with the delivered product, saying that it was not what they expected. The project manager is surprised, because the agile development team delivered the product several iterations early. What is one way that the project manager could have avoided this result?

options.text: Required team sign off for each of the constant changes to the requirements
options.rationale: Team sign-off on every requirement change adds bureaucracy and still does not involve the customer.

options.text: Set aside more resources for product testing after changes are made
options.rationale: More testing after changes checks quality but cannot reveal that the customer expected something different.

options.text: Made sure that the customer was aware of the value of demos
options.rationale: If the customer had valued and attended demos, they would have seen the product evolving and corrected course early.

options.text: Ensured that the team fully participated in developing the project scope
options.rationale: The team's involvement in scope is useful, but the gap here was the customer's feedback, not the team's.

questions.explanation: Iteration reviews and demos exist so that customers see working product regularly and shape it. When a customer is surprised at the end, it usually means they were not engaged in those feedback points.
questions.mindset: Keep the customer in the feedback loop through regular demos.

questions.stem: Early in a project, the project manager realizes that one of the key team members is not prepared to perform the assigned task. How should the project manager address this issue?

options.text: Ensure training is built into the resource management plan.
options.rationale: Building training into the resource plan is generic and does not address this person's specific gap now.

options.text: Review the training requirements with the team member.
options.rationale: Reviewing the training requirements with the team member identifies their gaps and a plan to close them.

options.text: Review each required task with the team member when it starts.
options.rationale: Reviewing each task as it starts gives support piecemeal and may come too late.

options.text: Escalate the issue to the resource's functional manager for resolution.
options.rationale: Escalating to the functional manager before trying to address the gap is premature.

questions.explanation: When a key team member is not ready for their work, the project manager works with them to identify what skills and knowledge are missing and plans how to close the gap — training, mentoring or shadowing.
questions.mindset: Close individual skill gaps with a plan made together.

questions.stem: A project is close to completion when an unidentified and influential stakeholder appears and threatens to put the project in jeopardy by not approving the closing documents. Which two actions should the project manager have done to avoid this? (Choose two)

options.text: The project manager should have carried out stakeholder identification during the initiation stage of the project.
options.rationale: Identifying stakeholders during initiation would have found this influential stakeholder early.

options.text: The project owner should have informed the project manager about the stakeholders of the project.
options.rationale: It is the project manager's responsibility to identify stakeholders, not the project owner's.

options.text: Identifying and analyzing stakeholders should have been performed as an ongoing task throughout the project duration.
options.rationale: Identifying and analysing stakeholders throughout the project would have caught them even if they emerged later.

options.text: The stakeholder should have come forward for proper identification at the beginning of the project.
options.rationale: Expecting stakeholders to come forward themselves is unrealistic.

options.text: Creating awareness of the stakeholders' concerns should have been continuously occurring throughout the project.
options.rationale: Awareness of known stakeholders' concerns does not find unidentified stakeholders.

questions.explanation: Stakeholder identification starts early and continues throughout the project. Influential stakeholders who are missed can derail acceptance at the end.
questions.mindset: Keep identifying stakeholders from start to finish.

questions.stem: A customer repeatedly complains, saying that a function developed by the development team does not seem to align with the original design. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the product owner to sit in on the next iteration review meeting to learn more about the development status for the product.
options.rationale: Having the product owner attend a review to learn the status does not address the customer's complaint.

options.text: Ask the quality assurance team to identify any mismatches in functionality compared to the initial design.
options.rationale: QA can find mismatches, but the customer's concern needs a shared discussion of corrective actions.

options.text: Ask the development team to rewrite the function so that it matches with the project scope.
options.rationale: Rewriting the function before understanding the gap may repeat the problem.

options.text: Schedule time during the next retrospective session to discuss all corrective actions and ask the customer to participate in the session.
options.rationale: Discussing corrective actions in a session that includes the customer builds shared understanding and agreement.

questions.explanation: Repeated customer complaints about alignment with the design call for a shared conversation. Bringing the customer into the discussion of corrective actions builds understanding and consensus.
questions.mindset: Resolve recurring complaints together with the customer.

questions.stem: A project team member continues to change a colleague's deliverable during every sprint. The colleague has asked the project manager to intervene. What action should the project manager take to address the concern?

options.text: Speak with the team member to determine the reason for the changes.
options.rationale: Talking with the team member to understand why they keep changing the deliverable is the first step to resolving the conflict.

options.text: Discuss any lack of quality in the deliverable with the colleague.
options.rationale: Raising quality concerns with the colleague presumes the changes are justified.

options.text: Review the performance of both team members with their functional managers.
options.rationale: Involving functional managers escalates before understanding.

options.text: Control the execution and delivery to ensure that the deliverables are not changed.
options.rationale: Controlling deliverables to prevent changes imposes a solution without understanding the cause.

questions.explanation: Recurring interference with a colleague's work has a reason. Understanding it from the person making the changes comes before deciding what to do.
questions.mindset: Understand the behaviour before correcting it.

questions.stem: A project manager provided video-based training for new software but several team members reported feeling unprepared to use it. What should the project manager have done to ensure effective training?

options.text: Tested the team members's understanding after they completed the training.
options.rationale: Testing understanding after training reveals the failure but does not prevent it.

options.text: Requested that the training department find more appropriate courses.
options.rationale: Finding other courses without understanding learning needs may repeat the problem.

options.text: Asked the team members to learn the required skills from the accompanying software manual.
options.rationale: Self-study from manuals may suit some but not all.

options.text: Conducted individual and team assessments on their preferred learning method.
options.rationale: Assessing individual and team learning preferences lets training be designed to suit the team.

questions.explanation: Different people learn in different ways. Assessing learning preferences before designing training makes it more effective.
questions.mindset: Fit training to how people learn.

questions.stem: A customer indicates that they would like to add functionality. Although this request is made during the execution phase of the project, the project manager finds that the cost for the addition would be small. The additional functionality, if successful, would increase the opportunity for profit. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Agree that the functionality would offer a great opportunity, but the proposed addition is out of scope.
options.rationale: Declaring it out of scope ignores a potentially valuable opportunity.

options.text: Schedule a meeting with the company's management team and present the customer's request for additional functionality as a good opportunity.
options.rationale: Presenting the request to management as an opportunity allows a decision on pursuing added value.

options.text: Move forward, using the project's management reserve to add the requested functionality.
options.rationale: Using management reserve without approval is inappropriate.

options.text: Identify an already-developed feature that could be combined with the new functionality and use the combination to meet the customer's request.
options.rationale: Combining features may not meet the customer's need.

questions.explanation: Customer requests that bring profitable opportunities should be surfaced to decision-makers rather than dismissed or implemented informally.
questions.mindset: Surface valuable opportunities to decision-makers.

questions.stem: During a challenging shareholder meeting, the customer indicates that they will reject an iteration's deliverable. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Send a request to the project sponsor, asking them to update the project charter then reassign the responsibilities and authorities.
options.rationale: Changing the charter and reassigning authority is disproportionate.

options.text: Meet with the project team to add new and improved features to replace the features that were rejected.
options.rationale: Adding features without understanding the concerns may not address them.

options.text: Work with stakeholders to create a shared approach that will address the issues of concern.
options.rationale: Working with stakeholders on a shared approach addresses the concerns collaboratively.

options.text: File a change request with the change control board (CCB) in order to add budget to the baseline.
options.rationale: Filing for extra budget presumes both the problem and its solution before the customer's concerns are understood.

questions.explanation: When a customer threatens to reject a deliverable, the project manager works with stakeholders to understand concerns and agree an approach.
questions.mindset: Agree the path forward with stakeholders.

questions.stem: A project manager in Location A works with a local team, while developers are in another remote location, and a quality assessor is in yet another remote location. The project manager is aware that these distances mean that the team could struggle with lag when needing to communicate. What could the project manager do to mitigate this issue?

options.text: Increase the number of standup sessions per day.
options.rationale: More stand-ups add meetings without reducing lag.

options.text: Source new team members locally.
options.rationale: Sourcing local members is costly and disruptive.

options.text: Create a fishbowl window.
options.rationale: A fishbowl window provides a persistent video link that lets distributed people engage spontaneously.

options.text: Decrease the need for team communications through backlog grooming.
options.rationale: Backlog grooming does not remove the need for communication.

questions.explanation: Distributed teams lose the spontaneous contact that colocated teams take for granted. Virtual workspaces such as a fishbowl window — an always-open video link during the working day — let people see and approach each other informally, reducing communication lag.
questions.mindset: Recreate proximity virtually.

questions.stem: A new project manager joins an existing team. The project manager is made aware that there are strong personalities on the team, which has resulted in management becoming involved to resolve team performance issues. What should the new project manager do when first joining this team?

options.text: Implement the plan that senior management has developed to resolve conflicts on the team.
options.rationale: Implementing management's plan before knowing the team may backfire.

options.text: Review the team velocity records and observe the team and interactions between the team members.
options.rationale: Reviewing velocity and observing interactions builds understanding before acting.

options.text: Follow the advice of the most vocal team member on how to improve team dynamics.
options.rationale: Following the loudest voice skews understanding.

options.text: Observe the team and determine who should be removed from the team.
options.rationale: Deciding whom to remove before understanding the team condemns people on reputation and may remove valuable contributors.

questions.explanation: A new leader joining a team known for friction first observes and gathers evidence — performance data and how people interact — before intervening. Acting on others' plans or on first impressions risks making the dynamics worse.
questions.mindset: Observe before intervening.

questions.stem: At what point in an agile project should a project manager engage stakeholders?

options.text: At the start of the project
options.rationale: Engagement only at the start leaves stakeholders out of later feedback.

options.text: At the end of the project
options.rationale: Engaging stakeholders only at the end removes their chance to shape the product while it is being built.

options.text: When challenges are encountered in the project
options.rationale: Engaging only when problems arise is reactive.

options.text: Throughout the project life cycle
options.rationale: Engaging stakeholders throughout the life cycle provides continuous feedback and alignment.

questions.explanation: Agile delivery depends on continuous stakeholder engagement. Stakeholders are involved from the start, give feedback at every increment, and are informed of challenges as they arise, so the product evolves with their needs.
questions.mindset: Engage stakeholders continuously.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on a small project that is critical for a larger program milestone. A new resource has been assigned to replace a key resource who had to leave the project. Unfortunately, an outside stakeholder claims that the person who assigned the new resource sent their weakest team member. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Assess the new resource’s ability to perform the necessary work by testing their communication skills with the current project team.
options.rationale: Testing communication skills is not the relevant evaluation.

options.text: Evaluate the skills of the new resource to see how the resource can provide value to the project.
options.rationale: Evaluating the new resource's skills gives evidence rather than relying on hearsay.

options.text: File a request with the project management office (PMO) manager in order to obtain a better resource.
options.rationale: Requesting another resource assumes hearsay is fact.

options.text: Address the concern with the new resource’s functional manager to mitigate any conflict within the project team.
options.rationale: Raising the concern with the functional manager acts on unverified claims.

questions.explanation: Judgements about people should be based on evidence. Evaluating the new resource's skills determines how they can contribute.
questions.mindset: Evaluate people on evidence, not rumour.

questions.stem: A project manager's team has been efficiently delivering expected results in an environment where budget and scope are fixed. Now, there is an increased demand for new skills due to changes in the market. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Meet the new demand by adding new resources with the required skills.
options.rationale: Adding new people breaks the fixed budget and brings onboarding costs.

options.text: Hire a third-party vendor who can provide resources with the needed skills.
options.rationale: A third-party vendor adds cost the fixed budget cannot absorb and does not build the team's own capability.

options.text: Change the distribution of partially dedicated resources with the needed skills.
options.rationale: Redistributing partially dedicated resources may not provide the skills.

options.text: Meet the new demand by upgrading the existing team members' skills.
options.rationale: Upgrading existing members' skills meets new demand within fixed constraints.

questions.explanation: When the market demands new skills but budget and scope are fixed, the sustainable response is to develop the existing team. Identifying the skills needed and upgrading team members' competencies meets the demand without breaking the constraints.
questions.mindset: Grow the team you have.

questions.stem: A project is following a strategic plan that includes key milestones that have been aligned with stakeholders. As the work is being executed, new tasks arise along with important dependencies that prevent the work from progressing as planned. The team is unable to determine who should make decisions and take action on the new tasks and dependencies. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Use a RACI chart to facilitate team task accountability.
options.rationale: A RACI chart clarifies who is responsible and accountable for new tasks.

options.text: Use a Gantt chart to ensure milestones are accomplished.
options.rationale: A Gantt chart shows schedule, not responsibility.

options.text: Ask the sponsors who have responsibility.
options.rationale: Asking sponsors for each task is inefficient.

options.text: Use a work breakdown structure (WBS) to ensure requirements are covered.
options.rationale: The WBS confirms what work exists, but it does not say who decides or acts on each task.

questions.explanation: When new tasks and dependencies appear and nobody knows who should act, a RACI chart makes responsibility and accountability explicit for each piece of work, so decisions are made and actions taken without delay.
questions.mindset: Clarify who is accountable for each task.

questions.stem: In an agile project initiation phase, a senior team member suggests using a new documentation tool based on experience on a previous project. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Discourage the use of the new documentation tool.
options.rationale: Discouraging the suggestion dismisses useful experience and discourages team members from proposing improvements.

options.text: Request the sponsor's approval of the new documentation tool.
options.rationale: Seeking sponsor approval for a documentation tool escalates a decision the team can make itself.

options.text: Ask the team for feedback regarding the new documentation tool.
options.rationale: Asking the team for feedback lets everyone weigh the tool's benefits and concerns before adopting it.

options.text: Arrange a team training session on how to use the new documentation tool.
options.rationale: Training everyone on the tool assumes the decision is made without team input.

questions.explanation: In agile teams, decisions about how the team works — including tools — are made collaboratively. Discussing a proposal openly surfaces concerns and builds the buy-in needed for successful adoption.
questions.mindset: Decide how the team works together with the team.

questions.stem: For quality assurance, a quality audit was conducted on the processes being used in the project execution plan. One of the nonconformance issues raised by the auditor was that attendance lists for the project risk review meetings were unavailable. Why is an attendance list important?

options.text: It is a document that is registered within the lessons learned register.
options.rationale: Attendance lists are records of meetings, not entries in the lessons learned register.

options.text: It is a record that shows the number of attendees at the meeting.
options.rationale: The number of attendees is less important than whether the right people were present.

options.text: It is standard practice on projects to conduct optional risk review meetings.
options.rationale: Risk reviews should be regular, not optional, so this is not why the list matters.

options.text: It is evidence that risk review meetings were held with the appropriate project team members.
options.rationale: An attendance list provides evidence that risk reviews took place with the appropriate people.

questions.explanation: Audits check that processes were followed. Records such as attendance lists provide evidence that required activities — like risk reviews with the right participants — actually happened.
questions.mindset: Keep evidence that processes were followed.

questions.stem: A project manager is planning the next release for the software development team. The team has completed two releases to date, and the product backlog for the next release has been confirmed. Which of the following tools should the project manager use to plan the duration for the next release?

options.text: Product roadmap
options.rationale: The product roadmap shows direction and themes, not the detailed effort needed for this release.

options.text: Resource calendar
options.rationale: A resource calendar shows availability but not how long the work will take.

options.text: Work breakdown structure (WBS)
options.rationale: Decomposing the confirmed release backlog into its work supports estimating the effort and duration of the release.

options.text: Burndown chart
options.rationale: A burndown chart tracks progress during a release rather than planning its duration.

questions.explanation: Planning a release's duration needs an understanding of the work it contains. Decomposing the confirmed scope, together with the team's demonstrated velocity from earlier releases, gives the basis for a duration estimate.
questions.mindset: Understand the work before estimating how long it will take.

questions.stem: A team member in a hybrid organization informs the project manager of a new way to execute an activity with a shorter duration. The project manager has not used the new process before, but a trusted team member explains that their previous experience with the process validates the efficacy of the new process. Which two actions should the project manager take? (Choose two).

options.text: Involve the team member's functional manager.
options.rationale: Involving the team member's functional manager is not needed to evaluate a process change.

options.text: Postpone the decision until the next sprint.
options.rationale: Postponing the decision wastes a potential improvement.

options.text: Update the work breakdown structure (WBS).
options.rationale: Updating the WBS presumes the change is adopted.

options.text: Assess the impact of adopting the new process.
options.rationale: Assessing the impact of the new process identifies its benefits and risks.

options.text: Communicate the impact with key stakeholders.
options.rationale: Communicating the impact to key stakeholders ensures they understand and support the change.

questions.explanation: A promising process improvement should be assessed for impact and the findings shared with key stakeholders before adoption. Trust in a team member's experience is a reason to evaluate, not to skip evaluation.
questions.mindset: Assess and communicate before changing how work is done.

questions.stem: Close to the end of a large project, some of the technical reports related to the delivered service were not ready. The project manager asked the team members for the missing documents, but the team claimed they had already fulfilled their assigned tasks. How should the project manager address this concern?

options.text: Review the hierarchical chart to confirm positions and relationships.
options.rationale: An organisation chart shows positions, not responsibility for specific deliverables.

options.text: Refer to the RACI chart to validate the assigned roles and responsibilities.
options.rationale: The RACI chart shows who is responsible for each deliverable, resolving the dispute about the missing reports.

options.text: Discuss the activity list and ensure that the team understands what work is required.
options.rationale: The activity list shows work, but not who is responsible for it.

options.text: Input all assumptions and constraints into the assumption log.
options.rationale: The assumption log is unrelated to assigning responsibility.

questions.explanation: When team members believe they have finished their assigned work but deliverables are missing, the question is who was responsible for what. The RACI chart records the agreed assignment of responsibilities and settles the gap objectively.
questions.mindset: Settle responsibility disputes with the RACI chart.

questions.stem: A project manager wants to ensure that virtual team meetings are effective. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Record all the meetings for participants who cannot attend.
options.rationale: Recording meetings helps absentees but does not make meetings effective.

options.text: Determine the best communication methods based on location.
options.rationale: Choosing communication methods that suit each location addresses time zones, language and technology differences.

options.text: Prioritize the agenda with items that require more discussion.
options.rationale: A prioritised agenda helps but does not address virtual-specific challenges.

options.text: Schedule meetings at convenient times for the majority of attendees.
options.rationale: Scheduling for the majority may exclude some attendees.

questions.explanation: Virtual meetings are effective when communication methods suit the participants' locations, time zones, languages and technology.
questions.mindset: Tailor communication methods to where people are.

questions.stem: A project manager was assigned to deliver new software for university students. In this project, the software is being delivered to a specific niche of people. To better understand this niche, the project manager needs to develop an archetype user. How should the project manager do that?

options.text: Create a persona character.
options.rationale: A persona describes an archetypal user with goals and behaviours, helping the team understand the niche.

options.text: Contract with an architecture firm.
options.rationale: An architecture firm designs buildings, not user archetypes.

options.text: Submit a public questionnaire.
options.rationale: A public questionnaire may not target the niche and is slower.

options.text: Publish a marketing plan.
options.rationale: A marketing plan promotes the product; it does not describe the goals and behaviours of a typical user.

questions.explanation: A persona is a fictional but research-based archetype of a user group, described through goals, behaviours and needs. Personas help a team design for a specific niche, such as university students, without surveying everyone.
questions.mindset: Design for users you can picture.

questions.stem: In order to determine a new hybrid approach for a project, the project manager decides that an assessment of the organizational culture is needed. The project manager should consider a balance between which two elements?

options.text: Exploration and stability
options.rationale: Exploration and stability are related but not the balance usually used to choose a hybrid.

options.text: Speed and traditional models
options.rationale: Speed and traditional models is not a recognised balance.

options.text: Flexibility and predictability
options.rationale: Flexibility and predictability are the key balance when tailoring a hybrid approach to culture.

options.text: Disruption and conformity
options.rationale: Disruption and conformity is not the relevant balance.

questions.explanation: Hybrid approaches balance adaptive flexibility with predictive control. Assessing culture shows where the organisation sits on that balance.
questions.mindset: Balance flexibility and predictability to fit the culture.

questions.stem: A team member is unhappy with their workload and feels they are not being supported enough. The project manager wants to meet with the team member to discuss their concerns and apply a compromise/reconcile conflict management approach. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Explain the project's constraints and priorities to the team member.
options.rationale: Explaining constraints first may make the team member feel unheard.

options.text: Listen to the team member's concerns and try to understand their perspective.
options.rationale: Listening to understand the team member's perspective is the first step in reconciling needs.

options.text: Suggest a revised workload that is more manageable for the team member.
options.rationale: Proposing a revised workload before listening may miss the real concern.

options.text: Offer to provide additional support to the team member.
options.rationale: Offering support before understanding may not address the issue.

questions.explanation: Every conflict-resolution approach, including compromise, starts with understanding the other person's perspective. Listening first shows respect, reveals the real issues behind the workload complaint and makes any agreed solution more likely to hold.
questions.mindset: Listen first.

questions.stem: The conflict about how to proceed has developed between two team members prior to a release. The team needs to work together to complete the product release. What should the project manager do first to defuse the situation?

options.text: Hire an agile coach to instruct the team members on how to manage their conflict without harming the project.
options.rationale: Hiring an agile coach is an expensive external step before understanding the conflict.

options.text: Observe the team members' interactions and talk with them about their complaints before applying a conflict resolution technique.
options.rationale: Observing and talking with both members before choosing a technique ensures the response fits.

options.text: Set up meetings with both team members and human resource management to remind them of the importance of the next delivery of the product.
options.rationale: Bringing human resources into a disagreement about how to proceed escalates it before the project manager has understood it.

options.text: Explain to the team members that they are wasting time engaging in a conflict and not delivering the product functionality.
options.rationale: Telling them they are wasting time is dismissive.

questions.explanation: Before choosing how to resolve a conflict, the project manager understands it: observing how the two team members interact and hearing their complaints. The right technique — collaborating, compromising or others — depends on what is really driving the disagreement.
questions.mindset: Analyse conflict before resolving it.

questions.stem: A customer's resources have not completed the required training. The project manager has to consider the risk it poses to the timely completion of the project. Customer resource training is a required project deliverable. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Communicate with the project stakeholders to address the risk.
options.rationale: Communicating with stakeholders, including the customer, addresses the risk collaboratively.

options.text: Revise the risk register and discuss it at the next project status meeting.
options.rationale: Waiting for the next status meeting delays action.

options.text: Dedicate additional post-implementation support to mitigate the risk.
options.rationale: Post-implementation support does not address the training deliverable.

options.text: Modify the project schedule to account for the training delay.
options.rationale: Adjusting the schedule for the delay accepts it before the customer has been engaged to resolve it.

questions.explanation: When a risk depends on the customer's own actions — here, completing required training — the most effective response is to engage the customer and other stakeholders directly, agreeing how the risk will be addressed before it affects completion.
questions.mindset: Engage the stakeholders who can resolve the risk.

questions.stem: A project manager is in the initiation phase of a new project and is preparing to develop a project team charter. The project team consists of members from different departments within the organization, and collaboration is vital for project success. What should the project manager do to create an effective project team charter?

options.text: Create the project team charter independently, outlining their expectations and goals for the team.
options.rationale: Writing the charter alone loses team ownership.

options.text: Hold a kick-off meeting with the team to collaboratively define the team's purpose, roles, responsibilities, and objectives.
options.rationale: Defining purpose, roles and objectives collaboratively builds commitment.

options.text: Delegate the task of drafting the charter to a senior team member with experience in project management.
options.rationale: Delegating the charter to one senior member limits input and ownership from the other departments.

options.text: Share a template of a generic project team charter with the team and invite them to modify it as needed to fit the project.
options.rationale: Modifying a generic template may miss the team's own agreements.

questions.explanation: A team charter captures values, agreements and operating guidelines. It is most effective when created by the team itself, because people commit to norms they helped define, which is especially important for cross-departmental teams.
questions.mindset: Create team charters with the team.

questions.stem: An agile project was scaled from the feasibility study phase to the implementation phase. Due to time constraints, the same team is assigned to the project, except for one team member who was replaced with a new team member. Many of the team members do not get along with the new team member and are unwilling to work in the next phase. How should the project manager ensure that the team is ready for the next phase?

options.text: Perform an incremental delivery assessment.
options.rationale: An incremental delivery assessment does not address team relationships.

options.text: Force the team to stay together.
options.rationale: Forcing the team together does not build commitment.

options.text: Request a formal team commitment.
options.rationale: Requesting a formal team commitment refreshes norms and commitment for the new phase.

options.text: Remove the new team member.
options.rationale: Removing the new member rewards the team for excluding a colleague and does not build a functioning team.

questions.explanation: When a team enters a new phase with changed membership, it is effectively a new team. Refreshing its norms and asking for a formal commitment from everyone helps members accept the newcomer and commit to the work ahead.
questions.mindset: Refresh commitment when the team changes.

questions.stem: Project team A is launching a complex program in collaboration with project teams B, C, and D. What should be the priority for project team A's project manager during the early stages of the project?

options.text: Host a team-building event with members from project teams A, B, C, and D.
options.rationale: Team-building helps relationships but not program coordination.

options.text: Include a metrics dashboard for project teams B, C, and D.
options.rationale: Dashboards come after dependencies are known.

options.text: Establish the same priorities as those of project teams B, C, and D.
options.rationale: Aligning priorities blindly may not suit each team.

options.text: Ask project teams A, B, C, and D to identify critical dependencies, risks, and major milestones.
options.rationale: Identifying dependencies, risks and milestones across teams is the foundation for coordinating the program.

questions.explanation: Early in a multi-team program, mapping dependencies, risks and milestones across teams is essential for coordinated planning.
questions.mindset: Map cross-team dependencies early.

questions.stem: An agile project team is struggling to keep track of the changes being applied to the product, because its process is cumbersome and error-prone. What should the project manager do to address the issue?

options.text: Clearly assign the responsibility for the process to a single person to ensure accountability in case of failure.
options.rationale: Assigning one person to own the process concentrates blame without fixing why the process is cumbersome.

options.text: Use the next retrospective to evaluate the process's effectiveness, and determine if changes are needed.
options.rationale: Evaluating the process in the next retrospective lets the team find the cause and agree practical improvements.

options.text: Seek the sponsor's approval to stop following this process and assume the risk of eliminating it.
options.rationale: Seeking approval to abandon the process removes a control without understanding what it is for.

options.text: Secure funds to acquire a software-based solution that can speed up the process and reduce the errors.
options.rationale: Buying a software tool is a solution chosen before the problem has been analysed.

questions.explanation: When a team's process is cumbersome and error-prone, the retrospective is the place to examine it. The team identifies what is not working and agrees improvements, which it is more likely to follow than a solution imposed from outside.
questions.mindset: Improve processes with the people who use them.

questions.stem: Before a project evaluation meeting, a key stakeholder complains that the project does not deliver the expected business benefits. The project manager needs to prepare for the meeting to effectively address the complaint. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Review the change control log for approved variances in the project deliverable.
options.rationale: The change log shows approved variations but not whether the project achieves its intended benefits.

options.text: Review the communications management plan and stakeholder engagement plan.
options.rationale: Communication and engagement plans describe how stakeholders are informed, not whether benefits are delivered.

options.text: Review the project performance metrics and acceptance test results.
options.rationale: Performance metrics and test results show delivery performance, not necessarily the business benefits.

options.text: Review the project objectives and success criteria.
options.rationale: Reviewing objectives and success criteria establishes what the project committed to achieve, the basis for addressing the complaint.

questions.explanation: A complaint that a project does not deliver expected benefits is judged against the agreed objectives and success criteria. Reviewing them first shows whether the concern reflects a real shortfall or a mismatch in expectations.
questions.mindset: Judge benefit complaints against the agreed success criteria.

questions.stem: A country implements new labor laws with specific requirements for labor health and safety. The company's existing procedures haven't been updated yet, but management informed all project managers of the regulations. What should the project managers do first?

options.text: Review the possible impacts of the updated regulations on their projects.
options.rationale: Reviewing the possible impacts of the new regulations on each project establishes what must change.

options.text: Update their project risk register for emerging risks.
options.rationale: Updating the risk register should follow an understanding of the impacts.

options.text: Request that the human resources department update the procedures.
options.rationale: Asking HR to update procedures is an organisational step, not the project manager's first action on their project.

options.text: Ask the corporate office for advice on how to define the best course of action.
options.rationale: Asking the corporate office for advice delays the project manager's own responsibility to assess impact.

questions.explanation: When new regulations are announced, project managers first review how they affect their own projects. That understanding drives risk updates, plan changes and requests for organisational procedures.
questions.mindset: Assess how new rules affect your project first.

questions.stem: A project is in the execution phase when new team members are onboarded. Before onboarding the new team members, what should the project manager do to reduce the impact of this action on project performance?

options.text: Conduct a session to update the existing social agreement on how the team will work collaboratively.
options.rationale: Updating the social agreement with everyone recognises that new members create a new team and lets all contribute to how it will work.

options.text: Schedule a session to let the existing team members explain to the new ones about the current social contract.
options.rationale: Having existing members explain the contract makes it one-way and denies newcomers a voice.

options.text: Organize a meeting with all of the team members to communicate the current social agreement.
options.rationale: Communicating the current agreement treats it as fixed rather than something to update.

options.text: Plan a meeting with the new team members to explain the rules included in the social contract.
options.rationale: Explaining rules only to new members sets them apart from the team.

questions.explanation: Adding people changes the team, so its working agreements should be revisited together. Updating the social contract with everyone builds shared ownership.
questions.mindset: Revisit team agreements when membership changes.

questions.stem: On an agile project, a team member raises concerns about health and safety issues related to the project deliverable. How should the project manager handle health and safety issues on projects?

options.text: Provide the customer with adequate documentation on health and safety information.
options.rationale: Documentation for the customer does not ensure the deliverable meets health and safety requirements.

options.text: Send the issue to the health and safety department.
options.rationale: Passing the issue to another department does not build the requirements into the work.

options.text: Design a health and safety policy for the organization.
options.rationale: Designing an organisational policy is beyond the project's scope.

options.text: Ensure that the necessary health and safety requirements are met in the definition of done (DoD).
options.rationale: Including health and safety requirements in the definition of done ensures every increment meets them.

questions.explanation: In agile projects, mandatory requirements such as health and safety are built into the definition of done, so no work is considered complete unless it complies.
questions.mindset: Build mandatory requirements into the definition of done.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned to a project that is transitioning the organization to adopt agile principles. The project scope definition is in progress, but the project team wants to have a less formal definition. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Review the scope and identify the desired deliverables and create contingency plans for identified risks.
options.rationale: Formal scope review and contingency plans contradict the team's desire for a lighter definition.

options.text: Organize a workshop with the product owner and project team to create a product backlog and acceptance criteria.
options.rationale: A workshop to create the product backlog and acceptance criteria provides a less formal but clear scope definition.

options.text: Create a communications website to share scope definition and product backlog with the project team.
options.rationale: A website shares information but does not define scope.

options.text: Meet with the project team to identify the mandatory requirements.
options.rationale: Identifying only mandatory requirements is incomplete.

questions.explanation: Agile teams define scope through the product backlog and acceptance criteria, created collaboratively with the product owner.
questions.mindset: Define agile scope through a backlog built together.

questions.stem: A customer is upset because a critical issue for a project deliverable has not been resolved by the agile team, even though troubleshooting has been running for several weeks. During the daily meetings, the team complains about the technical challenge and their lack of knowledge to resolve the issue. Which two actions should the project manager take to resolve this situation? (Choose two)

options.text: Escalate the case to a functional manager to bring a technical expert to the team.
options.rationale: Escalating to a functional manager to bring in a technical expert addresses the knowledge gap.

options.text: Explain the situation to the customer and include an action plan.
options.rationale: Explaining the situation and an action plan to the customer rebuilds trust.

options.text: Keep the team working on the sprint backlog in order to accomplish the next release milestone.
options.rationale: Continuing the sprint without resolving the issue leaves the customer's problem open.

options.text: Update the issue and risk logs, including the action plan to resolve the issue.
options.rationale: Updating logs should already have happened and does not resolve the issue.

options.text: Set up a new release date for this deliverable with the product owner.
options.rationale: Setting a new release date before having a solution may be premature.

questions.explanation: When a team lacks the knowledge to resolve a critical issue, the project manager removes the impediment by bringing in expertise and keeps the customer informed with a clear plan.
questions.mindset: Bring in expertise and keep the customer informed.

questions.stem: A project manager is managing a long-term project that is behind schedule. The client is concerned that the project will be delayed. Which two actions should the project manager take to address the client's concerns? (Choose two)

options.text: Create a new baseline schedule.
options.rationale: A new baseline hides the delay rather than recovering it.

options.text: Review the change control process.
options.rationale: Reviewing change control does not address the delay.

options.text: Add more resources to critical path tasks.
options.rationale: Adding resources to critical path tasks (crashing) shortens the schedule.

options.text: Perform a risk reserve analysis.
options.rationale: Analysing risk reserves may inform cost decisions but does not bring the schedule back on track.

options.text: Run some activities concurrently.
options.rationale: Running activities concurrently (fast-tracking) also shortens the schedule.

questions.explanation: When a project is behind and the client fears delay, the schedule is compressed on the critical path. Crashing adds resources to critical tasks; fast-tracking runs activities in parallel. Both recover time, at the cost of money or added risk respectively.
questions.mindset: Compress the schedule on the critical path.

questions.stem: A project is challenged by a multitude of problems resulting in defects and stakeholder complaints. The project manager has been contemplating a quick and effective approach to address the problems. Which two actions should the project manager take? (Choose two)

options.text: Gather the project team members and have a brainstorming session.
options.rationale: Brainstorming is useful but less systematic for diagnosing multiple problems.

options.text: Refer to the organizational process assets (OPAs) to assess lessons learned.
options.rationale: Reviewing lessons learned in the OPAs is slower and indirect when the project needs to diagnose its own current problems.

options.text: Use a trend analysis to engage some of the project team members.
options.rationale: Trend analysis looks at performance over time rather than root causes.

options.text: Use an Ishikawa diagram to help identify the problems.
options.rationale: An Ishikawa diagram systematically identifies causes of problems.

options.text: Use a Pareto chart to identify how the challenges of the project should be addressed.
options.rationale: A Pareto chart shows which few causes account for most problems, directing effort.

questions.explanation: Cause-and-effect diagrams identify causes; Pareto analysis ranks them so that effort goes to the few causes creating most problems.
questions.mindset: Find causes, then fix the vital few.

questions.stem: A project manager is managing a construction project that is 40% through the execution phase. The project sponsor has asked the project manager to ensure that all key stakeholders are still committed to the project. How should the project manager assess the stakeholders' current engagement levels?

options.text: By reviewing and updating the communications management plan
options.rationale: The communications plan describes information flows, not engagement levels.

options.text: By analyzing the most updated issue log
options.rationale: The issue log shows problems, not engagement.

options.text: By asking key stakeholders to submit a signed declaration
options.rationale: A signed declaration is not a practical engagement assessment.

options.text: By reviewing the stakeholder engagement assessment matrix
options.rationale: The engagement assessment matrix compares current and desired engagement for each stakeholder.

questions.explanation: The stakeholder engagement assessment matrix shows where each stakeholder currently is and where they should be, supporting engagement decisions.
questions.mindset: Assess engagement against what is needed.

questions.stem: The development phase of a new product has concluded. The validation test is about to start, but the test lead disagrees with the criteria for the test. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Understand the reason for the disagreement and submit a change request to the change control board if appropriate.
options.rationale: Understanding the disagreement and submitting a change request if appropriate handles it properly.

options.text: Implement a plan to change the test criteria so that the validation test can be started as scheduled.
options.rationale: Changing criteria without approval bypasses change control.

options.text: Keep the validation test criteria unchanged because such changes will impact the project schedule.
options.rationale: Refusing change without understanding may miss a real problem.

options.text: Explain how changes may impact the project and convince the test lead to go along with the original test criteria.
options.rationale: Persuading the test lead without understanding ignores their concern.

questions.explanation: When a key participant disagrees with agreed criteria just before a test, the project manager first understands why. If the concern is valid, the change goes through change control; if not, the reasons for keeping the criteria can be explained.
questions.mindset: Understand disagreements, then use change control.

questions.stem: A project manager leads a project team on a project. This project's goal is to enhance a product's capability in the market. What should be the top consideration when defining the team's key performance indicators (KPIs)?

options.text: Alignment with an individual's growth and development
options.rationale: Individual growth matters but is not the top consideration for team KPIs here.

options.text: Alignment with the customer's needs
options.rationale: Aligning KPIs with customer needs keeps the team focused on the product's market capability.

options.text: Alignment with the project manager's goals
options.rationale: The project manager's goals are not the measure of value.

options.text: Alignment with the sponsor's business goals
options.rationale: Sponsor goals matter but customer needs are the key driver here.

questions.explanation: KPIs shape what a team pays attention to, so they should reflect what creates value. For a project enhancing a product's market capability, aligning team KPIs with customer needs keeps the team focused on what the market will reward.
questions.mindset: Measure what matters to the customer.

questions.stem: In order to function optimally, a project team should have a project charter that states the vision or purpose of the project and a clear set of working agreements. To achieve this, which question should the project charter answer?

options.text: Why is this project being done?
options.rationale: Why the project is being done expresses its purpose and vision.

options.text: Why did the organization prioritize this project?
options.rationale: Why it was prioritised is portfolio information.

options.text: What are the key risks and their mitigation?
options.rationale: Key risks belong in planning documents; they do not express the project's purpose.

options.text: Who will be doing the work?
options.rationale: Who does the work is resource information and does not explain why the project exists.

questions.explanation: A team charter needs to state the project's vision or purpose. Answering 'why is this project being done?' gives the team a shared reason for the work, which guides decisions and working agreements.
questions.mindset: Start with why.

questions.stem: At daily standup meetings, several team members complain that they cannot concentrate due to a noisy work environment. Who is responsible for solving this problem by creating a more conducive work environment?

options.text: The project sponsor.
options.rationale: The sponsor is not responsible for day-to-day working conditions.

options.text: The team members.
options.rationale: Team members raise the issue but cannot always change the environment.

options.text: The product owner.
options.rationale: The product owner focuses on the backlog and value, not on the team's physical working conditions.

options.text: The project manager.
options.rationale: The project manager removes impediments, including a poor working environment.

questions.explanation: Removing impediments to the team's work, including a poor working environment, is part of the project manager's servant-leadership role. A conducive environment lets the team focus and deliver value faster.
questions.mindset: Clear obstacles to focus.

questions.stem: A geographically distributed project team has development issues between the colocated and virtual teams, causing productivity to decrease. What should the project manager do to address these issues?

options.text: Force the team members to work from one location.
options.rationale: Forcing everyone into one location ignores why the team is distributed and may be impossible.

options.text: Obtain special expertise to advise the team members.
options.rationale: Outside experts may advise, but the team still needs agreed ways to handle friction between locations.

options.text: Develop protocols for resolving conflicts between team members.
options.rationale: Protocols for resolving conflicts between members give colocated and virtual members a fair, agreed way to work through problems.

options.text: Set up face-to-face meetings with project team members.
options.rationale: Face-to-face meetings are often impractical for a distributed team and do not create lasting ways to resolve conflict.

questions.explanation: Mixed colocated and virtual teams develop friction when some members feel excluded or information flows unevenly. Agreed communication and conflict-resolution protocols give everyone the same routes to raise and settle issues, restoring productivity.
questions.mindset: Give distributed teams agreed ways to resolve conflict.

questions.stem: A project manager recently took over a project from a project manager who left the company. The new project manager is aware that the previous project manager had a very authoritarian style of management and made all the decisions regarding the project. The new project manager notices that a senior supervisor's morale is low. What should the new project manager do?

options.text: Increase the supervisor's level of authority.
options.rationale: Increasing authority presumes the cause is a lack of empowerment before it has been established.

options.text: Identify the cause of the morale issue.
options.rationale: Identifying the cause of the low morale gives the new project manager the understanding needed to respond appropriately.

options.text: Modify the role of the supervisor in the project.
options.rationale: Changing the supervisor's role is a solution chosen before understanding the problem.

options.text: Speak with the supervisor and update the project issue log.
options.rationale: Speaking with the supervisor is useful, but logging an issue treats a morale problem administratively.

questions.explanation: Low morale after a change in leadership may have many causes. The new project manager first gathers information to understand the cause before choosing a response.
questions.mindset: Find the cause of low morale before acting.

questions.stem: In a multidisciplinary project, a project manager is delegating some project management activities to several team members. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Develop a project communications management plan and distribute it to the stakeholders.
options.rationale: A communications plan is important but does not clarify who is responsible for the delegated activities.

options.text: Develop a mentoring plan and include it in the project status report.
options.rationale: A mentoring plan may help, but roles must be clear first.

options.text: Develop an organizational breakdown structure (OBS) and a work breakdown structure (WBS).
options.rationale: OBS and WBS show structure and work but not detailed responsibility for delegated management activities.

options.text: Develop a responsible, accountable, consult, and inform (RACI) chart.
options.rationale: A RACI chart clearly defines who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed for each delegated activity.

questions.explanation: Delegation works only when responsibilities are clear. A RACI chart makes roles for delegated activities explicit, avoiding gaps and overlaps.
questions.mindset: Clarify roles before delegating.

questions.stem: A project manager works in an organization where the culture encourages virtual teams. New challenges arise periodically in this environment, and the project manager currently is in the early stages of a new agile project. What should the project manager do to help the team overcome these challenges?

options.text: Perform a strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats (SWOT) analysis to quickly identify the team's status and take appropriate action.
options.rationale: A SWOT analysis quickly shows the team's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats in a virtual setting, informing targeted action.

options.text: Place a hold on all activities and gather the team for a meeting to discuss the new challenges identified so they can be immediately addressed.
options.rationale: Halting all activities to meet is disruptive and unnecessary.

options.text: Wait until the next daily scrum meeting to address the challenges so that the entire team knows what is going on and the issues can be discussed.
options.rationale: Waiting for the next scrum delays understanding recurring challenges.

options.text: Work with the product owner to determine the best course of action for the team to remove any impediments.
options.rationale: The product owner focuses on the product; these challenges are about how the team works.

questions.explanation: Understanding a team's situation before acting allows targeted support. A structured assessment such as SWOT helps identify where virtual teams need help.
questions.mindset: Assess the team's situation before intervening.

questions.stem: A project manager decided that using an agile approach for a new project will deliver the best outcomes. Some of the team members were resistant to using agile techniques and decided to use predictive approaches to carry out their work. What should the project manager have done at the beginning of the project?

options.text: Performed a skills assessment of the team
options.rationale: A skills assessment shows capability but does not win people over to the approach.

options.text: Advocated the use of agile techniques
options.rationale: Advocating agile techniques at the start helps team members understand the benefits and adopt the approach.

options.text: Engaged only the resources who were comfortable using agile
options.rationale: Engaging only comfortable resources may be impossible and avoids the change.

options.text: Hired agile consultants to lead the team
options.rationale: Agile consultants may help but do not replace the PM's advocacy.

questions.explanation: Adopting new ways of working is change management. People need to understand why the approach is being used and how it helps them before they will commit to it.
questions.mindset: Make the case for new ways of working from the start.

questions.stem: During an agile iteration, Task 1 cannot be completed on time due to unexpected challenges. Another team within the project is depending on timely completion of Task 1 in order to fulfill their part of the project. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Meet with both teams separately and ask them to figure out a way to meet the required deadlines and complete the project on time.
options.rationale: Asking both teams separately to find a way shifts the problem without coordination.

options.text: Meet with the product owner to reprioritize the iteration backlog, so that it does not impact other teams or obligations.
options.rationale: Reprioritising the iteration backlog with the product owner limits the impact on the dependent team.

options.text: Increase the number of team members for the project team and increase the iteration length, ensuring that the work will be completed according to schedule
options.rationale: Adding people and lengthening the iteration breaks the timebox.

options.text: Let team members know you want them to do their best under difficult circumstances, and make sure to note the iteration's challenges in lessons learned.
options.rationale: Encouragement and lessons learned do not address the dependency.

questions.explanation: When a task another team depends on will be late, the product owner reprioritises the backlog to protect dependencies and obligations.
questions.mindset: Reprioritise to protect cross-team dependencies.

questions.stem: A project manager observes that team members are in a low mood after demos. Feedback from stakeholders is constantly causing concern for the team. As a result, the team rushes through product demos, and the interaction between the team and stakeholders is minimal. Which action should the project manager take?
