options.text: Meet with the stakeholders and find out the root cause of their feedback. Work with the stakeholders to rectify the problems.
options.rationale: Resolving feedback with stakeholders alone leaves the team's confidence and communication issues unaddressed.

options.text: Verify that the project requirements are suitable and that the team members can do the work.
options.rationale: Requirements and capacity checks should already be done.

options.text: Coach the team to be more confident in their work and communicate properly with the stakeholders.
options.rationale: Coaching the team to be confident and communicate well with stakeholders improves demos and morale.

options.text: Consult the stakeholder matrix and identify whether any of these people are known to be difficult.
options.rationale: Labelling stakeholders as difficult does not help.

questions.explanation: Teams that fear stakeholder feedback need support to communicate confidently. Coaching turns feedback into constructive interaction.
questions.mindset: Coach teams to engage confidently with feedback.

questions.stem: An efficient, empowered agile innovation team does NOT understand why required approvals from the legal department are allowed to delay their progress. Eventually, the team confronts the product owner in a heated exchange. The product owner replies that the approvals are needed to check for existing patents which would block the product from going to market. How should a project manager prevent such conflicts?

options.text: Require that supporting department stakeholders attend the daily meetings to report progress.
options.rationale: Supporting departments attending stand-ups adds overhead.

options.text: Ensure that the product owner can be easily approached to respond to team questions and concerns.
options.rationale: An approachable product owner answers team questions early, preventing frustration.

options.text: Require the team to move a story to the Kanban blocked column if they have concerns about progress.
options.rationale: Moving stories to a blocked column records the issue but does not explain it.

options.text: Ensure that the product owner presents the team the rationale behind the refinement work flow.
options.rationale: Presenting the refinement workflow helps but less than ongoing access.

questions.explanation: Teams accept constraints when they understand them. Easy access to the product owner lets questions be answered before they become conflict.
questions.mindset: Keep the product owner approachable.

questions.stem: A newly launched product prototype is receiving a number of customer complaints. To reduce negative feedback, the team comes up with an action plan. At the end of the quarter, however, the project manager found there was no significant reduction in complaints. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Identify the key performers on the team and recognize them appropriately.
options.rationale: Recognising performers does not address why the plan failed.

options.text: Identify the team members who lack the required skills and train them.
options.rationale: Training presumes the problem is a skills gap when the plan itself or its measures may be wrong.

options.text: Revisit and reevaluate the project’s key performance indicators (KPIs).
options.rationale: Revisiting KPIs checks whether the action plan measures and targets the right things.

options.text: Report the status to the executive management team and seek help.
options.rationale: Reporting to executives and asking for help before analysing why the plan failed gives them nothing to act on.

questions.explanation: When an action plan does not improve results, the metrics and targets may be wrong. Revisiting KPIs makes sure the team measures and works on what drives the outcome.
questions.mindset: Recheck what you measure when results do not move.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned to take over an ongoing project. During the quality review, the team discovered that 40% of the deliverables have defects and require rework, with an expected worsening trend. What should the project manager's first step be?

options.text: Evaluate the cost of the rework.
options.rationale: Evaluating rework cost measures the damage but does not stop it.

options.text: Review the quality management plan.
options.rationale: The quality plan may need revisiting, but only once the cause of the defects is known.

options.text: Review the user stories.
options.rationale: Reviewing user stories assumes the defects come from requirements before the cause has been analysed.

options.text: Perform a root cause analysis
options.rationale: Root cause analysis finds the cause of defects so they can be prevented.

questions.explanation: A high and worsening defect rate means something systematic is wrong. Root cause analysis identifies the underlying causes so corrective action can stop the trend, rather than just costing the rework or reviewing documents.
questions.mindset: Find the cause before counting the cost.

questions.stem: During a project review meeting, an end user reports that the personal computers supplied for testing are experiencing performance degradation. Which three immediate actions should the project manager take to address this issue?

options.text: Record the issue in the issue log.
options.rationale: Recording the issue in the issue log creates a formal record of the problem and its impact.

options.text: Change the project scope.
options.rationale: A hardware performance problem does not justify changing the project scope.

options.text: Assign ownership for the issue.
options.rationale: Assigning an owner makes someone accountable for driving the issue to resolution.

options.text: Buy new personal computers.
options.rationale: Buying new computers presumes the solution before the cause of the degradation is known.

options.text: Implement a resolution of the issue.
options.rationale: Implementing a resolution addresses the problem.

questions.explanation: Issue management follows a simple pattern: record the issue so it is visible, assign an owner so someone is accountable, and drive it to a resolution. Jumping to purchases or scope changes skips understanding the problem.
questions.mindset: Log it, own it, resolve it.

questions.stem: One day before starting a task, the technical lead proposed a new implementation approach that could reduce the schedule by one week. However, if the approach does not work, the task will be delayed by three days. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Initiate a change request to reduce the schedule by one week.
options.rationale: A change request presumes the approach will work.

options.text: Tell the technical lead that the new approach is not feasible.
options.rationale: Dismissing the approach wastes an opportunity.

options.text: Refer to the network diagram to determine the float for this task.
options.rationale: Checking float shows whether a three-day risk is affordable against a one-week gain.

options.text: Communicate the possible three-day delay to the sponsor.
options.rationale: Warning the sponsor about a possible three-day delay is premature before checking whether float can absorb it.

questions.explanation: A proposal that could save a week but might cost three days is a schedule risk decision. Checking the task's float on the network diagram shows whether the downside can be absorbed without delaying the project, which decides whether the opportunity is worth taking.
questions.mindset: Check float before taking schedule risks.

questions.stem: A project team is small and the team members have known each other for a long time. The team's project is in the execution phase. Recently, a team member told the new project manager that another team member has been complaining about how the project is being managed. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Preview the current stakeholder engagement plan for the way to resolve the difficulty.
options.rationale: The stakeholder engagement plan does not address internal team issues.

options.text: Schedule a team meeting which will lead to the creation of a new social contract.
options.rationale: A team meeting to create a new social contract involves everyone in agreeing how to work together.

options.text: Notify team members that they should submit anonymous recommendations for a new social contract.
options.rationale: Anonymous recommendations avoid open discussion and do not build a shared agreement the whole team owns.

options.text: Send a survey to team members, requesting suggestions for dealing with the dissatisfaction.
options.rationale: A survey collects input but does not build agreement.

questions.explanation: Dissatisfaction inside a small, long-standing team is best addressed openly. A team meeting to create a new social contract lets everyone contribute to how the team will work, turning complaints into agreed norms.
questions.mindset: Rebuild agreements together.

questions.stem: A project team is unexpectedly audited. Several nonconformances were identified during the audit. Which three actions could the project manager have taken to prevent this situation? (Choose three)

options.text: Monitored conformance and quality standards.
options.rationale: Monitoring conformance to quality standards throughout would have caught nonconformances before an auditor did.

options.text: Anticipated potential nonconformance items.
options.rationale: Anticipating likely nonconformance items lets the team address them proactively.

options.text: Asked that the team remain ready for an audit.
options.rationale: Keeping the team audit-ready makes compliance part of normal work rather than a scramble.

options.text: Ensured that the auditors were experienced.
options.rationale: The auditors' experience does not change whether the project conforms.

options.text: Rejected the unexpected audit request.
options.rationale: Refusing an audit is not a legitimate way to avoid findings and may breach governance.

questions.explanation: Audits test whether work conforms to standards. The best preparation is continuous: monitor conformance, anticipate likely gaps and keep the team working as if an audit could happen at any time.
questions.mindset: Stay audit-ready by working to standard every day.

questions.stem: During a status meeting, a team member alerts the project manager that the delivery timeline for a component prototype is unattainable due to the unanticipated complexity of the requirements. After confirming the impending delay, the project manager must take action to address the situation. How should the project manager address this issue? (Choose two)

options.text: Identify the extent to which the complexity will impact the rest of the project.
options.rationale: Identifying how far the complexity affects the rest of the project reveals knock-on effects before they become serious.

options.text: Delegate prototype development to a more experienced team member.
options.rationale: Delegating to someone more experienced may help, but the requirements themselves are more complex than planned.

options.text: Allocate additional funding to the development budget to expedite delivery.
options.rationale: Extra funding does not by itself resolve unanticipated complexity.

options.text: Assign additional resources to prototype development and proceed as planned.
options.rationale: Adding resources and proceeding as planned ignores that the plan is no longer achievable.

options.text: Prioritize the requirements and concentrate on the most important ones.
options.rationale: Prioritising the requirements focuses effort on what matters most within the time available.

questions.explanation: Complexity cannot be removed, but the project can adapt: understand how far its effects reach, then prioritise requirements so the most important ones are delivered despite it.
questions.mindset: Understand complexity's reach, then prioritise.

questions.stem: A colocated project team is facing communication and collaboration issues. Some team members have roles that require them to work different hours, some arriving early, others leaving later. At a recent weekly meeting, several team members were absent. What is the best way for the project manager to ensure the team can attend all necessary meetings?

options.text: Encourage team members to work the same hours.
options.rationale: Asking everyone to work the same hours ignores role requirements.

options.text: Discuss the meeting with the missing team members.
options.rationale: Briefing absent members afterwards repeats the message and does not solve the attendance problem.

options.text: Create an information radiator for public display.
options.rationale: An information radiator shares information but does not replace meetings.

options.text: Schedule team meetings during overlapping core hours.
options.rationale: Scheduling meetings during overlapping core hours lets everyone attend.

questions.explanation: When a colocated team's members work staggered hours for their roles, meetings held outside the shared window will always miss someone. Scheduling them in the overlapping core hours lets everyone attend and hear the same message.
questions.mindset: Meet when everyone is there.

questions.stem: An organization is adopting an agile approach to fulfill its customer's requirements. Prior to that, the organization worked with specialized resources and project managers who were assigned to the project for a fixed amount of time. What should the organization change to better adopt the agile approach for resource planning?

options.text: The product owner should request specialists to be assigned to the team only when they are required.
options.rationale: Bringing specialists in only when needed keeps the old model and creates handoffs.

options.text: The team should consist of generalists and specialists capable of adapting to changing requirements.
options.rationale: A stable team of generalists and specialists can adapt to changing requirements, as agile expects.

options.text: The agile team should decide on which customer requirements will be developed and delivered.
options.rationale: Deciding which requirements to deliver is the product owner's role, not a resourcing change.

options.text: Customer involvement should be reduced in order to avoid disruptions and confusion.
options.rationale: Reducing customer involvement contradicts agile principles.

questions.explanation: Agile resource planning favours stable, cross-functional teams with a mix of T-shaped generalists and specialists, able to adapt as requirements change.
questions.mindset: Build stable, cross-functional teams for agile work.

questions.stem: A large transformation project has moved its project management office (PMO) to a virtual environment. There have been performance issues with the PMO team regarding the daily tasks they perform, which are now affecting the project. Which three actions should the project manager take to improve the performance of the PMO team? (Choose three)

options.text: Nurture confidence among the PMO team members by providing them with the required training on project management tools.
options.rationale: Training on project management tools builds confidence and capability for virtual work.

options.text: Hire a new senior manager for the virtual teams to improve collaboration between departments.
options.rationale: A new senior manager adds hierarchy without addressing the team's working conditions.

options.text: Suggest that management dissolves the virtual team or moves the PMO to a colocated area.
options.rationale: Dissolving the virtual team or relocating it ignores why it moved and is disruptive.

options.text: Build a collaborative environment by having regular connections among the PMO team members.
options.rationale: Regular connections among team members build collaboration in a virtual setting.

options.text: Provide access to communication tools to help the virtual teams connect better with the stakeholders.
options.rationale: Access to communication tools helps the virtual team connect with stakeholders.

questions.explanation: Virtual teams perform well when they have the skills, tools and regular contact they need. Training, collaboration routines and communication tools address those needs directly.
questions.mindset: Equip virtual teams with skills, tools and connection.

questions.stem: The project teams are having difficulties coordinating their tasks due to several constraints and dependencies. The project management office (PMO) suggests a monthly project report be distributed to stakeholders. However, the customer is concerned about not knowing the progress and what is holding up the project. What three solutions can the project manager use to resolve this situation? (Choose three)

options.text: Add a daily meeting to review project status and impediments.
options.rationale: A daily meeting on status and impediments makes blockers visible quickly.

options.text: Share missing performance information in the monthly status meeting.
options.rationale: Sharing missing information monthly is still too infrequent for the customer.

options.text: Add a daily or weekly project status report that includes dependencies.
options.rationale: A more frequent status report including dependencies gives the customer timely visibility.

options.text: Adapt a project status report to include missing information.
options.rationale: Adapting the report to include missing information tailors it to stakeholder needs.

options.text: Ask vendors to provide a monthly status report for the customer.
options.rationale: Monthly vendor reports are too infrequent and do not address the team's dependencies.

questions.explanation: When stakeholders cannot see progress or blockers, reporting must become more frequent and more relevant, including dependencies and impediments.
questions.mindset: Report as often and as specifically as stakeholders need.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on a global project with team members in several different countries. To manage communications, the project manager plans to hold virtual meetings and on-site visits once a month. What should the project manager do next while working with this team?

options.text: Ask the IT manager of each site to manage the technical components of the virtual meetings.
options.rationale: Delegating technical meeting management to IT managers does not set team norms.

options.text: Request the team members' résumés and become familiar with the teams' experiences.
options.rationale: Reviewing résumés is useful but not the next step.

options.text: Propose and establish a team charter with the rules and principles to be followed.
options.rationale: A team charter sets rules and principles that guide a global team.

options.text: Request the budget for weekly in-person meetings with the entire team to allow for direct contact.
options.rationale: Weekly in-person meetings for a global team are expensive and unnecessary.

questions.explanation: Global teams need explicit agreements. A team charter defines values, agreements and operating guidelines that help prevent and resolve problems.
questions.mindset: Set shared rules early for global teams.

questions.stem: During the execution phase of a project, the project manager is reassigned to another project. A new project manager takes over and quickly realizes that the project is facing issues with the quality and scheduling of some deliverables. Which of the following should the new project manager do first?

options.text: Update the project plan to reflect the new schedule and quality requirements.
options.rationale: Updating the plan before understanding the problems is premature.

options.text: Review the project schedule and focus on delivering the project on time and within budget.
options.rationale: Focusing on time and budget ignores the quality problems.

options.text: Meet with the project team to assess the situation and develop a plan to address the issues.
options.rationale: Meeting the team to assess the situation and plan a response uses their knowledge of the issues.

options.text: Evaluate the project team's skills and ask the project sponsor for additional resources.
options.rationale: Asking for more resources before understanding the issues is premature.

questions.explanation: A project manager taking over a project with quality and schedule problems first understands them. The team knows the details of what is going wrong, so meeting with them to assess the situation and develop a plan together comes before re-planning or requesting resources.
questions.mindset: Understand problems with the team before re-planning.

questions.stem: A project manager needs to ensure that all data security requirements are covered during a data warehouse development project’s execution phase. Each of the databases created during different project phases will have a specific data security policy to comply with governmental data security laws. The project manager wants to plan to meet these requirements. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Plan a database development specification, then regularly check to ensure the developer aligns with the specification.
options.rationale: Specifications and checks help development but do not provide formal compliance reviews.

options.text: Arrange for review of the data security status on a quarterly basis, and recommend remedial steps if noncompliance is found.
options.rationale: Planned periodic reviews of data security status with remedial steps provide formal compliance checks.

options.text: Tell the database developer to submit documentation of data security items and the steps they take to correct items that do not meet specifications.
options.rationale: Asking developers to self-report lacks independence.

options.text: Add a quality assurance specialist resource to the project team, who will be responsible for monitoring the data security quality of the project.
options.rationale: A QA specialist helps but is not a review plan.

questions.explanation: Compliance with data protection law benefits from scheduled formal reviews, at regular intervals or milestones, with corrective action when needed.
questions.mindset: Plan formal compliance reviews.

questions.stem: The government of a country intends to construct a multibillion-dollar railway across three major cities and hires a contractor to oversee construction. The project's design will be finalized within a few months of signing the contract, but the government has time constraints and expects the project to be completed within 24 months. The project manager wants to ensure a balanced distribution of risk between the government and the contractor. Which two techniques should be considered during the development of the project management plan? (Choose two)

options.text: Fixed-price increments
options.rationale: Fixed-price increments share risk by pricing each defined portion as the design matures.

options.text: Not-to-exceed time
options.rationale: Not-to-exceed time caps effort but does not balance risk between parties.

options.text: Early cancellation option
options.rationale: An early cancellation option protects the buyer only.

options.text: Dynamic scope option
options.rationale: A dynamic scope option suits flexible scope, not a fixed infrastructure design.

options.text: Graduated time and materials
options.rationale: Graduated time and materials adjusts rates with performance, sharing risk.

questions.explanation: When design is not yet final but timelines are fixed, contract techniques that share risk between buyer and seller help balance incentives.
questions.mindset: Choose contract terms that share uncertainty fairly.

questions.stem: An agile project is in the first of six iterations. The team is located globally, so the meetings are in a virtual environment. After the fifth daily meeting, the project manager realizes that not all members are actively participating. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the team members why participation is lacking.
options.rationale: Asking why participation is lacking is useful but less active than guiding the team.

options.text: Engage and guide the team to encourage all members to participate.
options.rationale: Engaging and guiding the team encourages everyone to participate in virtual meetings.

options.text: Ask each team member individually to participate in future meetings.
options.rationale: Asking each member separately is slower and treats a group dynamic as individual failings.

options.text: Allow the team to find their own way to fully participate.
options.rationale: Leaving it to the team may not resolve the issue early.

questions.explanation: Participation in virtual meetings does not happen automatically. The project manager actively engages and guides the team — creating space for each voice, using the tools well — so everyone contributes from the first iteration.
questions.mindset: Facilitate inclusion in virtual meetings.

questions.stem: During project execution, a project manager is informed that some resources will soon be removed from the project. What should the project manager do to address this situation?

options.text: Schedule a meeting to keep the stakeholders informed.
options.rationale: Informing stakeholders is part of the response but does not deal with the loss.

options.text: Inform the stakeholders at the next scheduled review meeting.
options.rationale: Waiting until the next scheduled review to mention it delays the planning response to a known loss of resources.

options.text: Update the risk register with this risk to project resources.
options.rationale: Recording a risk is useful, but the loss is already known.

options.text: Request resource leveling.
options.rationale: Resource leveling adjusts the schedule to the reduced resources.

questions.explanation: When the project learns it will lose resources, the schedule must be adjusted to the capacity that remains. Resource leveling rebalances activities against available resources, minimising the impact on the project.
questions.mindset: Re-level the schedule when resources change.

questions.stem: A customer is performing a weekly visit to a project site to inspect the final stage of product development. The quality manager alerts the project manager that the customer has been very unprofessional and reprimanded the team members during previous weekly visits. What should the project manager do to address this incident?

options.text: Draft a letter complaining about the behavior of the customer inspector.
options.rationale: A complaint letter escalates without understanding.

options.text: Allow the week to pass by, then send a complaint to the customer.
options.rationale: Letting the matter drift and complaining later leaves the team exposed to the behaviour in the meantime.

options.text: Discuss the matter with the project manager's senior management team.
options.rationale: Involving senior management may be needed later, but first the project manager should establish what happened.

options.text: Understand the situation by speaking with the team members and the customer.
options.rationale: Speaking with team members and the customer establishes the facts.

questions.explanation: Reports that a customer has been unprofessional must be investigated before acting. Speaking with the team members and the customer establishes the facts, so the response — whether a conversation or escalation — is fair and well founded.
questions.mindset: Gather facts from both sides before acting.

questions.stem: During product demonstration, a stakeholder suggests that the product does not meet expectations. What artifact should the project manager use to assess the stakeholder's suggestion?

options.text: Minimum viable product (MVP) description
options.rationale: The MVP description defines the minimum scope for release, not the acceptance conditions for each story.

options.text: Definition of done (DoD)
options.rationale: The definition of done is the team-wide quality checklist, not the story-specific conditions the stakeholder cares about.

options.text: Definition of ready (DoR)
options.rationale: The definition of ready governs when a story can enter a sprint, not whether it met expectations.

options.text: Acceptance criteria on the user story
options.rationale: The story's acceptance criteria state what the stakeholder agreed would make the feature acceptable, so they are the basis for assessing the suggestion.

questions.explanation: When a stakeholder says a demonstrated feature does not meet expectations, the reference point is the acceptance criteria agreed for that story. They show whether the gap is a failure to meet what was agreed or a new or changed expectation.
questions.mindset: Assess feedback against the agreed acceptance criteria.

questions.stem: A team member with sufficient experience and knowledge informs the project manager about a conflict with another team member and asks for advice and assistance. The project manager schedules a meeting to discuss the conflict with the team members involved. What should the project manager do during the meeting to resolve the conflict?

options.text: Determine a resolution together.
options.rationale: Determining a resolution together with both team members produces a solution they own and repairs the relationship.

options.text: Mandate the solution unilaterally.
options.rationale: Mandating a solution may end the argument but leaves resentment and does not build their ability to resolve conflict.

options.text: Separate the team members.
options.rationale: Separating the team members avoids the conflict and loses their collaboration.

options.text: Identify who instigated the issue.
options.rationale: Looking for who started it assigns blame instead of solving the problem.

questions.explanation: Collaborative problem-solving turns conflict into a joint search for a solution. When the people involved shape the resolution, it is more durable and relationships improve.
questions.mindset: Resolve conflict with the people involved, not for them.

questions.stem: After emailing a recent project status report, the project manager learns that a number of recipients are no longer involved with the project. The project manager needs to verify the distribution list for future status reports. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Review and update the communications management plan.
options.rationale: The communications management plan defines who receives which reports, so it is where the distribution list is corrected.

options.text: Review and update the schedule management plan.
options.rationale: The schedule management plan describes how the schedule is managed, not report recipients.

options.text: Review and update the responsibility assignment matrix.
options.rationale: The RAM assigns work responsibilities, not communication distribution.

options.text: Review and update the resource management plan.
options.rationale: The resource management plan covers resources, not report distribution.

questions.explanation: Report distribution is defined in the communications management plan. When stakeholders change, the plan is updated so the right people receive the right information.
questions.mindset: Keep distribution lists current in the communications plan.

questions.stem: A project team is working on a complex technology project. A competitor introduces a product with a new feature, forcing the team to make changes to keep their product from becoming obsolete. The software that the team was using was outdated and could not accommodate the development of the new feature and must be replaced with new-to-market software. The team is excited, but they do not have experience working with the new software. What should the project manager do to address this knowledge gap?

options.text: Train the team to use the new software.
options.rationale: Training the enthusiastic existing team on the new software closes the gap and retains their product knowledge.

options.text: Hire new team members with software knowledge.
options.rationale: Hiring new members adds cost and onboarding time and loses the team's context.

options.text: Ignore the technological advancements.
options.rationale: Ignoring the technology would leave the product obsolete.

options.text: Discuss the new product features with the competitor.
options.rationale: Discussing features with a competitor is inappropriate.

questions.explanation: When new tools are needed, training the existing team builds capability quickly and keeps valuable product knowledge in place.
questions.mindset: Train the team you have on the tools they need.

questions.stem: A project manager works in a matrix organization. Following a reorganization, several key project resources are reassigned to another project. The project no longer has the resources needed to successfully deliver the project. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Refuse to release the newly reassigned resources.
options.rationale: Refusing to release resources ignores the functional manager's authority in a matrix.

options.text: Review the communications management plan.
options.rationale: The communications plan does not recover resources.

options.text: Review resource allocation and utilization plans.
options.rationale: Reviewing internal allocation plans does not address the loss of key people.

options.text: Review resource needs with the functional manager.
options.rationale: Reviewing resource needs with the functional manager explains the impact and seeks a workable solution.

questions.explanation: In a matrix, resource decisions are negotiated with functional managers. The project manager explains the impact and works with them to minimise it.
questions.mindset: Negotiate resource needs with those who control them.

questions.stem: Team members are transferred from a predictive project to a newly formed agile team. The new team members are expressing dissatisfaction about the additional training they are required to complete in the internal project team chat channel. How should the project manager address this situation?

options.text: Ignore the complaints and assume that the new team members will adapt over time.
options.rationale: Ignoring complaints allows resistance to grow.

options.text: Schedule a meeting to discuss the concerns and provide clarity on the training's importance.
options.rationale: Meeting to discuss concerns and explain the training's importance addresses resistance constructively.

options.text: Remove the additional training requirement to alleviate team members' dissatisfaction.
options.rationale: Removing training leaves the team unprepared for agile work.

options.text: Send a memo outlining the mandatory training and consequences for non-compliance.
options.rationale: A memo threatening consequences forces compliance without addressing why the new members see no value in the training.

questions.explanation: Resistance to required training usually reflects unclear purpose. Open discussion that explains why it matters builds acceptance.
questions.mindset: Explain the why behind required change.

questions.stem: A project manager receives complaints from a project sponsor because of a delay in developing a prototype. The project manager responds that the delay was due to a lack of knowledge in a specific skill that was needed by the cross-functional project team. How could the project manager avoid this type of situation in the future?

options.text: Create training sessions at the start of the project, so all necessary skills are learned.
options.rationale: Training everyone at the start may not cover all needs and is inefficient.

options.text: List required skills for the project and organize the project team based on those skills.
options.rationale: Listing required skills and forming the team around them avoids missing capability.

options.text: Consult with the project sponsor to add training once the lack of a specific skill becomes apparent.
options.rationale: Adding training only when the gap becomes apparent is reactive.

options.text: Empower team members to problem solve where skills may be lacking, using the skills they do have.
options.rationale: Empowering the team does not create missing skills.

questions.explanation: Resource planning starts from the skills the work requires. Listing those skills and organising the team around them — including where a specialist is needed — prevents the kind of gap that delayed the prototype.
questions.mindset: Plan the team around the skills the work requires.

questions.stem: Regular check-ins with the delivery team reveal low morale and a lack of efficiency. What should the project manager do to address these concerns?

options.text: Perform a skill assessment.
options.rationale: A skills assessment presumes the cause is capability.

options.text: Conduct teambuilding exercises.
options.rationale: Team-building presumes the cause is relationships.

options.text: Remove all project roadblocks.
options.rationale: Removing all roadblocks is vague and presumes impediments are the cause.

options.text: Conduct a satisfaction evaluation.
options.rationale: A satisfaction evaluation helps identify the source of low morale before acting.

questions.explanation: Before addressing low morale and efficiency, the project manager identifies the cause, for example with a satisfaction survey.
questions.mindset: Measure before you fix.

questions.stem: A team member could not be reached by email or phone during the week that they were absent. The team member had not notified anyone on the team prior to their absence. Due to the absence, several successor activities are behind schedule, impacting the project’s critical path. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Add a new resource who can complete the work package in a professional manner.
options.rationale: Adding a new resource is premature and slower.

options.text: Discuss the situation with the team member, and work with them to identify a workable solution.
options.rationale: Discussing with the team member and agreeing a solution addresses the situation constructively.

options.text: Require that the team member complete the work package more quickly when they return.
options.rationale: Demanding faster completion ignores the cause.

options.text: Ask the functional manager for additional support on the project, including assignment of a new resource.
options.rationale: Asking the functional manager for replacement escalates prematurely.

questions.explanation: When a team member's unexplained absence harms the schedule, the project manager talks with them to understand and agree a way forward.
questions.mindset: Talk first, then plan recovery.

questions.stem: During a one-year project, a team delivered everything as requested and defined by the product owner and met all of the sprint goals. The project was on track regarding schedule, scope, and budget. A few months after the project release, the product satisfaction surveys show that the customer's level of satisfaction is surprisingly low. What should the project manager do to prevent this situation in the future?

options.text: Hold a kick-off meeting at the beginning of the project.
options.rationale: A kick-off meeting alone does not keep customers involved.

options.text: Improve application of test automation techniques.
options.rationale: Test automation improves quality, not fit to customer needs.

options.text: Increase project management office (PMO) involvement.
options.rationale: More PMO involvement does not add customer input.

options.text: Conduct periodic reviews with customer involvement.
options.rationale: Periodic reviews with customers ensure the product meets their needs.

questions.explanation: Meeting internal targets does not guarantee customer satisfaction. Regular customer reviews keep the product aligned with real needs.
questions.mindset: Involve customers in reviews throughout.

questions.stem: In an ongoing project, performance is continuously evaluated to determine benefits. Which two actions should the project manager do at the beginning of the project? (Choose two)

options.text: Ensure approval of the performance parameters with the stakeholders.
options.rationale: Approval of performance parameters by stakeholders ensures agreement on how benefits are measured.

options.text: Hold regular meetings with all of the stakeholders.
options.rationale: Regular meetings are useful but not the key setup activity.

options.text: Agree on the requirements for measurement tracking.
options.rationale: Agreeing measurement tracking requirements ensures data is collected consistently.

options.text: Review the project administration on a regular basis.
options.rationale: Reviewing administration is ongoing, not set up.

options.text: Simulate and predict the performance parameters for key stakeholders.
options.rationale: Simulating and predicting performance parameters is not needed to set up benefit measurement; agreeing what and how to measure is.

questions.explanation: Continuous benefit evaluation depends on agreement at the start: stakeholders approve the performance parameters, and everyone agrees how measurements will be tracked. Without that, later results are open to dispute.
questions.mindset: Agree metrics and measurement at the start.

questions.stem: A project manager is preparing to start a project and notices that the project team is having difficulties communicating and collaborating. The team has never worked together before. The project manager wants to understand each individual's behavior and tailor the leadership style to create a more effective team environment. Which tools or techniques should the project manager use in this situation? (Choose two)

options.text: Personality assessments
options.rationale: Personality assessments reveal individual behaviours and preferences.

options.text: Weekly teleconferences
options.rationale: Weekly teleconferences do not reveal behaviour.

options.text: One-on-one coaching
options.rationale: One-to-one coaching lets the PM understand individuals and tailor leadership.

options.text: Technical assessments
options.rationale: Technical assessments measure skills, not behaviour.

options.text: Cultural assessments
options.rationale: Cultural assessments address groups rather than individuals.

questions.explanation: Understanding individual behaviour helps leaders adapt their style. Personality assessments and coaching provide that insight.
questions.mindset: Understand individuals to lead them well.

questions.stem: A project manager has been engaged by a managing director to transform the project management office (PMO) from a waterfall structure focused on software development to an agile PMO. The manager of the PMO has been particularly resistant to the change. Upon investigation, the project manager realizes that the manager's resistance is due to a lack of agile knowledge may make them seem incompetent. How should the project manager proceed?

options.text: Ask the managing director to intervene with the PMO manager to explain why this is necessary.
options.rationale: Asking the managing director to intervene may increase defensiveness.

options.text: Ask the project team to support the transformation regardless of the PMO manager's negativity.
options.rationale: Asking the team to push ahead regardless of the PMO manager isolates a key stakeholder and deepens resistance.

options.text: Implement a change management strategy to ensure that the process meets governance requirements.
options.rationale: A governance-focused change strategy does not address the fear.

options.text: Implement a training program on agile for all staff to ensure there is congruency of learning for everyone.
options.rationale: Training all staff, including the PMO manager, builds knowledge and removes fear of seeming incompetent.

questions.explanation: Resistance rooted in lack of knowledge is best addressed through training that includes everyone, reducing fear and building support.
questions.mindset: Address resistance at its root.

questions.stem: On an agile project, a team member has been taking smaller, easier user stories from the backlog, not those with the highest priority. How should this be addressed?

options.text: Remind the entire project team that the highest priority user stories need to be taken from the backlog first.
options.rationale: Reminding the whole team treats one person's behaviour as a general problem and does not uncover why it happens.

options.text: Instruct the team member to select larger and more challenging user stories in the subsequent iterations.
options.rationale: Instructing the member to pick harder stories ignores the reason they are avoiding priority work.

options.text: Meet with the team member to understand why they pick easier stories and tailor the workload approach as needed.
options.rationale: Meeting the team member to understand why they choose easier stories reveals the cause — workload, skills, confidence — so the response can fit.

options.text: Retrain the team member on the core technologies used to build the product to address the skill gap.
options.rationale: Retraining assumes a skills gap before the cause has been established.

questions.explanation: When a team member consistently avoids high-priority stories, the behaviour has a reason. Understanding it privately first lets the project manager respond appropriately, whether by pairing, training, workload changes or clarifying expectations.
questions.mindset: Understand the reason before correcting the behaviour.

questions.stem: A company is transitioning from a predictive to an agile project management approach. The project manager has noticed that team members have valuable ideas on how to improve productivity. How can the project manager leverage these ideas?

options.text: Make use of project retrospective sessions for discussions and learning.
options.rationale: Retrospectives give the team a regular forum to share and act on improvement ideas.

options.text: Use iteration planning to discuss and adopt new ways of working.
options.rationale: Iteration planning focuses on what to deliver next, not on improving how the team works.

options.text: Develop and share guidelines for team training and mentoring.
options.rationale: Training and mentoring guidelines help development but do not capture the team's own ideas.

options.text: Engage with the product owner to facilitate fast-racking of the transition.
options.rationale: Fast-tracking the transition with the product owner does not use the team's ideas.

questions.explanation: Retrospectives are the agile mechanism for continuous improvement: the team reflects, shares ideas and commits to changes. They are the natural place to harness team members' ideas about productivity.
questions.mindset: Channel team ideas into retrospectives.

questions.stem: A project manager is beginning a new project and is starting to form the project team. The project manager has not worked with anyone from this team previously, and most of the team members do not know each other, and some are located in different countries. Which two actions should the project manager take to help the team work more closely together? (Choose two)

options.text: Identify the cultural differences and potential conflict areas to mitigate these going forward.
options.rationale: Identifying cultural differences and potential conflict areas early lets the project manager prevent misunderstandings.

options.text: Allocate a budget for the team members to temporarily relocate for the duration of the project.
options.rationale: Relocating the team temporarily is expensive and impractical.

options.text: Arrange virtual team building sessions that allow team members to get to know each other.
options.rationale: Virtual team-building sessions help geographically dispersed members get to know each other and build trust.

options.text: Select team members who have previously worked together to be allocated to the project.
options.rationale: Choosing only people who have worked together is rarely possible and limits the team.

options.text: Identify experienced team members to provide mentoring for the less experienced team members.
options.rationale: Mentoring helps skills development but does not bring the team together.

questions.explanation: New, geographically dispersed teams need deliberate effort to build relationships. Understanding cultural differences and creating virtual opportunities to connect help the team work closely together.
questions.mindset: Build connection deliberately in new dispersed teams.

questions.stem: While working on a long project with many changes, a project manager is informed by a team member that some users are uncomfortable with certain product functionalities released in the previous iteration. Which action should the project manager take?

options.text: Ensure that the team assignments are clear.
options.rationale: Clarifying team assignments does not address user discomfort with released functionality.

options.text: Obtain stakeholder feedback and team insights.
options.rationale: Gathering stakeholder feedback and team insights on the release lets the team adapt the product to users' needs.

options.text: Communicate the changes to the team.
options.rationale: Communicating changes to the team does not address the users' concerns.

options.text: Update the change log and issue log.
options.rationale: Updating logs records the matter without understanding or resolving it.

questions.explanation: Iterative delivery relies on feedback after each release. When users are uncomfortable with functionality, gathering their feedback and the team's insight guides the next adjustments.
questions.mindset: Use each release's feedback to shape the next.

questions.stem: A project manager is beginning a new financial software project in a very competitive environment. The regulations for compliance are clear, but the requirements are not clear. The customer stresses that they need results as soon as possible. Which implementation approach should the project manager choose for this project?

options.text: Repeating and refining project phases in multiple iterations.
options.rationale: Iterating to refine phases helps unclear requirements but does not by itself deliver usable results early.

options.text: Progressing through a linear sequence of stages.
options.rationale: A linear sequence of stages delays results and suits clear requirements.

options.text: Embracing change and focusing on delivering value.
options.rationale: Embracing change describes a mindset rather than the specific delivery strategy needed.

options.text: Focusing on delivering the project in multiple increments.
options.rationale: Delivering in multiple increments gives the customer usable value early while requirements are clarified.

questions.explanation: When customers need results quickly and requirements are unclear, incremental delivery puts usable value in their hands early and incorporates their feedback, while fixed compliance rules are built into each increment.
questions.mindset: Deliver in increments when speed and clarity are both lacking.

questions.stem: A project manager realizes that some newly hired team members have not been as productive as expected. The project has a very rigid timeline, and the lower-than-expected productivity issue is putting the project at risk. What should the project manager do to address this issue?

options.text: Provide additional training to the new team members.
options.rationale: Formal training takes time away from a rigid timeline and may not cover project-specific know-how.

options.text: Conduct job shadowing within the project team.
options.rationale: Job shadowing within the team transfers practical knowledge quickly from experienced colleagues.

options.text: Institute project milestone completion incentives.
options.rationale: Incentives do not give new hires the knowledge they lack.

options.text: Notify the team that productivity must improve.
options.rationale: Telling the team productivity must improve does not help the new hires.

questions.explanation: On tight timelines, learning from experienced colleagues through shadowing is a fast, practical way to bring new hires up to speed.
questions.mindset: Connect those who need knowledge with those who have it.

questions.stem: A project team has complete access to all project-related data, including visual data and information like the Gantt chart, prioritization matrix, story map, and other inputs. However, a project team member repeatedly requests more granular details on a work package than the Gantt chart indicates. The Gantt chart is confirmed to be comprehensive and current, and the other project team members feel that the current Gantt chart is sufficiently detailed. What should a project manager do to address this situation?

options.text: Create a new communication channel with granular updates.
options.rationale: A new channel duplicates information already available.

options.text: Ensure that the team member understands the granular information retrieval process.
options.rationale: Making sure the team member knows how to retrieve granular information lets them find the detail they need.

options.text: Remind the project team member that the Gantt chart was the agreed format.
options.rationale: Reminding them of the agreed format does not help them find detail.

options.text: Continue to ignore the project team members' requests.
options.rationale: Ignoring a team member's repeated requests damages trust and leaves them unable to do their work well.

questions.explanation: When information exists but a team member cannot find it, the answer is to help them use the available artefacts rather than creating new channels.
questions.mindset: Help people find the information that already exists.

questions.stem: A team is transitioning from a predictive to an agile approach. Which two obstacles are the team most likely to encounter? (Choose two)

options.text: Management provides freedom for the team to decide.
options.rationale: Freedom for the team to decide supports agile; it is not an obstacle.

options.text: Management continues to control the processes of delivery.
options.rationale: Management continuing to control delivery processes is a common obstacle in agile transitions.

options.text: Management would like the team to learn and adapt.
options.rationale: Wanting the team to learn and adapt supports agile.

options.text: Management support is lacking for team empowerment.
options.rationale: Lack of management support for empowerment is a common obstacle.

options.text: Management expects the team to keep their performance level.
options.rationale: Expecting performance to be maintained is reasonable, though transitions may dip.

questions.explanation: Agile transformations often stall when management retains command-and-control habits and does not support team empowerment.
questions.mindset: Watch for management habits that block empowerment.

questions.stem: The project manager needs to survey the necessary parties to reach a consensus and build a common vision for the project. To achieve better results, who should be engaged in the development of a common vision strategy?

options.text: The client and the delivery team
options.rationale: The client and delivery team alone exclude other stakeholders.

options.text: The delivery team and the project sponsor
options.rationale: The delivery team and sponsor alone exclude other stakeholders.

options.text: The project team and the stakeholders
options.rationale: The project team and stakeholders together build a vision that everyone supports.

options.text: The project owner and the client
options.rationale: The project owner and client alone exclude the team.

questions.explanation: A common vision needs input from both those who do the work and those affected by it, so everyone supports the direction.
questions.mindset: Build the vision with both the team and the stakeholders.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a new implementation project with a global project team. As team members are in different geographical locations and time zones, the project manager has to decide on the most effective team engagement strategy. What is the first action the project manager should take?

options.text: Develop a communications management plan.
options.rationale: A communications management plan designs how a global team will communicate across time zones.

options.text: Set up daily conference calls to track work.
options.rationale: Daily conference calls may not suit all time zones.

options.text: Ask all team members to utilize an online task board.
options.rationale: An online task board is a tool, not an engagement strategy.

options.text: Ask team members to align their work schedules.
options.rationale: Asking a global team to align their schedules across time zones is unrealistic and ignores local working hours.

questions.explanation: With team members spread across locations and time zones, engagement starts with a deliberate communications plan: who needs what information, through which channels, when and how often. Tools and meeting cadences follow from that plan.
questions.mindset: Plan communication before choosing tools.

questions.stem: In the middle of a release, the project manager is replaced. Feedback provided by the team to the new project manager hinted at team friction caused by the previous project manager's constant demands for rapid delivery. What approach should the new project manager adopt to quickly establish credibility with the team?

options.text: Do what the team needs to be done, maintain the action log, and provide feedback.
options.rationale: Serving the team is good but assumes understanding of what they need.

options.text: Help the team succeed with excellent service, on-time commitments, and an adequate budget.
options.rationale: Service and commitments are expected; they do not build credibility quickly after friction.

options.text: Assess the culture of the team, and observe and interact with them.
options.rationale: Assessing the culture and observing and interacting with the team shows the new PM how best to serve them.

options.text: Have the team explain what is needed, create tasks, and report progress on those tasks.
options.rationale: Asking the team to explain needs and report progress keeps a directive style.

questions.explanation: A new project manager following a leader whose demands caused friction builds credibility by first understanding the team: observing how it works, assessing its culture and interacting with its members. That understanding lets the new leader serve the team in ways it values.
questions.mindset: Observe and understand before leading.

questions.stem: The execution of a construction project in a remote area requires team members to live together in corporate dormitories when they are required to be onsite. Several team members approach the project manager to complain about the way one team member behaves after work. They have expressed concerns that the behavior is negatively impacting team morale and cohesion. What should the project manager do to address this issue?

options.text: Call a meeting to discuss the problem with the team.
options.rationale: A general meeting may embarrass the person without a framework.

options.text: Plan a team-building session to discuss the problem.
options.rationale: Team-building does not address the specific behaviour.

options.text: Move the team member in question to a new dormitory.
options.rationale: Moving the team member to another dormitory relocates the problem rather than addressing the behaviour.

options.text: Review the team norms and discuss this with the team.
options.rationale: Reviewing team norms and discussing them with the team addresses behaviour against agreed expectations.

questions.explanation: Team agreements define acceptable behaviour, including when it affects the team outside working hours in shared settings.
questions.mindset: Use team norms to address behaviour that affects the team.

questions.stem: As part of the project sprint review, stakeholders appear uninformed and are unable to agree on how to move the project forward. What should the project manager do first to ensure stakeholders are able to approve the project deliverables?

options.text: Review the communications management plan.
options.rationale: Reviewing the communications plan shows why stakeholders arrived uninformed and how to give them what they need to make decisions.

options.text: Perform a systemic stakeholder analysis.
options.rationale: A systemic stakeholder analysis is broader and slower than fixing the communication gap that is already visible.

options.text: Include the stakeholders in daily standup meetings.
options.rationale: Bringing stakeholders into daily stand-ups burdens both them and the team and is not what stand-ups are for.

options.text: Colocate the team to guarantee better teamwork.
options.rationale: Colocating the team does not inform the stakeholders.

questions.explanation: When stakeholders come to reviews uninformed and unable to decide, the communication approach is not meeting their needs. Reviewing and adapting the communications plan ensures they receive the right information in time to approve deliverables.
questions.mindset: If stakeholders are uninformed, fix how you inform them.

questions.stem: A project’s single sponsor has been replaced by a steering committee due to a significant increase in project size. How should the project manager approach this change?

options.text: Tailor communications to the new steering committee, recognizing that there has been a change in stakeholder structure.
options.rationale: Tailoring communication to the new steering committee recognises that a group of decision-makers needs different information and formats from a single sponsor.

options.text: Follow the initial project plan, recognizing that the sponsor is the key stakeholder and the new committee members work in a lesser capacity.
options.rationale: Treating the committee as secondary to the original sponsor ignores the new governance structure.

options.text: Schedule a low-key introductory meeting with the new steering committee and the team, while continuing to follow the initial project plan.
options.rationale: A low-key introduction while following the old plan does not adapt communication to the new decision-makers.

options.text: Ensure that the new steering committee members receive the project’s current status report.
options.rationale: Sending the current status report is a one-off action and does not adapt ongoing communication.

questions.explanation: Changes in governance change who needs what information. When a steering committee replaces a single sponsor, the project manager adapts communication — content, format and cadence — to the committee's needs.
questions.mindset: Adapt communication to the governance you now have.

questions.stem: A project manager is preparing for an organization-wide software system replacement project that will have a significant impact on business operations. It is crucial to provide training to ensure that everyone within the organization can effectively use the new software system, but training resources are limited. What is the most effective action the project manager should take to ensure successful training for all organization members?

options.text: Incorporate a detailed training and coaching component as a project deliverable.
options.rationale: Making training and coaching an explicit project deliverable ensures it is planned, resourced and delivered despite limited resources.

options.text: Determine the specific needs and requirements of different user functions.
options.rationale: Understanding needs of different user groups is valuable, but on its own it does not secure training delivery.

options.text: Recruit additional trainers to ensure adequate training coverage throughout the organization.
options.rationale: Recruiting more trainers may not be possible with limited resources.

options.text: Prioritize training efforts by identifying which features are most essential.
options.rationale: Prioritising features for training helps focus but does not ensure everyone is trained.

questions.explanation: When successful adoption depends on training, it should be part of the project's scope rather than an afterthought. Treating training and coaching as deliverables secures planning, resources and accountability.
questions.mindset: Make adoption activities part of the scope.

questions.stem: A project manager is experiencing issues with the functional manager of a project team member. The functional manager has given the team member another assignment and has told the team member that the previous project should be a lower priority. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Escalate the issue to senior management.
options.rationale: Escalating to senior management resolves the priority conflict at the level that sets organisational priorities.

options.text: Communicate the importance of the project to the team.
options.rationale: Communicating the project's importance to the team does not change the functional manager's instructions.

options.text: Refer the functional manager to the project charter.
options.rationale: Pointing the functional manager to the charter may not change their decision.

options.text: Request additional resources for your project.
options.rationale: Requesting additional resources does not resolve the priority conflict.

questions.explanation: When a functional manager deprioritises a project, the conflict is about organisational priorities. Senior management can settle which work takes precedence.
questions.mindset: Take priority conflicts to those who set priorities.

questions.stem: For an agile project, some team members have other commitments or responsibilities. The project manager faces the challenge of not having a team that is fully dedicated to the project. How should the project manager ensure good velocity, cycle duration, and on-time iteration completion with a nondedicated team? (Choose two)

options.text: Tell team members to log their time to guarantee that they prioritize their time effectively.
options.rationale: Logging time does not make people prioritise the project.

options.text: Request that the product owner and stakeholders provide cross-functional team members.
options.rationale: Cross-functional team members reduce handoffs and dependencies on others.

options.text: Get buy-in from the product owner and stakeholders for obtaining full-time team members.
options.rationale: Full-time team members provide the stable capacity agile relies on.

options.text: Revisit the resource log to ensure the most skilled resources are on the project.
options.rationale: Reviewing the resource log does not address dedication.

options.text: Deploy additional team members, irrespective of the story points or iterations.
options.rationale: Adding members regardless of story points increases overhead.

questions.explanation: Agile teams deliver predictably when they are dedicated and cross-functional. The project manager works with the product owner and stakeholders to secure such a team.
questions.mindset: Secure dedicated, cross-functional teams for agile work.

questions.stem: A member of a development project team informs the project manager that the operating system is not going to be installed on time due to a late upgrade by the supplier. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Determine the impact of the situation.
options.rationale: Determining the impact of the late installation guides how to respond.

options.text: Modify the schedule to reflect the situation.
options.rationale: Modifying the schedule before knowing the impact is premature.

options.text: Inform the stakeholders about the problem.
options.rationale: Informing stakeholders is part of the response, after impact is known.

options.text: Have the project team brainstorm a solution.
options.rationale: Brainstorming solutions comes after understanding impact.

questions.explanation: A supplier delay is a trigger for impact analysis. Before re-planning, informing stakeholders or brainstorming, the project manager quantifies how the late installation affects the schedule, budget and resources, which then shapes the right response.
questions.mindset: Quantify impact before responding.

questions.stem: A project team has been efficiently delivering results. The product upgrade they are working on must be released in three months or else a competitor’s new product will make their obsolete. Citing this reason, the product owner makes a sudden request for a feature revision. However, no one on the project team is capable of doing the work. The project sponsor is willing to extend the budget but CANNOT extend the schedule. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Meet the new demand by adding new resources with the required skills.
options.rationale: Adding resources with the required skills meets the new demand within the fixed schedule, using the available budget.

options.text: Recommend suspending the project until a firm decision can be made.
options.rationale: Suspending the project wastes the market window.

options.text: Discuss options with the project sponsor and choose the best one.
options.rationale: The sponsor has already set the constraints; the solution is clear.

options.text: Challenge the request and initiate customer research to determine whether the new feature is desirable.
options.rationale: Challenging the request delays delivery when the reason is compelling.

questions.explanation: When the release date is fixed by the market but the sponsor can extend the budget, and no one on the team has the needed skills, the fastest way to meet the demand is to add resources who already have them. Training takes time the project does not have.
questions.mindset: When time is fixed and money is not, buy capability.

questions.stem: A software delivery team at a large bank is frustrated by the documentation requirements put in place by the governance department in charge of their change control board (CCB). The project manager approaches the governance department and requests that they work together to reduce the amount of paperwork required from the delivery team, explaining that it slows them down and adds overhead costs. This is an example of what kind of leadership?

options.text: Servant leadership
options.rationale: Working with governance to reduce the team's paperwork is servant leadership: removing obstacles for the team.

options.text: Transactional leadership
options.rationale: Transactional leadership exchanges rewards for performance.

options.text: Directive leadership
options.rationale: Directive leadership instructs the team what to do; here the project manager is removing an obstacle on the team's behalf.

options.text: Constructive leadership
options.rationale: Constructive leadership is not a standard style.

questions.explanation: Servant leaders put the team's needs first and remove obstacles to its work, including organisational ones such as excessive documentation. Negotiating with governance to lighten the load on the team is a clear example.
questions.mindset: Serve the team by removing organisational friction.

questions.stem: A project team, distributed across three different countries, is having a difficult time arranging meetings. The team members are also unclear about the project requirements and are having trouble getting their questions answered. What should be done to increase project success?

options.text: Work independently until it is necessary to integrate the work.
options.rationale: Working independently while requirements are unclear risks rework.

options.text: Review the communications management plan and increase information sharing.
options.rationale: Reviewing the communications plan and increasing information sharing addresses unanswered questions.

options.text: Increase the frequency of team meetings to discuss any questions.
options.rationale: More meetings are hard to arrange for this team.

options.text: Bring questions to the functional managers to resolve issues across the team.
options.rationale: Functional managers are not the source of requirements answers.

questions.explanation: Distributed teams need communication designed for their constraints. Improving information sharing helps unclear questions get answered.
questions.mindset: Design communication for a distributed team's reality.

questions.stem: A company is implementing an agile approach for a new project. Which action should the project manager take to ensure they are acting as a servant leader?

options.text: Keep strict control of the team and their activities.
options.rationale: Strict control is directive, not servant leadership.

options.text: Serve as a backup in case a team member becomes ill.
options.rationale: Acting as a backup is not the essence of servant leadership.

options.text: Ensure the team follows all processes as defined without question.
options.rationale: Enforcing processes without question contradicts agile values.

options.text: Understand the bottlenecks and support the team to remove them.
options.rationale: Understanding bottlenecks and helping remove them is servant leadership.

questions.explanation: Servant leadership focuses on the team's needs so it can perform at its best. In agile teams, a key part of that is understanding what is slowing the team down and helping remove those bottlenecks, rather than controlling or policing the team.
questions.mindset: Remove bottlenecks for the team.

questions.stem: During a daily standup, some team members realized they were not all prioritizing the requirements in the same way. This could impact the current iteration's goals. What should the project manager do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Schedule an iteration review session and update backlog priorities.
options.rationale: An iteration review is for inspecting the increment, not clarifying priorities now.

options.text: Meet with the team and product owner to clarify priorities.
options.rationale: Meeting the team and product owner clarifies priorities and aligns work with the iteration goal.

options.text: Ask the project sponsor to redefine the prioritized values.
options.rationale: The sponsor does not order the backlog; asking them to redefine priorities bypasses the product owner.

options.text: Define priorities based on the urgency of requirements and risks.
options.rationale: The project manager does not define backlog priorities; that is the product owner's role.

questions.explanation: When team members interpret priorities differently during an iteration, the product owner — who owns backlog priority — clarifies them directly with the team, protecting the iteration goal.
questions.mindset: Clarify priorities with the product owner.

questions.stem: A project team is creating a stakeholder engagement assessment matrix to govern stakeholder management activities during project execution. The team learns that a key stakeholder is aware of the project, but is unsupportive of the outcome. What type of stakeholder is this?

options.text: Resistant
options.rationale: Resistant stakeholders are aware of the project but do not support it.

options.text: Leading
options.rationale: Leading stakeholders actively work for success.

options.text: Neutral
options.rationale: Neutral stakeholders are aware but neither supportive nor resistant.

options.text: Supportive
options.rationale: Supportive stakeholders are aware and back the project, which is the opposite of this stakeholder.

questions.explanation: The stakeholder engagement assessment matrix classifies stakeholders as unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive or leading. Someone who is aware of the project but opposes its outcome is resistant, and needs a plan to move them toward the desired level.
questions.mindset: Know where stakeholders stand.

questions.stem: A stakeholder complains that a product component is not easy to use. What should be the immediate next step for the project manager?

options.text: Check if the component meets the design and performance specifications.
options.rationale: Checking the component against specifications shows whether the problem is non-conformance or a design issue.

options.text: Collaborate with the stakeholder to confirm the acceptance criteria for the product.
options.rationale: Confirming acceptance criteria is useful after checking conformance.

options.text: Ask a user experience expert to meet with the stakeholder and explain the component design.
options.rationale: An expert explanation presumes the design is correct.

options.text: Raise a change request according to the stakeholder’s requirement concerns.
options.rationale: Raising a change request before knowing whether the component meets its specifications is premature.

questions.explanation: A usability complaint may reflect a defect or a gap in the design itself. Checking the component against its design and performance specifications first shows which, so the response — fix, change request or explanation — fits the real cause.
questions.mindset: Check conformance before changing designs.

questions.stem: In an environment subject to various elements of ambiguity and change, what should an agile project manager do to keep track of artifacts? (Choose two)

options.text: Update the artifacts frequently and quickly in a transparent fashion.
options.rationale: Updating artefacts frequently and transparently keeps them useful when ambiguity and change are constant.

options.text: Define which technology to use in the project management plan.
options.rationale: Specifying technology in the management plan fixes tools up front rather than keeping artefacts current.

options.text: Define which technology to use in the communications management plan.
options.rationale: Specifying technology in the communications plan does not keep artefacts up to date.

options.text: Increase the use of social computing tools.
options.rationale: Social computing and collaboration tools make artefacts visible and easy for everyone to update.

options.text: Use historical information from previous projects as a template.
options.rationale: Historical templates may not fit an ambiguous, changing environment.

questions.explanation: In uncertain, changing environments, artefacts are only valuable if they reflect current reality. Frequent, transparent updates and collaborative tools keep them current and visible to the whole team.
questions.mindset: Keep artefacts current and visible when things keep changing.

questions.stem: In the most recent sprint review meeting, the client announced that they need to implement two of the five modules committed for the project in a few weeks. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Conduct a brainstorming meeting.
options.rationale: Brainstorming generates ideas but does not replan the release around the client's new need.

options.text: Employ the nominal group technique.
