options.rationale: The nominal group technique ranks ideas but is not a release planning event.

options.text: Conduct a release plan meeting.
options.rationale: A release planning meeting reprioritises the work so the two urgent modules are delivered first.

options.text: Use prototypes to refine the design.
options.rationale: Prototypes refine design but do not reorganise delivery timing.

questions.explanation: When a client needs some modules much sooner, release planning is where the team reorganises the high-level plan to deliver the most urgent value first.
questions.mindset: Replan the release when priorities change.

questions.stem: After a few iterations, the project manager feels that even though the team is completing the work as planned, the team is not completely comfortable with some of the agile processes followed in the project. When should the project manager talk about this and make adjustments?

options.text: At the next daily standup meeting.
options.rationale: The daily stand-up is for coordinating the day's work, not reflecting on process.

options.text: At the lessons learned workshop.
options.rationale: A lessons learned workshop at the end is too late for adjustments now.

options.text: At the next retrospective meeting.
options.rationale: The retrospective is where the team reviews its way of working and agrees adjustments.

options.text: At the next iteration planning meeting.
options.rationale: Iteration planning focuses on what to deliver next, not on how the team works.

questions.explanation: When the team seems uncomfortable with parts of its process, even while delivering, the retrospective is the right place to raise it. It is the agile event dedicated to inspecting how the team works and agreeing adjustments.
questions.mindset: Adjust the process in the retrospective.

questions.stem: A developer has completed the deliverable for a feature. The product owner is not sure how to assess the quality of the deliverable. Considering that the project is using an agile approach, what kind of tool or technique should the product owner use?

options.text: Expert judgment
options.rationale: Expert judgement relies on others' opinions rather than seeing the working deliverable.

options.text: Decision making
options.rationale: Decision-making techniques help choose between options but do not assess a deliverable.

options.text: Demonstrations/reviews
options.rationale: Demonstrations and reviews let the product owner see the working deliverable and give feedback.

options.text: Checklists
options.rationale: Checklists help but do not replace seeing the product work.

questions.explanation: In agile, the product owner assesses a completed feature by seeing it work. Demonstrations and reviews show the working deliverable, let the product owner compare it with expectations and give feedback the team can act on quickly.
questions.mindset: Assess working product by seeing it work.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned to a new project. The requirements are still evolving, but there is a need to deliver business value quickly. What approach should the project manager take in this situation?

options.text: Develop mitigation strategies to address the risks of evolving requirements.
options.rationale: Mitigating risks of evolving requirements treats change as a threat rather than something to manage.

options.text: Use a product backlog and complete the highest priority requirements first.
options.rationale: A product backlog delivering the highest-priority requirements first provides business value quickly despite evolving requirements.

options.text: Ensure scope changes are documented in the requirements traceability matrix.
options.rationale: Documenting changes in a traceability matrix is heavy for rapidly evolving requirements.

options.text: Develop a feature burndown chart and show progress on requirements.
options.rationale: A burndown chart tracks progress but does not decide what to deliver.

questions.explanation: When requirements evolve and value is needed quickly, a prioritised backlog lets the team deliver the most important features first and adapt as requirements change.
questions.mindset: Deliver the highest priorities first when requirements evolve.

questions.stem: A company has decided to utilize a diverse international team that will work virtually. This will be the first time that the team is working together. The project manager is creating a communication plan for the project. What should the project manager do in order to build an effective project communications management plan?

options.text: Study the impact of cultural differences on communication.
options.rationale: Studying how cultural differences affect communication lets the plan avoid miscommunication.

options.text: Implement a one-way email push communication method.
options.rationale: One-way email push removes the dialogue a new international team needs to build understanding and trust.

options.text: Create a cloud-based resource folder for the project team.
options.rationale: A shared folder is useful but not the basis of the plan.

options.text: Appoint a skilled communications manager for the project.
options.rationale: Appointing a communications manager does not address cultural understanding.

questions.explanation: Effective communication planning for international teams starts with cultural awareness of communication styles and norms.
questions.mindset: Plan communication around cultural differences.

questions.stem: A project manager notices that a critical team member has lost interest in the project. The team member's lack of interest has led to decreased productivity. How should the project manager address this issue?

options.text: Escalate this issue to the human resources (HR) manager.
options.rationale: Escalating to HR before speaking with the team member treats a motivation problem as a disciplinary one.

options.text: Replace the team member with a more interested team member.
options.rationale: Replacing a critical team member is disruptive and discards their knowledge before the cause is understood.

options.text: Schedule a meeting with the team member to identify the cause.
options.rationale: Meeting to identify the cause addresses the issue directly.

options.text: Increase the team member's salary and bonus opportunities.
options.rationale: Offering more money assumes pay is the cause, which may well not be the case.

questions.explanation: A critical team member losing interest is a signal that something has changed for them. A private conversation to understand the cause — role, workload, recognition, personal factors — allows the project manager to respond in a way that actually restores engagement.
questions.mindset: Find out why interest has dropped.

questions.stem: An adaptative project team is globally distributed and the team members speak different primary languages. Daily meetings are conducted virtually in a common language. The project manager is made aware that there are some communication issues. Differences in pronunciation, accent, and vocabulary make it extremely difficult for some members to understand each other. What should the project manager tailor to improve the daily meeting and avoid misunderstanding?

options.text: Use the call to verbally summarize the work status as reported by the team members.
options.rationale: Verbal summaries do not solve accent and vocabulary difficulties.

options.text: Use an electronic task board to give a visual representation of work status and progress.
options.rationale: An electronic task board gives a visual representation that is easier to understand across language differences.

options.text: Ask for a change in the project's budget to provide access to a translation service.
options.rationale: A translation service adds cost and delay to a daily meeting and still relies on spoken communication.

options.text: Ask all team members to report on work completed, upcoming work, and blockers.
options.rationale: Asking everyone to report the standard three questions verbally repeats the format that is causing misunderstanding.

questions.explanation: When accents and vocabulary make spoken updates hard to follow, visual tools reduce reliance on language. An electronic task board shows each person's work and progress in a form everyone can read at their own pace.
questions.mindset: Use visuals to bridge language gaps.

questions.stem: The research and development team is planning to build a new facility that will focus on improving existing products the organization has developed. It will be a multi-year initiative. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Develop a scope management plan that will focus on the expected objectives of the initiative.
options.rationale: A scope management plan focused on objectives defines how scope will be defined and controlled for the initiative.

options.text: Develop a business case document that covers the return on investment (ROI) of the initiative.
options.rationale: The business case is typically developed before the project manager plans.

options.text: Develop a resource management plan to cover resources and contingency planning.
options.rationale: Resource planning depends on knowing the scope, so it follows scope planning.

options.text: Develop a communications management plan to address stakeholder needs.
options.rationale: Communication planning follows scope planning.

questions.explanation: For a new multi-year initiative, planning starts with how scope will be defined, validated and controlled against the expected objectives. Resource, communication and other plans build on that scope foundation.
questions.mindset: Define how scope will be managed first.

questions.stem: A project manager is concerned about delivering the planned business value because the product owner is not engaged. What should the project manager do to address the concern?

options.text: Review and update the communications management plan.
options.rationale: The communications plan concerns information flows, not engagement.

options.text: Review and update the stakeholder engagement plan.
options.rationale: Reviewing the engagement plan and adapting the strategy addresses the disengaged product owner.

options.text: Review and update the resource management plan.
options.rationale: The resource plan does not address engagement.

options.text: Review and update the risk management plan.
options.rationale: The risk management plan describes how risk is managed; it does not engage a disengaged product owner.

questions.explanation: A disengaged product owner threatens value delivery because they own priorities and acceptance. The project manager reviews the stakeholder engagement plan to assess whether the current strategy works and adapts it to re-engage them.
questions.mindset: Adjust engagement strategies when key people disengage.

questions.stem: A stakeholder on an agile project has attended the sprint demo where the team shows the minimum viable product (MVP) as defined by the product owner. During the session, the stakeholder complains that there were no release notes or technical product guides provided. Which two actions should the project manager take? (Choose 2)

options.text: Explain that technical product guides are not part of the agile process.
options.rationale: Claiming guides are not part of agile misrepresents agile.

options.text: Tell the stakeholder to contact the product owner for documentation.
options.rationale: Redirecting to the product owner avoids responsibility.

options.text: Clarify the stakeholder's need for release notes and technical product guides.
options.rationale: Clarifying the need is reasonable but less direct.

options.text: Acknowledge the stakeholder's concerns over missing documentation.
options.rationale: Acknowledging the concern shows the stakeholder is heard.

options.text: Provide the release notes and technical product guides as soon as possible.
options.rationale: Providing the documentation promptly addresses the need.

questions.explanation: Agile values working product over comprehensive documentation, but documentation that users genuinely need is still part of delivering value. Acknowledging the stakeholder's concern and providing the release notes and guides promptly addresses it.
questions.mindset: Acknowledge concerns and deliver what users need.

questions.stem: An agile project team has not completed the tasks within the current iteration. During a meeting, the project sponsor gives the team a final date for task completion. How should the project manager proceed?

options.text: Request that a functional manager becomes a team lead to ensure processes are followed.
options.rationale: A functional manager as team lead contradicts self-organisation.

options.text: Appoint a team leader to take responsibility for the team's iteration planning and completion.
options.rationale: Appointing a team leader for iteration planning undermines team ownership.

options.text: Advise the project sponsor that the team is responsible for managing work within iterations.
options.rationale: Advising the sponsor that the team manages its work within iterations protects agile roles.

options.text: Advise the team to comply with the new schedule provided by the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Telling the team to comply with an imposed date overrides self-management.

questions.explanation: In agile, the team plans and manages the work within its iterations. When a sponsor imposes a completion date on iteration work, the project manager protects that ownership and helps the sponsor understand how the team commits and delivers.
questions.mindset: Protect the team's ownership of its iteration.

questions.stem: A geographically distributed project team disagrees about status reporting. Some team members prefer detailed reports, while others prefer them to be brief. Some team members want to send daily status reports, while others want to send weekly status reports. How should the project manager resolve the issue?

options.text: Ask the team to adhere to the communications management plan.
options.rationale: Adhering to the communications management plan ensures consistent status reporting.

options.text: Escalate the reporting issue to the project sponsor for guidance.
options.rationale: Escalating a disagreement about report format and frequency to the sponsor is premature when an agreed plan already covers it.

options.text: Request that the team resolve the issue amongst themselves.
options.rationale: Leaving the team to resolve it may produce inconsistency.

options.text: Change the existing template for status reporting to accommodate.
options.rationale: Changing the template for everyone's preferences creates inconsistency.

questions.explanation: The communications management plan defines how and when information is reported, ensuring consistency across a distributed team.
questions.mindset: Use the agreed plan to settle reporting preferences.

questions.stem: A developer is expressing concerns about the time spent on daily standups, updating stories, creating tasks, and reviewing dependencies between stories instead of developing code. Other team members support the comment. What should a servant leader do next?

options.text: Ask for suggestions on how to manage their time more effectively.
options.rationale: Asking for time-management suggestions frames the ceremonies as the problem without explaining their value.

options.text: Reduce the interactions among team members to increase development time.
options.rationale: Reducing team interaction undermines the collaboration agile relies on.

options.text: Explain the definition of an information radiator to the project team.
options.rationale: Explaining information radiators addresses one artefact, not the concern about ceremonies and practices.

options.text: Acknowledge the developer's frustration and emphasize the benefit of each activity.
options.rationale: Acknowledging the frustration and explaining the benefit of each activity coaches the team on why the practices help them deliver.

questions.explanation: Developers new to agile may see ceremonies as overhead. A servant leader acknowledges the concern and coaches the team on how each practice — stand-ups, story updates, dependency reviews — helps them deliver faster and with fewer surprises.
questions.mindset: Coach the team on why practices matter, not just what they are.

questions.stem: A product development project has run into design issues. As a result, the team has decided to change the approach of the product design phase from a predictive to an iterative approach. What should the project manager do to ensure a smooth transition between approaches?

options.text: Schedule a workshop with the team to plan the upcoming iterations.
options.rationale: Planning the upcoming iterations with the team in a workshop builds shared understanding of how the new approach will work.

options.text: Work with the team to establish a team site and product artifacts.
options.rationale: Setting up a team site and artefacts is useful, but not the key to a smooth transition.

options.text: Meet with the product manager to analyze upcoming user stories.
options.rationale: Analysing user stories with the product manager excludes the team from planning the change.

options.text: Work with the product manager to define the number of iterations.
options.rationale: Defining the number of iterations with the product manager is a detail that the team should help plan.

questions.explanation: Switching a phase from predictive to iterative changes how the team works. Planning the first iterations together in a workshop builds understanding and commitment for a smooth transition.
questions.mindset: Plan a change of approach together with the team.

questions.stem: An experienced project manager joins an ongoing project and wants to estimate the amount of time required to tackle several complex tasks. The team uses a kanban board but is open to new approaches. The project manager suggests using story points. What is the first thing the team should do before implementing this new approach?

options.text: Calculate the story points only for new backlog items.
options.rationale: Estimating only new items leaves the team without a shared reference scale.

options.text: Estimate the story points required for the entire task board.
options.rationale: Estimating the whole board at once is a large effort before the scale is understood.

options.text: Convert all work in progress (WIP) items to story points.
options.rationale: Converting the current work-in-progress items to story points helps the team build a shared understanding of the scale using work they know well.

options.text: Measure and track story points over several sprints.
options.rationale: Measuring over several sprints is what comes after the team has started estimating.

questions.explanation: Introducing relative estimation requires a shared scale. Calibrating it on familiar work in progress helps the team understand what a point means before estimating new work.
questions.mindset: Calibrate new estimation methods on familiar work.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on an internal project and notes that the visions and goals of other department leaders are not clear. This creates confusion and ambiguity within the project team, and it is becoming difficult to distinguish between the wish list and scope items. Which document should the project manager review to clarify this situation?

options.text: Project Charter
options.rationale: The project charter documents the project's vision, objectives and high-level scope, clarifying what is in and out.

options.text: Communications Management Plan
options.rationale: The communications plan describes information flows, not goals.

options.text: Risk Register
options.rationale: The risk register lists uncertainties; it does not define the project's vision, goals or scope boundary.

options.text: Stakeholder Engagement Plan
options.rationale: The engagement plan covers stakeholder strategies, not scope.

questions.explanation: When stakeholders' visions blur the line between wish list and scope, the charter is the authorised statement of what the project is for and what it includes.
questions.mindset: Use the charter to separate scope from wishes.

questions.stem: During a weekly team meeting, the project manager reviewed task progress and found that a senior team member did not follow the plan. They performed tasks by personal preference, without communicating with the project manager. The senior team member is an expert and a critical resource for the project. How should the project manager address this?

options.text: Discuss this with the resource personally, then update the resource management plan if necessary.
options.rationale: Talking to the resource personally is right, but the resource management plan is not where working agreements are recorded.

options.text: Discuss this with the functional manager, then update the resource management plan if necessary.
options.rationale: Going to the functional manager first escalates before understanding the reason.

options.text: Discuss this with the functional manager, then update the team charter if necessary.
options.rationale: Escalating to the functional manager and changing the charter skips the conversation with the person.

options.text: Discuss this with the resource personally, then update the team charter if necessary.
options.rationale: Discussing it personally first, then updating the team charter if the working agreements need to change, addresses the behaviour and the norms.

questions.explanation: When an expert departs from the agreed plan, the project manager first talks with them to understand why. If their approach reveals a better way, the team's working agreements can be updated.
questions.mindset: Talk to the person first; update agreements if needed.

questions.stem: An organizational change program has met with internal resistance, a risk which was previously identified. A logistics manager is particularly affected, due to reduction of the team size and the rate of change driven by an agile planning of the predictive implementation. The manager's supervisor formally requests the change program to delay implementation for the logistics team. What should the project manager do next in response to this request?

options.text: Work with the program sponsor to re-prioritize the program backlog sequence.
options.rationale: Reprioritising the backlog may be part of the response but not the first step.

options.text: Request that the sponsor escalate the strategic issue to the executive committee.
options.rationale: Escalating to the executive committee is premature.

options.text: Perform root-cause analysis on the key factors causing the manager’s resistance.
options.rationale: Root cause analysis may help, but the risk was already identified with responses planned.

options.text: Review the risk register and implement the relevant risk response for the case.
options.rationale: Reviewing the risk register and implementing the planned response uses the preparation already made for this resistance.

questions.explanation: When an identified risk such as resistance to change materialises, the planned response in the risk register is the starting point for action.
questions.mindset: Use planned responses when anticipated risks occur.

questions.stem: Several items remain in the Kanban blocked column despite the team’s efforts to address them. The retrospective reveals that all the impediments can be traced back to a particular department head. Previously, the project manager has tried to educate this stakeholder, but they still show resistance. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Ask the department head for budgetary compensation proportional to the delays incurred due to lack of cooperation.
options.rationale: Demanding budgetary compensation is adversarial.

options.text: Use stakeholder analysis to identify an aligned senior stakeholder to influence the department head.
options.rationale: Using stakeholder analysis to find an aligned senior stakeholder who can influence the department head is an appropriate escalation.

options.text: Ask the team members to find other stakeholders who can help workaround the department head's barriers.
options.rationale: Working around the department head avoids the problem.

options.text: Set up an information radiator ranking stakeholders according to their active support of the project goals.
options.rationale: Ranking stakeholders publicly damages relationships.

questions.explanation: When a stakeholder remains resistant despite education, the project manager uses influence networks to address the resistance.
questions.mindset: Use influence networks when direct engagement fails.

questions.stem: An agile development team changes a design element in a project. Testing results improve dramatically over the next two iterations. At the third iteration retrospective, the product owner is unhappy to learn about the change to the original design and asks the team to redo the work based on the original design. How can the project manager prevent such situations?

options.text: Set out all decision path conditions in the ground rules and correct any deviations as early as possible.
options.rationale: Rigid decision rules do not replace ongoing collaboration.

options.text: Request additional funding from the product owner for re-work due to lack of collaboration with the team.
options.rationale: Requesting funds from the product owner is adversarial.

options.text: Ensure regular engagement with the product owner and run catch-up meetings if necessary.
options.rationale: Regular engagement with the product owner ensures changes affecting scope are agreed.

options.text: As servant leader, help the team to focus by removing all impediments.
options.rationale: Removing impediments is good but does not address product owner involvement.

questions.explanation: The product owner has authority over the product and its scope. When the team changes a design element without them, even for good reasons, rework can follow. Regular engagement with the product owner keeps design decisions aligned with their intent.
questions.mindset: Keep the product owner involved in design decisions.

questions.stem: A functional manager who is also a project stakeholder has time constraints and delegates project responsibilities to someone else on the functional team. This person becomes a new stakeholder. The new stakeholder is NOT attending meetings. How should the project manager engage this new stakeholder?

options.text: Examine the stakeholder engagement plan with the new stakeholder and assess their level of engagement.
options.rationale: Reviewing the engagement plan with the new stakeholder and assessing their engagement starts a tailored strategy.

options.text: Present the project schedule and the specific, assigned tasks to the new stakeholder.
options.rationale: Handing over the schedule and task list informs the new stakeholder but does not engage them or learn their needs.

options.text: Request that the functional manager briefs this new stakeholder and ask that they send them to all relevant meetings.
options.rationale: Asking the functional manager to enforce attendance is indirect.

options.text: Ask the new stakeholder to pair with a more experienced stakeholder to learn responsibilities.
options.rationale: Pairing with another stakeholder is a learning tactic, not a way to understand and plan this person's engagement.

questions.explanation: When a functional manager delegates their role, the delegate is effectively a new stakeholder. Reviewing the engagement plan with them and assessing their current engagement lets the project manager tailor how they will be involved.
questions.mindset: Engage delegated stakeholders as new stakeholders.

questions.stem: An R&D executive, who is a project stakeholder, occasionally visits the agile team’s work area to give instructions about urgent feature work. The team begins work. During sprint reviews, the product owner becomes upset that the team worked on the requested features. How should the project manager address the problem?

options.text: Escalate to ensure that the executive no longer interferes with the team.
options.rationale: Escalating to stop the executive's involvement damages the relationship.

options.text: Meet with the executive and product owner to agree on a work flow.
options.rationale: Agreeing a workflow between the executive and product owner restores order.

options.text: Require that the executive issues change requests for new items.
options.rationale: Formal change requests are not how agile teams receive new work; the backlog and product owner are.

options.text: Give the executive access to add new items to the backlog.
options.rationale: Giving direct backlog access bypasses the product owner.

questions.explanation: An executive giving the team work directly bypasses the product owner and disrupts priorities. Agreeing a workflow between the executive and the product owner channels urgent requests through the backlog, so the team works on what the product owner has prioritised.
questions.mindset: Route stakeholder requests through the product owner.

questions.stem: A company is losing market share to disruptive competitors with new business models. A cross-functional agile team has been formed to recommend ways to recover market share. How can the team increase their chance of producing successful recommendations?

options.text: Gain a deep understanding of why customers are disappointed by the company's products.
options.rationale: Customer disappointment matters but ignores competitors' value.

options.text: Focus on enabling profitable delivery of unique, high-quality and innovative products.
options.rationale: Profitable, high-quality products are good but not specific.

options.text: Understand how the competitors’ business models can reach more consumers at a lower cost.
options.rationale: Understanding competitors' cost advantages is only part of the picture; it ignores what customers actually value.

options.text: Focus on understanding the value consumers seek and the value competitors offer.
options.rationale: Understanding the value consumers seek and competitors offer targets recommendations.

questions.explanation: Market share follows value as customers perceive it. A team recommending how to recover share needs to understand both the value customers are seeking and the value competitors are offering, rather than focusing on a single dimension.
questions.mindset: Compete on understanding value.

questions.stem: A new project team is setting early priorities, and they plan to gain the customer's trust by delivering value as quickly as possible. Team member mentions that they have worked with the project sponsor on other projects. How should the project manager connect these two facts and create an advantage for the project team?

options.text: Make team member the project leader since they already know the sponsor.
options.rationale: Making someone leader because they know the sponsor is not merit-based.

options.text: Ask team member to tell the whole team everything they know about the sponsor so that the team can work better.
options.rationale: Sharing everything about the sponsor is inappropriate.

options.text: Explore how team member can use personal influence with the sponsor to increase the project's potential for benefits realization.
options.rationale: Using the team member's influence with the sponsor helps benefits realisation.

options.text: Discuss whether team member has a conflict of interest in order to maintain an ethical standard.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests a conflict of interest; treating the relationship as a problem wastes a useful connection.

questions.explanation: Existing relationships are an asset. A team member who knows the sponsor can use that personal influence to help the team understand the sponsor's needs and priorities faster, supporting early value delivery and benefits realisation.
questions.mindset: Use relationships to understand stakeholders.

questions.stem: The latest software build for a virtual reality headset release did NOT include urgent change requests already implemented by the electronics workstream. The product owner informed the software team about the change during a daily meeting, but NO ONE recorded it. What should the project manager to avoid this problem in the future?

options.text: Refine the product backlog with the team and product owner before the next iteration.
options.rationale: Refinement before the next iteration is too late.

options.text: Increase the frequency of backlog refinement meetings and note the change in the retrospective.
options.rationale: More frequent refinement meetings add overhead and still would not have captured a change announced verbally in a daily meeting.

options.text: Run an ad-hoc retrospective and add the agreed urgent change process to the team charter.
options.rationale: An ad-hoc retrospective and team charter update creates a process for urgent changes.

options.text: Privately remind the team lead that the role requires fast and proactive problem solving.
options.rationale: Blaming the team lead is not servant leadership.

questions.explanation: When a process gap lets an urgent change slip through, the team fixes the process promptly. An ad-hoc retrospective agrees how urgent changes will be captured and handled, and recording it in the team charter makes the agreement stick.
questions.mindset: Fix process gaps promptly and record the agreement.

questions.stem: A project manager is planning the construction of a new public library. The community and project stakeholders are having difficulty agreeing on the key features to be included in the final design. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Facilitate a workshop to gather input from all stakeholders
options.rationale: A workshop gathers input but may not resolve disagreement.

options.text: Define the differences between essential and non-essential features
options.rationale: Defining essential features presumes agreement.

options.text: Involve the design consultants to mediate stakeholder discussions
options.rationale: Handing mediation to the design consultants moves a stakeholder facilitation task away from the project manager.

options.text: Identify the root cause of the stakeholders' inability to agree on the project scope
options.rationale: Identifying the root cause of disagreement lets the PM facilitate a resolution.

questions.explanation: When stakeholders cannot agree on key features, the project manager first understands why: conflicting needs, missing information, power dynamics or unclear priorities. Knowing the root cause lets them facilitate the right discussions and negotiations to reach consensus.
questions.mindset: Understand disagreement before facilitating.

questions.stem: A project manager convenes an emergency session with the software development team to address significant bugs that are delaying the project's delivery. The product owner suggests conducting a thorough root cause analysis (RCA) to identify the underlying issues. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Collaborate with the team to discuss the RCA suggestion and decide collectively on the next steps
options.rationale: Discussing the RCA suggestion with the team and deciding together draws on everyone's knowledge and builds commitment to the next steps.

options.text: Encourage a lead developer to take charge of the RCA process, fostering team autonomy
options.rationale: Handing the RCA to one lead developer before the team has agreed to it removes the collective decision.

options.text: Coordinate with the quality assurance lead to refine testing processes based on the RCA outcomes
options.rationale: Refining testing based on RCA outcomes assumes the analysis has already been done.

options.text: Organize the session to ensure all team members contribute their insights and potential solutions
options.rationale: Making sure everyone contributes ideas is good facilitation, but it skips deciding whether and how to do the RCA.

questions.explanation: When a significant problem stalls delivery and someone proposes a root cause analysis, the team decides together how to proceed. Collective decisions draw on everyone's insight and build ownership of the fix.
questions.mindset: Decide how to tackle problems together with the team.

questions.stem: A project manager overseeing the launch of a new e-commerce platform discovers that the finance department has concerns about not being involved in the cost estimations and their potential impact on the projected returns. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Amend the stakeholder engagement plan to better integrate finance in future phases
options.rationale: Amending the engagement plan for later phases does not deal with the concerns now.

options.text: Document the exclusion of the finance team as a risk to project success
options.rationale: Documenting the exclusion as a risk records it but does not engage the finance team.

options.text: Maintain the project timeline but plan a financial review before the final phase
options.rationale: Deferring a financial review until the final phase leaves the concern unaddressed for too long.

options.text: Organize a meeting with the finance team to understand the concerns
options.rationale: Meeting the finance team to understand their concerns addresses them early, before they grow into delays.

questions.explanation: Stakeholders who feel excluded from decisions that affect them should be engaged promptly. Understanding their concerns early avoids larger problems later.
questions.mindset: Engage concerned stakeholders early.

questions.stem: During a critical phase of a software development project, a key developer notifies the project manager that they will need to take an unexpected leave, impacting the completion of a crucial backlog item scheduled for demonstration in the upcoming sprint review. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Insist that the developer work remotely during their leave to ensure the backlog item is completed on time
options.rationale: Insisting the developer works during leave is inappropriate.

options.text: Escalate the issue to senior management and demand that they assign an additional resource immediately
options.rationale: Demanding resources from senior management escalates too early.

options.text: Reevaluate the sprint goals and backlog priorities, consult with the team about adjustments, and communicate the revised plan to stakeholders
options.rationale: Reevaluating the sprint goal and priorities with the team, then communicating the revised plan, responds realistically to the loss.

options.text: Cancel the upcoming sprint review, citing the lack of progress on the crucial backlog item
options.rationale: Cancelling the sprint review removes a key feedback opportunity.

questions.explanation: When a key person becomes unavailable mid-sprint, the team reassesses what can be achieved, the product owner adjusts priorities and stakeholders are informed of the revised plan.
questions.mindset: Adjust the sprint plan to the capacity you have.

questions.stem: A project manager is preparing for a sprint planning session for a new feature in a healthcare management system. This meeting aims to determine the amount of work for the upcoming sprint. Which two pieces of information are essential for the project manager to ensure the meeting is productive and effective? (Choose two.)

options.text: Current project phase timeline
options.rationale: The phase timeline gives context but does not size the sprint.

options.text: Product Market Place Goal
options.rationale: A market goal is strategic context, not planning input for a sprint.

options.text: Updated risk assessment
options.rationale: A risk assessment is useful but not essential to sizing the sprint's work.

options.text: Detailed product backlog
options.rationale: A detailed, prioritised product backlog provides the candidate work for the sprint.

options.text: Team performance metrics
options.rationale: Team performance metrics such as velocity show how much work the team can take on.

questions.explanation: Sprint planning combines what to work on (the prioritised backlog) with how much the team can do (its performance metrics, such as velocity).
questions.mindset: Plan sprints from the backlog and the team's capacity.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading an intricate biotechnology research project characterized by significant ambiguity and unpredictability. A suggestion has been made to introduce a system to gauge the quality of the project outputs effectively. What hybrid techniques should the project manager employ to ensure quality assurance?

options.text: Combine weekly sprints with quarterly external audits to validate project standards
options.rationale: Quarterly external audits are too infrequent for an ambiguous, fast-changing research environment.

options.text: Merge traditional milestone reviews with agile sprint demonstrations
options.rationale: Milestone reviews with sprint demos help, but they are periodic checks rather than built-in quality practices.

options.text: Adopt pair programming and customer feedback sessions
options.rationale: Pair work and regular customer feedback build quality into the work and validate it continuously.

options.text: Integrate continuous integration tools with formal quality control checkpoints
options.rationale: Continuous integration with formal checkpoints suits software more than research outputs.

questions.explanation: In uncertain environments, quality is maintained by building it in continuously: peer collaboration catches errors early and customer feedback confirms outputs meet needs.
questions.mindset: Build quality in continuously when uncertainty is high.

questions.stem: A project team in a digital marketing project discovers that their key design software license has expired, halting the team work on a critical campaign visuals. What is the most effective initial action for the project manager to take?

options.text: Request that the team manually sketch the campaign concepts while awaiting license renewal
options.rationale: Manual sketching is an inefficient workaround.

options.text: Have the team work with the IT department to renew the license
options.rationale: Having the team work with IT diverts them from their work.

options.text: Prioritize other aspects of the campaign that don't require design software
options.rationale: Prioritising other work helps but does not remove the blocker.

options.text: Coordinate with the IT department to promptly renew the software license
options.rationale: Coordinating with IT to renew the licence removes the impediment quickly.

questions.explanation: When an expired licence halts critical work, the project manager removes the impediment directly — coordinating the renewal with IT — so the team can resume as quickly as possible without being pulled into administrative tasks.
questions.mindset: Remove blockers yourself so the team can keep working.

questions.stem: A project manager is overseeing the development of an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system and has decided that a combination of Scrum and Kanban methodologies would be most effective. However, the product owner is unsure about how to begin organizing and prioritizing work. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Guide the product owner on developing and prioritizing a comprehensive product backlog
options.rationale: Guiding the product owner to build and prioritise a product backlog gives them the foundation to organise the work.

options.text: Have a team member explain the integration of Scrum and Kanban principles to the product own to enhance understanding
options.rationale: Having a team member explain methodology integration misses the immediate need.

options.text: Recommend that the project team use visual management tools to improve workflow visibility
options.rationale: Visual tools help workflow but not backlog ownership.

options.text: Teach the product owner how to map out process flows to better understand task sequencing
options.rationale: Process mapping is not the product owner's key need.

questions.explanation: A product owner unsure how to organise work needs coaching on the product backlog, the primary tool for prioritising value.
questions.mindset: Coach product owners on building and ordering the backlog.

questions.stem: On an agricultural development project, a key team member expresses dissatisfaction with the current risk management strategy, feeling it doesn't adequately address the potential for unpredictable weather conditions affecting crop trials. What action should the project manager take first?

options.text: Implement a contingency fund specifically for weather-related delays
options.rationale: A contingency fund is a response chosen before the risk is reassessed.

options.text: Consult with external agricultural experts to gather insights on managing weather-related risks
options.rationale: External experts may add insight later, but the first step is to review the plan with the team that raised the concern.

options.text: Reevaluate the risk management plan and risk register with the entire team to incorporate feedback on weather-related risks
options.rationale: Reevaluating the risk plan and register with the team incorporates the concern.

options.text: Adjust project timelines and milestones to allow for greater flexibility in response to weather changes
options.rationale: Changing timelines and milestones is premature before the risk has been reassessed.

questions.explanation: When a team member feels an important risk is not adequately addressed, the project manager reviews the risk management plan and register with the team. That incorporates their knowledge and may reveal a gap in the current responses.
questions.mindset: Revisit risk plans when the team raises concerns.

questions.stem: During the rollout of a new IT system within a large corporation, the project manager observes that discussions in stakeholder meetings are frequently derailed by a participant who delves into technical details irrelevant to the meeting's objectives. This behavior is causing meetings to overrun and is reducing the time available to cover all agenda items, leading to dissatisfaction among stakeholders. What action should the project manager take to ensure meetings are more focused and productive?

options.text: Emphasize the meeting agenda at the start and kindly remind participants to keep discussions on-topic
options.rationale: Emphasising the agenda and gently reminding participants to stay on topic keeps meetings focused and respectful.

options.text: Allocate specific times for open discussion at the end of meetings to cater to additional topics
options.rationale: Open discussion time at the end may still overrun.

options.text: Introduce a meeting co-facilitator to help steer conversations back to the agenda when they go off-course
options.rationale: A co-facilitator adds cost and complexity when clear agenda-setting by the project manager would do.

options.text: Implement a suggestion box for topics that require further discussion outside of the scheduled meetings
options.rationale: A suggestion box delays relevant discussion and does not keep the meeting itself on track.

questions.explanation: Meetings stay productive when their purpose and agenda are clear and reinforced. Restating the agenda at the start and gently steering discussion back on topic keeps meetings focused without singling anyone out.
questions.mindset: Keep meetings on purpose with gentle facilitation.

questions.stem: A project manager has begun a complex airport expansion project. Although the project is in the initiation phase, the sponsor keeps asking for concrete dates for the most important project milestones. When will the project manager be able to provide the requested information?

options.text: After initial risk assessments are completed to estimate timelines
options.rationale: Initial risk assessments are not enough for concrete dates.

options.text: At the end of the planning phase, once detailed schedules and risk assessments are completed
options.rationale: Concrete milestone dates are available once detailed planning and risk assessments are complete.

options.text: During the execution phase, when the project is underway and progress can be measured
options.rationale: Waiting until execution to give milestone dates leaves the sponsor without commitments they need for planning.

options.text: Once the project charter is signed, as it will outline the initial milestones
options.rationale: The charter gives only high-level milestones.

questions.explanation: Concrete, reliable milestone dates come from detailed planning — schedules built on estimates and informed by risk assessment. In initiation the project manager can give only high-level targets; firm dates follow at the end of planning.
questions.mindset: Commit to dates once planning supports them.

questions.stem: A project manager is overseeing a large-scale infrastructure project in a hierarchical organization. The project team members are used to receiving direct instructions, and their performance reviews are based on task completion percentages. After discussing with the sponsor, the project manager realizes that some tasks need to be reassigned to meet the next milestone. This change could be perceived as a negative reflection on the current assignees' performance. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Assign the tasks to the most skilled team members without further discussion
options.rationale: Reassigning without discussion may be seen as blame.

options.text: Hold a team meeting to explain the changes and collaborate on reassigning tasks
options.rationale: A team meeting to explain and collaborate reduces feelings of blame.

options.text: Privately ask a senior team member to take over the tasks and inform the others of the reassignment
options.rationale: Quietly giving the tasks to a senior member and announcing it later can fuel suspicion and feelings of blame.

options.text: Send an email to the team outlining the task changes and the reasons behind them
options.rationale: An email explains the change but gives no chance for dialogue in a culture sensitive to perceived performance judgements.

questions.explanation: In a hierarchical culture where task completion drives performance reviews, reassigning work can feel like a verdict on people. Explaining the reasons openly and collaborating on the reassignment preserves trust and reduces any sense of blame.
questions.mindset: Reassign work openly.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a city park renovation project. During a status meeting with city officials, the project manager provides an update about a significant deliverable. Some of the officials claim they were not informed about this deliverable. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Confirm if the project scope has been updated to include the deliverable
options.rationale: Checking scope does not address the communication gap.

options.text: Meet with these officials to review the communication plan and clarify the deliverable
options.rationale: Meeting officials to review the communication plan clarifies the deliverable and fixes gaps.

options.text: Check the attendance records of these officials at prior project meetings
options.rationale: Checking attendance records looks for someone to blame instead of fixing how information reaches the officials.

options.text: Review the project documentation to ensure the deliverable was communicated
options.rationale: Reviewing documentation alone does not re-engage the officials.

questions.explanation: When stakeholders say they were not informed about a deliverable, the communication approach has not worked for them. Meeting them to review the communication plan and clarify the deliverable closes the gap and prevents future misunderstandings.
questions.mindset: Fix communication gaps with those affected.

questions.stem: A project manager is overseeing the construction of a new office building. A key stakeholder complains that they never received the structural integrity test status reports. The project manager provides the reports, and the stakeholder notices that an important aspect of the structure was not tested. Which tool should the project manager have used to prevent this situation?

options.text: Communication log
options.rationale: A communication log records what was sent but does not define needs.

options.text: Requirements traceability matrix
options.rationale: The traceability matrix links requirements to tests and would have exposed the untested aspect.

options.text: Stakeholder register
options.rationale: The stakeholder register records stakeholders' requirements and expectations, including which reports they need.

options.text: Quality management plan
options.rationale: The quality management plan defines standards but not stakeholder reporting.

questions.explanation: The stakeholder register records each stakeholder's requirements, expectations and information needs. Had the stakeholder's need for structural test reports been captured there, they would have been planned for and delivered.
questions.mindset: Record stakeholder needs in the register.

questions.stem: A project manager is overseeing the development of a new healthcare facility. The project team is struggling to understand some critical aspects of the project's scope. A senior subject matter expert (SME) from the organization's headquarters is available for one week. What should the project manager do to benefit from the SME's presence?

options.text: Conduct a workshop with the SME to address the team's challenges
options.rationale: A single workshop addresses immediate challenges but may not build lasting understanding across the team.

options.text: Discuss with the SME the specific scope issues the team is facing
options.rationale: Discussing issues only with the project manager leaves the team without the knowledge they are missing.

options.text: Arrange for the SME to provide training sessions to the team
options.rationale: Training sessions from the SME during their week on site build the team's understanding of the scope and their confidence.

options.text: Have the SME review the project documentation for alignment
options.rationale: A document review by the SME does not transfer knowledge to the team.

questions.explanation: When scarce expertise is available for a short time, the project manager uses it to build the team's capability. Structured training transfers knowledge that stays with the team after the expert leaves.
questions.mindset: Use scarce experts to build lasting team capability.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading an agile project developing a new customer relationship management (CRM) system. Midway through the project, the team receives feedback from the legal team regarding new data protection laws that the project must adhere to. Which two actions should the project manager take next? (Choose two.)

options.text: Direct the product owner to prioritize data protection features in future sprints
options.rationale: Directing the product owner to reprioritise before understanding the laws is premature and oversteps the product owner's role.

options.text: Request detailed information about the new laws from the legal team
options.rationale: Requesting detailed information about the new laws from the legal team clarifies exactly what must be complied with.

options.text: Have the legal team Implement the compliance measures
options.rationale: The legal team advises on law but does not implement product changes.

options.text: Plan immediate integration of the compliance requirements to mitigate any legal risks
options.rationale: Planning immediate integration before understanding the requirements risks rework.

options.text: Conduct an impact analysis with the team to understand the implications of the new laws
options.rationale: An impact analysis with the team shows how the new laws affect the product and backlog.

questions.explanation: New legal requirements mid-project are first understood — details from the legal experts and impact analysis with the team — before backlog changes are prioritised with the product owner.
questions.mindset: Understand new legal requirements before changing the backlog.

questions.stem: In the middle of a software development project following a predictive lifecycle, a significant portion of the software is set for incremental delivery to the client. The experienced team responsible for this portion has expressed a desire to take on more decision-making responsibilities, traditionally handled by the project manager after each delivery. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Schedule a meeting with senior management to seek their guidance on adjusting the decision-making process.
options.rationale: Seeking senior management guidance escalates a delegation decision the project manager can make.

options.text: Support the team's initiative to take on decision-making responsibilities while retaining final approval authority for critical decisions.
options.rationale: Supporting the experienced team's decision-making while retaining approval for critical decisions balances empowerment with accountability.

options.text: Maintain the traditional decision-making structure where the project manager oversees all decisions, regardless of the team's readiness.
options.rationale: Keeping all decisions with the project manager ignores the team's readiness and slows delivery.

options.text: Consult with the project sponsor to explore the option of delegating key post-delivery decisions to the team.
options.rationale: Consulting the sponsor about delegating team-level decisions is unnecessary.

questions.explanation: Experienced teams can take on more decision-making, which increases ownership and speed. In a predictive context, the project manager can delegate while keeping approval of critical decisions.
questions.mindset: Delegate decisions to ready teams, keeping oversight where it matters.

questions.stem: On an infrastructure project to upgrade city water systems, the project manager is struggling to finalize the project schedule due to unpredictable regulatory review times and potential delays in securing necessary equipment. What scheduling technique should the project manager adopt to manage the planning effectively under these conditions?

options.text: Rolling wave planning
options.rationale: Rolling wave planning details near-term work and refines later work as regulatory and equipment uncertainties resolve.

options.text: Backward pass analysis
options.rationale: A backward pass calculates late dates but does not handle uncertainty in inputs.

options.text: Dependency structuring
options.rationale: Dependency structuring helps sequencing but does not deal with unknown durations.

options.text: Lead and lag optimization
options.rationale: Optimising leads and lags fine-tunes timing but cannot plan around unknowns.

questions.explanation: When later work depends on uncertain events, rolling wave planning lets the project manager plan near-term work in detail while keeping later phases at a higher level until information emerges.
questions.mindset: Plan in waves when the future is uncertain.

questions.stem: In a major software development project, the project manager finds that several team members are reluctant to use new project management software, believing it to be overly complicated and not beneficial for their tasks. What should the project manager have initially done to facilitate the adoption of the new software by the team?

options.text: Encouraged team leaders to use the software their meetings to set an example for the rest of the team
options.rationale: Leaders modelling usage helps, but it does not give everyone the skills to use the software.

options.text: Implemented a rewards system for early adopters who effectively integrate the new software into their workflow
options.rationale: Rewards for early adopters encourage some but leave others without understanding.

options.text: Conducted one-on-one sessions understand individual resistances and tailor support accordingly demonstrate
options.rationale: One-to-one sessions help understand resistance but are slow for a large team.

options.text: Organized a comprehensive training session to demonstrate the functionalities and benefits of the new software
options.rationale: Comprehensive training that demonstrates functionality and benefits gives everyone the skills and the reasons to adopt.

questions.explanation: New tools are adopted when people know how to use them and see their benefit. Training that demonstrates both prevents resistance.
questions.mindset: Show people how and why before expecting them to adopt.

questions.stem: Your project is nearing completion. You have monitored and controlled quality through testing, and risks with mitigations throughout the project life. The project sponsor is concerned that she won't know if the product being delivered has the desired effect on her business area once it is released. What will you do next?

options.text: Consult the Quality Management Plan, to ensure the quality is right for the sponsor.
options.rationale: The quality plan ensures product quality, not whether the business benefits arrive.

options.text: Consult the Benefits Management Plan, and act in accordance to that process.
options.rationale: The benefits management plan describes how and when benefits are measured after release, answering the sponsor's concern.

options.text: Consult the Business Case, to see the proposed benefits from the change.
options.rationale: The business case lists proposed benefits but not how they will be tracked.

options.text: Consult the Risk Register, for any remaining risks that might reduce the effect.
options.rationale: Remaining risks may affect benefits, but the register does not measure them.

questions.explanation: The benefits management plan explains which benefits the project should produce, when they are expected and how they will be measured, including after release. It answers a sponsor's question about whether the product will have the desired effect on the business.
questions.mindset: Use the benefits plan to show how impact will be measured.

questions.stem: In the development stage of an innovative mobile application, the agile project team discovers the need for an advanced software library that wasn't initially anticipated, which is crucial for enhancing the app's functionality. What should the project manager do to effectively manage this unforeseen requirement?

options.text: Organize a strategic meeting with the product owner to reassess the project's priorities and integrate the new software library requirement
options.rationale: Meeting the product owner to reassess priorities integrates the new requirement into the backlog appropriately.

options.text: Update the project timeline to reflect the expected delay due to the integration of the new software library
options.rationale: Updating the timeline for a delay presumes the outcome before reprioritising.

options.text: Identify this new need as a project risk, and seek immediate advice from the project steering committee
options.rationale: Escalating to a steering committee is unnecessary for a backlog decision.

options.text: Delegate the task of integrating the new software library to a specialist within the project team without delay
options.rationale: Delegating integration immediately skips prioritisation.

questions.explanation: In agile projects, a newly discovered requirement is not simply added or refused. The product owner reassesses backlog priorities with the team so the new need is weighed against existing work and scheduled where it adds most value.
questions.mindset: Prioritise new needs with the product owner.

questions.stem: Throughout a project, it becomes apparent that team members from different departments have differing perspectives on what the final outcome of the project should be. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Facilitate a session to revisit and clarify the project's goals with the entire team.
options.rationale: Facilitating a session to clarify goals with the whole team aligns different departmental perspectives.

options.text: Meet with the project sponsor to ensure alignment on the project’s objectives.
options.rationale: Sponsor alignment is useful but does not align the team.

options.text: Make sure the project outcome is aligned with the project charter and scope statement.
options.rationale: Checking alignment with documents does not resolve the team's differing views.

options.text: Assign the department heads the responsibility of resolving these differences.
options.rationale: Delegating to department heads may deepen divisions.

questions.explanation: When team members from different departments hold different views of the outcome, the project manager brings them together to revisit and clarify the project's goals. A shared understanding reached as a team is more durable than alignment settled only with the sponsor or delegated to departments.
questions.mindset: Align the team on the goal together.

questions.stem: A project manager is overseeing the construction of a new manufacturing facility when an economic downturn may suddenly threatens the project's viability. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Adjust the project's financial forecasts to account for the economic downturn
options.rationale: Adjusting financial forecasts addresses one effect only.

options.text: Suggest to the project sponsor that the project should be postponed
options.rationale: Recommending postponement before analysing the new risks is premature and may be unnecessary.

options.text: Redirect some project resources to support other essential projects within the organization
options.rationale: Redirecting resources is not the project manager's decision.

options.text: Identify and document the new risks and create mitigation strategies
options.rationale: Identifying and documenting new risks with mitigation strategies manages the threat.

questions.explanation: An economic downturn introduces new risks to a project's viability. The project manager identifies and documents them and plans mitigation, giving decision-makers a structured basis for any decision about the project's future.
questions.mindset: Turn external threats into managed risks.

questions.stem: A project manager discovers that recent legislative updates necessitate additional security enhancements to the project. Although the development team has incorporated these enhancements without exceeding their budget, the project manager realizes that the allocated budget for quality assurance and testing is quickly being depleted due to these unplanned requirements. What action should the project manager take to manage the escalating costs associated with the increased scope of testing?

options.text: Propose a temporary reallocation of resources from less critical project activities to support the expanded testing requirements
options.rationale: Reallocating resources informally changes the plan without approval.

options.text: Have the sponsor analyze potential cost-saving measures within the project to reallocate funds towards the testing budget
options.rationale: Asking the sponsor to find savings shifts the PM's responsibility.

options.text: Submit a formal change request to revise the project's cost baseline, accommodating the extra expenses incurred in the testing phase
options.rationale: A formal change request to revise the cost baseline handles the extra expense through governance.

options.text: Adjust the project's financial strategy to ensure the newly identified testing needs are adequately funded without compromising project quality
options.rationale: Adjusting the financial strategy informally bypasses change control.

questions.explanation: When new requirements push costs beyond the baseline, the extra spending is not absorbed informally. A formal change request to revise the cost baseline documents the reason, gets approval through governance and keeps the budget accurate.
questions.mindset: Revise baselines formally.

questions.stem: A project manager is overseeing the upgrade of an old manufacturing system to a new automated solution, aligning with the organization's operational process changes. The project charter is approved, and the PMO has provided templates for all new projects. What should the project manager prioritize?

options.text: Align the project plan with the organization's strategic goals, working closely with senior management.
options.rationale: Strategic alignment should already be established by the charter.

options.text: Develop a training and communications management plan, ensuring collaboration with the team.
options.rationale: A training and communications plan supports adoption of the new automated solution and addresses resistance.

options.text: Create a detailed budget and schedule regular reviews with the finance department.
options.rationale: Budget reviews matter but do not address the organisational change.

options.text: Coordinate with operational departments to minimize disruption during the upgrade.
options.rationale: Minimising disruption matters, but people must be prepared for the change.

questions.explanation: Projects that change how people work need to prepare those people. With the charter approved and templates available, the project manager prioritises a training and communications plan, built with the team, to support adoption and reduce resistance to the new automated solution.
questions.mindset: Prepare people for operational change.

questions.stem: On a high-stakes software development agile project, the project manager notices a pattern where numerous team members are either late or entirely miss the daily virtual scrum designed to facilitate project cohesion. What action should the project manager take to enhance the efficacy and attendance of these daily sessions?

options.text: Work with the team to identify a project's communication protocol that will work with them to ensure timely participation in the daily scrum
options.rationale: Working with the team on a communication protocol builds commitment to timely participation.

options.text: Identify a time that could potentially crease attendance and punctuality
options.rationale: Changing the time helps but lacks team agreement.

options.text: Transition to an asynchronous communication model to allow team members to update their status at their convenience
options.rationale: Asynchronous updates lose the scrum's interaction.

options.text: Solicit input from project stakeholders on effective methods to improve team engagement and meeting attendance
options.rationale: Asking stakeholders how to improve the team's stand-up attendance looks outside the team for a problem the team should own.

questions.explanation: When many team members are late or absent from the daily scrum, the fix is a shared agreement. Working with the team on a communication protocol that suits them builds commitment to timely participation, rather than imposing a new time or dropping the meeting.
questions.mindset: Agree participation norms with the team.

questions.stem: A project manager needs to prioritize multiple projects within a portfolio and requires accurate budget estimates. The process must align with agile principles while ensuring reliable financial planning. How should the budget for each project be estimated?

options.text: Calculate costs by evaluating individual task estimates from the team, considering their current workload.
options.rationale: Bottom-up estimates from the team, considering workload, align with agile and produce reliable budgets.

options.text: Leverage the combined expertise of the sponsor, product owner, and agile coach to derive budget estimates.
options.rationale: Estimates from sponsor, product owner and coach exclude the people doing the work.

options.text: Use analytics software to model potential costs based on predictive analysis and historical data.
options.rationale: Analytics software may not reflect current team capacity.

options.text: Have the product owner conduct a thorough requirements analysis with the team to forecast project budgets.
options.rationale: Requirements analysis alone does not produce budgets.

questions.explanation: Reliable estimates come from the people doing the work. Team-based bottom-up estimates support agile principles and planning.
questions.mindset: Estimate with the people who do the work.

questions.stem: Following the approval of the project charter, the project manager begins working with the team to organize the project's scope into smaller, detailed components. What is the project manager primarily working on?

options.text: Creating a project RACI chart
options.rationale: A RACI chart assigns roles to work; it comes after the work has been broken down.

options.text: Project schedule network diagram
options.rationale: A network diagram sequences activities once they have been identified.

options.text: Work breakdown structure
options.rationale: Decomposing the scope into smaller, detailed components is creating the work breakdown structure.

options.text: Scheduling the execution phases for the project's tasks
options.rationale: Scheduling execution phases follows the WBS and activity definition.

questions.explanation: The WBS is a hierarchical decomposition of the total scope into deliverables and work packages. It is the foundation for estimating, scheduling and assigning responsibility.
questions.mindset: Break scope down before you schedule it.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading the development of a new customer support software system. During a sprint, a developer encounters ambiguity regarding the acceptance criteria of a feature. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Convene a meeting with the project steering committee to discuss the feature's requirements.
options.rationale: Taking a story-level question to the steering committee is disproportionate and slow.

options.text: Initiate a discussion in the next team meeting to gather collective input on the feature.
options.rationale: Waiting for the next team meeting delays the developer and does not involve the person who defines the criteria.

options.text: Refer the question to the technical architect to provide an expert interpretation of the requirements.
options.rationale: The architect can interpret technically, but the product owner owns what the feature must achieve.

options.text: Collaborate with the product owner to resolve the ambiguity in the acceptance criteria.
options.rationale: The product owner defines acceptance criteria, so clarifying them together resolves the ambiguity quickly.

questions.explanation: Ambiguity in acceptance criteria is resolved with the product owner, who owns what each backlog item must deliver. Quick clarification keeps the developer moving and the work aligned with intent.
questions.mindset: Resolve acceptance questions with the product owner.

questions.stem: During the execution phase of a software development project, the team encounters a technical challenge that jeopardizes the scheduled delivery of key functionalities. The technical team has, indicated a delay. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Schedule an emergency meeting with all stakeholders to brainstorm solutions
options.rationale: Gathering all stakeholders to brainstorm is heavy before the issue is understood and recorded.

options.text: Initiate a quick training session for the technical team to enhance their problem-solving capabilities
options.rationale: Training may help later but does not address the immediate issue.

options.text: Record the problem, its current impact, and urgency in the project's issue log for structured tracking
options.rationale: Recording the problem, its impact and urgency in the issue log makes it visible and tracked for resolution.

options.text: Organize a team-building event to boost morale and encourage innovative thinking for problem resolution
options.rationale: A team-building event does not address a technical issue.

questions.explanation: A problem that threatens delivery is an issue to be recorded, owned and tracked. The issue log gives structure to its resolution and supports prioritisation.
questions.mindset: Record issues so they get resolved, not just discussed.

questions.stem: During a pivotal project phase, it was revealed that critical stakeholders did not attend a meeting focused on confirming the project's strategic alignment and expected business benefits, resulting in their feedback being overlooked. This oversight has led to conflicts within the decision-making process. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Initiate a discussion to directly address and understand the concerns leading to the conflict
options.rationale: Directly discussing the concerns with the stakeholders addresses the conflict and brings their input back into decisions.

options.text: Distribute a detailed meeting summary and request written feedback from the absent stakeholders
options.rationale: A summary and written feedback request is slower and less effective at resolving conflict.

options.text: Conduct a formal risk analysis to evaluate the impact of missing stakeholder input
options.rationale: A formal risk analysis does not resolve the stakeholders' concerns.

options.text: Develop a contingency plan to navigate potential project delays or changes
options.rationale: Contingency planning addresses consequences rather than the conflict itself.

questions.explanation: When key stakeholders missed a critical decision and conflict follows, direct engagement to understand their concerns is the fastest route to resolution.
questions.mindset: Engage stakeholders directly when their input was missed.

questions.stem: During a crucial phase of the project, a pivotal team member informs the project manager of their impending resignation, intending to submit their notice to their line manager soon. This revelation comes at a time when their contribution is critical to meeting the project's upcoming deadlines. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Have a senior team member do a meeting to reassess task allocations and address any concerns
options.rationale: Having a senior member run the meeting delegates the project manager's responsibility.

options.text: Update the project risk register to reflect the potential impact on the project timeline
options.rationale: Updating the risk register is too passive when the departure is effectively certain.

options.text: Brief the project stakeholders on the situation to set realistic expectations about potential delays
options.rationale: Briefing stakeholders about delays is premature before planning mitigation.
