questions.stem: Faced with a constrained budget and a tight deadline for launching a new product development project, the project manager discovers that the current financial resources will not suffice to cover all the projected activities. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Propose a phased project approach to stakeholders, focusing on critical development phases first
options.rationale: Phasing the project is a possible option, but it should come from exploring alternatives first.

options.text: Document the financial shortfall in the project status report, highlighting potential impacts on the timeline
options.rationale: Documenting the shortfall reports the problem without doing anything to solve it.

options.text: Have the PMO identify priority areas, and allocate budget to critical development stages
options.rationale: The PMO does not own the project's budget allocation; that is the project manager's responsibility.

options.text: Engage with the team to explore options for reallocating existing budget items to cover key tasks
options.rationale: Working with the team to reallocate budget towards key tasks seeks to meet core objectives within available funds.

questions.explanation: When funds will not cover all planned activities, the project manager first works with the team to explore reallocating the existing budget so that the key tasks and core objectives remain funded before seeking changes to scope, phasing or funding.
questions.mindset: Explore options within the budget with the team.

questions.stem: During a significant landscape redesign project, the project manager finds a cutting-edge irrigation system that could drastically reduce water usage and maintenance costs. Introducing this system would necessitate a modest increase in both the project budget and timeline. What action should the project manager take first?

options.text: Assess the project's existing budget and timeline
options.rationale: Reviewing the existing budget and timeline alone does not evaluate the proposed system's value.

options.text: Initiate a pilot project within the current scope
options.rationale: A pilot within current scope may be impossible given the extra cost and time required.

options.text: Draft a detailed analysis comparing the long-term savings and environmental benefits of the new system against the initial increase in project costs and timeline for stakeholder review
options.rationale: A cost-benefit analysis of long-term savings against the extra cost and time gives stakeholders what they need to decide.

options.text: Showcase the compatibility of the new irrigation system with the project's sustainability goals and report findings to stakeholders
options.rationale: Showing sustainability alignment is only part of the case and omits the cost and schedule impact.

questions.explanation: An opportunity that requires more budget and time is a change for stakeholders to decide on. The project manager prepares an analysis comparing long-term savings and environmental benefits against the extra cost and time, so the decision is well informed.
questions.mindset: Present opportunities with a full cost-benefit case.

questions.stem: During a critical phase of a healthcare software implementation project, the project manager realizes that the project team is struggling to maintain pace with rapid iterations and frequent changes in project requirements, indicating a need for better cohesion and flexibility. Which two practices should the project manager implement to improve team performance and project fluidity? (Choose two.)

options.text: Foster a culture of continuous dialogue and collaboration among team members
options.rationale: A culture of continuous dialogue and collaboration helps the team keep pace with rapid iterations.

options.text: Embrace a mindset of flexibility and willingness to adapt to project shifts
options.rationale: A flexible, adaptive mindset lets the team absorb frequent changes in requirements.

options.text: Implement regular retrospectives to identify and act on improvement opportunities
options.rationale: Retrospectives are a good practice, but the source favours the underlying collaborative and adaptive mindset.

options.text: Organize training sessions on agile methodologies for enhanced team understanding
options.rationale: Training on agile methods builds knowledge but does not directly change how the team works together.

options.text: Schedule brief daily check-ins to keep the team aligned and informed
options.rationale: Daily check-ins align the team but do not by themselves build flexibility or cohesion.

questions.explanation: A team struggling with rapid iterations and changing requirements needs cohesion and adaptability. Continuous dialogue and collaboration, together with a mindset that embraces change, address the core challenges of working in an agile way.
questions.mindset: Collaboration and adaptability sustain agile teams.

questions.stem: As a project manager in charge of a new sustainability initiative, you've introduced a groundbreaking environmental monitoring system. However, you notice that your project team is hesitant to adopt this technology, leading to delays in the implementation phase. What is the most effective measure to ensure team adoption and project progression?

options.text: Implement a reward system for early adopters of the technology
options.rationale: Rewards may prompt a few early adopters but do not address why the team is hesitant.

options.text: Arrange for a series of brief, informative sessions on how the technology contributes to project goals
options.rationale: Brief sessions explain the purpose but may not give enough depth or hands-on experience to overcome hesitation.

options.text: Conduct an extensive workshop with the team that examines the technology
options.rationale: An in-depth workshop examining the technology builds understanding, relevance and hands-on confidence.

options.text: Enlist the help of environmental experts to explain the importance of the technology to the team's work
options.rationale: Outside experts can explain importance, but the team needs practical familiarity with using the system.

questions.explanation: Hesitation to adopt new technology usually comes from unfamiliarity. An extensive workshop that examines the system in depth, shows its relevance to the initiative and gives hands-on practice addresses that directly and gets implementation moving.
questions.mindset: Build familiarity to drive adoption.

questions.stem: Launching a project to introduce a new health information system across multiple clinics, the project manager realizes there are discrepancies between the project scope and the latest health data protection regulations. While the project's leadership team advises proceeding as planned, anticipating that these discrepancies will be resolved in due time, the project manager is concerned about potential compliance issues. What is the most appropriate initial step for the project manager?

options.text: Conduct an in-depth analysis of the health data protection regulations and outline a detailed compliance plan
options.rationale: Analysing the regulations in depth and outlining a compliance plan tackles the discrepancies and gives a basis to communicate changes.

options.text: Initiate a risk assessment session to evaluate the impact of potential non-compliance on the project
options.rationale: A risk assessment of non-compliance evaluates consequences but does not set out how to comply.

options.text: Arrange a consultation with a legal expert in health data protection to advise on compliance strategies
options.rationale: A legal expert can support the analysis, but the project manager still needs a plan for the project.

options.text: Redesign the project scope to include only those elements currently in compliance with existing regulations
options.rationale: Cutting scope to compliant elements is drastic and may remove essential functionality unnecessarily.

questions.explanation: Proceeding with known discrepancies against data protection law is a serious risk, whatever leadership expects. The project manager analyses the regulations thoroughly and develops a compliance plan, which then provides a clear basis for discussion with leadership and the team.
questions.mindset: Don't proceed on hope when compliance is at stake.

questions.stem: At the beginning of a green building project, the project manager is tasked by the lead architect to engage a key supplier known for their sustainable materials. However, this supplier is reluctant to collaborate, believing the project's environmental goals do not align with their business model. What action should the project manager take to encourage supplier participation?

options.text: Propose a trial period for the supplier to assess the project's commitment to sustainability
options.rationale: A trial period asks the supplier to invest effort before its concerns are addressed.

options.text: Refer the matter to the lead architect, suggesting the need for higher-level negotiations
options.rationale: Referring the matter to the architect gives away the project manager's responsibility to engage the supplier.

options.text: Initiate a campaign to highlight the project's sustainability achievements and future plans
options.rationale: A general publicity campaign is not targeted at this supplier's specific reservations.

options.text: Conduct a detailed presentation for the supplier outlining the project's environmental impact and mutual benefits
options.rationale: A presentation of the project's environmental impact and mutual benefits addresses the supplier's doubts directly.

questions.explanation: A supplier reluctant because it sees no alignment needs to be shown the fit. A detailed presentation of the project's environmental impact and the mutual benefits of working together targets the supplier's reservations and encourages it to reconsider.
questions.mindset: Show suppliers the mutual benefit.

questions.stem: Following a directive to enhance operational efficiencies within a multinational corporation, the executive team has requested an update on the progress and remaining tasks for all ongoing Agile projects. What methodology should the project manager employ to accurately convey this information?

options.text: Time-tracking analysis
options.rationale: Time tracking shows hours spent, not the work completed and remaining.

options.text: Resource allocation report
options.rationale: A resource allocation report shows who is assigned, not progress against scope.

options.text: Progress milestone review
options.rationale: A milestone review suits predictive projects and gives a less continuous view of agile progress.

options.text: Sprint burnup chart
options.rationale: A burnup chart shows work completed against total scope over time, conveying progress and what remains.

questions.explanation: For agile projects, a burnup chart visually shows how much work has been completed against the total scope over time. Executives can see both progress and the remaining work, and changes in scope are visible as movement of the total line.
questions.mindset: Show agile progress with burnup charts.

questions.stem: You have been allocated to a new project team with members from different parts of the functional business area. It soon becomes clear that very few of them have worked on a project before. There is also a lot of miscommunication and re-work occurring amongst the team, which is starting to cause delays. What will you do next?

options.text: Set a daily stand-up with your team to ensure they update what they completed.
options.rationale: A stand-up adds reporting but does not give an inexperienced team the shared foundation it lacks.

options.text: Review the Resource Assignment Matrix with your team and ensure they are doing their job.
options.rationale: Checking the responsibility matrix to police people does not address confusion about how to work together.

options.text: Help the team set their vision and objectives, roles and responsibilities, and team operations.
options.rationale: Helping the team set its vision, objectives, roles and ways of working builds the one-team foundation it needs.

options.text: Send your team members on training in their roles to increase their capability.
options.rationale: Role training may help later, but the immediate need is a shared understanding of how the team works.

questions.explanation: A team drawn from different business areas with little project experience needs more work up front to become one team. Establishing a shared vision and objectives, clear roles and responsibilities and agreed team operations reduces miscommunication and rework.
questions.mindset: Build a shared vision, roles and ways of working early.

questions.stem: During the integration phase of an international IT project, the project manager notices frequent miscommunications between the on-site and offshore teams, primarily due to cultural misunderstandings and language nuances. The project manager has individually spoken with members from both teams and confirmed that these differences are hindering project progress. What should the project manager do to enhance understanding and cooperation between the teams?

options.text: Implement a mandatory language proficiency course for all team members
options.rationale: Mandatory language courses are slow and do not address cultural misunderstanding.

options.text: Facilitate workshops that allow both teams to share their cultural norms and communication preferences
options.rationale: Workshops for both teams to share cultural norms and communication preferences build mutual understanding directly.

options.text: Assign a bilingual team liaison to translate and mediate communications between the teams
options.rationale: A liaison adds an intermediary layer rather than improving the teams' own understanding.

options.text: Require all project communications to be conducted in written form to reduce misunderstandings
options.rationale: Forcing all communication into writing reduces collaboration and does not resolve cultural gaps.

questions.explanation: Miscommunication between on-site and offshore teams rooted in culture and language is addressed by building mutual understanding. Workshops where both teams share their norms and communication preferences promote open dialogue, respect and better cooperation.
questions.mindset: Build cultural understanding between teams.

questions.stem: As part of a company-wide project to enhance IT security, the project manager schedules a series of educational webinars for employees. A leader from a department not yet covered in the initial rollout expresses interest in attending one of the early sessions. What action should the project manager do to best support the initiative's goals and engage interested stakeholders?

options.text: Limit webinar attendance to only those departments scheduled for the early phases of the rollout
options.rationale: Restricting attendance discourages an interested leader and slows wider adoption.

options.text: Suggest the department leader wait for a tailored session specific to their department's needs
options.rationale: Asking the leader to wait wastes their enthusiasm and delays preparation of their team.

options.text: Encourage the department leader to join an upcoming webinar to gain early insights and prepare their team
options.rationale: Welcoming the leader to an early webinar uses their interest to build awareness and prepare their department.

options.text: Provide recorded versions of the webinars exclusively to those in the initial rollout phases
options.rationale: Restricting recordings to early phases unnecessarily limits access to useful material.

questions.explanation: Organisation-wide change benefits from stakeholders who want to engage early. Encouraging the interested department leader to join an upcoming webinar builds awareness, helps them prepare their team and supports adoption across the company.
questions.mindset: Welcome early interest in organisational change.

questions.stem: A project manager is tasked with integrating advanced artificial intelligence (AI) features into an existing software product. However, the current project team lacks the Al expertise required for successful implementation. What should the project manager do to ensure the project's success despite the team's current skill limitations?

options.text: Initiate targeted Al training programs for the project team
options.rationale: Targeted AI training builds the capability the team needs for this project and future ones.

options.text: Partner with an Al technology firm to provide expert consultation
options.rationale: Outside consultants help, but the team would still lack the skills to build and maintain the features.

options.text: Facilitate workshops that encourage innovative problem-solving techniques
options.rationale: Problem-solving workshops do not provide the specific AI expertise required.

options.text: Deploy automated tools to assist the team with Al-related tasks
options.rationale: Automated tools cannot substitute for expertise the team does not have.

questions.explanation: When the team lacks a critical skill, the project manager closes the gap. Targeted AI training equips the team to implement the features successfully and builds lasting capacity, rather than relying only on outside help.
questions.mindset: Build the skills the project needs.

questions.stem: You are nearing the end of a difficult project where the vendor providing the system to your company has taken longer than anticipated. The deliverables have been quality tested, validated and verified. Your project sponsor is keen to finish the project and close it off. What will you do next?

options.text: Review the risk register and issues register for outstanding risks and issues.
options.rationale: Outstanding risks and issues are part of closure, but with a vendor involved the procurement closure comes first.

options.text: Review the project management plan and approved change requests.
options.rationale: The plan and change requests were used during delivery; they are not the closing inputs specific to this situation.

options.text: Review the procurement agreement and accepted deliverables.
options.rationale: Reviewing the procurement agreement and accepted deliverables confirms the contract is fulfilled so the project can close.

options.text: Review the requirements management plan and requirements traceability matrix.
options.rationale: Requirements traceability was relevant to validation, which is already complete.

questions.explanation: When a vendor has delivered and the deliverables have been verified and validated, closing the project includes confirming the procurement agreement has been fulfilled. The agreement and the accepted deliverables are key inputs for closing the project or phase.
questions.mindset: Close procurements before closing the project.

questions.stem: As the project manager for an innovative smart home device project, you receive a request from the stakeholder to incorporate advanced Al capabilities to improve device usability. This addition is expected to significantly enhance the product but comes late in the development cycle, with a challenging deadline for integration. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Conduct an impact analysis to determine how the integration of advanced Al capabilities affects the project timeline and budget
options.rationale: An impact analysis on timeline and budget shows what the late AI request would really cost.

options.text: Suggest focusing on launching the current version without Al and adding it as a feature in the next product release
options.rationale: Deferring to a future release may be right, but that decision needs the impact analysis first.

options.text: Increase the project team's working hours to meet the demand of integrating the new feature within the existing timeline
options.rationale: Longer working hours are unsustainable and ignore the change process.

options.text: Negotiate for additional resources to specifically focus on developing and integrating the Al functionalities
options.rationale: Negotiating resources assumes the change will be approved before its impact is known.

questions.explanation: A valuable but late request still needs its impact understood. An impact analysis of the AI integration's effect on schedule and budget gives the project manager and stakeholders the information needed to decide whether and when to include it.
questions.mindset: Analyse the impact of late changes before deciding.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading the development of a new public library. During the planning phase, it comes to light that the library's proposed location is a popular site for an annual book fair, which was not considered in the initial consultations. The oversight raises concerns about the fair's future and the library's community relations. What should the project manager do to ensure the project aligns with community interests and maintains positive relations?

options.text: Redesign the library layout to include a dedicated space for the annual book fair without additional stakeholder input
options.rationale: Redesigning without stakeholder input repeats the original mistake of not consulting.

options.text: Organize a discussion forum with book fair organizers and community members to explore how the library project can accommodate the fair
options.rationale: A forum with fair organisers and community members lets the project explore how to accommodate the fair.

options.text: Prepare a risk management plan specifically for mitigating the backlash from book fair enthusiasts
options.rationale: A plan to mitigate backlash treats the community as an opponent rather than a partner.

options.text: Suggest relocating the book fair to a less central but still accessible location without consulting the event organizers
options.rationale: Relocating the fair without consulting organisers would damage community relations.

questions.explanation: An important community stakeholder was missed in the initial consultations. Bringing the book fair organisers and community members together to explore how the library can accommodate the fair corrects the oversight and builds positive relations.
questions.mindset: Engage stakeholders you missed as soon as you find them.

questions.stem: As the project manager for a software development project, you're informed that due to budget reallocations, several developers will be reassigned to other projects, creating unease among your team about project timelines and their roles. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Implement a revised project schedule that accelerates timelines to demonstrate the project can proceed without additional resources
options.rationale: Accelerating the schedule with fewer people ignores the team's concerns and adds pressure.

options.text: Facilitate a session to discuss the reassignments, emphasizing the strategic vision and how team contributions are critical to both the project and the broader company objectives
options.rationale: A session on the reassignments that restates the vision and each person's importance addresses unease directly.

options.text: Introduce a mentorship program pairing remaining team members with experienced mentors to bolster confidence and skill sets in light of reduced staffing
options.rationale: Mentorship may help later but does not address the immediate uncertainty.

options.text: Launch a cross-training initiative to diversify the skill sets of remaining team members, ensuring the project's critical functions are covered
options.rationale: Cross-training helps coverage but does not address the team's concerns about their roles.

questions.explanation: When reassignments leave the team uneasy about timelines and roles, the project manager first talks openly with them. Discussing the changes, restating the strategic vision and showing how each contribution matters restores clarity and morale.
questions.mindset: Address uncertainty openly and reconnect people to the vision.

questions.stem: During the implementation phase of a citywide public transportation improvement project, a city council member requests a specialized update that goes beyond the scope of regular briefings provided to the public and city officials. The team utilizes advanced simulation software and traffic flow analyses to plan and monitor progress. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Provide a tutorial on how to interpret the simulation software results
options.rationale: A software tutorial presumes what the council member wants to know.

options.text: Invite the council member to a workshop on traffic flow analysis techniques used in the project
options.rationale: A workshop on analysis techniques may not answer their actual question.

options.text: Engage directly with the council member to clarify what specific data or insights are needed
options.rationale: Engaging directly to clarify the specific data or insights needed allows a precisely tailored response.

options.text: Compile a comprehensive report using data from both the simulation software and traffic analyses
options.rationale: A comprehensive report may bury the information they actually want.

questions.explanation: When a stakeholder asks for a specialised update, the project manager first clarifies exactly what they need. Understanding the specific data or insight sought allows a tailored response rather than generic material that may miss the point.
questions.mindset: Clarify the request before producing the answer.

questions.stem: Following a critical review session of a healthcare software project, a project manager notes that the output from one of the software engineers is not up to the project standards. What is the most appropriate form of communication for the project manager to utilize in addressing the software engineer's performance concerns?

options.text: Send a group email highlighting the importance of meeting project standards without naming individuals
options.rationale: A group email is vague and may embarrass or confuse the whole team.

options.text: Schedule a formal one-on-one meeting to discuss the performance issues and development plan
options.rationale: A formal one-to-one meeting addresses the performance issue privately and agrees a development plan.

options.text: Issue a formal performance improvement plan through the company's HR system
options.rationale: A formal HR improvement plan is an escalation before any conversation has taken place.

options.text: Initiate a team-wide meeting to discuss project standards and individual contributions collectively
options.rationale: Discussing individual performance in a team meeting is inappropriate and damaging.

questions.explanation: Performance concerns about one team member are addressed privately and constructively. A formal one-to-one meeting conveys the seriousness of the issue professionally and allows the project manager to agree a development plan with the engineer.
questions.mindset: Handle individual performance privately.

questions.stem: Leading a software development agile project for a multinational corporation, a project manager faces the challenge of managing a team spread across multiple time zones. The project manager has previously encountered issues with such teams regarding inconsistent work quality and missed deadlines. What action should the project manager take to ensure high-quality deliverables and adherence to the timeline?

options.text: Initiate frequent virtual stand-ups to clarify project goals, synchronize team efforts, and address any issues promptly
options.rationale: Frequent virtual stand-ups keep a dispersed team aligned on goals and surface issues before they cause delays.

options.text: Develop a comprehensive training program on time management and productivity tools for all team members
options.rationale: Time-management training does not address the lack of alignment across time zones.

options.text: Distribute a detailed weekly report template for team members to fill out, summarizing their progress and challenges
options.rationale: Weekly reports are slow and one-way, so problems surface too late.

options.text: Organize a quarterly in-person meet-up for team building and detailed project review discussions
options.rationale: Quarterly meet-ups build relationships but are too infrequent to keep daily work aligned.

questions.explanation: Inconsistent quality and missed deadlines in distributed teams often stem from poor alignment. Frequent virtual stand-ups give the team a regular rhythm to clarify goals, synchronise effort and resolve issues promptly, sustaining momentum across time zones.
questions.mindset: Keep distributed teams aligned with frequent touchpoints.

questions.stem: A project manager is tasked with launching a new drug product, which requires adherence to stringent health and safety regulations. It's critical for the launch to comply with these regulations to avoid penalties and ensure public safety. What should the project manager do to next to guarantee compliance with these health and safety regulations?

options.text: Arrange for regular training sessions on regulatory compliance for the project team
options.rationale: Training helps the team, but the specific compliance risks have not yet been identified.

options.text: Assess and document potential-compliance risks related to health and safety regulations
options.rationale: Assessing and documenting compliance risks gives a structured basis for managing every regulatory requirement.

options.text: Implement a quality control system to continuously monitor the product against regulatory standards
options.rationale: Quality control monitors the product later but depends on knowing which requirements carry risk.

options.text: Organize a consultation with legal experts specializing in regulations to review project alignment
options.rationale: Legal experts may help, but the project first needs its own structured view of compliance risks.

questions.explanation: Launching a drug product under stringent health and safety regulations requires a proactive approach. Assessing and documenting the potential compliance risks lets the team plan responses in a structured, informed way instead of reacting to problems later.
questions.mindset: Identify compliance risks early and manage them.

questions.stem: During the critical testing phase of an enterprise software upgrade, the project manager identifies that testing is significantly behind schedule, posing a risk to the planned go-live date. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Escalate the issue to the company's executive management for immediate intervention
options.rationale: Escalating to executives before understanding the delay is premature.

options.text: Conduct a detailed session with the team to pinpoint the specific causes of the delays
options.rationale: A detailed session with the team pinpoints the specific causes, so any response is well targeted.

options.text: Seek additional funding to contract external testing services to catch up on the schedule
options.rationale: External testers may help, but spending money before diagnosing the cause may not fix it.

options.text: Implement overtime hours for the testing team to accelerate progress and meet the deadline
options.rationale: Overtime treats the symptom and may not address why testing is behind.

questions.explanation: When testing falls well behind schedule, the project manager first diagnoses why. A detailed session with the team pinpoints the causes of the delay, so that subsequent actions are informed rather than premature or misdirected.
questions.mindset: Diagnose a delay before acting on it.

questions.stem: During the construction phase of a new city park, conflicts have emerged between the landscape designers and environmental consultants over the choice of plant species and their environmental impact. What are the most effective actions for the project manager to take first to resolve these conflicts? (Select two.)

options.text: Delay any decisions on plant species until further research can be conducted
options.rationale: Delaying decisions stalls the construction and leaves the conflict unresolved.

options.text: Organize individual meetings with the landscape designers and environmental consultants to understand each group's concerns
options.rationale: Meeting each group separately helps the project manager understand each side's concerns without inflaming tensions.

options.text: Initiate a workshop with all stakeholders to democratically vote on the plant species selection
options.rationale: Voting on plant species ignores expertise and turns a technical disagreement into a popularity contest.

options.text: Escalate the issue to the city council for a final decision to avoid further delay in the project timeline
options.rationale: Escalating to the city council is premature before the project manager has tried to resolve the conflict.

options.text: Conduct private, targeted discussions with key representatives from both sides to find a middle ground
options.rationale: Private discussions with key representatives from both sides help find a middle ground.

questions.explanation: Before bringing conflicting groups together, the project manager can understand each side's position privately. Individual meetings and targeted discussions with key representatives reveal the core issues and open a route to compromise without escalating tension.
questions.mindset: Understand each side before bringing them together.

questions.stem: During a critical software implementation project, the project manager identifies a significant slowdown in the integration phase, attributed to the team's unfamiliarity with the new software's API. This issue threatens to delay project milestones. What should the project manager do first to address the team's skill gap without rising the budget?

options.text: Initiate a collaborative problem-solving meeting to identify alternative integration strategies or solutions
options.rationale: A collaborative problem-solving meeting draws on the team to find integration approaches without extra cost.

options.text: Delegate the integration tasks to a more experienced team within the organization, reducing the learning curve
options.rationale: Handing the work to another team removes learning and may not be possible.

options.text: Invest in a fast-tracked external training program specifically focused on the new software's API for the team
options.rationale: External training adds cost, which the question rules out.

options.text: Hire an external consultant with expertise in the software to lead the integration phase and train the team concurrently
options.rationale: An external consultant also raises the budget and creates dependency.

questions.explanation: With no extra budget, the project manager relies on the team's collective knowledge. A collaborative problem-solving meeting can identify alternative integration strategies and build internal expertise, keeping the work moving without new costs or dependencies.
questions.mindset: Solve impediments with the team's collective knowledge.

questions.stem: During the planning of a new development project, a recently enacted zoning law changes the permissible building heights within the project's area. The project team has been informed of this change. What is the most effective course of action for the project manager to take?

options.text: Proceed with planning until the legal department informs you to update the plan
options.rationale: Waiting for the legal department to prompt an update delays the response to a known change.

options.text: Update the project documentation to reflect the change in zoning laws and its impact on the project scope
options.rationale: Updating the project documents to reflect the zoning change and its scope impact keeps planning aligned with the law.

options.text: Schedule a meeting with local government officials to seek exceptions for the current project
options.rationale: Seeking exceptions from officials is speculative and may not succeed.

options.text: Consult with legal counsel to understand the implications of the zoning law change on the project
options.rationale: Legal advice may help on details, but the known height restriction should already be reflected in the plans.

questions.explanation: A new zoning law directly limits building heights in the project area. Updating the project documentation to reflect the change and its impact on scope keeps planning grounded in current constraints and supports informed decisions with stakeholders.
questions.mindset: Reflect external changes in the plan promptly.

questions.stem: In the late stages of launching a marketing campaign project, it's identified that a critical piece of content is not ready because a team member fell behind schedule. This issue came to light during a presentation to the marketing department, causing concern about meeting the launch deadline. What action should the project manager do first?

options.text: Have a confidential discussion with the team member to understand the reasons for the delay and explore solutions together
options.rationale: A private discussion to understand the delay and find solutions together respects the team member and addresses the cause.

options.text: Delegate the unfinished tasks to another team member who has the capacity to expedite completion
options.rationale: Reassigning the work without talking to the team member may damage morale and miss the cause.

options.text: Organize a session for the team to collectively brainstorm ways to expedite the remaining work
options.rationale: A team brainstorm puts the individual's delay in front of everyone before it is understood.

options.text: Seek advice from a senior manager on how to handle the team member's delay in task completion
options.rationale: Asking a senior manager for advice is an unnecessary escalation of a matter the project manager can handle.

questions.explanation: When one person's work is late, the project manager speaks with them privately to understand why and to agree a way forward. This maintains dignity and morale while tackling the cause of the delay.
questions.mindset: Understand individual delays privately first.

questions.stem: The project manager for a renewable energy initiative receives a suggestion from an environmental consultant to incorporate a new technology that could improve project outcomes but also extend the timeline and increase costs. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Forward the suggestion to the project's CCB for an approval
options.rationale: The change control board needs an assessed change; forwarding it unassessed is premature.

options.text: Arrange a project team meeting to discuss the feasibility and implications of integrating the new technology
options.rationale: Discussing feasibility and implications with the team is the first step in assessing the proposed change.

options.text: Consult with industry experts to gauge the potential benefits and drawbacks of the new technology
options.rationale: External experts may be consulted later, but the team's assessment of the project impact comes first.

options.text: Conduct a preliminary risk analysis to understand how the new technology might affect project risks
options.rationale: A risk analysis covers only one aspect of the change's implications.

questions.explanation: A suggestion that would extend the timeline and increase cost is a change that must be assessed before any approval. The project manager first discusses its feasibility and implications with the team, forming the basis of a change request.
questions.mindset: Assess a change before submitting it for approval.

questions.stem: In the midst of a renewable energy project, a team member notices a significant risk related to equipment procurement that could potentially derail the project timeline. The concern is promptly communicated to the project sponsor, who then requests the project manager for a detailed assessment and action plan. Which document should the project manager consult with the team to outline predefined approaches to address this procurement risk appropriately?

options.text: Risk register
options.rationale: The risk register records identified risks with their planned responses and owners.

options.text: Issue log
options.rationale: The issue log tracks current problems, not predefined responses to risks.

options.text: Risk response strategy
options.rationale: A 'risk response strategy' is not a separate standard project document.

options.text: Risk management plan
options.rationale: The risk management plan sets out the overall approach, not responses to specific risks.

questions.explanation: To outline predefined approaches to a specific procurement risk, the project manager consults the risk register with the team. It records each identified risk together with its planned responses, owners and triggers.
questions.mindset: Specific risk responses live in the risk register.

questions.stem: In finalizing an infrastructure upgrade project, the project manager needs to ensure that all critical operational knowledge has been transferred to the client's maintenance team effectively. What approach should the project manager employ to confirm the thoroughness of the knowledge transfer?

options.text: Schedule face-to-face sessions with maintenance team members and project team to validate understanding and application of the operational knowledge
options.rationale: Face-to-face sessions let the project team check the maintenance team's understanding and application directly.

options.text: Develop and administer a formal assessment to the maintenance team on key operational procedures
options.rationale: A formal test checks recall of procedures but not the ability to apply the knowledge.

options.text: Create an interactive online module for the maintenance team to complete, covering all necessary operational information
options.rationale: An online module delivers information but does not confirm that it has been understood.

options.text: Facilitate a roundtable discussion with key project and maintenance team members to evaluate the depth of knowledge transfer
options.rationale: A roundtable is useful but less thorough than validating each person's understanding.

questions.explanation: Confirming knowledge transfer means checking understanding and application, not just delivery. Face-to-face sessions between the project and maintenance teams let the project team validate each person's grasp of operational knowledge and clarify gaps immediately.
questions.mindset: Validate knowledge transfer, don't assume it.

questions.stem: In a software development project, the project manager notices that the various project teams have differing priorities and methodologies, leading to inconsistencies and delays in project milestones. The project manager realizes the need for a unified approach to streamline processes and improve collaboration among the teams. What is the most effective course of action for the project manager to ensure consistent progress across all teams?

options.text: Implement a centralized project management tool to enhance communication and task tracking
options.rationale: A central tool helps tracking but does not reconcile differing priorities and methods.

options.text: Conduct a workshop to align all teams on the project's objectives and establish a shared methodology
options.rationale: A workshop aligning all teams on objectives and a shared methodology addresses the source of inconsistency.

options.text: Assign a liaison from each team to facilitate better understanding and integration of work practices
options.rationale: Liaisons help communication but leave the underlying differences in place.

options.text: Reallocate project resources to prioritize tasks according to the urgency and importance of project milestones
options.rationale: Reallocating resources does not resolve the lack of a common approach.

questions.explanation: Inconsistencies and delays caused by teams working to different priorities and methods need a common foundation. A workshop to align all teams on project objectives and establish a shared methodology integrates their work and supports consistent progress.
questions.mindset: Align teams on goals and a common approach.

questions.stem: While implementing an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system, the agile project manager receives several requests for additional features from department heads, potentially affecting the project's scope and timeline. What should the project manager do to address these feature requests effectively?

options.text: Direct the department heads to submit their requests after the ERP system goes live
options.rationale: Deferring all requests until after go-live ignores potentially valuable features.

options.text: Have the product owner integrate the feature requests into the product backlog for prioritization
options.rationale: The product owner adds the requests to the backlog and prioritises them against existing work.

options.text: Advise the department heads that all project changes are frozen to avoid deviations from the planned schedule
options.rationale: A change freeze is contrary to agile's openness to changing requirements.

options.text: Request detailed business cases for each feature to assess their impact before adding them to the project plan
options.rationale: Detailed business cases for each feature add heavy predictive overhead to an agile project.

questions.explanation: In an agile project, new feature requests go to the product owner, who adds them to the product backlog and prioritises them against existing items. This absorbs change in a controlled way aligned with strategic goals.
questions.mindset: Channel new requests through the backlog.

questions.stem: In the implementation stage of a critical network security project, it is revealed that a specialist responsible for key parts of the configuration will be taking emergency leave. What should the project manager do to address the specialist's imminent absence and keep the project on schedule?

options.text: Facilitate a discussion with the project team to redistribute the specialist's responsibilities effectively among existing members
options.rationale: Redistributing the specialist's work with the team keeps configuration moving using existing skills.

options.text: Suggest pausing the project until the specialist can return and resume their duties
options.rationale: Pausing the project wastes time and may not be necessary.

options.text: Contact an external consulting firm to temporarily fill the specialist's role
options.rationale: External consultants add cost and onboarding time, and should be considered only if the team cannot cover.

options.text: Request an immediate extension of the project deadline to accommodate the delay
options.rationale: Asking for an extension concedes the delay before trying to cover the work.

questions.explanation: A sudden absence is a resource problem to manage. Working with the team to redistribute the specialist's responsibilities uses the collective skills already available and keeps the project on schedule without outside help.
questions.mindset: Cover absences with the team first.

questions.stem: Near the completion of an extensive software development project, it's noted that one developer's innovative solutions have greatly enhanced the project's outcomes, distinguishing their contribution from the rest of the team. What is the most appropriate way for the project manager to acknowledge this outstanding contribution?

options.text: Create a feature in the company newsletter highlighting the developer's innovative work
options.rationale: Newsletter coverage may not suit someone who prefers not to be in the spotlight.

options.text: Organize a casual team lunch where the developer's efforts can be informally recognized by peers
options.rationale: A casual lunch is pleasant but may undersell an outstanding contribution.

options.text: Submit a recommendation for the developer to be considered for a prestigious industry award
options.rationale: An industry award nomination may not match what the developer values.

options.text: Identify a form of recognition that aligns with what the developer values most, whether it be professional development opportunities, a specific form of public acknowledgment, or something personal
options.rationale: Recognition tailored to what the developer values makes it meaningful and appreciated.

questions.explanation: Recognition motivates most when it matches what the person values. Finding out whether the developer would value development opportunities, a particular public acknowledgement or something personal ensures the recognition is relevant and appreciated.
questions.mindset: Tailor recognition to the individual.

questions.stem: As the project manager for a novel online education platform, you're faced with divergent views among stakeholders regarding the balance between interactive content and accessibility features. The development team is split on which aspects to prioritize, potentially affecting the project timeline. What action should the project manager take to navigate this impasse effectively?

options.text: Deploy conflict resolution techniques specifically designed to address and integrate the diverse viewpoints into a unified strategy
options.rationale: Structured conflict resolution techniques help integrate the differing views into one agreed strategy.

options.text: Conduct a poll within the team and among stakeholders to democratically decide the project's focus areas
options.rationale: A poll turns a complex trade-off into a popularity contest and may leave a disgruntled minority.

options.text: Facilitate a focused group discussion leveraging design thinking principles to foster innovative solutions and choose the best solution
options.rationale: Design thinking can generate ideas, but the priority is resolving the entrenched disagreement.

options.text: Suggest the team separately debates and reaches a consensus without managerial intervention
options.rationale: Leaving the team to debate without facilitation risks the impasse continuing and delaying the project.

questions.explanation: When stakeholders and the team are split on priorities and the impasse threatens the timeline, the project manager confronts the divergence using structured conflict resolution techniques. These build understanding and lead to a unified strategy that integrates the different viewpoints.
questions.mindset: Use structured conflict resolution to reach a shared strategy.

questions.stem: You are managing your team through difficult project, which has been made more difficult by many team members being new and inexperienced, and not having the right capability to get the work done. You are getting pressure from your steering committee to improve the performance of your project. What will you do next?

options.text: Use Tuckman's ladder of Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing with your team.
options.rationale: Tuckman's model describes team development stages; it is not an action that builds capability.

options.text: Use co-location, a shared knowledge portal, training and team assessments.
options.rationale: Co-location, a shared knowledge portal, training and team assessments build capability and improve performance.

options.text: Use conflict management, influencing and emotional intelligence to get your team onside.
options.rationale: Interpersonal skills help engagement but do not fix the lack of capability.

options.text: Use brainstorming and root cause analysis to get to the heart of the problem.
options.rationale: Root cause analysis is unnecessary here because the cause, inexperience, is already known.

questions.explanation: An inexperienced team lacking capability needs to be developed. Team development tools such as co-location, shared knowledge resources, training and team assessments improve competencies and interaction, which in turn improves project performance.
questions.mindset: Develop the team's capability to lift performance.

questions.stem: As a project manager overseeing the rollout of a new online banking platform, ensuring that customers can seamlessly transition and utilize the platform is critical. The project sponsor emphasizes the importance of excellent customer support following the launch. What action should the project manager take to fulfill this requirement?

options.text: Coordinate with the customer service department to extend their hours in the weeks following the launch
options.rationale: Longer call-centre hours help, but they offer only one channel and are temporary.

options.text: Initiate a temporary dedicated hotline for new platform inquiries and issues
options.rationale: A temporary hotline is a single, short-lived support channel.

options.text: Set up a series of self-pace webinars for customers, focusing on platform features and common troubleshooting steps
options.rationale: Self-paced webinars help learning but do not offer live support for urgent problems.

options.text: Create a comprehensive online help center that includes tutorial videos, a searchable knowledge base, and options for live support
options.rationale: A comprehensive help centre with tutorials, a searchable knowledge base and live support meets varied customer needs.

questions.explanation: Excellent support after launch means customers can get help in the way that suits them, when they need it. A comprehensive online help centre combines self-service learning with live support, easing the transition to the new platform.
questions.mindset: Support the customer's transition in several ways.

questions.stem: At the outset of an initiative to introduce smart city technologies, it's discovered that the input from a crucial environmental expert was not included during the preliminary discussions on the project's environmental impact assessments. What document is most likely in need of revision due to this omission?

options.text: Stakeholder Register
options.rationale: The stakeholder register lists all stakeholders; an omitted key expert means it needs updating.

options.text: Stakeholder Engagement Plan
options.rationale: The engagement plan would be updated too, but the root omission is in stakeholder identification.

options.text: Project Schedule
options.rationale: The schedule is not the document that records who should be consulted.

options.text: Communication Plan
options.rationale: The communication plan depends on the stakeholders already identified in the register.

questions.explanation: If a crucial expert was left out of the discussions, the expert was probably never identified as a stakeholder. The stakeholder register records who may affect or be affected by the project, so it is the first document to update.
questions.mindset: Missed stakeholders start with the stakeholder register.

questions.stem: Just assigned to lead a new technology integration project, the project manager learns that no foundational project documentation exists, leaving the team uncertain about project scope, deliverables, and timelines. What action should the project manager take to establish a solid foundation for the project's success?

options.text: Initiate the project by focusing on high-priority tasks and develop the documentation as these tasks progress
options.rationale: Starting tasks without foundational documents continues the uncertainty about scope and timelines.

options.text: Instruct department heads to compile their respective sections of the project documentation to streamline the process
options.rationale: Asking department heads for separate sections produces a fragmented plan without shared ownership.

options.text: Look into industry-standard project management templates to quickly draft the necessary documentation
options.rationale: Templates help with format but not with the content the team needs to agree.

options.text: Engage the entire project team in a comprehensive planning session to collaboratively develop all critical project management documents
options.rationale: A collaborative planning session produces agreed documentation and a shared understanding of scope, deliverables and timelines.

questions.explanation: A project with no foundational documentation lacks agreed scope, deliverables and timelines. Engaging the team in a comprehensive planning session produces those documents collaboratively, giving everyone a shared understanding and commitment.
questions.mindset: Plan with the team to build shared understanding.

questions.stem: To enhance project communication and address emerging issues, a project manager organizes bi-weekly meetings with the development team of a software project. What should the project manager prioritize at the beginning of these meetings?

options.text: Detail the current status of the project's schedule and any deviations
options.rationale: Schedule status may be discussed, but it is not how an effective meeting starts.

options.text: Meeting agenda, times and topics to cover
options.rationale: Starting with the agenda, timings and topics focuses the meeting on what must be addressed.

options.text: Reevaluate the project's scope in light of recent developments
options.rationale: Re-evaluating scope is not a routine start to a communication meeting.

options.text: Gather feedback for a continuous improvement process
options.rationale: Feedback for improvement is usually gathered at the end, not the start.

questions.explanation: Effective meetings begin with a clear agenda. Setting out the topics and timings at the start ensures everyone knows what will be covered and what decisions or actions are needed, making the bi-weekly meetings focused and productive.
questions.mindset: Open meetings with a clear agenda.

questions.stem: In the midst of executing a high-stakes software development project, several unexpected software bugs and team miscommunications have led to project delays, causing tension within the team and concern from the project sponsor about meeting key deliverables on time. What should the project manager do to alleviate these issues and steer the project back on track?

options.text: Conduct team-building events focused on enhancing team collaboration and open communication
options.rationale: Team-building that strengthens collaboration and open communication tackles the miscommunication driving delays and tension.

options.text: Host a problem-solving workshop where team members can collaboratively identify solutions to technical issues
options.rationale: A problem-solving workshop addresses the technical bugs but not the underlying miscommunication and tension.

options.text: Increase the frequency of progress review meetings to closely monitor team performance and progress
options.rationale: More review meetings increase scrutiny and may worsen tension.

options.text: Arrange for a professional mediator to address and resolve interpersonal conflicts within the team
options.rationale: A professional mediator is excessive when there is no entrenched conflict between specific people.

questions.explanation: The delays stem partly from miscommunication, and they have created tension. Activities that rebuild trust and open communication address the team dynamics that underlie both the technical and interpersonal problems.
questions.mindset: Rebuild trust and communication when tension grows.

questions.stem: You have planned the scope, schedule, cost and resources with your team. You have also identified a large number of risks within your project. You are in the process of assigning the probability and impact to the risks when one of the risks occurs. Your project sponsor immediately worries about a worst case scenario. What will you do next?

options.text: Utilise the management reserve for your project to mitigate the risk.
options.rationale: The management reserve is for unknown risks; this risk had been identified.

options.text: Review (or create) the risk response in the risk register then use the appropriate contingency reserve to implement it.
options.rationale: Using the planned (or newly created) response and the contingency reserve deals with an identified risk as intended.

options.text: Perform quantitative analysis on the risk to ensure you know how much it will cost.
options.rationale: Quantitative analysis takes time and does not act on a risk that has already happened.

options.text: Accept the risk for now, as the risk analysis is not yet complete.
options.rationale: Accepting a risk that has occurred because analysis is incomplete leaves it unmanaged.

questions.explanation: An identified risk has occurred during qualitative analysis. The project manager uses the response in the risk register, creating one if needed, and draws on the contingency reserve set aside for known risks, rather than the management reserve meant for unknown risks.
questions.mindset: Identified risks use contingency reserve.

questions.stem: In the midst of a complex IT project, feedback from an executive sponsor indicates dissatisfaction with the detailed nature of the project updates, which they find cumbersome and distracting from key insights. What measure should the project manager implement to refine the communication process with the executive sponsor?

options.text: Transition to a streamlined weekly email summary highlighting critical points and decisions needed
options.rationale: A shorter email may still miss what the sponsor wants to see.

options.text: Utilize a project management tool that allows the sponsor to view real-time updates at their convenience
options.rationale: A real-time tool leaves the sponsor to find insights in the detail they already dislike.

options.text: Conduct a detailed discussion with the sponsor to identify their preferences for information and report format
options.rationale: Discussing the sponsor's preferences for content and format lets the updates be tailored precisely.

options.text: Schedule brief, focused update calls with the sponsor to review major milestones and address any concerns
options.rationale: Brief calls are a format chosen without understanding the sponsor's actual preferences.

questions.explanation: When a sponsor finds updates too detailed, the project manager asks what they need rather than guessing. Understanding the sponsor's preferences for information and format allows updates to deliver clear, actionable insights without extraneous detail.
questions.mindset: Ask stakeholders how they want to be informed.

questions.stem: During an iterative development project for a new software tool, a developer who was recently added to the team suggests implementing a cutting-edge testing technique that differs significantly from the project's standard practices. The rest of the team has expressed reluctance to deviate from known methods. What should the project manager do to address the team's reluctance and explore the potential of the new method?

options.text: Instruct the new developer to maintain the status quo to preserve team harmony and project pace
options.rationale: Telling the developer to keep the status quo shuts down a potentially valuable improvement.

options.text: Assign the developer to less critical tasks to avoid any potential disruption to the established testing process
options.rationale: Sidelining the developer avoids the discussion and wastes their idea.

options.text: Facilitate a session where the new developer can present the proposed testing method, detailing its advantages and implementation process
options.rationale: A session where the developer presents the method lets the team evaluate its benefits and implementation openly.

options.text: Recommend the developer prepare a detailed report on the proposed method for review at the project's conclusion
options.rationale: Deferring review to the project's end loses the chance to benefit now.

questions.explanation: Iterative projects benefit from continuous improvement. Letting the new developer present the proposed testing method, with its advantages and implementation, allows the team to evaluate it critically and addresses reluctance through understanding rather than dismissal.
questions.mindset: Give new ideas a fair hearing.

questions.stem: Ahead of a crucial update meeting, a project manager learns about a potential unforeseen delay in a project segment that involves an external contractor. The full extent of how this will affect the project timeline is not yet known. What two actions should the project manager take before addressing this in the meeting? (Choose two.)

options.text: Liaise with the external contractor to understand the reasons behind the delay
options.rationale: Talking to the contractor helps understand the cause, but the source prioritises assessing impact and recording it.

options.text: Perform a detailed assessment to gauge the overall impact of the delay on the project
options.rationale: A detailed impact assessment tells stakeholders how the delay affects the whole project.

options.text: Delay the discussion until stakeholders notice the delay themselves
options.rationale: Waiting for stakeholders to notice is not transparent and damages trust.

options.text: Compare this situation with documented outcomes from similar incidents in other projects
options.rationale: Comparisons with other projects add little before this delay's own impact is known.

options.text: Record the delay in the project risk register and discuss it openly in the stakeholder meeting
options.rationale: Recording the delay and discussing it openly keeps it tracked and stakeholders informed.

questions.explanation: Before raising a possible delay in a key meeting, the project manager assesses its likely impact on the project and records it so it is tracked. Presenting it openly with this analysis keeps stakeholders properly informed.
questions.mindset: Assess, record and disclose emerging delays.

questions.stem: At the conclusion of an enterprise software implementation project, a department head suggests the addition of a new analytics feature to improve data visualization capabilities. This feature was not covered in the project's initial scope but is considered by the department head to be a straightforward enhancement that can be managed by the current IT staff. What action should the project manager take in response to the department head's suggestion?

options.text: Assess the feasibility of incorporating the new/analytics feature within the existing project's without formalizing it
options.rationale: Considering the feature informally without formalising it bypasses change control.

options.text: Consult with the finance team to assess the potential financial implications and budget adjustments required for the additional feature
options.rationale: Finance input is only one part of evaluating the proposal.

options.text: Coordinate a meeting with key project stakeholders to evaluate the added value versus the effort and risk of incorporating the new feature
options.rationale: A stakeholder meeting to weigh value against effort and risk evaluates the request properly before any decision.

options.text: Draft a supplemental project charter for the analytics feature addition, pending executive approval
options.rationale: A supplementary charter is premature before the value of the feature has been evaluated.

questions.explanation: A new feature suggested at project close is outside scope, however simple it may seem. Evaluating its value against the effort and risk with key stakeholders ensures a sound decision about whether to add it or handle it separately.
questions.mindset: Evaluate out-of-scope ideas with stakeholders before acting.

questions.stem: You have been assigned to a new project, where the work is behind schedule and the team are not working together well. The team is relatively new, and conflicts are arising. Team members are blaming each other for work not done, and some people are not showing up to work on the project at all. What will you do next?

options.text: Meet with the functional manager to agree on the team members' time requirements.
options.rationale: Agreeing time requirements with the functional manager addresses attendance only, not conflict and blame.

options.text: Meet with your team to set a team charter and define roles & responsibilities.
options.rationale: A team charter with agreed roles and responsibilities creates a shared basis for working together.

options.text: Meet with the project sponsor to gain additional funding for resources who can work together.
options.rationale: Seeking funding for different people abandons the current team without trying to improve it.

options.text: Escalate the issue to the steering committee as soon as possible as a project risk.
options.rationale: Escalating to the steering committee is premature before trying to develop the team.

questions.explanation: A new team with conflicts, blame and absenteeism lacks shared agreements. Meeting to set a team charter and define roles and responsibilities establishes a collaborative team environment with clear expectations.
questions.mindset: Set team agreements and roles to resolve early dysfunction.

questions.stem: You have recently completed a project for a new product and have been asked to manage it after its release to keep it relevant in today's marketplace. Half of your existing project team are rolling off to other projects soon, and your project budget is nearly depleted. What will you do next?

options.text: Create a business case and project charter for your project sponsor to approve.
options.rationale: A new business case and charter treat product management as a one-off project.

options.text: Retain as many of your current project staff to continue work on the product.
options.rationale: Keeping staff helps, but without secured funding the team cannot be sustained.

options.text: Raise a change request for your current project to add scope and continue making changes.
options.rationale: Stretching the completed project with change requests confuses project delivery with ongoing product management.

options.text: Secure funding for a stable team, then use current research to form a suite of projects to improve the product.
options.rationale: Securing funding for a stable team and forming improvement projects from research sustains the product through its lifecycle.

questions.explanation: Managing a product after release is product management, which spans the lifecycle. It needs sustainable funding for a stable team and a stream of improvement work informed by current market research.
questions.mindset: Manage products with stable teams and ongoing funding.

questions.stem: You are delivering a critical change and several key stakeholders in your organisation have added seemingly unnecessary steps for you to take, with extra approvals, reports and meetings. They are also restricting the people you need from working on your project in a larger capacity. What will you do next?

options.text: Go directly to the people you need to avoid extra back-and-forth with the stakeholders.
options.rationale: Going around stakeholders to reach their people damages relationships and increases resistance.

options.text: Raise a risk in the risk register on the lack of access to sufficient resources.
options.rationale: Logging a resource risk records the symptom but does nothing to change the stakeholders' behaviour.

options.text: Communicate more often with the stakeholders and gain a deeper awareness of their ideas and situation.
options.rationale: Communicating more and understanding their ideas and situation addresses why stakeholders are adding hurdles.

options.text: Show your stakeholders the Resource Assignment Matrix and project roles & responsibilities.
options.rationale: Showing the responsibility matrix asserts the plan without engaging their concerns.

questions.explanation: Stakeholders who add approvals and restrict resources are often not engaged appropriately. More frequent communication and a deeper understanding of their ideas and situation, ideally face to face, turns them from obstacles into supporters.
questions.mindset: Engage resistant stakeholders more, not less.

questions.stem: You are managing a project team mostly made up of men. Recently Jane was hired for her high expertise in the brands that make up your industry. You notice she has been left out of some key meetings, and others are overlooking her opinions. You also notice she is paid significantly less than her male colleagues. What will you do next?

options.text: Make steps to update her pay to the same range as the others on your project, and ask her opinion and advice specifically during each meeting (along with others in your team).
options.rationale: Correcting her pay and actively seeking her input address both the unfair treatment and her exclusion.

options.text: Take the lower pay as a win for your project, as it will help keep costs low and her colleagues don't need to know.
options.rationale: Treating unequal pay as a cost saving is unethical and breaches stewardship obligations.

options.text: Ask Jane to write down her knowledge of the industry, just in case she leaves.
options.rationale: Asking her to document knowledge in case she leaves ignores the unfair treatment that might make her leave.

options.text: No need to rock the boat - this is just how people work in this industry.
options.rationale: Accepting unfairness as 'how the industry works' fails the project manager's duty of integrity.

questions.explanation: Integrity and stewardship require fair and respectful treatment of team members, including pay, access to opportunity and inclusion. The project manager acts to correct the pay disparity and actively includes Jane's expertise in team discussions.
questions.mindset: Act on unfair treatment; include every expert voice.

questions.stem: During one of your working group meetings, a stakeholder raises the concern that the product you are working on will be discontinued in the next five months. You were not aware of this, and your project budget has already been approved until the scheduled delivery, which is in five months also. What will you do next?

options.text: Keep the project going as it is - the discontinued product isn't your responsibility.
options.rationale: Continuing a project for a product about to be discontinued wastes resources on something with no value.

options.text: Set a meeting with your project sponsor to share the information and a recommendation to terminate the project.
options.rationale: Sharing the information with the sponsor and recommending termination respects governance and the organisation's resources.

options.text: Change the scope of the project to meet a different product so your project can remain relevant.
options.rationale: Changing scope to a different product is a decision outside the project manager's authority.

options.text: Ask for additional funding to see if you can improve the product instead of discontinuing it.
options.rationale: Seeking funds to rescue the product oversteps the project's purpose and authority.

questions.explanation: Projects exist to deliver value. If the product will be discontinued when the project delivers, that value disappears. The project manager takes the information to the sponsor with a recommendation to terminate, leaving the governance decision to the sponsor.
questions.mindset: Recommend stopping when the value is gone.

questions.stem: You have collected the requirements for your project and are creating the scope statement and work breakdown structure. During this process you notice some functionality in your database system that will help a different project you are aware of within your Project Management Office (PMO). What will you do next?

options.text: Place the feature in the other project's backlog, and ask them to prioritise it as soon as possible.
options.rationale: Putting work into another project's backlog without their agreement bypasses their product owner and sponsor.

options.text: Raise the functionality in your risk register as a threat, with the response to "mitigate".
options.rationale: Beneficial functionality is an opportunity, not a threat to be mitigated.

options.text: Add the scope to your project and complete it as soon as possible.
options.rationale: Adding the scope to your project without approval causes scope creep.

options.text: Raise the functionality in your risk register as an opportunity with the response to "exploit", and meet with the other project team and sponsor to discuss.
options.rationale: Recording it as an opportunity to exploit and discussing it with the other team and sponsor makes the benefit available properly.

questions.explanation: Systems thinking looks at how the project interacts with others. Functionality that could help another project is an opportunity. Recording it and discussing it with the other project team and sponsor allows it to be exploited without bypassing their governance.
questions.mindset: Record and share opportunities across projects.

questions.stem: You are working on a high profile project. Several high-ranking senior executives want to take the credit for this initiative, while limiting the impact to their own resources. This has led to several conflicts and a scope statement that is unclear, leading to a risk of project failure. What will you do next?

options.text: Create a scope statement yourself to avoid further conflict.
options.rationale: Writing the scope yourself sidesteps the executives and will not gain their agreement.

options.text: Facilitate a discussion with the executives as a neutral third party, focusing on agreed project goals.
options.rationale: Neutral facilitation around agreed goals helps the executives reach consensus on scope.

options.text: Limit your project resources to the executives until they can agree on a way forward.
options.rationale: Restricting resources to pressure executives is manipulative and damages relationships.

options.text: Escalate the issue to the project steering committee and ask them to resolve the problem.
options.rationale: Escalating to the steering committee may be needed later, but facilitation should come first.

questions.explanation: Leadership is not the same as authority. When senior executives conflict over priorities, the project manager can facilitate as a neutral third party, focusing the discussion on agreed project goals to build consensus and clarify scope.
questions.mindset: Facilitate neutrally around shared goals.

questions.stem: You are managing a project where the majority of the product has been planned up-front, but an external system is needed from a vendor in partial pieces where the requirements are unclear. Half of your stakeholders want to use a waterfall approach, and the other half are advocating for an Agile approach. What will you do next?

options.text: Use an Agile methodology. The fixed scope is low risk, and you can capture changes using Agile.
