options.rationale: Agile alone ignores that most of the product has been planned in advance and is stable.

options.text: Use a Waterfall methodology and ask the team to plan the uncertain scope better.
options.rationale: Waterfall alone cannot handle a vendor component whose requirements are still unclear.

options.text: Proceed with a hybrid method to start, with pre-planned scope but Agile ceremonies that promote feedback.
options.rationale: A hybrid approach with pre-planned scope plus agile feedback ceremonies suits the project's mix of certainty and uncertainty.

options.text: Use a combination of Waterfall and Agile to capture all the requirements and keep stakeholders happy.
options.rationale: Combining methods to 'keep everyone happy' is not tailoring to the project's needs.

questions.explanation: Tailoring fits the method to the project's context. Where most of the scope is well defined but part is uncertain, a hybrid approach uses up-front planning for the known work and agile feedback loops for the uncertain vendor component, refined as the project proceeds.
questions.mindset: Tailor the approach to the certainty of each part.

questions.stem: You are working on a project where senior users have been testing the product as parts are released. They have found some missing requirements and defects. Their manager is worried that the project won't deliver a product that is fit for purpose, without defects and within the timeframe needed. What will you do next?

options.text: Perform some of the testing yourself to ensure a quality product.
options.rationale: The project manager doing testing does not build quality into the team's work.

options.text: Help every team member to focus on quality, from correct acceptance criteria to a developed and tested product.
options.rationale: Helping every team member focus on quality, from clear acceptance criteria to tested work, builds quality in.

options.text: Limit testing until the very end of the project so you can do it all in one go when the product is completely ready.
options.rationale: Deferring testing to the end finds defects late, when they are most expensive to fix.

options.text: Increase the testing on your project and add more testing resources so no defect goes unnoticed.
options.rationale: Adding testers catches more defects but does not prevent missing requirements.

questions.explanation: In adaptive projects quality is everyone's responsibility. Clear acceptance criteria, well-understood requirements and testing throughout development build quality into the product rather than inspecting defects out at the end.
questions.mindset: Build quality in; it is everyone's job.

questions.stem: You are working through the risk assessment with your team, who are having trouble coming up with ideas for risks. You decide to give them some guidance on types of complexity that might affect your new product. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask them to brainstorm Qualitative and Quantitative risks.
options.rationale: Qualitative and quantitative are analysis methods, not categories to prompt risk ideas.

options.text: Ask them to perform the Five Whys and Ishikawa analysis.
options.rationale: The Five Whys and Ishikawa diagrams analyse the causes of known problems, not future risks.

options.text: Ask them to brainstorm around possible unwanted human behaviour, system behaviour, ambiguity and technical innovation impacts.
options.rationale: Prompting on human behaviour, system behaviour, ambiguity and technical innovation targets the sources of complexity.

options.text: Ask them to perform a retrospective to discover what isn't working well, and what still puzzles us.
options.rationale: A retrospective reviews past work rather than identifying risks for a new product.

questions.explanation: Complexity often arises from human behaviour, system interactions, uncertainty and ambiguity, and technical innovation. Using these as prompts helps a team that is struggling to identify risks think systematically about what could affect the new product.
questions.mindset: Use sources of complexity to prompt risk ideas.

questions.stem: You are working in an Agile team and the business representative would like to get an idea of the risk associated with a particular feature. What will you do next?

options.text: Show the risk management plan from your project management plan to the business representative.
options.rationale: The risk management plan describes the approach, not the risks of a particular feature.

options.text: Ask the development team if they like the feature.
options.rationale: Whether the team likes a feature says nothing about its risk.

options.text: Hold a pre-mortem, where each team member writes reasons they think the task or feature might fail so these can be discussed.
options.rationale: A pre-mortem has each member write down why the feature might fail, surfacing risks for discussion.

options.text: Check your gut-feel for the feature, and if it doesn't feel right look into it deeply.
options.rationale: Gut feel is not a structured way to assess risk.

questions.explanation: A pre-mortem imagines that a feature has failed and asks why. Team members write down their reasons individually, then discuss them in turn, which produces a broad set of feature-level risks for the business representative.
questions.mindset: Imagine failure to find risks early.

questions.stem: A risk has been raised in your project around insufficient building materials. One risk response assigned to the functional manager suggests to use a brand new material, which has not been fully tested in a building project. Half of your stakeholder group are happy with this risk response, but the other half are not, and refuse to sign off on it. What will you do next?

options.text: Suggest a quantitative risk approach to give a more accurate financial impact.
options.rationale: Quantitative analysis of financial impact does not resolve disagreement about the response itself.

options.text: Suggest they proceed with the proposed risk response, and ensure it is followed through.
options.rationale: Proceeding without stakeholder agreement ignores a key criterion for a valid response.

options.text: Suggest a different risk owner, as an executive may have more power to respond to the risk.
options.rationale: Changing the owner does not address stakeholders' objections to an untested material.

options.text: Suggest a different risk response, as they should be timely, cost effective, realistic, and agreed to by relevant stakeholders.
options.rationale: A different response is needed: responses must be timely, cost-effective, realistic and agreed by stakeholders.

questions.explanation: An effective risk response must be appropriate to the risk's significance, timely, cost-effective, realistic in context, agreed by relevant stakeholders and owned by someone. A response that half the stakeholders reject fails these criteria, so another is needed.
questions.mindset: Risk responses need stakeholder agreement.

questions.stem: Your project is starting to go off track due to a large amount of uncertainty in the requirements and resources. At a significant cost, you have managed to reign in these issues, however your project management office would like you to brainstorm ways to improve with your team so that they do not happen again. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask your team to increase the project Contingency Reserve, to allow for these impacts.
options.rationale: More contingency absorbs the impact but does not prevent the problems recurring.

options.text: Ask your team to change the project methodology from Waterfall to Agile.
options.rationale: Switching methodology is a large change that may not suit the project.

options.text: Ask your team to use short feedback loops, continuous improvement, and transparent planning.
options.rationale: Short feedback loops, continuous improvement and transparent planning build adaptability to uncertainty.

options.text: Ask your team to check their work twice before sending it to the next part of the process.
options.rationale: Double-checking work addresses errors, not uncertainty in requirements and resources.

questions.explanation: Uncertainty in requirements and resources calls for adaptability and resilience. Short feedback loops, continuous learning and improvement, and transparent planning help the team spot and respond to change early, preventing costly disruption.
questions.mindset: Build adaptability through feedback and improvement.

questions.stem: As your project progresses, many of the business stakeholders are starting to voice their concerns, to question some of the changes, and even miss key meetings while trying to sabotage your efforts. What will you do next?

options.text: Communicate the vision and benefits for the change clearly, along with the impact to their work.
options.rationale: Clearly communicating the vision, benefits and impact on their work addresses the causes of resistance.

options.text: Create an impact over influence chart to determine who should be engaged appropriately.
options.rationale: A stakeholder chart analyses who to engage but does not address the resistance itself.

options.text: Escalate the matter with your project sponsor, and arrange for different stakeholders.
options.rationale: Escalating and replacing stakeholders is unrealistic and damages relationships.

options.text: Map the current state and the proposed future state of the change for the stakeholders.
options.rationale: Mapping current and future states helps, but on its own it does not explain the benefits and impact on people's work.

questions.explanation: Resistance to change often comes from lack of understanding or change fatigue. Communicating the vision, goals and benefits of the change, along with its impact on how people work, helps stakeholders understand why and what it means for them.
questions.mindset: Explain the why and the impact to reduce resistance.

questions.stem: You are analysing your stakeholder through an impact over influence chart and have found more than 100 different groups of people, and over 3000 impacted stakeholders. Other parts of your project are starting to fall behind as you try to keep up with the large amount of people. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask your project team to engage different groups of stakeholders so everyone is covered.
options.rationale: Spreading engagement across the team without priorities still attempts to cover everyone equally.

options.text: Clearly prioritise the stakeholders then engage and communicate with the highly impacted and influential groups early and often.
options.rationale: Prioritising stakeholders and engaging the most impacted and influential groups early and often makes engagement manageable.

options.text: Monitor the stakeholders for signs of stress and respond to groups most stressed about the project.
options.rationale: Reacting to signs of stress is not a planned engagement approach.

options.text: Create a SharePoint page for changes that any stakeholder can gather information from anytime.
options.rationale: A self-service page is passive and will not engage the key groups adequately.

questions.explanation: With too many stakeholders to engage individually, prioritisation is essential. Focusing engagement on the most impacted and influential groups, early and often, uses limited time effectively while other groups receive appropriate but lighter communication.
questions.mindset: Prioritise stakeholders when there are too many to engage equally.

questions.stem: You are managing a project which communicates to the customer using mostly pull communication so far. When monitoring the engagement of your stakeholders, you notice a trend that they are not clear on the impacts or benefits of the project. You decide to add push communication to your communication plan. What will you do next?

options.text: Create a webpage using SharePoint with all the project information, that your stakeholders can see.
options.rationale: A web page is pull communication, which is what the project already relies on.

options.text: Push for more funding on your project, and communicate this to your project sponsor.
options.rationale: Pushing for funding is unrelated to the communication method.

options.text: Push your stakeholders to engage in more two-way communication.
options.rationale: Two-way communication is interactive, not push communication.

options.text: Send a weekly email to stakeholders with a project update, including the impacts and benefits.
options.rationale: A weekly email update is push communication that delivers the impacts and benefits directly to stakeholders.

questions.explanation: Push communication is sent to specific recipients, for example by email, memo or status report. Pull communication is accessed when people choose to look. Adding a weekly email that explains impacts and benefits makes sure stakeholders receive the message.
questions.mindset: Push important messages to stakeholders.

questions.stem: You have taken over on a project with a vendor where scope and requirements have been missed. You notice that miscommunication and mixed messages are common. You set a meeting with your team and the vendor's team. The meeting is extremely important to get right. What will you do next?

options.text: Speak slowly and clearly with the vendor's team, at a louder volume if necessary.
options.rationale: Speaking slowly and loudly does not check understanding and can come across as condescending.

options.text: Confirm they hear your message, determine if they agree, and identify nuanced or unintended messages they may have received.
options.rationale: Confirming the message was heard, checking agreement and identifying unintended meanings closes the communication loop.

options.text: Only communicate with the vendor in writing, so you have a trail of proof if anything goes wrong in the future.
options.rationale: Writing-only communication slows collaboration and focuses on blame rather than understanding.

options.text: Prepare a claim for the mishandled scope of your project through your procurement team.
options.rationale: Preparing a claim escalates conflict before communication has been fixed.

questions.explanation: Where miscommunication has caused missed scope, the project manager uses quick feedback loops. Confirming that the message was heard, checking whether the other party agrees and uncovering any nuances or unintended messages ensures real shared understanding.
questions.mindset: Close the loop to confirm understanding.

questions.stem: You have collected the requirements for your project, matched them to project scope, and broken them down into smaller parts and the activities required. In doing this, you notice that the manager of the marketing department has added extra scope that is unrelated to your current project. What will you do next?

options.text: Start an open dialogue with the functional manager, raise the incorrect scope items and their impacts.
options.rationale: An open dialogue with the functional manager finds out why the scope was added and explains its impact.

options.text: Override the marketing manager's decision on scope as you are the senior project manager.
options.rationale: Overriding the manager is confrontational and assumes authority the project manager may not have.

options.text: Raise a change request for the additional scope and let the Change Control Board decide.
options.rationale: A change request is premature before understanding whether the scope was a mistake or previously approved.

options.text: Place the additional scope into the product backlog for the product owner to prioritise it.
options.rationale: Putting unrelated scope into the backlog legitimises work that may not belong to the project.

questions.explanation: Unexpected scope in the requirements might be a mistake, a previously approved addition or something else. Open dialogue with the functional manager about the items and their impact clarifies the situation, reflecting a team culture of transparency and courage.
questions.mindset: Talk openly before acting on unexpected scope.

questions.stem: Your project team are protected by a union agreement. You notice that they don't know how to use the product you are improving, are slow to respond and regularly complain about the work. Your project sponsor has had enough and threatens to shut the project down if improvements can't be made. What will you do next?

options.text: Set up a new project with different team members and transfer the project work to that team.
options.rationale: Replacing the team with others in the same organisation risks the same result.

options.text: Set a clear project purpose and vision and pair your team with the customer to show them how they are making a positive difference.
options.rationale: A clear purpose and vision, plus contact with customers, shows the team the difference they make and builds intrinsic motivation.

options.text: Tell your project team that they will lose their jobs in they don't improve the speed of their work.
options.rationale: Threatening jobs may entrench the behaviour and is inappropriate, especially with a union agreement.

options.text: Create a project Gantt Chart schedule and burndown chart so the project work is transparent to all.
options.rationale: Transparency charts show the problem but do not motivate the team.

questions.explanation: A disengaged team often lacks a sense of purpose. Setting a clear vision and connecting the team with customers shows them the positive difference their work makes, which builds intrinsic motivation far more effectively than threats or replacement.
questions.mindset: Connect the team to purpose to motivate it.

questions.stem: During a key scope meeting, an argument arises. The business manager accuses the technology manager of not delivering to their needs on past projects, and the technology manager accuses the business manager of changing requirements that impact the delivery schedule. The meeting is at risk, with the stakeholders being closed off to any further discussion. What will you do next?

options.text: Take the side of the technology manager, as scope that impacts delivery should be controlled.
options.rationale: Siding with the technology manager escalates the conflict and alienates the business.

options.text: Take the side of the business manager, as we should always deliver to the customer's specification.
options.rationale: Siding with the business manager escalates the conflict and alienates technology.

options.text: Facilitate to keep communication respectful, focus on the issue in the present and search for alternatives together.
options.rationale: Facilitating respectful communication, focused on the present issue, and exploring alternatives together can turn conflict into better decisions.

options.text: Ensure they both agree to the change control process to avoid disagreements in the future.
options.rationale: Agreeing change control helps later, but does not resolve the current confrontation.

questions.explanation: Conflict handled well leads to better decisions. The project manager keeps the discussion respectful, focuses on the issue rather than the person and on the present rather than the past, and helps both parties search for alternatives together.
questions.mindset: Focus conflict on the issue, the present and solutions.

questions.stem: You are working on a project where the project team is completely distributed around the country in multiple sites, including working from home. Some of the project team members have not been able to contribute to the project, and there are concerns from the program that the project will fall behind. What will you do next?

options.text: Raise a request to the program to co-locate all your project team members as soon as possible.
options.rationale: Co-locating a team spread across the country is impractical and costly.

options.text: Proceed with daily stand-ups and working group meetings with any team members in your area.
options.rationale: Holding meetings only with local members excludes the distributed team further.

options.text: Set team leaders for each area around the country, to report back to you as the centralized project leader.
options.rationale: Area team leaders add a reporting layer but do not help remote members contribute.

options.text: Use technology to maintain ongoing contact with audio and video for meetings, with a team web site to keep all project information available.
options.rationale: Audio and video meetings, ongoing contact and a shared team site let distributed members participate fully.

questions.explanation: Distributed teams need technology to work as one. Using audio and video for meetings, messaging for ongoing contact and an open project site for information lets team members in any location contribute and stay informed.
questions.mindset: Use technology to include distributed team members.

questions.stem: You are initiating a project to a sales team where the process will change significantly, even though the outcome of a completed sale will remain the same. The functional manager is concerned about the change and any disruption it might bring. What will you do next?

options.text: Kick of the project with multiple deliveries to deliver small parts and reduce the change impact.
options.rationale: Multiple partial deliveries of a process change could leave the sales team using a mix of old and new processes.

options.text: Kick off the project work with a single delivery at the end of the project when the process change is complete.
options.rationale: A single delivery at the end rolls out the complete new process at once, minimising disruption.

options.text: Kick off the project with continuous delivery in mind, to ensure fast value to the business.
options.rationale: Continuous delivery suits software features, not a sales process that must change as a whole.

options.text: Kick off the project using periodic deliveries, delivering value as it is ready.
options.rationale: Periodic deliveries of a process change would repeatedly disrupt the sales team.

questions.explanation: The right delivery cadence depends on what is delivered. A process re-engineering project may deliver nothing usable until the whole new process is ready. A single delivery at the end avoids the disruption of repeated partial changes.
questions.mindset: Choose the delivery cadence that fits the change.

questions.stem: You are working on a project where the requirements are clear but the solution ideas are uncertain. The product owner and the technical experts can't be sure which ideas will work in practice, and which ones won't. The organisation cannot afford to get this project wrong, as they have previously made mistakes and customers are starting to leave. What will you do next?

options.text: Use an Incremental development approach for the project.
options.rationale: Incremental delivery provides features progressively but does not focus on refining uncertain solution ideas.

options.text: Use an Iterative development approach for the project.
options.rationale: An iterative approach refines ideas through repeated cycles and feedback before a single release.

options.text: Use a Predictive development approach for the project.
options.rationale: A predictive approach needs certainty about the solution, which is missing.

options.text: Use a hybrid development approach for the project.
options.rationale: A hybrid approach is unnecessary when the requirements are clear and only the solution is uncertain.

questions.explanation: When requirements are clear but it is uncertain which solution ideas will work, an iterative approach tests and refines ideas through repeated cycles. The final solution is delivered once it has been proven, reducing the risk of another costly mistake.
questions.mindset: Iterate when the solution is uncertain.

questions.stem: You are working on a new product for your organisation where the requirements are complex and are likely to change a few times as the project progresses. The organisation also needs usable parts of the product to be released as soon as possible to try and capture some of the market they are aiming for, away from their competitors. What will you do next?

options.text: Recommend an Iterative development approach.
options.rationale: Iterative refines a solution but does not by itself deliver usable parts early.

options.text: Recommend a Predictive development approach.
options.rationale: A predictive approach struggles with requirements that are expected to change.

options.text: Recommend an Adaptive development approach.
options.rationale: An adaptive approach handles changing requirements and delivers usable parts early.

options.text: Recommend a Hybrid development approach.
options.rationale: Hybrid is unnecessary here because nothing in the project calls for predictive elements.

questions.explanation: Complex requirements that will change, combined with the need to release usable parts early to capture the market, point to an adaptive approach. A clear vision guides the work, and requirements are refined through user feedback as increments are delivered.
questions.mindset: Use adaptive approaches for changing requirements and early value.

questions.stem: A new project has been kicked off in your organisation due to a recent government inquiry into your industry, which found multiple processes with significant regulatory oversight that need to change. The inquiry ordering these changes has given you a due date of 10 months' time before you start incurring penalties. What will you do next?

options.text: Proceed, with an Agile development approach to deliver change as quickly as possible.
options.rationale: Agile's speed does not by itself meet the process and documentation needs of heavy regulatory oversight.

options.text: Proceed, with a Hybrid development approach to respond to changes while planning up front.
options.rationale: Hybrid could work, but the regulatory environment points most strongly to a predictive approach.

options.text: Proceed, with a Predictive methodology to ensure quality control.
options.rationale: A predictive approach provides the defined process, documentation and demonstration that regulators require.

options.text: Proceed, with an Iterative methodology to improve using feedback.
options.rationale: Iterative refinement does not by itself provide the formal controls required.

questions.explanation: Environments with significant regulatory oversight often call for a predictive approach. The required processes, documentation and evidence of compliance are easier to plan and demonstrate when the work is defined in advance.
questions.mindset: Heavy regulation favours predictive control.

questions.stem: Your organisation is moving to an Agile way of work. Your project team are strongly opposed to using Agile as they have been burned using iterations, when executives used the team velocity to try and force the team to work faster instead of keeping a sustainable pace. What will you do next?

options.text: Add extra resources to your team to deliver faster and avoid executives getting involved.
options.rationale: Adding resources does not address the team's concerns about how velocity is misused.

options.text: Proceed with a predictive development approach, and deal with the consequences later.
options.rationale: Reverting to predictive ignores the organisation's move to agile.

options.text: Ask your team to work with Agile, velocity and iterations despite their hesitations.
options.rationale: Forcing iterations and velocity on a team that has been burned by them deepens resistance.

options.text: Suggest the team uses flow-based scheduling, with a Kanban board for visual work.
options.rationale: Kanban's flow-based scheduling avoids sprints and velocity while keeping agile benefits and visual work.

questions.explanation: Agile is broader than Scrum. Kanban uses flow-based scheduling without sprints or velocity, optimising delivery around capacity and reducing waste. It lets a team wary of velocity misuse adopt agile while keeping a sustainable pace.
questions.mindset: Choose an agile approach that fits the team's context.

questions.stem: Your team have not worked on projects before, and don't know about waterfall, agile, or any of the different models. You project may also have requirements that are certain or uncertain, with varying levels of risk, so are not sure which approach to use as you begin this new project. What will you do next?

options.text: Use Waterfall and plan everything up front, so the team have more stability.
options.rationale: Planning everything up front may not suit uncertain requirements.

options.text: Use general phase definitions such as Feasibility, Design, Build, Test, Deploy and Close.
options.rationale: Generic phases such as Feasibility, Design, Build, Test, Deploy and Close apply to any approach and are a sound starting point.

options.text: Use Agile to ensure you can respond to change while your team's capability increases.
options.rationale: Choosing agile before understanding the requirements and risks may not suit the project.

options.text: Don't use any project approach - it doesn't matter as long as the work is getting done.
options.rationale: Working with no approach at all invites chaos and poor results.

questions.explanation: All projects pass through the general phases of feasibility, design, build, test, deploy and close; predictive projects do them once, while agile projects repeat them for each increment. These phases give an inexperienced team a common starting framework.
questions.mindset: Start from the phases every project shares.

questions.stem: You a project manager in an organisation with a directive Project Management Office, and are currently in between projects. The PMO asks you to prepare for an upcoming project in the accounting area by meeting with the functional manager there. You have no team, no scope or requirements and not timeline as yet. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask the functional manager for their wish-list of improvements, so you can take these to your PMO.
options.rationale: A wish list gathers ideas but does not define a coordinated approach or desired outcomes.

options.text: Create a project management plan so the project, scope, budget and schedule are more clear.
options.rationale: A project management plan cannot be written before the project is defined and authorised.

options.text: Create a small backlog of work and start your first sprint, then progressively update the backlog as the project progresses.
options.rationale: Starting sprints without a vision or team is premature.

options.text: Progressively elaborate the vision statement and project charter to define a coordinated approach.
options.rationale: Progressively elaborating the vision and charter defines the outcomes and a coordinated approach.

questions.explanation: Before a project can be planned, its purpose must be defined. Progressively elaborating a vision statement and project charter, working with the functional manager, identifies the desired outcomes and a coordinated path to achieve them.
questions.mindset: Define the vision and charter first.

questions.stem: You are working on a project where part of the project delivers a high value, high risk component. Another part of the project delivers a routine change to the system. Your project sponsor wants to gain the business value as quickly as possible, but your project team want to start with the work they are familiar with first. What will you do next?

options.text: Prioritise the high risk items at the end of the project.
options.rationale: Leaving high-risk work until the end exposes the project to late surprises after most of the investment is made.

options.text: Prioritise the high risk items at the start of the project.
options.rationale: Tackling high-risk, high-value items early reduces uncertainty and delivers value sooner.

options.text: Use an incremental approach and deliver part of the routine and high risk work in each sprint.
options.rationale: Splitting both types across every sprint delays learning about the high-risk work.

options.text: Plan out the work in detail and secure a scope baseline, with formal change controls to reduce uncertainty.
options.rationale: A detailed baseline with formal change control does not reduce the technical risk of novel work.

questions.explanation: Novel or risky work is best tackled early, before large investment, to reduce uncertainty. Routine work can wait until the last responsible moment. Prioritising the high-value, high-risk component first also meets the sponsor's wish for early value.
questions.mindset: Tackle high-risk, high-value work first.

questions.stem: You are working on an agile project where the functional area you are delivering to only has a high level idea of the system requirements they will need. The functional manager suggests a Work Breakdown Structure, however your team feel that is more for a predictive (waterfall) delivery approach. What will you do next?

options.text: Use and create a WBS anyway, as it is just a tool.
options.rationale: A WBS can be used, but it is not the natural fit for this agile team.

options.text: Use rolling wave planning, and keep the work at a high level until you are ready to work on it, when you can plan in detail.
options.rationale: Rolling wave planning is a valid concept, but agile decomposition into epics and stories fits better.

options.text: Note the high level themes or epics, decompose them into features, and again into user stories.
options.rationale: Breaking themes and epics into features and user stories decomposes the work in a way that suits agile delivery.

options.text: Ask the functional area for more detailed requirements before the project begins.
options.rationale: Waiting for detailed requirements contradicts agile's progressive refinement.

questions.explanation: Agile projects decompose work too, from themes or epics into features and then user stories. This decomposition fits incremental delivery, lets high-level requirements be refined as the team learns and respects the team's preferred approach.
questions.mindset: Decompose agile work from epics to stories.

questions.stem: You are an Agile project manager and have begun creating user stories with your Agile project team to go into the product backlog. You have created the card, added requirements, criticality and acceptance criteria. What will you do next?

options.text: Place the card on the Kanban board so the team can clearly see the future work.
options.rationale: Placing the card on the board skips the conversation that builds shared understanding.

options.text: Have a conversation with developers about how the software will be used, confirm the acceptance criteria and definition of done.
options.rationale: Discussing the story with developers and confirming acceptance criteria and the definition of done completes the card, conversation and confirmation cycle.

options.text: Prioritise the card in the upcoming sprint backlog to ensure the work gets done.
options.rationale: Prioritising the card into a sprint comes after it has been discussed, estimated and confirmed.

options.text: Advise the project sponsor and risk manager of the feature details to ensure risk captured.
options.rationale: Risk capture for a single story does not need the sponsor and risk manager at this stage.

questions.explanation: User stories follow the three Cs: card, conversation and confirmation. After writing the card, the team discusses the story to check understanding, find gaps and estimate effort, then confirms the acceptance criteria before the story is prioritised.
questions.mindset: Card, conversation, confirmation.

questions.stem: After gathering your project requirements, project scope, and breaking it down into activities, you need to estimate the project schedule with your team. After some analysis and discussion, your team come up with a range of 53 to 75 days assigned across all tasks. What will you do next?

options.text: The estimate is high accuracy but low precision – ask the team to come back with a more precise estimate.
options.rationale: A wide range signals low accuracy, not high accuracy.

options.text: The estimate is low accuracy but high precision – ensure the estimates become more accurate as the project unfolds.
options.rationale: A wide range reflects low accuracy; the day-level units give precision; the estimates should become more accurate as the project unfolds.

options.text: The estimate is in high confidence but low precision-proceed as is and adjust using an incremental approach.
options.rationale: The width of the range points to uncertainty rather than high confidence.

options.text: The estimate is in low confidence but high accuracy - allow the team to become more confident as the project unfolds.
options.rationale: A wide range does not indicate high accuracy, and confidence is not the issue being tested.

questions.explanation: Accuracy concerns how close an estimate is to the true value, so a wide range such as 53 to 75 days indicates low accuracy. Precision concerns exactness, and estimates expressed in days are relatively precise. Accuracy improves as the project progresses and more is known.
questions.mindset: Distinguish accuracy from precision.

questions.stem: You are working on a business case where you know that the industry is undergoing a significant change at the moment, and there could be many different impacts to your project benefits before it is delivered completely. The project sponsor asks you for the best estimate of benefits you can give under the circumstances. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask your team for a probabilistic estimate.
options.rationale: A probabilistic estimate gives a range with associated probabilities, reflecting the industry uncertainty.

options.text: Ask your team for a deterministic estimate.
options.rationale: A deterministic estimate is a single number that hides uncertainty.

options.text: Ask your team for an absolute estimate.
options.rationale: An absolute estimate gives specific figures and implies certainty that does not exist.

options.text: Ask your team for a relative estimate.
options.rationale: Relative estimates compare items to each other; they do not quantify benefits under uncertainty.

questions.explanation: When significant industry change makes benefits uncertain, a probabilistic estimate is the most honest and useful. It presents a range of outcomes with probabilities or confidence levels, giving the sponsor a realistic picture for the business case.
questions.mindset: Express uncertain estimates as ranges with probabilities.

questions.stem: You have noted nine epics for delivery as part of your most recent project. Your team have broken down these epics into user stories, and would like to see the effort involved for these deliverables. You ask your team to find the smallest user story, size it with a “1”, and then determine the size of the other cards based on how they compare to the original card. What approach are you taking?

options.text: Relative estimating with your team.
options.rationale: Sizing stories by comparison with a reference story is relative estimating.

options.text: Deterministic estimating to determine the effort.
options.rationale: Deterministic estimating produces a single value, not a comparison.

options.text: Absolute estimating to get an estimate with absolute certainty.
options.rationale: Absolute estimating uses actual units such as hours, and no estimate is ever certain.

options.text: Probabilistic estimating with the highest probability items.
options.rationale: Probabilistic estimating assigns probabilities to ranges, which is not what the team is doing.

questions.explanation: Relative estimating sizes work by comparing it with other work. Setting the smallest story as a reference of 1 and sizing the rest in relation to it is a classic agile technique for estimating effort without absolute units.
questions.mindset: Estimate agile work relative to a reference.

questions.stem: You are working on a project to build a new parkland for the community. The person in charge of parkland design approaches you as they are not sure what they are supposed to be working on. What will you do next?

options.text: Review the Project Scope Statement to see what the team is delivering.
options.rationale: The scope statement describes the project's overall scope, not individual assignments.

options.text: Review the WBS Dictionary to see the detailed description of the scope of the work and who it is assigned to.
options.rationale: The WBS dictionary describes each work package in detail, including who it is assigned to.

options.text: Review the Requirements Traceability Matrix to see where the scope comes from.
options.rationale: The traceability matrix links requirements to deliverables but does not assign work.

options.text: Review the Assumption Log, to see who we assume should do the work.
options.rationale: The assumption log records assumptions, not work assignments.

questions.explanation: The WBS dictionary gives a detailed description of each work package, including its scope, acceptance criteria, responsible person, schedule and cost information. It tells the parkland designer exactly what they are supposed to deliver.
questions.mindset: Work package detail lives in the WBS dictionary.

questions.stem: You have taken over as Project Manager for a project that has had issues delivering on time. You review the Earned Value Management and find the corresponding SPI and CPI values are 0.86 and 1.12. You advise the project sponsor, who asks you to bring the project back on track within the next two months. What will you do next?

options.text: Apply schedule crashing to bring the project back on track.
options.rationale: With CPI above 1 there is budget available, so crashing can buy back time.

options.text: Apply fast tracking to bring the project back on track.
options.rationale: Fast tracking adds risk and does not take advantage of the budget surplus.

options.text: Update the Risk Register and assign the risk of project failure to an executive with the power to bring it back on track.
options.rationale: Assigning the risk of failure to an executive abdicates the project manager's responsibility.

options.text: Reduce the project scope to bring the project back on track.
options.rationale: Reducing scope is a last resort when budget is available to recover the schedule.

questions.explanation: An SPI of 0.86 means the project is behind schedule, while a CPI of 1.12 means it is under budget. With money available, crashing—adding resources or paying to expedite critical path work—is the best way to recover time.
questions.mindset: Under budget and behind schedule: consider crashing.

questions.stem: You are working on a change that includes stakeholders at all levels from front-line workers to senior executives. After performing stakeholder analysis you and your team group the stakeholders according to their level of influence and the impact the change will have on them. The project sponsor asks what engagement strategy you will use for the front-line workers. What will you do next?

options.text: Manage them Closely
options.rationale: Manage closely is for stakeholders with high influence and high impact.

options.text: Monitor them only
options.rationale: Monitor only is for low influence and low impact, but front-line workers are highly impacted.

options.text: Keep them Satisfied
options.rationale: Keep satisfied is for stakeholders with high influence and low impact.

options.text: Keep them Informed
options.rationale: Front-line workers have low influence but high impact, so they should be kept informed.

questions.explanation: On an impact/influence grid, stakeholders with high influence and high impact are managed closely, high influence and low impact are kept satisfied, and low influence and low impact are monitored. Front-line workers have low influence but are highly impacted, so they are kept informed.
questions.mindset: Match engagement to impact and influence.

questions.stem: You are working on a project where you have been completing the deliverables in sequence, and the project work is starting to fall behind. The project sponsor asks you to speed up the work and reduce the time for the project to be delivered, but also makes it very clear that there is no more money to use when speeding up the work. What will you do next?

options.text: Apply leads and lags to your project schedule.
options.rationale: Leads and lags adjust dependencies but are not the main compression technique here.

options.text: Apply fast tracking to your project schedule.
options.rationale: Fast tracking runs sequential activities in parallel, compressing the schedule without extra cost.

options.text: Apply schedule crashing to your project.
options.rationale: Crashing adds resources or overtime, which costs money the sponsor has ruled out.

options.text: Apply resource levelling to your project.
options.rationale: Resource levelling usually lengthens the schedule rather than shortening it.

questions.explanation: Fast tracking compresses the schedule by performing activities in parallel that would normally be done in sequence. It adds risk but not direct cost, unlike crashing, which adds people, overtime or expediting costs.
questions.mindset: No money for compression: fast-track.

questions.stem: You are working directly with the project sponsor, in the initial phase of a brand new project. The project sponsor asks for your help in creating a document that formally authorises the project, including details such as the cost-benefit analysis, feasibility study, and high level risks. What will you do next?

options.text: Prepare a project milestone chart, and review with the project team
options.rationale: A milestone chart is a scheduling tool, not an authorising document.

options.text: Prepare a Business Case, and review with the functional manager and receiving team
options.rationale: The business case is an input to the charter; it does not formally authorise the project.

options.text: Prepare a Project Charter, and review with the portfolio governing body for approval
options.rationale: The project charter formally authorises the project and is approved through governance.

options.text: Prepare a Project Management Plan, and host a project kick off meeting to begin
options.rationale: The project management plan comes after the project has been authorised.

questions.explanation: The project charter formally authorises a project and gives the project manager authority to use resources. The business case, cost-benefit analysis and feasibility study are inputs that link the project to strategic objectives, and the charter is approved through the governing body.
questions.mindset: The charter authorises the project.

questions.stem: Your team are new to agile, and had previously been working with Waterfall. Your key customer asks you for a project schedule. The project team believes using a project schedule is from the old waterfall way of working and they shouldn't have to create one. What will you do next?

options.text: Create a project Gantt chart to visualise the activities within the project.
options.rationale: A Gantt chart imposes predictive detail the team rightly considers unsuitable.

options.text: Determine the project's planned versus actual value, instead of working with a schedule directly.
options.rationale: Earned value compares planned and actual value but is not a schedule for the customer.

options.text: Advise the customer that we don't need to plan ahead in an adaptive way of work.
options.rationale: Saying agile teams do not plan ahead is wrong; adaptive approaches plan incrementally.

options.text: Ask your team to develop a high level release plan like a product roadmap, showing the features to be included in each release.
options.rationale: A high-level release plan or roadmap shows which features come in each release, giving the customer a schedule view.

questions.explanation: Adaptive projects still plan, but incrementally. A high-level release plan or product roadmap shows the features expected in each release, giving the customer a meaningful schedule while leaving detail to be planned iteration by iteration.
questions.mindset: Agile schedules are release plans and roadmaps.

questions.stem: You are working in a project team that has recently moved to an Agile way of work. Your business analysts want to gather the requirements, solutions, match them to the scope and do a WBS for the whole deliverable. Your product owner says this will take too long, and is not agile enough for their needs. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask your team to review the scope management plan for the proper process.
options.rationale: The scope management plan does not resolve the tension between up-front analysis and agile delivery.

options.text: Break the deliverable down into smaller pieces so you can deliver those faster.
options.rationale: Breaking down the deliverable is part of the answer but lacks the prioritisation and timeboxing needed.

options.text: Ask your team to timebox work on the highest priority items in the backlog, update the estimates then reprioritise as necessary.
options.rationale: Timeboxing the highest-priority backlog items, then re-estimating and reprioritising, delivers value quickly and adapts as the team learns.

options.text: Review the project charter for the high level scope, and use this to begin delivery quickly.
options.rationale: The charter's high-level scope alone does not give the team prioritised work to start on.

questions.explanation: Adaptive approaches work from a prioritised backlog in timeboxes. The team estimates and delivers the highest-priority items, then the backlog is reprioritised for the next timebox, avoiding lengthy up-front analysis of the entire deliverable.
questions.mindset: Work in timeboxes from a prioritised backlog.

questions.stem: When reviewing the current progress with your project sponsor, they notice that the system solution is missing a critical piece that will impact the benefit of the project. The project sponsor approves this scope. Your project has a Planned Value of $520,000 and an Actual Cost of $535,000. What will you do next?

options.text: Work with the PMO to unlock the project management reserves for the extra work
options.rationale: Management reserve covers unforeseen in-scope work and may be controlled by the PMO.

options.text: Ask the Product Owner to reprioritise the backlog and see if the new work will fit.
options.rationale: Reprioritising a backlog does not provide funding, and the project is already over cost.

options.text: Perform the work within your normal budget as your project is on track.
options.rationale: The project is over budget (AC exceeds PV), so it cannot absorb extra work in its normal budget.

options.text: Raise a change request for the changes and gain approval from the Change Control Board.
options.rationale: The sponsor has already approved the scope, so the remaining question is funding.

questions.explanation: Management reserve is set aside for unforeseen work within the project's scope. With the sponsor approving the missing piece and the project already spending more than planned, the project manager works with the PMO, which may control the reserve, to release funds.
questions.mindset: Unforeseen in-scope work draws on management reserve.

questions.stem: You are in the planning stages of an Agile project where the functional manager and senior users have provided the high level requirements and scope. You have been asked to put together a project team that will be able to deliver quickly. What will you do next?

options.text: Select project members from each city to ensure diversity of knowledge within the team.
options.rationale: Spreading members across cities adds diversity but slows collaboration.

options.text: Put together a resource management plan outlining the resources required.
options.rationale: A resource management plan documents needs but does not by itself create a team that delivers quickly.

options.text: Ask your PMO for current available resources and assign them to the work.
options.rationale: Taking whoever the PMO has available may not produce a cohesive or effective team.

options.text: Select a small team that can work in the same area so they can solve problems as they arise.
options.rationale: A small co-located team benefits from osmotic communication and solves problems as they arise.

questions.explanation: Small teams working in the same space benefit from osmotic communication: they overhear and share information naturally and resolve problems quickly. For an agile project that must deliver fast, this is the preferred team set-up.
questions.mindset: Small co-located teams deliver fast.

questions.stem: You are putting together a project team to deliver an accounting system to offices around the country. The accounting system you are moving to has not been used by anyone in your organisation before. The project is quite high risk, and the delivery needs to be right the first time. What will you do next?

options.text: Select a small team that can work in the same area so they can solve problems as they arise.
options.rationale: A small co-located team does not address the lack of expertise in the new system.

options.text: Use a predictive project approach and source part of your team externally if they have skillsets in the new system.
options.rationale: A predictive approach suits a high-risk single delivery, and external specialists bring skills the organisation lacks.

options.text: Train existing internal staff in the new system then have them work on the project.
options.rationale: Training internal staff first takes time and does not guarantee getting it right first time.

options.text: Perform a make or buy analysis on the different software options.
options.rationale: The system has already been chosen, so a make-or-buy analysis is not relevant.

questions.explanation: When a project is high-risk, must be right first time and involves a system no one internally knows, a predictive approach and experienced external specialists reduce risk. The value of outside skills is weighed against their cost.
questions.mindset: Bring in expertise the organisation lacks for high-risk work.

questions.stem: You are putting together a project plan for a change that affects nearly ten thousand stakeholders in your organisation. You have identified the affected stakeholders, analysed and prioritised them, and are putting together a communication plan to ensure the right engagement is made. What will you NOT include in your plan?

options.text: Why should information be shared with stakeholders?
options.rationale: Why information should be shared is a standard communication planning consideration.

options.text: What is the best way to provide information?
options.rationale: The best way to provide information is a core communication planning question.

options.text: How can they make changes to the communication plan?
options.rationale: How stakeholders can change the plan is not one of the standard considerations in planning communications.

options.text: When and how often is information needed?
options.rationale: When and how often information is needed is a standard planning consideration.

questions.explanation: Communication planning considers who needs information, who has it, why it should be shared, what each stakeholder needs, when and how often it is needed and the best way to provide it. A mechanism for stakeholders to change the plan is not among these considerations.
questions.mindset: Plan who, what, why, when and how for communications.

questions.stem: You put together a resource plan for a large amount of physical inventory to be purchased from overseas. You ordered the inventory during project execution, however global supply chains were impacted and the shipment was delayed by three months, significantly impacting your project. What should you have done differently?

options.text: Hired a resource manager to take care of the resource tasks on your project.
options.rationale: A resource manager adds a role but does not by itself address lead-time planning.

options.text: Planned strategically about the timing from order to delivery to usage, managing resource risks and their responses.
options.rationale: Strategic planning of order-to-delivery-to-usage timing, with managed resource risks, would have anticipated the delay.

options.text: Ensured a means to track the inventory from arrival on site to the delivery of an integrated product.
options.rationale: Tracking inventory on site happens after arrival and would not have prevented the shipping delay.

options.text: Sourced the inventory locally to reduce the impact of global supply chains.
options.rationale: Local sourcing may not be available or economic; the lesson is to plan timing and risk.

questions.explanation: Projects with significant physical materials must plan strategically around the timing from order to delivery to use, and manage associated risks such as global logistics delays. Ordering during execution without accounting for lead time and supply risk left the project exposed.
questions.mindset: Plan physical resource lead times and risks.

questions.stem: You are half way through your agile project when there is a significant change to the project scope, after it was found that the project would not be able to deliver the benefits it had promised. You check your project budget and there are contingency and management reserves available. What will you do next?

options.text: Take the project scope change to the change control board for approval.
options.rationale: A change control board is a predictive mechanism; agile teams adapt through the backlog.

options.text: Use the available contingency reserves to make the appropriate change to project scope.
options.rationale: Reserves are about funding; the change itself is managed through the backlog.

options.text: Review the change management plan for the change control process.
options.rationale: Reviewing a change management plan adds predictive process to an agile project.

options.text: Reprioritise the product backlog, including the new scope and begin work on the highest priority straight away.
options.rationale: Reprioritising the backlog to include the new scope lets the team adapt and start on the highest-value work.

questions.explanation: Agile projects accommodate change by reprioritising the product backlog rather than through baseline change control. When new scope is needed to deliver the promised benefits, the product owner adds and orders it, and the team works on the highest-priority items.
questions.mindset: In agile, change flows through the backlog.

questions.stem: You have recently taken over on a project that is behind schedule, and slightly over budget. You raise an issue at the steering committee meeting, where they advise that there is no additional funding available and the project must finish on time. You believe you can optimise the project process to try and bring the project back on track. What will you do next?

options.text: Add additional people and resources to the project to speed it up.
options.rationale: Adding people costs money that is not available and may increase complexity.

options.text: Utilise the project's contingency reserve to source the resources you need.
options.rationale: Contingency reserve is for identified risks, and no extra funding is available anyway.

options.text: Perform project activities in parallel, completing multiple items at once instead of one at a time.
options.rationale: Fast tracking may help, but the project manager wants to optimise the process itself.

options.text: Use Lean production methods to reduce non-value add activities, and retrospectives for the team to suggest improvements.
options.rationale: Lean methods remove non-value-added activities, and retrospectives draw on the team's improvement ideas.

questions.explanation: With no extra funding and a fixed deadline, the project manager optimises the process. Lean methods remove non-value-added work, and retrospectives let the team suggest improvements, improving flow without adding people or cost.
questions.mindset: Optimise the process when resources are fixed.

questions.stem: Your Project Management Office (PMO) is optimising all the projects within their portfolio. They ask for your advice in tracking the type of work each team member is doing and how long it takes, suggesting that they categorise and record their work in addition to the work itself. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask your team to record and categorise their work, as gathering project data is important.
options.rationale: Manual recording and categorising adds non-value-added work for the team.

options.text: Recommend an automated reporting tool where possible, as categorising their work is non-value added.
options.rationale: Recommending automated reporting respects the PMO request while recognising that categorising work is non-value-added.

options.text: Recommend an automated reporting tool where possible, as recording their work is value added
options.rationale: Recording time is not value-added work for the customer, so the justification is wrong.

options.text: Ask your team to ignore the request and focus on delivering customer value only.
options.rationale: Ignoring the PMO disregards governance and the organisation's legitimate needs.

questions.explanation: Time spent recording and categorising work does not directly benefit the customer, so it is non-value-added. The project manager respects the PMO's request but recommends automating the reporting so the process is efficient as well as effective.
questions.mindset: Minimise non-value-added overhead.

questions.stem: You are working on an agile project as a scrum master, where the functional manager has worked with some people in your development team before. She approaches them directly to see if they can add a feature to the product in the current sprint. What will you do next?

options.text: Adjust the sprint backlog to allow for the additional feature.
options.rationale: Changing the sprint backlog for a direct request disrupts the sprint and bypasses the product owner.

options.text: Adjust the product backlog to add the customer requirement.
options.rationale: The product owner, not the scrum master, decides what goes into the product backlog.

options.text: Ask the manager to speak with the Product Owner for product priorities, then protect the team from direct requests in the future.
options.rationale: Redirecting the manager to the product owner and shielding the team from direct requests protects focus and flow.

options.text: Ask the manager to create a change request so it can go through the proper process.
options.rationale: A formal change request is a predictive process that does not fit sprint-based working.

questions.explanation: The scrum master protects the team's focus and acts as a diversion shield. Requests for new features go to the product owner, who manages priorities, and the team is shielded from direct requests that would disrupt the current sprint.
questions.mindset: Shield the team; route requests to the product owner.

questions.stem: Part of your project management plan is a detailed communications plan, which has the stakeholders on the project, their communication needs, and how information will be communicated. While this is being signed off by the project sponsor, you receive many ad-hoc requests for information from new stakeholders. What will you do next?

options.text: Review the communications management plan to include the stakeholders, the information they need and their communication preferences.
options.rationale: Updating the communication plan to cover the new stakeholders and their needs addresses the gap.

options.text: Create an information radiator and ask the stakeholders to pull the information they need.
options.rationale: An information radiator is one tool, but the plan still needs to reflect these stakeholders' needs.

options.text: Ignore the new requests, as you have captured all the stakeholders you need to in your plan.
options.rationale: Ignoring new stakeholders risks disengagement and missed requirements.

options.text: Ask the new stakeholders to review your communications management plan to see how you are distributing information.
options.rationale: Asking stakeholders to review the plan pushes the planning work onto them.

questions.explanation: A large number of ad-hoc requests for information shows that communication planning did not meet stakeholder needs. The project manager reviews the communication management plan to include the new stakeholders, the information they need and their preferences.
questions.mindset: Ad-hoc requests signal a communication plan gap.

questions.stem: You are working on a high value construction project to include smart-home components within multi-million dollar buildings. After completing a make-orbuy analysis, you find that it will cost $700,000 to make the new system, or $500,000 to buy it from a vendor. You prepare a procurement management plan to purchase it. What will you do before conducting a procurement?

options.text: Work with your project team to complete as much of the system in-house as possible.
options.rationale: The make-or-buy analysis has already led to a decision to buy, so building in-house contradicts it.

options.text: Work with contracting professionals to develop the RFP, SOW and terms and conditions.
options.rationale: Working with contracting professionals to prepare the RFP, SOW and terms and conditions readies the procurement.

options.text: Adjust your stakeholder register to include the new vendor, and add the scope to your work breakdown dictionary.
options.rationale: Stakeholder register and WBS updates do not prepare the bid documents.

options.text: Work with your project team to develop an RMP, SMP, and list of resources.
options.rationale: Risk, schedule and resource plans are not the procurement documents needed before going out to bid.

questions.explanation: Before conducting a procurement, the project manager and technical team members work with contracting professionals to develop the bid documents: the request for proposal, statement of work, terms and conditions and other documents needed to go to market.
questions.mindset: Prepare bid documents with contracting professionals.

questions.stem: A missing item has been uncovered in the project scope that your project team cannot deliver. The item is not complex and seems to be fairly readily available from various sources. You are ready to move to source selection and choose a vendor that will meet their needs. What will you do before sending out bid documents to vendors?

options.text: Prepare a Request for Proposal for vendors to provide a solution to your needs.
options.rationale: An RFP suits complex scope where vendors propose solutions, which is not the case here.

options.text: Prepare a Request for Quote to determine the best price from the vendors.
options.rationale: An RFQ follows once suitable vendors are known and price is the deciding factor.

options.text: Prepare a Request for Information to gather more information and viable sources from the market.
options.rationale: An RFI gathers market information and identifies viable sources before bid documents go out.

options.text: Review the procurement management plan for your project's procurement process.
options.rationale: The procurement management plan is useful, but the question asks about the step before issuing bid documents.

questions.explanation: A request for information gathers information from the market, including viable sources, before bid documents are sent to selected vendors. An RFQ is used when price decides, and an RFP when the scope is complex or the buyer wants the vendor to propose a solution.
questions.mindset: Use an RFI to survey the market first.

questions.stem: You are working on a project where part of the work is planned carefully upfront, and another part is subject to change. You negotiate terms and conditions, including cost, delivery and payment dates. The vendor is concerned about confusion that might occur between the pre- planned and changeable work. What will you do next?

options.text: Use a Firm Fixed Price contract, to ensure cost is fixed but scope can remain flexible.
options.rationale: A firm fixed price contract fixes cost and scope, which does not suit changeable work.

options.text: Use a time and materials contract, to ensure only the time and materials used are paid for.
options.rationale: Time and materials suits the changeable work but gives little control over the pre-planned work.

options.text: Adjust your project plan to suit either a predictive or adaptive approach to reduce the confusion.
options.rationale: Forcing one approach ignores that the project genuinely has both kinds of work.

options.text: Use a master agreement for the overall contract, with adaptive work placed in an appendix.
options.rationale: A master agreement for the whole contract, with adaptive work in an appendix, separates stable and changeable work clearly.

questions.explanation: When some deliverables are predictive and others adaptive, a master agreement governs the overall contract, and the adaptive work is placed in an appendix or supplement. Changes to adaptive scope can then occur without renegotiating the whole contract.
questions.mindset: Use a master agreement for mixed contracts.

questions.stem: You are working on an agile project where there are vastly differing levels of product knowledge within your team. The scrum master suggests that you try to gain knowledge by osmosis, because the project information may be lost when only communicating by email. What will you do next?

options.text: Co-locate the team to capture the benefit of each person's tacit knowledge.
options.rationale: Co-locating the team lets tacit knowledge pass by osmosis through everyday interaction.

options.text: Refer to the organisational process assets to capture the team's explicit knowledge.
options.rationale: Organisational process assets hold explicit knowledge, not the tacit knowledge being sought.

options.text: Refer to the project's knowledge management system to capture the project's explicit knowledge.
options.rationale: A knowledge management system captures explicit, codified knowledge, not experience and insight.

options.text: Create a process to capture the team's tacit knowledge.
options.rationale: Tacit knowledge is difficult to capture through a formal process.

questions.explanation: Learning by osmosis means absorbing information from one's surroundings, which requires people to work together physically. Co-location allows tacit knowledge—experience, insight and practical skill—to flow between team members in a way that email and documents cannot.
questions.mindset: Share tacit knowledge through proximity.

questions.stem: You are working as a Product Owner, and have placed high level information about the product in the product backlog, and the highest priority feature at the top. Senior users informing the project are unable to clearly articulate their requirements, and are concerned that the product will not truly meet their needs. What will you do next?

options.text: Proceed with the highest priority item during the first sprint.
options.rationale: Starting on the top item ignores the users' concern that the product may not meet their needs.

options.text: Work with the customer to create mock-ups and prototypes to discover what works for them.
options.rationale: Mock-ups and prototypes help users who cannot articulate requirements discover what works for them.

options.text: Ask your stakeholders to submit a change request and update the project scope accordingly.
options.rationale: Change requests do not help users who cannot yet say what they need.

options.text: Begin breaking the work down into user stories to place in the sprint.
options.rationale: Breaking work into stories still depends on requirements the users cannot articulate.

questions.explanation: When users cannot articulate their requirements, prototypes, mock-ups, storyboards and demonstrations help evolve them. Users can react to something tangible—'I'll know it when I see it'—so the product converges on what they need.
questions.mindset: Use prototypes when users can't describe what they need.

questions.stem: You are gathering requirements for a new feature in a customer management system. The product owner has given a user interface feature as the next highest priority, and you are co-located with the team receiving the benefits. What will you do next?

options.text: Show the customer team how the new user interface will look, as they will be using it.
options.rationale: Showing the design to the customer is useful but does not document requirements for developers.

options.text: Communicate the requirements to developers with a coherent, logical flow of ideas.
options.rationale: Clear communication matters, but the requirements still need to be elicited and documented.

options.text: Elicit requirements into user stories using acceptance criteria that is clear, verifiable and traceable.
options.rationale: Eliciting requirements into user stories with clear, verifiable and traceable acceptance criteria gives developers what they need.

options.text: Show the mock up or prototype to the developers and ask them to develop based on that.
options.rationale: A prototype alone may lack the detail developers need to build the feature correctly.

questions.explanation: Elicitation draws out requirements from those who hold them. Documenting them as user stories with acceptance criteria that are clear, verifiable and traceable gives developers a sound basis for building the user interface that the co-located customer team needs.
questions.mindset: Elicit and document requirements with clear acceptance criteria.

questions.stem: You are working in an agile team who are trying to break down the project requirements and scope. They have created a scope statement and work breakdown structure, but are not sure how it will work now that they are using sprints and user stories. What will you do next?

options.text: Assign activities to each of the scope items in the WBS, and place them on a Gantt Chart.
options.rationale: Gantt charts and activity lists are predictive tools that do not fit sprints.

options.text: Create a product roadmap with the team, using the lowest, most detailed part of the WBS.
options.rationale: A roadmap built from the lowest WBS level mixes approaches and loses the value-based grouping.

options.text: Group the work by large themes of customer value, shown as Epics, then break them down into smaller user stories to complete in each sprint.
options.rationale: Grouping work into epics by customer value, then breaking them into user stories for each sprint, fits agile delivery.

options.text: Ask the team to trace the requirements properly using a Requirements traceability Matrix.
options.rationale: A traceability matrix tracks requirements but does not structure the work for sprints.

questions.explanation: In agile, scope is organised by themes of customer value. Large epics group related functionality and are broken down into user stories small enough to complete within a sprint, replacing the WBS as the way of decomposing scope.
questions.mindset: Organise agile scope as epics and stories.

questions.stem: Your project team are trialling an agile way of work. The Product Owner has a clear vision for the product. There is confusion in the team as to how much work should be done on a user story before it is taken to the sprint review, and how they will know a story is complete. What will you do next?

options.text: Refer to the user story acceptance criteria and your team's Definition of Done.
options.rationale: The story's acceptance criteria and the team's definition of done together define when work is complete.

options.text: Review the user story with multiple customers and senior users to ensure it is correct.
options.rationale: Reviewing each story with many customers is not how completion is defined.

options.text: Ask the product owner to sign off on the completed user story.
options.rationale: Product owner sign-off depends on the acceptance criteria and definition of done being met.

options.text: Ensure quality testing on the user story is completed and passed.
options.rationale: Quality testing is carried out against the acceptance criteria; testing alone does not define completion.

questions.explanation: Completion in agile is defined in advance. Each user story's acceptance criteria state what it must do, and the team's definition of done sets the quality standard for all work. Together they tell the team when a story is ready for the sprint review.
questions.mindset: Acceptance criteria plus definition of done define complete.

questions.stem: You have been working closely with the quality manager of your project, planning the budget for the project phase that is due to begin in the next two months. They mention the need to budget for appraisal costs, to avoid quality issues in the future. What will you do next?

options.text: Ensure there is enough for training the staff to reduce the number of errors.
options.rationale: Training is a prevention cost, not an appraisal cost.

options.text: Ensure there is enough for a quality tester to verify the deliverables against agreed specifications.
options.rationale: A tester verifying deliverables against specifications is an appraisal cost.

options.text: Ensure there is enough to create a quality assurance plan.
options.rationale: Creating a quality assurance plan is quality planning, which is a prevention cost.

options.text: Ensure there is enough to allow for rework or rectification when defects are found.
options.rationale: Rework is an internal failure cost, which appraisal aims to reduce.

questions.explanation: The cost of quality has four categories. Prevention costs include training and quality planning; appraisal costs include testing, inspection and audits; internal failure costs include rework and scrap; and external failure costs include warranty claims and complaints.
questions.mindset: Appraisal means inspection and testing.

questions.stem: Your agile project has recently had multiple quality issues. Project features have been prioritised by the Product Owner, and broken down into user stories. What will you do to help reduce the cost of quality issues the most?

options.text: Quality test each user story according to its acceptance criteria before release.
options.rationale: Testing each story helps, but it finds defects after requirements and design errors are built in.

options.text: Advise the team that any quality defects will come out of their bonus.
options.rationale: Threatening bonuses creates fear without improving how quality is built in.

options.text: Perform testing all in one go at the end, to reduce the cost of testing resources.
