options.rationale: Testing everything at the end finds defects when they are most expensive to fix.

options.text: Ensure a "triad" of developer, tester and customer is involved during requirements and design
options.rationale: Involving a developer, tester and customer during requirements and design prevents defects when change is cheapest.

questions.explanation: The cost of change rises sharply the later a defect is found: fixes are cheapest in requirements and design and most expensive in production. Involving a developer, tester and customer early gets requirements, design and acceptance criteria right, reducing costly defects.
questions.mindset: Prevent defects early, where change is cheapest.

questions.stem: You are working in an agile team where executives in the team you are delivering to are asking for a large display of reports to be created every two weeks, showing how the project is tracking and updating them on the cost and benefits. What will you do next?

options.text: Collect the planned value versus earned value to show the executives any variance in the plan.
options.rationale: Earned value reports are predictive measures that add reporting overhead to an agile team.

options.text: Co-locate the team with the executives so they can answer any questions as they arise.
options.rationale: Co-locating executives with the team is impractical and does not replace a suitable way of showing progress.

options.text: Suggest a demonstration of the feature developed during each sprint instead, and a burndown chart of future product features.
options.rationale: Demonstrating features each sprint and using a burndown chart shows real progress and value without heavy reporting.

options.text: Create the desired reports for the executives to keep them happy.
options.rationale: Producing reports just to keep executives happy wastes effort that could deliver value.

questions.explanation: Measurement is valuable when it leads to action. Agile teams show progress by demonstrating working features at each sprint review and using live information radiators such as burndown charts, rather than preparing large periodic reports.
questions.mindset: Demonstrate working product instead of heavy reports.

questions.stem: Multiple features have been released, but they are not having the effect the product owner believes they should. Your team are using some Key Performance Indicators to track performance, and you agree to move to more Leading indicators. What could you use as examples of Leading indicators for your project?

options.text: An increase in customer usage once the feature is released, such as sales and repeat purchasing.
options.rationale: Customer usage after release measures outcomes that have already happened, so it is lagging.

options.text: Stakeholders who are not engaged and lack of a risk management process.
options.rationale: Disengaged stakeholders and the lack of a risk process predict future problems, so they are leading indicators.

options.text: Velocity of the work completed each sprint and cycle time of user stories.
options.rationale: Velocity and cycle time measure work already completed, so in this framework they are lagging.

options.text: Variance in the schedule between planned and actual time taken.
options.rationale: Schedule variance measures past performance and is a lagging indicator.

questions.explanation: Leading indicators predict future changes or trends; lagging indicators measure what has already happened. Disengaged stakeholders, a missing risk management process and poorly defined success criteria predict trouble, whereas work completed and schedule variance are lagging.
questions.mindset: Leading indicators predict; lagging indicators report.

questions.stem: You are working in an agile project team that has increased in size and complexity since the project began. In reviewing the throughput of work with your team, you notice fewer and fewer user stories being completed, and the roadmap of features scheduled to go live is being pushed out. What will you do next?

options.text: Place a limit on the work in progress and work with the team to reduce the cycle time.
options.rationale: Limiting work in progress reduces context switching and shortens cycle time, restoring throughput.

options.text: Increase meetings with the team so everyone can collaborate together.
options.rationale: More meetings take time away from finishing work.

options.text: Ask the team to work overtime until the number of features reduces.
options.rationale: Overtime is unsustainable and does not fix the multitasking causing the slowdown.

options.text: Put a Pull system in place, where the team can pull work only when they are ready.
options.rationale: A pull system helps, but without WIP limits the team can still take on too much at once.

questions.explanation: As a team grows in size and complexity, members often juggle too many items, and throughput falls. Limiting work in progress reduces multitasking and context switching, shortening cycle time so that more stories are completed and the roadmap is recovered.
questions.mindset: Limit WIP to finish more.

questions.stem: You are working on an agile project where the project customer wants a reliable way to measure the project performance, and you know you first need a baseline. What measures will you show to your customer as part of your agile project?

options.text: Start and finish dates.
options.rationale: Start and finish dates are largely fixed in agile and do not measure performance.

options.text: Project team velocity.
options.rationale: Velocity is a team planning tool and is not a reliable performance measure for customers.

options.text: Rate of Features completed.
options.rationale: The rate of features completed shows the customer the value actually being delivered.

options.text: Schedule and Cost variance.
options.rationale: Schedule and cost variance are predictive measures; in agile, cost and time are usually fixed.

questions.explanation: In agile projects with a stable team, cost and time are usually fixed and scope varies. The meaningful baseline and performance measure for the customer is the rate at which features are delivered, showing the value produced over time.
questions.mindset: Measure agile performance by features delivered.

questions.stem: The product owner has worked with a team of senior users to gather feature ideas. They now have a list of more than fifty ideas for your team to develop, which is far too many to complete in the timeframe you have. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask the new product owner to return to the senior users and ask for a shortened list.
options.rationale: Asking for a shorter list avoids the product owner's responsibility to prioritise.

options.text: Start work on the smallest features first, to ensure you are delivering value quickly.
options.rationale: Smallest-first does not ensure the most valuable features are delivered.

options.text: Workshop the features with a wider audience to get a completely diverse view on their priority.
options.rationale: A wider workshop adds opinions but does not replace prioritisation by value.

options.text: Ask the new product owner to prioritise the features using cost to benefit, then deliver in priority order until time or money runs out.
options.rationale: Prioritising by cost-benefit and delivering in order until time or money runs out maximises value delivered.

questions.explanation: The product owner prioritises features by business value, using measures such as cost-benefit ratio, return on investment or net present value. Delivering in priority order ensures the most valuable features are completed first, whatever the constraints.
questions.mindset: Deliver in order of value.

questions.stem: Your agile project team has only recently formed. The product is still unclear, and there have been disagreements and minor conflicts over the past two weeks as the team find their rhythm. You would like things to improve, but can't quite pinpoint or address the problem. What will you do next?

options.text: Hold a workshop with your team to ask them why they are unhappy.
options.rationale: Asking why the team is unhappy assumes the cause and may not produce candid answers.

options.text: Have the team complete a Net Promoter Score with comments, and ask for improvement ideas at the next retrospective.
options.rationale: A Net Promoter Score with comments measures sentiment, and the retrospective turns it into improvement ideas.

options.text: Raise the issue with their line managers, to ensure all levels are aware of and working on the issue.
options.rationale: Raising the issue with line managers escalates prematurely and may undermine trust.

options.text: Have the team pair up together for their tasks, so they can learn from each other.
options.rationale: Pairing is a useful practice but does not identify the underlying problem.

questions.explanation: When the problem in a forming team cannot be pinpointed, measure it. A Net Promoter Score or satisfaction score with comments, or a mood chart, reveals how people feel, and the retrospective is where the team turns those insights into improvements.
questions.mindset: Measure sentiment, then improve in retrospectives.

questions.stem: The project has faced serious impacts in getting materials, with supply chains being disrupted and a global pandemic, and is currently three weeks behind schedule. You take this information to the next project steering committee meeting, where they advise they need more information on how much the project will end up costing. What will you do next?

options.text: Use the current project budget with no deviations until it runs out.
options.rationale: Spending the budget until it runs out gives no forecast of the final cost.

options.text: Use the project burndown chart to see the burn-rate of accounting funds.
options.rationale: A burndown chart tracks remaining work, not the final cost of the project.

options.text: Use a regression analysis on the current rate of spending to see where the final cost will end up.
options.rationale: Regression analysis may work but is not the standard forecasting measure.

options.text: Use the project's estimate at completion to show the steering committee the most likely final cost.
options.rationale: The estimate at completion forecasts the most likely final cost from performance to date.

questions.explanation: The estimate at completion forecasts the total cost of the project based on performance so far. A common formula is EAC = BAC ÷ CPI, where CPI = EV ÷ AC. It gives the steering committee the most likely final cost.
questions.mindset: Forecast final cost with EAC.

questions.stem: You are working on an agile project where the project sponsor and executive managers require lengthy reports about the project work each week. This takes you and the project team a considerable amount of time to do, and reduces time spent creating the actual product. What will you do next?

options.text: Reuse most of the information each week so your time spent on them is reduced.
options.rationale: Reusing report content still wastes time and may produce stale information.

options.text: Suggest the leaders come to the sprint review and gather what they need from the information radiator.
options.rationale: Inviting leaders to the sprint review and pointing them to information radiators gives them current information without extra reports.

options.text: Ask your project sponsor to wait until a steering committee meeting for the information.
options.rationale: Making the sponsor wait reduces transparency.

options.text: Share your working project schedule and budget with the executives instead of creating the reports.
options.rationale: Sharing working documents is still push reporting and may not suit the sponsor's needs.

questions.explanation: Agile teams show completed work at the sprint review and use information radiators—big visible charts such as task boards and burndown charts—that anyone can pull information from. This keeps leaders informed without lengthy weekly reports.
questions.mindset: Let stakeholders pull information from radiators.

questions.stem: You are working on a project that has planned as much as they can up-front. You would like them to move to a more agile way of work. Currently, the work is hidden, the team catches up only once a week in a working group, and it is hard to see what each person is working on and keep track of it. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask your team to report on their work in a written status update each day so you can keep track.
options.rationale: Daily written reports add administrative burden and are not visible to the team.

options.text: Have more working group meetings so you are always up to date on what your team is working on.
options.rationale: More working group meetings increase overhead without making the work visible.

options.text: Ask the team to move their work to a central, visible task board, then have a short meeting each day to discuss progress on the cards.
options.rationale: A central task board with a short daily meeting makes work visible and surfaces progress and impediments.

options.text: Remove the team meetings altogether and trust your team to get the work done.
options.rationale: Removing meetings entirely further reduces visibility and coordination.

questions.explanation: Moving towards agile, the team makes work visible on a task board where cards move from to do to in progress to done. A short daily meeting to discuss progress and raise impediments keeps everyone aligned without heavy reporting.
questions.mindset: Make work visible and synchronise daily.

questions.stem: You are working on a hybrid project, where the majority of the work has been planned up front. The team manages their work via a Kanban board, and report on progress and blockers each day. As the project evolves, stakeholders have added more and more scope to the product, with one executive raising an urgent feature that needs to be added. What will you do next?

options.text: Limit the number of cards in the "Ready" or "To Do" column, and ask the Product Owner to work with stakeholder requests, noting the need to swap the new item for an existing item.
options.rationale: Limiting cards in 'Ready' and having the product owner trade new items for existing ones controls scope growth.

options.text: Match the number of user stories to the team's velocity, to ensure a sustainable pace.
options.rationale: Velocity matching is a Scrum practice; this team uses Kanban and needs a WIP limit.

options.text: Work with the stakeholder to raise a change request, and note the outcome in the change log.
options.rationale: A formal change request suits the predictive part but not the Kanban-managed work.

options.text: Review the impact of the scope change with the stakeholder using the WBS dictionary.
options.rationale: The WBS dictionary does not help decide which work to swap out.

questions.explanation: On a hybrid project using Kanban, a WIP limit on the ready column controls how much work can be queued. The product owner handles stakeholder requests, making clear that adding an urgent feature means swapping it for an existing item.
questions.mindset: New work in means other work out.

questions.stem: You are working as a product owner in an agile team, where the main measure of project success is the number of features delivered into production. Over the past six months, the team have delivered the highest number of features your organisation has ever seen, however customers are starting to complain about issues and bugs in the product. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask the team to work harder in delivering more features, to fix the product issues.
options.rationale: More features will worsen quality if the metric remains unchanged.

options.text: Adjust the product metrics to include customer satisfaction and quality measures.
options.rationale: Adding customer satisfaction and quality measures balances behaviour that was driven by counting features alone.

options.text: Add a slack card of 5 points into the sprint backlog, to deal with the technical debt.
options.rationale: A slack card helps with technical debt but does not change the incentive causing it.

options.text: Remove customer comments and feedback until you have finished delivering all the features.
options.rationale: Ignoring customer feedback hides the problem and damages the product.

questions.explanation: The Hawthorne effect means that what is measured influences behaviour. Counting only features drove the team to maximise output at the expense of quality. Adding quality and customer satisfaction measures balances the incentives.
questions.mindset: Balance metrics; you get what you measure.

questions.stem: You have been working on a project for the past eight months. Your project team have been approached by multiple stakeholders for reporting on various performance measures about the project and the product area. Now, a large amount of their time is spent on creating these reports for others. They have escalated this issue to you. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask the project stakeholders to stop interacting with your project team.
options.rationale: Cutting stakeholders off from the team damages relationships and transparency.

options.text: Spend a portion of your project budget to automate the reports for your stakeholders.
options.rationale: Automating reports reduces effort but may still produce measures no one acts on.

options.text: Work with the team, including the stakeholders, to only measure things that will facilitate a decision, help avoid an issue or increase project performance.
options.rationale: Measuring only what supports decisions, avoids issues or improves performance cuts wasted reporting while meeting real needs.

options.text: Invite your stakeholders to your sprint reviews, so they can see a working feature in practice.
options.rationale: Sprint reviews show working features but do not settle which performance measures are worth reporting.

questions.explanation: Measuring and reporting data is meant to support learning and improvement. Agreeing with the team and stakeholders to measure only what facilitates a decision, helps avoid an issue or improves performance removes unnecessary reporting and frees the team to deliver.
questions.mindset: Measure only what drives decisions or improvement.

questions.stem: You are working on a project where there is a significant amount of uncertainty about the requirements. There is also a legislative change coming, and no one knows what it will mean for your industry. As a project manager, how will you deal with this uncertainty?

options.text: Perform additional planning for your project to improve your view on scope management.
options.rationale: More planning cannot remove uncertainty that cannot yet be predicted.

options.text: Hold additional retrospectives, to capture challenges and improvements from your team.
options.rationale: Retrospectives capture learning but do not prepare for unknown legislative outcomes.

options.text: Create a risk assessment of all possible project risks, with their risk ratings and owners.
options.rationale: A risk assessment helps with identifiable risks but not with outcomes nobody can yet foresee.

options.text: Gather information and prepare for multiple outcomes, and build team resilience through processes and training.
options.rationale: Gathering information, preparing for multiple outcomes and building resilience are the recommended responses to uncertainty.

questions.explanation: General uncertainty cannot be predicted precisely. Effective responses include gathering information, preparing for multiple possible outcomes, using set-based design and building resilience into the team and its processes so it can adapt as the situation becomes clearer.
questions.mindset: Prepare for several futures when the future is uncertain.

questions.stem: You are working on a project with a vendor where there is significant ambiguity involved and multiple options the team could go with. Many outcomes are possible that have varying degrees of impact to improve the situation. What will you do next?

options.text: Use experiments and prototypes, and progressive elaboration to work your way through it.
options.rationale: Experiments, prototypes and progressive elaboration work through situational ambiguity step by step.

options.text: Ask your team for additional reporting around the different options so you can make an informed decision.
options.rationale: More reports do not resolve ambiguity; they add analysis without testing options.

options.text: Add all the different options into your project scope, so all your bases are covered.
options.rationale: Adding every option to scope is wasteful and uncontrolled.

options.text: Work more closely with your senior users so they can inform you of the product requirements.
options.rationale: Senior users cannot remove the ambiguity inherent in multiple possible outcomes.

questions.explanation: Situational ambiguity arises when several options and outcomes are possible. Experiments, prototypes and progressive elaboration let the team test options and refine its understanding as information emerges, rather than committing prematurely.
questions.mindset: Experiment through ambiguity.

questions.stem: You are working on a project to improve some software that has been in production for over 17 years, and has been modified extensively over that time. It also integrates with many other systems within your organisation. You cannot decide which features to deliver first. How will you deal with the complexity?

options.text: List out the possible features you can deliver and prioritise them by cost over benefit.
options.rationale: Cost-benefit prioritisation is difficult when the system's interdependencies obscure the true costs and benefits.

options.text: Simulate decoupling connecting parts to simplify the number of variables, then reframe your view by brainstorming with a diverse set of stakeholders.
options.rationale: Decoupling and simulation simplify the system, and brainstorming with diverse stakeholders reframes the problem.

options.text: Provide an incentive for your project team for whoever can solve this complex problem.
options.rationale: Incentives for individuals do not address systemic complexity.

options.text: Form a business-case for a third party system to replace the existing, complex system, to transfer the risk of delivery.
options.rationale: Replacing the system is a drastic decision that does not deal with the complexity in front of the team.

questions.explanation: Methods for dealing with complexity include systems-based approaches such as decoupling and simulation, reframing through diverse perspectives, and process-based approaches such as iteration and stakeholder engagement. Together they make a heavily modified, interconnected system manageable.
questions.mindset: Simplify and reframe complex systems.

questions.stem: You are working on a project that requires a very particular programming skillset that is not very common. It is also the hottest job-market the industry has seen in two decades, people are hard to come by and leave often. The programming language is also evolving at a quick pace. What will you do next?

options.text: Develop the product from scratch in a more common programming language.
options.rationale: Rewriting in another language is a drastic, costly change that may introduce new risks.

options.text: Ask your whole team to learn the programming skillset, to cover the risk.
options.rationale: Having the whole team learn a fast-evolving language is costly and does not ensure retention.

options.text: Use alternatives analysis to gather different options, and ensure a sufficient cost reserve to help complete your project.
options.rationale: Alternatives analysis and a sufficient cost reserve are recommended responses to volatility.

options.text: Raise a risk to your project completion, with the threat of project team member skillsets.
options.rationale: Recording the risk is a start, but it does not provide a response to volatility.

questions.explanation: Volatility is rapid, unpredictable change, such as fluctuating availability of skills or materials. Recommended responses include alternatives analysis to identify options and holding cost reserves to absorb the effects of change.
questions.mindset: Handle volatility with alternatives and reserves.

questions.stem: Your project team have found a significant data vulnerability in one of the features planned in your product backlog, where customer data is exposed without password access. This feature is partially made by a third party vendor, and the relationship is owned by a functional manager in your organisation. What will you do next?

options.text: Avoid the risk and wait for the third party vendor to fix the vulnerability.
options.rationale: Waiting for the vendor is not avoidance; it leaves customer data exposed.

options.text: Transfer the risk by asking a different vendor to create a feature with no vulnerability in their design.
options.rationale: Engaging a different vendor is not the project manager's decision while the relationship belongs to the functional manager.

options.text: Escalate the threat to the manager with appropriate authority to act on the response.
options.rationale: Escalating to the manager who owns the vendor relationship puts the threat with someone who has authority to act.

options.text: Accept the risk and move on the other features so the work continues to get done.
options.rationale: Accepting a serious data exposure is irresponsible.

questions.explanation: Escalation is the appropriate response when a threat is outside the project's scope or beyond the project manager's authority. The vendor relationship belongs to a functional manager, so the vulnerability is escalated to them to act.
questions.mindset: Escalate threats beyond your authority.

questions.stem: You brainstorm risk responses with your project team and project sponsor, and decide you cannot transfer a certain high impact risk. You also cannot avoid the risk, and there is no one in the organisation to escalate it to. Your project sponsor agrees that you should actively accept the risk. What will you do next?

options.text: Develop a contingency plan that would be triggered if the event occurred.
options.rationale: Active acceptance includes a contingency plan that is triggered if the risk occurs.

options.text: Shift the ownership to a third party to manage the risk and bear the impact if it does occur.
options.rationale: Shifting ownership to a third party is transference, which has been ruled out.

options.text: Act to eliminate the threat or protect the project from its impact only.
options.rationale: Eliminating the threat or protecting the project from its impact is avoidance, which is not possible here.

options.text: Take action to reduce the probability of its occurrence, and the impact of the threat.
options.rationale: Reducing probability and impact is mitigation, not acceptance.

questions.explanation: Active acceptance means acknowledging a risk and preparing a contingency plan to use if it occurs; passive acceptance does nothing. Avoidance eliminates the threat, transfer shifts ownership, escalation passes it to a higher authority and mitigation reduces probability or impact.
questions.mindset: Active acceptance means a contingency plan.

questions.stem: You are working on a project to build a new customer database system for an engineering team. In working with the requirements, you realise that this system can also work with other teams within your organisation, and the effort to add those teams is quite small. What will you do next?

options.text: Work with the other teams and their managers to escalate the opportunity.
options.rationale: Escalation is for opportunities outside the project manager's authority, which is not the case here.

options.text: Work with those other teams and their managers to exploit the opportunity.
options.rationale: Exploiting the opportunity acts to ensure the other teams benefit.

options.text: Work with those other teams and their managers to enhance the opportunity.
options.rationale: Enhancing increases the probability of an opportunity, which is already certain given the small effort.

options.text: Work with the other teams and their managers to accept the opportunity.
options.rationale: Accepting acknowledges the opportunity but does nothing to realise it.

questions.explanation: Opportunity responses include exploit (ensure it occurs), escalate (pass to a higher authority), share (allocate to a third party best placed to capture it), enhance (increase its probability) and accept (acknowledge only). A low-effort benefit for other teams should be exploited.
questions.mindset: Exploit opportunities you can secure.

questions.stem: You are working as a product owner in an agile team, and during a recent risk review the team have uncovered various risks that will impact your project. You brainstorm risk responses with your team. The project customer would like them to be mitigated as soon as possible. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask your team to work on the risk responses and get them done as soon as possible.
options.rationale: Working on every response immediately ignores their value compared with feature work.

options.text: Ignore the risks initially, some may dissipate over time and only the important ones will be left.
options.rationale: Ignoring identified risks lets threats grow and technical debt accumulate.

options.text: Assign the risk responses to all stakeholders around your project team to share the load.
options.rationale: Spreading responses across stakeholders loses accountability and focus.

options.text: Prioritise the risks by comparing the expected monetary value of the risk to the anticipated return on investment of upcoming deliverables.
options.rationale: Comparing each risk's EMV with the ROI of upcoming deliverables lets risk work be prioritised in the backlog.

questions.explanation: In agile, risk responses belong in a risk-adjusted backlog prioritised alongside features. Comparing the expected monetary value of each risk with the expected return of upcoming deliverables lets the product owner schedule risk work where it adds most value.
questions.mindset: Prioritise risk responses alongside features.

questions.stem: You are planning a project where supply chains have been impacted, and the requirements are complex and intertwined with other areas of the business. Your project sponsor asks you to manage these risks before the project moves to execution. What will you do next?

options.text: Move to project execution, so you can work through risks as they happen.
options.rationale: Moving to execution without managing known risks ignores the sponsor's request.

options.text: Move to an agile way of work so you can deliver faster and also deal with the complexity.
options.rationale: Switching to agile does not by itself manage supply chain or complexity risks.

options.text: Note the risks with appropriate controls, and add a contingency reserve in the project budget.
options.rationale: Recording the risks with controls and adding a contingency reserve prepares for identified risks.

options.text: Assign a management reserve to your project budget and deal with the risks before moving to project execution.
options.rationale: Management reserve is for unknown risks; these risks are already identified.

questions.explanation: Reserves set aside time or money to handle risk. Contingency reserve covers identified risks should they occur, while management reserve covers unknown, unplanned in-scope work. Known supply and complexity risks call for controls plus contingency reserve.
questions.mindset: Known risks need contingency reserve.

questions.stem: You are working on an agile project and delivering a usable feature every few weeks. The project sponsor is from a waterfall background and is concerned that there is not enough focus on risk. They would like to hold a regular risk review with a wide group of stakeholders. What will you suggest instead?

options.text: There is no need for a separate meeting as risk is everyone's responsibility in an agile team.
options.rationale: Saying risk is everyone's responsibility does not show the sponsor how risk is managed.

options.text: Use daily stand-ups to report blockers early, and fortnightly demonstrations of the product to catch any stakeholder dissatisfaction.
options.rationale: Daily stand-ups surface blockers early, and regular demonstrations reveal stakeholder concerns, serving as ongoing risk reviews.

options.text: Use the Kanban board to see the work and how it flows from the backlog to "done".
options.rationale: The Kanban board visualises work but does not by itself surface risks.

options.text: Hold the risk meeting, but only with the immediate project team to avoid unnecessary participants.
options.rationale: A separate meeting with the immediate team duplicates what agile ceremonies already provide.

questions.explanation: Agile teams build risk management into their ceremonies. Daily stand-ups report blockers before they become threats, frequent demonstrations surface stakeholder dissatisfaction, and retrospectives identify improvements, giving the sponsor frequent, meaningful risk review.
questions.mindset: Agile ceremonies are continuous risk reviews.

questions.stem: Your Project Management Office has no prescribed way of work, so are working with a vendor who supplies an eXtreme Programming framework at a significant cost. Your organisation is using it, but projects are still running behind schedule, over budget, and with low customer satisfaction. What will you do next?

options.text: Tailor the approach to suit the organisation, operating environment and project needs.
options.rationale: Tailoring the approach to the organisation, environment and project addresses why the framework is not working.

options.text: Use a waterfall approach instead, to ensure the proper planning is completed for every project.
options.rationale: Switching to waterfall for every project is another one-size-fits-all choice.

options.text: Switch to Scrum instead, as it is a more popular framework and has been tested in the market.
options.rationale: Switching to Scrum because it is popular repeats the same mistake with a different framework.

options.text: Tighten the controls around the project environment with a more directive PMO approach.
options.rationale: Tighter PMO control does not address the mismatch between the framework and the projects.

questions.explanation: Projects operate in complex environments with competing demands. Tailoring the chosen approach to the organisation, its operating environment and each project's needs is more effective than adopting a framework unchanged or swapping to another popular one.
questions.mindset: Tailor frameworks; don't adopt them blindly.

questions.stem: Your Project Management Office is in the middle of a company-wide "ways of working" transformation. They have taken a popular project framework and are tailoring it to the organisation with branded templates and processes that meet their existing governance requirements. You have been asked to help finalise the process. What will you do next?

options.text: Gather feedback from the functional business areas to ensure the process meets their needs.
options.rationale: Feedback is useful but does not complete the tailoring process.

options.text: Roll out the new way of working to the PMO as a pilot first, then to the rest of the organisation.
options.rationale: A pilot helps rollout but does not build tailoring into the approach.

options.text: Enable a process for tailoring based on size and complexity, and implement ongoing improvement.
options.rationale: Enabling tailoring by project size and complexity, with ongoing improvement, completes the tailoring process.

options.text: Form a working group comprised of executives and project professionals.
options.rationale: A working group adds governance but does not define how tailoring works.

questions.explanation: Tailoring follows a sequence: select the initial development approach, tailor it for the organisation, tailor it for each project and implement ongoing improvement. Having tailored for the organisation, the PMO now needs project-level tailoring and continuous improvement.
questions.mindset: Tailor for the organisation, then for each project.

questions.stem: You are a manager of a PMO in a large organisation, which has recently undertaken a company- wide way of working transformation. You need to select an initial development approach for your projects, which you will then tailor to suit them further. What will you do next?

options.text: Use the framework that best engages your executive team through easy-to-use graphics and presentations.
options.rationale: Choosing a framework for its presentation appeal ignores project characteristics.

options.text: Select the most popular current framework to keep up with what other organisations are doing.
options.rationale: Popularity is not a basis for selecting an approach.

options.text: Select multiple development approaches as a baseline for your organisation.
options.rationale: Selecting several baselines at once complicates rather than guides tailoring.

options.text: Use a suitability filter to assess the most appropriate development approach.
options.rationale: A suitability filter assesses project characteristics to indicate a predictive, hybrid or adaptive approach.

questions.explanation: A suitability filter helps teams assess whether a project's characteristics suit a predictive, hybrid or adaptive approach. The selected approach becomes the base, which is then tailored to the organisation and each project.
questions.mindset: Select approaches with a suitability filter.

questions.stem: Your organisation is starting to move to an agile way of work and they are setting up a Value Delivery Office (VDO) to complement the existing PMO. The executives in the area have begun working through what the function looks like and the roles and responsibilities that might exist. They approach you for help. What will you tell them?

options.text: The VDO is responsible for the value delivered, and owns the programs within the organisation.
options.rationale: A VDO enables rather than owns programmes or value; ownership sits elsewhere.

options.text: The VDO focuses on coaching project teams, building adaptive skills and capabilities and mentoring sponsors and product owners to be more effective.
options.rationale: A VDO coaches teams, builds adaptive capability and mentors sponsors and product owners.

options.text: The VDO is responsible for agile resources such as scrum masters and product owners to be allocated effectively to project teams.
options.rationale: Allocating agile roles is a resource management function, not the VDO's enabling focus.

options.text: The VDO creates the organisational framework to be used on each project throughout the company.
options.rationale: Imposing one framework on every project is a controlling role, not the VDO's.

questions.explanation: A value delivery office plays an enabling role rather than a management or oversight function. It coaches project teams, builds adaptive skills and capabilities across the organisation and mentors sponsors and product owners to be more effective.
questions.mindset: A VDO enables; it does not control.

questions.stem: You have been planning a project for the last two months, gathering requirements and scope and assigning tasks to a schedule. As you get closer to the execution phase of your project you need to decide what delivery approach you will use. The requirements are likely to change, require a medium amount of compliance, but can be released in one go. What will you do next?

options.text: Set up a Predictive delivery approach with your team.
options.rationale: Predictive delivery handles changing requirements poorly.

options.text: Set up an Incremental delivery approach with your team.
options.rationale: Incremental delivery releases in multiple increments, but a single release is needed here.

options.text: Set up an Agile or adaptive delivery approach with your team.
options.rationale: Adaptive delivery typically releases incrementally, which is not required.

options.text: Set up an Iterative delivery approach with your team.
options.rationale: Iterative delivery refines the product through feedback while releasing it in one go.

questions.explanation: Iterative delivery gathers feedback and improves the product over repeated cycles, then releases it once. It suits requirements that are likely to change when the product can be delivered as a single release, and it can accommodate a medium level of compliance.
questions.mindset: Changing requirements with one release: iterate.

questions.stem: You have been asked to make a process improvement in the accounting area of your organisation. You have been assigned a small team of nine people, each with all the skills you need to complete the project. The team is co-located, and have unlimited access to the project customer. How will you tailor your delivery approach?

options.text: Use a predictive / waterfall delivery approach.
options.rationale: Predictive suits work that needs extensive up-front planning, which this context does not.

options.text: Use an agile / adaptive delivery approach.
options.rationale: A small, cross-functional, co-located team with customer access is ideal for adaptive delivery.

options.text: Use an incremental delivery approach.
options.rationale: Incremental describes a release pattern and does not make full use of this team's characteristics.

options.text: Use a hybrid delivery approach.
options.rationale: Hybrid suits projects needing two different approaches, which is not the case here.

questions.explanation: Agile and adaptive approaches work best with small teams of fewer than about nine to twelve people who are cross-functional, co-located and have close access to the customer. This team has all of those characteristics.
questions.mindset: Small, cross-functional, co-located team: go adaptive.

questions.stem: You have been working as a project manager in an organisation for some time, where an agile- centric delivery approach and way of work has been selected and tailored for the organisation. Over the past few months, you notice several things that are not working and could be improved as you begin new projects. What will you do next?

options.text: Review the product backlog to see the flow of features going through project teams.
options.rationale: The product backlog shows feature flow but not the problems with the way of working.

options.text: Look into issues, threats and quality assurance statistics.
options.rationale: Issue and quality statistics are useful inputs but do not engage leaders in improving the approach.

options.text: Suggest a retrospective with PMO leaders to determine ongoing improvement opportunities.
options.rationale: A retrospective with PMO leaders identifies what works and what to improve in the tailored approach.

options.text: Review a control chart and value stream map to see non-value-added activities and remove waste in the process.
options.rationale: Control charts and value stream maps can help, but a retrospective is the agile way to find broader improvements.

questions.explanation: Tailoring is not a one-off exercise; the chosen approach needs ongoing improvement. In an agile environment, a retrospective with PMO leaders is the natural way to identify what is working, what is not and which improvements to make.
questions.mindset: Improve the way of working through retrospectives.

questions.stem: You have been working on a project to deliver a new customer data system, and have noticed that the work is starting to slow down. Fewer user stories are appearing in your sprint backlog, as they are not ready. You hold a retrospective with your team and discover that there are long delays waiting for requirements and acceptance criteria approvals. What will you do next?

options.text: Streamline approval decisions through fewer people (such as a Product Owner) authorised to make decisions up to certain value thresholds.
options.rationale: Streamlining decisions through fewer authorised people, such as the product owner, removes the approval bottleneck.

options.text: Ask your team to place the user stories in the sprint backlog, reducing the need for customer approval.
options.rationale: Skipping customer approval undermines quality and accountability.

options.text: Note the long delays as a risk to your project, with a high likelihood as it is currently happening.
options.rationale: Logging the delay as a risk does not resolve an issue that is already happening.

options.text: Escalate the issue to the functional manager to ensure approvals are happening quickly.
options.rationale: Escalating may help once but does not fix the approval process.

questions.explanation: When work waits on approvals, the tailoring response is to streamline decision-making through fewer people authorised to decide up to set value thresholds. Giving the product owner that authority keeps stories flowing into sprints.
questions.mindset: Streamline decision rights to remove delays.

questions.stem: You have been assigned to take over an existing project as the previous project manager leaves for another opportunity. In working with your team you notice there is a large amount of work currently in progress all at once, with team members working on multiple items at a time and constantly contextswitching between tasks. What will you do next?

options.text: Add more people to your project to get the work done at a faster rate.
options.rationale: Adding people increases coordination overhead and does not fix multitasking.

options.text: Use value stream mapping and Kanban boards to visualise the work and brainstorm solutions with your team.
options.rationale: Value stream mapping and Kanban boards make the work visible so the team can identify problems and solutions.

options.text: Ask your team to work overtime to cover the extra work and bring it back into line.
options.rationale: Overtime worsens fatigue without reducing context switching.

options.text: Review the scope of the project and reduce items with a low impact to customer satisfaction.
options.rationale: Scope reduction may help later but does not tackle the flow problem.

questions.explanation: Too much work in progress causes constant context switching. Value stream mapping and Kanban boards make the flow of work visible, helping the team identify bottlenecks and agree solutions such as WIP limits.
questions.mindset: Visualise work to fix flow.

questions.stem: The product owner has prioritised the product backlog of features, and the team creates user stories with estimates and places enough to fill a two week sprint. You notice that the pieces being completed are being rejected by the customer for defects and missed requirements. What will you do next?

options.text: Create the project scope from scratch with the project team and customers so it is correct.
options.rationale: Redefining the whole scope is disproportionate to a quality problem.

options.text: Have an "Iteration zero" planning sprint with your project team to set it up for success.
options.rationale: An iteration zero sets up a project but does not fix quality in ongoing sprints.

options.text: Add more feedback loops such as shoulder checks, peer review, unit and system testing.
options.rationale: Adding feedback loops such as shoulder checks, peer reviews and testing catches defects before customer review.

options.text: Have less frequent customer demonstrations, so they only see the product when it is correct.
options.rationale: Fewer demonstrations would hide defects rather than prevent them.

questions.explanation: When deliverables are rejected for defects and missed requirements, the tailoring response is to add more verification and feedback loops: peer reviews, shoulder checks, pair programming and unit, system and regression testing, so defects are found earlier.
questions.mindset: Add feedback loops to raise quality.

questions.stem: Your project team has started to find their rhythm, yet you notice that they seem disengaged in their work and are dragging their feet on normal tasks. You check your project budget and note that the team are all paid fairly for the market and within the same range for the role. What will you do next?

options.text: Look for ways to reward team members with bonuses above their normal pay rate.
options.rationale: Bonuses are hygiene factors and do not create lasting motivation once pay is fair.

options.text: Move team members around to different roles frequently, so they experience job variety.
options.rationale: Frequent role changes can disrupt people rather than motivate them.

options.text: Give the team a paid day off to show how much you appreciate their work.
options.rationale: A paid day off is a one-off gesture, not a lasting motivator.

options.text: Establish ways for the team to grow and advance, such as career paths or learning pathways.
options.rationale: Growth and advancement opportunities are motivators that increase satisfaction and engagement.

questions.explanation: Herzberg's theory distinguishes hygiene factors, such as pay and policies, from motivators, such as achievement, growth and advancement. With pay already fair, more money will not motivate; career paths and learning opportunities will.
questions.mindset: Once hygiene factors are met, motivate through growth.

questions.stem: You are working as a project manager on a regulatory change for your organisation. You notice that the team are not communicating as well as they could be. You put together a plan to improve team communication by increasing its effectiveness and richness. What will you do?

options.text: Include methods that will handle multiple information cues, facilitate rapid feedback, and utilise natural language.
options.rationale: Rich communication handles multiple cues, gives rapid feedback and uses natural language, as face-to-face does.

options.text: Include methods to escalate issues easily, with executives being open for anything the team needs.
options.rationale: Escalation paths are useful but do not make everyday communication richer.

options.text: Include ways to get sign off in writing, so it can be recorded and reviewed later when needed.
options.rationale: Written sign-offs are low in richness and slow to give feedback.

options.text: Include communication that ensures everyone gets a voice and input into decisions.
options.rationale: Giving everyone a voice is valuable but is not what makes a communication channel rich.

questions.explanation: Cockburn's model plots communication channels by effectiveness and richness. Rich media handle multiple information cues, allow rapid feedback, establish personal focus and use natural language; face-to-face conversation is the richest.
questions.mindset: Rich communication is interactive and immediate.

questions.stem: Your deliverables have been signed off by the Product Owner and are ready to be released to the customer, which is the financial analytics team of your organisation. The new system will be quite a change from their normal day-to-day work. The team already have the desire to use the new system. What will you do next?

options.text: Tell them the vision and why the change is necessary.
options.rationale: Explaining the vision builds awareness, which has already been achieved.

options.text: Use training and education to show them the new processes and systems.
options.rationale: Training and education provide knowledge, the next step once desire exists.

options.text: Give them unlimited hands-on practice so they can get used to the new system.
options.rationale: Hands-on practice builds ability, which follows knowledge.

options.text: Include rewards, recognition, feedback and measurement.
options.rationale: Rewards and recognition reinforce change, the final step.

questions.explanation: The ADKAR model runs Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability and Reinforcement. The analytics team already wants the change, so the next step is knowledge: training and education on the new processes and systems.
questions.mindset: Follow ADKAR: after desire comes knowledge.

questions.stem: You are leading a large organisational change that affects more than a thousand people across multiple teams. You have engaged with the senior managers of that area, created a brief vision statement that summarises the change, and created a strategy to realise the vision. You communicate the vision throughout the change process. What will you do next?

options.text: Release multiple usable features to the affected teams so they can get used to it gradually.
options.rationale: Releasing features is delivery, not a step in Kotter's model.

options.text: Anchor the changes into corporate culture by telling success stories and recognising people who embody the change.
options.rationale: Anchoring changes in the culture is the final step, not the next one.

options.text: Address the obstacles to change, including outdated processes and people resistance.
options.rationale: Removing obstacles, such as outdated processes and resistance, follows communicating the vision.

options.text: Set goals for continued improvement on the change throughout the organisation.
options.rationale: Building on the change comes after short-term wins.

questions.explanation: Kotter's eight steps are: create urgency, form a coalition, create a vision, communicate it, remove obstacles, create short-term wins, build on the change and anchor it in the culture. Having communicated the vision, the next step is to remove obstacles.
questions.mindset: After communicating the vision, remove obstacles.

questions.stem: You are a project manager assessing the risk of future releases with your team. You have a clear set of requirements from your customer, however there are a range of possible correct solutions, that may or may not get the outcome the customer needs. There are a range of known unknowns. How will you approach this situation?

options.text: Use current best practices to make decisions.
options.rationale: Best practice suits obvious situations with clear cause and effect.

options.text: Use emergent practices that allow you to probe the environment, sense the situation, and respond with action.
options.rationale: Probe-sense-respond suits complex situations with unknown unknowns.

options.text: Assess the facts, analyse the situation and apply known good practices.
options.rationale: Complicated situations with known unknowns and several right answers call for assessing facts, analysing and applying good practice.

options.text: Sense where there is some stability then take steps to try and stabilise the situation.
options.rationale: Acting to stabilise suits chaotic situations with no clear cause and effect.

questions.explanation: The Cynefin framework classifies situations as obvious, complicated, complex or chaotic. Known unknowns with a range of correct answers indicate a complicated situation, handled by sensing the facts, analysing them and applying good practice.
questions.mindset: Complicated: sense, analyse, respond.

questions.stem: You have been asked to initiate a project to deliver a new system. The requirements are not clear, and it will take some work to uncover them. The system has been used by some team members but not all and has a medium level of uncertainty around it. How will you approach this project?

options.text: Release small usable features and improve your approach based on feedback.
options.rationale: Releasing small usable features and improving with feedback suits medium uncertainty in requirements and technology.

options.text: Do additional planning up-front to ensure every component is thought of.
options.rationale: More up-front planning cannot remove requirements that must be discovered.

options.text: Split the team into two and work on different parts of the system to simplify it.
options.rationale: Splitting the team does not reduce the uncertainty.

options.text: Form a business case for starting from scratch with new, easier to use technology.
options.rationale: Starting from scratch with new technology adds risk without addressing unclear requirements.

questions.explanation: The Stacey matrix assesses uncertainty in requirements and technology to classify a project as simple, complicated, complex or chaotic. Moderate uncertainty on both suits an agile approach: releasing small features and adapting based on feedback.
questions.mindset: Moderate uncertainty: deliver small and adapt.

questions.stem: Your project team came together from different parts of the organisation, and were introduced formally to each other. Now you notice there is some conflict within the team. Some people don't respect others' decisions, are not working together well, and there are some personality clashes within the team. What will you do next?

options.text: Help team members get to know each other, their names, position on the team, and other background information.
options.rationale: Getting to know each other belongs to the forming stage, which the team has passed.

options.text: Help the team understand their roles and responsibilities and form a regular rhythm of meetings, collaboration and work.
options.rationale: Clarifying roles and establishing a working rhythm helps the team move from storming to norming.

options.text: Help the team jockey for position within the team, and foster healthy conflict.
options.rationale: Encouraging jockeying for position prolongs storming rather than resolving it.

options.text: Help the team complete the project work and disperse to work on other things
options.rationale: Completing work and dispersing describes the adjourning stage.

questions.explanation: Tuckman's model runs forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning. Conflict, disrespect and personality clashes indicate storming. Clarifying roles and responsibilities and establishing a regular rhythm of work helps the team progress to norming.
questions.mindset: Help storming teams reach norming.

questions.stem: You have formed a new project team and have worked through the purpose and mission of the project with them. You expanded on who is on the project team and the skills and abilities each person brings. You would like to foster a high performing culture and ensure the team is able to deliver as soon as possible. What will you do next?

options.text: Work through changes on the project team and the project such as deliverables and stakeholders.
options.rationale: Working through changes to team and project belongs to the renewal stage, much later.

options.text: Decompose the high level plan into greater detail, including a detailed schedule or backlog.
options.rationale: Detailed decomposition is implementation, which comes after goals and commitment.

options.text: Define a plan to achieve the project goals, including milestone schedules, release plans and high- level budgets.
options.rationale: Defining the plan is commitment (the 'how'), which follows goal clarification.

options.text: Clarify the goals of the team and what you are here to deliver.
options.rationale: Clarifying the team's goals and what it will deliver (the 'what') follows orientation and trust building.

questions.explanation: The Drexler/Sibbet team performance model runs orientation (why), trust building (who), goal clarification (what), commitment (how), implementation, high performance and renewal. With purpose and team members covered, the next step is clarifying goals.
questions.mindset: Why, who, then what, then how.

questions.stem: Your team members have raised an issue as they believe the current project scope will not reach the intended project goal of increasing customer retention. You take their concerns to the Project Sponsor who controls the funding and resources. The sponsor dismisses them and directs you to proceed with the scope currently set. What will you do next?

options.text: Problem solve with the sponsor and find a resolution.
options.rationale: Problem solving is often preferred, but the sponsor has already dismissed the concerns after discussion.

options.text: Compromise with the sponsor so each party gets what a part of what they want.
options.rationale: Compromise is not realistic when the sponsor, who controls funding, has given a clear direction.

options.text: Accommodate the sponsor to maintain harmony and good will.
options.rationale: Accommodating the sponsor maintains the relationship when the other party has more power and has decided.

options.text: Force the issue so the sponsor accepts the change in requirements from the team.
options.rationale: Forcing against a more powerful sponsor who controls funding is likely to fail and damage the relationship.

questions.explanation: The Thomas-Kilmann model describes conflict modes chosen according to relative power and the importance of the relationship. With a sponsor who holds the power and has already dismissed the concerns, accommodating preserves goodwill while the direction is followed.
questions.mindset: Choose the conflict mode that fits power and relationship.

questions.stem: The functional manager raises a concern that they have not been engaged correctly and the program is missing some key requirements as a result. You believe you have captured all the items required. Your program manager asks you to handle the situation and approach it from a win-win perspective. What will you do next?

options.text: Escalate the decision to the steering committee to ensure your point of view is heard.
options.rationale: Escalating to the steering committee sets up a win-lose contest.

options.text: Demonstrate integrity, find mutual trust, and look at the situation from their point of view.
options.rationale: Integrity, mutual trust and seeing the manager's point of view are the foundations of a win-win outcome.

options.text: Choose to give some lee-way in your approach so the functional manager can add their requirements.
options.rationale: Simply giving way to the manager's demands is lose-win, not win-win.

options.text: Get your requirements baselined first then compete with the manager to ensure a win.
options.rationale: Competing to win produces win-lose and damages the relationship.

questions.explanation: Covey's 'Think win-win' principle rests on character, mutual trust and the ability to see a situation from the other party's point of view. Approaching the functional manager this way seeks an outcome that works for both sides.
questions.mindset: Win-win starts with trust and empathy.

questions.stem: You have been planning a project to deliver a process change for the past four weeks. The requirements and scope have been signed off by the business owner, and the team are moving into delivery and execution. The work begins in line with the project plan and scope. What will you do next?

options.text: Monitor and control the work being done to ensure it meets its goals.
options.rationale: Monitoring and controlling the work as it is executed ensures it meets its goals.

options.text: Execute the project work to complete the work defined in the project plan.
options.rationale: Execution has already begun, so the next activity is to monitor and control it.

options.text: Plan the project work to ensure sufficient understanding.
options.rationale: Planning has already been completed and signed off by the business owner.

options.text: Formally sign off and complete the project phase.
options.rationale: Closing comes after the work is completed and accepted.

questions.explanation: The process groups are initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, and closing. They can overlap and iterate, and once work is being executed it must be monitored and controlled to confirm it is meeting the plan and goals.
questions.mindset: Execution is always paired with monitoring and control.

questions.stem: You are working as a Product Owner. While your sales and revenue have been increasing over the past eight months, the overall profit for your product has decreased by 17%. Your executive manager asks you to address the situation. What will you do next?

options.text: Stop the current work and set a planning session with your team to address the situation.
options.rationale: Stopping all work is disruptive and delays value while the cause is unknown.

options.text: Ask your team to work overtime on the current features in your backlog and get the work done.
options.rationale: Overtime on current features does not address why profit is falling.

options.text: Perform benchmarking with a similar yet non-competitive company, and add any process improvements to your product backlog.
options.rationale: Benchmarking against a similar non-competing company reveals process gaps to add to the backlog.

options.text: Look for opportunities to partner with other products in your organisation and increase your sales further.
options.rationale: Increasing sales does not help if the cost of producing or selling is rising.

questions.explanation: Rising revenue with falling profit means the product costs more to produce or sell. Benchmarking against a similar but non-competing organisation reveals process improvements, which the product owner can add to the backlog for the team to deliver.
questions.mindset: Benchmark to find process improvements.

questions.stem: You have been given authority to manage the upcoming features your team will release. You do not have a high enough level of expertise in the product, so you gather senior users from the product's area to create a features list. Each stakeholder wants their feature to be delivered first. How will you prioritise them and move forward?

options.text: Go with the features wanted by the top level executives first, to avoid issues later on.
options.rationale: Executive seniority is not a measure of business value.

options.text: Perform a MOSCOW analysis with the stakeholders.
options.rationale: MoSCoW with competing stakeholders risks every feature becoming a 'must have'.

options.text: Perform a root cause analysis and go with features that address the root cause.
options.rationale: Root cause analysis is for specific problems, not for prioritising a feature list.

options.text: Use a cost benefit analysis and compare the time needed to recover the project cost.
options.rationale: Cost-benefit analysis and payback period prioritise features objectively by business value.

questions.explanation: When every stakeholder wants their feature first, an objective measure of value is needed. Cost-benefit analysis and payback period—the time to recover the investment—are accepted ways to rank features by business value.
questions.mindset: Prioritise objectively by value.

questions.stem: You are creating a business case and project charter with a small initial project team. You have a high level feature, decomposed into smaller release milestones, and you would like to note a high- level schedule using wideband delphi or a high-level version of planning poker. What will you do next?

options.text: Hold a round of cards with points on them, where each team member places their cards in the centre for the total estimate.
options.rationale: Placing cards to add up a total misdescribes planning poker, which reaches consensus rather than summing.

options.text: Ask subject matter experts to complete multiple rounds of estimates individually, compare, and explain the highest and lowest estimates for each
options.rationale: Wideband Delphi uses repeated rounds of individual expert estimates, discussing the highest and lowest each round.

options.text: Show the wideband high level range from lowest to highest for each feature.
options.rationale: Showing a range is an output, not the technique itself.

options.text: Find the business functionality for each feature and estimate the effort based on that.
options.rationale: Estimating from business functionality describes function point analysis.

questions.explanation: Wideband Delphi asks subject matter experts to estimate individually over several rounds, comparing results and explaining the highest and lowest estimates each time until they converge. Planning poker is an agile variation of the technique.
questions.mindset: Delphi converges expert estimates through rounds.

questions.stem: You have been asked to help facilitate a senior planning meeting in your organisation. High level executives have made a presentation on the strengths and opportunities of the organisation, painting a rosy picture. Revenue has fallen recently, and the chief executive asks you to level out their analysis a more complete view. What will you do next?

options.text: Add your organisation's competitors and compare their products.
options.rationale: Competitor comparison informs threats but does not complete the analysis.

options.text: Showcase the pipeline of upcoming work to be delivered in the next quarter.
options.rationale: The work pipeline is operational detail, not strategic analysis.

options.text: Add in the background and abilities of the executive team, that will allow the organisation to deliver.
options.rationale: Executive backgrounds would add more strengths, making the picture more one-sided.

options.text: Brainstorm and capture the weaknesses of the organisation and threats to the organisation.
options.rationale: Adding weaknesses and threats completes the SWOT analysis and balances the picture.

questions.explanation: A SWOT analysis considers strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. The executives have presented only strengths and opportunities, so capturing internal weaknesses and external threats completes the analysis and gives the balanced view requested.
questions.mindset: A complete SWOT includes weaknesses and threats.

questions.stem: You are adding an essential feature to your product roadmap. Your team believe they can complete the feature in six weeks, however the feature is quite large and a bit more complicated than normal. One of your lead developers says they worked on a similar feature in another company, and it took around four months to complete. What will you do next?

options.text: Use relative estimating, assigning the amount of points your team agree on to the product roadmap.
options.rationale: Relative points assume the team understands the feature, which the lead's experience calls into question.

options.text: Use analogous estimating, and place the feature with around four months to complete.
options.rationale: Analogous estimating uses the similar past feature to give a quick, experience-based estimate.

options.text: Use parametric estimating, and place the feature with around four months to complete.
options.rationale: Parametric estimating uses a statistical relationship with unit rates, not a single past example.

options.text: Use function point estimating to show the amount of business functionality in the feature.
options.rationale: Function points measure functionality, not the elapsed time the roadmap needs.

questions.explanation: Analogous estimating uses the actual duration of a similar past piece of work to estimate new work quickly, with moderate accuracy. The lead developer's experience of a similar four-month feature provides that analogy.
questions.mindset: Use similar past work as an analogy.

questions.stem: You have a prioritised product backlog of features, and have decomposed the next feature to be delivered into user stories, small enough to complete in one sprint of two weeks. The team would like to estimate the effort involved on those user stories, but are unsure on how to proceed. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask each team member to add their own estimates as they complete the acceptance criteria.
options.rationale: Individual estimates made during the work are not a team estimate made in advance.

options.text: Estimate the effort for the overall feature to reduce the need for individual story estimates.
options.rationale: Estimating only the whole feature loses the story-level detail needed for sprint planning.

options.text: Help the team perform relative estimating together, where the stories are sized in points relative to the smallest piece.
options.rationale: Sizing stories together in points, relative to the smallest, is the standard agile method.

options.text: Base the estimates on cost per hour, and add them after the work is done to ensure it is correct.
options.rationale: Estimating after the work is done is recording, not estimating.

questions.explanation: User stories are most commonly estimated relatively: the team compares each story with the smallest one and assigns story points, often on a Fibonacci-like scale such as 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 and 13.
questions.mindset: Estimate stories together, relatively.

questions.stem: You are half way through your current sprint of two weeks. The work is progressing well, however you notice that there is not enough work ready and elaborated for when the next sprint begins. What will you do next?

options.text: Hold a backlog refinement meeting and work with the team to identify the work that could be accomplished.
options.rationale: Backlog refinement elaborates and prioritises items so there is ready work for the next sprint.

options.text: Raise the issue as a blocker in the daily stand-up and ask your team to swarm around the problem.
options.rationale: A lack of ready work is not a blocker for the current sprint's work.

options.text: Raise the issue in the next retrospective and take an action for the team.
options.rationale: Waiting for the retrospective means the next sprint may start without ready work.

options.text: Place the cards on the Kanban board so the team can see the work and get started.
options.rationale: Unrefined cards on the board are not ready to be worked on.

questions.explanation: Backlog refinement progressively elaborates and reprioritises backlog items so that enough work is ready for the next iteration. Holding a refinement session mid-sprint ensures the team can plan the next sprint effectively.
questions.mindset: Refine the backlog ahead of the next sprint.

questions.stem: You have completed a make-or-buy analysis in your project and found that part of your deliverable is best created by an external vendor. You work with your project team to create the procurement strategy, source selection criteria and statement of work. What will you do next?

options.text: Gather seller proposals, including technical details and price (separately).
options.rationale: Proposals are gathered after sellers understand the requirements.

options.text: Meet with prospective sellers to ensure all vendors have a common understanding of the procurement.
options.rationale: A bidder conference gives all prospective sellers a common understanding before they bid.

options.text: Perform source selection analysis on what you want from prospective vendors.
options.rationale: Source selection criteria have already been created.

options.text: Create the procurement agreement for the third party vendor to provide their specified services.
options.rationale: The agreement is created after a seller has been selected.

questions.explanation: With the procurement strategy, source selection criteria and statement of work complete, the next step is to conduct procurement. A bidder conference ensures all prospective sellers share a clear, common understanding before they prepare proposals.
questions.mindset: Hold a bidder conference before proposals.

questions.stem: One of the stakeholders in your project has raised a change request, after some of the deliverables contained defects and a missed requirement. Your project has a formal change control process, as opposed to a more agile prioritised product backlog. What will you do next?

options.text: Gather feedback from other stakeholders to see if they also need the change.
options.rationale: Surveying other stakeholders is not part of the formal change control process.

options.text: Note the change in the change log, then place the requested item in the next sprint.
options.rationale: Putting the item into a sprint bypasses the formal process in use.

options.text: Take the change to the CCB, then communicate the decision to approve or reject the change.
options.rationale: Taking the change to the CCB and communicating its decision follows the formal change control process.

options.text: Raise the request as an issue that will affect your project schedule and budget.
options.rationale: Raising an issue records a problem but does not decide on the change.

questions.explanation: Where formal change control applies, the change control board reviews change requests and approves or rejects them. Its decisions are recorded and communicated to the appropriate stakeholders.
questions.mindset: Follow the change process that is in place.

questions.stem: Your agile project has recently gained some new stakeholders after a department restructure. They complain to you that they are not seeing enough traction of work delivered through the project, and are worried it will not meet their requirements. What will you do next?

options.text: Invite them to the daily stand up, so they can see the work that happens on a daily basis.
options.rationale: The daily stand-up is for the team to coordinate, not a showcase for stakeholders.

options.text: Invite them to iteration planning, so they can choose what the team works on.
options.rationale: Iteration planning is where the team plans the work; priorities are set by the product owner.

options.text: Invite them to the retrospective, so they can raise their issue there and come up with a solution.
options.rationale: The retrospective is the team's own improvement meeting.

options.text: Invite them to the Iteration Review, so they can see the usable increment the team delivers.
options.rationale: The iteration review demonstrates the usable increment and invites stakeholder feedback.

questions.explanation: The iteration or sprint review demonstrates the work completed during the iteration to customers and stakeholders. Inviting the new stakeholders shows them real progress and gives them the chance to influence the product so it meets their needs.
questions.mindset: Show stakeholders working increments at the review.

questions.stem: You have recently taken over a project. Your project team approach you to say there is a regulatory approval that has not been granted yet, and it may block development of your project in the next five months. You check your project documentation but cannot see any mention of this. What will you do next?

options.text: Hold a risk review meeting, capture it as a risk, and ensure an adequate risk response.
options.rationale: A risk review captures the unrecorded approval as a risk and ensures an adequate response is planned.

options.text: Hold a retrospective with your team to capture what challenges the team are facing.
options.rationale: A retrospective looks at team challenges, not an unrecorded external dependency.
