options.text: Adjust your product roadmap to reflect the changes to the timeframe of that deliverable.
options.rationale: Changing the roadmap assumes the delay will happen before the risk is assessed.

options.text: Escalate the regulatory approval to the project steering committee.
options.rationale: Escalation may be needed later but only once the risk is understood and a response considered.

questions.explanation: A pending regulatory approval that could block development in five months is an unrecorded risk. A risk review identifies and analyses it, records it in the register and ensures an adequate response is in place before it can affect the project.
questions.mindset: Capture new risks and plan responses.

questions.stem: You are an agile project manager, and holding daily stand-ups with your team. You notice people accusing other team members of not doing their job and there are some tasks that are not mentioned anywhere and no one is responsible for. The team velocity has slowed in the last three sprints. What will you do next?

options.text: Refer to the team charter, and the team roles and agreed ways of managing conflict.
options.rationale: The charter is a useful reference, but the team needs to solve the problem together.

options.text: Raise it as an issue in the next retrospective and come to a solution with the team.
options.rationale: Raising the issue at the retrospective lets the team explore the causes of blame and unowned tasks and agree a solution.

options.text: Assign team roles to those you think are best suited.
options.rationale: Assigning roles yourself is directive and bypasses the team's self-organisation.

options.text: Work with your team to size user stories correctly, so velocity improves.
options.rationale: Resizing stories does not address blame and unowned work.

questions.explanation: The agile way to tackle team dysfunction is to problem-solve with the team. The retrospective is the regular forum where the team examines how it works, including conflict and unowned tasks, and agrees improvements to its process.
questions.mindset: Solve team problems together in the retrospective.

questions.stem: You are managing a large construction project. Due to some delays, the project schedule has been pushed back by one week. As a result, one of the project risks has increased slightly, but is still within the acceptable limits. What will you do next?

options.text: Hold a risk review to update the risk response and owners.
options.rationale: A full risk review is unnecessary when the risk remains within acceptable limits.

options.text: Raise a change request for the change to the project schedule.
options.rationale: A change request may not be needed for a delay that stays within tolerances.

options.text: Capture the change in your project reporting and take it to the next status meeting.
options.rationale: Reporting the change and discussing it at the status meeting keeps stakeholders informed proportionately.

options.text: Update the sprint backlog to reflect the delayed work.
options.rationale: A sprint backlog does not apply; nothing suggests this construction project is run in sprints.

questions.explanation: A one-week delay that slightly raises a risk still within acceptable limits calls for a proportionate response. The project manager records it in project reporting and discusses it at the regular status meeting, where progress and performance are reviewed.
questions.mindset: Respond proportionately to changes within tolerance.

questions.stem: You are working as a Project Manager and your team is about to deliver the completed system to the customer. During the final round of testing, the customer points out that a major piece of functionality is missing, which should have been in scope but was not previously thought of. What will you do next?

options.text: Deliver the system to the customer as it is with the promise to add the functionality later.
options.rationale: Delivering an incomplete system with a promise leaves the customer without required functionality.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to accept the risk and move on.
options.rationale: The sponsor accepting the risk does not deliver functionality that should be in scope.

options.text: Utilise your project budget's Contingency Reserves to add the functionality before release.
options.rationale: Contingency reserve is for identified risks; this missing functionality was never identified.

options.text: Utilise your project's Management Reserves as part of the budget to add the required functionality before release.
options.rationale: Management reserve covers unforeseen work within scope, such as this missed functionality.

questions.explanation: Management reserve is withheld from the budget for management control and covers unforeseen work that is within the project's scope. Functionality that should have been in scope but was never identified is exactly such work.
questions.mindset: Unforeseen in-scope work: management reserve.

questions.stem: You are a project manager in an agile team developing new features for an app. An executive stakeholder with a high influence in the organisation approaches you and asks you to add a feature that they like. They asked their friends, who think it is a good idea too. What will you do next?

options.text: Place the feature in the product backlog and prioritise it, using cost-versus-benefit.
options.rationale: Adding the feature to the backlog and prioritising it by cost versus benefit handles the request objectively.

options.text: Raise a change request to add the new feature into the scope baseline.
options.rationale: Scope baselines and change requests are predictive mechanisms, not agile ones.

options.text: Gather the requirements for the new feature and ask your team to elaborate on it.
options.rationale: Elaborating the feature before it is prioritised may waste effort on low-value work.

options.text: Analyse the impact to your project schedule and cost, the add the feature to your project scope.
options.rationale: Adding it to scope after impact analysis is also a predictive approach.

questions.explanation: In agile, new requests, including those from influential executives, go into the product backlog and are prioritised against other items using an objective scheme such as cost versus benefit. This keeps the team working on the most valuable work.
questions.mindset: Prioritise every request on value, whoever asks.

questions.stem: During User Acceptance Testing a senior user points out a major change needed to the project scope for it to be successful. You realise you may not have enough money or resources to complete your project, but will need approval to increase either. What will you do next?

options.text: Review the Change Management Plan for the correct change control process, including approvers on the Change Control Board.
options.rationale: The change management plan sets out the change control process, including the CCB approvers.

options.text: Review the Configuration Management Plan to find out who can configure the scope change.
options.rationale: The configuration management plan covers version control of items, not approval of changes.

options.text: Review the Scope Management Plan to see how changes to scope should be handled.
options.rationale: The scope management plan covers defining and validating scope rather than the approval process.

options.text: Review the Quality Management Plan to see rules for User Acceptance Testing and their results.
options.rationale: The quality management plan covers testing, not approval of scope and budget changes.

questions.explanation: The change management plan defines the change control process, including who sits on the change control board and approves changes. A significant scope change that affects budget and resources must follow this process.
questions.mindset: Check the change management plan for how to approve changes.

questions.stem: Your project team have planned the requirements, scope, schedule and cost for constructing a new building in your organisation. An executive from another area approaches you, as your project is funded and about to begin execution, and asks if you can help them deliver a website as part of your work. What will you do next?

options.text: Raise the request as an issue in your project's issue log.
options.rationale: Recording it as an issue misrepresents a request for new work.

options.text: Add the website to your project scope and adjust your project scope, schedule and cost.
options.rationale: Absorbing unrelated scope into a funded building project is scope creep.

options.text: Raise a change request for the added scope and review the impact to your project schedule and cost.
options.rationale: A change request would add work that is unrelated to the building project.

options.text: Offer to help them create a business case for the new idea and get funding for a new project.
options.rationale: Helping the executive build a business case for a separate, funded project is the right route.

questions.explanation: A website is unrelated to constructing a building and needs different skills and scope. It should be a separate project with its own funding, so the project manager helps the executive prepare a business case, which typically precedes a charter and formal approval.
questions.mindset: Unrelated work belongs in its own project.

questions.stem: A new executive has started in the functional area you are delivering to. They are concerned the project is not delivering what they need, and they put pressure on you to deliver more than was originally agreed. You agree to meet and talk through the Scope Baseline so you are on the same page. What will you do next?

options.text: Gather the Requirements Traceability Matrix and Feature Gantt Chart.
options.rationale: The traceability matrix and a feature Gantt chart are not components of the scope baseline.

options.text: Gather the Feature list and current Sprint backlog.
options.rationale: Feature lists and sprint backlogs are agile artefacts, not the baseline.

options.text: Gather the approved Scope Management Plan.
options.rationale: The scope management plan explains how scope is managed but is not the baseline.

options.text: Gather the Project Scope Statement, WBS and WBS dictionary.
options.rationale: The scope statement, WBS and WBS dictionary are the components of the scope baseline.

questions.explanation: The scope baseline consists of the approved project scope statement, the WBS and the WBS dictionary. Reviewing these with the new executive shows exactly what was agreed and provides a basis for discussing any additional requests through change control.
questions.mindset: Scope baseline: scope statement, WBS, WBS dictionary.

questions.stem: You are working in a new agile team, where the work has started to slow and there is uncertainty and low team engagement. You set time to create a team charter with your team, agree on roles and responsibilities and team cadence. What will you do next?

options.text: Set a team goal for them to be more engaged in the work over the next three months.
options.rationale: Setting an engagement goal does not give the team a reason to engage.

options.text: Create a product vision statement, showing the value you are bringing and the "why" behind the work.
options.rationale: A product vision statement explains the value and the 'why', inspiring the team to contribute.

options.text: Ask the team to contribute more to all pieces of work during each team meeting.
options.rationale: Asking for more contribution in meetings does not address the lack of purpose.

options.text: Raise it as a people issue for your project and manage it with the project steering committee.
options.rationale: Escalating a team engagement issue to the steering committee is premature.

questions.explanation: With a charter, roles and cadence in place, the team still needs a reason to care. A concise product vision statement sets out the purpose and value of the work and inspires the team to contribute.
questions.mindset: Give the team a clear 'why'.

questions.stem: You are integrating a third party system as part of your project. The developers in your project team have not worked with this system before, but they believe the language and layout is the same and they should be able to implement it, adding a bit of time for the uncertainty. They give a high-level estimate of five weeks. What will you do next?

options.text: Note the estimate of five weeks and update the assumption log with the technical assumption.
options.rationale: Recording the estimate and the technical assumption behind it in the assumption log keeps it visible and testable.

options.text: Don't add the estimate, break down the integration into user stories and use a bottom-up approach.
options.rationale: A detailed bottom-up estimate is unnecessary for a high-level estimate.

options.text: Check the estimate using parametric estimating, to increase its accuracy.
options.rationale: Parametric estimating needs historical data that the team does not have for this system.

options.text: Gather your whole team and customers together, and estimate using wideband delphi (planning poker).
options.rationale: A full wideband Delphi session is disproportionate for this estimate.

questions.explanation: The estimate rests on the assumption that the new system works like familiar ones. Recording the estimate and logging the assumption means it can be monitored and revisited if it proves false.
questions.mindset: Log the assumptions behind estimates.

questions.stem: Your agile project has delivered three features so far and is halfway through delivering the latest improvement. During a brainstorming session, one of your customers comes up with a new feature idea. You check the benefit it could have, and it is high. The complexity is low. What will you do next?

options.text: Add money to your budget to accommodate the additional feature as soon as possible.
options.rationale: Adding budget is premature and not how agile teams absorb new ideas.

options.text: Elaborate on the feature, break it down into user stories, and estimate them.
options.rationale: Elaborating the feature comes after it has been prioritised.

options.text: Place the item in the backlog and reprioritise it to be next.
options.rationale: Adding the high-benefit, low-complexity item to the backlog and prioritising it next maximises value.

options.text: Create a business case for the new feature outlining the benefit and costs involved.
options.rationale: A separate business case adds heavy overhead for a small, high-value feature.

questions.explanation: A backlog is an ordered list of work. A new idea with high benefit and low complexity is added to the backlog and prioritised near the top, so the team delivers it soon after the current improvement.
questions.mindset: High value, low effort goes to the top of the backlog.

questions.stem: One of the senior users testing your product found is was missing a key requirement that he had assumed would be there. It was not noted in the project scope, which has been baselined. You check the impact to cost and schedule, raise a change request on his behalf, and take it to the change control board where it is approved. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask your team to elaborate and turn the requirement into user stories.
options.rationale: Elaborating user stories is agile work and comes after the change is recorded and communicated.

options.text: Place the new requirement into the sprint backlog for the next sprint.
options.rationale: This project uses a baselined, predictive scope, not a sprint backlog.

options.text: Add the missed requirement to the issue log and problem solve with your team to ensure it does not happen again in the future.
options.rationale: The approved change is not an issue to be logged.

options.text: Note the outcome in the change log and communicate it to your stakeholders.
options.rationale: Recording the outcome in the change log and communicating it completes the change control step.

questions.explanation: After the change control board approves a change, the decision is recorded in the change log and communicated to stakeholders. The change log tracks all submitted changes and their status.
questions.mindset: Log and communicate change decisions.

questions.stem: You are working on a hybrid project to replace an aging customer system that has just had a feature upgrade release. The senior developer raises a concern during the daily stand-up that the system doesn't seem to be able to connect to some parts of the organisation after the upgrade. What will you do next?

options.text: Re-plan the project to ensure the correct scope is worked on that will connect to the organisation.
options.rationale: Re-planning the project is disproportionate before the problem is understood.

options.text: Raise it in the issue log, assign it to a responsible party and work with them to find a resolution.
options.rationale: Recording the connection problem in the issue log with an owner ensures it is tracked and resolved.

options.text: Raise the concern as a risk and brainstorm risk responses with your team.
options.rationale: The problem is already happening, so it is an issue rather than a risk.

options.text: Escalate the issue to the technical manager so they can resolve it.
options.rationale: Escalating without recording and owning the issue loses track of it.

questions.explanation: A problem that is already happening is an issue. It is recorded in the issue log, assigned to a responsible party and followed up until resolved, keeping it visible and managed.
questions.mindset: Record issues and assign owners.

questions.stem: You are working on an agile project, where your project team have raised multiple risks to project delivery. Some of the risks may impact your cost and schedule significantly. Your program manager asks you to manage them using a risk adjusted backlog. What will you do next?

options.text: Adjust your risk register to include the work not completed if the risks are triggered.
options.rationale: The risk register is not the backlog, and recording unfinished work does not address risks.

options.text: Adjust your backlog velocity so your end date is not impacted by the raised risks.
options.rationale: Adjusting velocity to protect the end date ignores the risks.

options.text: Gather risk mitigation responses from your retrospectives and assign them to an owner.
options.rationale: Retrospectives are not the main source of risk responses.

options.text: Place at least one risk response in each sprint to manage and close.
options.rationale: Placing risk responses into each sprint builds them into planned work so risks are actively addressed.

questions.explanation: A risk-adjusted backlog includes work to address threats and opportunities alongside features. Planning risk responses into each sprint ensures they are worked on and closed rather than left as a separate list.
questions.mindset: Put risk responses into sprints.

questions.stem: You are delivering a project to a functional area in your organisation. The project is highly complex and there are many risks to project delivery. The functional manager would like to see the biggest risks that are assigned to her. What will you do next?

options.text: Show her the risk adjusted backlog.
options.rationale: A risk-adjusted backlog lists risk work in priority order, not risk owners and ratings.

options.text: Show her the risk register.
options.rationale: The risk register records each risk with its owner, probability, impact and planned responses.

options.text: Show her the risk management plan.
options.rationale: The risk management plan describes the approach to risk management, not individual risks.

options.text: Show her the qualitative risk assessment.
options.rationale: A qualitative assessment rates risks but is recorded in the register alongside ownership.

questions.explanation: The risk register is the repository for identified risks, recording each risk's owner, probability and impact, and planned responses. It lets the functional manager see the biggest risks assigned to her.
questions.mindset: Individual risks and owners live in the risk register.

questions.stem: Your project has been in progress for the past six months. Someone you have not met before approaches you and says they have not been engaged sufficiently, even though he believes his team is highly impacted by the change. He advises he may block the project as a result. What will you do next?

options.text: Perform stakeholder engagement assessment with the stakeholder.
options.rationale: An engagement assessment comes after the stakeholder has been identified and recorded.

options.text: Add him to the stakeholder register, including his salary and interests information.
options.rationale: Salary is not relevant stakeholder information.

options.text: Add him to the stakeholder register, including his impact and influence information.
options.rationale: Recording him in the register with his impact and influence establishes where he fits before engagement is planned.

options.text: Raise a risk to project delivery due to the nature of his actions.
options.rationale: Raising a risk treats the stakeholder as a threat rather than engaging him.

questions.explanation: A newly discovered stakeholder must first be identified and recorded. The stakeholder register captures his details, assessment and classification, such as impact and influence, which then shape how he is engaged.
questions.mindset: Identify and classify new stakeholders first.

questions.stem: You are a product owner on an agile project and have created a product backlog of features in a prioritised order for delivery. You ask the team to break down the first feature into user stories, and estimate their effort. What will you do next?

options.text: Create an iteration plan with your team.
options.rationale: An iteration plan matches the estimated stories to the team's velocity for the upcoming sprint.

options.text: Create the product roadmap with your team.
options.rationale: The roadmap already exists as the prioritised feature backlog.

options.text: Perform a sprint review with your team.
options.rationale: A sprint review happens at the end of a sprint, which has not yet started.

options.text: Begin daily stand-ups with your team.
options.rationale: Daily stand-ups begin once the sprint is under way.

questions.explanation: With features prioritised and the first feature broken into estimated user stories, the next step is iteration planning. The team selects stories that fit its average velocity to form a detailed plan for the sprint.
questions.mindset: Plan the iteration after stories are estimated.

questions.stem: You have worked with your project customer to create a list of features that will bring the most value to them. They would like to see when some of this value will be delivered and the expected outcomes of each. What will you do next?

options.text: Show the features at the next sprint review so the customer can see what they look like.
options.rationale: A sprint review shows features after they are built, not when they will be delivered.

options.text: Place the features on a release plan and show this to the customer.
options.rationale: A release plan sets expectations for the dates, features and outcomes across multiple iterations.

options.text: Check the features against the velocity chart to see when they might be delivered.
options.rationale: A velocity chart shows past throughput, not a plan for delivery.

options.text: Place the features into the next sprint plan and show this to your customer.
options.rationale: A single sprint plan covers only the next iteration.

questions.explanation: A release plan sets expectations for when features will be delivered and the outcomes they will bring over several iterations. It is the agile tool for showing the customer when value will arrive.
questions.mindset: Show future delivery with a release plan.

questions.stem: You are in the planning stages of your project, where you need to find out exactly what the project customer needs so you can find a solution and make it happen. Your business analysts are new to their roles and are not sure on what their process will be. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask the business analysts to begin writing user stories to place in a sprint.
options.rationale: Writing stories before a requirements process is defined leaves the analysts without direction.

options.text: Create the project management plan to outline how the project will be delivered.
options.rationale: The overall plan is broader; the analysts need the specific requirements process.

options.text: Work with the business analysts to create a requirements management plan.
options.rationale: A requirements management plan describes how requirements will be analysed, documented and managed.

options.text: Create a work breakdown structure on the project scope.
options.rationale: A WBS decomposes scope; it does not define how requirements are elicited.

questions.explanation: The requirements management plan is a component of the project management plan that describes how requirements will be analysed, documented and managed. It gives new business analysts a clear process to follow.
questions.mindset: Define how requirements will be managed.

questions.stem: You are working on a new software application with a lot of complex interdependencies. The senior user providing and testing most of the requirements is concerned that some of those dependencies will cause errors upon release, if they are not checked thoroughly. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask the senior user for a written list of all his requirements, then check they are included in the project scope.
options.rationale: Listing requirements checks scope coverage, not whether dependencies are tested.

options.text: Raise a risk on the software complexity with the project team.
options.rationale: Raising a risk records the concern but does not show how testing will address it.

options.text: Create an affinity diagram with the senior user.
options.rationale: An affinity diagram groups ideas; it does not plan testing.

options.text: Review the test plan with the senior user.
options.rationale: Reviewing the test plan with the senior user confirms that complex dependencies will be tested thoroughly.

questions.explanation: A test plan describes what will be tested, which tests will be run and how. Reviewing it with the senior user confirms that complex interdependencies are covered and gives an opportunity to add tests where they are not.
questions.mindset: Address quality concerns through the test plan.

questions.stem: You are planning your project and have captured the requirements from the project customer. You ask your team to plan the project scope, but they need to see exactly what needs to be delivered and how each part relates to each other. What will you do next?

options.text: Create a product breakdown structure with your project team.
options.rationale: A product breakdown structure shows all product components and how they relate in a whole-part hierarchy.

options.text: Create the requirements traceability matrix with your project team.
options.rationale: The traceability matrix links requirements to deliverables but does not show the product structure.

options.text: Create the risk breakdown structure with your project team.
options.rationale: A risk breakdown structure organises risks, not deliverables.

options.text: Create the scope management plan with your project team.
options.rationale: The scope management plan describes how scope is managed, not what the product contains.

questions.explanation: A product breakdown structure is a hierarchical tree of a product's components and deliverables arranged in whole-part relationships. It shows the team exactly what must be delivered and how the parts relate.
questions.mindset: Show product structure with a product breakdown.

questions.stem: You are working on a project where you discover a certain negative risk with a potential impact of $2,000,000. You meet with your project stakeholders who determine that this is within their risk appetite, provided you meet a risk threshold of 10%. What will you do next?

options.text: Note the acceptable risk level as a threat of $200,000 (10%).
options.rationale: A 10% threshold is a variation around the objective, not a threat of $200,000.

options.text: Note the acceptable risk level as a threat of $1,800,000 to $2,200,000 (10% variance).
options.rationale: A 10% threshold around $2,000,000 gives an acceptable range of $1,800,000 to $2,200,000.

options.text: Note the impact as outside the acceptable risk level of $2,000,000.
options.rationale: The stakeholders have said the risk is within their appetite.

options.text: Note the impact as an opportunity of $200,000 (10%).
options.rationale: A negative risk is a threat, not an opportunity.

questions.explanation: Risk appetite is how much uncertainty stakeholders will accept; risk threshold measures the acceptable variation around an objective. A 10% threshold around $2,000,000 means an acceptable range from $1,800,000 to $2,200,000.
questions.mindset: Thresholds define acceptable variation.

questions.stem: You have planned and begun the current sprint, where the project team have committed to delivering and releasing a particular feature. You need to see how the team are tracking towards their sprint goal. What will you do next?

options.text: Review the team Kanban board.
options.rationale: A Kanban board shows work status but not progress against the sprint over time.

options.text: Review the team velocity chart.
options.rationale: A velocity chart shows completed work across sprints, not progress within this sprint.

options.text: Review the sprint burndown chart.
options.rationale: A sprint burndown chart compares remaining work with the ideal trend for the current sprint.

options.text: Perform a sprint review with the team.
options.rationale: A sprint review occurs at the end of the sprint, too late to track progress.

questions.explanation: A sprint burndown chart plots the work remaining in the sprint against an ideal trend line. It shows at a glance whether the team is on track to meet its sprint goal.
questions.mindset: Track sprint progress with a burndown.

questions.stem: You are a program manager on a large scale agile program, where each project team has its own scrum master. You need to know the rate at which work is flowing through each team, so you can see if there are any blockers or issues and whether they will remain on track. What will you do next?

options.text: Raise your query at scrum of scrums, so each team knows what they need to do.
options.rationale: Raising a query at the scrum of scrums does not give data on flow rates.

options.text: Attend the sprint review of each team at the end of the sprint.
options.rationale: Attending every sprint review is time-consuming and shows outcomes rather than rates.

options.text: Review the schedule management plan for managing the schedule.
options.rationale: The schedule management plan describes how scheduling works, not current throughput.

options.text: Review the team velocity charts, and what was committed versus completed.
options.rationale: Velocity charts show each team's rate of delivery and committed versus completed work.

questions.explanation: The velocity chart tracks the rate at which deliverables are produced, validated and accepted in each interval. Comparing committed and completed work across teams shows whether each is on track and where blockers may exist.
questions.mindset: Use velocity to see delivery rates.

questions.stem: Your project has been executing for the past five months, and due to an organisational change a new project sponsor has come on board. He asks where the project is up to and whether it is on track. You tell him, but he wants more information. What will you do next?

options.text: Show him the signed project charter, to ensure he honours the original project agreement.
options.rationale: The charter shows the original authorisation, not current progress.

options.text: Show him the project management plan, including the schedule management plan.
options.rationale: The management plans describe how the project is run, not where it stands.

options.text: Review the status report and previous status report with the sponsor.
options.rationale: The current and previous status reports show progress, trends and forecasts.

options.text: Invite him to the next sprint review so he can see the progress made.
options.rationale: Waiting for a sprint review delays the information, and this may not be an agile project.

questions.explanation: A status report describes the project's current status, including progress since the last report and cost and schedule forecasts. Reviewing the current and previous reports with the new sponsor shows where the project is and how it is trending.
questions.mindset: Use status reports to show progress and trend.

questions.stem: Your agile project needs a third party vendor to help complete the work. The product owner has multiple features on their product roadmap which may change over time, making the scope of your project uncertain. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask your product owner to fix the features and scope so the project is more certain.
options.rationale: Fixing scope in an agile project removes the flexibility it depends on.

options.text: Create a cost plus incentive fee contract with your procurement team.
options.rationale: A cost-plus-incentive-fee contract suits scope that is not well defined or likely to change.

options.text: Create a firm fixed price contract with your procurement team.
options.rationale: A firm fixed price contract suits well-defined scope, not an evolving roadmap.

options.text: Use the external vendor funding to create a project team in-house and complete the project.
options.rationale: Diverting vendor funding to an in-house team ignores the need for the vendor's help.

questions.explanation: Cost-reimbursable contracts pay the seller's actual costs plus a fee, making them suitable when scope is uncertain or likely to change. Variants include cost plus fixed fee, cost plus incentive fee and cost plus award fee.
questions.mindset: Uncertain scope suits cost-reimbursable contracts.

questions.stem: You have completed a make-or-buy analysis and you agree to hire a third-party vendor to complete part of your product. You create the statement of work and have a list of acceptable sellers that meet the source selection criteria. The work is not complex and they understand the scope. What will you do next?

options.text: Send a request for proposal to the sellers.
options.rationale: An RFP is for complex scope where sellers propose solutions.

options.text: Send a request for information to the sellers.
options.rationale: An RFI gathers market information, which is no longer needed.

options.text: Send a request for quotation to the sellers.
options.rationale: An RFQ suits clear, simple scope where price is the main factor.

options.text: Hold a bidders conference to ensure all sellers are on the same page.
options.rationale: A bidder conference is unnecessary when sellers already understand the scope.

questions.explanation: With a complete statement of work, qualified sellers and simple, well-understood scope, a request for quotation is appropriate. RFPs suit complex work where sellers propose solutions, and RFIs gather information before bidding.
questions.mindset: Simple, clear scope: request quotes.

questions.stem: Your project is new and the team have just come on board. There have been multiple disagreements and the work is slow as they try to understand where they fit in the project and the team. What will you do next?

options.text: Create a definition of ready and definition of done with your team.
options.rationale: Definitions of ready and done cover work quality, not team behaviour and roles.

options.text: Create a project charter with your team.
options.rationale: The project charter authorises the project; it does not set team agreements.

options.text: Create a project management plan with your team.
options.rationale: The management plan is broader and does not set out team values and ground rules.

options.text: Create a team charter with your team.
options.rationale: A team charter records values, agreements and operating guidelines, clarifying expectations.

questions.explanation: A team charter records the team's values, agreements and operating guidelines and sets clear expectations for behaviour. It helps a new team understand where each member fits and how to work together.
questions.mindset: Set team agreements early with a team charter.

questions.stem: You have created a high level view of the features your project will deliver, and prioritised them. The development team is ready to start work, but they don't know where to start as the information is too high level. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask the team to begin with the highest priority item first.
options.rationale: Starting on a high-level feature leaves the team without enough detail to work from.

options.text: Help the team break the features down into User Stories to place in a sprint.
options.rationale: Breaking features into user stories gives the team work items small and clear enough to start in a sprint.

options.text: Hold a retrospective with the team to understand what is blocking them.
options.rationale: A retrospective is for improving the process; the blocker here is simply the level of detail.

options.text: Reprioritise the features into an order that makes sense for the developers.
options.rationale: Reordering features does not add the detail the team needs.

questions.explanation: A user story is a brief description of an outcome for a specific user, detailed enough for team members to work on. Breaking prioritised features into stories turns a high-level view into sprint-ready work.
questions.mindset: Break features into stories the team can work on.

questions.stem: You are working on a project as an Agile Project Manager. The executive manager who will own the product you are delivering would like to focus primarily on set processes and tools to manage to project. What will you recommend to them instead?

options.text: To focus on the definition of success as defined by the project manager
options.rationale: Success is defined with stakeholders, not by the project manager alone, and this is not the manifesto's advice.

options.text: Focus primarily on the individuals and interactions involved
options.rationale: The Agile Manifesto values individuals and interactions over processes and tools.

options.text: Focus primarily on the scope of the project
options.rationale: Scope matters, but the manifesto's counterpoint to processes and tools is people.

options.text: Focus primarily on the schedule of the project
options.rationale: Schedule matters, but it is not the value the manifesto places above processes and tools.

questions.explanation: The Agile Manifesto values individuals and interactions over processes and tools. Projects are delivered by people for people, and the quality of their interactions largely determines whether a project succeeds.
questions.mindset: People and interactions over processes and tools.

questions.stem: You are a project manager working on an Agile project, and want your team to maximise the value they bring to the customer. What can you eliminate in order to maximize project value?

options.text: Daily stand-ups
options.rationale: Daily stand-ups support coordination and are not waste.

options.text: Unnecessary features
options.rationale: Unnecessary features consume effort without adding value, so eliminating them maximises value.

options.text: Sprint reviews
options.rationale: Sprint reviews gather the feedback needed to deliver value.

options.text: Testing
options.rationale: Removing testing would increase defects and rework.

questions.explanation: Maximising value means eliminating waste, including unnecessary features, partially done work, delays, extra processes, task switching, waiting, defects and handoffs. Features nobody needs are a major source of waste.
questions.mindset: Eliminate waste, starting with unneeded features.

questions.stem: You are working on a project and the team have recently moved to an Agile way of work. One of the team members is confused about Scrum and what typically happens after the sprint review. What will you tell them happens next?

options.text: Hold a sprint retrospective with the team
options.rationale: The sprint retrospective follows the sprint review and precedes the next sprint planning.

options.text: Perform product backlog refinement with the product owner
options.rationale: Backlog refinement is ongoing and is not the event that follows the review.

options.text: Perform story card elaboration with the three amigos (Business Development, Testing)
options.rationale: Story elaboration with the three amigos is a practice, not the next Scrum event.

options.text: Hold a Daily Scrum
options.rationale: The daily scrum takes place during the sprint, not after the review.

questions.explanation: In Scrum, the sprint review is followed by the sprint retrospective, where the whole team reflects on the sprint and agrees improvements before the next sprint planning meeting.
questions.mindset: Review, then retrospective, then planning.

questions.stem: You are managing a project as an Agile project manager and a business representative for the product you are delivering asks you how many defects were found in the latest round of testing. You don't know the answer. What should you do?

options.text: Guess the number then change the subject
options.rationale: Guessing and changing the subject is dishonest and damages trust.

options.text: Tell the business partner you will send an e-mail to him with the information
options.rationale: Emailing later is slower than showing the visible information already available.

options.text: Take him into the team area, where the "information radiator" with project information is displayed
options.rationale: Showing the information radiator gives the business representative current, transparent information.

options.text: Ask the business partner to call the Scrum Master to get a correct answer
options.rationale: Redirecting to the scrum master is unhelpful when the information is on display.

questions.explanation: Agile teams rely on visual management and transparency. Information radiators in the team area display velocity, the Kanban board, backlog, burndown, test results and issues, so anyone can see the latest information.
questions.mindset: Point stakeholders to visible information.

questions.stem: You are working on an Agile project and the project team have just finished an iteration. All tasks for the iteration have been completed, and you are ready to move to the next iteration, but are not sure what the team should work on. What will you do next?

options.text: Follow the project plan developed early in the project.
options.rationale: A plan made early in the project may no longer reflect current priorities.

options.text: Follow the PMO, who has already determined how the project should progress
options.rationale: The PMO does not decide the content of agile iterations.

options.text: Ask the product owner, who continuously prioritizes the backlog
options.rationale: The product owner continuously prioritises the backlog, which determines the next work.

options.text: Ask the project coach or team leader to determine the next iteration
options.rationale: The coach or team leader does not set product priorities.

questions.explanation: The product owner represents the customer and continuously prioritises the product backlog by value. The team takes its next work from the top of that backlog.
questions.mindset: The product owner's backlog sets what's next.

questions.stem: You are the project manager on an Agile project that is half way through. The project sponsor is starting to raise concerns that the project will not be completed in the allotted time. What will you do to gather the information necessary to answer the project sponsor?

options.text: Review the Kanban board and the current WIP
options.rationale: The Kanban board and WIP show current work, not whether the project will finish on time.

options.text: Check the product backlog for remaining features
options.rationale: The backlog shows remaining features but not the rate of progress.

options.text: Review the team velocity, product burndown chart and other key performance indicators
options.rationale: Velocity, the product burndown and other KPIs combine rate and remaining work to forecast completion.

options.text: Have a team meeting and log everyone's status
options.rationale: Logging everyone's status is slow and does not give a forecast.

questions.explanation: Forecasting agile completion needs both the rate of progress and the remaining work. Team velocity and the product burndown chart provide exactly this, giving the sponsor a reliable, evidence-based answer.
questions.mindset: Forecast from velocity and remaining work.

questions.stem: You are working with the team on the team charter and have outlined the project vision, mission, agreed meeting times and accepted team behaviour. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask the team to get to work straight away, because Agile teams move swiftly.
options.rationale: Starting without agreeing when work is complete leads to confusion and rework.

options.text: Send the Team Charter to the project sponsor for their sign off, so the project can begin.
options.rationale: A team charter is an agreement among the team and does not need sponsor sign-off.

options.text: Agree on and include the “definition of done" for team features and tasks.
options.rationale: Agreeing the definition of done makes clear when work is complete and what success looks like.

options.text: Set a meeting for two weeks time so you can continue to develop the charter iteratively.
options.rationale: Delaying the charter slows the team without adding value.

questions.explanation: The definition of done is an essential part of the team charter. It ensures everyone agrees when a task or feature is complete—defined, developed, tested, reviewed and released—and when to pull the next item.
questions.mindset: Agree the definition of done early.

questions.stem: You are working on an Agile project, gathering requirements from the business stakeholders with the Product Owner. During the discussion, different people seem to have different understandings of what the feature will look like. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask the stakeholders to elaborate their ideas better, and set another meeting in a week's time.
options.rationale: Waiting a week delays alignment and may not resolve differing interpretations.

options.text: Park that feature for now and begin work on a feature that is elaborated better.
options.rationale: Parking the feature avoids the problem rather than resolving it.

options.text: Draw a storyboard prototype of the requirement so all stakeholders can see it adjust it and agree.
options.rationale: A storyboard prototype lets stakeholders see, adjust and agree the feature together.

options.text: Give your understanding of the feature and ask the stakeholders to agree or disagree.
options.rationale: Imposing your own understanding may not reflect what stakeholders need.

questions.explanation: When stakeholders have different mental pictures of a feature, a visual model such as a storyboard or wireframe creates a shared understanding. Everyone can see the flow, suggest changes and reach consensus quickly.
questions.mindset: Visualise requirements to align understanding.

questions.stem: You are working as a project manager with an Agile project team. The project sponsor sits on another floor, and prefers to communicate by email only. What will you do next?

options.text: Ensure you communicate by email only with the project sponsor so they are comfortable.
options.rationale: Email-only communication loses the richness and immediacy agile teams rely on.

options.text: Stop communicating with the project sponsor until they at least come to a few project meetings.
options.rationale: Stopping communication with the sponsor is unacceptable.

options.text: Ask the project sponsor to co-locate with the Agile team for a few days a week, to ensure face to face communication and access to the visual project information.
options.rationale: Inviting the sponsor to spend time with the team gives face-to-face communication and access to visual information.

options.text: Set meetings with the project sponsor so you can update them personally.
options.rationale: Personal update meetings help, but they do not give the sponsor access to the team's visual information.

questions.explanation: Agile teams value face-to-face communication, which allows questions, immediate feedback and reading body language. Encouraging the sponsor to co-locate with the team for part of the week also gives them direct access to boards and charts.
questions.mindset: Bring stakeholders close to the team.

questions.stem: You are working as an Agile project manager in a new project team. Many project team members are despondent, and do not show up for the meetings and ceremonies you have set. What will you do next?

options.text: Raise a risk in the risk register around project goals, and ask the project sponsor to mitigate the risk.
options.rationale: Treating disengagement as a risk for the sponsor to handle abdicates leadership.

options.text: Have a coaching session with the team teaching the "what” and “why” behind Agile ceremonies, and ensure each meeting has a clear outcome, time and agenda.
options.rationale: Coaching the team on the purpose of the ceremonies and running focused meetings rebuilds engagement.

options.text: Cancel all meetings for now, and write some documentation for the team what you'd like them to do.
options.rationale: Replacing meetings with documentation removes interaction.

options.text: Make the decisions yourself and dictate the outcomes to the team.
options.rationale: Dictating decisions contradicts agile leadership and self-organisation.

questions.explanation: Agile leaders coach teams, remove blockers and encourage interaction. Explaining what each ceremony is for and why it matters, and making every meeting purposeful with a clear agenda and outcome, helps disengaged team members see the value in taking part.
questions.mindset: Coach the why behind agile practices.

questions.stem: You are planning the next iteration in your Agile team, as the Agile lead. The team is going to select user stories from the prioritized release backlog, elaborate the user stories, and estimate the work needed for each user story. The number of stories selected is based on:

options.text: What the scrum master says, as he or she knows best.
options.rationale: The scrum master does not decide how much the team commits to.

options.text: The team's "Velocity", which is the rate at which a team can complete work.
options.rationale: The team's velocity—its average rate of completing work—guides how many stories to select.

options.text: What the team wants to work on, to ensure individuals work within their strengths.
options.rationale: Selecting by individual preference ignores the team's capacity.

options.text: The Feature Driven Development model to be completed.
options.rationale: Feature driven development is a different method, not a basis for sprint sizing.

questions.explanation: Velocity is the average amount of work a team completes in an iteration, measured in points, stories or another unit. The team uses its velocity from previous iterations to decide how much to take into the next.
questions.mindset: Plan sprints from average velocity.

questions.stem: Your Agile team leader works through servant leadership to the team, and has built a safe environment for disagreement. How has this empowered the team to move forward without obstacles?

options.text: The team is able to create a list of reasons why tasks cannot be completed.
options.rationale: A list of excuses is not the product of a safe environment for disagreement.

options.text: The team has no conflict as they get along so well.
options.rationale: Getting along well is not the same as having no conflict; healthy teams disagree.

options.text: The team leader takes responsibility for all decisions made in the project.
options.rationale: Servant leaders empower the team to decide rather than taking every decision themselves.

options.text: The team is encouraged to participate in discussion and disagreement in order to make better decisions.
options.rationale: Encouraging open discussion and disagreement leads to better decisions and surfaces risks and alternatives.

questions.explanation: Psychological safety allows team members to disagree constructively. Open discussion surfaces risks and alternative ideas and leads to better decisions, which is how servant leadership removes obstacles to progress.
questions.mindset: Safe disagreement leads to better decisions.

questions.stem: New projects go through the Tuckman Model of forming, storming, norming, and performing. You have just taken the lead of a new project with a newly formed team, but are surprised to find little conflict and that the forming stage has gone so quickly. Which of the following might be the reason?

options.text: The team members have worked together on previous projects and are following the same Agile ceremonies and methods.
options.rationale: Members who have worked together before and share practices move through forming and storming quickly.

options.text: You have made all the project decisions so they don't have to worry.
options.rationale: Making all decisions yourself undermines team development.

options.text: The team is in line for a promotion, so they want to get along.
options.rationale: Promotion prospects are not a reliable explanation for smooth team formation.

options.text: The team members really care about the product being delivered.
options.rationale: Caring about the product helps, but it does not explain a rapid forming stage.

questions.explanation: Teams normally pass through forming, storming, norming and performing. Members who have worked together before and share the same agile practices already know each other and how to work together, so they progress quickly.
questions.mindset: Shared history speeds team formation.

questions.stem: You are an Agile project manager leading a new software project. During the last retrospective there was very little engagement and feedback, and the team seem to be losing interest in the work. What will you do to improve the situation?

options.text: Hold another retrospective to try and extract more information.
options.rationale: Repeating a retrospective that yielded little is doing the same thing and expecting a different result.

options.text: Align the project goals to each team members' personal goals.
options.rationale: Aligning project goals with each member's personal goals and strengths rebuilds interest and commitment.

options.text: Hold a vote on whether to continue the project or not.
options.rationale: Voting on whether to continue the project is not the team's decision and does not address engagement.

options.text: Get executive management involved so team members raise their engagement.
options.rationale: Pressure from executives is unlikely to create genuine engagement.

questions.explanation: When team members lose interest, the project manager looks for what motivates each person. Understanding their strengths and aligning their personal goals with the project's goals makes people care more and work harder naturally.
questions.mindset: Connect personal goals to project goals.

questions.stem: You are working as a project manager in a team that is moving to an Agile way of work. You have previously engaged the team in a single weekly meeting, with email as the primary communication. What changes will you make in the new Agile team?

options.text: Ensure reports are created weekly for executive management.
options.rationale: Weekly executive reports do not change how the team communicates.

options.text: Set up a teleconference with different parts of your project team.
options.rationale: Teleconferences are less rich than face-to-face communication.

options.text: Co-locate the team where possible and focus on frequent face-to-face communication.
options.rationale: Co-location and frequent face-to-face communication are the agile norm, allowing information to flow by osmosis.

options.text: Have frequent one-on-ones with your project team to get their point of view in private.
options.rationale: Private one-to-ones do not replace frequent team interaction.

questions.explanation: Agile values individuals and interactions. Co-locating the team lets information flow by osmosis, and frequent face-to-face conversation is the recommended way to communicate, replacing weekly meetings and email.
questions.mindset: Agile teams talk face to face, often.

questions.stem: While on an Agile project team, you prioritise the backlog of features with the product owner, and agree what you will work on first. Your project sponsor wants to know how long it will take to deliver some value. How will you estimate how long each of these features will take to complete?

options.text: Break down the feature into tasks or user stories, then estimate how long those tasks will take to complete with the dev team.
options.rationale: Breaking features into stories and having the development team estimate them gives a bottom-up estimate.

options.text: Take the total number of people in the team, multiplied by the hours worked, divided by the number of features in the backlog.
options.rationale: Dividing total hours by the number of features ignores the size of each feature.

options.text: Ask the sponsor how many iterations the project is funded for, then plan to complete the features by the end of that time.
options.rationale: Fitting features to funded iterations is planning to a constraint, not estimating.

options.text: Find a similar feature delivered by another part of the organisation, and use your estimate.
options.rationale: Another area's estimate may not reflect this team's capability or context.

questions.explanation: Agile favours bottom-up estimating by the people who will do the work. Breaking a feature into stories or tasks and having the development team estimate them gives a realistic view of the effort and time needed to deliver value.
questions.mindset: Let the team estimate small pieces.

questions.stem: The product owner has worked with the development team to list all work to be done, write up user stories for each feature and place them in the product backlog. What will you do next?

options.text: Groom the backlog to ensure only important items are being worked on.
options.rationale: Grooming is part of the answer but does not describe taking work through iterations.

options.text: Create the schedule management plan to ensure you know when each item can be delivered.
options.rationale: A schedule management plan is a predictive artefact, not the next agile step.

options.text: Sort the items by business priority, place them in an iteration, complete the items then remove them from the backlog.
options.rationale: Sorting by business priority, pulling items into iterations and removing them when complete is how the backlog drives delivery.

options.text: Move the items into the requirements traceability matrix so you can report on their progress.
options.rationale: A traceability matrix is not used to manage agile work in progress.

questions.explanation: The product backlog is the source of truth for agile requirements. Items are ordered by business priority, pulled into iterations, completed and removed, and the backlog is continually reprioritised so the most valuable work comes first.
questions.mindset: The backlog drives what gets built next.

questions.stem: You are working with your Agile project team to estimate each task and how long they might take. The team is finding it difficult to give an exact figure, and worries that it might impact project delivery. What can you show them, to estimate more accurately?

options.text: Ask them to estimate by whole iteration to give a little room for variation.
options.rationale: Estimating per iteration is too coarse and still asks for exact figures.

options.text: Estimate the cards in full days instead of effort per card.
options.rationale: Full-day estimates still demand precision the team finds difficult.

options.text: Use comparative estimates or relative sizing such as T-shirt sizing or story points.
options.rationale: Relative sizing with T-shirt sizes or story points avoids exact time predictions and is easier to do well.

options.text: Prioritise the backlog based on customer value.
options.rationale: Prioritising by value is important but is not an estimation technique.

questions.explanation: Agile teams commonly use relative sizing, such as story points or T-shirt sizes, rather than exact durations. Velocity is then measured in the same units, which makes forecasting easier and more reliable than predicting exact times.
questions.mindset: Size relatively when exact times are hard.

questions.stem: You are an Agile project manager and talking through the iteration with the product owner. They have created the list of items in the product backlog, but there is confusion in the team about who should perform the process of story card sizing. What will you tell them?

options.text: The Product Owner works through the backlog to size the story cards.
options.rationale: The product owner prioritises the backlog but does not size the work.

options.text: The Agile team work together to size the story cards, relying mostly on information from the developers and testers.
options.rationale: The team sizes stories together, relying mainly on the developers and testers who will do the work.

options.text: The Agile team leader or scrum master works to size the story cards for the team.
options.rationale: The scrum master facilitates estimation but does not size stories for the team.

options.text: The customer sizes the story cards to ensure maximum value.
options.rationale: The customer defines value, not the effort needed to deliver each story.

questions.explanation: Story sizing is done by the agile team, drawing mainly on the developers and testers who will do the work. The product owner clarifies the stories, and the scrum master facilitates.
questions.mindset: Those who do the work size the work.

questions.stem: You are an Agile team leader and talking through the process for your first retrospective. The team is curious as to what they should do. What is the way a team retrospective would normally work?

options.text: Discuss what was successful, what could be improved, and incorporate those into future iterations.
options.rationale: Discussing what went well, what could be improved and acting on it is the core of a retrospective.

options.text: Discuss what the team liked about working with each other.
options.rationale: Discussing what people like about each other misses improvement of the process.

options.text: Discuss what went wrong, and make sure the team knows who is to blame
options.rationale: Assigning blame destroys the safety a retrospective depends on.

options.text: Discuss the validity of the features being developed.
options.rationale: Validating features belongs in the sprint review with stakeholders.

questions.explanation: A retrospective helps the team improve its process by asking what went well, what could be improved and what still puzzles people, then building agreed improvements into future iterations.
questions.mindset: Retrospectives improve the process, without blame.

questions.stem: You are the Agile project manager analysing the risk for each feature in your backlog by assigning a probability and an impact score to each risk, then multiplying them to calculate risk severity. How will the Agile team handle items with the highest risk?

options.text: Change the requirements to remove the risk.
options.rationale: Changing requirements to remove risk may remove value the customer needs.

options.text: Schedule them later in the project so you can deliver maximum value first.
options.rationale: Leaving high-risk items to the end keeps uncertainty high throughout the project.

options.text: Schedule them earlier in the project to reduce the risk impact over time.
options.rationale: Scheduling high-risk items early reduces uncertainty and exposure as the project progresses.

options.text: Place all the high-risk items in a "risk iteration" where the focus is on reducing risk.
options.rationale: A dedicated risk iteration delays value and isolates risk work unnecessarily.

questions.explanation: Risk is highest early in a project. Tackling the highest-risk items first reduces uncertainty and exposure to late surprises, so overall project risk falls steadily as work is completed.
questions.mindset: Burn down risk by doing risky work early.

questions.stem: You are working through the iteration with your Agile team, and are having trouble completing one of the story cards in the sprint. It is dependent on something else being done and the contact is away. What will you do next?

options.text: Raise a blocker at the next daily stand-up (or before) so the team can swarm around the problem and solve it quickly.
options.rationale: Raising the blocker promptly lets the team swarm on it and find help quickly.

options.text: Bring the piece of work in-house so you don't have to worry anymore.
options.rationale: Bringing work in-house may not be possible and bypasses the team.

options.text: Ask the product owner to remove that feature for now, you can revisit it later.
options.rationale: Dropping the feature is premature when the blocker might be solved quickly.

options.text: Add cost to the budget and find a third party to complete the work.
options.rationale: Adding cost for a third party is disproportionate to a temporary dependency.

questions.explanation: Agile teams solve problems together. Blockers are raised as soon as possible, at the latest at the daily stand-up, so the team can swarm on them, bring in any help needed and keep work moving.
questions.mindset: Raise blockers early and swarm.

questions.stem: Feedback in many different forms is one of the most important parts of a successful Agile product delivery. Which of the below is an Agile method for gathering and using feedback to improve?

options.text: Having a once-weekly working group meting with project stakeholders
options.rationale: A weekly working group is not an agile feedback mechanism based on the product.

options.text: Conducting sprint reviews or demonstrations that include all stakeholders
options.rationale: Sprint reviews and demonstrations gather stakeholder feedback on working increments regularly.

options.text: Sending out project reports to project stakeholders to view.
options.rationale: Sending reports is one-way and gathers little feedback.

options.text: Asking stakeholders for feedback only development is blocked.
options.rationale: Asking for feedback only when blocked is far too infrequent.

questions.explanation: Demonstrating the usable increment at each sprint review gathers stakeholder feedback quickly and often, rather than only at the end. Retrospectives provide a complementary feedback loop on the team's process.
questions.mindset: Demonstrate increments to gather feedback.

questions.stem: You are working on an Agile project where the product business representative is pushing for more and more features to be delivered in each iteration. You know what they are asking is not possible, based on your team's current velocity. What will you do next?

options.text: Show them the team velocity chart and the points allotted to cards in the backlog, and ask them to prioritise the features at the next sprint planning.
options.rationale: Showing velocity against backlog points lets the business representative prioritise within real capacity.

options.text: Add more members to the team so you can get the work they want done.
options.rationale: Adding people is costly and may slow the team in the short term.

options.text: Ask for another business representative who understands technology better.
options.rationale: Asking for a different representative dismisses a legitimate customer.

options.text: Remove some of the features yourself and see if anyone notices.
options.rationale: Secretly dropping features is dishonest and damages trust.

questions.explanation: When a customer asks for more than the team can deliver, the project manager shows them the evidence: the team's velocity against the points allocated in the backlog. Inviting them to prioritise gives them control over value without overburdening the team.
questions.mindset: Align expectations with capacity data.

questions.stem: You are working on a traditional waterfall project and the organisation wants to move to an Agile way of work. The functional manager wants to get the benefit of certain Agile tools they have heard about that are used to uncover potential problems before they occur. What will you do next?

options.text: Write the change into your project management plan and circulate it with project stakeholders.
options.rationale: Updating the plan document does not give visibility of emerging problems.

options.text: Set a weekly working group meeting with your project stakeholders to discuss the project.
options.rationale: A weekly meeting is too infrequent to detect problems early.

options.text: Iteration planning
options.rationale: Iteration planning is a single event rather than a way of detecting problems continuously.

options.text: Make the product backlog, iteration Kanban board, and velocity chart all visible in a co-located team area.
options.rationale: Visible backlogs, Kanban boards and velocity charts expose problems and blockers as they arise.

questions.explanation: Visual management is a key agile way to detect problems early. Displaying the backlog, the iteration Kanban board and velocity chart in the team area lets everyone see progress, blockers and signs that work is going off course.
questions.mindset: Make work visible to spot problems early.

questions.stem: You are new to your Agile project, and the team are working through the forming stages. How do you help the team improve as the project progresses?

options.text: Ensure the team holds a project post-mortem and captures the lessons learned at the end of the project.
options.rationale: A post-mortem at the end is too late for the team to benefit on this project.

options.text: Hold a retrospective with the whole team at the end of each iteration and build those lessons learned into each new iteration.
options.rationale: Retrospectives at the end of each iteration let the team apply lessons immediately.

options.text: Ask the product owner to show the team where they can improve to deliver the features they want.
options.rationale: The product owner focuses on the product, not the team's process improvement.

options.text: Rotate tasks and roles amongst the team during each new iteration.
options.rationale: Rotating roles every iteration can disrupt a forming team.

questions.explanation: Agile teams hold a retrospective at the end of each iteration to ask what went well, what did not, what they learned and what still puzzles them. Improvements are then built into the next iteration, so the team improves quickly throughout.
questions.mindset: Improve every iteration, not just at the end.

questions.stem: You are the Agile project manager working through the product requirements for the product owner and executive project sponsor. The project sponsor raises concerns that the development team do not fully understand the requirements. What will you do next?

options.text: Show them the project management plan, which will have the scope statement listed in the scope baseline.
options.rationale: The scope statement is predictive and does not demonstrate the team's understanding.

options.text: Ask the team to create a high-level prototype of the requirements, then discuss and review with all stakeholders.
options.rationale: A prototype reviewed with all stakeholders exposes misunderstandings and builds consensus quickly.

options.text: Show them the project schedule, outlining each feature and their delivery date
options.rationale: A schedule shows dates, not whether requirements are understood.

options.text: Hold a retrospective with the team to gather feedback and improve.
options.rationale: A retrospective looks at the team's process, not requirements understanding.

questions.explanation: Agile teams use quick visual mock-ups or prototypes, such as storyboards, wireframes or models, to check their understanding of requirements. Reviewing a prototype with the sponsor and stakeholders reveals gaps and builds consensus.
questions.mindset: Prototype to confirm understanding.

questions.stem: When working in an Agile team it is common to use prototypes, demonstrations and reviews, wireframes and storyboards to elicit feedback from the customer or product owner. What is the benefit of using these tools?

options.text: So the development team don't have to create the real thing.
options.rationale: Prototypes support understanding; they do not replace building the real product.

options.text: So the team can get together and have another meeting.
options.rationale: The purpose is feedback and agreement, not an extra meeting.

options.text: It allows users to create new forms that will be required for the new system.
options.rationale: Prototypes are not a way for users to design new forms for the system.

options.text: It allows the product owner to discuss and agree on requirements with their stakeholders.
options.rationale: Visual models let the product owner discuss and agree requirements with stakeholders before development.

questions.explanation: Prototypes, demonstrations, wireframes and storyboards give stakeholders something concrete to react to. The feedback helps the product owner and stakeholders agree requirements and features before money is spent on full development.
questions.mindset: Use visual models to agree requirements early.

questions.stem: You are finishing up the first iteration on your Agile project and have set a retrospective meeting for the whole team. One member of the team asks why we have this meeting and if they really need to go. What will you tell them?

options.text: It helps the team prioritise product features for the next iteration.
options.rationale: Prioritising features is the product owner's job, supported by backlog refinement and planning.

options.text: It allows the team to blame others when things go wrong.
options.rationale: Retrospectives are explicitly blame-free; blaming others destroys the trust they rely on.

options.text: It's an opportunity for the whole team to look at their way of work and improve.
options.rationale: The retrospective lets the whole team examine its way of working and agree improvements.

options.text: It showcases a part of the product so everyone can see what was delivered.
options.rationale: Showcasing the product is the purpose of the sprint review.

questions.explanation: The retrospective is held at the end of each sprint for the whole team to reflect on how they work: what went well, what did not and what still puzzles them. Agreed actions are built into future iterations.
questions.mindset: Everyone attends retrospectives to improve how the team works.

questions.stem: You have been working on an Agile project for some time and have been blocked by the need for expertise in another team. You need to overcome organisational silos. What will you do?

options.text: Work with the various managers of team members you need and have them dedicate the necessary individuals to the cross-functional team.
options.rationale: Working with managers to dedicate the needed people to the cross-functional team removes the silo blocker.

options.text: Raise a change request for review by the project Change Control Board as the work will be delayed.
options.rationale: A change request does not resolve the missing expertise.

options.text: Raise an issue in the issue log for review and management by the project team
options.rationale: Logging an issue records the blocker but does not bring in the needed skills.

options.text: Work with the risk team to raise a project risk, assign it to an owner and create controls for those risks.
options.rationale: Treating a current blocker as a risk misclassifies it and does not solve it.

questions.explanation: The whole-team approach brings all the skills a project needs into one cross-functional team. Working with the relevant managers to dedicate people with the missing expertise removes dependence on other silos.
questions.mindset: Bring needed skills into the team.

questions.stem: A significant change has been made to the project scope after finding a serious system flaw. This scope change will impact the scope, cost and schedule of the project. You analyse the impacts to each, raise an issue in the issue log and are about to raise a change request. What will you do next?

options.text: Review the configuration management plan for the baselined project items.
options.rationale: The configuration management plan covers baselined items but not the approval process.

options.text: Add the detail as a project delivery risk in your project risk register.
options.rationale: The change is already known; recording it as a risk misclassifies it.

options.text: Update the change log and implement the changes required.
options.rationale: Implementing changes before approval bypasses change control.

options.text: Check the Change Management plan for the Change Control Board members and process.
options.rationale: The change management plan defines the CCB members and the process the request must follow.

questions.explanation: Perform Integrated Change Control uses a change control board to review, approve, defer or reject changes. The change management plan documents the process and roles, so the project manager checks it before submitting the change request.
questions.mindset: Follow the change management plan to reach the CCB.

questions.stem: Five major defects have been found during quality testing, resulting in the scope changing significantly and affecting your schedule and budget. You have analysed the impacts and raised change requests for each. The Change Control Board has approved two changes, rejected two changes and deferred one. What will you do next?

options.text: Record the outcomes in the change log and communicate the deferred and rejected changes to the change requestor.
options.rationale: Recording the outcomes in the change log and informing requestors of deferred and rejected changes closes the loop.

options.text: Review and re-prioritise the project scope to fit must-have items into delivery.
