options.rationale: Reprioritising scope is premature and ignores the CCB's decisions.

options.text: Raise a risk in the risk register for threats to the benefit of your project.
options.rationale: A benefits risk may exist, but the immediate step is to record and communicate decisions.

options.text: Raise a claim on the affected changes to give them a better chance of approval.
options.rationale: Raising a claim to push rejected changes undermines governance.

questions.explanation: All change request outcomes are recorded in the change log. Approved changes are implemented, and deferred or rejected changes are communicated to the person or group who requested them.
questions.mindset: Record and communicate every change decision.

questions.stem: You are working through the scope of a newly kicked-off project, and the senior user is unsure on how the requirements and scope come together to create a deliverable that will work for him and the functional manager. Your program manager suggests you use "decomposition" in this circumstance. What will you do next?

options.text: Estimate activity resources for who is required to deliver the item.
options.rationale: Estimating resources comes after the work has been decomposed.

options.text: Define the project scope for the functional manager.
options.rationale: Defining scope for the functional manager does not show how it breaks into deliverables.

options.text: Create a WBS and Define Activities in your schedule.
options.rationale: Decomposition is used to create the WBS and define activities, showing how scope becomes deliverables and work.

options.text: Create the Project Charter and Project Management Plan for a clear view of the project.
options.rationale: The charter and plan are higher-level documents, not decomposition.

questions.explanation: Decomposition means breaking work into smaller, more manageable parts. It is a technique of both Create WBS and Define Activities, and shows the senior user how requirements and scope build up into deliverables.
questions.mindset: Decompose scope into WBS and activities.

questions.stem: You have been assigned to take over a project in your organisation that has gone off track, with scope creep causing the schedule and cost to increase. You can't quite understand the current cadence and way of working within the team, so you decide to find out their development approach, including any modifications. What will you do next?

options.text: Review the Project Charter, as this was the original agreed document.
options.rationale: The charter authorises the project but does not describe the development approach.

options.text: Review the schedule management plan, as this will have team cadence schedules.
options.rationale: The schedule management plan covers scheduling, not the overall development approach.

options.text: Review the Project Management Plan, as this will house the cadence approach.
options.rationale: The project management plan documents the development approach and any modifications.

options.text: Review the Stakeholder Register, for stakeholder cadence needs.
options.rationale: The stakeholder register records stakeholders, not the team's way of working.

questions.explanation: The development approach—predictive, iterative, agile or hybrid—and any modifications to it are documented in the project management plan. Reviewing it shows the new project manager how the team is meant to work.
questions.mindset: The development approach lives in the project management plan.

questions.stem: You are working on a complex engineering project, where a significant amount of risk has been found with your team and the customer. The functional manager approaches to ask if she can work with your team to plan any risk responses. You agree to help her update the Risk Register, with:

options.text: Risk triggers, agreed response strategies, and residual risks after mitigation
options.rationale: Plan Risk Responses adds triggers, agreed strategies and residual risks to the register.

options.text: Risk contingency reserves, quantitative analysis and financial impact responses.
options.rationale: Quantitative analysis and reserves are other processes and outputs.

options.text: The list of risks, their probability and impact, and their overall risk rating.
options.rationale: Probability, impact and ratings come from risk analysis, which is already done.

options.text: Risk owners, risk assumptions, and risk mitigations.
options.rationale: Owners and mitigations are part of it, but assumptions are not the main update from response planning.

questions.explanation: Plan Risk Responses updates the risk register with agreed response strategies, triggers and warning signs, and residual risks expected to remain. This is the process the functional manager is joining.
questions.mindset: Response planning adds triggers, strategies and residual risks.

questions.stem: You are the project manager on a high profile software project that involves automation technology not used before in your company. Because of this, your team have no resources to complete that part of the project. The steering committee approves outsourcing this work to a suitable vendor. What will you do next?

options.text: Perform a make-or-buy analysis to ensure a correct decision.
options.rationale: The make-or-buy decision has already been made and approved.

options.text: Approach your procurement department for suitable contracts to proceed with, such as Cost plus Incentive Fee.
options.rationale: The contract type is part of planning, but the SOW and selection criteria are the core outputs needed now.

options.text: Create the procurement statement of work and source selection criteria.
options.rationale: Creating the procurement SOW and source selection criteria are key outputs of Plan Procurement Management.

options.text: Review current agreements and change requests impacting third-party work.
options.rationale: No vendor agreements exist yet to review, because procurement has not begun.

questions.explanation: Once outsourcing is approved, Plan Procurement Management produces the procurement statement of work, source selection criteria, bid documents and procurement strategy. These define what is being bought and how sellers will be chosen.
questions.mindset: Define the SOW and selection criteria before going to market.

questions.stem: You are a project manager working in the initial phases of a project, and trying to put together a document for your stakeholders to have your project approved. You remember the Five Cs of communication from your studies, and decide to use them here. What will you do next?

options.text: Connect each part of the communication.
options.rationale: 'Connect each part' is not one of the Five Cs.

options.text: Create a bond between the message sender and receiver.
options.rationale: Creating a bond is not one of the Five Cs of written communication.

options.text: Ensure clear purpose and expression directed to the needs of the reader.
options.rationale: Clear purpose and expression directed to the reader's needs is one of the Five Cs.

options.text: Care about the subject and the person.
options.rationale: Caring about the subject is not one of the Five Cs.

questions.explanation: The Five Cs of written communication are correct grammar and spelling, concise expression, clear purpose and expression directed to the reader's needs, coherent logical flow of ideas and controlling the flow of words and ideas.
questions.mindset: Write for the reader: the Five Cs.

questions.stem: You have been working with the stakeholders on your project for some time, and the communication has been getting more and more tense with each interaction. You perform a stakeholder engagement assessment and discover the majority of your stakeholders are either resistant or neutral. What will you NOT do next?

options.text: Ensure you are listening actively with each interaction, speaking less and listening more.
options.rationale: Active listening supports effective communication and should be done.

options.text: Increase your awareness of cultural and personal differences.
options.rationale: Awareness of cultural and personal differences supports communication and should be done.

options.text: Identify, set and managing stakeholder expectations.
options.rationale: Identifying, setting and managing expectations supports communication and should be done.

options.text: Escalate the stakeholder issue to their functional manager to bring them back in line.
options.rationale: Escalating to bring stakeholders 'into line' is coercive and will increase resistance.

questions.explanation: Effective communication is supported by active listening, awareness of cultural and personal differences, managing expectations and developing skills such as negotiation and conflict resolution. Escalation to force compliance is not among them.
questions.mindset: Listen and understand; don't force compliance.

questions.stem: You have been working on a large database transfer project, when the manager for data in your organisation identifies the aging systems as a threat to your project. You review this with your project team and decide to perform qualitative risk analysis on the threat. What will you do next?

options.text: Review the quality of the data that led to the risk identification.
options.rationale: Data quality assessment is part of it, but the core step is assessing probability and impact.

options.text: Assign a probability of occurrence and an impact if it does occur.
options.rationale: Qualitative analysis assesses probability and impact to prioritise risks.

options.text: Perform analysis on a range of outcomes to see the possible financial impact.
options.rationale: Analysing a range of financial outcomes is quantitative analysis.

options.text: Add a risk trigger, mitigation and owner to the threat.
options.rationale: Triggers, mitigations and owners come from response planning.

questions.explanation: Perform Qualitative Risk Analysis prioritises individual risks by assessing their probability of occurrence and impact, along with other characteristics. This determines which risks need further analysis or action.
questions.mindset: Qualitative analysis: probability and impact.

questions.stem: You are managing a project that has formed organically around an important process improvement. You have been given limited resources and a very small budget form the project sponsor. You are planning Risk Management with your team, but you do not have the resources to complete all the necessary risk tasks. Which step will you remove in such a project?

options.text: Perform Qualitative Risk Analysis.
options.rationale: Qualitative analysis is essential for prioritising risks on any project.

options.text: Perform Quantitative Risk Analysis.
options.rationale: Quantitative analysis is costly and mainly suited to large, complex or strategic projects.

options.text: Identify Risks.
options.rationale: Risks must always be identified, however small or constrained the project.

options.text: Plan Risk Management.
options.rationale: Planning risk management sets the approach, however lightweight.

questions.explanation: Quantitative risk analysis requires extra time, data and cost. It is most appropriate for large, complex or strategically important projects, so a small project with limited resources can omit it.
questions.mindset: Tailor risk processes; quantitative analysis is optional.

questions.stem: You are the project manager on a waterfall project, and you have planned the requirements, scope and schedule with your team. You now need to create the cost estimates for your project. What will you NOT include as part of your cost estimates?

options.text: Contingency amounts to account for identified risks.
options.rationale: Contingency for identified risks can be part of cost estimates.

options.text: The known cost of project changes and managing project change.
options.rationale: The cost of project changes is not known in advance and is not a component of cost estimates.

options.text: Indirect costs at the activity level, if they are included in the project estimate.
options.rationale: Indirect costs can be included at activity level if part of the project estimate.

options.text: A management reserve for unforeseen scope changes.
options.rationale: The source treats management reserve for unforeseen scope as part of the estimates.

questions.explanation: Cost estimates may include contingency for identified risks and indirect costs where they are included in the project estimate. The cost of future changes is not known at estimation time, so it is not part of the estimates.
questions.mindset: Estimate known work and risk allowances, not unknown changes.

questions.stem: You have just taken over as project manager on a difficult waterfall project. Multiple project stakeholders have approached you and asked to make changes to different parts of the scope, cost and the delivery (schedule) of the project. You are trying to figure out which items need change approval, and which can just be done. What will you do next?

options.text: Review the Change Management Plan for the change approval process.
options.rationale: The change management plan describes the change process but not which items are baselined.

options.text: Refer the Scope Management Plan for scope items that need approval.
options.rationale: The scope management plan covers scope only, not cost and schedule items.

options.text: Review the Configuration Management Plan for baselined items.
options.rationale: The configuration management plan identifies which items are baselined and therefore need change approval.

options.text: Examine Requirement Traceability Matrix for the requirement requestor.
options.rationale: The traceability matrix links requirements to deliverables, not to change approval.

questions.explanation: The change management plan explains how changes are processed, but the configuration management plan identifies which project items are under configuration control and baselined. Those items must go through change control; others can simply be updated.
questions.mindset: Baselined items need change approval.

questions.stem: You are new to a project and are approached by the functional manager. No one has been able to tell them exactly what the project is about, and what they need to be aware of, including high level scope, schedule, risks, and who approved it in the first place. What will you do next?

options.text: Check the project activity list and schedule.
options.rationale: The activity list and schedule give detail but not the purpose, risks or approver.

options.text: Hold a sprint review to see what the team have developed so far.
options.rationale: A sprint review shows increments, not the project's authorisation and high-level scope.

options.text: Review the project charter and identify the stakeholder impacted by the change.
options.rationale: The charter summarises purpose, high-level scope, milestones, risks, stakeholders and the approver.

options.text: Visit the project management office (PMO) to gather organizational process assets.
options.rationale: Organisational process assets are general, not specific to this project.

questions.explanation: The project charter contains the high-level information needed to get up to speed: purpose, high-level requirements and deliverables, summary milestones, key risks, stakeholders and who authorised the project.
questions.mindset: The charter is the project's summary and authority.

questions.stem: The project manager on your project recently left, and you agreed to see the project through as it is nearly complete. The deliverables have been accepted, and you just need to communicate the release to any and all affected stakeholders in the way they agreed. What will you do next?

options.text: Review the Communication Management Plan for how communication is managed.
options.rationale: The communications management plan describes how information is distributed to stakeholders as agreed.

options.text: Review the Stakeholder Engagement Plan for how stakeholders prefer to be engaged.
options.rationale: The engagement plan focuses on engagement strategies rather than communication mechanics.

options.text: Review the Stakeholder Register for the people you need to communicate to.
options.rationale: The register identifies stakeholders but not how they agreed to be communicated with.

options.text: Review the Resource Management Plan for the resources affected by your project.
options.rationale: The resource management plan concerns team and physical resources.

questions.explanation: The communications management plan describes how project communications are planned, structured, implemented and monitored, including stakeholders' communication requirements, the information to be shared and the methods agreed.
questions.mindset: Communicate as the communications plan specifies.

questions.stem: You have been working on a project in your organisation for some time. In the latest working group meeting, the project sponsor adds a new executive member to the group. As soon as they arrive, they raise a new scope item that was not in the original plan. What will you do next?

options.text: Raise a change request to change the scope baseline.
options.rationale: A change request comes after analysing the new scope item's impact.

options.text: Update the stakeholder register with the new stakeholder details.
options.rationale: Recording the new executive in the stakeholder register is the immediate next step.

options.text: Raise an issue for the scope change in the issue log.
options.rationale: A new scope request is a potential change, not a current problem for the issue log.

options.text: Update the change log with the initial details of the scope change.
options.rationale: The change log is updated once a change request has been raised.

questions.explanation: A new executive has joined the project, so the first step is to add them to the stakeholder register with their role, requirements, influence and classification. Their scope request then goes through impact analysis and change control.
questions.mindset: Register new stakeholders before acting on their requests.

questions.stem: Your project team have been complaining about poor stakeholder engagement in a certain part of the organisation for some time. It is now impacting the project schedule and you may need to use your contingency reserve to crash the schedule and bring it back on track. What will you do next?

options.text: Review the cost management plan and access the appropriate contingency reserve.
options.rationale: Using contingency before understanding the cause may waste reserves on a symptom.

options.text: Perform root cause analysis on the problem with your team.
options.rationale: Root cause analysis with the team identifies why engagement is poor so it can be fixed.

options.text: Raise the engagement as a risk and escalate it immediately to the functional manager.
options.rationale: Escalating without analysis skips assessment of the problem.

options.text: Change the way of working to agile to increase stakeholder engagement.
options.rationale: Changing to agile will not immediately fix poor engagement.

questions.explanation: Poor engagement is now affecting the schedule. Root cause analysis identifies why it is happening, so the project manager can address the cause before spending contingency on crashing or escalating.
questions.mindset: Find the root cause before spending reserves.

questions.stem: You are delivering a brand new product line into your organisation, partly utilising a third party system. You have been working with the functional manager and her team to gather their expert judgement throughout development, when they raise a concern that the third party system is being discontinued and losing support in the next 12 months. What will you do next?

options.text: Update the Risk Register.
options.rationale: Discontinuation in 12 months is a future risk, so it belongs in the risk register.

options.text: Update the Issue Log.
options.rationale: The issue log records current problems, not future ones.

options.text: Ignore the concern, you can still deliver the product without the system.
options.rationale: Ignoring an expert's warning is irresponsible.

options.text: Escalate the concern to the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Escalation is premature before the risk is analysed.

questions.explanation: A system that may lose support in 12 months is an uncertain future event that could affect delivery and benefits: a risk. Risks can be identified at any time and are recorded in the risk register for analysis and response.
questions.mindset: Future problems are risks; record them.

questions.stem: You have joined a car manufacturing company as a new project manager. Senior Management have asked you to take the necessary steps that will enable you to kick-start a project in a corresponding area for designing a new electronic dashboard. What will you do next?

options.text: Review the marketplace conditions and current industry standards.
options.rationale: Market research may inform the business case but is not the step to start the project.

options.text: Create a cost benefit analysis and feasibility study for a business case.
options.rationale: The business case normally precedes the project and is owned by the sponsor.

options.text: Gather the high level requirements, scope, milestones and risks for a project charter.
options.rationale: Developing the charter with high-level requirements, scope, milestones and risks formally starts the project.

options.text: Start the project through a kick-off meeting immediately, and begin gathering resources.
options.rationale: A kick-off meeting comes after the project is authorised and planned.

questions.explanation: Develop Project Charter is the key initiating step. The charter formally authorises the project and gives the project manager authority to use resources, summarising high-level requirements, scope, milestones and risks.
questions.mindset: Start projects with a charter.

questions.stem: Your project team have just finished defining the scope of the project. They have matched the scope to the original requirements on a Requirements Traceability Matrix. The team cannot agree on what to do next. What will you ask them to do?

options.text: Ask your quality team to verify the scope so your project can proceed.
options.rationale: Verification by quality comes later, after deliverables are produced.

options.text: Approach the project sponsor for acceptance of the project scope.
options.rationale: Scope acceptance is validation of deliverables, not of the scope definition.

options.text: Break down the scope into activities and place them on a project schedule.
options.rationale: Scheduling activities follows the WBS, not scope definition.

options.text: Review the Scope Management Plan for direction on creating the Work Breakdown Structure.
options.rationale: The scope management plan explains how to create the WBS, the next scope process.

questions.explanation: Scope planning runs Collect Requirements, Define Scope and Create WBS. The scope management plan describes how the scope statement, WBS and scope baseline are created, so the team should consult it next.
questions.mindset: Define scope, then create the WBS.

questions.stem: You have just taken over a project that is approximately half-way through, and has used around 75% of its budget. A change to one of the features has been requested after extensive user acceptance testing, and your project team cannot agree on what to do next or whether changes should be made. What will you do next?

options.text: Check the Change Management Plan for details on how to make changes.
options.rationale: The change management plan sets out the change process, but the source points to the scope plan for managing scope.

options.text: Check the Requirements Traceability Matrix for how the requirements should be traced.
options.rationale: The traceability matrix does not tell the team how to handle changes.

options.text: Blame the previous project manager loudly for not having a process to deal with this situation.
options.rationale: Blaming the previous project manager is unprofessional and unhelpful.

options.text: Check the Scope Management Plan for details on how to manage the scope.
options.rationale: The scope management plan documents how scope is defined, monitored and controlled.

questions.explanation: The scope management plan documents how project and product scope are defined, validated, monitored and controlled. Consulting it shows the team how requested feature changes should be handled.
questions.mindset: Plans tell you how to manage scope.

questions.stem: You have been asked to work on a process improvement within your team. Your manager has secured a developer to assist you with automating the process once it is streamlined, but you will need to make sure they understand the process thoroughly, including the criteria to test the automation against. What will you do next?

options.text: Gather your team and the developer and create a flowchart together.
options.rationale: A flowchart with the team and developer shows the process steps and decision points to automate and test.

options.text: Gather your team and create an affinity diagram together.
options.rationale: An affinity diagram groups ideas; it does not map a process.

options.text: Gather your team and the developer and perform a cost-benefit analysis for the automation.
options.rationale: A cost-benefit analysis does not help the developer understand the process.

options.text: Gather your team and create a quality management plan together.
options.rationale: A quality management plan is broader and does not map the process itself.

questions.explanation: A flowchart shows a process from start to finish, including decision points and the people or systems involved. Building it together gives the developer a thorough understanding of the process and the criteria to test against.
questions.mindset: Map the process before automating it.

questions.stem: You are working on a new project where the design and project work, including all the scope and cost have been planned up front. However, part of the project relies on a vendor creating a new add-on for your project, which will be subject to multiple changes as the core product is created. What project development lifecycle approach will you recommend to the team?

options.text: A Predictive or Waterfall approach, as the work is planned up-front.
options.rationale: Predictive alone does not handle the changing vendor add-on.

options.text: An Iterative approach, as changes will need to be made before the final delivery
options.rationale: Iterative suits the add-on but ignores the pre-planned core.

options.text: An Incremental approach, so you can deliver parts continuously and align them.
options.rationale: Incremental delivery does not address the mix of fixed and evolving work.

options.text: A Hybrid approach combining pre-planned activities, iterations and ceremonies that promote collaboration and feedback.
options.rationale: Hybrid combines predictive planning for fixed work with adaptive practices for evolving work.

questions.explanation: A hybrid life cycle combines predictive and adaptive approaches. Well-understood, fixed elements follow a predictive life cycle, while evolving elements such as the vendor's add-on use iterations and feedback.
questions.mindset: Mix approaches when work differs in certainty.

questions.stem: The project you are managing has defined the scope and created the Scope Baseline with the Scope Statement, WBS and WBS dictionary. The project sponsor is unhappy with the planning progress and would like to know how much this scope will cost to deliver. What is the next best action you should take?

options.text: Create the project budget, including contingency and management reserves.
options.rationale: A budget cannot be created before activities, durations and resources are known.

options.text: Define and sequence activities and estimate their durations.
options.rationale: Defining, sequencing and estimating activities provides the basis for cost estimates.

options.text: Create the Resource Management Plan
options.rationale: The resource management plan helps, but activities must be defined first.

options.text: Review the project charter for the high level project scope, schedule and costs
options.rationale: The charter's high-level costs are too broad for a reliable answer.

questions.explanation: Costs are estimated from the work required. After the scope baseline, the next steps are to define and sequence activities and estimate their durations and resources; only then can reliable cost estimates and a budget be produced.
questions.mindset: Know the work before costing it.

questions.stem: You are working on a project charter for the initiating stage of a new project that will deliver a new data system. You approach your enterprise data team and ask them for an estimate to deliver these changes, however your project sponsor believes a third-party vendor will provide the best solution. What will you do next?

options.text: Create the project charter and let the steering committee decide.
options.rationale: Leaving the decision to the committee without analysis gives them nothing to decide on.

options.text: Perform make-or-buy analysis with a payback period.
options.rationale: Make-or-buy analysis, including payback period, compares in-house and vendor options objectively.

options.text: Ask the enterprise data team for their lowest quote to ensure they win.
options.rationale: Asking for a low quote to ensure the in-house team wins is biased.

options.text: Take an agile approach to the project and deliver it in increments.
options.rationale: Delivery approach does not resolve the make-or-buy question.

questions.explanation: Make-or-buy analysis compares producing something internally with buying it. Techniques such as payback period, net present value and cost-benefit analysis give an objective basis for choosing between the enterprise data team and a vendor.
questions.mindset: Decide make or buy with objective analysis.

questions.stem: You are working on a project where the functional manager is unhappy with the changes being brought about to his part of the organisation. He argues constantly, misses key meetings, demands multiple sign-offs to slow progress and more. The project sponsor asks you to go for a win/win approach to this conflict. What will you do next?

options.text: Smooth and accommodate the manager, emphasising areas of agreement.
options.rationale: Smoothing and accommodating is a lose-win outcome.

options.text: Collaborate and problem solve with the manager.
options.rationale: Collaborating and problem solving is the only mode that produces a win-win outcome.

options.text: Compromise and reconcile with the manager.
options.rationale: Compromise means both sides give something up, a partial loss for both.

options.text: Force and direct the manager, pushing your viewpoint and the expense of others.
options.rationale: Forcing is win-lose at the expense of others.

questions.explanation: Of the conflict resolution modes, only collaborating and problem solving aims for an outcome where both parties' needs are met. Smoothing is lose-win, compromise leaves both partly unsatisfied and forcing is win-lose.
questions.mindset: Win-win requires collaboration.

questions.stem: You are working on a large multi-year project. You realise that the estimates from a year ago are extremely inaccurate, and the project is off track. You would like to try a different approach that gives a high level view of future work, and a detailed view of near-term work. What will you do next?

options.text: Recommend a Decomposition approach.
options.rationale: Decomposition breaks work down but does not by itself vary detail over time.

options.text: Recommend the process in the Schedule Management Plan.
options.rationale: Following the existing schedule process repeats what produced inaccurate estimates.

options.text: Recommend an Iterative approach to development.
options.rationale: Iterative development is a delivery approach, not a planning technique for near and far work.

options.text: Recommend a Rolling Wave Planning approach.
options.rationale: Rolling wave planning details near-term work and keeps future work at a high level.

questions.explanation: Rolling wave planning is a form of progressive elaboration: near-term work is planned in detail, while work further out is planned at a higher level and elaborated as it approaches. It suits long projects where distant estimates are unreliable.
questions.mindset: Plan near work in detail, far work at a high level.

questions.stem: You are in the initiating stages of a project working for a car manufacturer. Their vehicles have been losing market share due to the high price of fuel, and the organisation wants to build more fuel efficient cars. You have been asked to put together a business case outlining the various options, with a specific order to perform benchmarking. What will you do next?

options.text: Find which competitor products have been benchmarked for future production.
options.rationale: Asking which competitor products have been benchmarked is not itself benchmarking.

options.text: Compare the specifications of popular branded fuel efficient cars available in the market with your products.
options.rationale: Comparing your products with popular fuel-efficient cars in the market is benchmarking.

options.text: Create a project charter to use as a benchmark for your future project management plan.
options.rationale: A charter is not a benchmark for a management plan.

options.text: Benchmark your current Scope, Cost and Schedule to use as values for project performance.
options.rationale: Baselining scope, cost and schedule is performance measurement, not benchmarking.

questions.explanation: Benchmarking compares actual or planned products, processes and practices with those of comparable organisations to identify best practice and ideas for improvement. Comparing specifications with successful fuel-efficient cars informs the business case options.
questions.mindset: Benchmark against comparable products.

questions.stem: When reviewing the project performance with your team, you notice the following: 1) Activity A, on the critical path, is delayed by 5 days. 2) Activity B, not on the critical path, is delayed by 10 days. 3) Activity C, on the critical path is delayed by 3 days 4) Activity D, not on the critical path, is delayed by 7 days. Where will you ask the team to focus their efforts on first, and then in which order, to bring the project back on track?

options.text: Activity A, Activity B, Activity D, Activity C.
options.rationale: This order puts a non-critical activity ahead of critical activity C.

options.text: Activity B, Activity D, Activity A, Activity C.
options.rationale: This order starts with non-critical activities, which have float.

options.text: Activity A, Activity C, Activity B, Activity D.
options.rationale: Critical path activities first (A then C, by size of delay), then non-critical by size of delay (B then D).

options.text: Activity B, Activity A, Activity D, Activity C.
options.rationale: This order mixes critical and non-critical work without logic.

questions.explanation: Delays on the critical path delay the project directly, so they are addressed first, largest delay first. Non-critical activities follow, again prioritised by the size of their delay relative to their float.
questions.mindset: Fix the critical path first.

questions.stem: As your project begins, it becomes clear the most of the business analysts, developers and testers are not familiar with system they will be modifying. The Project Sponsor asks you to address this as a potential future quality issue, and asks you to add a series of training sessions for the team, with associated cost. What will you do next?

options.text: Add it as Appraisal Costs, and take the change request to the CCB for approval.
options.rationale: Appraisal costs cover inspection and testing, not training.

options.text: Add it as Preventive Costs, and take the change request to the CCB for approval.
options.rationale: Training prevents future defects, so it is a prevention cost.

options.text: Add it as Internal Failure Costs and take the change request to the CCB for approval.
options.rationale: Internal failure costs arise from defects found before release.

options.text: Add it as Sunk Costs and take the change request to the CCB for approval.
options.rationale: Sunk costs are money already spent, not planned training.

questions.explanation: Within the cost of quality, prevention costs include training and quality planning; appraisal costs include testing and audits; failure costs arise from defects. Training the team to avoid future quality issues is a prevention cost.
questions.mindset: Training is a prevention cost of quality.

questions.stem: You have finished project planning. All baseline documents are approved and the project team is ready to begin project execution or delivery. Your team have planned and estimated the activity resources required. What will you do next?

options.text: Define with the team how to estimate, acquire, manage, and use team and physical resources.
options.rationale: Defining how resources are managed is Plan Resource Management, already done.

options.text: Estimate team resources and the type and quantities of materials, equipment, and supplies necessary to perform project work.
options.rationale: Estimating resources is Estimate Activity Resources, already done.

options.text: Obtain team members, facilities, equipment, materials, supplies, and other resources necessary to complete project work.
options.rationale: Obtaining the team and physical resources is Acquire Resources, the next step in execution.

options.text: Monitor the planned versus actual utilization of resources and taking corrective action as necessary.
options.rationale: Monitoring utilisation comes once resources are in use.

questions.explanation: Resource management runs Plan Resource Management, Estimate Activity Resources, Acquire Resources, Develop Team, Manage Team and Control Resources. With planning and estimating complete, the next step is to acquire the resources.
questions.mindset: After estimating resources, acquire them.

questions.stem: You have been working on a large waterfall project for some time, and one of the business analysts working with you has shown interest in taking on higher duties and moving into a project management role. What advice will you give them?

options.text: To work on their soft skills for communication, conflict management and negotiation.
options.rationale: Soft skills are part of leadership, but only one side of the talent triangle.

options.text: To ensure they can create a Project Charter and Project Management Plan.
options.rationale: Creating documents is a narrow technical skill.

options.text: To work on their knowledge and skills in Project Management, Leadership, and Strategic and Business Management.
options.rationale: The talent triangle covers ways of working (technical project management), power skills (leadership) and business acumen.

options.text: To work on their contract and procurement skills for hiring and vendors.
options.rationale: Procurement is one narrow area of technical skill.

questions.explanation: PMI's Talent Triangle describes the skill areas project managers need: technical project management (ways of working), leadership (power skills) and strategic and business management (business acumen). Developing all three prepares the analyst for the role.
questions.mindset: Develop all three sides of the talent triangle.

questions.stem: You are working as a project manager in an organisation with a new Project Management Office. They advise all project managers to fulfil their numerous roles within their sphere of influence, including the Project, the Industry, and their professional discipline. What is your responsibility when it comes to the Organisation?

options.text: Proactively interact with other project managers for demands on the same resources, funding, and alignment of project goals to the organisation.
options.rationale: Working with other project managers on shared resources, funding and alignment is the organisational sphere.

options.text: Communicate within your project consistently and predictably.
options.rationale: Communicating within the project is the project sphere.

options.text: Ensure an understanding of changing market niches and standards.
options.rationale: Understanding market niches and standards is the industry sphere.

options.text: Educate other professionals in the organisation regarding the value of project management.
options.rationale: Educating other professionals about project management is the professional discipline sphere.

questions.explanation: Project managers influence several spheres. Within the organisation, they interact proactively with other project managers over shared resources, funding and alignment of goals. The project, industry and professional discipline are separate spheres.
questions.mindset: In the organisation, coordinate with peers on shared demands.

questions.stem: You have just joined an organisation, and are about to be allocated to an existing project, delivering a new Human Resources system. You have heard that the project is behind its delivery milestones, and it is over budget by $40.000 so far. There are multiple stakeholders with differing needs. What will you do first?

options.text: Create a project management plan, outlining the processes for each phase of the project.
options.rationale: The project already has a plan to review; writing a new one is premature.

options.text: Perform a stakeholder engagement assessment, to see who is sabotaging the project.
options.rationale: Starting with who is sabotaging assumes bad intent and targets stakeholders too soon.

options.text: Start by understanding how the organisation works, including its politics and power.
options.rationale: Understanding how the organisation works, including politics and power, is the first step for a new joiner.

options.text: Meet with the project sponsor to understand why the project is off track.
options.rationale: Meeting the sponsor is useful, but the project manager is not yet on the project and must first understand the organisation.

questions.explanation: As a newcomer not yet assigned to the project, the project manager first learns the internal enterprise environmental factors: culture, politics, power and how things get done. That understanding underpins every later interaction with stakeholders.
questions.mindset: Understand the organisation's politics and power first.

questions.stem: You are working in an organisation where a large change is happening to multiple departments. You have been asked to manage this change as a project, and allocate people within your project team with sufficient leadership skills. What will you NOT look for in potential candidates?

options.text: People who build trust, balance opposing goals and apply persuasion and conflict resolution.
options.rationale: Building trust, balancing goals and resolving conflict are core leadership qualities.

options.text: People who give feedback constructively and accept feedback constructively.
options.rationale: Giving and accepting constructive feedback is a leadership quality.

options.text: People who can describe the products, goals and objectives of the project.
options.rationale: Being able to articulate the vision and objectives is a leadership quality.

options.text: People who ensure the work is done their way, to ensure the fastest approach.
options.rationale: Insisting on one's own way is dictatorial and not a leadership quality to seek.

questions.explanation: Leadership qualities include integrity, vision, collaboration, building trust, managing conflict and giving and receiving feedback. Insisting that work is done one's own way, without regard for others, is not a quality to look for.
questions.mindset: Leaders collaborate; they don't dictate.

questions.stem: You have started as a junior project manager on an internal process improvement project within your existing team. Your program manager asks that you be aware of and use the various forms of power available to you. What is the best type of power available to you in this situation?

options.text: Informational power.
options.rationale: Informational power, from access to knowledge within the team, is available to a junior project manager.

options.text: Situational power.
options.rationale: Situational power arises from unusual circumstances, which do not apply here.

options.text: Positional power.
options.rationale: A junior project manager has limited positional power.

options.text: Punitive or coercive power.
options.rationale: Punitive or coercive power is unavailable to a junior project manager and damages relationships.

questions.explanation: A junior project manager has little positional, reward or coercive power. Working within their existing team, their strongest source of influence is informational power: their knowledge of the team's process and access to its expertise.
questions.mindset: Use the power you actually have.

questions.stem: You are working on a new waterfall project where the scope and cost have been planned up front. As the project progresses, you notice several tasks going off-track and falling behind. Luckily these tasks are not on the critical path, have several days of float available, and you can adjust their dates without affecting the overall project. What technique are you using to keep your project on track?

options.text: Resource smoothing.
options.rationale: Resource smoothing adjusts activities within their float without changing the end date.

options.text: Resource levelling.
options.rationale: Resource levelling can change the critical path and delay the project.

options.text: Schedule fast tracking.
options.rationale: Fast tracking overlaps activities to shorten the schedule.

options.text: Schedule crashing.
options.rationale: Crashing adds resources to shorten the schedule.

questions.explanation: Resource smoothing adjusts activities within their available float so the project end date is not affected. Levelling can extend the schedule, while fast tracking and crashing are compression techniques.
questions.mindset: Smoothing stays within float.

questions.stem: About a third of your project team have worked on a similar project in the past. They have gathered requirements and created a high level scope. It is time to estimate the size and effort involved, however the customer believes things are taking too long and would like to see some progress as soon as possible. What will you do?

options.text: Ask the customer to wait so you can plan the project properly.
options.rationale: Making the customer wait ignores their need to see progress.

options.text: Estimate the scope using parametric estimating.
options.rationale: Parametric estimating needs detailed unit data that the team does not yet have.

options.text: Break the high level scope into smaller parts using a WBS.
options.rationale: Decomposition takes time and delays the estimate the customer wants.

options.text: Estimate the scope using analogous estimating.
options.rationale: Analogous estimating uses the team's similar past project to estimate quickly at a high level.

questions.explanation: Analogous estimating uses information from a similar past project to estimate a new one. It is quick, works with only high-level scope and suits a team where members have delivered similar work.
questions.mindset: Use analogous estimating for quick, early estimates.

questions.stem: You have been asked to monitor the changes to a product before completing your next project phase. You review the control chart. The data is within the upper and lower limits. You have an upward trend of four data points, and six points above the average line. What will you do next?

options.text: Proceed with the next phase, as the process is within control.
options.rationale: The data is within limits and does not break the trend or run rules, so the process is in control.

options.text: Delay the next phase and rework the current release, as the process is out of control.
options.rationale: The process is in control, so rework is unnecessary.

options.text: Ask the project sponsor to validate the released deliverable.
options.rationale: Validation by the sponsor is separate from interpreting the control chart.

options.text: Proceed with quality testing to verify the created deliverables.
options.rationale: The control chart already shows the process is stable.

questions.explanation: A process is typically considered out of control if a point falls outside the control limits, if seven or more consecutive points fall on one side of the mean, or if there is a sustained trend in one direction. Four rising points and six above the mean do not meet these rules.
questions.mindset: Apply control chart rules before reacting.

questions.stem: You are in the process of planning the resources required for your project. Work on your project has not started, as your team are not sure what they should be doing. You decide to create the resource management plan with your team. What output do you specifically need from this plan?

options.text: Stakeholder Register, to identify and classify people involved in the project.
options.rationale: The stakeholder register comes from stakeholder identification, not resource planning.

options.text: Project Charter, with the high level roles & responsibilities for the project.
options.rationale: The charter is created in initiation, not resource planning.

options.text: Requirement traceability matrix, with who requested and signs off on each requirement.
options.rationale: The traceability matrix comes from requirements work.

options.text: Roles & responsibilities, with Role, Responsibilities, Authority and Competence.
options.rationale: Roles and responsibilities, with authority and competence, are a key part of the resource management plan.

questions.explanation: Plan Resource Management defines roles and responsibilities: each role, its responsibilities, the authority it holds and the competence it needs. This tells team members what they should be doing.
questions.mindset: Define role, responsibility, authority and competence.

questions.stem: A quality assurance manager has been hired externally to test the project and manage defects. She executed the process in the quality management plan with her testing team, where they found a high number of low impact defects. You need to see where the biggest impacts are. What will you do next?

options.text: Use a histogram to show the most common defects.
options.rationale: A histogram counts occurrences of each defect type, showing which are most common.

options.text: Use a flowchart to show the most common defects.
options.rationale: A flowchart maps a process; it does not count defects.

options.text: Use a matrix diagram to show the most common defects.
options.rationale: A matrix diagram shows relationships between factors, not frequency.

options.text: Use an affinity diagram to show the most common defects.
options.rationale: An affinity diagram groups ideas; it does not quantify them.

questions.explanation: A histogram is a bar chart showing how often each category occurs. Counting defects by type reveals the most common ones, and ordered from highest to lowest it becomes a Pareto chart that highlights where to focus.
questions.mindset: Count defects to find where to focus.

questions.stem: The project you are working on has recently started and the team has come together from many different parts of the organisation, each with their own agenda. There are lots of small conflicts within the team and little work getting done. The program manager asks you to use your positional power to resolve these conflicts as the team starts to find its rhythm. What will you do?

options.text: Withdraw from the conflicts so the team can work through them.
options.rationale: Withdrawing leaves the conflicts unresolved and is not using positional power.

options.text: Force a decision for the conflicts.
options.rationale: Using positional power to decide is forcing, which resolves conflicts quickly.

options.text: Smooth and accommodate all sides in the conflicts.
options.rationale: Smoothing emphasises agreement rather than using authority.

options.text: Problem Solve the conflicts with the team.
options.rationale: Problem solving is collaborative and does not rely on positional power.

questions.explanation: Using positional power to resolve conflict means forcing a decision. It usually gives a win-lose outcome but can resolve many small conflicts quickly, which is what the program manager has asked for while the team finds its rhythm.
questions.mindset: Positional power resolves conflict by forcing.

questions.stem: During your project, your company was taken over by another, larger company, and the project management office and its policies were changed. The project customer has already formally accepted the deliverables, the project has completed delivery and is ready to be closed. What will you do next?

options.text: Refer to the Project Charter for the closing procedures.
options.rationale: The charter does not contain closing procedures.

options.text: Refer to the scope management plan for deliverables' acceptance.
options.rationale: Acceptance has already happened, so the scope management plan is not the next step.

options.text: Gather details on the accepted deliverables, any agreements and procurement documentation.
options.rationale: Accepted deliverables, agreements and procurement documentation are the inputs to closing the project.

options.text: The project cannot be closed as the project outcomes need to be measured and accepted.
options.rationale: The project can be closed; benefits are measured after closure.

questions.explanation: Inputs to Close Project or Phase include the accepted deliverables, agreements on closure and procurement documentation. Gathering these allows the project to be formally closed under the new organisation's procedures.
questions.mindset: Gather closure inputs to close formally.

questions.stem: One of your stakeholders with a very high influence within the company has raised an urgent change that they want to be implemented within the next two weeks. You check the change management plan and see that changes can be approved by the project manager. You raise a change request and review the impact to the project schedule and cost. What will you do next?

options.text: Review the configuration management plan to see which documents are baselined.
options.rationale: The configuration management plan identifies baselined items, which is already known here.

options.text: Review the schedule earned value reports for your project.
options.rationale: Earned value reports have already fed the impact analysis.

options.text: Decide on the changes, approve the changes, and track the changes.
options.rationale: With authority to approve, the project manager decides, approves and tracks the change.

options.text: Review the Requirement Traceability matrix for requirement acceptance and sign off.
options.rationale: The traceability matrix is not needed to approve this change.

questions.explanation: The change management plan gives the project manager authority to approve changes. Having raised the request and analysed its impact on schedule and cost, the project manager decides, approves and tracks the change.
questions.mindset: Use delegated authority within the change process.

questions.stem: You are in the process of measuring the outcome of one of your deliverables on the business. The data shows that there seems to be an improvement but the range of results is very wide. You are able to get very clear results, however. Based on these results, what will you do next?

options.text: The process has high precision but low accuracy. The equipment should be adjusted.
options.rationale: The diagnosis is right, but the problem lies in the deliverable's process, not equipment.

options.text: The process has high precision but low accuracy. The deliverable process should be improved.
options.rationale: Clear, exact results show high precision; the wide range shows low accuracy, so the process should be improved.

options.text: The process has high accuracy but low precision. The equipment should be replaced.
options.rationale: A wide range indicates low, not high, accuracy.

options.text: The process has high accuracy but low precision. Additional features should be added.
options.rationale: A wide range indicates low accuracy, and adding features does not address it.

questions.explanation: A wide range of results indicates low accuracy, while clear, exact measurements indicate high precision. The process that produces the deliverable needs improvement to bring results closer to the target.
questions.mindset: Wide range means low accuracy.

questions.stem: In the last few months, your project team have had a large amount of conflict, finding their role and place within the team. They are starting to work together and adjust their work habits and behaviours to support the team. As a leader, what will you do next?

options.text: The team are in the performing stage, work with them to maintain as they move towards adjourning.
options.rationale: The team has only just started working together, so it is not yet performing.

options.text: The team are in the forming stage, work with them to find their roles and work through the coming conflict.
options.rationale: The team has already passed through forming and the conflict of storming.

options.text: The team are in the norming stage, work with them to become performing.
options.rationale: A team adjusting habits to support each other after conflict is norming, and the leader helps it reach performing.

options.text: The team are in the storming stage, work with them to normalise their role in the team.
options.rationale: The conflict is behind them, so they are past storming.

questions.explanation: In Tuckman's model, a team that has worked through conflict and is adjusting its habits and behaviour to support each other is norming. The leader helps it build on this to reach the performing stage.
questions.mindset: Help norming teams move to performing.

questions.stem: You have used a project charter and statement of work to create a project management plan. You present the plan to key stakeholders, including the project sponsor and you sense a high level of dissatisfaction by the customer executives. They do not believe the project will produce the results they had expected. What should you do next?

options.text: Request a written statement from the customer, detailing their concerns.
options.rationale: A written statement delays resolution and keeps the customer at a distance.

options.text: Proceed as normal. Your project plan will produce a convincing product for the customer.
options.rationale: Proceeding ignores clear dissatisfaction from key customers.

options.text: Arrange a change request, re-plan your project where necessary and go ahead with the project work.
options.rationale: A change request and re-plan before understanding expectations may miss the mark again.

options.text: Work together with your customer to create a narrative Scope statement outlining the deliverables.
options.rationale: Creating the scope statement with the customer aligns deliverables and acceptance criteria to their expectations.

questions.explanation: When customers doubt that the plan will deliver what they expect, the project manager works with them directly. Developing the scope statement together, with deliverables and acceptance criteria, aligns the project with their expectations.
questions.mindset: Define scope with the customer.

questions.stem: You have planned, executed and monitored a project to completion. The customer has just received the finished product and you would like to close the project. The customer advises you that they are not happy with the received product, that your team didn't listen when they raised quality concerns, and they are raising a claim against your company. What will you do next?

options.text: Raise a change request for their proposed changes and update your project plan.
options.rationale: A change request does not settle a claim about delivered work.

options.text: Call their bluff: take the claim to a dispute, then an appeal if necessary.
options.rationale: Going straight to dispute escalates costs and damages the relationship.

options.text: Review the claims process in the contract and negotiate with them to settle the claim.
options.rationale: The contract's claims process, with negotiated settlement, is the preferred way to resolve claims.

options.text: Review the earned value report for any impact to the schedule and cost of your project.
options.rationale: Earned value reports do not address the customer's claim.

questions.explanation: Claims are handled through the process set out in the contract, and negotiation is the preferred way to settle them. Litigation or other dispute resolution is a last resort.
questions.mindset: Settle claims by negotiation under the contract.

questions.stem: You are in the process of creating a project charter for your part of the organisation, to try and gain resources for an automated process improvement. The project sponsor is also the functional manager in charge of the resources for the area. She rejects your project charter, noting that you have outlined everything you want from her team, but nothing about what her area will get in return. What will you do next?

options.text: Rework the project charter to include the benefits management plan and success measures.
options.rationale: Including the benefits management plan and success measures shows the sponsor what her area gains.

options.text: Escalate the charter to the project sponsor's manager, as this project is important.
options.rationale: Escalating over the sponsor's head damages the relationship.

options.text: Ask the project sponsor to work Agile, and start delivering a minimum viable product (MVP).
options.rationale: Switching to agile does not address the missing benefits.

options.text: Begin work on the Requirements Management Plan, as this will show the sponsor how their requirements will be added and tracked.
options.rationale: A requirements plan shows how requirements are handled, not the benefits to her area.

questions.explanation: A charter should show what the organisation gains. Including the benefits management plan—target benefits, strategic alignment and timeframe—and success measures such as ROI or payback period shows the sponsor why the investment of her team's time is worthwhile.
questions.mindset: Show stakeholders what they gain.

questions.stem: You are working on a complex, high-value project to replace the telecommunications system across your organisation. You have created a Request For Quote for vendors to respond to, including source selection criteria and a statement of work, and you have selected a seller based on multiple vendor responses. What will you do next?

options.text: Record the new vendor in your Stakeholder Register, and begin engaging them to deliver the project.
options.rationale: Recording the vendor as a stakeholder comes after the contract is awarded.

options.text: Draft an appropriate contract such as Fixed Price Incentive Fee, and proceed with the implementation.
options.rationale: Drafting a contract and proceeding skips the approval required for a high-value award.

options.text: Place the approved RFQ in your procurement management plan, and proceed with delivery of the project.
options.rationale: The RFQ is a bid document, not something placed in the plan for delivery.

options.text: Approach organisational senior management for approval to award the contract.
options.rationale: Complex, high-value procurements usually need senior management approval before award.

questions.explanation: Final approval of complex, high-value or high-risk procurements generally requires organisational senior management approval before the contract is awarded. Only then is the contract signed and the vendor engaged.
questions.mindset: Get approval before awarding major contracts.

questions.stem: You have been planning your project using a waterfall methodology, and need to estimate the resources required with your team. Your project management office recently stopped using third parties or offsite workers and mandated resources to be onsite only. You review the activity list based on your project scope and realise that some essential project resources currently work offsite. What will you do next?

options.text: Discuss available options with the Project Sponsor.
options.rationale: Discussing with the sponsor is useful once options have been analysed.

options.text: Perform alternatives analysis on the impact of both onsite and offsite workers for your project.
options.rationale: Alternatives analysis weighs options for meeting resource needs within the onsite constraint.

options.text: Update the resource management plan with the onsite worker mandate.
options.rationale: Updating the plan with the mandate does not address the skills gap.

options.text: Update the resource calendar with the available people, locations and dates before baselining your project plan.
options.rationale: Updating calendars assumes the resourcing question is already solved.

questions.explanation: Alternatives analysis evaluates options for performing project activities within constraints. It helps the project manager find the best way to secure essential skills given the new onsite-only mandate.
questions.mindset: Analyse alternatives when constraints bite.

questions.stem: You have been working on a project where your organisation wanted only onsite workers, while you believed the project needed specific skills that were only available offsite. You worked through the various options and agreed to use the onsite workers available. As your project progresses however, it becomes clear that it is not being done to specification and you really do need the offsite workers. The project is going off track. What will you do next?

options.text: Update the issue log, and the resource calendar with the resource requirements.
options.rationale: Logging the issue records it but does not resolve the resource shortfall.

options.text: Use problem solving with your team, and negotiation with your Project Sponsor.
options.rationale: Problem solving with the team and negotiating with the sponsor are Control Resources techniques that address the gap.

options.text: Gather work performance information from your team, and raise a change request.
options.rationale: A change request may follow, but first the resourcing problem needs solving and negotiating.

options.text: Raise a risk in the risk register, and brainstorm risk responses with your team.
options.rationale: The problem is already happening, so it is an issue, not a risk.

questions.explanation: Control Resources uses techniques such as problem solving and negotiation. Working with the team to understand the gap and negotiating with the sponsor for the offsite skills tackles the cause of the off-track work.
questions.mindset: Solve resource problems and negotiate for what you need.

questions.stem: You are working on a very high risk infrastructure project that is critical to your organisation. The team are experienced in this area after working on this project for the past 12 months. During a working group meeting, they mention they are stuck and cannot implement part of the project. You raise an issue in the issue log and decide to problem solve with your team. What will you do next?

options.text: Escalate the problem outside your team, as they clearly cannot move forward.
options.rationale: Escalating outside an experienced team may bring in people less familiar with the work.

options.text: Review the lessons learned register for lessons to past similar problems.
options.rationale: Lessons learned may help, but structured problem solving is the next step.

options.text: Define the problem with data, identifying the root cause, and generating possible solutions.
options.rationale: Defining the problem with data, finding the root cause and generating solutions is structured problem solving.

options.text: Raise a risk to project delivery and note the impact and likelihood of the risk.
options.rationale: The problem is already happening, so it is an issue, not a risk.

questions.explanation: Structured problem solving defines the problem with data, identifies the root cause, generates possible solutions, chooses and implements one and checks it worked. The experienced team is well placed to do this.
questions.mindset: Solve problems systematically with data.

questions.stem: You are creating a high level project charter which has now been approved. The Project Sponsor expects you to get to work straight away, but you do not know who to approach or who is available to help you deliver this project. What will you do next?

options.text: Identify stakeholders with an organisational breakdown chart, and include this in your project plan.
options.rationale: Identifying stakeholders with an organisational breakdown chart shows who to approach and who can help.

options.text: Create a RACI or Resource Assignment Matrix so your team know what is expected of them.
options.rationale: A RACI can only be built once you know who is involved in the project.

options.text: Review and update the resource calendar with resource working days and start dates.
options.rationale: Resource calendars need to know who the resources are first.

options.text: Review the high level stakeholders in the project charter and begin your project.
options.rationale: The charter's stakeholders are high-level and starting work immediately skips identification.

questions.explanation: After the charter is approved, the next step is Identify Stakeholders. An organisational breakdown chart is one way to find the people and groups who are affected or can help, before assigning responsibilities or scheduling resources.
questions.mindset: Identify stakeholders right after the charter.

questions.stem: You have been assigned to address the fast-moving competition that is rapidly taking market share from your company. Your executive manager advises you the company only has around 12 months before jobs will be lost, but there are currently no projects to address these concerns. As a project manager, what will you do next?

options.text: Ask the executive manager to come up with project ideas to address the situation.
options.rationale: Asking the executive to come up with ideas passes back the task the project manager was given.

options.text: Perform benchmarking against various companies for process improvement opportunities.
options.rationale: Benchmarking helps generate ideas but is only one input to a full business case.

options.text: Create a project charter with high level scope, milestones and cost for approval.
options.rationale: A charter needs a justified project first, which comes from the business case.

options.text: Create a project business case, including business need, situation analysis and solution options.
options.rationale: A business case with the business need, situation analysis and solution options establishes what project to start.

questions.explanation: Before a project can be chartered, a business case sets out the business need, analyses the situation and evaluates solution options. With competitive pressure and no project yet defined, this is the first step.
questions.mindset: Justify the project with a business case first.

questions.stem: You have just started work in a project that has been in development for the past six months. You notice it has been through a large amount of project steps that you are unfamiliar with, such as concept development, feasibility study, commissioning, milestone review and more. These don't match the normal phases of design, build and test. What will you do next?

options.text: Advise the project to reduce and update its phases, for less admin and faster delivery.
options.rationale: Changing established phases before understanding them may breach governance.

options.text: Advise the project to adhere to the normal project phases of Design, Build and Test as per the PMBOK Guide
options.rationale: The PMBOK Guide does not prescribe fixed phases; organisations define their own.

options.text: Adhere to the project's phases, and familiarise yourself with the organisation's process.
options.rationale: Adhering to the organisation's phases and learning its processes respects its governance and ways of working.

options.text: Remove phases altogether and work through the waterfall delivery in one big release.
options.rationale: Removing phases ignores the organisation's governance and approvals.

questions.explanation: Organisations define their own life cycle phases, governance and approvals as part of their enterprise environmental factors and process assets. A new project manager follows these and learns the organisation's way of working before suggesting changes.
questions.mindset: Learn and follow the organisation's governance.

questions.stem: The project management office is looking to you for help in hiring and coaching new project managers, and they ask you to interview the next candidate for roles in upcoming projects. In speaking with the candidate, they do not have any industry experience. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask them whether they prefer waterfall or agile, to see if they work the same way as your organisation.
options.rationale: A preference for waterfall or agile says little about project management capability.

options.text: Ask them whether they would like a different job within the company, with less focus on industry experience.
options.rationale: Steering the candidate to another job judges them only on industry experience.

options.text: Ask them if they can dictate and command a team to get fast results.
options.rationale: Seeking a command-and-control style risks harming team safety and long-term performance.

options.text: Ask them what their focus on a project would be: the schedule, selected financial reports, or the issue log.
options.rationale: Asking about focus areas such as the schedule, financials and issues tests core project management skills.

questions.explanation: A capable project manager combines technical project management, leadership and business skills. Without industry experience, the candidate can still show sound focus on core artefacts such as the schedule, financial reports and the issue log.
questions.mindset: Assess project management capability, not just industry experience.

questions.stem: Your project charter has recently been approved, and you are gathering the customer requirements that will form the basis of your project. The project customer advises they have been burned by previous project deliveries in the past, where the project did not deliver what they really needed. What will you do next?

options.text: Create an initial list of requirements as part of a solid requirements management plan.
options.rationale: An initial list without customer involvement may repeat past failures.

options.text: Call a focus group with customer experts and brainstorm requirements with them.
options.rationale: A focus group with customer experts brainstorming requirements involves them directly.

options.text: Perform benchmarking between the area process and external organisations.
options.rationale: Benchmarking compares with others but does not capture this customer's needs.

options.text: Create a requirements traceability matrix to ensure requirements are tracked properly.
options.rationale: A traceability matrix tracks requirements but does not gather them.

questions.explanation: Collect Requirements uses techniques such as interviews, focus groups, brainstorming and questionnaires. For a customer who has been let down before, direct collaboration through a focus group and brainstorming ensures their real needs are captured.
questions.mindset: Involve the customer directly in gathering requirements.

questions.stem: You are a project manager brought on during the very early phase of the project. The project sponsor has asked you to create a report on whether this project can be completed in time, at what cost, and what benefit is expected. What is the Project Sponsor asking for?

options.text: A Project Charter
options.rationale: A charter authorises a project; it does not assess feasibility.

options.text: A commercial database
options.rationale: A commercial database is a source of information, not a report on viability.

options.text: A Feasibility Study
options.rationale: A feasibility study assesses whether the project can be delivered, at what cost and with what benefit.

options.text: A project management plan
options.rationale: A management plan explains how the project will be managed once approved.

questions.explanation: A feasibility study, often part of the business case, examines whether a project is viable: whether it can be completed in time, at what cost and with what benefit. It helps the sponsor decide whether to proceed.
questions.mindset: Test viability with a feasibility study.

questions.stem: Your deliverables have recently been quality checked by a specialist testing team, and passed with flying colours. You take them to the Project Sponsor for approval so you can move to project closure. The project sponsor accepts all the deliverables except two. One she notes as a defect, and one as a missed requirement. What will you do next?

options.text: Make the changes as soon as possible to avoid further delays.
options.rationale: Making changes without a change request bypasses control.

options.text: Raise an issue in the issue log, as this will delay your project.
options.rationale: Logging an issue does not initiate the formal fix.

options.text: Raise a change request for the items, along with the reasons for non-acceptance of those deliverables.
options.rationale: Raising change requests with the reasons for non-acceptance puts the fixes through proper control.

options.text: Proceed as normal to project closure - you have delivered them as per the project needs.
options.rationale: Proceeding to closure ignores the sponsor's rejection.

questions.explanation: When deliverables are not accepted during Validate Scope, change requests are raised for them, documenting the reasons for non-acceptance. This ensures defect repairs and missed requirements are handled through change control.
questions.mindset: Non-accepted deliverables lead to change requests.

questions.stem: You have been planning your project using a waterfall methodology. The project team have collected the requirements from the customer, who is eager to begin work as soon as possible.
