You set a meeting with the business analysts in your team to create the Scope Statement based on these requirements. What will you do next?

options.text: Include the Scope description, deliverables, acceptance criteria and exclusions.
options.rationale: The scope statement includes the scope description, deliverables, acceptance criteria and exclusions.

options.text: Include the Scope description, Work Breakdown Structure and WBS dictionary.
options.rationale: The WBS and dictionary belong to the scope baseline, not the statement.

options.text: Include the Scope Management Plan, Statement of Work, and Requirements Traceability Matrix.
options.rationale: These are other plans and documents, not scope statement content.

options.text: Include the Project Charter, Project Management Plan, and Accepted Deliverables.
options.rationale: The charter, management plan and accepted deliverables are separate documents, not scope statement content.

questions.explanation: The project scope statement describes the scope, major deliverables, acceptance criteria and exclusions. Together with the WBS and WBS dictionary it forms the scope baseline.
questions.mindset: Scope statement: description, deliverables, acceptance, exclusions.

questions.stem: You have been assigned to a project that is behind schedule. Some of your team approach you and ask what they should be working on. You check with your team and one of your senior analysts recommends you work together to create the Work Breakdown Structure Dictionary. What will you do next?

options.text: Create a scope breakdown with unique identifier, description, and acceptance criteria.
options.rationale: This describes WBS dictionary content, which does not tell people who does what.

options.text: Work with the senior analyst to create a Resource Assignment Matrix instead, and coach them on the difference between a RAM and WBS Dictionary.
options.rationale: A resource assignment matrix shows who is assigned to each work package, answering the team's question.

options.text: Gather the project scope and break it down into smaller work packages.
options.rationale: Decomposing scope creates the WBS, not assignments.

options.text: Create a scope breakdown with unique identifier, description and resource requirements.
options.rationale: Resource requirements alone do not assign work to people.

questions.explanation: The team needs to know what each person should work on. A resource assignment matrix links work packages or activities to team members, making assignments clear. Coaching the analyst on how it differs from the WBS dictionary builds their understanding.
questions.mindset: Use a RAM to show who does what.

questions.stem: The project charter has been approved, you have identified the stakeholders you will be working with and who will be impacted. As the project progresses, you notice multiple stakeholders who seem to be actively trying to sabotage your project and efforts. What will you do next?

options.text: Review the stakeholder engagement assessment matrix and invite feedback from the people who are resistant.
options.rationale: Assessing engagement and inviting feedback from resistant stakeholders targets the problem directly.

options.text: Remove the people who seem to be slowing your project from your project team.
options.rationale: Removing people does not address why stakeholders resist.

options.text: Escalate the problem stakeholders to their functional managers for disciplinary action.
options.rationale: Seeking disciplinary action escalates conflict and deepens resistance.

options.text: Review the Impact over Influence matrix to determine how to engage with the stakeholders.
options.rationale: Impact and influence analysis helps prioritise, but engagement levels show who is resistant and what to do.

questions.explanation: The stakeholder engagement assessment matrix compares current and desired engagement levels. Reviewing it and inviting feedback from resistant stakeholders helps the project manager understand their concerns and engage them using communication and interpersonal skills.
questions.mindset: Assess engagement and listen to resisters.

questions.stem: Your project involves nearly a dozen teams who are dispersed around the country at different sites, with thousands of impacted stakeholders. The executives in these areas are concerned with the changes the project will bring, and are starting to push back on your planning efforts. What will you do next?

options.text: Create the project charter, and arrange for sign off by the executives.
options.rationale: The charter is already approved on a project in progress.

options.text: Create the communications management plan to ensure their communication needs are met.
options.rationale: The communications management plan ensures dispersed executives receive the information they need.

options.text: Raise a change request for the project, and arrange to co-locate all the teams.
options.rationale: Co-locating a dozen teams across the country is impractical.

options.text: Create the requirements traceability matrix, so you can trace the executives' requirements back to the scope you deliver and keep them engaged.
options.rationale: A traceability matrix tracks requirements but does not meet communication needs.

questions.explanation: With many dispersed teams and thousands of stakeholders, clear planned communication is essential. The communications management plan sets out stakeholders' needs and how information will be collected, created and distributed, addressing executives' concerns.
questions.mindset: Plan communications for dispersed stakeholders.

questions.stem: A number of risks have been raised on your project. You perform qualitative analysis to get a subjective risk rating, but your project customer is not satisfied. They would like you to perform additional qualitative risk analysis, beyond impact and likelihood. What will you analyse next?

options.text: Simulation, Sensitivity analysis, Decision tree analysis.
options.rationale: Simulation, sensitivity and decision trees are quantitative techniques.

options.text: Cost of Failure, Cost of Appraisal, Cost of Prevention.
options.rationale: These are cost of quality categories, not risk parameters.

options.text: Executive needs, Political needs, Promotion needs.
options.rationale: These are not risk parameters and would politicise risk analysis.

options.text: Urgency, Proximity and Strategic impact.
options.rationale: Urgency, proximity and strategic impact are additional qualitative risk parameters.

questions.explanation: Beyond probability and impact, qualitative risk analysis can assess parameters such as urgency, proximity, dormancy, manageability, controllability, detectability, connectivity and strategic impact to prioritise risks more effectively.
questions.mindset: Assess risk beyond probability and impact.

questions.stem: One of the risks on your project is significantly large, and could seriously impact your company if it ever came about. It has captured the attention of high ranking executives, who have each proposed a response and thinks theirs is the best. You decide to solve the argument with a Decision Tree. What will you do next?

options.text: Rate the risks for their probability and impact to get a risk rating for each.
options.rationale: Rating probability and impact is qualitative analysis, not a decision tree.

options.text: Note each of the options on a vertical bar chart for their impact sensitivity on cost.
options.rationale: A bar chart of cost sensitivity describes a tornado diagram.

options.text: Note the various response options with their cost impact, and their probability of occurrence.
options.rationale: A decision tree lays out each response option with its cost and the probability of outcomes.

options.text: Perform a simulation of each of the responses against multiple criteria to test their impact.
options.rationale: Simulation is a different quantitative technique.

questions.explanation: A decision tree maps decision options with their costs or benefits and the uncertain outcomes that follow, each with a probability. Calculating expected values lets the team compare the executives' proposed responses objectively.
questions.mindset: Compare options objectively with a decision tree.

questions.stem: You have recently become a project manager for a large organisation and you are not sure what to expect. Your colleague tells you that the organisation is large enough to have a substantial project management office, and it is a directing PMO. What will you do next?

options.text: Collaborate with the other project managers in the PMO to find a project that suits your skillset.
options.rationale: In a directive PMO, project managers do not choose their own projects.

options.text: Get started on a business case in your work area to initiate a project.
options.rationale: Initiating projects is not how assignments work in a directive PMO.

options.text: Await to be assigned to a project by the PMO.
options.rationale: A directive PMO manages projects directly and assigns project managers who report to it.

options.text: Review the project management frameworks, templates and tools mandated for use by the PMO.
options.rationale: Mandated frameworks are characteristic of a controlling PMO.

questions.explanation: PMOs can be supportive (providing templates and guidance), controlling (requiring compliance with frameworks) or directive (managing projects directly and assigning project managers). In a directive PMO, the project manager waits to be assigned.
questions.mindset: Know your PMO type.

questions.stem: The project customer approaches you as they are worried that the project is not delivering fast enough. You review the project schedule and cost so you can see how the project is tracking. The Actual Cost is $648,000. The Earned Value is $601,000. The Planned Value is $629,000. What will you tell them?

options.text: The project is ahead of schedule and over budget.
options.rationale: SV is negative, so the project is behind schedule, not ahead.

options.text: The project is ahead of schedule and under budget.
options.rationale: Both variances are negative, so neither ahead of schedule nor under budget.

options.text: The project is behind schedule and over budget.
options.rationale: SV = EV − PV = −$28,000 (behind) and CV = EV − AC = −$47,000 (over budget).

options.text: The project is behind schedule and under budget.
options.rationale: CV is negative, so the project is over budget, not under.

questions.explanation: Schedule variance is EV − PV = $601,000 − $629,000 = −$28,000, so the project is behind schedule. Cost variance is EV − AC = $601,000 − $648,000 = −$47,000, so it is over budget.
questions.mindset: Negative SV: behind; negative CV: over budget.

questions.stem: The people and resources involved in your project are currently costing a large amount of money, and your project sponsor comments about it frequently. You check how the project is tracking. Planned Value is $840,000. Earned Value is $795,000. Actual Cost is $755,000. What will you do next?

options.text: Utilise the project contingency reserves to bring the project schedule back on track.
options.rationale: Contingency reserve is for identified risks, not general schedule recovery when the budget is healthy.

options.text: Raise a change request to reduce the project scope and bring the cost back on track.
options.rationale: Cutting scope is unnecessary when the project is under budget.

options.text: Reduce the project resources to bring the project cost back on track.
options.rationale: Cutting resources would make the schedule slip further, and cost is already under control.

options.text: Add more resources to bring the project schedule back on track.
options.rationale: The project is under budget but behind schedule, so adding resources can recover time.

questions.explanation: SV = EV − PV = $795,000 − $840,000 = −$45,000, so the project is behind schedule. CV = EV − AC = $795,000 − $755,000 = +$40,000, so it is under budget. Despite the sponsor's comments, adding resources to recover the schedule is justified.
questions.mindset: Read the numbers, not the perception.

questions.stem: Team members from parts of the organisation have been assigned to your project at an agreed level of 50% availability. As the project progresses, you notice they are being pulled back into their normal roles. You also notice that your project is falling behind schedule. What will you do next?

options.text: Talk with the project steering committee, and arrange for more resources to assist your project.
options.rationale: Asking for more resources does not fix the loss of already committed ones.

options.text: Talk with functional managers. Negotiate clear and written assignments with reliable scheduling priorities.
options.rationale: Negotiating clear, written assignments with the functional managers secures the agreed availability.

options.text: Raise a risk to project delivery and assign it to the functional managers to mitigate.
options.rationale: Assigning a risk to functional managers does not address a problem already happening.

options.text: Raise an issue in the issue log, and raise it at the next project working group.
options.rationale: Logging the issue records it but does not resolve it.

questions.explanation: When team members are repeatedly pulled back into their normal roles, the project manager works directly with their functional managers. Negotiating clear written assignments with reliable priorities secures the agreed availability.
questions.mindset: Negotiate firm resource commitments.

questions.stem: You have been planning a project with the manager of a functional area who needs to increase their profit by 57% in the next three years. You are helping him put together a business case. He has come up with 18 different project ideas to reach the goal but will take approximately seven years. The manager pushes you to find a way to do them in three. What will you do next?

options.text: Prioritise the ideas based on impact and cost, and note Required, Desired or Optional next to each in the business case.
options.rationale: Prioritising ideas by impact and cost and labelling them required, desired or optional focuses the plan on what matters most.

options.text: Advise the manager that good things take time to deliver.
options.rationale: Telling the manager to wait does not help achieve the goal.

options.text: Add the appropriate amount of cost for extra resources to your project plan to get the work done.
options.rationale: Adding cost may not make seven years of work fit into three.

options.text: Set a meeting with the functional area experts and ask them to pick the top ideas for delivery.
options.rationale: Asking experts to pick ideas lacks objective criteria.

questions.explanation: A business case analyses the situation and applies decision criteria to options, often classifying them as required, desired or optional. Prioritising the 18 ideas by impact and cost shows which ones can deliver most of the profit goal within three years.
questions.mindset: Prioritise options by impact and cost.

questions.stem: Your project charter has been approved and your stakeholder analysis reveals multiple impacted highly paid executives with the power to influence your career. As you approach some of these stakeholders, they raise their concerns about the project, how it is progressing, and what it involves. What will you do next?

options.text: Perform an Impact over Influence analysis on all your stakeholders.
options.rationale: More analysis delays addressing the executives' concerns.

options.text: Create your project management plan and review its detail regularly with the impacted or influential stakeholders.
options.rationale: Developing the plan and reviewing it regularly with influential stakeholders addresses concerns and builds engagement.

options.text: Circulate the signed project charter to anyone who needs convincing that the project is needed.
options.rationale: Circulating the charter to convince people is one-way and unlikely to answer their questions.

options.text: Reduce your communication with most stakeholders - they can't resist what they don't know
options.rationale: Reducing communication increases uncertainty and resistance.

questions.explanation: After the charter and stakeholder identification, the project management plan defines how the work will be done. Reviewing it regularly with impacted and influential executives answers their questions about what the project involves and keeps them engaged.
questions.mindset: Engage influential stakeholders through the plan.

questions.stem: You have just created your project management plan and are reviewing it with your stakeholders. It includes the subsidiary plans of scope management, schedule, cost, resources and quality. Some of your stakeholders raise concerns that they cannot see what needs to be baselined, or how to measure the project performance and changes. What will you do next?

options.text: Advise your stakeholders the information they need is in the subsidiary plans.
options.rationale: The subsidiary plans listed do not show what is baselined or how changes are processed.

options.text: Meet as often as needed with your project stakeholders to increase their engagement and acceptance of your project.
options.rationale: More meetings do not supply the missing plan components.

options.text: Show them the project budget timeline with costs projected on a schedule.
options.rationale: A budget timeline is only part of the performance baseline.

options.text: Create the configuration management plan, change management plan and performance measurement baseline with your team, and include them in your project plan.
options.rationale: Adding the configuration and change management plans and the performance measurement baseline completes the plan.

questions.explanation: The configuration management plan identifies what is baselined, the change management plan explains how changes are processed and the performance measurement baseline integrates scope, schedule and cost to measure performance. All are components of the project management plan.
questions.mindset: A complete plan shows baselines and change control.

questions.stem: Part of your project work needs to be outsourced to a supplier. You are asked to ensure that cost for the outsourced portion of the project does not exceed $1.2 million, and if the work comes in under cost and ahead of schedule, you may provide additional money to the supplier. What sort of contract will you work with your procurement office to prepare?

options.text: Create a Firm Fixed Price contract for the seller.
options.rationale: A firm fixed price has no incentive for early or under-cost delivery.

options.text: Create a Fixed Price Incentive Fee contract for the seller.
options.rationale: Fixed price incentive fee sets a ceiling and rewards better cost and schedule performance.

options.text: Create a Cost Plus Fixed Fee contract for the seller.
options.rationale: Cost plus fixed fee has no ceiling and no incentive.

options.text: Create a Cost Plus Award Fee contract for the seller.
options.rationale: Cost plus award fee uses subjective criteria and has no price ceiling.

questions.explanation: A fixed price incentive fee contract sets a price ceiling above which the seller bears all costs, and adds financial incentives for meeting or beating agreed metrics such as cost and schedule. It suits a $1.2 million cap with rewards for early, under-cost delivery.
questions.mindset: Cap plus reward: fixed price incentive fee.

questions.stem: You take the completed scope to your project sponsor for them to accept. The Project Sponsor advises she cannot accept the deliverables as she doesn't know the outcomes of testing, and whether the scope met her requirements or needs further changes. What will you do next?

options.text: Set a meeting with the Project Sponsor directly to address their concerns.
options.rationale: Meeting without evidence does not answer the sponsor's questions.

options.text: Review the Requirements Traceability Matrix and show the Sponsor how each requirement is met by project scope.
options.rationale: The traceability matrix shows coverage but not test outcomes.

options.text: Review the Quality Report together with your testing leader, and note which items may need change requests.
options.rationale: The quality report summarises test findings and recommended corrective actions, showing the sponsor the state of deliverables.

options.text: Review the Change Requests for the project, to show the Sponsor whether any corrective actions needed to be made.
options.rationale: Existing change requests do not show current testing outcomes.

questions.explanation: The quality report summarises Control Quality findings, including test results and recommended corrective actions such as rework or repairs. Reviewing it with the testing lead shows the sponsor the state of the deliverables and identifies any needing change requests.
questions.mindset: Show test evidence before seeking acceptance.

questions.stem: Multiple unforeseen events have happened that have set your project behind schedule, and in trying to bring it back on track you have spent a considerable amount of money. Now the project sponsor has threatened to stop the project unless they can see how much the project will cost them by the time it is finished. What will you do next?

options.text: Perform Reserve Analysis on the remaining contingency and management reserves.
options.rationale: Reserve analysis shows remaining reserves, not the total forecast cost.

options.text: Create a project Estimate at Completion and compare it to the Budget at Completion.
options.rationale: An estimate at completion compared with the budget at completion shows the likely final cost.

options.text: Create the To Complete Performance Index with your project team to meet your project goal.
options.rationale: TCPI shows the efficiency needed to meet a target, not the likely final cost.

options.text: Review the Cost Performance Index (CPI) to see how the project cost is tracking.
options.rationale: CPI shows current cost efficiency but not the final cost.

questions.explanation: The estimate at completion forecasts the total cost based on performance so far. Comparing it with the budget at completion shows the sponsor the likely final cost and how far it differs from the original budget.
questions.mindset: Forecast final cost with EAC versus BAC.

questions.stem: Your project plan includes an estimate of how long the project will take (via a project schedule), how much it will cost and the resources that will be required. The Project Sponsor believes that the project can be done with around 34% fewer resources, which will save them some money and keep their area within budget. What will you do next?

options.text: Dismiss the Sponsor's comments as uneducated, and proceed with your plan as it is.
options.rationale: Dismissing the sponsor is disrespectful and unprofessional.

options.text: Reduce the resources in your project plan so the project can meet your Sponsor's expectations.
options.rationale: Cutting resources without analysis risks failure.

options.text: Create a basis of estimates with your project team and review this with your Sponsor to agree on a way forward.
options.rationale: A basis of estimates explains assumptions, constraints and ranges, so the sponsor can agree a way forward.

options.text: Raise a risk to your project delivery in the Risk Register, if the plan goes ahead with fewer resources.
options.rationale: Logging a risk does not resolve the disagreement.

questions.explanation: The basis of estimates documents how estimates were produced, including assumptions, constraints and ranges. Reviewing it with the sponsor explains the resource needs and supports an informed agreement.
questions.mindset: Explain estimates with their basis.

questions.stem: You have joined a new project team and are moving to an Agile way of work. Part of this is co-locating the team to gain the benefit of osmotic communication. Your project sponsor asks what this means. What do you tell them?

options.text: The team is able to meet more frequently when co-located.
options.rationale: Meeting more often is a benefit of co-location, but it is not osmotic communication.

options.text: It is easier to hand off work to someone if it meets their strengths.
options.rationale: Handing off work by strengths is unrelated to osmotic communication.

options.text: It is a written process made available to everyone in the team for transparency.
options.rationale: A written process is explicit communication, not osmotic.

options.text: The team will overhear conversations and information in the common area that will help them solve future problems.
options.rationale: Osmotic communication is overhearing useful background information in a shared space.

questions.explanation: Osmotic communication is the incidental overhearing of conversations and information in a shared space, which often proves useful later. It is a key benefit of co-locating agile teams.
questions.mindset: Co-location lets information flow by osmosis.

questions.stem: You are working with an Agile team who are not co-located. They are in various locations around the country. As the Agile lead, how will you get the benefit of Agile without a co-located team?

options.text: Utilise group messaging software, daily teleconference stand-ups, an electronic Kanban and backlog.
options.rationale: Messaging, virtual stand-ups and electronic boards and backlogs give distributed teams frequent contact.

options.text: Ask the organisation to re-locate the team to ensure everyone is in the same place.
options.rationale: Relocating the whole team is often infeasible and costly.

options.text: Hire or find new team members from within the organisation who are in the same place so you can co-locate.
options.rationale: Replacing team members to co-locate is disruptive.

options.text: Remove all meetings so people can focus on their work without distraction.
options.rationale: Removing meetings eliminates the communication agile relies on.

questions.explanation: When co-location is not possible, electronic tools can provide much of its benefit: group messaging, daily virtual stand-ups and electronic Kanban boards and backlogs keep a distributed team in frequent contact.
questions.mindset: Use virtual tools when co-location is impossible.

questions.stem: You are leading an Agile team that has members in various locations around the country. You have arranged daily stand-ups via phone, with electronic Kanban and backlogs, but the team is not able to meet face to face. What else will you do to increase the team working together and getting to know each other?

options.text: Have a team board with their backgrounds and pictures.
options.rationale: A picture board is informative but does not build working relationships.

options.text: Swap roles throughout the team so each member gets a feel for what others do.
options.rationale: Swapping roles can disrupt delivery and does not ensure people work together.

options.text: Pair up team members to work on tasks, and rotate the pairs for each feature.
options.rationale: Pairing members on tasks and rotating pairs builds relationships through real collaboration.

options.text: Have a virtual lunch and learn where team members share something about themselves.
options.rationale: A virtual lunch helps socially but offers less sustained interaction than working together.

questions.explanation: Pairing is a common agile practice that can apply to most tasks. Pairing members of a distributed team and rotating pairs for each feature gives them regular one-to-one collaboration, building relationships and shared knowledge.
questions.mindset: Pair and rotate to build distributed teams.

questions.stem: You are showing the project sponsor around the team area for your Agile project and see the burndown chart next to the team Kanban board. The project sponsor asks what the chart tells you. What will you say?

options.text: It shows how many team members are moving on and off the project.
options.rationale: A burndown chart does not track team membership.

options.text: It shows the remaining tasks versus what was planned for a given iteration.
options.rationale: It shows the work remaining against the plan for the iteration.

options.text: It shows the automated tests run as part of continuous integration.
options.rationale: Automated test results are shown in other displays.

options.text: It shows the return on investment for the delivered features.
options.rationale: Return on investment is not shown on a burndown chart.

questions.explanation: A burndown chart plots the work remaining in an iteration against the planned trend. The same idea can be applied to features over a release or to risks, measured in hours, tasks, cards or story points.
questions.mindset: Burndown shows remaining work against plan.

questions.stem: You are working through the feature backlog with the functional manager of the organisation, who is the product owner for your Agile team. They ask about the velocity chart that is hanging in the team area. What do you tell them it is?

options.text: The number of points, tasks or features completed by the team in each given iteration.
options.rationale: A velocity chart shows the amount of work completed by the team in each iteration.

options.text: The number of team members working on the Agile project over the life of the project.
options.rationale: A velocity chart does not show how many people are on the team over time.

options.text: How fast each team member completes their work each day.
options.rationale: Velocity is measured for the team per iteration, not per person per day.

options.text: The speed with which the project budget is being used up.
options.rationale: Budget burn is tracked separately from velocity.

questions.explanation: Team velocity is the amount of work completed in an iteration, measured in points, hours, stories, tasks or features. A velocity chart shows this for each iteration and helps with planning and forecasting.
questions.mindset: Velocity is team output per iteration.

questions.stem: In 2001, a group of individuals, representing the most widely used lightweight software development methodologies, agreed on a common set of values and principles which became known as the Agile Manifesto. Which of the following is one of the Agile Manifesto's core values?

options.text: Developer negotiation over feature collaboration.
options.rationale: This inverts and invents terms; it is not a manifesto value.

options.text: Product owner interaction over Scrum Master delegation.
options.rationale: This is not one of the four manifesto values.

options.text: Customer collaboration over contract negotiation.
options.rationale: Customer collaboration over contract negotiation is one of the four Agile Manifesto values.

options.text: Getting things right over getting the right things.
options.rationale: This is a play on words, not a manifesto value.

questions.explanation: The Agile Manifesto's four values are individuals and interactions over processes and tools, working software over comprehensive documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation and responding to change over following a plan.
questions.mindset: Know the four Agile Manifesto values.

questions.stem: You are working with your project team in a way that ensures you Analyse the requirements, then Design, Build and Test for those requirements, repeating them until the product is correct, and adjusting your product or approach as necessary before releasing in one large feature. Which project lifecycle are you using?

options.text: A Predictive project lifecycle approach.
options.rationale: Predictive plans up front and releases once, with little iteration.

options.text: An Agile project lifecycle approach
options.rationale: Agile combines iteration with frequent incremental releases, not one large release.

options.text: An Incremental project lifecycle approach
options.rationale: Incremental releases small pieces of value, not one large feature.

options.text: An Iterative project lifecycle approach
options.rationale: Iterative repeats analyse-design-build-test until right, then releases once.

questions.explanation: An iterative life cycle repeats analysis, design, build and test, adjusting the product or approach from feedback until it is right, and then releases it in one go. Incremental delivers in pieces, and agile combines both.
questions.mindset: Iterate until right, release once: iterative.

questions.stem: You are working on a project with clear procedures based on past projects. The product is clear and the risks are fairly well known as the organisation has done this before. Which is true from the below?

options.text: It is definable work, you can choose a predictive project lifecycle.
options.rationale: Definable work with known risks suits a predictive life cycle.

options.text: It is definable work, you can choose an Agile project lifecycle.
options.rationale: Agile suits high-uncertainty work, not work that is clearly defined.

options.text: It is high-uncertainty work, you can choose an incremental project lifecycle.
options.rationale: The work is clearly defined with well-known risks, so it is not high-uncertainty work.

options.text: It is high-uncertainty work, you can choose an iterative project lifecycle.
options.rationale: The work is not high-uncertainty, so an iterative life cycle is unnecessary.

questions.explanation: When the product is clear, procedures are established and risks are well known, the work is definable. A predictive life cycle, planning most of the project up front and delivering once, suits it. Adaptive life cycles suit high-uncertainty work.
questions.mindset: Definable work suits predictive life cycles.

questions.stem: You are an Agile project manager leading a project team who is used to a Waterfall way of work. The project sponsor wants to plan the entire project up front so they can see when the project will be delivered. You tell them that Agile uses adaptive planning. Why might this be a better alternative?

options.text: Adaptive planning allows the project sponsor to adapt to the project plan over time.
options.rationale: Adaptive planning adapts the plan, not the sponsor to the plan.

options.text: Adaptive planning allows the team to deliver usable features while continually reprioritising next pieces based on business value.
options.rationale: Adaptive planning delivers usable features while reprioritising upcoming work by business value.

options.text: Adaptive planning ensures that the users can adapt to the product delivered by the project team.
options.rationale: The product is adapted to users, not users to the product.

options.text: Adaptive planning is stable after the prototype is complete.
options.rationale: Adaptive planning continues throughout the project, not just after a prototype.

questions.explanation: Adaptive planning delivers value incrementally and lets the product owner reprioritise remaining work by business value as the project progresses. It gives the sponsor usable results early and a plan that reflects reality.
questions.mindset: Adaptive planning delivers value and adapts priorities.

questions.stem: You are the Scrum Master and about to begin a new iteration in your Agile project. New features have been added to the backlog, and the team are unsure of which of those features to work on next. How will you guide the product owner and the team when analysing next priority?

options.text: Analyse the value of each feature with the product owner, versus the effort and risk of each item with the Agile team.
options.rationale: Weighing each feature's value, with the product owner, against its effort and risk, with the team, gives a balanced priority.

options.text: Focus on the shortest tasks first so you can deliver value quickly.
options.rationale: Doing the shortest tasks first ignores both business value and risk.

options.text: Choose to deliver the entire project at the end so the project sponsor can see it all together.
options.rationale: Delivering everything at the end loses agile's early value.

options.text: By asking the customers what they want delivered first.
options.rationale: Customers inform value, but the product owner decides priority.

questions.explanation: The product owner decides priority on behalf of the customer and business. Good prioritisation weighs each feature's value against the effort and risk the team identifies, and high-risk items are often tackled early.
questions.mindset: Prioritise by value against effort and risk.

questions.stem: You are working through the backlog with the product owner and estimating the story cards with the development team. The team are unsure if their estimates are accurate enough. Some of the team have worked on similar projects in the past. What will you recommend they use?

options.text: Analogous estimating, using actual effort from a similar feature on a different project.
options.rationale: Actual effort from a similar feature on another project provides a grounded analogous estimate.

options.text: T-shirt sizing, using broad Small, Medium or Large sizes to accommodate variation.
options.rationale: T-shirt sizing is broad and does not improve accuracy.

options.text: Three point estimating, where the team gives the average of an optimistic, pessimistic and most likely estimate.
options.rationale: Three-point estimating helps with uncertainty, but the team has relevant past data to draw on.

options.text: The product owner should estimate the story cards as they are getting the benefit of the delivered features.
options.rationale: The product owner prioritises by value but does not estimate the team's effort.

questions.explanation: When team members have delivered similar work before, analogous estimating uses the actual effort from that feature to calibrate new estimates. It complements the usual bottom-up approach and improves confidence in accuracy.
questions.mindset: Calibrate estimates with similar past work.

questions.stem: You are working with your Agile team on your first iteration. The feature has been chosen by the product owner and the team breaks it down into user stories to work on. What is a user story?

options.text: A piece of functionality small enough to be completed in one to three days.
options.rationale: A user story is a small piece of functionality, typically completed within one to three days.

options.text: A description of a group of features from the viewpoint of the customer.
options.rationale: A group of features is an epic, not a user story.

options.text: A story about the end-user so the team understands the feature completely.
options.rationale: A user story describes what a user needs, not a narrative about the user.

options.text: A prioritised backlog that the team can choose features from.
options.rationale: A prioritised backlog is the list that contains stories.

questions.explanation: A user story is a small unit of work written from the user's perspective, typically 'As a…, I want…, so that…'. The source's rule of thumb is that a story should be completable in one to three days; larger stories are split.
questions.mindset: Stories are small, user-focused units of work.

questions.stem: You have begun a new project in a new organisation, and the project team mentions you are working in an iterative project environment. How do you know you are working within an iterative project life cycle?

options.text: The team iterates around one idea to make sure that idea is right.
options.rationale: Iterating on one idea is vague and does not define the life cycle.

options.text: You are improving the product or result through successive prototypes or proofs of concept.
options.rationale: Improving the product through successive prototypes or proofs of concept characterises an iterative life cycle.

options.text: The project sponsor says that the project lifecycle is iterative.
options.rationale: A statement by the sponsor does not tell you how the work is actually done.

options.text: You are using Agile sprints or iterations to manage your work.
options.rationale: Sprints can be used in several life cycles, including incremental and agile.

questions.explanation: An iterative life cycle improves the product through successive prototypes or proofs of concept, gathering feedback each time, and then releases the finished product in one go.
questions.mindset: Successive prototypes mean iterative.

questions.stem: In 2001, a group of individuals, representing the most widely used lightweight software development methodologies, agreed on a common set of values and principles which became known as the Agile Manifesto. Which of the following is another of the Agile Manifesto's core values?

options.text: Developing as much as possible to see what gets the best result.
options.rationale: Building as much as possible is not a manifesto value and creates waste.

options.text: Finding a product owner over finding a development team.
options.rationale: Finding a product owner over a development team is not one of the four manifesto values.

options.text: Cross functional team members over executive buy-in.
options.rationale: Cross-functional team members over executive buy-in is not one of the four manifesto values.

options.text: Responding to change over following a plan.
options.rationale: Responding to change over following a plan is one of the four Agile Manifesto values.

questions.explanation: The four Agile Manifesto values are individuals and interactions over processes and tools, working software over comprehensive documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation and responding to change over following a plan.
questions.mindset: Value responding to change.

questions.stem: You are working on a project where the organisation wants to move towards an Agile way of work. Which two project lifecycles combine to create an Agile environment?

options.text: Iterative and Predictive lifecycles.
options.rationale: Predictive is not part of an agile life cycle.

options.text: Incremental and Predictive lifecycles.
options.rationale: Predictive is not part of an agile life cycle.

options.text: Iterative and Incremental lifecycles.
options.rationale: Agile combines iterative refinement with incremental delivery.

options.text: Predictive and Agile lifecycles.
options.rationale: Agile is the result, not one of the components.

questions.explanation: An agile life cycle combines iterative development, which improves the product through feedback, with incremental delivery, which releases small pieces of value frequently.
questions.mindset: Agile = iterative + incremental.

questions.stem: You have come on board a new project team and have been advised that the project works with a predictive style project lifecycle. How will you know you are working in a "Predictive" or Waterfall style approach?

options.text: The bulk of planning is done up front, then executed in a single, sequential process.
options.rationale: Most planning up front, then sequential execution, defines a predictive life cycle.

options.text: The bulk of the planning is done up front, then prototypes are created to gather feedback before releasing in one go.
options.rationale: Up-front planning with prototypes before one release describes iterative.

options.text: A product roadmap is created and smaller features are designed and released as part of the whole.
options.rationale: A roadmap with small releases describes incremental.

options.text: The project uses feature sprints, Kanban boards and retrospectives to manage their work.
options.rationale: Sprints, Kanban and retrospectives describe agile.

questions.explanation: A predictive or waterfall life cycle does most planning up front and then executes in a single sequential process. It suits definable work where risks are well understood.
questions.mindset: Plan up front, execute in sequence: predictive.

questions.stem: You are working as a project manager in an Agile team. Which of the below are NOT examples of execution practices you will see in Agile?

options.text: Test at all levels, where the team applies end-to-end testing and unit testing (of an individual story or feature). Agile teams prefer automated tests.
options.rationale: Testing at all levels, often automated, is an agile execution practice.

options.text: Test-Driven Development, where the team writes automated tests before writing the product code to help mistake-proof the product.
options.rationale: Test-driven development is an agile execution practice.

options.text: Spikes, which are time-boxed research or experiments and useful for estimation, acceptance criteria definition, or learning some critical technical or functional element.
options.rationale: Spikes are an agile practice for research and learning.

options.text: Project management plan, where the project is planned is detail up front to avoid misunderstanding by project stakeholders.
options.rationale: A detailed up-front project management plan is a predictive artefact, not an agile execution practice.

questions.explanation: Agile execution practices include testing at all levels with automation, test-driven development and spikes—time-boxed research to reduce uncertainty. A detailed up-front project management plan belongs to predictive approaches.
questions.mindset: Recognise agile practices.

questions.stem: The business partner or product owner continuously refines, or grooms, the product backlog. This includes adding new stories, reprioritizing stories, and removing stories when needed. What role does the development team take during this process?

options.text: Developing the cards as soon as they are added to ensure maximum value.
options.rationale: Developing cards as soon as they are added bypasses prioritisation.

options.text: Removing cards from the backlog that do not make sense to complete.
options.rationale: The product owner, not the team, decides which cards to remove.

options.text: Estimating the work needed for each card so the product owner can prioritise based on value and effort.
options.rationale: The team estimates each card so the product owner can prioritise by value and effort.

options.text: Coming to daily stand-ups to report on what was done yesterday and what will be done today.
options.rationale: Stand-ups are separate from backlog refinement.

questions.explanation: During backlog refinement, the product owner adds, reorders and removes stories while the development team estimates the work. Estimates let the product owner prioritise based on value and time to deliver.
questions.mindset: The team sizes; the product owner prioritises.

questions.stem: You have been estimating story cards with your Agile project team, but the effort captured has not been matching the time it ends up taking to complete. What is the most likely reason for this occurring?

options.text: The team have not included sick days in the estimate.
options.rationale: Sick days affect capacity, not story estimates.

options.text: The team have not included testing or refactoring in the estimate.
options.rationale: Omitting testing and refactoring is a common cause of underestimation.

options.text: The team have not included time to merge the code for continuous integration.
options.rationale: The source identifies time to merge code for continuous integration as the missing element.

options.text: The team have not included the time it takes for the daily stand-up.
options.rationale: Stand-up time is team overhead, not part of story estimates.

questions.explanation: Story estimates should include all the activity needed to finish a card, including integration, testing, refactoring, complexity and risk. Leaving out work such as merging code for continuous integration makes estimates consistently too low.
questions.mindset: Estimate everything needed to finish a story.

questions.stem: The 12th principle of Agile is "At regular intervals, the team reflects on how to become more effective, then tunes and adjusts its behaviour accordingly." In practice, this is a Retrospective. But what is the practical reason for including Retrospectives in an Agile team?

options.text: It reduces the communication time between the project sponsor and the developers.
options.rationale: Retrospectives are team-focused and do not address sponsor communication time.

options.text: It ensures features are released on schedule and on budget.
options.rationale: Retrospectives do not by themselves guarantee schedule or budget outcomes.

options.text: It helps the team learn about and improve their process over time.
options.rationale: Retrospectives help the team learn about and improve its process over time.

options.text: It keeps the team focused on the main feature to deliver the most business value.
options.rationale: Focusing on business value is the product owner's role through backlog prioritisation.

questions.explanation: The twelfth agile principle calls for regular reflection and adjustment. Retrospectives put it into practice, giving the team structured, regular feedback so it can learn about its process and improve continuously.
questions.mindset: Reflect regularly to improve.

questions.stem: Retrospectives are typically held at the end of an iteration, but an Agile team can also hold retrospectives at any other time. What is NOT a time that an Agile team might hold a retrospective?

options.text: When the team completes or ships something new.
options.rationale: Completing or shipping something is a natural time to reflect.

options.text: When more than a few weeks have passed since the previous retrospective.
options.rationale: A long gap since the last retrospective is a reason to hold one.

options.text: When the team appears to be stuck and completed work is not flowing.
options.rationale: When work is stuck, a retrospective helps find out why.

options.text: When the feature backlog has not been created and work is yet to begin.
options.rationale: Before any work or process exists there is nothing to reflect on, so a retrospective is not useful.

questions.explanation: Retrospectives gather feedback on a process that is already in use. Teams hold them after shipping, when too much time has passed or when work gets stuck, but not before any work has begun.
questions.mindset: Retrospect on real experience.

questions.stem: You are in a new project team and working through which project lifecycle or way of work to use in order to deliver the products to your customer, and how far to modify it. What are some of the project factors that will influence your tailoring decisions to use Agile or other methods?

options.text: Which project lifecycle the customer wants to use.
options.rationale: The customer's preference is a consideration but not a project factor that determines fit.

options.text: What the latest lifecycle is - the latest one must be the best and will be most interesting to upper management.
options.rationale: Novelty is not a reason to choose a life cycle.

options.text: Whether the flow of work is often interrupted by various delays or impediments, and is easily definable or highly uncertain.
options.rationale: How often flow is interrupted and whether the work is definable or uncertain are key tailoring factors.

options.text: Project approaches should never be tailored - we should follow one approach to the letter so we make no mistakes.
options.rationale: Tailoring is expected; rigid adherence ignores context.

questions.explanation: Tailoring decisions depend on project factors such as whether the work is definable or highly uncertain, how often flow is interrupted by delays or impediments, and the team's experience. These factors point towards more predictive or more adaptive approaches.
questions.mindset: Tailor to the nature of the work.

questions.stem: You are in the forming stages of a new project team, and deciding on the way of work to use when operating as a team. What are some of the factors that will influence how you tailor the project lifecycle?

options.text: The demand pattern for value or delivery: is it steady or sporadic?
options.rationale: The demand pattern is one factor, but not the only one listed that applies.

options.text: The rate of process improvement required by the team.
options.rationale: The required rate of process improvement is one factor, but not the only one listed.

options.text: Is more than one team is needed to build the product?
options.rationale: Whether several teams are needed is one factor, but not the only one listed.

options.text: All of the above.
options.rationale: All of these factors influence how the project life cycle is tailored.

questions.explanation: Many factors influence how a life cycle is tailored, including the demand pattern for delivery, the rate of process improvement needed, whether several teams are involved, the certainty of the work and the team's experience. All the listed factors apply.
questions.mindset: Many factors shape tailoring.

questions.stem: You are delivering features through your Agile project and the project sponsor and product owner are happy with the progress. Your project sponsor raises a concern about future items and what that development looks like. What will you show them?

options.text: The Project Management Plan, that has outlined the project delivery in full.
options.rationale: A full up-front plan is predictive and not how agile shows future work.

options.text: The product backlog, that has the list of features the team will deliver.
options.rationale: The backlog lists features but not when they are planned.

options.text: The product roadmap, that shows planned future features and their approximate dates, similarly to a Gantt Chart.
options.rationale: The product roadmap shows planned future features and approximate release dates at a high level.

options.text: The team velocity chart, that shows how much the team completes each iteration.
options.rationale: Velocity shows capacity, not future features.

questions.explanation: A product roadmap is a high-level visual of planned releases and features over time, similar to a schedule but built around agile releases. It is revised as priorities change and answers questions about future development.
questions.mindset: Show future plans with a product roadmap.

questions.stem: Your Agile team is estimating story cards using planning poker. For one of the larger features, some of the team has estimated three points, while the others have estimated eight points. How will you guide the team to come to an estimate?

options.text: Ask them to average out the points and assign that value to the card.
options.rationale: Averaging hides the different understandings behind the estimates.

options.text: Change the method of estimating to accommodate the team decision.
options.rationale: Changing method avoids the useful discussion that differing estimates provoke.

options.text: Change the feature to make it easier to estimate on.
options.rationale: Changing the feature to make it easier to estimate is not the purpose of estimation.

options.text: Ask the high and low estimates to discuss their reasons, and the team to estimate again until a consensus is reached or more information is needed.
options.rationale: The high and low estimators explain their reasoning and the team re-estimates until consensus.

questions.explanation: In planning poker, widely differing estimates reveal different assumptions. The highest and lowest estimators explain their reasoning, then the team estimates again, repeating until consensus or until it decides more information is needed.
questions.mindset: Discuss outliers, then re-estimate.

questions.stem: The Agile team is working through a particularly complex feature that is difficult for the team find a solution for. As the Agile lead, you recommend a spike. What is a spike?

options.text: A shifting of the feature into another iteration.
options.rationale: Moving a feature to another iteration is deferral, not a spike.

options.text: A time-boxed task to explore or investigate an issue.
options.rationale: A spike is a time-boxed task to explore or investigate an issue.

options.text: A short meeting at the beginning of the day to discuss tasks in progress.
options.rationale: A short meeting at the start of the day to discuss tasks is the daily stand-up, not a spike.

options.text: A demonstration of the feature to the product owner.
options.rationale: A demonstration to the product owner is a review.

questions.explanation: A spike is a time-boxed piece of research or experimentation, separate from development work, used to reduce uncertainty about a difficult problem. It helps the team find a solution or estimate more reliably.
questions.mindset: Use spikes to reduce uncertainty.

questions.stem: The Agile manifesto has twelve clarifying principles added to it to help projects and teams understand the Agile values. Which of the below is a correct clarifying principle?

options.text: Tailor the project approach to suit the project and the team.
options.rationale: Tailoring is good practice but not one of the twelve principles.

options.text: Ensure executive buy-in by reporting frequently to your managers.
options.rationale: Frequent reporting to managers is not an agile principle.

options.text: Deliver working software frequently, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, with a preference to the shorter timescale.
options.rationale: Delivering working software frequently, preferring shorter timescales, is one of the twelve principles.

options.text: Ensure complete planning for your product and release once tested thoroughly.
options.rationale: Complete up-front planning is predictive, not agile.

questions.explanation: One of the twelve agile principles is to deliver working software frequently, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, with a preference for the shorter timescale. Frequent delivery provides early value and feedback.
questions.mindset: Deliver working software frequently.

questions.stem: The Agile manifesto has twelve clarifying principles added to it to help projects and teams understand the Agile values. Which of the below is another correct clarifying principle?

options.text: Business people should dictate to the development team what to do and how to do it.
options.rationale: Business dictating to developers contradicts agile collaboration.

options.text: Developers can code and release products at a schedule that suits them, for complete autonomy.
options.rationale: Developers releasing on their own schedule ignores business collaboration.

options.text: Business people and developers mustn't work together, but they can chat about their work over lunch.
options.rationale: Limiting interaction to lunch contradicts the principle of daily collaboration.

options.text: Business people and developers must work together daily throughout the project.
options.rationale: Business people and developers working together daily is one of the twelve principles.

questions.explanation: One of the twelve agile principles states that business people and developers must work together daily throughout the project. Close, continuous collaboration keeps the product aligned with business needs.
questions.mindset: Business and developers collaborate daily.

questions.stem: The Agile manifesto has twelve clarifying principles added to it to help projects and teams understand the Agile values. Which of the below is also a correct clarifying principle?

options.text: Build projects around a core idea, then brainstorm frequently to get the job done.
options.rationale: Frequent brainstorming around a core idea is not an agile principle.

options.text: Find the right executive support and ensure they tell you the product requirements.
options.rationale: Executives dictating requirements contradicts customer collaboration.

options.text: Deliver frequently whether an item has been tested or not, as quality is everyone's responsibility.
options.rationale: Delivering untested work contradicts the focus on technical excellence.

options.text: Build projects around motivated individuals. Give them the environment and support they need and trust them to get the job done.
options.rationale: Building projects around motivated individuals and trusting them is one of the twelve principles.

questions.explanation: One of the twelve agile principles is to build projects around motivated individuals, give them the environment and support they need and trust them to get the job done. Leaders remove blockers and enable flow.
questions.mindset: Trust and support motivated people.

questions.stem: The twelve Agile clarifying principles also match up with the best advice for projects, leadership and communication. Which of the below is a correct clarifying principle when it comes to project communication?

options.text: The most efficient and effective method of conveying information to and within a development team is face to face conversation.
options.rationale: Face-to-face conversation is the most efficient and effective way to convey information, per the principles.

options.text: Communication is always done in writing to ensure you have ongoing proof the communication occurred.
options.rationale: Writing everything down for proof is not an agile principle.

options.text: Agile teams ensure downward communication only so the executive in charge directs the product features and work.
options.rationale: Downward-only communication contradicts agile collaboration.

options.text: When communicating ensure to use various forms such as telephone, writing, face-to- face, and ensure variety.
options.rationale: Variety of channels is not the principle; face-to-face is preferred.

questions.explanation: One of the twelve agile principles states that the most efficient and effective way to convey information to and within a development team is face-to-face conversation, which is why agile teams favour co-location.
questions.mindset: Prefer face-to-face conversation.

questions.stem: The Agile manifesto has twelve clarifying principles added to it to help projects and teams understand the Agile values. Identify a correct clarifying principle from the options below.

options.text: Union attendance is the best measure of team happiness.
options.rationale: Union attendance is not an agile principle or a measure of progress.

options.text: Working software is the primary measure of progress.
options.rationale: Working software is the primary measure of progress, according to the principles.

options.text: Finding risks is the only way to avoid failure.
options.rationale: Finding risks is useful, but this is not one of the principles.

options.text: Learning new things keeps a team engaged.
options.rationale: Learning is valuable, but this is not one of the twelve principles.

questions.explanation: One of the twelve agile principles states that working software is the primary measure of progress. Progress is shown by what actually works, not by documents or activity.
questions.mindset: Measure progress by working product.

questions.stem: You are working through a sprint planning meeting with your team. The team have sized up the cards and prioritised the backlog. What will you do next to determine how much work can be done during this iteration?

options.text: Count up the user stories that the product owner wants completed by the end of the iteration.
options.rationale: The product owner's wishes do not determine the team's capacity.

options.text: Check the team's velocity against the number of points for the story cards you want to complete.
options.rationale: Comparing velocity with the points of the desired stories shows what can realistically be done.

options.text: Ask the Scrum Master to allocate work to each team member in the fairest manner possible.
options.rationale: The scrum master does not allocate work; the team self-organises.

options.text: Look at other teams and what they did in the last iteration to give the best idea for your team.
options.rationale: Other teams' results do not reflect this team's capacity.

questions.explanation: Velocity is the average amount of work the team completes per sprint. Comparing it with the total points of the stories the product owner wants shows how much can realistically fit, and the selection can then be adjusted.
questions.mindset: Plan to velocity.

questions.stem: You are the Agile lead or Scrum Master for your Agile team and planning for the next iteration is about to begin. What will you do first?

options.text: Break down the features into user stories.
options.rationale: Features should already be broken into stories before iteration planning.

options.text: Write the story card acceptance criteria with the team.
options.rationale: Acceptance criteria are refined before or during planning, but prioritisation comes first.

options.text: Choose which stories the team will work on in the iteration.
options.rationale: Stories are chosen after priorities are confirmed.

options.text: Work with the product owner to prioritise the highest value ones to work on.
options.rationale: Working with the product owner to prioritise the highest-value stories is the first step in planning.

questions.explanation: At the start of iteration planning, the product owner confirms the priority of the stories, based on business value. The team then selects what it can complete given its velocity.
questions.mindset: Start planning with value priorities.

questions.stem: You are the Agile project manager working on a software project, and the development team have identified a major risk for the delivery of a certain feature. That feature is not scheduled until very late in the project. What will you do next?

options.text: Wait until later in the project, as the problem may be fixed by other features going in.
options.rationale: Waiting leaves a major risk unaddressed until late, when it is most costly.

options.text: Ask the developers to find a way to proceed without that feature.
options.rationale: Dropping the feature may remove value the customer needs.

options.text: Plan a spike around the risk, identify a solution then prioritise that feature earlier in development.
options.rationale: A spike explores the risk and finds a solution, and prioritising the feature earlier reduces exposure.

options.text: Remove all other story cards from the current sprint so the team can swarm around the issue and fix it.
options.rationale: Stopping all other work is disproportionate; a time-boxed spike by some of the team is enough.

questions.explanation: Agile teams tackle risks early. A time-boxed spike investigates the risk and finds a way forward, and moving the feature earlier in the backlog means the uncertainty is resolved before much investment depends on it.
questions.mindset: Investigate and front-load risky features.

questions.stem: You are working in a new Agile team and have reviewed the team velocity over the past three iterations. The maximum number of points completed was 35, and the fewest was 25. What will you do next?

options.text: Push the team to complete five more than the maximum, and roll over any incomplete cards to the next iteration.
options.rationale: Pushing beyond the team's maximum is unsustainable and contrary to agile practice.

options.text: Set 35 as the Work in Progress (WIP) limit, and adjust it during future iterations if the team is able to pull more work than assigned.
options.rationale: The source sets 35 as a WIP limit, adjusting it if the team can pull more work.

options.text: Add more people to the team to complete the work, because 35 is not enough.
options.rationale: Adding people is premature and increases coordination overhead.

options.text: Reduce the number of features in the product backlog to suit the team velocity.
options.rationale: Cutting the backlog to fit velocity removes value rather than planning realistically.

questions.explanation: Agile teams work at a sustainable pace. Using the known velocity to cap the work taken on avoids overburdening the team, while members can still pull in more work when they finish early, and the limit can be reviewed.
questions.mindset: Plan to a sustainable pace.

questions.stem: You are working on the product backlog with your Agile project team, and creating user stories to be prioritised. Which of the below is the best answer for what should go into a user story card?

options.text: Key risks of the project and the feature being delivered, with their owners and mitigations.
options.rationale: Project risks and mitigations belong in the risk register, not on a story card.

options.text: A wireframe of the feature to be developed that developers can work with.
options.rationale: A wireframe can support a story but is not what the card must contain.

options.text: The requirement, its criticality, expected development and test duration, and the acceptance criteria for that story.
options.rationale: A story card holds the requirement, its criticality, expected development and test effort and acceptance criteria.

options.text: The benefit of the feature so key stakeholders are aware of what they will get.
options.rationale: The benefit is useful context but is only part of a complete card.

questions.explanation: A good user story card contains the requirement, its criticality, expected development and test effort and clear acceptance criteria, giving the team enough information to prioritise, estimate and verify the work.
questions.mindset: Story cards carry requirement and acceptance criteria.

questions.stem: The executive management in your organisation has assembled a new team, and dictated that they will use Agile for their product development. As the project progresses, there is confusion about the product scope and what the definition of done looks like. As an Agile Project Manager, what will you recommend to the executive team?

options.text: Select a person from each part of the organisation to assist, to ensure diversity.
options.rationale: Diversity is useful but does not bring the requirement owners into the team.

options.text: Have the functional manager select their friends or favourite team members.
options.rationale: Choosing friends or favourites is not a sound basis for team formation.

options.text: Encourage a self-organizing team to form, including the people who asked for the requirements and outcomes in the first place.
options.rationale: A self-organising team including those who defined the requirements and outcomes brings ownership and product expertise.

options.text: Hire external consultants to run the project and create the product.
options.rationale: External consultants lack the organisation's product knowledge and ownership.

questions.explanation: Confusion about scope and the definition of done often means the people who understand the requirements are not in the team. A self-organising team that includes those who asked for the outcomes brings ownership and expertise that cannot easily be bought.
questions.mindset: Put the people who own the outcomes in the team.

questions.stem: You are running an Agile project and meet with the team for the next sprint planning meeting. What will you do next?

options.text: Negotiate the scope and costs of the project with the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Negotiating project scope and cost with the sponsor is not part of sprint planning.

options.text: Walk through three questions with the team-What did I do yesterday? What will I do today? Is anything blocking me?
options.rationale: The three questions belong to the daily stand-up.

options.text: The development team demonstrates the working feature to the product owner, who marks it as complete.
options.rationale: Demonstrating work to the product owner happens at the sprint review.

options.text: The product owner shares the updated backlog, and the team discusses it to ensure a shared understanding.
options.rationale: The product owner shares the updated backlog and the team discusses it to reach a shared understanding.

questions.explanation: Sprint planning starts with the product owner presenting the updated, prioritised backlog. The team discusses the items to ensure a shared understanding before selecting the work for the sprint.
questions.mindset: Start sprint planning from a shared view of the backlog.

questions.stem: You are working with a team that is new to Agile and are using Scrum to manage the project. The business representative is confused about the difference between a sprint review and a sprint retrospective. What will you tell them?

options.text: Sprint reviews demonstrate the work completed in the sprint. Sprint retrospectives look at all the work completed in the project.
options.rationale: A retrospective looks at how the team worked during the sprint, not all project work.

options.text: Sprint reviews discuss what is worked on in the sprint. Sprint retrospectives are done at the end of the project for a lessons learned opportunity.
options.rationale: Retrospectives happen every sprint, not only at the end of the project.

options.text: Sprint reviews review the lessons learned. Sprint retrospectives look at the history of the product retrospectively.
options.rationale: Reviews demonstrate product; retrospectives are for process lessons, not product history.

options.text: Sprint reviews are for product demonstrations. Sprint retrospectives are for lessons learned.
options.rationale: Sprint reviews demonstrate the product; retrospectives capture lessons to improve the process.

questions.explanation: The sprint review demonstrates the work completed to stakeholders and gathers feedback on the product. The sprint retrospective is the team's lessons-learned session on its own process: what went well, what did not and what to change.
questions.mindset: Review the product; retrospect on the process.

questions.stem: The Agile team for which you are the project manager has determined several key features to deliver to the customer. How should the team handle these feature ideas?

options.text: The features should be prioritized, developed, tested and delivered incrementally
options.rationale: Prioritising, developing, testing and delivering incrementally gives value early with quality.

options.text: The features should be delivered quickly, whether or not they are complete, to gather feedback
options.rationale: Delivering incomplete features sacrifices quality, which remains everyone's responsibility.

options.text: The features should be delivered according to the project plan
options.rationale: Following a fixed plan is predictive and ignores changing priorities.

options.text: All features should be delivered at the end of the project
options.rationale: Delivering everything at the end loses early value and feedback.

questions.explanation: Agile combines iterative development with incremental delivery. Features are prioritised by value, developed, tested and delivered in increments the customer can use, with quality built in throughout.
questions.mindset: Prioritise, build, test and deliver in increments.

questions.stem: While meeting with the customers or business owners, they introduce several pieces of new functionality into the product backlog list. The deadline for the product cannot be changed. What will you do next?

options.text: Tell the team to work overtime in order to deliver the project
options.rationale: Overtime is unsustainable and contrary to agile's sustainable pace.

options.text: Stand by your team and tell the customers the project will not be delivered on time
options.rationale: Telling customers the project will be late ignores the flexibility of scope.

options.text: Be sure the customers understand that lower priority features may not be completed at all
options.rationale: Customers must understand that with a fixed deadline, lower-priority features may not be completed.

options.text: Place the new features in a "parking lot" that can be completed if time allows
options.rationale: A parking lot hides the trade-off instead of making it explicit through prioritisation.

questions.explanation: Agile welcomes change even late, but with a fixed deadline and a sustainable pace, scope is the variable. Customers need to understand that adding features means lower-priority ones may not be completed at all.
questions.mindset: With fixed time, scope flexes.

questions.stem: You are working on a project as an Agile project manager. You look at the product backlog and ensure several features, or minimum viable products (MVPs) can be scheduled for delivery throughout the duration of the project. Why is this a good idea?

options.text: To show executives that progress is being made by the development team
options.rationale: Showing progress to executives is a side effect, not the main purpose.

options.text: To keep the project duration short
options.rationale: Incremental delivery does not necessarily shorten the project.

options.text: To enable users to test the product for quality, and give feedback
options.rationale: User feedback is valuable, but the primary reason is early value.

options.text: To enable the business to get value quickly, as features are delivered
options.rationale: Scheduling MVPs throughout lets the business gain value as each is delivered.

questions.explanation: Minimum viable products are usable in their own right. Scheduling several for delivery throughout the project lets the business realise value early, while also gathering feedback on how they are used.
questions.mindset: Deliver usable value early and often.

questions.stem: You are working on a complex software project but see that the team uses a whiteboard, and writes tasks on cards or sticky notes. The business representative seems put off by the use of these low-tech tools on such a high profile technology project. What will you tell them?

options.text: The team are using low-tech tools so low-tech people can understand them.
options.rationale: The board is not about the audience's technical ability.

options.text: A whiteboard is actually a complex thing, they just don't know it yet.
options.rationale: This dismisses the concern rather than explaining the practice.

options.text: The team is using the principle of visual management, and by using a physical board it is transparent to anyone who needs the information.
options.rationale: Visual management makes information transparent to anyone who needs it, and a physical board does this well.

options.text: The team will drop everything and develop a new software-based Kanban board to avoid embarrassment.
options.rationale: Rebuilding the board to avoid embarrassment wastes effort and misses the point.

questions.explanation: Visual management is a lean principle adopted by agile teams. Low-tech, high-touch tools such as physical Kanban boards make key information visible at a glance to anyone who walks through the team area.
questions.mindset: Make information visible, even on a whiteboard.
