questions.stem: You are working with your agile team, and they are confused about when the best time is to determine the acceptance test criteria for the feature or story card. What time will you tell them?

options.text: When the first iteration is complete
options.rationale: Waiting until after the first iteration is too late for work already done.

options.text: During estimation and elaboration of the card, with the product owner, business analysts and development team
options.rationale: Acceptance criteria are defined during estimation and elaboration, with the product owner, analysts and team.

options.text: Before the product or feature is prioritised
options.rationale: Before prioritisation, the story may not be detailed enough to define tests.

options.text: At the end of the project
options.rationale: Defining acceptance criteria at the end of the project is far too late to guide the work.

questions.explanation: Acceptance criteria and tests are designed before development, during story elaboration and estimation, often in 'Given, When, Then' form. Defining them early ensures everyone agrees what done means.
questions.mindset: Define acceptance criteria before building.

questions.stem: You working as an Agile project manager in a team with many stakeholders who have not worked on an Agile project before. Some of these stakeholders come to you with valid concerns about the Agile methods being used. As a servant leader or project coach, what will you do to make them more comfortable with the process?

options.text: Educate the stakeholders, address their concerns, and keep them engaged
options.rationale: Educating stakeholders, addressing their concerns and keeping them engaged builds comfort with the new approach.

options.text: Tell them is has worked in the past, it will work here too
options.rationale: Saying it worked before dismisses valid concerns.

options.text: Dictate to the stakeholders that this is how all future projects must be executed
options.rationale: Dictating a method undermines trust and engagement.

options.text: Go back to a Waterfall style project management method
options.rationale: Reverting to waterfall abandons the approach without addressing concerns.

questions.explanation: Stakeholders new to agile often have valid concerns. A servant leader educates them about the approach, addresses their concerns and keeps them engaged, helping them become comfortable with the new way of working.
questions.mindset: Educate and engage stakeholders new to agile.

questions.stem: A team new to Agile has worked closely with the product owner and has identified the highest value features of the project. What is one reason to break those features down into increments and deliver them as soon as possible?

options.text: To get all the work out of the way so the team can relax.
options.rationale: Delivering to get work out of the way is not a value-driven reason.

options.text: So the project lifecycle can be shortened.
options.rationale: Incremental delivery does not necessarily shorten the life cycle.

options.text: So the product owner can report to her executive manager that work is being done.
options.rationale: Reporting activity is not the purpose of incremental delivery.

options.text: To reduce the risk of the feature no longer providing value for the customer.
options.rationale: The longer delivery takes, the greater the risk the feature no longer provides value.

questions.explanation: Value can decay over time as markets and needs change. Delivering the highest-value features in increments as soon as possible reduces the risk that they will no longer provide the intended benefit by the time they arrive.
questions.mindset: Deliver value before it decays.

questions.stem: You are an Agile project manager working closely with the Scrum Master and Agile team. The Scrum Master mentions that Agile works differently with risk compared to a traditional project. He sets a meeting with you and the team to talk through Agile risks. What will you do next?

options.text: Ensure the team notes and schedules high-risk activities early in the project so that they are mitigated quickly.
options.rationale: Scheduling high-risk activities early reduces risk quickly as the project progresses.

options.text: Ensure the team identifies risks, places them in a register and mitigates them by the end of the project.
options.rationale: Mitigating risks only by the end of the project leaves exposure high throughout.

options.text: Ensure the team keeps the risk register to itself, so other stakeholders don't think less of the project.
options.rationale: Hiding the risk register from stakeholders undermines transparency.

options.text: Ensure risk is only captured around people because an Agile team prefers individuals and interactions over processes and tools.
options.rationale: Agile values do not limit risk management to people-related risks.

questions.explanation: Agile teams deliver incrementally and deal with risk early. Noting high-risk activities and scheduling them near the start of the project reduces uncertainty and future risk as work progresses.
questions.mindset: Front-load risky work.

questions.stem: You are a project manager on an Agile project that requires an external third party to develop software for one of your features. You have worked with the project team to gather the requirements and backlog of product features. You begin working with your procurement department on a contract for the vendor. What will you do next?

options.text: Request that the contract is one that accommodates changes to product scope.
options.rationale: A contract that accommodates changes to scope fits agile delivery, where scope evolves.

options.text: Go back to the business and ask them to deliver the feature
options.rationale: Asking the business to deliver the feature ignores the decision to use a vendor.

options.text: Raise a risk to the delivery of your project based on the external vendor
options.rationale: Raising a risk does not produce a suitable contract.

options.text: Find an existing "time and materials" contract from the organisation's Organisational Process Assets.
options.rationale: Reusing an old contract without checking fit may not suit this work.

questions.explanation: Agile projects usually fix schedule and quality while scope evolves. A vendor contract must therefore accommodate changes to product scope so the relationship can adapt as the backlog changes.
questions.mindset: Agile vendor contracts must allow scope change.

questions.stem: You are an Agile project manager tasked with evolving your part of the organisation into Agile. What is NOT something you would do, when making this change?

options.text: Treat the change as an Agile project, with its own backlog of changes that could be introduced by the team based on perceived value.
options.rationale: Treating the transformation as an agile project with its own backlog is a recommended practice.

options.text: Treat each of the changes as an experiment, tested for a short period of time to determine suitability or the need for further refinement.
options.rationale: Treating changes as short experiments is a recommended practice.

options.text: Use Kanban boards to track progress, showing new approaches in use as "done", and things being tried as "in progress".
options.rationale: Tracking adoption on a Kanban board is a recommended practice.

options.text: Direct the teams to take on Agile in one go, moving ahead without wavering.
options.rationale: Directing teams to adopt agile all at once contradicts agile's incremental, experimental approach.

questions.explanation: An agile transformation can itself be run in an agile way: a backlog of changes prioritised by value, each tried as a short experiment and tracked on a Kanban board. Imposing everything at once contradicts the approach being adopted.
questions.mindset: Adopt agile incrementally.

questions.stem: As an Agile project manager, you understand the need to operate with openness and transparency with your team and stakeholders. How will you encourage knowledge sharing throughout the project?

options.text: Tell your team what to do during work hours, so they can learn from you.
options.rationale: Telling people what to do is directive and does not create shared knowledge.

options.text: Write a process document for the team to read through in their spare time.
options.rationale: A process document to read in spare time is passive and unlikely to be read.

options.text: Make key information visible in the team area, and ensure all impacted stakeholders are invited to the daily stand-up, retrospectives, and even iteration planning.
options.rationale: Visible information and open invitations to agile ceremonies spread knowledge throughout the project.

options.text: Form a key group of executive stakeholders to share project information with, to ensure your good reputation within the company.
options.rationale: Sharing only with executives for reputation's sake undermines transparency.

questions.explanation: Agile teams share knowledge through visible information in the team area and by inviting stakeholders to stand-ups, retrospectives and planning. Openness and interaction spread knowledge far better than documents alone.
questions.mindset: Share knowledge openly and visibly.

questions.stem: The team are planning their first upcoming sprint on an Agile project. They have worked with the product owner who has gathered a backlog of features in prioritised order. As an Agile project manager, what must you do to ensure you can plan future sprints correctly?

options.text: Find the best performer in the team so you know who you can rely on.
options.rationale: Finding the best performer does not help plan team capacity.

options.text: Find your team's velocity over the next few sprints so you can set a sustainable pace.
options.rationale: Establishing velocity over the first few sprints enables realistic, sustainable planning.

options.text: Set a working group meeting to gain executive buy-in.
options.rationale: Executive buy-in is not what enables accurate sprint planning.

options.text: Create the project management plan and draw out the schedule in advance.
options.rationale: A detailed schedule in advance is a predictive approach.

questions.explanation: Sprint planning is based on velocity, the average amount of work the team completes per sprint. A new team needs a few sprints to establish its velocity, which then supports planning at a sustainable pace.
questions.mindset: Establish velocity to plan sustainably.

questions.stem: You are working on the requirements for the next iteration and a decision needs to be made by the team. The product owner suggests using a show of hands to indicate whether team members are for or against the decision. As the Agile project manager, you object to this approach. Why?

options.text: Agile is about software, and the team should use software to vote on the decision.
options.rationale: Using software to vote does not solve the problem with simple for-or-against voting.

options.text: The decision may not go in your favour, so it's best to just do it yourself.
options.rationale: Deciding alone because a vote may go against you undermines the team.

options.text: Decisions should take time to work through, not be voted on quickly.
options.rationale: Speed is not the objection; visible voting without discussion is.

options.text: By making their decisions visible, team members may be influenced by others in the team (especially executives) without the benefit of discussion.
options.rationale: Visible votes let members be swayed by others, especially seniors, without discussion of alternatives.

questions.explanation: A simple show of hands allows no discussion and lets people be influenced by others' visible votes, particularly those more senior. Techniques that encourage discussion or hide initial votes lead to better, more independent decisions.
questions.mindset: Avoid decision methods that invite undue influence.

questions.stem: You are at the beginning of a new iteration and about to plan and decide what gets worked on in the upcoming sprint. You decide to invite all project stakeholders to the planning meeting to decide what to work on next. Why is it important that all stakeholders are involved in decision-making?

options.text: So you can keep an eye on what they are doing
options.rationale: Monitoring stakeholders is not the purpose of involving them.

options.text: So business representatives can report back to their managers on the project
options.rationale: Reporting back to managers is a side effect, not the reason.

options.text: So the team feels important, with lots of stakeholders present
options.rationale: Making the team feel important is not the reason for involvement.

options.text: So the project stakeholders don't reject a decision that wasn't theirs
options.rationale: Stakeholders involved in decisions own them and are less likely to reject them.

questions.explanation: Involving stakeholders in decision-making gives them ownership. People who helped make a decision are more committed to it and to the project, and less likely to reject or undermine it later.
questions.mindset: Involvement builds commitment.

questions.stem: There are multiple project life-cycles you can choose from, depending on the type of project, environment, deliverable and stakeholders. You are working on a project that requires features of an overall product to be delivered on a regular basis. What sort of project lifecycle will you choose to work with?

options.text: Waterfall project lifecycle
options.rationale: A waterfall life cycle delivers the whole product once, at the end.

options.text: Agile project lifecycle
options.rationale: Agile does deliver regularly, but incremental specifically describes delivering features in increments.

options.text: Iterative project lifecycle
options.rationale: Iterative refines the product and delivers once.

options.text: Incremental project lifecycle
options.rationale: An incremental life cycle delivers features in increments of value throughout the project.

questions.explanation: An incremental life cycle delivers the product in increments of usable value throughout the project. Iterative refines through feedback before one release, and agile combines both.
questions.mindset: Regular feature delivery: incremental.

questions.stem: You are working on a project where two high-ranked executives keep derailing project meetings with their own agenda, and adding their own scope and requirements that are often conflicting. As a result the project is off-track and is at risk of not delivering any value. What will you do?

options.text: Stop inviting the executives to project meetings, and ask your team to stop communicating with them altogether.
options.rationale: Excluding executives damages relationships and does not resolve the conflict.

options.text: Write down the conflicting requirements and ask your team to deliver them in order of one each per executive, to keep everyone happy.
options.rationale: Delivering one requirement per executive ignores value and does not resolve conflicts.

options.text: Ensure clear roles & responsibilities for anyone involved with the project, then facilitate a session to problem solve a way forward with the key stakeholders.
options.rationale: Clarifying roles and facilitating a problem-solving session helps key stakeholders reach consensus.

options.text: Gather all the requirements from everyone involved on the project, prioritize them against their cost to benefit ratio, then deliver them in that order.
options.rationale: Prioritising by cost-benefit helps, but it does not address conflicting agendas and unclear roles.

questions.explanation: Stakeholders with conflicting agendas and unclear roles create confusion. Clarifying roles and responsibilities, then facilitating a problem-solving session, helps the executives build consensus on a way forward.
questions.mindset: Clarify roles, then facilitate consensus.

questions.stem: You have just taken over a project that is behind schedule. The previous Project Manager was brought on during a company crisis, and used a directive leadership style to force work through. The team have been together for 8 months now but are still in the "storming" stage, with conflict a common occurrence. What will you do first?

options.text: Continue the directive leadership style, using your Positional Power to force work through the team until they eventually move into "Norming".
options.rationale: Continued directive leadership has kept the team storming for eight months.

options.text: Set a clear vision and mission and create a Team Charter with the team, remove blockers and shield the team from external politics.
options.rationale: A clear vision, a team charter, removing blockers and shielding the team help it move beyond storming.

options.text: Remove any people who think differently to you on the team, so you can get consensus with team decisions more quickly.
options.rationale: Removing people who disagree destroys diversity and trust.

options.text: Ensure that all the project stakeholders know it was the previous Project Manager to blame for the project's current troubles, so your reputation is not tarnished.
options.rationale: Blaming the previous project manager is unprofessional and does not help the team.

questions.explanation: A team stuck in storming under directive leadership needs a different approach. Setting a clear vision and mission, agreeing a team charter, removing blockers and shielding the team from politics are servant leadership practices that help it progress.
questions.mindset: Lead with vision and support, not force.

questions.stem: The project you have taken over recently was behind schedule. It has seen some improvement with some minor releases, but the team are still struggling to deliver consistently. Your Project Sponsor is starting to question whether you are right for the job. What will you do next?

options.text: Do a team assessment of skills against key performance indicators, support team development, then verify the results.
options.rationale: Assessing skills against KPIs, supporting development and verifying results improves consistent delivery.

options.text: Ask the Project Sponsor for additional funding, as more people on the project should help you deliver more frequently.
options.rationale: More people may not help and adds coordination overhead.

options.text: Ask the team to work overtime, including weekends, to speed up the project delivery.
options.rationale: Overtime including weekends is unsustainable and harms morale and quality.

options.text: Work with the project team and Sponsor to reduce the project scope so the project is no longer behind.
options.rationale: Reducing scope treats the symptom rather than improving performance.

questions.explanation: Supporting team performance means appraising performance against key indicators, supporting development where gaps exist and verifying that the changes are working. This builds consistent delivery over time.
questions.mindset: Assess, develop and verify team performance.

questions.stem: You are working as a Project Manager on a project where the Project Sponsor makes all decisions on project requirements and scope. There is also a very competent Senior User from the business who is part of the project team. The Sponsor is a high-level executive leading multiple teams, and does not have time for scope discussions. What will you do next?

options.text: Set a single all-hands full-day requirements and scope meeting with the Project Sponsor, to get all the scope out in one go.
options.rationale: A single all-day session is unrealistic for a busy executive and cannot anticipate every decision.

options.text: Move your project team to co-locate with the Project Sponsor, so you can have regular discussions and get answers quickly.
options.rationale: Moving the team to sit with a busy executive sponsor is impractical.

options.text: Come up with a list of project requirements based on your experience so far, to help speed up the process.
options.rationale: Inventing requirements from your own experience risks building the wrong product.

options.text: Work with the project sponsor to give the Senior User the authority over scope decisions.
options.rationale: Giving the capable senior user authority over scope decisions uses team strengths and speeds decisions.

questions.explanation: Empowering team members means organising around their strengths and delegating appropriate decision-making authority. Working with the sponsor to give the competent senior user authority over scope removes a bottleneck.
questions.mindset: Delegate decisions to capable people.

questions.stem: You are a program manager overseeing multiple Agile projects within your organization. One of the projects is very important but has consistently had trouble delivering valuable features, with only one released in the last four months. The backlog is not clear, and the team are not aligned on what to do. What will you do?

options.text: Perform a training needs assessment with the team and set aside time and funding to uplift the Product Owner and Scrum Master's skills.
options.rationale: A training needs assessment and funded development for the product owner and scrum master addresses the capability gap.

options.text: Sit down with the team and create a Product Backlog yourself so they can see how it's done.
options.rationale: Creating the backlog yourself fixes the symptom once without building capability.

options.text: Start reducing the team members on that team and assign them to other teams who are performing better.
options.rationale: Taking people away from a struggling team makes its delivery worse, not better.

options.text: Swap members of the team with other project's team members who are more capable, to ensure an even spread across all your projects.
options.rationale: Swapping team members spreads the problem rather than solving it.

questions.explanation: An unclear backlog and misaligned team point to gaps in key roles. Assessing training needs and investing in the product owner's and scrum master's skills builds lasting capability, and the outcomes of training can then be measured.
questions.mindset: Build capability where the gap is.

questions.stem: You are in the initiating stages of a project. The Project Charter has been approved, and initial funding released. You have been tasked with building a project team in an organization where the project maturity is low. What will you do?

options.text: Start creating the first few User Stories as part of your 'Iteration zero", then estimate the resources required to complete them.
options.rationale: User stories before a team exists puts the cart before the horse.

options.text: Ask the Project Sponsor for the best people from their business area to fill project roles, so you know they understand the project changes.
options.rationale: The sponsor's best people may not match the project's needs.

options.text: Use Parametric estimating to estimate the resources required for your project based on high- level deliverables, assess team skills regularly, and ensure knowledge sharing with an open team portal.
options.rationale: Estimating resource needs, assessing skills regularly and sharing knowledge openly builds a suitable team.

options.text: Bring an existing project team from a previous project over to begin your new project, so you know they will work together well already.
options.rationale: An existing team may not have the skills this project needs.

questions.explanation: Building a team involves deducing resource requirements, continuously assessing and refreshing skills and maintaining knowledge transfer. Estimating needs from deliverables, reviewing skills and sharing knowledge through an open portal support this in a low-maturity organisation.
questions.mindset: Build the team from the project's needs.

questions.stem: You are running the daily stand-up as an Agile project lead and neutral facilitator for the team. Work seems to be being developed, but is not being released. Upon pushing a little further, one of the Testers raises a blocker and notes that there is not an adequate test environment to create test data and complete proper tests in. What will you do?

options.text: Ask the developers to perform user acceptance testing on their work so the work is not slowed down.
options.rationale: Developers doing acceptance testing on their own work undermines quality.

options.text: Remove the requirement for testing so the items can be released and value can be delivered. Agile is about moving fast.
options.rationale: Removing testing sacrifices quality; agile does not mean skipping tests.

options.text: Ask the testers to find a way to make it work, testing is their responsibility and they should be taking the lead for their own work.
options.rationale: Pushing the problem back to testers ignores the project manager's role in removing blockers.

options.text: Note the blocker, review it after the Stand-Up, escalate it to the appropriate area and check in on it daily until it is solved.
options.rationale: Recording the blocker, escalating it appropriately and following up daily until solved removes the impediment.

questions.explanation: Removing impediments is a core project leader responsibility. The blocker is noted at the stand-up, discussed afterwards, escalated to the people who can fix it and followed up daily until resolved.
questions.mindset: Own and chase blockers until they are removed.

questions.stem: During a retrospective, your team advise that a high ranking executive from another part of the business keep approaching them to do work, which slows down existing work on the project. That executive, while they are not your Sponsor, also has the power to fire you or remove project funding. You decide to approach them and negotiate the situation. What will you do?

options.text: Review the situation with your team and force your viewpoint on the Executive, so they no longer approach you or the team.
options.rationale: Forcing your viewpoint on a powerful executive risks the project and your role.

options.text: Brainstorm best alternative to a negotiated agreement with your team and attempt to problem solve an agreement with the other Executive.
options.rationale: Preparing a best alternative to a negotiated agreement and problem solving with the executive sets up a sound negotiation.

options.text: Ask your team to just agree with the executive, but not do any of their work, to smooth things over.
options.rationale: Agreeing but not doing the work is dishonest and will backfire.

options.text: Set a meeting with the executive and your team to redo your deliverables list with ones primarily from that executive to keep them happy.
options.rationale: Rebuilding deliverables around one executive abandons the project's objectives.

questions.explanation: Effective negotiation starts with analysing the bounds of agreement and knowing your best alternative to a negotiated agreement. With that preparation, the project manager can problem-solve with the executive to protect the team's focus while respecting their power.
questions.mindset: Prepare a BATNA, then problem-solve the negotiation.

questions.stem: You are working on a project to deliver a major system change to retail workers in a large department store. You have worked closely with the Functional Manager of that area, and are analyzing the remaining stakeholders in your stakeholder matrix, and what to do with the front-line retail workers. What will you do?

options.text: Class them as high-impact, low-influence: Keep informed
options.rationale: Front-line workers are highly impacted but have low influence, so they are kept informed.

options.text: Class them as high-impact, high-influence: Collaborate
options.rationale: They do not have high influence over the project.

options.text: Class them as low-impact, low influence: Monitor
options.rationale: They are highly impacted by the system change.

options.text: Class them as low-impact, high-influence: Maintain Confidence
options.rationale: They are not low-impact, and do not hold high influence.

questions.explanation: Front-line retail workers must use the new system every day, so they are highly impacted, but they have little influence over the project. In an impact/influence grid, this group is kept informed.
questions.mindset: High impact, low influence: keep informed.

questions.stem: Your project has just had its first release of a deliverable, which has taken 4 months to deliver. The team showcased it to the receiving functional manager and her team. Upon viewing it, the functional manager advises that this was not what she wanted at all, and threatens to go to the Project Sponsor to either change the project team, or remove funding. What will you do?

options.text: Ask the functional manager to accept the deliverable anyway, as they are technically not part of the project team.
options.rationale: Asking for acceptance of something that does not meet needs ignores the problem.

options.text: Tell the Functional Manager that it was the project team's fault. With you in charge, this will not happen again.
options.rationale: Blaming the team damages trust and does not fix the misunderstanding.

options.text: Facilitate a meeting with the functional manager and the project team to investigate potential misunderstandings and reach a consensus to move forward.
options.rationale: A facilitated meeting to investigate misunderstandings and reach consensus rebuilds shared understanding.

options.text: Remove the deliverable and go back to the drawing board, starting with new requirements that you think the functional manager might like based on their response.
options.rationale: Guessing new requirements repeats the mistake that caused the problem.

questions.explanation: When a deliverable does not match what the customer expected, the root cause is usually a misunderstanding. Facilitating a meeting with the functional manager and the team to investigate what was misunderstood and agree a way forward builds shared understanding.
questions.mindset: Resolve mismatched expectations together.

questions.stem: You are working in an organization that is new to Agile, and have just built your initial team to start your project. The team is located in different cities around the country and the world. You have heard that an Agile team needs to be co-located. What will you do?

options.text: Ask for funding to move your team from their locations to your current city so they can gain the benefit of co-location.
options.rationale: Relocating a global team is costly and often impossible.

options.text: Create a virtual Kanban board, online project portal as an information radiator, and check in with video conferencing for stand-ups, planning and retrospectives.
options.rationale: Virtual boards, an online portal and video for agile ceremonies engage a distributed team effectively.

options.text: Fire the project team and hire new team members only in your area, to get the full benefit of Agile.
options.rationale: Replacing the team to force co-location is disruptive and wasteful.

options.text: Stop working in an Agile way and go back to a more Predictive method. Ask your team for fewer check-ins and less collaboration, so you don't have to worry about their locations.
options.rationale: Abandoning agile and reducing collaboration makes matters worse.

questions.explanation: Virtual teams can still work in an agile way. A virtual Kanban board, an online project portal acting as an information radiator and video conferencing for stand-ups, planning and retrospectives provide much of the benefit of co-location.
questions.mindset: Engage virtual teams with the right tools.

questions.stem: You have brought together a new project team to deliver a system that has never been done before in your organization. The organization is also moving to a more Agile way of work. The project team are quite new in working together, and working in projects. What will you do?

options.text: Take a directive approach to your project leadership, ensuring the new team does exactly what you say, when you say it.
options.rationale: A directive approach undermines a new team's development and ownership.

options.text: Take on most of the project work yourself, and plan it all up-front so you can tell in advance if there are going to be issues.
options.rationale: Doing most of the work yourself and planning everything up front ignores the team and the agile move.

options.text: Raise the new team as a project issue and take it to your project's steering committee, to get access to staff with more experience.
options.rationale: Treating the team as an issue to escalate does not help them develop.

options.text: Set ground rules with a Team Charter, then check in at each Retrospective to see if the team still understands them and feel they can follow them.
options.rationale: Setting ground rules in a team charter and revisiting them at retrospectives gives a new team a clear, evolving foundation.

questions.explanation: A new team needs clear ground rules. Agreeing them in a team charter and checking at each retrospective that they are still understood and followed creates an environment that fosters adherence and lets the rules evolve.
questions.mindset: Set ground rules and revisit them.

questions.stem: You have just been allocated to a project where the team has been working together for the past six months. The Project Coordinator has shown signs that they want to improve their life, and even gain a promotion in the future. What will you do?

options.text: Ensure the Project Coordinator is focused primarily on their job. You don't want the project to go off track.
options.rationale: Ignoring the coordinator's aspirations misses a mentoring opportunity.

options.text: Tell the Project Coordinator that they can get a promotion if they work hard enough, and you will put in a good word for them.
options.rationale: Vague promises of promotion are not mentoring.

options.text: Set time with the Project Coordinator to review their career plan, discuss career pathways, and recommend certifications and methods of study to get there.
options.rationale: Reviewing their career plan, pathways and study options is effective mentoring.

options.text: Refer the Project Coordinator to your boss, to help set them gain visibility in the organization and get more options for promotion.
options.rationale: Passing them to your boss avoids your own mentoring role.

questions.explanation: Project managers mentor relevant stakeholders by recognising opportunities and allocating time. Reviewing the coordinator's career plan, discussing pathways and recommending certifications and study supports their growth.
questions.mindset: Make time to mentor.

questions.stem: The project you are working on is on schedule, but has been marred with conflict and politics for its duration so far. You ask your team to complete a Myers Briggs Type Indicator test (MBTI). The results show that the Project Coordinator is Extroverted and prefers Thinking, while the team is primarily Introverted and prefers Feeling. What will you do?

options.text: Take the MBTI test yourself, then use the results to review how you and the team work with the Project Coordinator. Work these into the Team Charter.
options.rationale: Using MBTI insights, including your own, to adjust how everyone works together and recording this in the charter applies emotional intelligence.

options.text: Replace the Project Coordinator with someone who is more compatible with your team. Ensure each new member does a MBTI test from now on.
options.rationale: Replacing someone for personality type is inappropriate and damages trust.

options.text: Ask the Project Coordinator to change their personality to be more suitable to the project team. After all, they are the odd one out.
options.rationale: Asking someone to change their personality is unrealistic and disrespectful.

options.text: Focus your efforts on the Project and keeping the plan on track. As long as you are getting results, it shouldn't matter whether the team is happy or not.
options.rationale: Ignoring team conflict harms performance and wellbeing.

questions.explanation: Personality indicators such as MBTI help people understand different working preferences. The project manager uses the results, including their own, to adjust how the team works with the coordinator, and captures agreements in the team charter.
questions.mindset: Use personality insights to adapt, not to exclude.

questions.stem: You have begun planning a large project with the input from your Project Sponsor and the help of your project team. The project is large, with a single very large deliverable that will take 14 months to finish and bring value to the business. The Project Sponsor is worried they will run out of time and money if not benefits can be made sooner. What will you do?

options.text: Split the project into four different projects with additional project teams to speed up delivery, then put them all together at the end.
options.rationale: Splitting into separate projects and integrating at the end still delays value.

options.text: Find a vendor to deliver the item instead. That way if it goes over schedule or budget they will have to manage it and your team will be free to get other work done faster.
options.rationale: Outsourcing does not bring value sooner and adds new risk.

options.text: Ask the Project Sponsor to reduce the scope of the project, so you can finish its delivery more quickly and everyone looks good.
options.rationale: Cutting scope to look good may remove essential value.

options.text: Ask the team to break the deliverable down into smaller usable pieces, with an initial part that will bring value sooner to the business as an MVP.
options.rationale: Breaking the deliverable into usable pieces, starting with an MVP, brings value to the business sooner.

questions.explanation: Executing with urgency means looking for ways to deliver value incrementally. Breaking the large deliverable into smaller usable pieces, starting with a minimum viable product, gives the business benefits sooner and reduces the risk of running out of time and money.
questions.mindset: Deliver an MVP first.

questions.stem: You have been working on a high-profile project with a large amount of business executives who will gain benefit from what you are delivering. You have made all the project information available in a Project portal as a method of Pull Communication for them. Recently, a lot of "noise" and unhappiness has come from those stakeholders. What will you do?

options.text: Send an email to those stakeholders reminding them that the project information is available in the Project Portal, and they can view it at any time.
options.rationale: Reminding people of the portal repeats the approach that is not working.

options.text: Begin regular reviews of the actual deliverables created with the business representatives, to confirm the communication is understood and feedback is received correctly.
options.rationale: Regular reviews of actual deliverables with business representatives confirm understanding and capture feedback.

options.text: Review the problem with your project Steering Committee, and ask that the business Stakeholders stop the noise and negativity around your project.
options.rationale: Asking the committee to silence stakeholders ignores their concerns.

options.text: Add a Push communication to your project stakeholders in the form of a Project Report via email, so they have more options for information.
options.rationale: Another report adds information but does not confirm understanding.

questions.explanation: Managing communications includes confirming that messages are understood and feedback is received. Regular reviews of real deliverables with business representatives turn passive pull communication into two-way engagement.
questions.mindset: Confirm understanding through two-way engagement.

questions.stem: You have been working on a project for some time, and it is only slightly behind schedule with a SPI of 0.96. Various Risks to delivery, including new Risks that will occur once the product is delivered have been raised by your project team members. What will you do next?

options.text: Do a large scale simulation (Monte Carlo) of all the different risks under different conditions, and a Sensitivity Analysis (Tornado Chart).
options.rationale: Large-scale simulation is disproportionate for a project only slightly behind schedule.

options.text: Note the items in the Issue Log to track and manage them to completion before the Project is delivered.
options.rationale: These are future events, so they belong in the risk register, not the issue log.

options.text: Set a meeting with the key risk owners, set risk Likelihoods and Impacts, note a strategy and an Owner to manage each Risk.
options.rationale: Assessing likelihood and impact and assigning a strategy and owner to each risk manages them properly.

options.text: Ask your project team to deal with each risk as they raise them, so you are not left with any outstanding work at the end of the project.
options.rationale: Asking the team to handle risks ad hoc lacks prioritisation and ownership.

questions.explanation: Newly raised risks, including those after delivery, need to be assessed and prioritised iteratively. The project manager works with risk owners to set likelihood and impact, choose a response strategy and assign an owner for each risk.
questions.mindset: Assess, prioritise and own each risk.

questions.stem: You are in the initiating stages of a project, and have been given an initial project team. Your team are gathering the project stakeholders needed to kick-off the project work. What will you do?

options.text: Set an all-hands project meeting with any stakeholder you have seen mentioned as an all day planning event to kick start the project.
options.rationale: An all-day meeting with everyone is inefficient and not based on analysis.

options.text: Classify the project stakeholders by Impact and Influence, and ensure high engagement and communication with stakeholders high in both.
options.rationale: Classifying stakeholders by impact and influence focuses engagement where it matters most.

options.text: Ask each stakeholder what they believe their contribution to the project will be, and classify them based on their own importance.
options.rationale: Letting stakeholders rate their own importance is not objective analysis.

options.text: Find a previous project's stakeholder map and copy the details from there, using analogous stakeholder mapping.
options.rationale: Copying another project's stakeholder map ignores this project's context.

questions.explanation: Engaging stakeholders starts with analysing and categorising them, for example by impact and influence. High engagement and communication are then focused on those who rate highly on both.
questions.mindset: Analyse stakeholders, then engage by category.

questions.stem: You are planning your project and finalizing the project costs. You have broken down the scope into work packages and estimated their duration and cost with your team. What will you do next?

options.text: Add a Contingency Reserve for the known project risks based on past projects, and a small Management Reserve for unforeseen issues to project scope.
options.rationale: Contingency for known risks, informed by past projects, plus a management reserve for unforeseen work gives a sound budget.

options.text: Add 50% to the total as part of your preliminary budget to account for any uncertainty in the estimates.
options.rationale: Adding an arbitrary 50% is not based on analysis.

options.text: Set aside 10% in a "miscellaneous" task on your project, that you can use as a pool of funding for any mistakes.
options.rationale: An unexplained 'miscellaneous' pool is poor practice.

options.text: Set the budget as your new Cost Baseline, so there cannot be any additional funding without approval in the future.
options.rationale: Baselining without reserves leaves no allowance for risk.

questions.explanation: After estimating work package costs, the budget adds a contingency reserve for identified risks, informed by lessons from past projects, and a management reserve for unforeseen in-scope work. The cost baseline then includes contingency.
questions.mindset: Budget for known and unknown risks.

questions.stem: Your project team have been used to working in a Predictive or Waterfall way of work, planning everything up front. As your company moves to a more Agile way of work, you have been asked to ensure the Project Schedule does not suffer, can still get done, and can still be reported on as necessary. What will you do?

options.text: Break down the project deliverables into work packages and then into Activities, and estimate the sequence and duration of those activities for your project Schedule.
options.rationale: Detailed activity sequencing is predictive and does not fit the agile move.

options.text: Ask the team to self manage their own work and pick items that they feel they want to work on. This will help their engagement.
options.rationale: Letting the team choose freely ignores priorities and the need to report.

options.text: Set a due date for the project 10 months out in the future, then plan backwards for everything that needs to get done to meet that deadline.
options.rationale: Planning backwards from an arbitrary deadline is not an agile scheduling method.

options.text: Estimate enough user story points for the next sprint to match the team's velocity, and set a high level Product Roadmap of upcoming features and their estimated timeframes.
options.rationale: Sprint planning to velocity and a high-level roadmap provide an agile schedule that can be reported on.

questions.explanation: Agile scheduling plans the near term in detail and the longer term at a high level. Estimating the next sprint to match velocity and maintaining a product roadmap with estimated timeframes lets the schedule be managed and reported on.
questions.mindset: Schedule agile work with velocity and a roadmap.

questions.stem: You have been working with a project team, delivering new items very quickly. The team were so focused on delivering items quickly that you didn't realize the deliverables were not working to the customer requirements. You will have to adjust your project approach. What will you do?

options.text: Ask the team to finish their deliverables more slowly.
options.rationale: Slowing down does not ensure deliverables meet requirements.

options.text: Break down the deliverables into smaller items that your team can work on, so there is smaller chance of mistakes.
options.rationale: Smaller items help but do not define what meets the requirements.

options.text: Note acceptance criteria on each work package from the Senior Users themselves, and check that quality with a Control Chart and Pareto Chart to track defects.
options.rationale: Acceptance criteria from senior users, with control and Pareto charts to track defects, build quality into delivery.

options.text: Tell your project sponsor that the customers or Senior Users from the receiving business have not given you enough detail to deliver correctly.
options.rationale: Blaming the customers does not fix the quality gap.

questions.explanation: Managing quality means defining the standard required and tracking against it. Acceptance criteria from senior users define what 'right' looks like, and tools such as control charts and Pareto charts show where defects arise so the team can improve.
questions.mindset: Define quality with users, then measure it.

questions.stem: You have been assigned to a project in your organization, and have been given a list of high-level features or deliverables that the Project Sponsor wants you to deliver. The project team are keen to get to work. What will you do?

options.text: Set the features on a schedule so you can report back to the Project Sponsor on when they will be delivered.
options.rationale: Scheduling unprioritised, undecomposed features gives unreliable dates.

options.text: Note any risks for the features and give them a rating for their likelihood of occurrence and the impact when they do happen.
options.rationale: Risk rating is useful later but is not the first step with a feature list.

options.text: Prioritize the features with the Sponsor, then work with your team to break the features down into Work Packages (or User Stories).
options.rationale: Prioritising features with the sponsor, then breaking them into work packages or stories, plans the scope properly.

options.text: Add contingency and management reserves to the high-level features to ensure there is enough to get the work done.
options.rationale: Adding reserves before understanding the work is premature.

questions.explanation: Planning scope means determining and prioritising requirements and breaking the scope down, whether into a WBS or a backlog. Prioritising with the sponsor and decomposing into work packages or stories gives the team a clear start.
questions.mindset: Prioritise, then decompose.

questions.stem: You are in the planning phase of your project, having finished the various project plans required to begin. Your Project Sponsor would like to receive regular updates as the project progresses. What will you do?

options.text: Ask the Project Sponsor to attend the daily stand-ups whenever they want an update. This will give real data from the ground.
options.rationale: Stand-ups are for the team, not structured sponsor reporting.

options.text: Combine your project plans (Scope, Schedule, Cost, Resources), calculate the PV and analyze EV and AC as the project progresses.
options.rationale: Consolidating the plans and tracking PV, EV and AC gives the sponsor integrated, regular performance updates.

options.text: Work through your project plans iteratively on a week-by-week basis, focusing on the Scope Management Plan first (then Schedule, etc).
options.rationale: Revisiting plans one at a time weekly does not produce integrated performance data.

options.text: Determine the project's BAC and EAC, so you can show the Project Sponsor the true progress as things are delivered.
options.rationale: BAC and EAC are useful, but they depend on the integrated baseline and EV tracking.

questions.explanation: Integrating planning activities means consolidating the subsidiary plans into one performance baseline. Planned value from that baseline, compared with earned value and actual cost as work progresses, gives the sponsor objective updates.
questions.mindset: Integrate plans and measure against them.

questions.stem: You are working on a new project in your organization, where the team is trying to move to an Agile way of work. The team are not sure how to handle Change Management, as they had a Change Management Plan in their previous Waterfall way of work. The PMO is not keen on having no documentation around change management. What will you do?

options.text: Ask the PMO to trust you. Agile is about moving fast and breaking things, and you can't move fast if you have to document everything.
options.rationale: Asking the PMO for blind trust ignores its legitimate need.

options.text: Tell the PMO that Agile is about working software over comprehensive documentation. As long as you are delivering, the change approach shouldn't matter.
options.rationale: Dismissing documentation disregards governance requirements.

options.text: Hold a Retrospective with your team to find out what works, what doesn't work, and what still puzzles them about the current Change Management approaches.
options.rationale: A retrospective may help, but the PMO needs a documented approach.

options.text: Create a few lines as a change management plan that outline the Product Owner's responsibility for Scope Changes, by reprioritizing the Product Backlog.
options.rationale: A short plan stating that the product owner manages scope change through backlog reprioritisation satisfies the PMO.

questions.explanation: Agile values working software over comprehensive documentation, but not no documentation. A brief change management plan describing how the product owner handles scope changes through the backlog meets the PMO's needs while fitting the agile approach.
questions.mindset: Document agile change control simply.

questions.stem: You are working on a project where a vendor is performing a large amount of the work. Lately they have not been performing well, with deliverables finished later and later. The last deliverable did not match your requirements at all. The manager representative for the Vendor disagrees, and will not budge. What will you do?

options.text: Review the Claims Process in your Procurement Management Plan, and engage the alternative dispute resolution if necessary.
options.rationale: The procurement plan's claims process, with alternative dispute resolution if needed, handles contested vendor performance.

options.text: Review the scope management process in your Scope Management Plan, and engage the WBS if necessary.
options.rationale: Scope management and the WBS do not resolve a contractual dispute.

options.text: Review the Statement of Work in your Procurement Management Plan with the Vendor.
options.rationale: Reviewing the SOW may help, but the parties already disagree and need the claims process.

options.text: Review the Source Selection Criteria and the Multi-Criteria Analysis with the Vendor, from your Procurement Management Plan.
options.rationale: Source selection criteria are no longer relevant after award.

questions.explanation: When a vendor disputes that its work fails the requirements, the claims administration process set out in the procurement plan and contract applies. Negotiation is preferred, with alternative dispute resolution if agreement cannot be reached.
questions.mindset: Use the claims process for vendor disputes.

questions.stem: You have just initiated a project, and the steering committee asks you to keep them updated on the main project activities. You perform a Communication Needs Analysis with them and determine a regular Push approach will work. What will you do?

options.text: Consolidate the project schedule, cost and risk into a versioned weekly project report, and assess its effectiveness with a Retrospective each month.
options.rationale: A versioned weekly report consolidating schedule, cost and risk, reviewed for effectiveness, meets the committee's push needs.

options.text: Place the project artifacts of scope, schedule and cost in the team area so the steering committee members can walk through and view them anytime.
options.rationale: Leaving artefacts in the team area is pull communication, which the committee did not choose.

options.text: Send a delegate to meet with the Steering Committee each week and review the project artifacts.
options.rationale: A delegate meeting does not guarantee consistent, versioned information.

options.text: Wait for the project steering committee to approach you, asking for information about the project. This way you are not bothering them and you know they want the information.
options.rationale: Waiting to be asked contradicts the agreed push approach.

questions.explanation: Managing project artefacts means determining what information is needed, keeping it up to date and version-controlled and assessing its effectiveness. A versioned weekly report pushed to the committee, with regular review, does this.
questions.mindset: Keep artefacts current, versioned and useful.

questions.stem: Your organization has recently completed a new system for the sales department. New features still need to be added as the functionality is not complete, but they are relatively straight forward. The Project Sponsor would like value to get value as soon as possible. What project approach will you recommend?

options.text: Predictive approach, so you can plan the features correctly before releasing them.
options.rationale: Predictive delays value until everything is planned and built.

options.text: An Agile approach, so you can plan each sprint and keep a sustainable pace.
options.rationale: Agile would work, but incremental most specifically describes regular small deliveries into an existing system.

options.text: An Iterative approach, so you can Iterate the new features into the existing system.
options.rationale: Iterative refines through prototypes and releases once, which delays value.

options.text: An Incremental approach, delivering small features on a regular basis (one to three months) into the main system.
options.rationale: Incremental delivery of small features every one to three months gives value early.

questions.explanation: With straightforward features to add to an existing system and a sponsor who wants value quickly, an incremental approach fits: small features are delivered regularly into the main system.
questions.mindset: Straightforward features, early value: incremental.

questions.stem: You are a Project Manager who has been tasked with initiating a new project for your area. You review the current organizational structure. There is a PMO, but it is Supportive, and operates in a Hybrid governance structure. What will you do?

options.text: Ask the PMO to assign a Manager to the project based on their pool of available resources.
options.rationale: A supportive PMO provides templates, not project managers.

options.text: Take complete control of the project to ensure the Scope, Budget, Schedule and other things are managed well.
options.rationale: Taking complete control ignores the functional manager's authority in a hybrid structure.

options.text: Work very closely with the Functional Manager of the receiving area to help manage Scope, Budget and Resources.
options.rationale: In a hybrid structure the project manager works closely with the functional manager on scope, budget and resources.

options.text: Let the Functional Manager do the project as they know their area
options.rationale: Handing over entirely ignores the project manager's role.

questions.explanation: A supportive PMO provides templates and guidance only. In a hybrid organisational structure, authority is shared between the project manager and functional managers, so the project manager works closely with the functional manager to manage scope, budget and resources.
questions.mindset: Match your approach to the governance structure.

questions.stem: You have been working on your project for some time, when one of your project team tells you about an issue with the materials. He heard the supplier was having trouble getting the materials from overseas, and that it might impact us receiving them in future deliveries. What will you do?

options.text: Raise the item in the issue log, with an owner, and manage it to completion.
options.rationale: A possible future delay is a risk, not an issue.

options.text: Raise the item in the Risk Register, with a likelihood and impact rating, a risk response and risk owner.
options.rationale: Recording the possible supply delay as a risk with rating, response and owner manages it proactively.

options.text: Immediately source a new supplier for the materials so you don't get caught out in the future.
options.rationale: Switching suppliers immediately is premature before assessment.

options.text: Change the project scope requirements with your team so you no longer rely on those types of materials.
options.rationale: Changing scope requirements is drastic for an unconfirmed risk.

questions.explanation: A possible future delay in materials is a risk. It is recorded in the risk register with likelihood and impact, a response and an owner. If it occurs, it becomes an issue.
questions.mindset: Uncertain future events are risks.

questions.stem: You are nearing the end of your project which has delivered a brand new system to the organization. There have been many challenges with the delivery and with the vendor, which you have managed to overcome. The Project Sponsor has accepted the product. What will you do next?

options.text: Verify the deliverables by reviewing the Quality Assurance tests and their results.
options.rationale: Verification by quality testing is complete; the sponsor has already accepted the product.

options.text: Tell the vendor verbally that their services are no longer required, as the Project Sponsor is happy.
options.rationale: Verbal dismissal of the vendor is not proper contract closure.

options.text: Collaborate with your team to agree on roles for knowledge transfer and the agreed approach.
options.rationale: Agreeing roles and the approach for knowledge transfer ensures continuity after the project.

options.text: Review the final versions of the Project Management Plan, and ensure they are up to date.
options.rationale: Updating plans is administrative and does not secure continuity.

questions.explanation: With the product accepted, the project must ensure continuity. Agreeing with the team who will transfer what knowledge, and how, prepares operations and support teams to run the new system after the project closes.
questions.mindset: Plan knowledge transfer for continuity.

questions.stem: You are in the closing phase of your project, after having delivered a large change for employees in the HR department. What will you do next?

options.text: Break down the project scope into smaller User Stories and estimate their effort, so your team can work on them.
options.rationale: Breaking scope into stories belongs to planning, not closure.

options.text: Perform a team assessment to see how your team is performing, fill any gaps and help them grow.
options.rationale: Team assessment is part of developing the team, not closing.

options.text: Raise a change request for any outstanding items so they are noted as "not complete" in the project management plan.
options.rationale: Outstanding items should be resolved or transferred, not recorded as incomplete through change requests.

options.text: Notify the vendor in writing that the project is closed, finalize and close all accounts, archive project information and lessons learned.
options.rationale: Formally notifying the vendor, closing accounts and archiving information and lessons learned are closure activities.

questions.explanation: Closing a project includes formally closing procurements with written notice to vendors, finalising and closing financial accounts, archiving project records and capturing final lessons learned.
questions.mindset: Close contracts, finances and records formally.

questions.stem: You are halfway through a large scale project for your organization when you are approached by the internal Audit department. Your industry is heavily regulated and a breach can mean large fines and even jail time for executives. The Audit team are asking for your project delivery approach, project cost and resources, and the value the project is delivering. What will you do?

options.text: Provide them your Project Charter and Project Management Plan, highlighting Cost and Resource Management, and the Benefits Management Plan.
options.rationale: The charter, management plan and benefits plan give auditors the approach, cost, resources and value they asked for.

options.text: Tell the audit team they will have to wait, as the project is not finished yet there is no value that has been delivered.
options.rationale: Value can be demonstrated through planned benefits; refusing an audit is unacceptable.

options.text: Ask your project team to provide their own updates on their roles, cost, time required and the value they provide, and collate this for the Audit team.
options.rationale: Collating individual updates is inconsistent and incomplete.

options.text: Show the Audit team your team area which holds all your project information and allow them to set time with you to ask questions if needed.
options.rationale: Showing the team area is informal and may not satisfy a regulatory audit.

questions.explanation: In a heavily regulated industry, supporting audits is part of compliance. The charter, project management plan with cost and resource management and the benefits management plan provide documented answers on approach, resources and value.
questions.mindset: Support audits with the right documents.

questions.stem: Your project is around half-way complete and has had a great deal of issues around resources and funding. Other executives from the business are starting to mention that they don't see the value your project is delivering and that it is a waste of company resources. What will you do?

options.text: Create or review your Project Management Plan, outlining the project scope, schedule and cost, so the executives can understand it.
options.rationale: The management plan covers scope, schedule and cost but not the benefits being questioned.

options.text: Use your Project Charter to create or review your Benefits Management Plan, outlining the project benefits, who will measure them and how, then showcase this to the executive team.
options.rationale: A benefits management plan setting out the benefits, how and by whom they are measured, shared with executives, demonstrates value.

options.text: Ask for a representative from the executive team to review and measure your project benefits. This way they will be more likely to support it.
options.rationale: Asking an executive to measure benefits misplaces ownership.

options.text: Ask the executive team to attend your Sprint Review, demonstrating the increment or feature and the value it provides.
options.rationale: A sprint review suits agile projects; this project's value needs a benefits view.

questions.explanation: When executives question a project's value, the project manager ensures benefits are identified, owned and measured. A benefits management plan derived from the charter, shared with the executive team, shows what value the project will deliver and how it will be tracked.
questions.mindset: Show value through a benefits plan.

questions.stem: You are a project manager on a project using Agile to deliver a change to a busy team in your organization. Recently there have been industry changes that require extra compliance and a completely different way of operating. What will you do?

options.text: Work with the Product Owner to create features that will meet the new industry changes, add them to the Product Backlog and prioritize them.
options.rationale: Adding features to meet the new industry requirements to the backlog and prioritising them adapts scope to the external change.

options.text: Note the industry change as a Risk, with the likelihood and impact, a risk owner, and risk response.
options.rationale: The change has already happened, so it is not a risk.

options.text: Write a Scope Statement and high level deliverables, then break them down into work packages.
options.rationale: A scope statement and work packages are predictive tools.

options.text: Start the project closure process with your Project Sponsor and archive the project documents, as the current project benefit has changed.
options.rationale: Closing the project is premature; the scope can adapt.

questions.explanation: External business environment changes, such as new regulations, are assessed for their impact on scope. In an agile project, the product owner adds features that address the changes to the backlog and prioritises them.
questions.mindset: Adapt the backlog to external change.

questions.stem: You have been assigned to a project that is half way through its delivery. You analyze the stakeholders involved in the project and find that the functional area you are delivering to will experience a significant change in the way they work. What will you do?

options.text: Invite the manager of the receiving area to your project stand-ups so they can see more detail on what is being delivered.
options.rationale: Stand-ups give a manager detail but do not prepare the whole area for change.

options.text: Write a large documentation manual on how the new system will operate and send this to the functional area stakeholders.
options.rationale: A large manual is unlikely to be read or effective.

options.text: Perform a Stakeholder Engagement Assessment to determine the level of engagement from the receiving area.
options.rationale: An engagement assessment helps, but the area needs active change support.

options.text: Announce the change well ahead of time, identify change champions, and provide training and resources.
options.rationale: Early announcements, change champions and training and resources support people through the change.

questions.explanation: Supporting organisational change involves building awareness, desire, knowledge and ability. Announcing the change early, identifying change champions and providing training and resources prepares the receiving area for new ways of working.
questions.mindset: Prepare people for change early.

questions.stem: You are working as a project manager, asking for proposals from a Third Parties to complete the work. Your brother works for one of the vendors bidding for the contract. You are part of the executive team which will accept a vendor. What should you do?

options.text: Discourage the vendor bid as it would be a conflict of interest
options.rationale: Discouraging the bid is unfair to the vendor and does not disclose the conflict.

options.text: Help your brother's vendor in the bid so you can work together
options.rationale: Helping your brother's vendor is a clear ethical breach.

options.text: Inform your company and the vendor of the relationship
options.rationale: Disclosing the relationship to your company and the vendor lets the conflict be managed transparently.

options.text: Don't tell anyone. Why complicate things?
options.rationale: Hiding the conflict is dishonest and breaches the code of ethics.

questions.explanation: A family relationship with a bidder is a conflict of interest. The ethical response is to disclose it to your organisation and the vendor so that the conflict can be managed, for example by removing yourself from the decision.
questions.mindset: Disclose conflicts of interest.

questions.stem: You are working as a project manager in a foreign country. It is customary that gifts be made to the government to obtain the necessary project approvals, however the country where your company is based does not allow this practice. What should you do?

options.text: Don't bother with getting project approvals
options.rationale: Skipping required project approvals is illegal and puts the project at risk.

options.text: Ensure you offer gifts to obtain the project approvals
options.rationale: Offering gifts for approvals breaches your home country's law.

options.text: Allocate additional hidden funds in the project to obtain the gifts
options.rationale: Hiding funds for gifts is both illegal and dishonest.

options.text: Do not offer gifts to obtain project approvals
options.rationale: Not offering gifts complies with the law of your home country and with ethical standards.

questions.explanation: Where local custom conflicts with the law of the country in which your company is based, you must comply with the law. Offering gifts to obtain government approvals is prohibited, so the project manager does not do it.
questions.mindset: Follow the law, even abroad.

questions.stem: You are working as a project manager and created the cost estimate to bid on a government contract, where the scope was set by the government. Your manager advises you to reduce the cost to win the contract by whatever means, but your analysis shows that reducing the cost estimate will make the project unable to meet the specified scope. What should you do?

options.text: Reduce the cost estimate and submit it
options.rationale: Reducing the estimate knowingly misrepresents what the scope will cost.

options.text: Formally communicate to your manager about the implications of reducing the cost
options.rationale: Formally explaining the consequences of reducing the estimate is honest and gives the manager what they need to decide.

options.text: Ask your manager to estimate instead
options.rationale: Handing estimation to the manager avoids responsibility.

options.text: Submit your estimate without reducing the cost
options.rationale: Submitting without discussion ignores the manager and the conflict.

questions.explanation: Project managers must be accurate and truthful in their estimates. Rather than cutting an estimate to win work, the project manager formally explains to the manager what reducing it would mean for delivering the specified scope.
questions.mindset: Be truthful about estimates.

questions.stem: You are working as a Project Manager and one of the stakeholders of the project raises a problem with the product requirements, stating they are not correct. Which document will you use to note this for further discussion and resolution?

options.text: Change Request
options.rationale: A change request may come later, once the problem is discussed and resolved.

options.text: Benefits Management Plan
options.rationale: The benefits plan does not track problems with requirements.

options.text: Issue Log
options.rationale: The issue log records current problems for discussion and resolution.

options.text: Requirements Traceability Matrix
options.rationale: The traceability matrix links requirements but does not track disputes.

questions.explanation: A stakeholder saying the requirements are wrong raises a current problem that needs discussion. The issue log records it, assigns an owner and tracks options until it is resolved, which may lead to a change request.
questions.mindset: Record current problems in the issue log.

questions.stem: A recent news article spread a rumour about a supplier who is providing services for the project you are working on. They are reportedly in the middle of a hostile takeover bid from another larger company. You need to ensure you project is able to continue. What should you do?

options.text: Ignore the news article - they don't know the supplier like you do
options.rationale: Ignoring the report leaves a potential risk unassessed.

options.text: Set a meeting and talk to executives in charge at the hostile bidder
options.rationale: Contacting the bidding company is inappropriate and outside your role.

options.text: Talk to the vendor and find the facts
options.rationale: Talking to the vendor directly establishes the facts before deciding on a response.

options.text: Stop working with the vendor immediately, get another vendor to do the work
options.rationale: Dropping the vendor on a rumour is premature and costly.

questions.explanation: Rumours about a supplier's takeover could affect the project. The project manager is direct and collaborative, raising the matter with the vendor to establish the facts and then deciding how to manage any risk.
questions.mindset: Check the facts with the supplier.

questions.stem: You are working on a global project in other country, where it is customary to honour the project manager of a successful project with gifts. The company you are working for has a policy to never accept gifts as it may be a conflict of interest. What should you do in this circumstance?

options.text: Accept the gift from the customer, it would be rude not to
options.rationale: Accepting the gift breaches company policy, however polite it may seem.

options.text: Tell the customer you don't accept gifts
options.rationale: A blunt refusal may cause offence without considering customs.

options.text: Discuss the situation with your manager and agree what to do - you must be aware of social customs in other countries but your company's rules take precedence over others.
options.rationale: Discussing it with your manager respects local customs while following company policy.

options.text: Accept the gift from the customer and give it to somebody else
options.rationale: Passing the gift on still means accepting it against policy.

questions.explanation: Project managers should be sensitive to local customs, but company policy takes precedence. Discussing the situation with your manager lets you agree a response that respects the customer while complying with the no-gifts policy.
questions.mindset: Respect customs; follow company policy.

questions.stem: You as a project manager are listing the things that must be done to close out the project. What should you do in regards to the contracts for your third party suppliers?

options.text: Issue a formal written notice of the project completion to the contractors
options.rationale: Formal written notice of completion closes the contracts with suppliers.

options.text: Put a legal notice in the newspapers indicating that all invoices must be submitted
options.rationale: A newspaper notice is not how contracts are closed.

options.text: Request final inspection reports for all vendor-supplied materials
options.rationale: Inspections happen before acceptance, not as contract closure.

options.text: Issue letters of recommendation for the project team
options.rationale: Letters of recommendation for the team are unrelated to supplier contracts.

questions.explanation: Closing procurements requires formal written notice to sellers that the contract is complete, after deliverables are accepted and any claims settled.
questions.mindset: Close contracts in writing.

questions.stem: You have been asked to prepare a document to gain the project sponsor's sign off to access their function's resources, that details the project goal and business case, high-level scope and requirements, high level dates and milestones, a high-level budget, and initial risk analysis. What are you creating?

options.text: Project Management Plan
options.rationale: The management plan comes after authorisation and is more detailed.

options.text: Project Charter
options.rationale: The charter authorises the project and gives access to resources, summarising goals, scope, milestones, budget and risks.

options.text: Risk Management Plan
options.rationale: The risk management plan covers only the risk approach.

options.text: Lessons Learned
options.rationale: Lessons learned are captured during and after the project.

questions.explanation: The project charter formally initiates the project and authorises the use of resources. It summarises the objective and business case, high-level scope and requirements, milestones, budget, initial risks and stakeholders, and is signed off by the sponsor.
questions.mindset: The charter authorises the project.

questions.stem: You are working on an Agile project and have been asked to create a document that lists team principles, agreements, and guidelines about the acceptable behaviour by team members. What are you working on?

options.text: The Team Guideline
options.rationale: 'Team guideline' is not the standard name for this document.

options.text: The Project Management Plan
options.rationale: The project management plan covers how the project is managed, not team behaviour.

options.text: The Project Charter
