options.rationale: The project charter authorises the project; it does not set team behaviour.

options.text: The Team Charter
options.rationale: The team charter lists team principles, agreements and guidelines for acceptable behaviour.

questions.explanation: A team charter records the team's values, principles, agreements and guidelines for acceptable behaviour. It sets clear expectations for how members work together.
questions.mindset: Team agreements live in the team charter.

questions.stem: You are working through your project and performing quality inspections on the product. During inspection, you notice a key part of the product is likely to be defective in the future. The team brainstormed, removed some scope and managed to make the product work without the defective component. This is:

options.text: Risk mitigation
options.rationale: Mitigation reduces probability or impact but keeps the risky element.

options.text: Transfer of risk
options.rationale: Transfer shifts the risk and its impact to a third party, such as an insurer.

options.text: Risk avoidance
options.rationale: Removing the risky scope so the threat can no longer affect the product is avoidance.

options.text: Work-around
options.rationale: A workaround responds to a problem that has already occurred.

questions.explanation: Risk avoidance eliminates a threat or protects the project from it entirely, for example by removing high-risk scope. Removing the likely defective component so the product works without it avoids the risk.
questions.mindset: Removing the source of risk is avoidance.

questions.stem: You are working on a project and it has become apparent that part of the product your company was creating they won't be able to complete. You decide to outsource it to a vendor, and offer a bonus to the vendor if the work is completed in two months. What type of contract will you use?

options.text: CPFF (Cost plus fixed fee)
options.rationale: Cost plus fixed fee has no incentive for speed.

options.text: FPWEA (Fixed price with economic price adjustments)
options.rationale: Economic price adjustment covers inflation, not performance incentives.

options.text: T&M (Time and materials)
options.rationale: Time and materials has no built-in bonus for early completion.

options.text: FPIF (Fixed price incentive fee)
options.rationale: Fixed price incentive fee allows a bonus tied to meeting a schedule target.

questions.explanation: A fixed price incentive fee contract sets a fixed price with an additional incentive tied to metrics such as schedule, cost or quality. Offering a bonus for completion in two months fits this type.
questions.mindset: Bonus for performance: incentive fee.

questions.stem: You are at the beginning of planning a new project, and have researched and gathered the requirements from the area, broken them down into deliverables and activities, which you believe could take 26 weeks to deliver. The project sponsor is asking you for an estimate on how long the project will take. What will you do next?

options.text: Tell the project sponsor 26 weeks.
options.rationale: A single figure implies precision the project does not have yet.

options.text: Tell the project sponsor that you will use an iterative approach, where value is delivered until the project stops.
options.rationale: Delivering until the project stops does not answer the sponsor's question.

options.text: Tell the project sponsor approximately 24 to 28 weeks.
options.rationale: A narrow range suits later stages, not the start of planning.

options.text: Tell the project sponsor approximately 20 to 45 weeks.
options.rationale: Early estimates carry a wide range, roughly −25% to +75%, giving about 20 to 45 weeks.

questions.explanation: Early in a project, estimates have a wide range, typically from −25% to +75%. Applied to 26 weeks, that gives roughly 20 to 45 weeks. The range narrows as more is known.
questions.mindset: Give early estimates as wide ranges.

questions.stem: You are working on a project where a competitor is also working on a similar feature, and being first to the market will have a significant impact on this year's profit. Your product owner would like to measure how quickly story cards are being completed, once they start being developed. What will you do next?

options.text: Check the Lead time of the story cards.
options.rationale: Lead time runs from request to delivery, not from the start of development.

options.text: Check the Gantt chart with assigned schedule activities.
options.rationale: A Gantt chart does not measure how fast stories complete once started.

options.text: Check the Cycle time of the story cards.
options.rationale: Cycle time measures elapsed time from when work starts on a story to when it is done.

options.text: Check the schedule network and precedence diagram.
options.rationale: Network and precedence diagrams show dependencies, not completion speed.

questions.explanation: Cycle time is the elapsed time for a unit of work to move through the process once started. Lead time runs from the request to delivery. The product owner's question concerns cycle time.
questions.mindset: Cycle time measures speed once work starts.

questions.stem: You are working on a project that has recently moved to a more agile way of work. The team have not completely taken on the Scrum approach however, and are comfortable working with a more flow-based approach moving user stories across a Kanban board. You are wanting to get an estimate on how much work can be completed in the next three months, based on the team's existing progress. What will you do next?

options.text: Multiply the velocity by the number of remaining user stories.
options.rationale: Velocity is a Scrum measure, and multiplying by remaining stories is meaningless.

options.text: Multiply the throughput of the team for the last month, by three.
options.rationale: Last month's throughput multiplied by three forecasts what can be completed in three months.

options.text: Multiply the lead time by the schedule performance index.
options.rationale: Lead time multiplied by SPI mixes unrelated measures.

options.text: Multiply the planned value by the actual value.
options.rationale: Multiplying planned value by actual value is meaningless.

questions.explanation: Flow-based teams forecast using throughput and cycle time rather than velocity. Throughput is the number of items completed in a period, so last month's throughput multiplied by three estimates three months' output.
questions.mindset: Forecast flow work with throughput.

questions.stem: Your product owner wants to bring the next feature forward so that it is done in parallel to the current feature, but is still released in the existing feature order. You make the necessary adjustments to the product backlog, and decide to adjust the product roadmap, which you have visualised as a Gantt chart. What will you do next?

options.text: Use a schedule lead on the feature, and change the feature to finish-to-start
options.rationale: Finish-to-start keeps the features sequential, so they would not run in parallel.

options.text: Use a schedule lag on the feature, and change the feature to start-to-start
options.rationale: A lag delays the feature rather than bringing it forward.

options.text: Use a schedule lead on the feature, and change the feature to finish-to-finish
options.rationale: A lead brings the feature forward, and finish-to-finish keeps its finish after the current feature.

options.text: Use a schedule lag on the feature, and change the feature to start-to-finish
options.rationale: A lag with start-to-finish neither brings the work forward nor keeps the release order.

questions.explanation: A lead brings an activity forward, while a lag delays it. A finish-to-finish relationship means the next feature cannot finish until the current one does, so the two can be worked on in parallel while keeping the release order.
questions.mindset: Use leads and relationship types to model overlap.

questions.stem: After reviewing your project schedule you notice you are behind by three weeks and the schedule will need to be compressed. Your project does not have enough budget to crash the schedule. You check with the lead for each area and review the schedule as to whether they can fast track their deliverables. What will you do next?

options.text: Fast track team items with discretionary dependencies.
options.rationale: Discretionary dependencies reflect preferences and can be changed to overlap work.

options.text: Fast track team items with mandatory dependencies.
options.rationale: Mandatory dependencies are inherent in the work and cannot be overlapped.

options.text: Fast track team items with external dependencies.
options.rationale: External dependencies are outside the team's control.

options.text: Fast track team items based on industry regulation.
options.rationale: Regulatory dependencies usually cannot be changed.

questions.explanation: Fast tracking overlaps activities normally done in sequence. Only dependencies based on preference, known as discretionary dependencies, can usually be changed; mandatory, external and regulatory dependencies generally cannot.
questions.mindset: Fast-track discretionary dependencies.

questions.stem: You are an agile project manager and your team have delivered three features to improve a customer app over the last three months. Your product owner needs to know if the features are having the desired effect. It is a large organisation and there are multiple measures available. What will you do next?

options.text: Ask them to gather the team velocity and throughput over the past three months.
options.rationale: Velocity and throughput measure team output, not customer outcomes.

options.text: Ask them to gather the Cost Benefit ratio over the past six months.
options.rationale: A cost-benefit ratio is an investment measure rather than evidence of customer response.

options.text: Ask them to gather the Net promoter score over the past six months.
options.rationale: Net promoter score measures customers' willingness to recommend, showing whether the features are improving satisfaction.

options.text: Ask them to gather the average app availability and uptime.
options.rationale: Availability measures reliability, not whether the features had the desired effect.

questions.explanation: To judge whether features are achieving their intended effect, the product owner needs outcome measures. Net promoter score, covering the period before and after release, gauges customer satisfaction and loyalty.
questions.mindset: Measure outcomes, not output.

questions.stem: Your project team are gathering solution ideas for a particular customer requirement, which is prioritised to be worked on next. The item is complicated and they have been trying to find a way forward for the past three weeks. There is not enough work for the upcoming sprint. What will you do next?

options.text: Start work on the item in the next sprint anyway and elaborate as the sprint begins.
options.rationale: Starting an unelaborated item risks wasting the sprint.

options.text: Arrange the right people to elaborate the issue with a spike, and timebox it to two days.
options.rationale: A time-boxed spike with the right people investigates the problem quickly and unblocks the item.

options.text: Deprioritise the item until the team can figure out the issue.
options.rationale: Deprioritising a high-priority item without investigating it loses value.

options.text: Adjust the project schedule to reflect the extra time taken on elaboration.
options.rationale: Adjusting the schedule accepts the delay without addressing it.

questions.explanation: When a high-priority item is stuck because the solution is unclear, a spike—short, time-boxed research with the right people—focuses effort on resolving the uncertainty so the item can be elaborated and planned.
questions.mindset: Unblock unclear work with a time-boxed spike.

questions.stem: You are working on an agile project and are planning your product backlog for the next three to six months. You have some high level feature ideas from various parts of your organisation, from front-line staff to executives, to direct customer research as well. There is currently not enough detail in each feature, and you are not sure if any are worth proceeding with. What will you do next?

options.text: Break down each feature into Epics and user stories, then size the work with your team.
options.rationale: Decomposing every feature before knowing if any is worthwhile wastes effort.

options.text: Add all of the items into your product backlog and work on the ones from managers first.
options.rationale: Prioritising by the requester's seniority ignores value.

options.text: Work with the requestors and your technical experts to create a business model canvas for each feature.
options.rationale: A business model canvas with requestors and experts evaluates each idea's value proposition, customers, costs and infrastructure.

options.text: Perform precedence diagramming on each feature to determine their dependencies.
options.rationale: Precedence diagrams show dependencies, not whether features are worth pursuing.

questions.explanation: The business model canvas is a one-page summary of a value proposition, customers, infrastructure and finances. It helps evaluate high-level feature ideas quickly before investing in detailed decomposition.
questions.mindset: Test ideas' value before detailing them.
